-> # NEW INVESTIGATION <-

<meta>catchword: rit, quod</meta>

Having refuted the Jesuit’s reasoning concerning the place where metals originate, let us proceed to another of his specific arguments. Metals, he says, do not possess the properties of sulfur and quicksilver; therefore, they were not born from them. Before we address these properties and his premise, I wish to overturn his conclusion through the thing itself, and demonstrate by the very act that metals consist of quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note>, into which they are resolved and from which they are composed. There are two paths among Alchemists: one called the **wet way**, which is performed through "waters" and solutions; the other called the **dry way**, which is performed through powders. Let us provide evidence of both—how metals, whether soft or hard, can be converted and resolved into running quicksilver within the space of an hour.

Let the example of the former be in **lead**, which should be filed, or made into shavings worn down by a chisel; or, having been melted, let it soon be finely powdered between two wooden plates (coated with chalk), producing a leaden sand almost like that found in hourglasses. For this analysis into its principles, let such a "water" be prepared: Take two ounces of purified <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid, a powerful solvent</note>, and dissolve in it one ounce of common quicksilver in a glass flask <note>original: *ampulla vitrea*</note> that is properly sealed, with a light coal fire placed beneath until it has turned into clear water. 

Afterward, remove it from the heat of the fire, and with the opening uncovered, gradually throw in one ounce of the shaved or powdered lead. For the water will spontaneously effervesce and bubble violently if you throw everything in at once or in too great a quantity. Then seal the mouth of the glass again and let it dissolve for a while; soon you will see the common quicksilver, which was previously dissolved in the water, sink down like a lime or a white powder, while the shavings of lead, before your very eyes if they are stirred, are gradually resolved into running quicksilver. 

This happens to such an extent that eventually three-quarters of an ounce of lead will become quicksilver, while about a fourth part (if all things were done correctly) remains as dross and the dregs of the sulfur of lead. When these things are finished, pour the aqua fortis into another glass vessel. Take out the remaining quicksilver made from the lead and pass it through leather or a linen cloth squeezed and tightened with a cord (as is the custom), and you will see how much <term>living Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurij vivi*</note> you have drawn out from the lead, and how much of the earthy and sulfurous dregs remains. 

Also, collect the white lime settling from the dissolution of the quicksilver first placed into the water; this can either be further precipitated into a red powder by aqua fortis, or be "revivified" back into its original weight of quicksilver through sublimation and boiling, with a piece of steel placed in common water, as is known to those skilled in chemical matters. Thus it will appear evidently to the eye how lead returns to the quicksilver from which it was created at the beginning, with the weight of the remaining dross also testifying to how much of the lead has passed into <term>hydrargyrum</term> <note>another name for mercury, from the Greek for "water-silver"</note>...

-> # CONCERNING ELIJAH THE ARTIST <-

<meta>catchword: rit, quod (continuation from previous page: "it differs nothing...")</meta>

it differs nothing from common mercury, except that it is a little more leaden-colored and sluggish, just as the specific nature of each metal requires. Conversely, that which is produced from iron is the most lively and agile of all. I am not arguing here why one Mercury should dissolve another—that is, why common mercury (dissolved into a transparent liquid) draws out the mercury residing within lead and lets it remain "alive" or liquid, while the first mercury from the solution settles entirely into a <term>calx</term> <note>A dry, powdery substance produced by heating a metal or mineral</note>. I only wish it to be noticed that these two Mercuries are clearly distinct, so that no one thinks they are being mixed. The mercury of the metal is "proximate" or direct, while the other, dissolved in water, is more "remote," acting as the agent through which the metallic one is drawn out. Thus, the metal is not resolved into a watery cloud or transparent liquid, but into <term>hydrargyrum</term> <note>original: *hydrargyrum*; a Greek-derived name for quicksilver or liquid mercury</note>.

There are other ways of resolving lead into Mercury without using any outside mercury at all, especially through such means after the lead has first been <term>calcined</term> <note>burned or roasted to a powder</note>. But because these cannot be done in a single moment, I will skip over describing them, lest a trial lasting several days bring weariness to the reader.

Let us move on to the harder metals, which we shall dissolve by **dry means**. Let us choose **steel**, as it is the core of purified iron. Take half an ounce of its filings and place them in a <term>crucible</term> <note>A ceramic or metal container used for melting materials at high temperatures</note>. Over this, place half an ounce of very finely ground <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>Ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to help dissolve or sublimate substances</note> mixed with an ounce of previously ground <term>mercury sublimate</term> <note>Mercury(II) chloride, a highly toxic white crystalline salt; the author specifies it should be prepared with salts and vitriol, not arsenic</note>. Soon the crucible should be placed in the middle of lightly glowing coals, under a chimney or in the open air. 

As soon as it feels the heat, the sal ammoniac and the sublimate will begin to rise. (One must beware of the odor, however, because of the poisonous nature of the Mercury, lest it be inhaled carelessly through the nostrils.) A little later, the sal ammoniac and the sublimate will begin to melt and flow. Once this has finished—which takes three or four moments and can be safely seen under a chimney—the crucible should be removed immediately and allowed to cool on its own. 

Afterward, when broken over a dish, it will show that the steel filings have, for the most part, turned into quicksilver. When collected in a dish or glass and strained through a linen cloth, it will be seen to be most clear and of such a lively nature that it almost leaps as it runs across a flat surface—so fiery is the nature of **Mars** <note>The alchemical name for iron or steel</note>. Indeed, it can hardly be kept in a wooden vessel without gradually evaporating away; it can only be preserved firmly sealed in glass. Nevertheless, it is a true and natural mercury, possessing every property of quicksilver. But one must be extremely careful that too much time does not pass during the resolution. For it flies away immediately—much faster than any other mercury from hard or soft metals—and it even mixes itself with the sal ammoniac...

# NEW DISQUISITION
Page 260

...of the mass of <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: *armoniaci*; ammonium chloride, a salt used to aid chemical reactions</note> and <term>mercury sublimate</term> <note>original: *Mercurij sublimati*; a highly toxic compound of mercury and chlorine used here as a solvent or reagent</note>. If anyone happens to doubt that this living mercury flows out from the sublimate itself, let him, if he wishes, catch the vapor in a receiver using an <term>alembic</term> <note>a distillation apparatus</note>, or perform the same process in a glass vial. He will see the original weight of the sublimate and sal ammoniac remains, once the dross of the iron—the earthy sulfur of the steel—and the resulting <term>hydrargyrum</term> <note>liquid mercury or quicksilver</note> have been removed.

It can also be proven by another reason that it does not flow from the sublimate: if, instead of iron filings, you put in a solid piece of steel, you will easily learn by experiment that no living mercury is left behind from the mercury sublimate (which, when boiled in water without iron, is not easily "revived" or returned to a liquid state). Therefore, that mercury is produced from the filed steel, and not from the sublimate. The same judgment applies to copper and silver. For they are prepared in a similar way, except that the powders thrown over them must be allowed to flow a little longer than in the case of resolved steel. 

From the mercury of copper (once the greening sulfur has been separated), a most precious <term>Mineral Turpeth</term> <note>original: *Turbith minerale*; a yellow mercuric sulfate used in historical medicine</note> is prepared with <term>oil of vitriol</term> <note>sulfuric acid</note> and spirit of wine. Taken in the quantity of a single grain with sugar of roses, this is an excellent and proven remedy against the **Plague**, even after infection, and indeed without any danger, provided it is taken before 24 hours have passed. I have tested this myself on my own family when danger forced my hand and all other things failed. Nor do I care that **Suchten** <note>Alexander von Suchten (c. 1520–1575), a famous alchemist and physician</note>, in a certain treatise on antimony, pronounces it a most dire poison when mixed with **Mars** <note>the alchemical name for iron</note>; I do not know if he was led to this by any experiment or not? In excess, **copper** and **iron** are hard; in deficiency, **tin** and **lead** are soft. Of these, the softness of lead corresponds to the hardness of iron on the opposite side; while the softness of tin corresponds to the hardness of copper.

### CONCERNING ELIAS THE ARTIST

Its <term>regulus</term> <note>original: *regulus*; the metallic heart or button found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</note>, produced by <term>calcining</term> <note>heating to a high temperature to cause oxidation or chemical change</note> with dry wine dregs and <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: *halinitro*</note>, pours out <term>hydrargyrum</term> <note>liquid mercury</note> just as iron, copper, and silver filings do, if it is ground by the same artifice through the "dry path" and resolved in a crucible like steel. We have shown thus far how metals may be resolved into mercury. Now, let us explain how metals may be composed from mercury by the benefit of metallic sulfur, so that their <term>genesis</term> <note>origin or creation</note> might be established, as will be clear in the formation of lead. Let lead be melted in a <term>cupel</term> <note>original: *testa*; a shallow earthenware dish used in assaying</note> and <term>reverberated</term> <note>heated in a furnace where the flame is deflected downward onto the material</note> by stirring it over coals until it turns into a <term>lime</term> <note>original: *calcem*; a powdery oxide</note> or yellowish powder. Into this dissolved solution, slowly pour as much of the reserved vinegar (the kind that contains the extraction of the soul of lead) as there is aqua fortis. You will immediately see the resolved mercury settle like a powder, having drawn into itself the "soul of Saturn." Once the liquid is poured off, melt that remaining matter of mercury (now reduced to powder) in a crucible by itself, and you will have from the mercury true, natural lead made by art. Thus, no one can deny that metals are born and produced from mercury and sulfur by a natural and true genesis.

# A NEW DISQUISITION

...qualities, let us be satisfied; it will not be tedious to briefly discuss these delusions. Metals, he says, do not possess the properties of sulfur and quicksilver. Why, I pray? Because, he says, nothing is more suitable for catching fire than sulfur; yet metals are not <term>inflammable</term> <note>original: *φλογιστὰ* (phlogista); a Greek term used to describe substances that can be set on fire</note>. How ridiculous! This is because the sulfur in metals has reached a state of <term>fixation</term> <note>the process by which a volatile substance is made stable and resistant to the effects of fire</note>. Thus, in <term>imperfect metals</term> <note>metals like lead or tin that oxidize or vaporize more easily</note>, the sulfur evaporates along with the raw mercury, even if it is not flammable. In <term>perfect metals</term> <note>noble metals like gold and silver that withstand high heat</note>, however, the sulfur has completely fixed the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *hydrargyron*</note>, so that it neither evaporates nor is consumed by fire.

To understand this better, one must know that <term>flammability</term> <note>original: *τὸ φλογιστὸν* (to phlogiston)</note> is indeed a property of all sulfur—and indeed, only of the sulfur implanted in all things—yet it is not always an active property. For it can be fixed, and that either perfectly or imperfectly. When it is imperfectly fixed and mixed with matter, it does not catch fire, yet it evaporates in the heat. When perfectly fixed, it remains. It is from this that the perfection or imperfection of metals—whether they evaporate or endure in the fire—chiefly arises. 

A remarkable proof of this is provided by <term>Antimony</term> <note>a brittle, silvery-white semi-metal often used in alchemical experiments</note>, which is not yet fixed enough to be extended by a hammer, but is only brittle and easy to melt. For in antimony, the sulfur that has congealed the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note> into an earthy mass—I speak of it as it remains in its compound state, without the artifice of <term>reverberation</term> <note>intense reflected heat</note>—does not catch fire. Instead, it evaporates completely in the fire along with the <term>Mercury</term>, for both are joined together by nature into a single mass. 

But if the sulfur is drawn out from Antimony by extraction, then it becomes like common sulfur, and just as <term>inflammable</term> <note>original: *φλογιστὸν*</note> as that is. I am not speaking of the "redness" that the <term>chemists</term> <note>original: *chymistae*; early laboratory practitioners</note> extract, but of the true, natural, greenish sulfur. You shall prove it by this method: <term>Take</term> <note>original: *Rec.*, an abbreviation for the Latin *Recipe*</note> equal parts of alum and saltpeter as much as is sufficient. Make <term>aqua valens</term> <note>literally "strong water," a concentrated acid</note>, or even take common <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note> as is customary, into which you should put half the weight of roasted salt. Afterward, grind the Antimony very finely, and place into a small amount of this water enough of the ground Antimony so that the water floats four fingers' depth above it. Add it gradually, however, so that the water does not boil over too violently. 

When the water has taken on a green color in the vial, the finest sulfur having been extracted, pour it out immediately. Then, by adding common warm water, the sulfur will settle at the bottom like common green sulfur. You will prove by this very act that it is <term>inflammable</term> <note>original: *φλογιστὸν*</note> and differs in no way from common sulfur in this regard. There are other ways of separating this sulfur by the "dry path"; for us, it is enough to have separated it by the "wet path" to achieve what we desire. Let us, therefore, gather our argument and overturn this <term>Jesuitical</term> <note>likely referring to a specific school of Aristotelian natural philosophy taught in Jesuit colleges that the author is refuting</note> claim regarding the properties of sulfur. For if the sulfur in antimony is not flammable (despite it being a metal that is not yet <term>ductile</term> <note>capable of being hammered thin</note>, and from which the sulfur burns once separated), how much less flammable will it be in the rest of the metals, whether they be perfect or imperfect...

### ->ON ELIAS THE ARTIST<-
<note>Elias the Artist was a messianic figure in alchemical lore, prophesied by Paracelsus as a master who would reveal the final secrets of nature; here, the title likely refers to the name of the treatise or the author's persona.</note>

Is it necessary for [sulfur] to retain the property of <term>inflammability</term> <note>original: *inflammationis*</note> in those metals where it has already reached a state of <term>fixation</term> <note>the chemical process of making a volatile substance stable in fire</note> even to the point of being <term>malleable</term>? The former is true, as is clear by experiment: for <term>antimony</term> <note>a brittle, metallic-looking mineral often used as a test case for metallic properties</note> melts before a bellows and will evaporate without catching fire. Therefore, the latter is also true—and all the more so, since sulfur reaches a greater state of fixation in a metal than it does in antimony. For once separated from metals, it is no longer set on fire because of a certain fixation, as is evident in lead, a matter we have discussed previously. 

The same reasoning applies to <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>, which does not solidify by cold—at least not by itself and alone. But when it solidifies into a metal along with sulfur and can be melted, it is "congealed" by cold, as can be seen in the <term>generation</term> <note>original: *genesi*; the formation or birth of a mineral</note> of lead from mercury; or as is evident in antimony, in which, however, no permanent fixation into a metal has been achieved through <term>extensibility</term> <note>the ability to be hammered or stretched, which was the defining characteristic of a "true" metal</note>.

It appears, therefore, that the Jesuit's argument is "limping" <note>original: *elumbia*; literally "weak in the loins," meaning a feeble or crippled argument</note>, and composed only for a sophisticated appearance; it offers, I know not what futility, but clearly nothing of solid reason. Let this be the response to him and to his accomplice <term>Pererius</term> <note>Benedictus Pererius (1535–1610), a prominent Jesuit philosopher who argued against the possibility of alchemy</note>, who writes as follows in his books *On the Common Principles and Affections of All Natural Things* <note>original: *de communibus omnium rerum naturalium principiis & affectionibus*</note>, Book 8, Chapter 19: 

*“Certain people,”* he says, *“most skilled in metallic matters, about which they have also written with subtlety and accuracy, affirm that the first and highest foundation upon which the art of Alchemy rests and is supported is nothing at all. From this, it can be understood that the art itself (if indeed it should be called an 'art' which has nothing of truth or certainty in itself) is empty and false. For Alchemists think the matter of all metals is sulfur and quicksilver: for which reason they profess that they can, from various mixtures of sulfur and quicksilver tempered together, produce any metal they wish—in which, surely, they are vehemently deceived. For if sulfur and quicksilver are the matter of gold and silver, then in the veins in which gold and silver are generated, some traces of sulfur and quicksilver would appear. Similarly, in veins of sulfur and quicksilver, some indications of gold and silver would be found. But those who have spent nearly their entire lives most curiously surveying and considering the veins and locations of metals have never been able to find any such thing. Therefore, the opinion of the Alchemists is false, and the gold which is made by them from sulfur and quicksilver is not true gold. For, as has been said, such is not the matter of true and natural gold, etc.”* 

Whether this hypothesis of the principles that compose metals is rightly denied by the Jesuit Pererius—and thus whether the production and generation of true and natural gold through chemistry should be exploded—we believe we have already shown sufficiently and more than enough. Whence it is no wonder that he is fascinated by preconceived false opinions of this kind, while the principles remain unknown...

# CONCERNING ELIAS THE ARTIST
<note>Elias Artista (Elijah the Artist) was a legendary figure in alchemy, prophesied by Paracelsus to appear during the "end times" to reveal all secret arts and perfect the world's knowledge.</note>

Therefore, what he adds—that the same may be said of gold, silver, and the rest—carries just as much weight as his previous reasoning. The remaining arguments, like those of a certain other man who argues from the <term>supposition of logical terms</term> <note>a scholastic method of defining things by their names and categories rather than their physical nature</note> that metals differ in species, do not hold unless they are applied to their own natural principles. For even if "lead" as a species is predicated of this individual piece of lead, and "metal" as a genus is predicated of this species, these things can nevertheless be said for the sake of distinction based on common speech, rather than the nature of the thing itself.

But the Jesuit continues. *“Either there is a single substance of metals,”* he says, *“and different qualities, or there is not a single substance. If there is a single substance, then these statements will be true: 'lead is gold,' and conversely, 'gold is lead.' Then it would also not be difficult to make gold from lead, since it would not be difficult to remove the qualities from lead—which are not held back by any peculiar form—and introduce those which belong to gold. We respond that it has been made sufficiently clear from the experiments regarding the substance of <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "hydrargyri," literally "water-silver"</note> cited above that all metals consist of it; and that depending on the difference of <term>sulfur</term> <note>in alchemy, sulfur represents the "soul" or "combustible" principle, while mercury represents the "spirit" or "fluid" principle</note>—whether it is fixed or not fixed—and their different mixing, metals are either imperfect and "combustible" by fire, or perfect and fixed. Therefore, since these things are evident to the eye, there is no need to struggle over these far-fetched little arguments.

Furthermore, if you look at the common folk, these propositions sound like paradoxes: "lead is gold." But if you look at the nature from within, they will not be so absurd. Hence lead is called **leprous gold** by the chemists; likewise, the internal parts of silver are gold. Such propositions are correctly understood from the nature of things, not from the speech and opinion of the common people. From this it follows that the purging of qualities and the introduction of the **gold-making form** through the ministry of art is easy, using a fixed metallic principle which removes the imperfect and perfects the matter.

*“But no one so far has been found,”* he says, *“of whom it is clearly established that he produced gold proven in every respect.”* To be sure, everything finally comes back to this: that we must demonstrate to these "un-skilled" men <note>original: "asistis," likely a derogatory term for those who lack practical alchemical experience</note> by the reality of the thing itself—against the empty quibbles of those who philosophize—that the transmutation of metals into gold is possible, and likewise that true, natural gold is produced from metallic principles. This is what we shall provide hereafter. # A NEW DISCOURSE
<meta>catchword: -rated [runt].</meta>

We have had Arnold of Villanova, a supreme physician and theologian in the Roman court, about whom I wrote in my *Counsel on the Observance of Fasting*. He was a great alchemist who agreed to submit the rods of gold he manufactured to every possible test. Is this not an example? I could bring forward the testimonies of most distinguished men, worthy of all credit, who saw these things with their own eyes and handled them with their hands. Not so long ago, with one part of the <term>tincture</term> <note>The "tincture" or "powder of projection" was the concentrated alchemical substance used to catalyze the transformation of base metal into gold.</note>, three thousand five hundred and eighty-four weights of lead were turned into gold, a portion of which is still preserved at Basel to this day.

But we do not wish to rely on unscientific arguments; instead, we refer our readers to the history of metallic transmutation by the most learned and noble Ewald von Hohenland, written for the defense of chemistry regarding these experiments. However, at this point, the Physicians rush in, boldly asserting that none of the more learned men have granted their assent to chemistry. But what Jean Fernel <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558) was a highly influential French physician who introduced the term "physiology."</note> determines concerning the hidden causes of things, the <term>Elixir of the Arabs</term>, and this whole matter in Book 2, Chapter 18 [of *On the Hidden Causes of Things*]; and what Marsilio Ficino <note>A celebrated Italian scholar and priest, one of the most influential humanist philosophers of the early Renaissance.</note> (two men superior to any Hercules) determines in Book 2 of *On Life from the Heavens*, Chapter 3, is before the eyes of everyone and on the lips of the learned. To refute them would be too reckless—to say nothing of Count Pico della Mirandola and others.

Indeed, we shall prove that the transmutation of metals is possible and natural through the experience of nature and art, provided we first respond to those who deny that the more perfect species of things can be produced in any way except one: that is, by a natural agent. They argue this because the generations of such things are supposedly fixed, both according to their active principle and matter, as well as the place in which they are made. This can be admitted thus far (as <insert>the alchemist</insert> Pietro Bono of Ferrara rightly notes) only insofar as art must employ those same principles closest to nature that are within the power of nature itself. For if other or merely similar principles were used, the result would not be the same as natural gold, but something different or only a likeness. 

We are not speaking here of <term>sophistical works</term> <note>In alchemy, "sophistication" refers to fraudulent or superficial methods, such as gilding or plating, that change the appearance but not the essence of the metal.</note> of whitening or reddening for the sake of color, but of that which exists within the very nature and essence of metals, according to a <term>univocal definition</term> <note>A term from logic meaning a definition that applies in exactly the same sense to different things; here, it means the alchemical gold is identical in every property to mined gold.</note>. If the metal sustains all the criteria and all the properties of gold, silver, copper, and so on, it must be that species. Hence Paracelsus openly testifies in his book *The Vexations of Alchemists* that true alchemy consists of nothing but being "of metals, from metals, through metals, and with metals." But as far as the location and the means of generation are concerned, the matter stands differently, as is clear from Book 9 of Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, who admits that when the agents and matter are similar, the operations are always similar, even if the mediums used are different, as others before us have demonst-

> *Albertus,* he says, *in his 30th book On Minerals, chapter 9, treating this question on the capacity of Alchemy, first sets out the opinion of Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works were foundational to medieval science and medicine.</note>, which was this: "Let the practitioners of alchemy know,"* (says Avicenna) *"that the species of metals cannot be changed, although something similar to them can be made. For I do not believe it possible that the <term>specific difference</term> <note>The essential quality that makes a substance what it is (e.g., what makes gold 'gold' rather than 'lead').</note> can be removed by any human skill; but the stripping away of <term>accidents</term> <note>The outward, non-essential qualities of a thing, such as color, weight, or hardness.</note> is not impossible, or at least their reduction. For the species of metals are not changed unless they are first reduced to the <term>first metallic matter</term> <note>The 'Prima Materia': the formless, fundamental substance that alchemists believed sat beneath the outward form of all metals.</note>, and thus by the help of art are led into the species of the metal which you desire."* And he says that Hastem <note>Likely a reference to the Arabic philosopher Al-Haytham or Haly Abenragel.</note>, a philosopher foremost in physics and mathematics, felt the same. Then Albertus adds those things which follow:

> It is necessary for us to say that skilled Alchemists operate no differently than skilled Physicians, who by purgative medicines purge corrupted materials harmful to health, and afterwards, through means that strengthen nature, assist the natural power so that by <term>digesting</term> <note>In alchemy and old medicine, 'digestion' refers to the slow application of heat to mature or transform a substance.</note> they bring about health, which health is the effect of both nature and art: but of the former effectively and principally, and of the latter instrumentally and organically. Thus the Alchemist first, by well-purifying the matter of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury; the original uses the shorthand "arg. vi." for "argentum vivum" (living silver).</note> and sulfur inherent in all metals, strengthens them; then they lead the elemental and celestial virtues inherent in such matter to the proportion of the metallic mixture they intend to introduce, and then nature itself works and not art, except by assisting organically and stripping away [the outward qualities], as we have said, and thus they are seen to bring forth and make true gold and silver. For what the elemental and celestial virtues do in natural vessels <note>The "vessels" of nature are the veins and cavities of the earth where metals grow.</note>, they also do in artificial vessels, if the artificial ones are formed in the manner of the natural; what nature does by the heat of the sun and stars, art does by the heat of fire: provided it is so tempered that it does not exceed the self-moving and informing power that is in the metals. For a celestial power is within this, which first mixed it, and this is inclined to this or that through the help of art. Alchemy, therefore, proceeds in this manner: that is, by corrupting one thing by removing it from its species, and with the help of those things which are in the matter, inducing the species of another. Therefore, of all alchemical operations, the best is that which proceeds from the same things from which nature proceeds, such as the purification of sulfur through <term>decoction</term> <note>The process of boiling or heating a substance to extract its essence.</note> and sublimation, and the purification of quicksilver, and the good mixing of these with the matter of the metal. For in these, and from their powers, every species of metal is induced. But those who whiten through white things and yellow through yellow things, while the species of the former metal remains in the matter, are without doubt deceivers and do not make true gold and silver; and in this way almost all proceed, either in whole or in part...

### CONCERNING ELIAS THE ARTIST

By this single experiment, all the arguments of the Aristotelians <note>The traditional followers of Aristotle who believed that the "species" or fundamental nature of a substance could not be changed into another</note> are blown away—specifically, how a part of steel can retreat back into vitriol <term>sulfate minerals</term>, and again be reduced from vitriol into copper, and thus truly be generated through the ministry of art by the benefit of nature, and not just the metal being superficially changed.

I add another shorter experiment. Let iron filings be calcined <term>heated to a powder</term> with an equal amount of ground sulfur, and let it be reverberated by stirring it over a ceramic dish until the sulfur is burned away; cast the residue, thus made white-hot, into boiling water, and place in it pure plates of steel. Copper will adhere to them in the form of a slime, which, when wiped off and melted, will be natural copper. This, says Paracelsus, is a smaller thing than transmuting iron or copper into gold—which God has not yet willed to be commonly known to everyone—but whatever the case may be, it abundantly overthrows the quibbles of the sophists.

Let us proceed, however, to the transmutation of silver into natural gold, proven by every trial <note>original: "specillo," literally a probe or surgical instrument, used here to mean an assaying tool</note> according to all the properties of gold. Yet let us proceed in such a way that we show only the possibility of art and nature, not the utility. For those who attack these things are unworthy of attaining anything further, since no one, as the legal experts say, should be forced to act for their own benefit. Paracelsus, when dealing with this matter against the Aristotelians in his *Book of Minerals*, chapter 7, "Concerning Sulfur," says shortly after the beginning:

> *It should be known that (unless God prevents it) there is a wonderful power within sulfur, so excellent that the natural light of man's reason is stunned; or if God does not prevent it, the error lies with the craftsmen who handle sulfur, which can easily happen. But be that as it may, such power and faculty exists in sulfur that no skilled person can exhaust it, and such virtue that it is a wonder to anyone. For it confounds (he says) Aristotle, who says species cannot be transmuted. Sulfur transmutes them. If that foolish Aristotle were still alive, it would turn him from a fool into a madman; he has been conquered more than by any woman.*

Thus says Paracelsus. But he does not show by what method this transmutation is to take place, except that while discussing mineral sulfur, he teaches how to make a "liver" <note>original: "epaticam," likely referring to "liver of sulfur," a chemical preparation involving sulfur and potassium</note> from it with linseed oil. When this is rightly distilled and rectified (he teaches the method in the second book of the *Archidoxes*), let any silver be placed into its red oil and left until the destined time limit; it will happen that it turns black and produces a "lime" <term>calx</term> of gold, namely in *aqua fortis* <term>nitric acid</term>. But he says it is not yet fixed gold, but "volatile" gold. However, if it reaches its perfect term, he says it accomplishes all things that must be accomplished, about which it is not useful to discuss further. Thus says Paracelsus.

...celsus. More regarding **fixed sulfur** <term>sulfur that has been rendered non-volatile by heat so that it no longer evaporates</term> can be found in the booklet *Concerning the Mortification of Things and its Metamorphosis* <note>original: "libello de mortificatione rerum ejusq; metamorphosi"</note>. But, having set aside the Theophrastean <note>Referring to the methods of Theophrastus Paracelsus</note> process, we wish to show how even crude, common sulfur may be transmuted and produce true, natural gold.

Take, therefore, one part lead and let it be melted in a crucible over burning coals; then, remove the crucible with **fire-tongs** <term>pyrolabe</term>, and before the lead congeals, cast in as much crude and "living" mercury <note>Liquid quicksilver</note> and stir it gently with a small stick. Next, have one part of common sulfur, which should be melted in another crucible; into this molten sulfur, cast the previously coagulated **mixture** <term>malagma</term> bit by bit and stir with a spatula. Take care that the sulfur does not catch fire or burn up before you have added everything. Then, once it has cooled naturally, grind it upon a marble or stone slab, and having placed it again in a crucible, let it be melted until the sulfur is burned away, and the material stays in flux long enough that it can be poured into a metallic rod, similar to molten antimony and just as brittle.

Take one part of this crushed material and one part of laminated silver, and arrange them **layer upon layer** <note>original: "stratum super stratum"</note> in a crucible. Place finely crushed **Venetian glass** <note>A high-quality glass often used as a flux to help metals melt and to protect them from the air</note> on top to the thickness of a finger. Do not overfill the vessel, lest the glass overflow. Let all these be continuously melted for the space of an hour with intense heat, so that the glass and the rest are in a constant state of flux.

Afterwards, allow it to cool, and having broken the crucible, take out the **button** <term>regulus; the mass of metal found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</term> from the bottom. Prepare a **cupel** <term>cineritium; a refining hearth made of bone ash</term> upon which lead is placed in the usual manner until it runs intensely. Then, introduce the button and **refine** <note>original: "fulmina," referring to the "brightening" or flash of light seen when precious metal is finally purified in a cupel</note> it after the manner of goldsmiths until pure silver remains. Let this silver be hammered into thin plates or granulated, then immediately cast into ***aqua fortis*** <term>nitric acid</term>. Once dissolved, it will yield shining specks of gold which will settle to the bottom like black powder. When these are washed with warm water, heated in a crucible, and melted, you will have grains of true natural gold, pure and clear, sustaining all the properties and tests of natural gold, both in medicine and in other uses.

Now, although we do not teach how to transmute the *entirety* of the silver into gold, but only a very light and tiny portion; nevertheless, because all parts of silver are homogeneous and similar, it is enough that even a speck of silver passes into true natural gold to demonstrate **metallic transmutation** to the eyes. Lest anyone think that gold was already present in the *aqua fortis* or mixed into the silver, lead, or mercury, or hidden within the sulfur, let him first examine each ingredient separately, if he wishes, by the criteria of fire and *aqua fortis*. Thus, he may know with greater certainty that this gold arises from no other source than transformation through the experiment of art. We could add other experiments of no small importance...

Having therefore fulfilled our promises (as can be experienced by the act itself), it remains for us to respond briefly to the empty objections of both Hagelius and Pererius <note>Christoph Hagel and Benedictus Pererius were prominent scholars of the 16th century who wrote on natural philosophy and magic</note>, as well as those who fruitlessly cry out that we are attempting to usurp the power of God. For we treat nothing here that is against nature, nor against the essential principles of metals, and therefore we in no way oppose the order of creation. We do, however, state beforehand that God is able to destroy and hinder any work, however natural, no less than the sowing of plants or the birth of animals: a fact which Physicians also frequently experience in their medicines, when nature does not always work but is sometimes suppressed by a higher cause. Indeed, we attribute all power of growth to Him alone who said **"LET IT BE"** <note>original: "FIAT"</note>, without whose blessing all things are reduced to nothing.

Let a forked rod of the present year—that is, one year old—be cut from a hazel or oak tree, whose "horns" <note>the two branches forming the fork</note> are equal and without defect. Some people, however, think that it should be cut before sunrise while the Moon is waxing, and especially around the day of the **Annunciation of Mary** <note>March 25th</note>. But we have observed none of these things. 

This being done, let two small forks be taken in each hand, facing each other, with the fingers pressed toward the sky, so that on both sides the ends of the rod's twigs protrude beyond the hand at each squeezed thumb. The main stem of the fork itself should turn inward between the two hands. Now, if someone wears silver buttons fixed to their tunic, even if they squeeze the rod with all their might in both hands, it will nevertheless make a circle by itself, and that cut part of the stem will turn itself inward toward the chest until it reaches the buttons. But if you are stripped of all metal and place silver or gold on the ground, then even if you who hold the rod resist and are unwilling, the cut part of the stem will turn outward until it strikes toward the metal with a most powerful judgment and motion. the sympathy of nature is to be admired: yet I myself have experienced it to be true in reality, and have seen it repeatedly in others. If the rod does not move in everyone's hand (as Hagelius says), surely who does not see that this too is reserved within the power of God? But let us now bring our Investigation to a conclusion <note>original: "ad umbilicum... perducamus," a Latin idiom meaning to reach the end or the navel of the matter</note>. For the other arguments Hagelius brings forward are of no weight or value. First, he concedes that metals are produced from the same causes and have the same operations, differing only according to "more" and "less." But if properties follow nature, these facts convince us much more that metals do not differ properly and fundamentally in their essence; it is far from the case that they support his view, since he wishes them to differ in species by an essential difference. For regarding the exception he makes for stones, their proximate essence is not the same: for they do not derive their origin proximately from **living Mercury** <term>Quicksilver or elemental mercury, considered the "mother" of all metals</term>. > *Furthermore, he adds: Nature neither wishes, nor is able, to transmute other metals into gold. She does not wish it: first, because she has never done so; second, because she produced each and every thing for certain and necessary uses, which would be entirely lost by a substantial change.*

I respond that I recognize not Nature, but God, the governor of nature, has provided for human needs through the diversity of metals; and therefore not every metal ends as gold. Rather, different metals are produced from the diversity of **fixed and volatile sulfur** <term>Sulfur was viewed as the "father" or active principle of metals, with "fixed" being stable and "volatile" being reactive</term> combined with pure or more impure Mercury. Insofar as they depart from a balanced state, some are produced through the hardness of combustible impurity, and others through an evaporable softness; but if these accidental qualities are separated, they serve transmutation no less than medicinal uses. Nor is it necessary that metals be entirely lost through this change. For no one can use gold for certain purposes compared to iron <note>The author points out that gold is too soft for tools, so iron will always be needed and kept in its own form</note>. Therefore, there is no fear of their abolition through the alchemical art. What of the fact that Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541)</note> confesses it is the same work and labor if someone wishes to change better metals into baser ones? Thus, there is no reason to fear their disappearance. As for his claim that nature has never done this, it is so far from the truth that even a beetle was transmuted by being caught in golden vapors; many such wonders are found in mines, unless one says that the gold vapor, upon the destruction and burning of the beetle, simply took on its external shape—a view I am inclined to support. But who has descended into the depths of nature, or who is so **Lynceus-eyed** <term>Referring to Lynceus of Greek myth, an Argonaut known for sight so sharp he could see through the earth</term> that he can say nature has never done this? Certainly, Petrus Bonus <note>A 14th-century alchemist and author of 'The Precious Pearl'</note> proves the contrary: all lead naturally contains a grain of silver, and tin, with a little preparation, leaves a grain of silver behind; these are manifest signs of a natural inclination toward perfection.

### ON ELIJAH THE ARTIST
<note>Elijah the Artist (Elias Artista) was a messianic figure in alchemical lore, predicted by Paracelsus to appear and reveal the ultimate secrets of nature and the transmutation of metals.</note>

festivities. He pointlessly attacks the idea that nature cannot transmute metals through heat and cold, as has already been seen previously regarding the natural transformation of iron into copper. Hagelius odiously repeats these same arguments in the question regarding the mutual transmutation of metals when he denies the substantial transmutation of metals with these petty questions in Thesis 88: *Is generation the work of nature alone? There remains one question, partly Physical and partly Theological: whether gold produced by art is true natural gold and retains all the properties of natural gold both in Medicine and in other things; and if not, whether it is illicit and contrary to the order of creation. Thus says Pererius. But he ought to have remembered, from the words of Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and theologian often cited as an authority in alchemy</note> produced by him, that there is one kind of gold and silver (so-called equivocally) made by those who "whiten with white" and "yellow with yellow" <note>This refers to charlatans who merely tint or plate metals to change their surface color without changing their essence</note>, who are beyond doubt deceivers. But we may certainly allow Pererius to "nod off" <note>original: dormitare; a reference to Horace's "even the great Homer nods," suggesting a great scholar has made a lapse in judgment</note> in his great work, especially since his judgment, drawn from philosophy, is much saner and more just than that of Hagelius—even though Hagelius undoubtedly looked to Pererius when he wrote in Thesis 84: *Lastly, there are those who do indeed consider gold...*

# NEW INQUIRY

...they deny that it has been done by any art thus far (for this is the summary of **Pererius's** <note>Benito Pereira (c. 1535–1610), a Jesuit philosopher who wrote extensively on physics and the boundaries of natural magic.</note> decision), yet they do not deny that it could, in an absolute sense, be done by skill. And yet, the same **Hagelius** does not blush to determine and decide against his ally Pererius that this can be done in no way at all. Such is the character of all those who are more devoted to language than to nature.

We respond, therefore, regarding Pererius’s "Alchemical gold," that everything he says is true if he understands those same things to apply to **sophisticated** <term>adulterated or "fake" gold that only looks real on the surface</term> gold and silver—that is, regarding **whitening and reddening** <term>original: albificationibus & rubificationibus; the alchemical stages of turning a metal white like silver or red like gold</term> only in color, while the **sulfur and quicksilver** <note>In alchemical theory, all metals were thought to be composed of varying ratios and purities of Sulfur (the soul/combustible element) and Quicksilver/Mercury (the spirit/fluid element).</note> of the previous metal remain in the same state of essence. And such "apparent" and sophisticated gold is a great poison; it is a sin to sell such a thing because of its **arsenical and narcotic qualities** in medicine. Whatever its nature, it is consumed by fire and eventually destroyed—indeed, it returns as if to dross after the proper criteria and examinations of fire, just like the gold tested six or seven times by **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar and saint credited with many alchemical discoveries.</note>. 

It appears, however, from Pererius’s evidence, that he speaks as if through a fog regarding the examinations of gold. To him, we oppose the most severe judgments prescribed in the works of **Geber** <note>The legendary father of alchemy, likely referring here to the Latin works of "Pseudo-Geber," the most influential medieval alchemical texts.</note> and **Peter Bonus of Ferrara** <note>A 14th-century alchemist and author of 'The New Precious Pearl'.</note>, the physician and chemist. We also oppose whatever else ought to be used to examine the properties of true natural gold, such as:
*   **Ignition** <gloss>testing by fire</gloss>
*   **Fusion** <gloss>melting</gloss>
*   **Extension under the hammer through every dimension** <gloss>malleability</gloss>
*   **Refining in the ash-cup** <term>original: cineritium; cupellation, a process where ores are treated under high heat to separate noble metals from lead and other base metals</term>
*   **Exposure to sharp vapors** <gloss>testing with acids</gloss>
*   **Extinction** <gloss>quenching the hot metal</gloss>
*   **Cementation** <term>original: cementum; a process of purifying gold by heating it with granulated materials</term>
*   The mixing of **re-burning agents**
*   Reduction after **calcination** <term>heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical constitution</term>
*   The easy or difficult acceptance of **quicksilver** <gloss>mercury</gloss>, and so on.

If, therefore, gold is produced that is proven by every test, and is not destroyed like "sophisticated" gold, but stands firm, having all the properties of natural gold and all its operations and reactions (as we say ours is), then it will not be merely *similar*, but *identical* to the natural, regardless of how much Pererius raves along with **Aegidius** <note>Likely referring to Aegidius Romanus (Giles of Rome), a medieval theologian.</note>. 

For as to what is brought up regarding the **serpents and small dragons** produced by the Egyptian Magicians and by Moses: the former was the result of diabolical illusion, the latter of divine power. We, however, presume neither, nor do we attempt such things; we follow only **natural forces**. 

Now, regarding the objection about **mice born from putrefaction** <note>A common medieval belief that life could spontaneously generate from decaying matter, like mice from rotting straw.</note> and how they differ in species from mice generated through seed—from which they infer that "chemical gold" differs from natural gold even if it has the properties of natural gold—this is entirely irrelevant. Truly, the true art of chemistry does not proceed from any principles other than natural ones, nor does it employ anything other than what nature has generated and continues to generate, through the application of mixing and proper preparation. Therefore, while there may be a difference in the underlying matter of those mice, there is no such difference in the **making of metals**.

Indeed, some go so far as to say that even if all the properties of natural gold...

# ON ELIAS THE ARTIST
<note>The title "Elias the Artist" refers to a legendary figure in alchemy, prophesied by Paracelsus, who would one day reveal all the secrets of nature and transform the world.</note>

### S 2

...nature contains that which is produced through chemistry, yet they refuse to accept it, who does not see that such people should be left to themselves, and that we should pray they receive a sound mind? For whatever possesses the same essential principles, and the same qualities and operations as a thing, is identical with that thing—as **Aristotle** testifies when discussing forms. For in the fourth book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Metaphysicorum"</note>, he argues from the works and accidents of things regarding the forms themselves: *That which performs the operations of an eye is an eye, but that which does not is not an eye.* Therefore, an eye made of stone or a blind eye is not called an eye (except in name), but rather an image of an eye; likewise, a **wooden saw** is not called a saw, but an image of a saw. The entire light of Nature testifies to this same truth.

But I admit that **sophistications** <term>fakes or "apparent" transmutations that only change the surface appearance</term> do not possess such properties. However, true gold produced by chemical operation, from the true principles and essential components of metals, contains all the properties of gold, as is evident by experiment. Therefore, if gold has any medicinal value (specifically raw gold), this chemical gold will also provide it—namely, to **gladden and comfort the heart**—and much more so than the other, as the alchemist **Plato** testifies in his *Third Book of Stars* <note>original: "3. stellicarum"; a medieval alchemical text pseudepigraphally attributed to Plato</note>, and **Hamech** in his commentary on the same, and likewise **Haly** in his *Secrets*. The same is said by the alchemist **Aristotle** in his book *The Secret of Secrets* <note>A famous medieval "handbook for kings" attributed to Aristotle, covering everything from politics to alchemy</note> and in his book on precious stones; though it is true that "sophisticated" chemical gold does the opposite, as was mentioned above.

Therefore, true gold must be distinguished from the counterfeit gold of the Alchemist, which is merely painted, altered, and adulterated. I have no desire to provide instructions for such sophistications, such as those read in the works of **Albertus Brunus** in his treatise *On Increase and Decrease*, or in the *Correctorium* of **Richard the Englishman**, or finally in the books *On Subtlety* by **Cardanus** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath; the author here implies Cardano’s "subtlety" is actually just deception</note> (if this can even be called subtlety), and everywhere among others. These works deal partly with **whitening** <term>original: albificationis; the process of making a metal look like silver</term> and partly with **reddening** <term>original: rubificationis; the process of making a metal look like gold</term>—that is, producing adulterated gold and silver that only display the color.

However, based on the principles and criteria of all the properties found in true chemical gold, one may conclude that we attempt nothing against the order of creation. For our gold is natural and true, produced by the benefit of nature alone through the ministry of art. Therefore, it is not something secretly added by the suggestion of the **Devil**, as is claimed by **Aegidius** and **Angelus** <note>Aegidius de Bellamera and Angelus de Ubaldis, two prominent 14th-century jurists who wrote legal opinions against alchemy</note>—the only two among the legal scholars who fruitlessly attack the chemical art—and after them, a certain "great man" in Germany, who was unskilled in these matters and deceived by others. Indeed, we proceed here from the essential and natural principles of metals, not from diabolical works. It is true that God, the Best and Greatest, is able to inhibit, hinder, or utterly destroy even the work of nature and art; but we do not, in truth, invade the office of divine power for that reason, since we do not produce this by command, will, or words alone, as...

# CONCLUSION FROM HIERO-
## NYMUS DE ZANETINIS, BY WHICH
### the disputation and arguments of Angelus are
### answered in chapter 1, Extravagantes, on accusations.

**Is alchemy a sin, and a condemned art?** <note>original: "An alchymia sit peccatum, & ars reprobata?"</note> Albericus in the *Dictionary of Civil Law* <note>Albericus de Rosate, a 14th-century Italian jurist</note> under the word "Alchemy" argues [it is], as does Joannes Andreae in the additions to the *Speculum* <note>The "Speculum Iudiciale" by Guillaume Durand, a standard legal manual</note> under the title "on the crime of forgery." So too Joannes de Anania in chapter 2 "on sorcery," and Petrus de Ancharano in chapter 1 of the same title. Baldus in chapter 1, "which things are royal," and Thomas [Aquinas] in the *Secunda Secundae* <note>The second part of the second part of the "Summa Theologiae"</note>, question 77, article 2. 

And finally, they seem to hold that practitioners do not seem to sin if they attribute their work to God: because they do not change one species into another (as is charged against them), because this is impossible: but they say that from one species of metal (namely tin) another species of metal (namely gold or silver) can be produced. Nor is this inconsistent. And we see sometimes that from a dead thing a living thing is produced, as in the worms from which silk is produced. For all metals proceed from the same principle, namely from **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <term>mercury, known in Latin as "argentum vivum"</term>: but by the power of the elements, certain ones have a greater influence in one place than in another, and in one region tin is formed, in another silver, in another gold, and therefore it is lawful: provided it is not done through magic art, or another art hateful to the laws. According to law 1, Code on Treasures, book ten: for they are to be praised. 

However, add the *Summa Angelica* <note>A widely used 15th-century handbook for confessors by Angelus de Clavasio</note>, under the word "Alchemy," which holds that the art is illicit for many reasons: first, because no one is found who possesses this kind of true art, although it is said of many—but it is found false by experience. Then, because we see that commonly those practicing it consume much [wealth], and one must judge by what commonly happens. Whence it is said of them in Timothy, chapter three: *Always learning, and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth* <note>2 Timothy 3:7</note>. They perform many experiments and never reach perfection: they consume time and life, nor does that which they work upon have the truth of gold or silver, but only the appearance. And therefore Alchemists are simply to be condemned. And this is clearly proven: because no one wants to do it in public, so that it appears they act wrongly: because they hate the light. And if they ever do produce something true, it is either done with loss when expenses are calculated, or from some deception.

<header>CONFIRMATION</header>
<meta>catchword: Alche-</meta>

...[by deception], by substituting real gold, or through some diabolical deception, which—in order to draw people toward such things—occasionally produces real gold for them through the secret addition of genuine gold. Since, therefore, such a practice is against the public utility (as is clear from the consumption of resources, and because practitioners commonly use these materials to make counterfeit money), those who perform it are simply to be condemned.

I, however, hold the common opinion: that this art is licit <note>legally and morally permissible</note>, because the arguments in the *Summa Angelica* <note>The "Summa Angelica de casibus conscientiae" by Angelus de Clavasio, a famous 15th-century handbook for confessors</note> do not prove that the art itself is illicit just because no one possesses the true art; for this is not due to a defect in the art itself. Nor do other arguments conclude this, as is evident in themselves. Thomas [Aquinas] and Albert [the Magnus] hold the same. 

As for whether profit from alchemy is licit and whether a sale is rendered unjust, Thomas says (in the place cited above) that if true gold is made through alchemy, it is not illicit to sell it as real. This is because nothing prohibits using art and certain natural means to produce natural effects. However, if it does not have the true "species" <note>essential nature or identity</note> of gold, then it is an unjust sale, as it is sophisticated <term>sophisticatum; in this context, "sophisticated" means adulterated, fake, or imitation</term> gold.

### *Response of Tommaso Arsoncini, Doctor of Both Laws, regarding the legal status of alchemy.*

To the proposed question of whether the art of alchemy is licit, I respond briefly: if the common opinion of the Doctors creates the law (as is established among all experts), it follows that alchemy is licit. The premise is true, because Oldradus, Baldus, Johannes Andreae, Panormitanus, Andreas Iferninus, Albericus de Rosate, Alberto Bruno, Guido Papa, and many others—both civil and canon lawyers—have approved it. 

One alone contradicts them: Angelus in his *Summa Angelica*. But besides the fact that the authority of a single Doctor against the common opinion is null, as everyone knows, there was certainly one great Canonist, Girolamo da Zanettini, who in chapter 1 "on accusations," responded most precisely to each and every one of his [Angelus’s] arguments. 

This is the adamantine <note>meaning unbreakable or rock-solid</note> foundation based on the authority of great and famous Doctors and legal consultants—not to mention the authority of Thomas Aquinas, who in two or three places most clearly approved of alchemy. Pliny also writes in Book 34, Chapter 4, that there were alchemists in the time of the Emperor Gaius <note>Caligula</note>. Nor is his statement relevant that their craft was not profitable. First, because in the question of whether alchemy is a licit art, we do not ask whether it is lucrative and fruitful, but only whether it is prohibited by divine or human law. Second, because it is possible that those craftsmen of whom he speaks were not sufficiently skilled, while others might be more skilled—as we commonly say "among craftsmen" <note>original: "inter artifices," a reference to the Digest (ff.) of Roman Law regarding the standards of skill expected in a contract</note>. Furthermore, the things that Suidas <note>The Suda, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world</note> relates about...

<page-num>279</page-num>
<header>### OF ALCHEMY.</header>

Alchemy tells of the artificial production of gold: that the Egyptians were able to sustain a long war against the tyrant Diocletian, relying on their art—that is, <term>gold-making</term> <note>original: *aurificio*; the Greek-derived term for the chemical production of gold</note>.

But let us look at some other arguments. For Aristotle writes in the second and fourth books of his *Metaphysics* that art imitates nature in certain things, and that many natural things can be produced and perfected by art. He names <term>Colchotar</term> <note>A reddish-brown residue of iron oxide left after the distillation of vitriol, used as a pigment or polishing powder</note> and <term>Calchantum</term> <note>Blue vitriol or copper sulfate, historically used in making inks and dyes</note> as examples, saying that those two <term>inks</term> <note>original: *atramenta*; a general term for dark substances like ink or vitriol</note> are not only "born" in minerals but can also be produced by art. A third example is given concerning Salt. For (as Pliny says in book 31) salt is either made or it is born <note>meaning it is either manufactured through evaporation or mined naturally</note>. In Poland there is mineral salt, while in France there is manufactured salt, and the latter has the same properties, nature, and efficacy as the former. A fourth example is <term>Electrum</term> <note>A naturally occurring or man-made alloy of gold and silver</note>, which Pliny in book 33, chapter 4, and many others write is not only natural but also artificial. Regarding this manufactured and artificial variety, legal texts speak in the Digest <note>The author provides several citations to the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the foundational body of Roman law, specifically regarding legacies and the acquisition of property</note>. A fifth example is <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note>, which the aforementioned Pliny in book 33, chapter 8, says is in one form native and in another manufactured; and for the sake of distinguishing the two, he calls the latter <term>Hydrargyrum</term> <note>Literally "water-silver"; Pliny distinguished between naturally occurring mercury and mercury extracted from ore</note>. Guillaume Philander, in his commentaries on Vitruvius, counts four types of it: two native and two manufactured. In the same place, he shows that <term>steel</term>, <term>sandarac</term> <note>A resin or a red arsenic sulfide pigment</note>, <term>verdigris</term> <note>The green pigment or "rust" that forms on copper</note>, <term>vitriol</term>, and <term>cinnabar</term> are produced by nature in some cases and by human art in others. Since these things are so, we can conclude without absurdity: just as art can imitate nature in so many other things, it is not inconsistent to say that it can also imitate nature in the processing of gold and silver. Certainly Cardano, in the sixteenth book of *On Subtlety*, writes (and many say this is known to them) that <term>copper</term> can be made from iron by applying vitriol. In the same book, Cardano testifies that a certain apothecary from Treviso converted quicksilver into gold in the presence of the most illustrious Prince of the Venetians and the wise senators. It is true that Julius Scaliger denies that he believes this, but he relies on a weak argument: namely, that if the Venetians had seen this—who are of such greed (as he writes) that they would even make a treaty with the Turk, the enemy of the Christian name—they would never have let that <term>apothecary</term> go. Instead, they would have forced him with tortures to reveal his art, and perhaps would have hanged him on the Sabbath. But it is likely that the apothecary, through public trust or perhaps by some other security or pledge, took precautions and provided for himself. Certainly, it is not honorable to suspect the worst of everyone regarding everything. It is well established that there were in previous centuries, and are now, many grave men who practiced this art and found it profitable for themselves.

...taught it. Among these were *Albertus Magnus* <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and bishop recognized as a Doctor of the Church; he was famously interested in the natural sciences</note>, the *Count of* *Trevisan*, *Augurellus*, *Avicenna* <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, the Persian "Prince of Physicians"</note>, *Geber* <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy</note>, *Lull*, *Bonus* *of Ferrara*, *Morienus*, as well as *Tolod.* and especially *Arnald of* *Villanova*, the supreme physician. We see even in our own times *Jean Fernel*—considered a prince in the medical art—held this same art to the highest degree <note>original: *ad unguem*; literally "to the fingernail," meaning with perfect precision</note> in his book *On the Secret Causes of Things*. He was practiced in it, although toward the end of the book, he playfully eludes the unwary reader by citing three verses from *Augurellus*. Yet, the authority of that one man, *Fernel*, outweighs the authority of many other contradicting physicians (as some say).

But principally, and before all else, in the question: "Is any art licit?" <note>Is a practice permitted by law and morality?</note>, one must consider whether it is prohibited by any divine or human law. For the licit and illicit are distinguished thus in the <term>Digest</term> <note>original: *ff.*; the *Pandects* or *Digest*, a massive compendium of Roman law organized by Emperor Justinian</note> under the sections on concubines, doubtful matters, and the laws concerning colleges and corporations. As for Divine Scripture, I certainly find no text where Alchemy and the making of gold are forbidden—even though the divine lawmaker *Moses* pursues innumerable vices and crimes in *Leviticus* and *Deuteronomy*. Nor do I think he would have prohibited distillations and the use of the <term>alembic</term> <note>A chemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling</note>, or the making of gold and silver, any more than he would the casting of jewelry, rings, and other such ornaments with which *Solomon* and other kings were adorned. Indeed, it is known to everyone how great the use of gold plates and gold leaf was among the people of God, especially in the Temple of Jerusalem. 

Furthermore, regarding <term>Civil Law</term> <note>The legal system derived from Roman law, as opposed to Church law</note>, certainly no letter can be shown in the *Digest*, the *Code*, the *Institutes*, or the *Novels* <note>The four components of the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the foundation of Western law</note> that pertains to the prohibition of Alchemy. On the contrary, the art of the **Founders** <note>Those who melt and cast metal</note> is approved, praised, and decorated with rewards in the law concerning the "excusal of craftsmen." Thus, "Vessel-casters" are frequently named as practicing a legitimate art (without controversy) in the laws of *Labeo* regarding prescriptive words, obligations, and legacies of gold and silver. And regarding the **Miners**, there can be no doubt that they practice a legitimate art according to the eleventh book of the *Code*. 

As for <term>Canon Law</term> <note>The internal legal system and regulations of the Catholic Church</note>, two texts are usually raised in opposition, but it is easy to answer both. The first is found in the decree *Spondent* <note>Referring to the 1317 papal bull *Spondent pariter* issued by Pope John XXII against alchemical fraud</note> concerning the crime of forgery. There, *Pope John XXII* reproaches Alchemists, yet he does not condemn them to death, but only to perpetual infamy. However, that text was not written infinitely or generally about all Alchemists, but specifically and properly only about those who (to use the words of the text) "forge gold or silver through **Sophistical** <note>Meaning deceptive, fake, or imitation</note> transformation." Therefore, it does not apply to those who produce no rejected or adul-

Therefore, all the Doctors—both of civil and canon law—paid no heed to that "extravagant" decree <note>original: *extravagantem Papę*; "Extravagants" were papal decrees not yet integrated into the official collections of Church law</note> of the Pope, as we said above. Furthermore, Giovanni Augurello, the great poet, freely dedicated and presented his short work on alchemy to Pope Leo X, and it is well known that this gift was most pleasing to him. Therefore, let this response to that text suffice—not to mention that many today do not accept the authority of that legislator who was Pope. They would say that if his authority is approved in one chapter, then it would also have to be approved in the next chapter, where he established certain rules for the Franciscans and other monks according to his own whim. <note>original: *l. qui non cogitur ff de judic.*; a reference to the Digest of Roman Law regarding judicial compulsion</note>

Another text that is opposed to us is found in the chapter *Bishops* <note>original: *c. episcopi*; a famous canon law text known as the *Canon Episcopi* which was used to prosecute witchcraft</note>, which is said to date from the Council of Ancyra <note>original: *Anquirensi*; the author notes this name is likely a corruption</note>, and it is written thus: *Whoever believes that any creature can be made, or transformed for better or worse into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator himself who made all things, is an infidel.*

First, the citation from a "Council of Ancyra" is ridiculous, as such a thing never existed nor could have. It should be corrected to the Council of AQUILEIA. But even more ridiculous is the citation of that text to condemn those who believe transformation can occur in another species. Certainly, this pertains to our question no more than the Emperor’s writing that it is possible for all things to be converted into money <note>original: *l. 2. C. de constit. pecunia*; a reference to the Justinian Code regarding the valuation of goods</note>. That text does not speak of the "species" (types) of metals or similar things, but of the "species" of persons—that is, of sorcerous women who claimed they were transformed at night into various species of animals and wandered through the woods and groves with Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt, often associated with folk-magic and "night-witches" in medieval law</note>. And so, in the section "Inasmuch as Satan," the text says: *Satan transforms himself into the species of different persons.*

Therefore, it is ridiculous to twist a text that speaks of the diabolical transformation of persons to the transformation of metals, which can be achieved through the industry and skill of certain craftsmen without any diabolical or magical artifice, as Thomas Aquinas shows in the aforementioned places. Indeed, there is another text under the same question in the chapter *No Wonder*, where it is written: *There are in physical things, throughout all the elements, certain hidden seminal reasons; when a temporal or causal opportunity is given to these, they break forth into their proper species.* <note>original: *occultae seminariae rationes*; an Augustinian concept suggesting God "pre-programmed" nature with the potential for all future developments</note> I will also add this: that our laws approve of medicine made from poisons or poisonous things, just as those things which nature...

<meta>This page concludes the legal defense of alchemy. Following the previous page's discussion on the Canon Episcopi and papal authority, the author now addresses the moral character of alchemists and the legal distinction between a craft and its practitioners. He argues that the misuse of a science by individuals should not lead to the condemnation of the science itself.</meta>

<page-num>282</page-num>

<header>
THE VINDICATION OF ALCHEMY.
</header>

...harmful things can be improved and transformed to a healthy state through art and skill, as the text on the Mithridatic antidote <note>Mithridatum was a famous "universal antidote" in the ancient world, named after King Mithridates VI of Pontus.</note> suggests in the Law *quod saepe*, section *venena* <note>original: *l. quod sæpè, §. venena, ff. de cont. empt.*; a reference to the Digest of Roman Law (Book 18, Title 1, Law 35, Section 2) regarding the sale of poisons for medicinal use.</note>.

There remains that argument: that many Alchemists make counterfeit money; many have also been sorcerers, impious, atheists, and necromancers. It is even said that Raymond Lull <note>A 13th-century Majorcan polymath and philosopher often associated with alchemical works.</note> and Paracelsus <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss-German physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals in medicine.</note> were tainted by magical arts. The piety and integrity of those who dispute this is to be praised; however, they must be asked to consider that the vices of the practitioners should by no means be blamed on the art itself. For the art is one thing, the artist another. The use of an art is one thing, its abuse another. In Law *quicunque* and the following law <note>original: *l. quicunque & l. ſeq. ff. ad leg. Corn. de falſ.*; referring to the Digest, Book 48, Title 10, regarding the Cornelian Law on forgery.</note>, the art of minting is approved; yet those who tint or forge gold or silver coins are condemned. Likewise, in Law 1 <note>original: *l. 1. ff. de extra ord. cognit.*; Digest Book 50, Title 13, on extraordinary legal proceedings.</note>, professors of the medical art are praised; yet among them there are said to be impostors who use incantations, curses, and exorcisms. Likewise, Mathematics <note>In this context, "Mathematics" often referred to astrology or divination.</note> is condemned simply in Law 2 <note>original: *l. 2. C. de malefic.*; Code of Justinian, Book 9, Title 18, "On sorcerers and astrologers."</note>, yet not all mathematicians are to be condemned, but only the impostors. Likewise, poisoners are punished with the death penalty in the Law *capitalium*, section *venenarii* <note>original: *l. capitalium. §. venenarii, ff. de pœn.*; Digest Book 48, Title 19, Law 38, Section 5, on punishments.</note>, even though poisons themselves are not condemned, as was just said from the Law *quod saepe*. 

But if arts were to be condemned because of the abuse of their practitioners, which one would be approved today? Jurisprudence, in which there are so many <term>shysters</term> <note>original: *rabulæ*; a derogatory term for petty, loud, or dishonest lawyers.</note>? Medicine, in which there are so many poisoners? Theology, in which there are so many Sophists? Therefore, judgment and discernment should be applied. Let the chaff be separated from the grain on the threshing floor; the bad fish from the good in the net; counterfeit coins from the honest ones in the State. Regarding those who fake gold or silver: let the sharpest punishments, investigations, and inquiries be established against forgers and corrupters of the currency. But (as the Jurist says), let the punishment for another’s crime be removed from those whom no fault touches <note>original: *l. ultim. d. bon. damnat.*; referencing the final law in the Digest title "On the property of the condemned," asserting individual responsibility.</note>.

# Preface to the Art-loving Reader.

> The Art <note>In this context, "The Art" refers specifically to Alchemy (the *Ars Magna*).</note> is righteous, true, and certain
> To him who is God-fearing and industrious,
> And employs the ways of Nature rightly;
> It makes him a master, and not a servant.
> Do not hasten, but stay upon the proper path,
> So shall you have much profit and joy;
> And if God grants it to you in your life,
> Then give most generously to the poor.
> Be faithful, and keep the Art in silence, <note>A reference to the "Hermetic silence," the traditional requirement that alchemists keep their secrets from the unworthy.</note>
> For that is certainly the will of God.
> Keep faith and belief, and remember me therein,
> So shall you remain free from all slander. <note>original: *nachred*; this refers to the public mockery or legal accusations of fraud that alchemists frequently faced.</note>
