# PROCLAMATION

## *To the Alchemical Reader.* <note>original: "Ad Lectorem Philochymicum." A "Philochymist" is literally a "lover of chemistry," a term used by early modern practitioners to distinguish themselves from mere "gold-cooks" or fraudulent "puffers."</note>

The work of the Art <note>The "Art" (*Ars*) refers to the Great Work of alchemy, the transformation of matter and the soul.</note> is righteous, true, and proven by certainty,
   Yet it is handed down only to the diligent and the pious.
Those who persevere on the right path, guided by Nature,
   Are not made servants, but rather become masters through this.
Beware of rushing; do not desert the proper track,
   For from here you shall reap both reward and joy.
And if the Lord grants this to you during your lifetime,
   Extend a generous hand to the poor.
Be faithful, and hide the Art within a silent mind,
   And believe for certain that God willed it to be so.
Keep your pacts and the faith you have pledged; be mindful of me;
   Thus you shall be safe and free from all mockery. <note>original: "scommate"; this refers to the public derision, taunts, or "scoffs" that alchemists frequently endured from skeptics or those they failed to enrich.</note>

**Alchemical Reader**, **Nature**, **the poor**, **The Lord**, **The Art**

## Of the Matter and Practice of the Stone
### of the Wise. <note>original: "Stein der Weisen." This is the famous Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and providing a universal cure.</note>

Ye God-fearing, pious, and dear ones,
Who practice yourselves in Art and virtue,
So as not to act against God or your neighbor,
But rather to serve for the good of everyone:
If you have the desire, I will show you
The great treasure that is justly praised,
According to God’s Word and the soul of man,
A golden well and a silver spring.
I am the very one of whom I speak;
The wealth of the world cannot equal me.
But I am a poisonous worm and dragon, <note>In alchemical symbolism, the "dragon" or "serpent" often represents the raw, chaotic state of matter (the *Prima Materia*) which must be "slain" or transformed.</note>
A fierce lion with an open maw.
All metals must cower before me;
If I catch them, they must break to pieces.
Yet when I, through the Artist’s hand, <note>The "Artist" is the alchemist, who works alongside Nature to perfect the substance.</note>
Am driven and bound to that end,
From me comes the highest Medicine,
Regardless of the fact that I am so poisonous.
I expel all sickness and maintain long life,
Yet I cannot strive against the will of God.
I am the true Unicorn of the ancients; <note>The unicorn was a symbol of the "Spirit of Mercury" or the *Monas*—the singular, pure essence that contains the power of healing and transformation.</note>
He who can split me apart,
And glue and seal me back together again
So that my body no longer breaks open,
He shall have cause to wonder
At what I can do by myself alone,
Which otherwise would not be possible for many.
So if it should perhaps be your desire
For me to reveal myself better to you,
I will spare no effort in doing so;
Only open up your reason and your senses,
And do not look upon me only superficially.
Not a single word too many is written here,
Nor has any been left out in vain.
I tell you this as certain and true:
That never before has it been so purely clear
As what has been written here by many Philosophers.

# ON THE MATTER AND PRACTICE
## Of the Philosopher’s Stone.

O my beloved ones, as many of you as are lovers of piety,
Whom it pleases to have studied Virtue and the Art; <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy, often called the "Sacred Art" or "Royal Art."</note>
An Art which is not contrary to God, nor does it serve
Any single group of men, but rather the public good.
Do you burn with the zeal for learning? Behold, I will teach you
A vast treasure, which it is right to cherish,
Yet placed second to the Word of the Lord and to your salvation.
A silvery fountain starts here, and here flows the gold-bearing Tagus. <note>The Tagus is a river in the Iberian Peninsula that was famous in antiquity for the gold found in its sands.</note>
I am the very one of whom I speak: all the kingdoms
And riches of the world cannot compare themselves to me:
Though I may be an unclean worm, and full of poison,
A terrifying Lion with a gaping throat. <note>In alchemical imagery, the "Green Lion" or "Poisonous Dragon" represents the raw, acidic, or corrosive state of the starting material.</note>
All metals, wherever they may be, fear me,
For those I am permitted to touch fall into pieces.
If, however, the learned skill and hand of the craftsman <note>original: "artificis" — the alchemist who "performs" the work.</note>
Should bind me, and constrain me with intricate knots;
The highest medicine shall be born from me, by the gift of the Gods,
However much I breathed out dire poisons before.
I drive away every kind of disease: I prolong life:
Yet I can do nothing against heavenly fate.
I am the unicorn of the ancients: <note>The unicorn's horn was believed to purify water and detect poison; in alchemy, the unicorn represents the "Spirit of Mercury" or the unique, singular essence of the Stone.</note> he who knows how to split me,
And is able to restore me again into a body
That cannot be dissolved—truly, he will marvel exceedingly
At my power, and also at what I alone can do,
Which is impossible for so many others. Therefore,
If by chance you wish to learn of me more deeply,
And you desire that I reveal myself to you more clearly,
It shall not be my fault: there will be no delay.
You must only sharpen your mind, and knock at the recesses of your soul,
And look through me not only outwardly, but also
Inwardly. Nothing mentioned here is in vain, nor is there
Anything written here that is more or less than what is right.
I assert truthfully that at no time has this
Been written so clearly for many sages. <note>original: "sophis" — referring to the *philosophi* or wise practitioners of alchemy.</note>

But what has driven me to this,
Would be much too long to recount;
So that I do not make you anxious,
And first reveal my form,
That follows now very soon.
By nature I have a gray body,
And yet I am neither man nor woman;
Both natures I have within me,
As my flesh and blood show.
The blood is masculine, the flesh feminine,
The power of both is spiritual.
I have the members of both man and woman,
Therefore I am called <term>Hermaphrodite</term>. <note>In alchemy, the Hermaphrodite (or Rebis) represents the union of opposites—sulfur and mercury, sun and moon, or masculine and feminine—within a single substance.</note>
I have my seat in the kingdom of the earth,
Where metals, minerals, and the like dwell,
Yet I am none of those as one might think,
But am thus united by nature,
According to my metallic form and shape:
Warm, moist, dry, and cold. <note>These are the four primary qualities of Aristotelian physics which combine to form the four elements.</note>
But I am not solid, but rather fusible
In the fire, and brittle in the cold.
The four <term>elements</term> are enclosed within me,
Flowed around by <term>Sulphur</term> and <term>Mercury</term>; <note>Sulphur and Mercury are the two philosophical principles believed to be the parents of all metals.</note>
Wild, rough, deadly, and poisonous,
Fixed, volatile, stable, and airy.
I am neither herb, animal, nor fat,
Neither <term>Arsenic</term>, <term>Vitriol</term>, <term>Alum</term>, nor <term>Salt</term>,
Neither <term>Sulfur</term>, nor other such minerals,
Nor am I gold, nor any other metal.
<term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Mercurius Philosophorum"</note> is my name;
I have only one root, and two stems.
Everyone treats me with contempt,
Because I have no outward beauty,
In my old gray coat;
And yet I am that very beehive
Which gives the best honey
For potentates, princes, and kings,
The noble, the ignoble, the poor, and the rich;
To me, indeed, every man is equal.

When it is quite noble, then you may praise it,
For it turns <term>Quicksilver</term>, <term>Copper</term>, <term>Tin</term>, and <term>Lead</term>
Into good silver that is permanent.
Proceed, at last it becomes red;
If you obtain that, then thank God.
The <term>Sun</term> <note>In alchemy, "Sol" or the Sun is the symbol for Gold.</note> is well-disposed to all metals
And converts them into the best gold.
In all things you should praise God.

    Yet no thing outside of me has the power to <term>tinge</term> <note>To "tinge" or "tincture" refers to the alchemical power to transform the properties and color of a base metal into a noble one.</note>.

## The Golden Poem.

One thing in the world stands before your eyes,
Which contains within itself the <term>secret of gold</term> <note>original: "Golds secret." This refers to the "seed" or hidden essence of gold believed to reside within the Prime Matter.</note>.
Its form is the Male; the Female figure
Is its material, which is so cold.
The Male remains <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "vest" (fest). In alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that can withstand the heat of fire without evaporating.</note>; the Female, she flows,
When one draws it out from its <term>ore</term> <note>original: "Miner."</note>.
Yet it is but one, Beginning and End;
Whereby the Male turns himself toward the Female.
<term>Dissolve</term>, file, wash, <term>coagulate</term> <note>These are standard laboratory steps: breaking down a solid into liquid (dissolve) and thickening a liquid into a solid (coagulate).</note>,
Until the golden youth takes shape.
Feed him anew with his own milk,
And repeat the work without fear,
Until everything flows and penetrates
Like wax; then add fine gold.
Thus the <term>body-spirit</term> <note>original: "Leibgeist." A term referring to the union of the volatile spirit and the physical body of the Stone.</note> will be well <term>leavened</term> <note>original: "gesewret." Comparing the alchemical process to the way yeast leavens bread; the "ferment" of gold makes the whole mass "rise" into perfection.</note>,
Ready for the work, full of colors.
The six <term>immature metals</term> <note>original: "vnzeitigen Metall." Alchemists believed that base metals (lead, tin, copper, iron, mercury, and silver) were simply "unripe" versions of gold that grew in the earth.</note>,
Through Art, [it shall] also heal all suffering.
This is the secret of Alchemy,
Given freely by God to the wise.

## SONG OF APOLLO. <note>original: "CARMEN APOLLINEUM." Apollo, the sun god, was the patron of both gold and the healing arts in alchemical tradition.</note>

Before the eyes of all, one single thing revolves,
Which holds within itself the <term>gold-making form</term> <note>original: "formam aurificam." The specific essence or "seed" required to transform base matter into gold.</note>.
The male provides the form, but the female
Governs the matter; the former remains <term>fixed</term>, but the latter <term>flees</term> <note>original: "fixa" and "fugit." In alchemy, "fixed" substances resist fire, while "fleeing" or "volatile" substances (like mercury) evaporate when heated.</note>.
And yet, though twofold, it is the same in origin—a single
THING, both the end and the beginning of its own <term>ore</term> <note>original: "Mineræ."</note>.
Join the wife to the husband, dissolve them once joined, let them <term>putrefy</term> <note>original: "putrefac." The "blackening" stage where the matter decomposes before it can be purified.</note>,
Wash, thicken, and fix them, so that a <term>golden boy</term> <note>original: "puer aureus." A common allegorical name for the Philosopher's Stone in its infant or developing state.</note> may emerge.
Nourish him with his own milk, and reshape him many times,
Until he may <term>tinge</term> <note>original: "Tingat." The ability of the Stone to "dye" or permeate a base metal to change its nature.</note> and flow, penetrating like soft wax.
Finally, let it be <term>fermented</term> <note>original: "Fermentatur." Just as yeast leavens a loaf of bread, adding a small amount of gold "ferments" the Stone, giving it the power to produce more gold.</note> with flakes of pure, welcoming gold;
In this way, the spirit enters the work.
Then you may choose to transform other metals through the art,
Or apply your hands to heal the <term>afflicted</term> <note>original: "affectis." This refers to the belief that the Stone was also a Panacea or Universal Medicine for the sick.</note>.
These are the mysteries of the whole art of Alchemy,
To be attempted only by the <term>divine sages</term> <note>original: "divinis sophis."</note>.

*There are those who often and extensively read chemical books,*

**A**lthough it was not my intention, for my own small part, to publish any further writing or speculation on chemical matters after my inquiry into **Elijah the Artist** <note>original: "Helia Artista." A legendary figure in alchemy, often prophesied as a messianic "herald" who would appear at the end of time to reveal all the secrets of nature and the arts. My aim is to bring to light this brief but clear **Elijah’s Guide** <note>original: "Chiragogia Heliana." From the Greek roots meaning a "hand-guide" or manual.</note> concerning the **Philosophical Gold** <note>original: "auro Philosophico." This refers not to common metallic gold, but to the perfected substance or "Stone" that has the power to transmute and heal.</note>, which has hitherto been little noticed. I wish to communicate it to those who are worthy, earnestly asking again and again that they would not find it burdensome to weigh it diligently, if perhaps they might be forewarned of certain things from this work.

For since I have followed this art for a very long time—not only with constant thoughts and theoretical study, and the inspection of many manuscripts (which I mention here and there), but also with manual labor and my own experience, which (as the proverb says) is the teacher even of fools—I have both attempted and discovered many things, though not without serious loss <note>original: "intertrimento." I hope I may be permitted to uncover for students of <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: "Chymiæ." ->### PREFACE.<-

...as far as I have reached. For although those **three essential principles** <note>original: "tria illa principia essentialia." In Paracelsian alchemy, these are Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the three substances that make up all material things.</note> of all things—which are now extracted from common gold and silver or other metals, and are now most powerfully sought out in their ores—accomplish what they can (for it is not our purpose to investigate these now) and are thus held and spoken of as **Philosophical and living gold**; nevertheless, if we listen to the Philosophers with a more refined ear, there is yet another gold, not a little more hidden than that one. 

Indeed, that gold is twofold, and it ought to be inquired into more deeply and brought forth more clearly into the light! One is that which is proper to the **Chemical Monarchy** <term>Chemical Monarchy: The supreme hierarchy or sovereign domain of alchemical secrets and natural laws.</term> and exists in the **First Entity** <note>original: "primo ente." The primary, uncorrupted state of a substance before it takes a specific form.</note> of the Universal Mineral; the other is that which looks toward preparing the **Tincture of the Sun** <note>original: "tincturam Solis." In alchemy, the 'Sun' (Sol) refers to gold. A 'tincture' is a potent liquid extract capable of transmuting metals or healing the body.</note>, about which we have discussed abundantly in this treatise, since it appears to be entirely hidden from most people. 

However, although I have abstained from the practice of all the alchemical arts for some time—partly because of the malevolence of certain people's minds poured out against me, partly because of the various dangers I have endured (which would be too long to recount here), and finally because of the offense to those who, since they grasp none of these things, do not wish their time to be wasted on them—it nevertheless happens that even the most prudent are sometimes accustomed to ask whether they should so greatly regret what they have learned from me, and whether I am going to cease "shaking empty husks" (as they themselves put it) from now on, or not? 

To these people, I could not fail to respond with this very **Hand-Guide** <note>original: "Cheirogagia." From the Greek roots for "hand" and "leading," meaning a manual or introductory guide.</note> of ours. Certainly, it is not because I do not think chemical study should be held in the highest regard; rather, it is because the use of my time and the necessity of my professional calling forbid me from the **business and practice** <note>original: "negotiationem & pragmateiam." Pragmateia is a Greek term for systematic practice or business.</note> of this matter. Therefore, this open Treatise concerning the as-yet-unknown Philosophical gold was written by me in my spare hours, not in the allegorical style of the Chemists (as is their custom), but plainly, so that the **Tincture of the Sun**, hidden until now, may be understood—with other things added, as far as it was proper to reveal them.

Silver.</note> into the Sun, besides tin and lead: It indeed omits **Mars** <note>Iron</note> and **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, except for how much can be drawn out from them in this regard through separation.* Likewise: *“This tincture,”* (he says) *“cannot transmute more than five parts with one part of itself, so that it remains fixed in **Saturn** <note>Lead</note> and Antimony itself, in **Quartation** <term>Quartation: A process of refining gold by alloying it with three parts silver and then separating them with acid.</term>, and in burning agents: Whereas, on the contrary, that true and ancient Great Philosophers' Stone can achieve an immense amount. So a little later on page 244: *“Furthermore, the reader must notice,”* (he adds) *“that stones which tinge particularly are not found to be of only one kind. This is followed by the tincture of the **Sun** and **Moon** for the red and for the white: which is succeeded by the tincture of **Vitriol** <term>Vitriol: A glassy crystalline metal sulfate, highly valued in alchemy for its acidic and transformative properties.</term> and of **Venus**, as well as the tincture of **Mars**, both of which also have the tincture of the Sun within themselves, if only they have first been brought to a lasting fixation. Other stones, both noble and ignoble, me*

...now they do not move [me]; regarding which I also do not wish anything to be said or written at this time, since they have no other power beyond medicine. Likewise, I will make no mention now of stones from animals or vegetables, which are designated only for medical uses, and they cannot perform any metallic work to provide even a single power from themselves; the power of all of these—mineral (I say) as well as animal and vegetable stones—is found gathered together in the **Philosophers' Stone**. The salts of all [these things] have no power of tinging <note>original: "tingendi" – the alchemical process of coloring or transmuting a base metal into gold or silver.</note>: but they are only keys for the preparation of the stones; otherwise, by themselves, they can do nothing, except for what pertains to the salts of metals and minerals (now I am saying something—if you truly wish to understand correctly—regarding what distinction I perceive between the salts of Minerals) which must by no means be omitted or rejected as far as tinctures are concerned, since we cannot do without them in the composition. This sublime and incomparable Philosopher (writing before Paracelsus) places here the foundation of the entire *Universal of Universals* <note>original: "Vniversalis universalissimi" – referring to the most potent, all-encompassing alchemical agent.</note>, and of all other stones and tinctures in the Mineral kingdom, outside of which Metallic tinctures (specifically in other things by themselves) ought not to be sought, a fact which he attests to in several places. Furthermore, in this passage he most clearly indicates that—besides the great original *Universal* of the seed and the initial mother <note>Likely referring to the "Prime Matter" or the Mercury of the Philosophers.</note> from which all other tinctures have come forth (though he does not name it by its explicit name)—there exist six distinct and different other Stones and Tinctures, of which one may tinge more powerfully than the next; to say nothing for now of "particular" <note>A "particular" in alchemy is a substance that can only transmute certain metals, whereas a "universal" works on all.</note> tinctures. And indeed, at the beginning of his *Triumphal Chariot of Antimony*, he describes for us the **Stone of Fire**, or the **Tincture of Antimony**, whose **Mercury** he teaches to precipitate with **oil of Vitriol from Mars** <note>Vitriol of Mars is iron sulfate; its "oil" is sulfuric acid distilled from it.</note>, and to dissolve it in its own sweet red oil (which is extracted from the **sulfur and salt of Antimony** by means of **spirit of wine** <note>Distilled alcohol.</note> and driven through a Retort <term>Retort: A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</term>), and afterward to fix it into a **tinging and flowing stone**. This is indeed a particular Tincture of Antimony, yet it is well known that Paracelsus so exalted it through subtle preparations, then reverberations, afterwards sublimations, then digestions, as well as separations and distillations, and finally various reductions and resolutions (as Paracelsus himself attests in the fourth book of his *Archidoxes*), that its admirable power can by no means be sufficiently investigated, through which it penetrates all metals, remaining immune to any diminishing of its virtue, and [bringing] them to...

...brings to perfection, being sufficient in itself for dyeing <note>original: "tingenda"—the alchemical process of "tinging" or transmuting a substance, often by changing its color and internal nature.</note> one thing after another, and propagating human bodies healthy and strong even unto the tenth generation. Sulphur, a mineral, is not unlike Antimony (for both ought to be categorized among the vitriolates), concerning which Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus, the influential 16th-century physician and alchemist.</note> says: *“That which is not in it,”* he says, *“we can achieve through it by the benefit of another,”* understanding the Magnetic Spirit of the World <note>original: "spiritum Mundi Magneticum"</note>, which is the true Magnesia of the Philosophers in the *Book of Minerals*, chapter 7. Truly, how the Stone of Fire <term>Stone of Fire: In Latin, *Lapis Ignis*. A specific medicinal and transmutative substance derived from the "inner heart" of Antimony.</term> ought to be prepared from the three internal parts of Antimony by the intervention of oil of vitriol from Venus <note>Venus is the alchemical name for copper.</note> and Mars <note>Mars is the alchemical name for iron.</note>, Basilius <note>Basilius Valentinus, a semi-mythical Benedictine monk and master alchemist.</note> teaches not only scattered throughout his *Triumphal Chariot* [of Antimony], but he seems to have dealt with it much more cohesively and in an open method in the manuscript of his practical manual.

Immediately following the Stone of Fire, he makes mention of the Philosophers' Stone, to which he indeed attributes first place—namely, in respect to other universal tinctures, but not truly to the "Universal of Universals," as will be discussed later. He asserts, however, that the Philosophers' Stone is made from the essence of gold: truly indeed, but as we shall hear, not without the addition of the Salt of Nature, both simple and composite: whence Chrysippus Fannianus <note>An alchemical author known for his work *On the Art of Metallic Transformation*.</note> not ineptly calls Alchemy as if it were *Halchemy* <note>A pun on the Greek word *hals*, meaning salt, suggesting that salt is the primary foundation of alchemical science.</note>.

The third is the Tincture of the Sun <note>The "Sun" or *Sol* refers to gold in alchemical terminology.</note>, most Philosophical, which follows closely after the Philosophers' Stone. This consists chiefly of gold alone, and that "Philosophical" gold described by us, by which name it differs from the Stone itself, although various preparations of it are held. For the Philosophers' Stone is indeed from the essence of gold, so that it is itself a tincture. But this Tincture of the Sun, in place of the fusible salt of nature, is contained in its own salt, and it comes forth from the three principles of gold (especially Philosophical gold) having been resolved, purified, and joined together, as we shall say toward the end.

The fourth Tincture, according to Basil's opinion, is the Tincture of Venus and Mars, melted into one—that is, from their white and red spirit of vitriol, which is the Mercury and Sulphur of both, together with their fixed salt, from which this tincture is prepared: although it is not perfected without common Gold, with which it must be incorporated; since it must first be fixed with it, as Basilius testifies in the book *On Natural and Supernatural Things*, chapter 2, page 28, in these very words: *“For when,”* he says, *“the Tincture of Gold <note>original: "Tinctura Solis"</note> is found more abundantly in nothing else than in Mars and Venus, like male and female, their bodies are destroyed, and their tinging spirit is driven out of them, which saturates the reserved and prepared gold with its blood, and through food and po-* <meta>catchword: -tum (drink)</meta>

...when they make their own substance fleeting and volatile. Furthermore, gold becomes volatile after it has been satiated with its own food and drink <note>Alchemical metaphors for solvents or chemical reagents that "feed" the metal during the process.</note>, reassuming its own blood, and dries it out through its own internal heat, with the benefit of an intervening vaporous fire. From this, victory emerges again, which renders the substance entirely fixed and highly enduring, so that the gold becomes a medicine that is more than fixed. Regarding this opinion, the same author <note>Basilius Valentinus</note> adds after two pages: *“Even if Mars <note>Mars is the alchemical name for Iron.</note> and Venus <note>Venus is the alchemical name for Copper.</note> do not lack for clothing <note>original: "vestitu"—referring to the outward "tincture" or transformative color/property of a metal.</note>, but are able to communicate it to the other five metals: nevertheless, I firmly assert that without the Lion (that is, gold as described and prepared above), they can accomplish nothing at all. This is because provision has not been made for the fixity of their Mercury, nor the malleability of their salt, as would be necessary for you to hunt for anything profitable from them; unless the Lion overcomes them again in the contest, so that they may celebrate a triumph on both sides—that is, so that both are brought not only to a state of being dissolved, but also to a state of perfect fixation on both sides, just as was taught before.”*

However, a great and memorable objection meets us here, and not without merit. For Basilius, on the twenty-ninth page of this chapter, not only clearly writes, *“That the Tincture <term>Tincture: A potent alchemical liquid or powder capable of transmuting base metals into gold or curing diseases.</term> of Venus and Mars can achieve nothing without resolved gold (as has just been said): but he also testifies, conversely, regarding common gold, whose tincture is to be mixed with the tincture of Venus and Mars: The Master (namely, gold) cannot impart anything of his own clothing to his subjects, since nature has granted him only a single honorary garment, unless the servant first enriches the Master.”* Likewise, a little later he adds: *“The King cannot communicate any inheritance of his kingdom to his servants, nor grant them an enduring courtly dress, unless he first receives a pension and tribute from his subjects, so that the Master and servant may thus be able to exist together.”* Since these things are so, one might rightly ask: In what way does the Tincture of the Sun <note>The Sun (Sol) is the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> differ from the Tincture of Venus and Mars or the others according to its essential difference? If, evidently, common gold cannot "tinge" <note>To "tinge" means to fundamentally change the nature or color of a metal through alchemy.</note> unless it is itself first tinctured by the spirit of its subjects? Some, attempting to untie this knot, have fled to the ore of gold and to Marcasites <note>A group of minerals, often iron pyrites, believed by alchemists to contain the "seeds" of metals.</note>, which I do not deny can do much, as they are not devoid of spirits. They contend, therefore, that the Tincture of the Sun is prepared from these, and not from molten gold. Others, on the contrary, hunt for this Tincture of the Sun not from gold simply resolved, but from gold first distinctly reduced into its principles, purified from there, and then joined together again. For those who add not the Sulphur of the Sun <note>The "soul" or active combustible principle of gold.</note>, but the Sun itself to the Mercury of gold, do not belong to this discussion. We—so as not to mock them <note>original: "oppedamus"—literally "to break wind at," a vulgar way of saying to dismiss or scoff at.</note> in this place—nonetheless respond briefly: namely, that for the Tincture of the sun, gold and silver as simply given by nature are not so much required as something more sublime...

### H E L I A N A.

sublimer and better, namely our **Gold of the Philosophers** <note>original: "aurum Philosophorum"—not common gold, but the perfected "Seed" or "Stone" used to transform other metals</note>, in which the tincturing spirit resides—of which we shall speak very soon, once we have first reviewed all the Basilian tinctures <note>The transformative recipes of Basilius Valentinus</note>.

Basilius therefore proposes a **fifth tincture** in **Jupiter** <note>Alchemical name for Tin</note> and **Saturn** <note>Alchemical name for Lead</note>, but only for the **coagulation of Mercury** <note>The process of solidifying liquid Quicksilver</note>—specifically into silver and gold—by means of their "red and sweet oil" drawn out by art, as Basilius suggests in more than one place. To this also belongs what **Paracelsus** teaches in his *Book of Vexations* concerning the composition of Saturn, the Moon <note>Silver</note>, and Mercury. 

At this point, I cannot remain silent: Basilius speaks of common Saturn and Jupiter; however, if they are still in their ores <note>original: "mineris"</note>, they possess a deeper source and power. Regarding this, in the *Triumphal Chariot of Antimony*, while speaking of the fixation of common Mercury, Basilius writes these words on page 87:

> *Mercury can be brought to no coagulation unless there is an addition of the remaining metallic spirits. This coagulation is poured out most effectively and powerfully in the **mother of Saturn** <note>Lead ore, or the "prime matter" associated with lead</note> above all others; and without this, it cannot be done, unless you possess the Stone of the Philosophers itself.*

So too, in his book *On Natural and Supernatural Things*, chapter 9, concerning Saturn, page 121:

> *Everyone should also know,* (he says) *that no transmutation of that metal can follow from Saturn, on account of its immense coldness, except for the coagulation of common Mercury: since the cold sulfur of lead can tame the hot, running spirit of Mercury and take it away, if the process is rightly established.*

To these things, a little later, he adds:

> *Therefore, do not utterly reject Saturn, nor mockingly cast it behind your back: for its nature and power are not yet known to many. For the **Stone of the Philosophers** has its first beginning of its celestial and more than shimmering color only from that metal; and through the influence of this planet, the "key of perseverance" is handed to it through putrefaction <note>The stage of decomposition where the matter turns black</note>: since no red can be made from yellow, unless it has first been made white from the beginning of black.*

These are his words; just as they are of a deeper inquiry, so they are understood to pertain to the more secret Saturn—namely the **PHILOSOPHICAL SATURN**, which exists from the putrefaction of the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and the **Salt of Nature**. Nevertheless, a certain excellent Doctor of Laws, whose "twin blossoms" are well known, strives to prove in his *Ruricola* that a very great power of a certain kind exists even in the ore of lead itself. The same is shown by the tincture called the **Aromatic of the Philosophers** made from the Mercury of lead, to say nothing of other minor particulars. Hence Paracelsus, in the aforementioned book of *Vexations* (or rather, the book of *Fixations*), cannot sufficiently praise that internal spirit of Saturn, which "kills" <note>In alchemy, to "kill" a metal often means to strip away its outward form or to fix its volatility</note> the remaining spirits of the metals, or their Mercuries:

<note>Cheiragogia: A Greek-derived title meaning "Hand-guiding" or "A Manual."</note>

...just as we ourselves have seen rods of the most refined gold produced from common Mercury, which a very learned man showed us for our inspection five years ago.

In the sixth and final place, **Basilius** mentions the **Tincture of Mercury itself**. This is prepared either by the means of the lime of eggs, as found in **Paracelsus's** *Book 5 on Open Ulcers*; or it is elevated from the vitriol of Venus <note>Copper</note> and Mars <note>Iron</note>, then resolved, distilled, and coagulated, as may be seen in the same author’s *On the Death of Things* in the *Metamorphosis*, and in the works of **Rupescissa**, whose short book on the tincture of Mercury we attribute to one of the parts of **Gratarolus** <note>Guglielmo Gratarolo, a 16th-century physician who compiled alchemical texts</note>. Alternatively, it is resolved and distilled through the benefit of a <term>malagma|An alchemical mixture or soft mass, often an amalgam of mercury and another metal</term> of Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, in which Mercury is calcined and coagulated with metals—a method **Basilius** seems to follow in his *On the Double Mercury of the Sun*, page 108, in the *Repetition of the Great Stone*. There are indeed many ways of working with Mercury: although it is most easily reduced to a liquid through the use of crushed charcoal and fire, which afterwards, by a certain artifice, extracts the soul from the Sun <note>Gold</note>. It is also precipitated by itself and fixed by the Tinctures of Mars, Venus, and the Sun; but it is especially nourished by its own milk, about which you might perhaps interpret that saying of the **Emmerian Sibyl** <note>A legendary prophetic figure</note> when she says:

> Sitting upon a spread seat, giving him his own right <note>original: "ius proprium"—this can mean "proper juice" or "rightful law" in an alchemical context</note>, that is, milk sent from heaven,

which can nevertheless be applied repeatedly to the universal Stone, found in the Sibylline fragments of **Philippus de Lignamine**, a Sicilian Knight. Regarding this, you may also accept the saying of **Geber**, who says:

> If you know how to fashion the Stone from Mercury alone (that is, from the mineral form, though prepared elsewhere), you will be a most excellent seeker of nature.

Hence **Basilius** says in the *Triumphal Chariot*, page 88:

> For Mercury (he says) is pure, clear, winged fire. Therefore it cannot be burned by any fire, nor can any fire capture it for its total destruction. Either it suddenly flees, resolving itself spiritually into an incombustible oil; or it remains constant after its fixation, so that no man can take anything from it. To this extent only: whatever can be made from gold can also be fashioned from Mercury through art. For after its proper coagulation, it is similar to gold in all respects, since it comes from one root, one trunk, and from unity with gold.

This agrees with what the same author says here and there regarding the "star of the Sun" and the "spirit or star of Mercury"; these two, joined by the radiant power of their strengths, open the inner chambers of deepest wisdom at a certain time. See the *Triumphal Chariot*, pages 71 and 72, as well as pages 91 and 92. If the treatise by **Basilius on the Star of the Sun and Mercury**—the former glowing red, the latter shining with snow-white brilliance—were not still suppressed by some, we would labor less in explaining Basilius's words.

<page-num>305</page-num>

# HELIANA.

Nor are we unaware that some apply this to the **ore of the Sun** <note>Gold; *minera Solis*</note>, the process of which is established through the **wet path** by means of nitre <note>saltpeter</note> and rock salt <note>original: *sale gemmæ*</note>, such that first the three principles <note>The Paracelsian Tria Prima: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> are sequestered, which are then purified by the spirit of wine <note>alcohol</note>. And first of all, the white **star of Mercury** rises, with the Sulphur and Salt remaining; the latter is extracted by distilled rainwater and separated from the sulphur, and soon, cleansed of all earthly dross, it grows together into vitriol <note>a crystalline sulfate</note> of triangular and quadrangular form. 

Once these three are purified, a new **ore of the Sun** is extracted anew, and the extract is cohobated <note>distilled and poured back repeatedly</note> several times by the pouring on of new **aqua regia** <note>a powerful mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note>, until the **mouth of the red Lion** (as they call it) is properly unlocked. When placed in digestion, it is circulated; after the water is drawn off, the **Mercurial spirit** rises. In this spirit, the previously prepared vitriol is first dissolved and digested until it has deposited all its dross. This oily water dissolves the previously prepared sulphur in double its own proportion. To these three parts, they add four of the **Mercurial star**, and thus digest them in a water bath for forty days, until all things pass into a green and viscous liquor, which afterwards in a physical furnace is very gently coagulated into a **Fixed Medicine** <note>A stable, potent alchemical elixir</note>.

Others, following the **dry path**, separate the ore from the gold, and having gently crushed the gold impregnated with its own spirit, they distill it through a retort, so that from a pound they elicit barely a dram of its **sweet spirit**. They enclose an ounce of this, prepared in sufficient quantity, in a vial and decoct it for six months according to the degrees of fire, until it turns toward a fixed redness. This redness penetrates **living mineral Mercury** <note>Quicksilver</note> collected without fire and renders it fit to turn the body of gold into a tincture. Whether these men or those others more correctly investigate the star of the Sun and the Mercury of **Basilius** <note>Basilius Valentinus</note>, I leave to the judgment of others, since it has not happened that I have seen Basilius’s *Treatise on the Star of the Sun*.

But to speak more openly about the Mercury known to the common people, we ought diligently to compare with one another what **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus</note> puts forward in his *Book of Minerals* concerning the freezing of the spirit of Mercury into a **Sapphire Stone** with oil of vitriol, with those things which his disciple **Phædro** <note>Georg Fedro, a 16th-century Paracelsian physician</note>, surnamed the Great, relates concerning the **soul of the Hermaphrodite** <note>The Rebis, or the unified principle of Sun and Moon</note>. It will then be clear to the princes of the Chemical Monarchy whence it arises, and how that **Sapphire flower of the Hermaphrodite** is prepared, which is a marvelous mystery of the greater world. Indeed, a dram of it (he says), after its projection upon three thousand drams of melted gold, and then cast into a thousand drams of copper, transmutes all of it into the purest gold.

<header>THE GUIDING HAND</header>

Rodochæus relates these things to Phædro; a process that remains hidden from some of us.

To these, we may rightly add what the most experienced man and profound investigator of Nature, **Joannes Isaacus Hollandus** <note>original: *Flander*; a reference to the 15th-century Dutch alchemist whose works were highly influential</note>—from whom all others of a later age learned, as if from a second **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>—contains in his treatise on the **oil of vitriol** <note>sulfuric acid</note>; likewise concerning the oils of **Mercury** and **Antimony** brought to a **fixed tincture** <note>a stable substance capable of transmuting other metals</note>. Nor can I pass over in silence that he teaches the same: that from several metals and minerals gathered together, oily spirits and salts grow together with gold and resolved Mercury into a **Tincture**. This tincture, prepared from one and the same kind of various minerals, may persistently color and transmute a thousand parts of silver into gold. No less inferior should be considered the Mercurial and solar tincture of the most illustrious Duke of Bavaria, Lord **George the Rich**, who is said by his ancestors to have established immense wealth from this art. Indeed, that ancient saying: *Make Mercury through Mercury by means of Mercurial water* (namely, from gold) exhibits the same thing to us in reality. Nor does **Palingenius** <note>Marcellus Palingenius Stellatus, author of the *Zodiacus Vitae*</note> seem to allude far from this same idea in *Capricorn*, book 10, when he says:

> *Seize this Arcadian youth, unfaithful and far too fleeting,*
> *And kill him by plunging him into the Stygian waters, etc.* <note>The "Arcadian youth" is a poetic metaphor for volatile Mercury; "killing" him refers to the process of "fixing" the metal so it no longer evaporates under heat.</note>

But enough of these things. For I hardly know whether we should refer here to what **Hohenheimer** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus</note>, that Swiss Doctor, puts forward in his book *The Treasure of Treasures*, where writing about minerals he says: *Nature* (he says) *produces the Mineral in the bowels of the earth, of which there are two kinds found in many places and borders of Europe: The best, in the figure of the macrocosm, is at the rising of the star of the Solar sphere. The other is in the Southern star, which is in its first flower, produced from the* <image-desc>manicule pointing right</image-desc> *mistletoe of the earth* <note>original: *visci terræ*; a Paracelsian term for a primordial mineral substance</note> *by the star, and which is found to be red in its first coagulation, in which the flowers and colors of all Minerals lie enclosed.* These words seem to be taken literally regarding the ore of gold and Mercury, because **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus</note> attributes all the colors of minerals to quicksilver, as if to the mother of metals (as does the great Phædro), just as can be seen in his booklet *On the Generation of Things* in his *Metamorphosis*. Although there is no lack of those who stubbornly apply these things to the translucent **red silver ore** (called *Rotguldigertz* by the Germans). I would rather think it suits some other ore instead of gold, which is indeed fertile with gold, but is not yet gold itself. To this, what **Basilius** <note>Basilius Valentinus</note> relates in his books on Natural and Supernatural matters is not dissimilar—

...in the third chapter he brings forth concerning the **spirit of Mercury** <note>the volatile essence or "soul" of mercury, believed to be the key to transmutation</note> on page forty-five in these words: *“Here someone might ask, and not without cause (he says), how this spirit of Mercury is to be obtained and prepared? Furthermore, take the best ore of gold you can have: grind both together in equal weight, before they have been made partakers of any fire,”* and the rest which follow in that same place.

It is known from a certain fertile ore of the **Sun** <note>the Sun is the alchemical symbol for Gold</note> and the liquor of Mercury—with the addition of its **menstruum** <note>a solvent used in alchemical extraction</note>—that a perpetual growth of gold occurred for a certain noblewoman: the gold rising first like grass of a green color, and then gradually with the tips turning into **Gold**, which could be harvested with shears. There is also a place where, when it has been sublimated, it grew into multicolored little branches, almost agreeing with the former description.

But it should be noted that **Basilius** <note>Basilius Valentinus, a legendary 15th-century alchemist</note> speaks of the spirit of Mercury and of **Sulfur** not in one way, but in various ways: now of the **Stone** <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note>, now of the tincture of **Venus** <note>Copper</note> and **Mars** <note>Iron</note>, now of the most universal substance. Hence, not long after in chapter four, concerning the spirit of **vitriol** <note>a sulfate mineral, often used to produce sulfuric acid</note> from Venus and Mars, he says: *“The genuine and true Sulfur is incombustible. For it is a true and pure spirit, from which incombustible oil is prepared: and it is that very thing (he says) from which the sulfur of gold also comes from the same root and is made.”* From these things it will not be difficult to conjecture what ought to be understood by the "best ore of gold" in different places, according to the variety of the subject he is dealing with. Therefore he adds: *“For this sulfur can rightly be called and baptized the sulfur of all Philosophers”* (just as it is also designated by **Paracelsus** in the eighth chapter of the *Book of Minerals* concerning vitriol, and by Basilius in the chapter on vitriol, page one hundred thirty-three). *“Since (he says) in it all wisdom is found, even unto the spirit of Mercury, which precedes it.”* But who that spirit of Mercury might be, about which he writes there—whether it is expressed in the tincture of Venus of my manuscript, namely the white spirit of vitriol of Venus from Mars, or the universal of the most universal—I leave to the judgment of the learned. For he says that from one root come both the star of the Sun and Mercury, and the Mercury and Sulfur of the Philosophers: first indeed the white spirit, which he expressly calls the **Mercury of the Philosophers**; for afterwards...

# THE GUIDING HAND

*The red spirit follows (he says), that is, the **sulfur of the Philosophers**, and the incombustible oil, namely from both the tincture of **Venus** <note>the alchemical name for Copper</note> and **Mars** <note>the alchemical name for Iron</note> coming together equally as one.* See what is contained in the chapter on vitriol <note>vitriol refers to sulfate minerals, often used as powerful solvents</note> in the same author on page 132, regarding how the Philosopher reasons analogically there about the **white spirit** for the white work, and the **red spirit** for the red work.

It appears, therefore, that the red ore of **Paracelsian Cinnabar** <note>a mercury sulfide mineral associated with the teachings of Paracelsus</note> and the red ore of **Basilian Mercury** almost agree. It can be understood that the best ore of gold for both—not only from those commonly given by nature, but also from others such as **Antimony**, the **Ore of Mars**, and especially the **vitriol of Venus** derived from Mars (to say no more)—can be utilized. But regarding these things in passing, or as the Greeks say, *in transit* <note>original: ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ (hōs en parodō)</note>, for the sake of better understanding **Basil**, who speaks of the spirit of Mercury in many ways; this is the habit of many experienced Chemists, who "put many feet into one shoe" <note>a metaphor suggesting they layer multiple meanings or processes into a single description</note>. For there are many ways which aim at one goal, not only through one path, but through many and indeed diverse ones, contrary to what many believe.

Since, therefore, our **Basil** distinctly recounts these six explicit **Tinctures** and mineral **Stones** which we have reviewed at length so far; meanwhile, however, on page 244 of his *Triumphal Chariot* <note>referring to Basil Valentine's famous work, "The Triumphal Chariot of Antimony"</note>, he openly professes at the same time: *“All these six Stones of metallic Tinctures were so sown from one seed and one initial mother, which clearly all of them received in their first generation”* (these are the words of Basil himself) *“that from the same, a true **Universal** similarly flowed forth.”* It is clearer than the midday sun that, besides and above the gold-making essence of both common and our **Philosophical gold** (for the Tincture must be imbued from the common Venus and Mars, but our **Tincture of the Sun** <note>the Sun is the symbol for Gold</note> consists primarily of the Philosophical), there is still something else. This thing is far more hidden, from which the most universal **Universal**, like a seventh and most perfect thing, proceeds. It arises from its own proper root—that is, earth and water—and thereby even excels the **Philosophers' Stone** itself, insofar as from this single source both the Stone itself and all other particular transmuting agents have initially arisen. Indeed, from this all the remaining things of the whole world—not only in the **Mineral kingdom** but also in the **Vegetable** and **Animal**—have received their life, still retain it, and were ordained by the Creator for growth. What kind of thing this is, and where it is situated, though it can be conjectured in some way from the preceding (with the **green line** <note>possibly a reference to the "Green Lion," a symbol for the raw solvent or vital force in alchemy</note> circling everywhere), yet we shall say more about this matter below.

# HELIANA
<note>The title likely refers to "Sun-matters" or alchemical secrets of gold, derived from the Greek 'Helios' for Sun.</note>

The whole question from here on, after we have thoroughly examined all the Tinctures and their multiplicity and diversity in the mineral kingdom, must be transferred by us to our **Philosophers' gold**. We must ask what that might be—namely, from what source the **Tincture of the Sun** <term>Tinctura Solis; the solar essence used to transmute "lesser" metals into gold</term> is most especially to be prepared, besides the "universal of universals" <note>the supreme alchemical substance mentioned on previous pages</note> and the rest of the things mentioned by us above.

We say, therefore, that this is that **Philosophers' gold** (for we are not speaking now of the others, nor of the "universal of universals"): namely, that which is produced by the Philosophers themselves from inferior metals of lesser value—not by separation alone, but by the benefit of **Nature** working through **Art** <note>the "Art" is Alchemy, which assists and accelerates natural processes</note> in the very act of transmutation. Therefore, it is not **common gold** <term>vulgare aurum; the ordinary metal used for coinage</term>, which is simply perfect in its own degree by nature. Because of this, it is in a state of expiration, or the decline of its seed, rather than being capable of being fruit-bearing for the purpose of progenerating another **Sun** <note>the Sun is the alchemical symbol for Gold</note>. 

On this matter, we must listen to the most experienced metallurgist, **Andreas Solea** <note>a 16th-century writer on mining and metals</note>, published by the most famous **Montanus**, who writes as follows in his little book *On Metallic Ores*, in the ninth chapter on the expiring metal in the second *Septuria* <note>original: "Septuria"; likely a division of seven or a specific volume in his work</note>: *When nature reaches gold with the body of a metal, it then descends again from a lack of nourishment because of hunger.* Likewise, at the end of the seventh chapter of the first *Septuria* concerning the **ascent and descent of metals**, after he has mentioned how beautifully nature, in ascending, calcines the entire body of the **Moon** <note>Luna/Moon is the alchemical name for Silver</note> (which lime <note>calx</note> is nothing other than the body of the **Sun**), he adds: *Truly, as far as the descent is concerned, you can easily perceive it from the ascent. For this is the difference: in the ascent, it acquires the Tincture before the body; here, however (namely in the descent), it loses it more quickly. Therefore, descending metals,* he says, *are much more imperfect than ascending ones.*

Furthermore, regarding where the seed and the Tincture might be fruit-bearing or non-fruit-bearing in metals, writing on this opinion in the second chapter of the same first *Septuria* concerning the **seed of metals**, he says: *The ascent and descent of metals could not happen unless they agreed in their seed and were related to one another.* Likewise, *Silver and gold have the same seed,* he says, *which in ascent transmutes silver into gold; in descent, however, it transfers it into copper.* Finally, concluding in the same place most clearly, he says: *It is necessary that the seed goes from its body into another, otherwise it is not fruit-bearing.* Thus far **Solea**, in whose manifold experience he who does not have faith will have faith in no one. It appears, therefore, the reason why from common...

# CHEIRAGOGIA
<note>original: "CHEIRAGOGIA"; Greek for "A Guiding Hand" or "Manual."</note>

Tinctures of gold are not made unless that gold is first exalted (as **Basil** says) by the tinging spirit of its subordinates <note>The "subordinates" are the "lesser" metals used to prepare or "exalt" the gold.</note>. For we must seek a more noble and perfect gold, which is produced in the "ascent" <note>Referring to the alchemical process of sublimation or the growth of the metal's power.</note>, in which there is a tinging and growing spirit and a fruitful seed—which indeed, by the indication of **Solea** himself, is the gold produced from inferior metals. *For to what other purpose,* says the **Count of Trevisan**, *would the nine-month period serve us?* (*namely, that which we must spend on the exaltation of common gold through the **Tincture of Venus** <term>Tinctura Veneris; the essence of copper used in the process</term>, as Basil teaches, until it can progenerate the **Philosophers' gold** for us*). *For truly we would take up this body,* he says, *just as it was created by nature.* You see here that it is not gold simply given by nature that produces Tinctures by itself, but another kind. Therefore, concluding, he adds: *Our gold is not the gold of the common people, as all Philosophers say, because common gold is dead: ours, however, is impregnated with spirit and alive.*

From this, **Jean de Meung** <note>original: "Iohannes Clopinellus de Mehum"; a famous medieval poet and alchemist.</note> in his *Response to the Lamentation of Nature* says: *Gold is known to be the treasure of all minerals; yet it has neither the form nor the matter of such power that it might exceed its own perfection.* For it has no greater power than that of perfecting itself, whatever the craftsman may attempt. To destroy it and reduce it back into its essence would be a foolish task, since nothing more of virtue or power can be obtained from it than it possesses from its own nature. No reduction occurs of those things which nature has perfected into a species or an individual unless they are first corrupted <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to breaking a substance down into its primal components (putrefaction) so it can be reborn.</note>. Even after corruption, the generation of a similar species does not occur unless there is a return to this genus. Therefore, the destruction of common gold does not pave the way for constructing it, because nothing can be constructed through its own destruction; for once the gold itself is dead, its substance dies along with it, so that no more **mercury** <term>argentum vivum; literally "living silver" or quicksilver, the base of the Stone</term> can be born from it, nor any metal, and the other things that follow there, which are worthy of note.

So that we may expressly and solidly confirm our opinion concerning the preparation of the **Philosophers' gold** from inferior metals, we shall bring forward the evident testimonies of several Philosophers. And first indeed **Basil** [Valentinus], writing in a manuscript declaration of his manual *Practice* concerning the **Tincture of the Sun** <term>Tinctura Solis; the solar or gold-making essence</term>, says these words: *You ought to know that our **Stone** is composed of its own essence, and transmutes other metals into true gold: which* GOLD (he adds) *MUST AGAIN BE DESTROYED and converted into a better Stone.* He indicates clearly enough here (I think) that this gold must first be constructed before it can be destroyed again, or converted into a better stone.

It cites several masters to prove that gold must be built up from lesser metals and then "destroyed" (broken down) to create the Philosopher's Stone.</summary>

Truly, regarding what is commonly discussed about the "soul" of gold being extracted, it must be known that it cannot transmute other substances, even if it induces a color. **Paracelsus** is a rich witness of this in the seventh chapter of his *Book of Minerals*, when he writes in these words: *“This is entirely true in itself: if the sulfur of gold is cast into silver, it colors it indeed, but does not fix it”* <note>original: "Hoc in se omnino verum est... non figit." To "fix" a metal means to make its transformation permanent and resistant to fire.</note>, which **Basil** also hints at in his *Repetition of the Great Stone*, page 113.

Correct, then, is **Sendivogius** <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist and pioneer of chemistry.</note> in his *Ninth Treatise on the Mixing of Metals*: *“Chemists,”* he says, *“know how to transmute iron into copper or Venus without the Sun <note>Gold</note>; but if they knew,”* he adds, *“how to manage Nature for these mutations of the Sun, they would certainly find a thing more precious than any treasure.”* What is this, I ask, other than not common gold, but our **Philosophical Gold**, from which the **Tincture of the Sun** <note>A concentrated alchemical medicine or "projection powder" capable of turning many parts of lead into gold.</note>, the most precious treasure, can afterwards be prepared? *“Therefore,”* he says, *“it must not be ignored which metals are to be joined together, and whose nature corresponds to nature.”* 

Finally, concluding, he says: *“therefore, there is one metal (a metal, he says) which has the power of consuming others”* (by corroding them, obviously). *“Why? For it is almost,”* he says, *“like their water and almost their mother: Only one thing, namely the **radical moisture** <term>Humidum radicale; the fundamental, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist within all matter</term> of the Sun and Moon, resists it, and is improved by it.”* 

It could altogether seem that he is speaking literally of common **Saturn** <term>Saturnus; the alchemical name for Lead</term>. But properly, gold and silver are not made better internally by common lead, though they may be purged externally. Therefore, you must understand this as referring to *another* Saturn, with whom if gold unites eleven times, it is cast down into death, and afterwards, placed in its **matrix** (namely, Mercury), it conceives and brings forth the best fruits. 

But since no other Saturn exists as a metal in actuality—besides the common one, or that which is made from the “soul” of the **Regulus of Antimony** <term>Regulus; the pure metallic heart of a mineral, often shaped like a star</term> by a "cementing" process, or from common Mercury resolved in **aqua fortis** <term>Strong water; Nitric Acid</term> by transmutation—these things are not inaptly referred to the **Tincture of Vitriol of Venus and Mars** <note>Copper and Iron vitriols. This suggests that the "water" or "mother" is actually an acidic salt derived from these metals.</note>. The first letters of these Latin words spell VITRIOL, a central alchemical acronym.</note>.

But regarding what Sendivogius adds—*if it couples eleven times* <gloss>gold</gloss> *with it* (for it does not transcend the **Alembic** <note>A glass apparatus used for distillation.</note> unless joined with gold many times, as can be seen in the manuscript *Practice of the Basilian Tincture of Venus*), *“it emits its seed, and is weakened almost unto death”*—this must be understood in such a way that it is finally **mortified** <note>killed or broken down</note> through putrefaction after the distillation of both, so that it can then be resuscitated into a new life. *"Then,"* he says, *"the steel conceives, and gives birth to a son clearer than the father"* (that is, clearer than common gold); *"that is, it generates for us the **Sun** or **Philosophical Gold**, from which the **Tincture of the Sun** subsequently arises out of the Philosophical Gold."* Hence he adds: *"Afterward, the seed of the one already born"* (that is, the <term>Sulfur of Philosophical Gold</term> <note>The active, "fiery" soul of the gold.</note>) *"is placed into its womb (that is, if it is mixed with its own Salt and Mercury), it purges it, and makes it a thousand times more fit to bring forth the best fruits"*; that is, it produces for us the Tincture from Philosophical Gold, which, after its fermentation, dyes a thousand parts, as Basil is the witness. 

But Sendivogius adds: *"There is also another steel, which is likened to this one, created by nature itself, which knows how to elicit from the rays of the Sun—with marvelous power and virtue—that which so many men have sought, and which is the beginning of our work."* By this, he means not so much the ore of **Mars** <note>Iron</note> (or native steel), but a certain mineral opposite to Mars, about which he says in his last treatise: *"Our Salt is Mercury."* Then he adds: *"Our Sun and Moon"* (from which, of course, <term>this Stone of the Philosophers</term> arises) **IS COVERED BY THE SPHERE OF SATURN** <note>original: "OBDUCTA EST SPHERA SATURNI." Saturn usually represents lead or the raw, "blacker than black" starting material, often associated with antimony in this context.</note>. This mineral receives the rays of gold (that is, its <term>fifth essence</term> <note>The quintessence; the purest part of a substance.</note>) into itself and, with marvelous power, promotes it into the **dyeing stone**. Nothing is more hidden than these things, yet nothing is more open—if only we have open eyes to understand the roots of minerals, both simple and compound.

In this same vein, Sendivogius says in his tenth treatise: *"Gold,"* he says, *"can give fruit and seed, in which the industry of the wise craftsman, who knows how to promote nature, multiplies itself."* But both in the "Practice" of the eleventh treatise and in the "Theory" of the third treatise, he strictly warns that we should not simply take common gold by itself for the Tincture of the Sun: *"In practice indeed, be warned of this,"* he says, *"lest you take the gold and silver of the common people. For these are..."*

dead. "Take ours," he says, "which are alive." But in Theory, hold this caution for yourself: he says not to seek that "point of Nature" in the metals of the common people, for it is not in them. But let us consult **Theophrastus Paracelsus** <note>The famous Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541).</note>, and let us see what he philosophizes to us about this our Philosophical gold, or rather, what he demonstrates through his practice. In his book *On the Nature of Minerals*, chapter 7, he teaches how to make a **Hepatic** <note>Liver-colored; original: "Epaticam."</note> substance from mineral sulfur, from which a red oil is later distilled. Writing in these words, he says: *"Here it must also be observed that any silver placed into this oil, if it remains for its proper time, is blackened and sends a solar calx* <note>A "calx" is a powder or residue left after heating/treating a metal. "Solar" refers to Gold.</note> *to the bottom. But before the proper time,"* he says, *"it is not a fixed calx, but something volatile and immature"* (let the word **immature** be noted here for what follows). *"But if it attains its term,"* he adds, *"and reaches the end, then* **IT ACCOMPLISHES EVERYTHING THAT IS TO BE ACCOMPLISHED: IT IS NOT GOOD TO SAY MORE OF THIS MATTER.**" From this single passage, it appears more than evidently what this gold born from silver can provide—about which he says it is not beneficial to reveal more. And yet he confesses that it performs all things which are to be performed, whatever the seeker of the Art desires. This is a remarkable passage which can in no way be dismissed or evaded; it suffices as a masterpiece to confirm our opinion—all the more certain because Theophrastus is the greatest of all. 

Furthermore, this oil of sulfur is nothing other than the **First Essence** <note>original: "primum ens." The fundamental spiritual/chemical blueprint of a substance.</note> of **vitriol**, which is proven both by its acidity and by the fact that if you mix as much spring water as you like with this oil of common sulfur, and then boil iron plates in this until a third remains, as soon as it is cooled, a very green vitriol is produced. A certain person, recently inserting our findings into his own apprenticeship, took this description word-for-word and foolishly sold it as the **Salt of Mars** <note>"Mars" is the alchemical name for Iron.</note>.

But let us return to Paracelsus. He writes in his *Manual*, where he deals with the practice and preparation of the **Tincture of the Sun** <note>Gold</note> (as is clear from the end, for there he speaks expressly of potable gold and the liquor of the Sun), in these words: *"Take,"* he says, *"immature mineral Electrum* <note>A naturally occurring alloy of gold and silver. Paracelsus considers the "immature" version to be more potent for alchemy.</note> *(that is, what is between the mature and the immature)."* What this...

->## HELIANA ##<-

(I ask) of electrum? Truly, **Electrum** is nothing else to **Paracelsus** than a metal made from another metal by art, so that even "white Venus" <note>A term for white copper or a silver-like alloy; original: *alba venus*</note> made from red Venus <note>Copper; original: *rubea*</note> is called such by him, however much it differs only in color and not in substance. Hence, in his *Book of Minerals*, in the chapter on Arsenic, he defines it thus: "Electrum," he says, "is a metal that proceeds from another metal" (namely, by the benefit of nature through art). Wherefore elsewhere he also calls the *crama* <note>A mixture or blend of metals; original: *crama*</note> of all metals joined to Mercury "Electrum," as if it were something drawn out from the seven metals. It follows, therefore, that by the name of Electrum he is not speaking here of common metals given simply by nature—whether found in their ores or as melted metals on their own—but of those things which are produced from others by art, such as when **Venus** (copper) is made from **Mars** (iron), which is far more excellent and of greater power (as experience teaches) than common copper.

So also gold produced from **Luna** (silver), which he taught above was made through the oil of hepatic sulfur <note>Literally "liver-colored" sulfur; original: *oleum epaticæ sulphuris*</note>, is much more excellent than the common kind, since it accomplishes all things (as Paracelsus says) that are to be accomplished; it can even be so exalted that it is a wonder to anyone. But why does he call it "mineral" and "immature"? Surely because it comes from what is mineral and immature. For it is made through minerals, specifically through the Oil of Sulfur from Silver, which is imperfect but nonetheless on the nearby path to being led most closely to maturity. Therefore, before it fully completes its term, it is "immature," still having foreign superfluities. For this reason, he teaches that one should wash and purge this electrum from all superfluity through *stybium* <note>Antimony; original: *stybium*</note> in the chemical manner, namely so that it may reach the exquisite grades of gold. 

What then? That gold itself (however much it is produced from Silver) is still an imperfect thing, and therefore in some way immature, in respect to the **Stone** and the **Tincture of the Sun** <note>The Philosopher's Stone or the solar elixir; original: *Tincturæ Solis*</note>. As **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus's first name.</note> himself explains, declaring not much later in the same place: *"Nature left it imperfect in this place, since it formed its matter, not the stone; which indeed, in respect to the stone and without preparation, is a thing half-finished and crippled."* This passage must be weighed accurately so that we understand what he calls the work of Nature respectively (such as the natural transmutation of silver into gold through the Oil of Hepatic Sulfur) and what he calls the work of art, namely in preparing the **Philosophical Tincture**. Because where Nature stops in the construction of our gold, there Art finally begins—namely, to prepare the Tincture of the Philosophical Sun. Although in both cases the craftsman approaches only as the minister of Nature, he spends more labor in the work of art and less in the work of nature. **Bartholomew Korndörffer** <note>Bartholomæus Korndørferus, a 16th-century alchemist known for his secret processes and claim to possess the Stone.</note>, who follows Theophrastus, agrees, to whom gold itself is still

Our gold is not common gold (he adds) and our silver is not the silver of the common folk: for since those things remain fixed in their own substance, they are dead, nor do they possess any powers in themselves, as can be seen in the *Book of Truth*, that is, the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum* — one of the earliest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among ancient sages</note>. # H E L I A N A. #

...(says Basilius) *our potable gold <note>original: aurum potabile — gold in a liquid, drinkable form, highly sought after as a universal medicine</note> is yet more perfect than that made from gold itself, which must first become spiritual before potable gold can be prepared from it,* as he states in chapter 6 of *On Natural Things* and chapter 7, page 93. For *this blue spirit, which is in both the sapphire gemstone and in the Moon <note>alchemical code for Silver</note>, is the sulfur and soul* (he says) *from which gold and silver receive their life.* Hence Basilius, in his repetition of the *Great Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>,* page 114, writes that *the spirit of the Moon is assigned to the spirit of the Sun just as a woman is to a man, both in the earth (where metals are first generated) and then above the earth through art.* Finally, *the white Tincture* (he says) *is situated in the Magnetic form <note>an attractive or essential essence</note> of that unique thing, in which the first essence of gold is likewise found.* Therefore, after describing the **Rectification of the Silver Tincture and its preparation**, he closes that chapter with these words: *If indeed you know* (he says) *the first mobile <note>original: primum mobile — the primary source of motion or the starting material that triggers the process</note> of all those things, there is no need (that is, for such great circulations of compositions),* SINCE YOU ARE ABLE TO COMPLETE THE WORK FROM ONE THING.

What this "one thing" might be in the Mineral kingdom of Nature must be investigated. But yet, so as not to leave the matter entirely untouched and thus abandon the Reader in the middle of the journey, he suggests throughout his work that our [subject] is not far from anyone. Thus, in *Natural Things*, chapter 4, page 56, he laments that *the sons of men do not observe this, but rather despise that which God has placed hidden in nature.* In the same vein, at the end of his memorial tablet, he says *the true root is vile <note>original: vilis — meaning cheap, common, or lowly</note>, even visibly exposed to the eyes of the common people themselves, yet unknown, and without many trials demonstrated, it remains hidden to man in darkness. For this whole World* (as *Bernard* <note>likely Bernard of Trevisan, a famous 15th-century alchemist known for his search for the First Matter</note> also testifies) *sees it, yet does not recognize it.* So, regarding the *Great Mystery of the Microcosm* near the end of page 220: *The First Matter <note>original: Prima materia — the primitive, formless base of all matter</note>, manifest to the whole world,* (he says) *is placed before the eyes, yet known to very few, and still to be found visibly in every place; namely Mercury, sulfur and salt, and Mineral water, or metallic liquor, as a center,* SEPARATED FROM ITS FORM, *and made from these three beginnings.* Most of all, at the end of the last chapter on Natural Things, he says that *all things which—after Antimony, Vitriol, Sulfur, and the Magnet—are especially endowed above others and related to those from which gold and silver receive their beginning, middle, and end, along with the true transmutation and alteration in particular,* have received their virtue, strength, and power FROM ONE THING, *in which all these lie hidden invisibly to be brought forth, together with all metals:* to which he adds, WHICH MATTER *is manifest before the eyes of all men. But because its virtue, power, and force are buried very deep in the depths, and thus unknown to most, even to the point that this matter is judged as nothing and unsuitable out of ignorance...*

...is considered and thought upon. *His name is called Hermes* (he says) *who carries a flying serpent as his emblem and has for a wife one who is called Aphrodite, who knows the hearts of all mortals: and yet all are one and one thing uniquely, and it is a unique essence* (he says) **WHICH IS COMMON IN ALL REGIONS, AND KNOWN IN ALL PLACES. ANYONE** (he says) **GRABS IT WITH THEIR HANDS:** *and uses it for vile things. The common person considers the precious thing to be vile, and rejects the precious. In summary, there is nothing else* (he says) *except water and fire, from which the earth was born with the help of air, and even now is preserved. With these words, he abundantly places the material of the interior root before the eyes of all.*

Here, therefore, as if at the finish line of the "Universal of the most universal" <note>The "Universal" refers to the Great Work or the Philosopher's Stone, which acts upon all things; the author is concluding this section on the primary mineral matter.</note>, we must come to a halt in the Mineral kingdom, after this review of almost all the Universal and particular Tinctures <note>term: Tincture — a potent alchemical substance capable of transforming or "dyeing" base metals into noble ones.</note> of which any knowledge has reached our ears.

It seemed good to add only one thing for the sake of those who think that outside of this "Universal of the most universal" there is absolutely nothing true or profitable, and who therefore deny that any particular works should be sought outside of it; indeed, they pull all the sayings of the Philosophers "by the hair" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to distort or force an interpretation.</note> toward the Universal alone. To these people, I would easily concede that if the Universal matter is possessed and rightly understood, most certain "particulars" can be prepared from it. But it does not follow that in the various branches of the Universal matter—like offshoots which may differ in appearance from the source—there is no power of transmutation present. This is testified by experience and acknowledged by the most learned men, such as **Chrysippus**, **Fannianus**, and **Thomas Aquinas** himself in his book *On Supercelestial and Inferior Bodies*, chapter 4 and following. Nor does it follow that because **Count Trevisan** <note>Bernard Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous alchemist who spent his life and fortune seeking the Stone.</note> in his whole life found no "particular" work of any importance, therefore no others can find it, or that such claims by others are false. For even if I remain silent about Count Bernard seeking the Universal (which you will certainly not find in any particular substance outside the universal), both he and others are sufficiently refuted by what **Basilius** <note>Basilius Valentinus, the legendary alchemist and monk.</note> produced—not only regarding the *Fire Stone* and the distinct *Tinctures of metals*, but also what **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus (Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim).</note> taught concerning **Liver of Sulfur** <note>original: Hepatica sulphuris — a chemical compound used in various alchemical recipes.</note> and the conversion of **Silver into Gold** <note>original: Luna in Solem.</note> through its oil. This is further supported by what **Bartholomew Korndorfer** reports regarding the **Stone Schist** <note>original: Lapide Schisto — likely a reference to a specific mineral or "cleavable stone" used in his recipes.</note> suitable for the fixing of Silver; although even Basilius himself, through ignorance, denies that any power of transmutation exists in common sulfur or in Korndorfer’s Schist (which is a certain very sharp Salt). Thus, there is no lack of those who, having obtained some universal or even particular Tincture, immediately and insolently proclaim that nothing else...

...that no Universal exists except their own: so are most of us Sophists <note>original: Supheni — Likely a reference to pretentious or self-proclaimed wise men who believe only their own path is correct.</note> to one another? But let it be enough that we have pointed a finger here in passing.
