## TREATISE
# ON THE EARTHLY
# HEAVEN,
### BY WENCESLAUS LAVINIUS
### *The Moravian.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' (transcribed as 'Vnus') featuring floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

[V]one is the bodily spirit <note>original: spiritus corporeus — a substance that is spiritual in nature but takes a physical, material form</note> first created by Nature, common, hidden, a precious thing of life: preserving the pure and good, and destroying the impure and bad. This is the end and the beginning of every creature, threefold in substance, consisting of salt, sulfur, and Mercury <note>These are the *Tria Prima*, the three primary components of all matter according to alchemical theory</note>, or a pure water, which coagulates, unites, and gathers, and waters all these lower places through the dry, the oily, and the moist, from a higher place (which is skillful and fit for receiving any form and figure whatsoever). Art alone, with Nature mediating, renders it visible to our eyes: in its womb it conceals and hides an infinite power and virtue: it is stuffed and full of the faculties and properties of heaven and earth. It is Hermaphroditic <note>Combining both active/male and passive/female principles</note>, and it gives growth: it mixes itself indifferently with all things because it has enclosed within itself all the seeds of the etheric globe <note>original: globi aetherei — the celestial or heavenly sphere</note>. For it is full of a swift and powerful fire, and descending from heaven it flows in and impresses its power upon the bodies of the earth; its porous womb, full of heat, is the Father of all things. Then this womb is filled with another vaporous fire, and continuously receives nourishment from the radical moisture <note>original: humore radicali — the fundamental, life-sustaining liquid within a substance</note>, which in that vast body assumes the body of mineral water, and this by the cooking of hot fire. This coagulable water, generating all things, becomes pure earth, which keeps itself enclosed by a firm union of the powers of the highest heavens. Therefore, because it is joined in the earth itself with heaven, by this beautiful name I call it THE EARTHLY HEAVEN.

Just as at first, for the adornment of the undigested mass <note>A reference to the *massa confusa* or the chaotic state of matter before the creation of the world</note>, primary Nature used separation, so Art, loving perfection, ought to imitate Nature. Nature removes substantial waste either through earthly slime into water, or through scorching: Art uses washing and digestion <note>original: elotione & digestione</note> either by water or by fire, and separates infection and impurity, purifying the pure souls

<header>PREFACE.</header>

# TO THE LOVERS OF CHEMISTRY
## TO THE FRIENDS OF THE SUN, HELIOPHI-
### lus, the Friend of Chemistry,

#### NICOLAUS NIGER HAPELIUS
#### Anagrammatized, Greetings.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'A' featuring interlaced floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

*To assert the truth of the gold-making art <note>original: "artis Chrysochemicae" — chemistry specifically focused on the creation of gold</note> (although it is held in very bad repute due to the deception of many, and is plainly outlawed by the prudent and otherwise learned as if it were nothing), it seemed right to establish this inquiry. In it, the causes of the art's difficulty are opened, and what should be thought of it is shown by certain signs, bringing to light the "Elias of the Art" <note>original: "HELIAS artis" — a legendary figure in alchemy, Elias the Artist, who was prophesied to reveal all hidden chemical secrets at the end of time</note>, as they call him. Therefore, Reader, lend a patient ear to this inquiry until you have weighed what Elias intends, so that you may more correctly understand the transformation of metals.*

*It is well known among those whose opinion is hostile to chemistry that none resist it more than Natural Philosophers <term>Physicos</term> and Theologians. Both draw from the principles and sources of nature to argue that metallic transformation is partly impossible <note>original: "ἀδύνατον" (adunaton)</note> and partly contrary to the order of creation; we shall discuss these arguments in the progress of this treatment. But as for those things which are purely Theological and have little or nothing in common with the principles of Natural Philosophy, we shall now briefly touch upon them in this preface. They are generally of two kinds: from Example and from Use. Examples of individuals and of universals.*

*An argument of the former kind is provided as follows:*

<meta>This page continues the preface by Nicolaus Niger Hapelius (Raphael Eglinus). Following the introduction of the "Elias of the Art" on the previous page, the author now presents the formal logical arguments often used by critics to debunk alchemy. He structures this section as a classic scholastic syllogism—a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises—to address the theological and philosophical objections to the transformation of metals.</meta>

All natural and lawful sciences were known to Solomon:
The science of the chemical art, which teaches the transformation of metals, was unknown to Solomon:

Therefore, the science of the chemical art concerning the transformation of metals must be considered neither natural nor lawful.

*The force of this proposition <note>This is the "Major Premise" of the author's logical argument</note> depends on the fact that Solomon was the wisest of all mortals, not only in the excellence of his right judgment, and in his political action and prudence, but also because he discoursed upon every question of natural things and physical contemplation—from the Cedar of Lebanon even to the hyssop on the wall, and of beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish. Because of this, the Kings of the whole earth, and especially that most sagacious Queen of the South <note>The Queen of Sheba</note>, came to hear him (as was the custom of ancient traveling philosophers <term>apodemicis</term>). [1 Kings 4 and 10]. Therefore, the major premise seems plainly irrefutable <note>original: "ἀνέλεγκτος" (anelegktos)</note>.*

*The minor premise <note>The claim that Solomon did not know alchemy</note> is proved by many arguments. For from the sacred scriptures it is clear (contrary to the delusions of some chemists) that such an abundance of riches belonged to Solomon not indeed from chemistry, but from the countless tributes, exactions, taxes, royal gifts, and bounties of the wealthiest provinces; and especially from the gold of Ophir brought from Tarshish. For because of the abundance of gold, silver became cheap, of which there was as much available in Jerusalem as there were stones. [1 Kings 10]. But if this abundance of gold were produced at home, or could be prepared by any chemical artifice, why would it be sought abroad through the danger of a three-year voyage across the seas? Why would earthly wealth be redeemed at the cost of souls <note>A reference to the physical and spiritual risks of maritime travel in the ancient world</note>, when it could be had at home for free? Thus indeed—*

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of alchemy by Nicolaus Niger Hapelius (Raphael Eglinus). Here, Hapelius begins his rebuttal, distinguishing between Solomon's divinely inspired wisdom and the mundane way he acquired his historical wealth, while suggesting a "God-given" science of metals still exists.</meta>

In 2 Chronicles 20, we read that the ships under Jehoshaphat were shattered by divine vengeance <note>Referencing the destruction of the fleet at Ezion-Geber, which the text uses to argue that "unnatural" wealth-seeking is punished</note>. It follows, therefore, that Chemistry is Vain, and consequently neither natural nor lawful.

*We respond to the major premise <note>The "major premise" refers to the first part of the logical argument presented on the previous page</note> that it cannot be accepted absolutely <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\pi\lambda\hat{\omega}\varsigma$" (haplōs)</note>, but must be understood with a certain condition. For it depends on the circumstances of the choice and the Vow, in which Solomon asked for neither glory, nor riches, nor the souls of his enemies, nor longevity for himself, but for the Wisdom to govern the people. And although God therefore voluntarily added glory and riches to his wisdom—such as fell to no other King—nevertheless, the gift of his wisdom is far different from the addition of his riches. For the former was not acquired through the study of disciplines or formal instruction, but was plainly God-given <note>original: "$\theta\epsilon\acute{o}\sigma\delta o\tau o\varsigma$" (theodotos)</note> and bestowed beyond the common way of things. Riches, however, were added in the common manner of gaining wealth, consisting of trade, tributes, taxes, and gold imported from elsewhere with King Hiram.*

*But if Solomon had requested riches instead of Wisdom, who does not see that God would have shown him a singular way of preparing wealth, just as He adorned him with exceptional Wisdom? Therefore, the argument is not so much dissolved as it is turned back <note>A "retort" in a formal debate: using the opponent's logic to prove the opposite point</note>. For from this it appears that there is some permitted method and reason for becoming wealthy that is not contrary to God, by which gold and silver can be multiplied—not in the common way, but through an exceptional, God-given <note>original: "$\theta\epsilon\acute{o}\sigma\delta o\tau o\nu$" (theodoton)</note> science, and not a diabolical one. This is true even if, considering the condition of his own vow, this science and exceptional method of gaining wealth was just as unknown to Solomon as it is accessible to very few today. And from this one may suspect why it is not expressly recorded that he lectured on fossils and metallic things, as he did on plants and animals. But who could doubt that by the gift of God there exists such an exceptional science of metallic things, by which both gold and silver are multiplied—certainly not against the order of nature, but from*
the order

He posits that a divinely sanctioned alchemy exists, even if it was not Solomon's specific path.</summary>

the order of nature, it could equally be possible, just as multiplication is accustomed to occur in plants; since it was said to all created things from the very beginning: *Increase and Multiply.* <note>Genesis 1:28. # AN INVESTIGATION
## INTO ELIAS, CONCERNING THE
### *Transformation of Metals, etc.*

Philippus Bombastus, that Swiss Hermit <note>original: "Eremitanus"; referring to his birth near the Abbey of Einsiedeln</note> who calls himself Aureolus Theophrastus (perhaps in the Academic fashion, or after the art he practiced) and indeed Paracelsus—which, as conjecture suggests, is a name derived from his family name, Hohenheim—was the first (so far as I know) to mention in his published books on chemistry and mineral matters a certain "Elias the Artist" who was to come after him. Alexander von Süchten follows him in his little book on the secrets of Antimony, as does the recently published (though written earlier) Basilius Valentinus, both writing that chemical books are to be opened to us by the Elias who is to come.

Led by this occasion, I wished to begin an investigation into the Elias of the art and the transformation of metals: namely, what <term>Spagirus</term> <note>A title for Paracelsus, derived from the "spagyric" art of separating and recombining natural elements</note> signifies by the name of Elias, what times he assigns to him, and what benefit may be hoped for from him. Then, having brought forward reasons and experiments against the opinions of the Jesuits Hagelius and Pererius, we shall show that the transformation of metals is real, and that—contrary to the old proverb—it is not a total loss of "oil and labor" <note>original: "oleum & operam perdi"; a Latin idiom for wasting time and resources</note> when spent on the study of <term>Chrysochymia</term> <note>The specific branch of alchemy dedicated to the making of gold</note>.

Now, although we are only attempting an investigation into Elias as he relates to Theophrastus [Paracelsus], we do not hesitate to offer our own judgment where the authority of Theophrastus wavers or is suspect to us. Meanwhile, we accept those things he presents which are consistent with nature and proven by the experience and use of many, so long as they do not oppose the faith. As for the man himself, now deceased, we commit him to God’s judgment, and we believe he should be read only with caution and discernment.

Regarding Elias the Artist, then, Theophrastus speaks of him in two different ways in his books. Once in a general sense, as in the eighth chapter of his book *On Minerals*, where he writes concerning vitriol in these words:

> *That which is of less value, God allows to be revealed; but that which is of greater importance (namely, the transformation into gold) still lies hidden from the common people, until the coming of Elias the Artist (some copies read: until the art of Elias, when he shall come).*

To which, for the sake of explanation—

# INVESTIGATION
<header>INVESTIGATION</header>

...he adds: For the arts have their Elijah just as much as is understood in other matters.

These things he said indefinitely and generally; everyone understands that they must be referred to the cycles of time in which all things reach their <term>akmē</term> <note>original: "ἀκμήν"; the peak, flower, or maturity of a process</note>. Therefore, regarding the hidden things of nature and the secrets of the arts, these words seem to be accepted just as our Lord and Savior says in the Gospel concerning the Gospel: *Nothing is so hidden that it shall not be revealed; and the Gospel of the kingdom shall be announced to all nations in the whole world, as a testimony to them, and then shall be the end.* For just as there is that Gospel Elijah <note>Referring to John the Baptist or the promised return of Elijah before the Day of Judgment</note>, by whose virtue and spirit all things shall be restored—who, in the precursor of the Lord, namely John the Baptist (in whom the Gospel was first promulgated in the New Testament), already then indeed came and shone forth, but at the end of the world the same shall flash forth far and wide in the spirit—so in the same way Paracelsus depicts for us a certain Elijah of the chemical arts. This figure is to bring their secrets into the open when those arts, now only taking root, shall flourish everywhere with great profit; more on this later. 

Again, Paracelsus is found to speak of this Elijah of the arts definitely and specifically, referring what was said generally to a specific hypothesis, and adapting it almost to one singular man. He does this not to take away the general meaning, but to teach that this collective name of "Elijah" is extended to a certain individual <term>kat’ exochēn</term> <note>original: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν"; pre-eminently or par excellence</note>. For just as the age of Cicero is said to have been a "golden age," in which the purity, elegance, and brilliance of the Latin language reached its absolute peak of maturity and beauty—which nevertheless unfolded its powers in Cicero alone above all others, and poured out all the riches of nature as if in a single heap—so if anyone were to say that an "Elijah of the Latin Language" then shone forth (meaning in many people during the time of Cicero, but in Cicero himself especially), I say he would have said nothing different from the opinion of Theophrastus <note>Paracelsus</note>, though in a different subject matter.

Therefore, he proposes this Elijah of the arts, and especially of chemistry, specifically <note>original: "κατ' ἐνῷ" (kat' enō); likely a Greek-inflected term for "individually" or "specifically"</note> in his books on minerals, in the first Treatise: *It is indeed true (he says), that many things still lie hidden in the earth, which*
<margin>I am ignorant of, along with others.</margin>
*I am ignorant of, along with others. For I know this, that God will henceforth reveal many wonders, and much more will be brought to light than has been known to us all before. This also is true: Nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed: therefore after me shall come one whose <term>magnale</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for a great work, a divine secret, or a miraculous power</note> does not yet live, who will reveal many things.* These things he says <term>maniōdōs</term> <note>original: "μανιωδῶς"; with prophetic frenzy or inspired madness</note> concerning a certain and unique man. He seems to explain the same in chapter 4 of *The Physical Tincture* when he says: *There are still more of these secrets which effect transmutation, although they are known to very few. For if they are revealed to anyone by God, yet the praise and proclamation...*

# INVESTIGATION
<header>H E L I A N A .</header>

...their [secrets] do not immediately become known to the common people, for God grants, alongside the art, the wisdom to hide them from others until the arrival of **Elijah the Artist**. For then, whatever is hidden shall be made manifest. Thus says he. Indeed, he promises then a golden age of grace, asserting that the gifts of the Spirit will exert themselves so brightly that he denies so much knowledge and wisdom has been heard of in any previous age; more on this matter later. 

A truly wondrous prophecy from the man, especially concerning a certain singular individual to come after him, whose great work <note>original: "magnale"; a Paracelsian term for a great work, essence, or virtue</note>, as he says, does not yet live while he himself is alive—that is, one who has not yet appeared in the nature of things. For let it be that those things which are still hidden from the common people shall come forth generally: indeed, those things which are now almost the "spoils of the Egyptians" (for so it pleases him to call those things now shut up in their hands <note>The author uses a biblical metaphor: just as the Israelites took the gold of Egypt during the Exodus, the "True Israelites" (true seekers) will reclaim the secrets of nature currently held by the unworthy</note>) must be handed down to the true Israelites and to the true Magi of Nature. Just as the Magi once did for Christ, these figures shall now open their treasures to Him as He is about to flee into Egypt in the person of His faithful. This was certainly the reason that drove me to think these things should be investigated by me as well. 

Yet from where did this peculiar announcement of the future come to Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus</note>? From where, and from what spirit, did this designation of some "Personal Elijah" to come after him proceed? Is it as Adam Nachemoser (so the inscription sounds) asserts in his *Theological Prognostication*, identifying a certain reformer whom he counts as the seventh of the world (in part 4, book 4, chapter six)? Nachemoser claims that from the year 1581, this figure would certainly and without exception carry the spirit of Elijah. In the same way, Theophrastus predicts for us his own Elijah—a master of the chemical arts and of nature. Did he do this by natural sagacity and mental apprehension (especially through the powder of the stone and the purified <term>physical tincture</term> <note>original: "tincturæ physicæ"; a legendary alchemical substance capable of perfecting or "tincturing" both metals and the human body</note>) or by some sidereal <note>relating to the stars or constellations</note> prophecy and celestial influence? Or perhaps by some peculiar inspiration of I know not what spirit? 

More could be investigated or discussed on this opinion from Paracelsus and Suchten <note>Alexander von Suchten, a 16th-century chemist and follower of Paracelsian thought</note>: But because these things are not proven to me, and judgment on unverified matters is rash, I willingly pass over them.

### Let us pass to the second part of the question, in which the "Time of Elijah" must be explained, along with its benefits.

Paracelsus distinguishes the age in which he himself lived—during which he declares himself the <term>Monarch of Secrets</term> <note>original: "Arcanorum Monarcha"</note>—from the age to come after him. He calls the former the "intermediate age." This latter age he calls "golden," an "age of grace," and the "last age" in his *Book of the Physical Tincture* (for those who doubt these are the treatises of Theophrastus are in error). In the fiftieth...

# INVESTIGATION
<header>I N V E S T I G A T I O N</header>

Therefore, he says that in his eighth year his **Theory** will be in full bloom, at which time everyone will join him and follow in his footsteps in investigating the **secrets of nature** <note>original: "arcanis naturæ"</note>. Likewise, an admirable **Practice** <note>original: "Praxim"</note> will follow with works and signs, so that it does not merely reach and be approved by the common folk and the lowest plebeians. These are his words. That these things are predicted to occur in the fifty-eighth year—not of the century in which he lived, but of the following one (namely that of 1600 <note>meaning 1658</note>)—appears from his books on *Minerals*, in the chapter on **Vitriol** <note>Vitriol: a term for sulfate minerals, considered by alchemists to hold the "secret fire" of nature</note>, where he writes about both his own century and the following one in these words: (for he departed from this life in the year of our Lord 1541.)

"It would be far better," he says, "even at this hour or at this time, to devote effort to these things (*namely the secrets of nature*) *than to indulge in drunkenness, lechery, and other kinds of wickedness. But now the times are such that lechery is the focus, until a third part of the world is killed by the sword; another consumed by plague; and the remaining third barely survives. Then the state of things will be restored to its proper place and to wholeness. But as things stand now, this cannot happen. Even the religious orders must perish and be completely removed from the world; otherwise, it cannot happen again and again.* (This last section is absent in the Cologne edition published in the fourth format by the heirs of **Arnold Birckmann** in the year 1570.) *Then truly,* he says, *will be the golden age; then man will reach a sound understanding and live in a human manner, not after the fashion of beasts, nor like pigs, nor in a den of thieves.* By these stages—the **Protasis**, **Epitasis**, and **Catastrophe** <note>These are terms from classical Greek drama: the introduction, the intensification of conflict, and the final resolution. Paracelsus uses them to describe the "drama" of human history leading to the Golden Age</note>—the **Helian** time <note>The era of Elijah the Artist</note> is established by **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, the birth name of Paracelsus</note>.

The **Protasis** <note>introduction</note> lies in the morals of his own century, by which it happens not only that the secrets of nature are neglected and withdrawn from most people by God’s just judgment, but also that an even more grievous evil is summoned (namely through a wicked life): the slaughter of a third part of humanity, as the **Epitasis** <note>the tightening of the plot or rising action</note> teaches. Hence in the seventh chapter of the books on *Minerals*, when **Paracelsus** deals with **Sulphur**, he says: *If it were not against God (for by this knowledge any man might be rich, but the Lord knows why He did not promise a tail to the goat <note>An old proverb meaning God provides only what is necessary or safe for a creature to have</note>), many could be helped by a shortcut; but because wealth seduces the poor man, takes humility and modesty from him, and transforms him into a rogue, it is better to have kept silent and left such men in poverty.* These are his words.

So we ourselves have seen that when a fruitful result was produced through a **chemical operation** in what are called **particulars** <note>term: "particularia," chemical processes that produce a specific result or a small amount of gold/silver, rather than the "Universal" transformation of the world</note>, the craftsman rarely repeated the same work—whether due to the diversity of materials (especially if one does not pay attention to what the matter depends on), or the inclemency of the weather, or the inequality of the vessels, or because of the regulation of the fire—

### HELIANA

...[reaching the] end <note>original: "nem", the terminal suffix of a word like *perfectionem* (perfection) or *finem* (end) from the previous page</note> (on which much depends), or is it because it did not seem right to God to grant growth to those things planted and watered? For the Lord alone, in His infinite wisdom, governs even the smallest movements of nature, so that they either achieve their effect or pass away. There is no reason, therefore, for us to deny that "everyone is the architect of their own fortune," though these ideas may not benefit the common people.

What should be said of the **Epitasis** <note>In classical drama, the *epitasis* is the part of the play where the action intensifies and complications arise.</note>? Since **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus (1493–1541), the Swiss physician and alchemist whose prophecies are being analyzed here.</note> predicts that a third part of men must first be killed before these things are made public and known everywhere? Indeed, even if Theophrastus were to be hissed off the stage and his divinations ignored, it still appears from the Holy Scriptures that after the immense slaughter of the godly—where death and hell (which are the gates of the underworld) will kill a quarter of the earth by sword, hunger, plague, and through the beasts of the earth (as in Apocalypse chapter six)—when the bodies of the saints lie there, and especially those of the witnesses of the Church in the streets of the great city, which is spiritually Sodom and Egypt (Apocalypse chapter eleven), specifically when their testimony is finished, near the time of the waning Beast who waits at the doors, then a third part of men will perish. 

For the Angels stationed at the boundary of the ancient Roman Empire, the Euphrates, will be released, prepared for the hour, day, month, and year, so that they might kill a third part of men (namely, the ungodly), according to Apocalypse chapter nine. Certainly, if there is anything to it, that Theophrastean "abolition of orders" seems to refer to this: that is, the abolition of the "orders of the Beast," <note>Usually referring to corrupt religious or institutional hierarchies.</note> not of pious Magistrates and Princes, but insofar as the Beast is full of names of blasphemy, which will be burned alive in fire along with the false prophet. As the most holy prophet **Daniel** testifies in explicit words concerning the Beast before John did, in chapter seven. Then, undoubtedly, things will be restored to their original state. For then the face of the Church will be renewed, and the kingdoms of the world will be subjected to the scepter of Christ; and with the Jews also converted to the faith, as we have testified elsewhere before this inquiry.

And here the Theophrastean **Catastrophe** <note>The final resolution or "unraveling" of a plot; here, the end of the current age.</note> also seems to apply, in which he says that the **Golden Age** will then come, when man will not live in a beastly manner according to his own likeness, and in a den of thieves and usurers, but as becomes a human being. For the Paracelsian distribution of times fits this, although I do not know by what Spirit it was predicted by him and referred to the **Peak** <term>akmēn: the highest point or culmination</term> <note>original: "ἀκμὴν"</note> of **Elijah the Artist**; when his Theory will flourish along with his Practice and will be spread everywhere, as he says, among the common people. From these destinies we perceive what the reason is why almost nothing of any importance from **chemistry** <note>original: "chymia"; in this era, the term covered both chemistry and alchemy.</note> reaches the common folk today; although everything is not only full of books, but among Christians...

# INQUIRY

...and among the Muslims <note>original: *Mahumetistas*; referring generally to the Islamic world where alchemy flourished</note> nothing is practiced more frequently everywhere than the **chemical art**, so much so that no corner of the world is without the scent of chemical smoke! What then? Is all hope lost? And before that **Elijan** point in time <note>referring to "Elias the Artist," a prophesied figure in Paracelsian thought who would arrive in the "end times" to reveal all secrets of nature</note>, will it not be permitted through **Theophrastus** <note>Paracelsus</note> for anyone to devote time to the chemical art unless they wish to lose themselves and their possessions entirely? 

Theophrastus does not say so. For although no kind of men is more prone to envy, nothing more varied and deceptive: yet in his book *On the Physical Tincture* <note>original: *Tinctura Physica*</note>, he openly writes the same: *Not only will the final age of grace and the golden age be joined to it, when these things are celebrated everywhere among the common people; but even now, he says he writes these things to promote the intermediate age, so they may be of use and ornament to lovers of truth.* And in his *Manual of Philosophers*, he says in clear words: *What I now write, I shall write so that the Astral disciples may perceive them, and use and enjoy them, and glory in them.* And he adds: *These things can also be perceived by the diligence of another who is not ashamed to learn, since they are not so heavy that they cannot be grasped through labor and industry.* 

These are his words. If they are considered, it will appear that Theophrastus [mentions] those born not only for this purpose—whom he calls "Astral" not only from the Angelic natures of the higher stars, but also from the stars of the Philosophical metals—while **Suchtenus** <note>Alexander von Suchten (c. 1520–1575), a notable chemist and follower of Paracelsus</note> calls them "Mental." Yet others, through labor and industry, for whom charcoal (as Theophrastus says elsewhere) is not beneath them <note>original: *non sordent*; meaning they are willing to do the "dirty" work of the laboratory furnace</note>, and who burn with the desire for experimentation, can attain these things somehow. In their number, I profess my name thus far, as long as these things do not conflict with my duty, the laws of Nature, and charity toward God and neighbor.

But having set aside the Paracelsian Elias, for whose sake we touched upon these matters (let the faith remain with him): we shall now, in the third and final place of our Inquiry, contend against those who either deny that the **transmutation of metals** can happen, or affirm that it opposes the order of the Creator, as if the power of God were being challenged. A grave accusation, if it were true. 

But we shall refute these hasty censures with reasons and demonstrations placed before the eye—that is, **experience**, which, as they say, is the mistress even of fools. In testimony of this matter, we sincerely profess above all that we attempt nothing here except by natural means, since without the movement of nature the whole art is vain, and the artist exists only as the servant and minister of nature, adding nothing of his own to it. We ask first, therefore, that we not be weighed down by prejudice: then, that (as is customary in every science) those with unwashed hands and **unlettered** readers <note>original Greek: *ἀναλφάβητοι* (analphabētoi); meaning the illiterate or those uninitiated in the "alphabet" of alchemy</note>—that is, those entirely unskilled in mineral matters and the criteria of metals—[do not judge.]

# HELIANA.

...those who lack knowledge of metals should approach this matter cautiously, lest they either deceive themselves when making judgments or betray their ignorance and malice when criticizing others. As the old proverb says, "only the craftsman can and should judge his own craft."

First, therefore, those who wish to judge these matters without ambiguity must learn from goldsmiths, silversmiths <note>original: *argyrocopis*</note>, and mining assayers about those solemn trials and examinations by which gold and silver are usually separated and sequestered from other metals. For the Lydian stone <note>the touchstone, a dark stone used to test the purity of gold and silver by the color of the streak left when the metal is rubbed against it</note> is not sufficient here; it can be deceived by sophisticated <note>deceptive or "sophistical"</note> works if other criteria are not added to the color produced by rubbing. Therefore, both princes and all Republics owe much not only to the Wardens and goldsmiths who use these tests to prevent simpler folk from being cheated by counterfeit currency and uncoined metal, but to the very inventors of these tests. These inventors must have been most skilled in mineral matters, as they had to investigate the causes of these things and prove them by experience, which could not be done without chemical practice <note>original: *negotiatione chymica*</note>. Consequently, not all Alchemists should be proscribed at once, even though we should not patronize impostors and charlatans—that is, the **pseud-alchemists** <note>original: *cakchymiſtis*; a derogatory term formed from the Greek *kakos* (bad) and alchemy</note>. There is no small difference between these frauds and the true seekers of nature and philosophers, a fact which is more than sufficiently proven in the faculty of medicine itself.

The first criterion, therefore, is the **Ash-fire** <note>the process of cupellation, used to refine precious metals</note>, which is also called "the lightning" <note>original: *fulmen*; referring to the sudden brightening or "blick" of the metal when the impurities are finally absorbed</note>, and the trial by lead. To make this test more rigorous, take ashes and sun-bleached bones burnt to whiteness; alternatively, use one part bones and two parts common ashes, purified with lye and burnt again. Take care that pig bones do not get in, as they would ruin everything. 

Grind everything finely and pass it through a sieve; afterward, sprinkle with water and moisten just enough so that they may be formed—either in molds (also called little mortars) into small dishes, which are also called **cupels** <note>original: *capellæ*; small porous bowls used in assaying</note>, or into shallow pans in earthen vessels—and let them be well smoothed with a pestle shaped for that purpose. But these things must be demonstrated by experience. After an hour or two has passed, once they have become white-hot in the small furnace upon what they call a "tile," the lead should be added—double, triple, or quadruple the amount, depending on the material being tested—and this should be done gradually. Sometimes fifteen weights of lead must be used in the most extreme examinations, if by no other means can the gold and silver be tamed and separated from the other metal-

### INVESTIGATION

...the dross and slag cannot be separated. Thus it happens that when lead is used, the other metals are burnt away and vanish into smoke, pushing the slag to the outside. Only gold and silver remain as the residue; because they alone endure in the fire, they are called "perfect" and "superior" metals. The others, however, are called "imperfect" and "inferior," arising from either fixed or non-fixed sulfur, as will be understood later, etc.

Another method of testing is by "strong water" <term>aqua fortis; nitric acid</term>, which they call **quartation** <term>quartatio; a process of refining gold by alloying it with silver</term>, so named because at least three parts of silver are required if a fourth part of gold mixed with that silver is to be properly separated by the strong water. If there is less silver, the strong water (unless the limit of the test is exceeded) will not dissolve it in the proper manner; if there is more silver, it promotes the dissolution, but almost "tears" the gold apart <note>i.e., it breaks the gold into such fine particles that they are difficult to recover</note>. Therefore, let the strong water be made from one part calcined vitriol <note>original: *vitrioli calcinati*; sulfates of copper or iron that have been heated to remove moisture</note>, another part raw vitriol, and a third part saltpeter <note>original: *salis nitri*; potassium nitrate</note>. This is generally the most common method.

However, as much saltpeter can be taken as there is vitriol, which will make the solution that much stronger—unless a portion of the dregs from strong water already made once before is added, which is called the **dead head** <term>caput mortuum; the useless chemical residue remaining after distillation</term>.

But books on these matters have been published by mint-masters, goldsmiths, and metallurgists; we refer our readers to those, and especially to the tenth book of Georgius Agricola’s *On the Nature of Metals* <note>original: *De re metallica*; the most famous Renaissance work on mining and metallurgy, published in 1556</note>. While these pages were being sent to the press, we happened by chance upon the most learned books of the famous Libavius <note>Andreas Libavius, a German chemist and physician known for his systematization of chemistry</note>, who is easily the prince of all those authors we have had the opportunity to see. He provides everything in abundance. Let the strong water be purged of all dross: namely, by dissolving a dram of silver in an ounce and a half of strong water in a glass flask with light heat applied. Once the silver is dissolved, it should be immediately thrown into the remaining strong water, whether there be one or two pounds of it. This will make the liquid look like white, turbid milk; then let it sit overnight to settle, and the water will be clarified, with all the dross pressed to the bottom of the vessel.

We use this clarified water to separate silver from gold filings. Heat is applied to the glass flask so that ounces of the metal—which has been beaten into thin leaves and rolled up like a cylinder—are covered with two ounces of strong water. If roughly a fourth part of gold is mixed with the silver, it will remain at the bottom as a single piece; if there is less gold, the filings and flakes will usually take on the appearance of a black powder. Once removed, these must be washed with lukewarm water and later heated in a crucible. The gold then reveals itself to the eye as it truly is; once removed, it may be rubbed against a testing touchstone or melted. But it is not our intent to pursue these technical matters further, since we have shown where they can be sought.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of metallurgical assaying and moves into a defense of the chemical principles of metal composition against academic critics. The previous page detailed the process of quartation using "strong water" (nitric acid).</meta>

### HELIANA

The third common method used by goldsmiths is to use **Antimony** <term>antimonium; often referring here to stibnite, used to purify gold by reacting with other metals</term> to create a **Regulus** <term>regulus; the metallic "button" or pure mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible</term> from metals mixed with gold. From this, they draw out pure gold; if it is placed in a crucible and purified by a flame drawn over it from burning coals with the help of bellows, it remains until all the **stibium** <note>original: *stybium*; an early name for antimony</note> or Antimony has evaporated. The residue of the regulus is then reduced, as is the custom, using dried wine dregs <note>tartar</note> and saltpeter.

The final method for testing gold and separating whatever has not been "fixed" is the **Royal Cement** <term>cementum regale; a dry refining process where gold is heated with salts but not melted</term>. This uses bricks ground very finely (twice the amount of the other ingredients), crushed salt, and calcined vitriol <note>sulfates heated to a powder</note>. These are layered one upon the other <note>original: *stratum superstratum*</note> over very thin plates or foil of gold placed in a small pot or crucible within the furnace, which is then well-sealed with clay. Finally, a charcoal fire is stoked so that the crucible remains constantly red-hot after the furnace has warmed up. However, care must be taken that the plates do not melt from excessive heat. This process is usually continued for several hours—three or four—by which the gold is refined.

These trials and criteria for recognizing gold and silver (which alone remain in the fire) must be thoroughly learned for this reason: without them, every method of judging or debating metals—let alone working with them—is blind. Therefore, those scoffing men <note>original: *nasutili*; literally "large-nosed" or "sharp-nosed" critics</note> who take up the censor’s rod against the Chemists should be sent away to the miners and goldsmiths. Let them learn there what the nature and power of metals are in the fire, and what the method of examination is, lest they appear "insane with reason" by trying to argue against lived experience. But with these things established, let us proceed to our main purpose.

There are those who deny that the transmutation of metals is possible, or—if they argue from the principles that compose metals—they deny that Chemists correctly identify **Mercury** <term>hydrargyrum; liquid silver or quicksilver</term> and **Sulfur** as their component principles. Thus Balthasar Hagelius, a Jesuit and Professor of Philosophy at the University of Ingolstadt, wrote in a disputation on metals and stones (published for the graduation of the Austrian respondent Andreas de Luchis in the year 1588, thesis 7). He writes under the title "On Matter" (for I wish to draw the foundations of this inquiry from that very Sect <note>the Jesuits</note> which now claims the inner chambers of philosophy for itself alone; once these foundations are refuted, the others, both ancient and modern, whose footsteps Hagelius follows, will collapse of their own accord). Thus, he says in the aforementioned thesis: *“The Alchemists, a new and most superstitious breed of men, most stubbornly contend that the principles of all metals are sulfur and mercury, or quicksilver.”* Explaining the same in thesis 12, he adds: *“The matter has returned to the chemists. Because they think they can manufacture metals from sulfur and mercury themselves, they contend, not without much puffing of breath, that nature also forges them from the same.”*

<header>INQUIRY</header>

This Jesuit considers this a most novel and superstitious class of men, even going against the professors of his own order, such as Delrio <note>Martin Delrio (1551–1608), a Jesuit theologian famous for his work on magic and the supernatural</note> and others. But how does he try to prove his undertaking? *Because metals are not made from sulfur and quicksilver,* <term>argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</term> *he says, it must be proven thus: If things are as the chemists want them, why are sulfur and quicksilver not found in all or most metallic veins, or metals in their own pits?* This is the Jesuit’s first argument, drawn from the origin of metals, or rather from their location. He then argues from the properties of the components. *And why,* he asks, *do they not possess the properties of sulfur and quicksilver? For what is more fit for catching a flame than sulfur?* Yet metals are not **flammable** <note>original Greek: $\phi\lambda o\gamma\iota\sigma\tau\dot{\alpha}$ (*phlogista*); substances that can be set on fire</note>. Likewise, *No quicksilver solidifies by cold, as experience and Aristotle in the "Meteorology," book 4, chapter 8, is the author. However, there is no metal that cold has not thickened: How then could it be made from mercury?* These are the Jesuit's principles by which he denies that metals consist of sulfur and quicksilver; we might perhaps meet these more rightly if, by applying a demonstration immediately to the eye—that is, by the deed itself—we were to overturn these vanishing little arguments, according to that saying of the Poet:

->There is no place for cleverness here; eyes will conquer when the matter is the judge:<-

Nevertheless, we shall respond briefly to the objections before we confirm the matter by the deed. As for his denial that sulfur and quicksilver are found in all or most metal mines where there are metallic veins, and conversely his denial that metals are in the pits of sulfur and quicksilver: who does not see that this happens because here there are only "metallic seeds," and indeed these are thrust out by nature and dispersed before the metals could be formed? But where there are veins of metal, quicksilver and sulfur do not appear as frequently because the constituent principles have already passed into the compounds—that is, they have hardened into metals. But if he wished to prove anything, he would have to prove that no quicksilver or sulfur is found *anywhere* in metallic veins. For this (even though he argues only with probability) is asserted not only by other physicists and philosophers (which the Jesuit has craftily avoided), but even certain noble chemists, deceived by less experienced miners, have felt this to be true. But we show that this is otherwise by eye-witnesses, worthy of trust and skilled in ores, and—what is relevant to the matter—those who are strangers to Alchemy. Thus says Mathesius. <header>INVESTIGATION</header>

...to demonstrate by fact that metals consist of <term>quicksilver<note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note></term>, into which they are resolved, and from which they are composed. There are two ways among the Alchemists: one which is called the "wet way," which is done through waters and solutions; the other which is called the "dry way," which is done through powders. Let us put forward a proof for both, showing how metals—both soft and hard—can be converted and resolved into running quicksilver in the space of even an hour.

Let an example of the first way be in lead, which may be filed or made into scrapings worn down by a tool; or it may be melted and pulverized into tiny pieces between two wooden plates, like the "lead sand" often used in hourglasses. For the <term>analysis<note>resolution into component parts</note></term> of this lead into its principles, such a "water" should be prepared:

Take two ounces of purified <term>aqua fortis<note>literally "strong water," the alchemical term for nitric acid</note></term>; dissolve in it one ounce of common quicksilver in a glass flask, well-stoppered, placed over a light coal fire until it has turned into clear water. Afterward, remove it from the heat of the fire, and with the mouth of the flask open, gradually throw in one ounce of lead filings or powder. For the water effervesces of its own accord and becomes turbulent if you throw it all in at once or too much at a time. Then, stop up the opening of the glass again, and allow the water to dissolve for a little while. 

Soon you will see the common quicksilver, which had previously been dissolved in the water, sink down like a lime or a white powder. The lead filings, however, before your very eyes, if they are shaken, will be seen to gradually resolve into running quicksilver—so much so that two and sometimes three parts of an ounce will become quicksilver from the lead; about a fourth part (if all things have been performed rightly) remains as the dross and dregs of the lead's sulfur. 

When these things are finished, pour the *aqua fortis* into another glass vessel. Take out the remaining quicksilver made from the lead, and pass it through leather or a linen cloth squeezed and constricted with a cord (as is the custom), and you will see how much <term>living Mercury<note>original: "Mercurii vivi"</note></term> you have drawn out of the lead, and how much earthy and sulfurous dross remains. Also, collect the white <term>calx<note>a powder produced by roasting or dissolving a metal</note></term> that settled from the first dissolution of quicksilver into the water; this can either be further <term>precipitated<note>chemically separated into a solid</note></term> into a red powder by *aqua fortis*, or "revivified" back into its original weight of quicksilver through sublimation and boiling, with a piece of steel placed in common water, as is known to those skilled in chemical matters.

Thus, it will appear evidently to the eye how lead returns into the quicksilver from which it was created at the beginning. The weight of the remaining dross also testifies to how much of the lead has turned into <term>hydrargyrum<note>Greek-derived term for mercury or quicksilver</note></term>. This mercury differs in no way from the common sort, except that it is a little more leaden and sluggish, just as the peculiar nature of each metal requires; just as, conversely, that which is made from iron is the most lively and agile of all. Nor do I dispute here why one Mercury...

For it flies off immediately, and far more quickly than any other of the hard or soft metals. It also mixes itself into the mass of sal ammoniac and mercury sublimate; if this happens, the mass must be washed in a mortar with hot water until the pure Mercury of Mars is separated. <meta>This page continues the author's polemic against critics of the mercury-sulfur theory of metals. Having previously described the synthesis of lead, the author now addresses the specific objection that metals cannot contain sulfur because they do not burn like sulfur does.</meta>

-> I N V E S T I G A T I O N <-

To satisfy our requirements, it will not be troublesome to briefly discuss these dreams. Metals, he says, do not possess the properties of sulfur and **mercury** <note>original: "argenti vivi"; literally "living silver"</note>. Why, I pray? Because, he says, nothing is more fit to catch flame than sulfur, yet metals are not **flammable** <note>original: "Φλογιστά" (phlogista); a Greek term used here to mean combustible or able to support fire</note>. Ridiculous. For sulfur in metals reaches a certain state of **fixation** <note>original: "fixationem"; the process by which a volatile substance is made stable in fire</note>, such that in imperfect metals, the sulfur may indeed evaporate along with the rawness of the **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii"</note>, even if it is not flammable; in perfect metals, however, it has thoroughly fixed the **mercury** <note>original: "hydrargyron"</note>, so that it neither evaporates nor is consumed by fire. So that this may be better understood, it must be known that **flammability** <note>original: "τὸ Φλογιστὸν"</note> is indeed a property of all sulfur—indeed, of only the sulfur implanted in all things—but it is not *always* its property. Truly, it can be fixed; and that which is imperfectly fixed and mixed with matter does not catch fire, yet it evaporates in the heat. That which is perfectly fixed remains. And from this arises the perfection or imperfection of metals that either evaporate or remain in the fire.

A remarkable proof of this matter is provided by **Antimony**, which is not yet fixed to the point of being extended by a hammer <note>i.e., it is not yet a malleable metal</note>, but is only brittle and easy to melt, as we have said. For in it, the sulfur—which has congealed the **mercury** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> into an earthy mass (setting aside the artifice of the **reverberatory furnace** <note>original: "reverberationis"</note>, as long as it remains a compound)—does not catch fire, but evaporates entirely in the fire along with the Mercury; namely, the two of them joined together by nature into a mass. But if the sulfur is drawn out from the Antimony by extraction, then it is like common sulfur, and just as **flammable** <note>original: "Φλογιστὸν"</note> as that is. I am not speaking of the redness which the chemists extract, but of the true, natural, greenish sulfur. You shall prove it by this evidence:

<term>Take</term> <note>original: "Rec." (Recipe)</note> of **Alum** and **Saltpeter** <term>equal parts</term> <note>original: "ana"</note> as much as suffices. Make a "strong water" <note>original: "aquam valentem"; a powerful acidic solvent</note>, or even take common **aqua fortis** <note>nitric acid</note>, as is the custom, into which you should put half its weight of roasted salt. Afterward, grind the **Antimony** very finely, and put enough of the ground Antimony into a small amount of this water so that the water floats four fingers' breadth above it. Add it gradually, however, lest the water bubble up too violently. When the water has taken on a green color in the vial—the most subtle sulfur having been extracted—pour it out immediately. When it is immersed in common lukewarm water, the sulfur will settle at the bottom, just like common green sulfur; you will prove by the act itself that it is **flammable** <note>original: "Φλογιστὸν"</note>, and differs in no way from the common sort in this regard.

Let us therefore gather our argument and overturn the **Jesuitical property** <note>original: "Iesuiticam proprietatem"; likely a jab at his opponent's deceptive or overly subtle logic</note> of sulfur. For if sulfur in Antimony is not flammable (which is not yet a malleable metal, and yet once separated, it burns), how much less is it necessary for the property of flammability to be preserved in the other metals, whether perfect or imperfect, in which the **fixation**—

"Certain men," he says, "highly skilled in metallic affairs, about which they have also written subtly and accurately, assert that the first and highest foundation upon which the art of **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchymiæ"</note> rests and is supported, is nothing: from which it can be understood that the art itself (if indeed it should be called an art, which contains nothing of truth or certainty in itself) is empty and false. For, as has been said, such is not the matter of true and natural gold, etc."

A second opinion is undertaken by Hagelius against the **Chemists** <note>referring to alchemists</note> concerning the defense of the distinction between metals; by this opinion, he wishes them to be distinguished by their species and essential difference, and from this, he concludes that metals cannot be transmuted into other metals. Therefore, as far as the distinction of metals is concerned, since they all grew together equally from **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: *hydrargyro*</note>, as has been demonstrated—and we have discovered by the very fact that they differ only according to whether the quicksilver is more or less pure, and whether the sulfur is fixed <note>stable in heat</note> or combustible—according to their various mixing via the salt or metallic earth occurring with the sulfur, we cannot indeed reject the opinion of those who deny that metals differ by a special essential difference. Rather, they differ only by reason of various **accidents** <note>original: *accidentium*; non-essential qualities like color or density that do not change the core identity</note> arising in the ores, which create the different metals.

But nevertheless, let us suppose for the sake of argument that they differ by a specific **form** <note>original: *forma*; the internal "blueprint" or essence of a thing</note>; can art not induce another form once one is destroyed? Surely it can, if the matter seeking the form is laid underneath, and by the impulse of a natural efficient cause and the proper aids, it breaks forth into reality. For we do not say that species are changed into species—such as **silver-ness** into **gold-ness**—but rather the individuals of those species, which are subject to destruction and generation and are changeable.

Let us see, then, how the **Jesuit** <note>referring to Benedict Pererius (1535–1610)</note> defends his opinion. He says, "It is the common opinion of many that only gold among metals has a perfect species, and all others are only certain rudiments and beginnings of gold; therefore, there is no other distinction among metals than between the perfect and the imperfect within the same species." Truly, we can argue against this opinion in this way. "Iron is not an imperfect mixture, such as Snow and other things which occur in the upper atmosphere <note>original Greek: *en tō meteōrō*</note>. For who would believe it? Therefore, it is a perfect mixture." What an excellent reason indeed—if this is what counts as reasoning, especially in philosophy and natural science! He says, "Who would believe it?" [...who] clearly demands this, and concludes that the mixture is perfect, because he and his followers do not believe it to be imperfect? Likewise, regarding what he adds—that the same may be said of gold, silver, and the rest—it carries just as much weight as his previous reasoning had. The remaining arguments, such as those of a certain other person who argues from the supposition of logical terms that metals differ in species, do not hold unless they are assigned to their own proper natural principles. For even if "lead" as a species is predicated of this individual piece of lead, and "metal" as a genus is predicated of this species; nevertheless, these things are said not because of the reality itself, but for the sake of distinction, according to the usage of speakers, not the nature of the thing.

From this, he concludes that there is not one single substance of metals.

We respond that it has been made sufficiently clear from the substance of **quicksilver** <note>original: *hydrargyri*; mercury</note>, through the experiments cited above, that all metals consist of it; and depending on the difference of fixed or non-fixed **sulfur**, and their different tempering, they are either imperfect and combustible by fire, or perfect and fixed. Therefore, since these things are evident to the eye, there is no need to contend over these far-fetched little reasons in a debater-like and fallacious manner. 

Furthermore, if you look at the common people, these propositions are like paradoxes: *lead is gold*. But if you look at nature from within, they will not be so absurd. Hence, by the **chemists** <note>alchemists</note>, lead is called **leprous gold**. Likewise, "the inner parts of silver are gold"—and similar propositions, when rightly understood, arise from the nature of things, not from the speech and opinion of the common crowd. From this, the purging of qualities is also easy, as is the introduction of the gold-making form by the **ministry of art** <note>alchemical practice</note> through a fixed metallic principle, which removes the imperfect and perfects the matter. 

"But no one has been found so far," he says, "of whom it is clearly established that he has made gold proven in every respect." # INQUIRY

For as to the claim that no one has yet been found (as the **Jesuit** <note>Referring back to the Jesuit scholar mentioned on page 355, likely Benedict Pererius</note> says) who is clearly established to have produced gold proven in every respect, there is no reason for us to refute this, especially since **Johannes Andreae** <note>A famous 14th-century canon lawyer</note> writes concerning **Arnold of Villanova** in his additions to the *Speculum*, under the title <italic>regarding the crime of forgery</italic> <note>original: "de crimine falsi"</note>. In our own days, we had Arnold of Villanova in the Roman court, a supreme Physician and Theologian—about whom I wrote a counsel regarding the observation of fasts—who was also a **Great Alchemist**. He allowed the small rods of gold which he made to be submitted to every test. Here is an example! But on this matter, Arnold’s own books exist, which testify that gold was made from lead. I could bring forward the testimonies of the most famous men, worthy of all credit, who saw these things with their own eyes and touched them with their hands; and not so long ago, with one part of a **tincture** <term>tincture: in alchemy, a potent substance or "medicine" capable of transforming base metals into gold; often synonymous with the Philosopher's Stone</term>, three thousand five hundred and eighty-four weights of lead were turned into gold, a portion of which is even now preserved at Basel. But we do not wish to deal in artificial arguments; instead, we refer the readers to the history of metallic transmutation by the noble **Ewald von Hohenlande**, for a defense of chemistry regarding these experiments. However, at this point, the Physicians push themselves forward, and they boldly assert that even the more learned among them have not granted their assent to chemistry. But what **Fernel** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a highly influential French physician</note> determines in *On the Hidden Causes of Things* concerning the **Elixir of the Arabs** and this whole matter (Book 2, Chapter 18), and what **Marsilio Ficino** <note>The famous Florentine philosopher who led the Platonic Academy</note> (two men superior to any Hercules) says in Book 2 of *On Caring for the Life of the Healthy* (Chapter 3), are before the eyes of everyone and on the lips of the learned. It would be too rash to refute them. To these, I add the **Count of Mirandola** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, a renowned Renaissance polymath</note>, to say nothing of many others.

But we shall prove that the transmutation of metals is possible and natural by the experiment of nature and art; and we shall first respond to that point which some deny—that more perfect species of things can be made except in one way, that is, by a natural agent—because the generations of such things are determined both according to an active principle and matter, as well as according to the place in which they are made. This can be admitted so far (as **Peter Bonus of Ferrara** <note>Author of the *Precious New Pearl*, an influential 14th-century alchemical text</note> rightly notes) insofar as the same principles nearest to nature must be applied by art as are within nature itself. For if other or similar principles were applied, the result would not be the same as natural gold, but something different or merely similar. We are not speaking of the sophisticated works of **whitening** or **reddening** in color <note>referring to "sophistical" alchemy, which only changed the surface color of a metal to look like silver or gold without changing its essence</note>, but of that which is within the very nature and essence of metals in their universal definition—if indeed metals differ by species—and which sustains all the criteria and all the properties of gold, silver, copper, etc.; hence **Paracelsus**...

<meta>This page continues the author’s practical demonstration of metallic transmutation, moving from the theoretical arguments of the previous page to specific chemical "experiments" intended to prove that iron can be transformed into copper, thereby refuting Aristotelian natural philosophy.</meta>

# H E L I A N A.
### (A TREATISE ON HELIUS)

Copper is generated, by the benefit of nature and the ministry of art, through common **sulfur**. Take one ounce of **oil of sulfur** <note>original: "olei sulphuris per campanam facti"; this refers to sulfuric acid produced by burning sulfur under a glass bell jar</note> made by the bell method, as is the custom, though it need not be rectified, and mix into it two ounces of spring water. Soon, heat very thin plates of steel or iron until they are glowing, and quench them many times in a vessel full of cold water until they are so hardened that they can be easily broken apart with pliers. Tear them into pieces the size of a fingernail and place them, dry, into the mixture of water and oil of sulfur in a vial. Stop up the vial and place it in a vessel filled with ashes <note>A "sand bath" or "ash bath" used to provide even, gentle heat</note>, under which you shall kindle a charcoal fire just enough so that it boils very gently for six hours. Soon, allow it to cool of its own accord, and you will find generated at the top of the cooled vessel a shining, green, and excellent **vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolum"; here meaning ferrous sulfate, or "green vitriol"</note>. Let this be dissolved in common water and boiled until a thin skin forms on the surface; then, place into the water bright and fresh plates of steel, and in a short moment, shimmering flakes of copper will adhere to them. Collect these and melt them, and you will have natural copper, ductile and fusible, possessing every property of copper. By this single experiment, all the arguments of the **Aristotelians** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who argued that the fundamental species of metals were fixed and could not be changed</note> are blown away—showing how iron can go backward into vitriol, and again from vitriol be reduced into copper, and thus truly be generated by the ministry of art and the benefit of nature, and not merely be a metal that has been changed in appearance.

I add another shorter experiment, though for a smaller quantity. Let iron filings be **calcined** <note>Reduced to a powder through heat</note> with an equal amount of crushed sulfur, and let it be "reverberated" <note>Heated in a furnace where the flames are reflected onto the material</note> by stirring it upon a tile until the sulfur is consumed. Throw the residue, while still red-hot, into boiling water, and insert pure plates of steel; copper will adhere to them in the form of a sludge, which, when wiped off and melted, will be natural copper. This, says **Paracelsus**, is a lesser thing than transmuting iron or copper into gold, which God has not yet willed to be commonly known to all; but whatever the case, it abundantly overthrows the quibbles of the **sophists** <note>A derogatory term for those who used clever but false arguments to deny the truths of alchemy</note>.

Let us proceed, however, to the transmutation of silver into natural gold, tested by every touchstone <note>original: "specillo"; a tool or stone used to test the purity of gold</note> according to all the properties of gold. Yet let us proceed in such a way that we show only the possibility of art and nature, not the utility <note>The author emphasizes that he is sharing this for scientific/philosophical proof, not for greed or profit</note>. For those who attack these things are unworthy of achieving anything further, since, as the legal experts say, no one should be compelled to act for their own benefit. When **Paracelsus** was dealing with this matter against the Aristotelians in his *Book of Minerals*, chapter 7, on sulfur, he says shortly after the beginning: "It must be known that (unless God prevents it) there is a wondrous power in sulfur, so excellent that the natural light of man is struck thin with wonder; or if God does not..."

prevents it; the error lies with the craftsmen who handle the sulfur, which can easily happen. But be that as it may, such power and faculty exist in sulfur that no skilled person can exhaust it; such a virtue, too, that it is a wonder to anyone. For it confounds (he says) *Aristotle*, who says that species cannot be transmuted. Sulfur transmutes them. If the foolish *Aristotle* were still alive, it would turn him from a fool into a madman, more than he was ever conquered by any woman <note>A reference to the popular medieval legend of "Aristotle and Phyllis," where the philosopher was so infatuated with a woman that he allowed her to ride him like a horse, proving that even the greatest intellect can be humbled by nature or passion.</note>. Thus says *Paracelsus*. But he does not show by what method this transmutation ought to be done, except that when treating mineral sulfur, he teaches how to make a hepatic <note>original: "epaticam"; meaning liver-colored or liver-like, likely referring to "liver of sulfur" (potassium polysulfide).</note> compound from it with linseed oil, which, when properly distilled and rectified (the method of which he teaches in the second book of the *Archidoxes*), any silver should be placed into its red oil and let it be left until the appointed term of time; so it will happen that it turns black and pours out a "calx" of gold <note>original: "calcem auri"; a powder or residue resulting from heating a metal.</note>, namely in *aqua forti* <note>nitric acid</note>, but it is not yet fixed gold, but volatile, he says: but if it reaches its perfect limit, he says, it accomplishes everything that is to be accomplished, about which it is not useful to discuss further. Thus *Paracelsus*. More regarding fixed sulfur can be found in the little book on the *Mortification of Things* and its *Metamorphosis*.

But we, setting aside the Theophrastean <note>Referring to Theophrastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus.</note> process, wish to show how even crude common sulfur transmutes and produces true, natural gold. Take, therefore, one part of lead, which should be melted in a crucible over burning coals; afterward, remove the crucible with fire-tongs <term>pyrolabe: from the Greek for "fire-taker," a tool for handling hot crucibles</term>, and before the lead congeals, cast in the same amount of crude and living *Mercury* <note>quicksilver</note> and stir gently with a small stick. Then have one part of common sulfur, which should flow in another crucible; into this melt, cast bit by bit the previously coagulated **malagma** <term>malagma: a soft, dough-like mass; in this context, a lead-mercury amalgam</term>, and stir it with a spatula, and beware lest the sulfur catch fire or be scorched before you have cast everything in. Then, once cooled of its own accord, grind it upon a marble or stone and, placed again in a crucible, let it be melted until the sulfur is consumed and the added material flows for so long that it can be poured into a metallic rod, similar to melted *Antimony* and brittle.

Of this ground material, take one part and one part of laminated silver and make layer upon layer in a crucible, and on top, let finely crushed **Venetian glass** be placed, to the thickness of a finger; nor should the vessel be overfilled, lest the glass flow out. Thus, for the space of an hour, let everything be continually melted with an intense fire, so that the glass and the rest are in a continuous flux. Afterward, allow it to cool, and having broken the crucible, take out the **regulus** <term>regulus: the metallic button or "little king" found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</term> at the bottom, and prepare a **cupel** <term>cineritium: a vessel made of bone-ash used in cupellation to separate precious metals from base metals like lead</term>, upon which lead is placed in the usual manner until it flows intensely; then cast in the regulus, and refine it <note>original: "fulmina"; literally "to strike with lightning," referring to the "brightening" or flash of the metal when it reaches purity during cupellation.</note> in the manner of goldsmiths, until...

<header>HELIANA</header>

<sig>Z 5</sig>

Let clean silver <note>original: "argentum mundum"</note> be subjected to the process. Whether in the form of thin plates or small grains, as soon as it is cast into *aqua fortis* <note>Nitric acid, a powerful solvent used by early chemists to separate gold from silver.</note> and dissolved, it will yield bright specks of gold. These will settle to the bottom like a black powder; once these are washed with lukewarm water, heated in a crucible, and melted, you will have flakes of true, natural gold—pure and unadulterated—possessing all the properties and passing all the tests of natural gold, whether for use in medicine or for any other purpose. And although we do not claim that the *entirety* of the silver is transmuted into gold, but only a very small and minute portion, nevertheless, because all parts of silver are uniform and similar in nature, it is sufficient that even a tiny flake of silver passes into true natural gold to demonstrate metallic transmutation to the eyes. Furthermore, lest anyone suspect that gold had perhaps been previously poured in or mixed with the silver, lead, or mercury, or had been hidden within the sulfur itself, let him first examine each substance separately, if he wishes, by the criteria of fire and *aqua fortis*. In this way, he may know with greater certainty that this gold arises from no other source than transformation through the experiment of the Art. But if anyone should somewhat "fix" the sulfur using lime, extract it with hot water, separate it with sprinkled vinegar, and finally soak it in a tartary quintessence of wine <term>quinta essentia: the "fifth essence" or most purified spirit of a substance, believed by alchemists to hold its medicinal or transformative power</term> distilled to a red and oily state, he will find his labor even more richly rewarded. We mention these things so that we may hand down the immediate natural principles of metals to be understood in detail, and to confirm and establish the legal experts in their accepted opinion—those who defend "chymia" <note>An early term for chemistry and alchemy combined.</note> against Angelus <note>Likely referring to a specific critic or legal authority of the time who argued against the legitimacy of alchemical gold.</note>. Indeed, we refer to this evidence those Princes and Republics who either doubt this business or hold an incorrect opinion of it.

Therefore, having fulfilled our promises (as can be proven by the act itself), it remains for us to respond briefly to the empty objections of both Hagelius <note>Christoph Hagel, a writer who commented on mining and metals.</note> and Pererius <note>Benito Pereira (1535–1610), a Jesuit philosopher who was often skeptical of alchemy and magic.</note>, as well as those who cry out in vain that we are attempting to usurp the power of God. We do nothing here against nature, nor against the essential principles of metals; therefore, we in no way oppose the order of creation. We will, however, preface this by saying that God is able to destroy or hinder any work, however natural it may be—no less than the sowing of plants or the generation of animals. Physicians often experience this in their own medicines: nature does not always operate, but is sometimes repressed by a higher cause. On the contrary, we attribute all power of growth to Him alone who said, "Let it be," without whose blessing all things are reduced to nothing. And I do not know whether we should also refer to this that which Hagelius touches upon regarding the forked rod <note>original: "virgula bifurcata"; a dowsing rod used to locate ore or water.</note> for seeking metals—namely, that it does not move for everyone. For that the practice is free from any vice is clear from its use...

we shall demonstrate. Let a one-year-old forked rod <term>virga bifurcata: a dowsing rod, often used by early modern miners to locate ore</term> be cut from a hazel or oak tree, whose branches are equal and without flaw. (Some people, however, believe that this rod must be cut before the sun rises while the moon is waxing, and ideally around the day of the Annunciation of Mary <note>March 25th; such astrological and religious timing was common in folk magic and early science</note>.) But we have deliberately observed none of these superstitions. This being done, let the two forks be taken into each upturned hand, with the fingers squeezed toward the sky, so that the ends of the fork-tips protrude outside the hand next to each squeezed thumb. The main stem of the fork should point outward from between the two hands. Now, if someone wears silver buttons <note>original: "argenteos globulos"</note> fastened to their tunic, even if they squeeze the rod with all their might in both hands, the rod will nevertheless make a circle by itself and turn that cut stem-part inward toward the chest, right up to the buttons. If, however, you strip off all metal and place silver or gold on the ground, then even if you who hold the rod resist and are unwilling, the cut part of the stem will turn outward until it strikes the metal with a most powerful indication and movement. What the reason for this thing might be remains hidden from the physicists; so wonderful is the sympathy of nature. Nevertheless, I have experienced it to be true myself, and I have seen it time and again in others. If it does not move in everyone's hand (as Hagelius <note>likely Christoph Hagel, a contemporary critic or author</note> says), surely who does not see that this too is reserved within the power of God?

But let us now bring our investigation to its center point. For the arguments that Hagelius brings forward elsewhere are of no weight or value. First, he concedes that metals are produced by the same causes and have the same operations, differing only by "more or less" <note>meaning they differ in degree, not in kind</note>. But if properties follow nature, these facts prove all the more that metals do not differ in their proper and constitutive essence; so far is he from supporting his own case, since he wants them to differ in species by an essential difference. For regarding what he excludes about stones, their immediate essence is not the same. For they do not take their immediate origin from "living mercury" <term>Mercurius vivus: quicksilver or elemental mercury</term>. Furthermore, what he brings up concerning the elements suggests a more imperfect mixture, **as in atmospheric phenomena** <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἐν τῷ μετεώρῳ"</note>. 

Regarding what he adds: *Nature neither wants nor is able to transmute other metals into gold. It does not want to because it has never done so; and because it produces each and every thing for other necessary uses, which would be entirely lost by a substantial change.* I respond that I acknowledge not "nature," but God, the moderator of nature, has provided for human needs through the diversity of metals. Consequently, not every metal is intended to end as gold, but arises from the diversity of fixed and volatile sulfur combined with pure or impure Mercury, and through a good mixture produces different things.
