HELIANA.

Metals are drawn away, insofar as they depart from a balanced state, some through a combustible hardness of impurity, others through an evaporable softness. But if these accidents <term>accidentia: in Aristotelian philosophy, non-essential qualities of a thing that can change without changing the thing's essence</term> are separated, they serve transmutation no less than they do medicinal uses. Nor is it necessary that metals be entirely lost through change. For no one can use gold for certain purposes where iron is required. Therefore, one should not fear their destruction through art. What of the fact that Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), a foundational figure in Swiss alchemy and medicine</note> admits it is a task of equal labor if one wished to change better metals into viler ones? Thus, there is no reason to fear their abolition. As for the claim that nature has never done this, it is so far from the truth that even a beetle <note>original: "scarabæum"</note>, caught by the vapors of gold, has been known to be transmuted, many such wonders being found in mines. Unless, of course, one were to say that the gold vapor, occupied by the destruction and burning away of the beetle, simply took on its external shape—a view I am happy to support. But who has descended into the depths of nature’s chasms, or who is so sharp-eyed <note>original: "Lynceus," referring to Lynceus of Messenia, an Argonaut famed for sight that could penetrate stone or see underground</note> as to say that nature has never done this? Certainly, Petrus Bonus <note>An Italian alchemist of the 14th century, author of the "Precious New Pearl"</note> proves the contrary: all lead contains a grain of silver by nature, and tin, with a little preparation, leaves a grain of silver behind; these are manifest signs of a natural inclination. Furthermore, his claim that nature cannot transmute metals through heat and cold is a vain pursuit, as has already been seen regarding iron naturally changed into copper.

These same arguments regarding the mutual transmutation of metals he odiously repeats when he denies the substantial transmutation of metals with these little questions in his eighty-eighth thesis: *Is it because generation is the work of nature alone? <note>original: "An quia generatio est opus solius naturæ?"</note> Is it because what nature is not accustomed to doing cannot be done by art? Is it because nothing in nature is done in vain?* Likewise, in his eighty-ninth thesis: *Furthermore (he says), metal is contained in metal neither in act nor in potency <term>virtute: "in virtue" or "potency," the inherent capacity to become something else</term>.* But how false and futile all these claims are is apparent through the mercury <term>hydrargyron: literally "water-silver," the Greek-derived term for quicksilver or mercury</term> elicited from metal, and through the construction of lead from Mercury, and other things revealed above. *But the corruption of these things,* he says, *results in something worse.* That much is true; but the Chemist does not merely corrupt; he also generates through means agreeable to nature, by the ministry of art. As for the claim that the gold produced by Alchemy is not established by cold—as the art of fire <term>pyrotechnia: here referring to the chemical and metallurgical use of fire</term> teaches—we say that cold is not properly the generator of things, but rather heat. Yet metals, when removed from the fire, consist [solidify] by cold, which applies no less to chemical gold, as fusion itself teaches, just as it applies to natural gold, which you will easily learn through experience. There remains one question, partly Physical and partly Theological: whether gold produced by art...

[made], whether it be true and natural, and whether it retains all the properties of natural gold both in medicine and in other matters; and if not, whether it be illicit and contrary to the order of creation.

The negative view is held by Pererius <note>Benedict Pererius (1535–1610), a Jesuit theologian who wrote extensively on the Book of Genesis and natural philosophy</note> in chapter 19 of the place cited above: *Gold,* he says, *which is made by Alchemists, although it may seem very similar to true gold, can nevertheless be recognized and judged to be false in many ways; namely, either by its weight, or because it does not withstand the force of fire, or because when cast into urine it loses its color; or because it cannot be drawn out into the thinnest plates; or finally because it does not have the natural properties of gold, among which that of comforting the human heart is especially commended.* <note>original: "Aurum, inquit, quod sit ab Alchymistis..."</note> Thus says Pererius. 

But he ought to have remembered the words of Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the Dominican polymath often cited as an authority on the transmutation of metals</note> produced by himself, that gold and silver are one thing when they are so called equivocally <term>equivocally: here meaning a thing that shares the name "gold" but not the actual substance, like a gilded imitation</term>—namely, the work of those who "whiten through white things and yellow through yellow things," <note>original: "per alba albificant, & per citrina citrinant"</note> who are undoubtedly deceivers—and another thing for those who proceed from the same materials from which nature proceeds. This is especially true since he himself acknowledges that Albert clearly declares which method <note>original: "nodus", literally "the knot" or "core difficulty"</note> of making true gold is possible, and which is impossible. 

But for our part, we may allow Pererius to "nod off" <note>A reference to the poet Horace’s remark that even the great Homer sometimes "nods" or makes a mistake</note> in this great work, especially since his judgment, drawn from philosophy, is much saner and fairer than that of Hagelius <note>Johannes Hagelius, a contemporary critic of Paracelsian alchemy</note>. Even though Hagelius undoubtedly looked to Pererius when he wrote in his 84th thesis: *Finally, there are those who deny that any gold has indeed been made by any art so far* (for this is the summary of Pererius’s decision) *but yet they do not deny that it could be made absolutely by artifice;* and yet the same Hagelius does not blush to determine and decide, against his allies Pererius and Delrio <note>Martin Delrio (1551–1608), a Jesuit famous for his work on magic and the supernatural</note>, that this can be done in no way at all. Such is the character of all those more studious of language than of nature. 

We respond, therefore, to Pererius’s "alchemical gold" that everything he says is true if he understands those things to be about sophisticated <term>sophisticated: in this historical context, it means "adulterated" or "counterfeit"</term> gold and silver; that is, regarding "whitenings" and "reddenings" only in color, while the sulfur and quicksilver <term>sulfur and quicksilver: in alchemical theory, these were the two "parents" or primary components of all metals</term> of the prior metal remain in their original state of essence. And such apparent and sophisticated gold is a great poison; it is a sin to sell such a thing for medicinal use because of its arsenical and narcotic qualities. Whatever it may be, it is eventually consumed and lost by fire—indeed, it returns as if to dross—after the proper criteria and examinations of fire, unlike the gold which was tested six or seven times by Albert. 

It appears from Pererius’s evidence, however, that he speaks "through a cloud" <note>original: "per nebulam," meaning unclearly or without direct knowledge</note> concerning the examinations of gold. ...extension <note>the ability to be beaten into thin sheets</note>, cupellation <note>original: *Cineritium*; a refining process where ores are heated in a "cupel" to separate noble metals from lead and other impurities</note>, exposure to sharp vapors, solution by *aqua regia* <term>aqua regia: "royal water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</term>, quenching, cementation <note>a process of purifying gold by heating it with granulated materials</note>, the mixing of burning substances, reduction after calcination <note>reducing a metallic powder back into solid metal after it has been oxidized by heat</note>, the easy or difficult reception of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, and so on. If, therefore, gold is produced that passes every test, and is not destroyed like a fake but persists, possessing all the properties of natural gold—all its operations and qualities (such as we claim ours to be)—it will not merely be similar to the natural, but identical with it, whatever Aegidius <note>likely Aegidius Romanus (Giles of Rome), a 13th-century philosopher</note> and Pererius <note>Benedict Pererius, the Jesuit critic mentioned on the previous page</note> may rave. 

For as to what is asserted regarding the serpents and little dragons made by the Magi and by Moses, the former was a work of diabolical illusion, while the latter was by divine power. We, however, presume neither of these, nor do we attempt such things, but follow only natural forces. 

Now, as to the objection regarding mice born from rot <note>referring to the theory of "spontaneous generation," where creatures were thought to arise from decaying matter</note> and how they differ in species from mice generated from seed—from which they infer that chemical gold differs from natural gold even if it has the properties of natural gold—this is entirely irrelevant. Indeed, the true art of chemistry does not proceed from any principles other than the natural principles of metals, nor does it employ anything else than what nature has generated and continues to generate, applying mixture and due preparation. Thus, while there may be a difference in the underlying matter of mice, there is certainly none in the making of metals. 

As for those who go so far as to refuse to accept alchemical gold even if it contains all the properties of natural gold, who does not see that such people should be dismissed and offered a prayer for a better mind? For whatever has the same essential principles, qualities, and operations of a thing, is the same as that thing, as Aristotle testifies when discussing forms. Thus, in the 4th book of his *Metaphysics* <note>this argument regarding function is more famously found in Aristotle's *On the Soul* or *Meteorology*, but the author cites the *Metaphysics*</note>, he argues from the works and accidents of things regarding their very forms: ***For that which performs the functions of an eye is an eye; but that which does not is not an eye.*** Therefore, ***a stone eye or a blind eye, because it does not perform the functions of an eye, is not called an eye, but an image of an eye; and a wooden saw is not called a saw, but an image of a saw.*** The entire light of Nature testifies to this same thing. 

But imitations, I admit, do not have such properties. Truly, gold produced by chemical operation from the true and essential principles that compose metals contains all the properties of gold, as is evident by experiment. Thus, if gold is used for medicine (for instance, in its raw state), even this chemical gold will prove effective—for example, to gladden and comfort the heart—and much more so, as the chemist Plato <note>referring to a pseudo-Platonic alchemical text, possibly the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> testifies in the 3rd book of *Stellicae* and Hamech in his commentary there, and similarly Haly in his *Secrets*. Likewise, the chemist Aristotle <note>referring to the *Secretum Secretorum*, a popular medieval text falsely attributed to Aristotle</note> in his book on the *Secret of Secrets* and on precious stones; although sophistical gold...

# INVESTIGATION

...which makes the chemical [process] the opposite of what was said above. Therefore, true gold must be distinguished from faked and merely altered alchemical gold.

Nor do I wish to include the methods of adulteration <term>sophistication: the act of faking or debasing metals to make them appear more valuable than they are</term>, such as those read in the works of Albertus Brunus <note>an Italian jurist who wrote on the legality of alchemy</note> in his treatise on *Increase and Decrease*, and in the *Correctorium* of Richard the Englishman <note>a 14th-century alchemical author</note>, and finally in the books *On Subtlety* by Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano, a famous 16th-century polymath</note> (if this can even be called subtlety), and commonly among others. These methods involve, in part, "whitening" <note>original: *albificationis*; making a base metal look like silver</note> and, in part, "reddening" <note>original: *rubificationis*; giving a metal the surface appearance of gold</note>—that is, processes that only present the color of counterfeit gold and silver, which we utterly condemn.

However, based on the principles and criteria of all the properties found in true chemical gold, one may conclude that we attempt nothing against the order of creation. Our gold is natural and true, produced by the benefit of nature alone through the service of art. Therefore, it is not secretly added by the devil's suggestion, as is claimed by Aegidius and Angelus—two legal experts who alone among their kind fruitlessly attack the chemical art—and after them, a certain great man in Germany, though he was great in status, he was unskilled in these matters and deceived by others. Indeed, we proceed here from the essential and natural principles of metals, not from diabolical works. Although God, the Greatest and Best, is able to restrain, hinder, or even utterly destroy the work of nature and art, we do not, in truth, invade the office of divine power; for we do not produce gold by command, will, and words (as occurs in divine miracles by divine decree), but only through the innate power of generating nature. We serve nature as ministers, bringing nothing to it from outside sources, nor from our own invention.

If these arguments are not enough to distinguish honest craftsmen from impostors, and to defend the truth of the art itself from the vanity of fraud or the deceptions of diabolical arts and the tongues of slanderers, let those who think otherwise teach us better things, and we will willingly obey more truthful views. Or let them at least respond to the *Apologies* of Claveus <note>Gaston DuClo, a defender of alchemy</note> and Libavius <note>Andreas Libavius, a famous chemist</note> written against the physician Thomas Erastus <note>a Swiss physician and fierce critic of Paracelsian alchemy</note>, or to the solutions of Bonus of Ferrara <note>Petrus Bonus, author of the *Precious New Pearl*</note>, the Aristotelian physicist. This has indeed been attempted by some, but clearly achieved by no one.

->*But if this is done in good faith, through the various and diverse airing of these matters,*<-
->*truth will emerge as if from a well, and the way of the Elias of the Art will finally*<-
->*come forth into the light; to which I have seen fit to devote*<-
->*this discussion until now.*<-
<note>Elias of the Art (Elias Artista) was a legendary figure in alchemy, prophesied by Paracelsus to appear at the end of time to reveal all the secrets of nature.</note>

<summary>On this page, the author argues that true alchemical gold is a product of nature assisted by art, rather than a diabolical trick or a surface-level counterfeit. He challenges critics of alchemy to respond to the leading defenders of the field before dismissing it as fraud.</summary>

<header>APHORISMS</header>

# THE BASILIAN APHORISMS OR CANONS
## Hermetic.

->*Concerning the Spirit, Soul, and Body of the Greater and Lesser Worlds.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'H' decorated with foliate patterns and a seated figure.</image-desc>Hermes "the Thrice-Greatest" <note>original: *τρισμέγιστος*; an ancient, legendary figure credited with the founding of alchemy</note> earned the title "Father of Philosophers" because of his investigation into the triple kingdom—Mineral, Vegetable, and Animal—and indeed for his inquiry into the three substances existing within a single created essence, in which he examined the entire power of Vegetable, Animal, and Mineral Nature.

2. A vegetative power resides in the nature of "volatile Mercury" <note>original: *Mercurii volantis*; in alchemy, Mercury represents the spirit or active, flowing principle</note>, which is white like solid snow, though not of the common variety. This is the Spirit of both the greater world <term>Macrocosm: the universe at large</term> and the lesser world <term>Microcosm: the human being</term>; upon this, the mobility and fluidity of human nature itself depends, according to the rational soul.

3. Furthermore, the animating force, serving as the "glue of the world," is the medium between Spirit and body and the bond of both. It is found in the Sulphur of a certain red and transparent oil, acting much like the Sun in the Greater World and the heart in the Microcosm.

4. Finally, mineral nature occupies the place of the body in the form of Salt. It possesses a wonderful power and scent when the salt has been separated from the dross <note>original: *scoria*; the rocky waste matter left after metal is smelted</note> of the earth. It differs from Mercury almost only in the thickness and consistency of its body.

5. These three substances in one created essence constitute the primordial matter <note>original: *limbum*; the "edge" or "border" of creation, often referring to the fundamental substance from which everything was made</note> of the lesser and greater worlds, from which the first man was formed when he was fashioned from the dust of the earth. To this is added the immortal rational soul of the Microcosm, inspired directly by God. Like a Queen, the soul is the moving and directing cause of these three substances and of all functions within man.

6. Moreover, just as the power of our bodies and our entire life remains whole if the Mercurial spirit (acting as the "radical moisture" <term>humidum radicale: the essential fluid believed to sustain life</term>) and the Sulphurous soul (acting as the "natural heat" <term>calidum naturale: the internal fire of a living being</term>), along with the consistency of Salt (which preserves from rot), work harmoniously together as one: so, conversely, the immortal soul must be separated from the body made of gathered dust if a defect arises in one or more of these three principles. If the defect is in the whole, it leads to death; if in a part, it leads to disease. This can be seen especially in the anatomy of the seven principal organs.

<summary>This page outlines the Hermetic theory that all things, including the human body and the universe, are composed of three essential principles: Mercury (Spirit), Sulphur (Soul), and Salt (Body). It explains that health and life depend on the balance of these three, while disease and death result from their separation or deficiency.</summary>

7. Nothing can heal this triple defect as effectively as that mass of the **limbus** <note>original: *limbi*; in Paracelsian philosophy, the "Limbus" is the primordial "clay" or chaotic matter from which the first human was formed</note>, from which the first man was fused, gathered into one from the three principles. This mass is capable of stirring and nourishing any power and force of nature, provided it has been properly turned into a fixed **astral body**.

8. From this, it is understood that the **Balsam** of the Hermetic subject <note>the substance being worked upon in the alchemical vessel</note> has a singular harmony with the human body. Thus, that Swiss "Monarch of Physicians," **Philippus ab Hohenheim** (also known as **Paracelsus**), in his book on the Physician’s Stone called the *Manual*, most rightly asserts that his Medicine can restore and preserve the health of the <term>Microcosm: the human being as a miniature reflection of the universe</term>—which was formed radically from the earthly *limbus* and the dust of the earth—as if by its own likeness; this is not merely an opinion, but a true and proper fact. The same can and should be justly said of this medicine of ours.

9. Indeed, this must be observed all the more because common medicine is too weak to radically protect and provide for those three principles of the microcosm and their harmony. For common medicine serves those three principles only as if by accident, since it is almost entirely occupied with the **four humors** <note>the traditional medical theory involving blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</note>.

10. Furthermore, **Mineral Chemical Medicine** prepared from metals and minerals is rarely prepared or administered correctly. For this reason, Paracelsus, in that same book, prefers his own medicine above all others. However, he does not deny that great **Arcana** <note>hidden secrets or powerful medicinal essences</note> also reside in other mineral things; but they require longer work and labor, and are not easily used correctly, especially by the unskilled, who do more harm than good when they encounter these things.

11. Let us therefore seek the **Limbus** of our <term>Microcosm</term> in which it is situated—that is, that viscous globe of earth, composed of <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Sulphur</term>, and <term>Salt</term>. Since it exists from a certain moisture, it can be beautifully called, according to **Geber** <note>original: *Gebrum*; referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century Persian alchemist</note>, the "moisture of moisture."

12. For just as the World, though created out of Nothing, owes its origin to the **Water** upon which the Spirit of the Lord brooded—with all things, both Heavenly and Earthly, proceeding from there—so this **Limbus** emerges from a Water that is not common, nor from heavenly dew, nor from Air condensed in the caverns of the Earth or in the Receiver itself, nor drawn from the abyss of the Sea, springs, wells, or rivers: But from...

12. From a certain <note>original: *perpessa*; literally "having suffered" or "endured," referring to matter that has undergone the "tortures" of chemical processing</note> substance, accessible to everyone but known to very few, which contains within itself everything necessary for the completion of the entire work, provided all external things are removed.

13. This Nature is a medium between the **Macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm: The "Greater World" or the universe at large</term> and the **Microcosm** <term>Microcosm: The "Lesser World" or the human being</term>. It is found everywhere and is available to the poor as well as the rich, as all the Philosophers claim. For it is cast out in the streets and trodden underfoot, even though it is the source of such miraculous operations. From this, those three principles of the body are to be restored.

14. This matter, dissolved into its own proper **Water** (for from Water all generation flows), is rotated through the four **Elements** <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note> until it passes into a fixed **Astral Nature** within the **Philosophical Egg** <note>original: *Ovo Phylosophico*; the sealed glass flask used in alchemy, so named because it nurtures the "chick" of the Stone</note>. It is called this because of the constant warmth, like a brooding hen sitting on her nest; otherwise, all hope of offspring would perish.

15. Thus the animal **Bird of Hermes** <note>original: *Avicula Hermetis*; a symbol for the volatile spirit or Mercury that must be "fixed" or stabilized</note>, once enclosed in its **Cage** (which is the **Furnace**), must be gradually stirred by the continuous heat of our vaporous fire until it hatches itself and heals all by its birth.

16. Just as we add nothing substantial to the matter in the preparation of the "enduring water" of the three Principles, and take nothing away from the three properties subsisting within it—but only remove the superfluous parts through preparation, that is, the heterogeneous elements, or the "dead earth" and tasteless water—so the **Hermetic Work** of the three prepared Principles is begun by joining them in a certain proportion. Specifically, the weight of the body should be about one and a half times that of the Spirit and Soul combined.

17. From then on, everything must be guided by continuous warmth <note>original: *fotu*; literally "fostering" or "incubation"</note>, so that the internal **Acting Nature** neither stops nor suffers from excess. Therefore, at the beginning, let there be a mild fire, the first degree being of about 4 threads <note>original: *filorum*; likely referring to the number of wicks in a lamp, a common way of measuring heat intensity in early chemistry</note>, until the matter turns black. Afterward, increase it to about 14 threads, until the matter washes itself and the appearing **Iris** <note>The "Peacock's Tail," a stage where many colors appear on the surface of the matter</note> fades into a gray color. From there, push it with about 24 threads until it reaches a perfect **Whiteness**, more brilliant than snow, flowing and fixed, which is the **Moon of the Microcosm**.

19. But if you desire to proceed to the perfect **Redness**, you shall continue the fire for 70 days, until the **Stone** turns...

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' with floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

IN the judging of any work, *Most Illustrious Prince, Most Clement Lord*, two kinds of people present themselves: one praising the work or the art; the other disparaging it. That the same thing happens in the judgment of the *Chemical* <term>Chemical: Referring here specifically to Alchemy, the "Hermetic Art" of transmuting metals and preparing medicines</term> art is clearer than daylight, as daily experience proves.

For one may find certain honorable men who embrace this art as pleasant and useful for many reasons, and acknowledge it as true; yet others are not lacking to whom it seems too absurd, useless, and uncertain. On account of its extreme uncertainty, it has been viewed with suspicion for so many centuries, especially because its final result—for the sake of which almost all labor in this field is undertaken—has been attained by almost no one famous, or certainly by only the very rarest of individuals.

Furthermore, they pursue with great hatred not only the art itself, but also those who set out to spread it through published books, and by this means seek to cultivate and propagate it.

For most people believe that these authors serve greed, and that they so entice the minds of wicked men with beautiful charms and the hope of great riches (with which they might satisfy their desires) that, uncontrolled and blinded, they cast themselves into total ruin. Thus they suffer the loss not only of their fortunes, but even of their reputation, health, and indeed their very souls.

# VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE PHILOSOPHERS
## ON ARRIVING
## at the Blessed Stone.

### The Opinion or Process of Albertus Magnus the Philosopher.

->From Book 3, *On Mineral Matters*, chapter 10.<- <note>original: *Lib 3. de rebus mineralibus*; a major work by Albertus Magnus on the nature of metals and minerals.</note>

<margin>
A careful description of the Vessel.
</margin>
<margin>
The method of the fire.
</margin>
Alchemists wishing to make the Elixir first take a wide lower vessel that can receive all the material—whether of purified sulfur or quicksilver, <note>Mercury.</note> or other things used in the Elixir. Then they provide that above this there should be a vessel having a long, narrow neck, and over the opening of that neck, let there be a lid made of clay in which there is a very small and narrow hole. Then they "inhume"—that is, they submerge—the bottom of the lower vessel in ashes, or dung; perhaps horse dung is better, which they call a horse-furnace <term>equi clibanum</term>; <note>A common alchemical heating method where the heat of fermenting manure provided a constant, gentle temperature.</note> and then they apply a very slow fire.

<margin>
The compression of the vapors.
</margin>
<margin>
The color of the fixed stone.
</margin>
<margin>
The Tincture.
</margin>
The description of the first vessel is like the shape of a urinal. <note>A standard glass flask with a rounded body and wide neck used in medical and chemical examinations.</note> And the second vessel stands over it and receives all the vapor that is released from it. The joint where the glasses or vessels meet is smeared very well with clay <note>This sealing process is known as "luting."</note> so that nothing can evaporate through that place. It then directs the received vapor upward into its long neck, which is gradually narrowed, and in this neck the vapor begins to be compressed <note>original: *præfocari*; literally "suffocated" or "choked," referring to the vapor being forced into a tight space.</note> and swirled about. That part of the vapor which is burnt off flies out as soot through the narrow hole in the lid of the neck. When it is thus compressed, it returns to a lemon-yellow substance, coiled within itself; once this is collected, it tints <term>tingit</term> any metal into the color of gold—and perhaps even more beautiful, if it be a noble elixir in which the Artist has made no error.

->Also from Book 3, chapter 6.<-

<margin>
The preparation and purification of Sulfur.
</margin>
The art of Alchemy has seen that a yellow Elixir can be made in no way other than through Sulfur. In Sulfur, however, it observed a strongly burning oiliness, such that it burns all metals and turns them black by burning when it is poured over them in a melted state. It commands, therefore, that the Sulfur be washed with sharp solutions and boiled for so long until no yellow water comes out from the boiling itself; and these washings must be sublimated until all the combustible oiliness leaves it. This is because only then does a subtle oily substance remain, which withstands the fire and is not consumed by it.

## II. THE PROCESS OF RAYMOND LULLY,
### *which he described here and there in his books: especially in the "Latest Testament," and in "The Light of Mercuries."* <note>Raymond Lully (Ramon Llull, c. 1232–1316) was a philosopher and mystic; many alchemical works were later attributed to him.</note>

<margin>Distillation of burning water from wine.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'I' featuring a robed figure holding a book and a staff, set within a decorative square frame.</image-desc>In the name of the Holy Trinity, take white or red wine, clear and fragrant (just as we taught in our book on the *Fifth Essence* <term>quinta essentia</term> <note>The "fifth element" or purest part of a substance, beyond earth, air, fire, and water.</note>) which we call the Liquor of Lunaria, <note>Moon-plant liquor; a symbolic name for the base of the work.</note> and which we call "blacker than black." Place it in putrefaction in a Water Bath <note>A *Balneum Mariae* or Marie’s Bath, a vessel placed in hot water to provide gentle, even heat.</note> for twenty days, to the end that through putrefaction the parts may be broken apart and can be better separated. Afterward, by distillation in the Bath, extract the burning water <term>aquam ardentem</term> <note>Strongly distilled alcohol or ethanol, so called because it is flammable.</note> with a very slow fire, which you shall rectify <note>Purify by repeated distillation.</note> until it is entirely without phlegm. <note>The watery, inactive residue left after distillation.</note> You will know this is achieved when, because of its heat, it burns a piece of linen cloth so thoroughly that no water remains.

<margin>How many times the water must be rectified.</margin>
And many think that the work requires rectification up to the seventh time: but I tell you (if you act with the proper slow fire) that three or four times suffices, lest by too much rectification something of the Fifth Essence evaporates.

<margin>Vegetable Quick-silver.</margin>
This burning water, after its reduction into the Fifth Essence—which happens through putrefaction and circulation—is called Vegetable Quick-silver, or Vegetable Mercury. And when you have such a sign, divide it into two parts, and keep one part for creating the menstruum: <note>A solvent used to dissolve solid materials.</note> and with the other part, draw out the "soul" from the "earth," in the manner I shall tell you.

<margin>Its names.</margin>
Properly called: Vegetable Sulfur, Sal Ammoniac <note>original: *Sal armoniacum*; in alchemy, this often refers to a volatile salt that "animates" a substance</note>, our Sulfur, Sulfur of Nature, Testamentary Mercury <note>original: *Mercurium Testamentarium*; a reference to Lully’s famous work, the *Testamentum*</note>, Salt of Tartar, or Salt of Niter: and many other names are also bestowed upon it.

<margin>N.B. Degrees of fire.</margin>
The fire of the Water-bath <note>original: *Ignis Balnei*; a gentle heat using a vessel of water</note> is called the fire of the first degree: the fire of the Ash-bath <note>original: *ignis cinerum*; a sand or ash-filled tray for higher heat</note> is called the fire of the second degree: and the burning fire <note>direct flame</note> is called the fire of the third degree.

<margin>A shortening of this work.</margin>
Furthermore, the aforementioned Sulfur can be wonderfully shortened <note>accelerated</note> in this manner: Take our liquid pitch, and place it in a cucurbit <note>a gourd-shaped distillation flask</note> over a fire of the third degree, and extract the Oil until only dry and burnt earth remains. Calcine this <note>burn it to ash</note> as I have taught you, and purify the earth: in this way, separate the salt from it. Upon this salt, give a fourth part of the Spirit which is in the second part of the water <note>highly rectified alcohol</note>, and digest it as described above, afterwards extracting the moisture. Repeating this, give another fourth part, digest, and dry it as before, until the earth is "pregnant" <note>fully saturated</note>: the sign will be that nothing more will distill over. Sublimate as before, and you will have Vegetable Sulfur, clean and pure, and of the same virtue as the first. The same can also be done with the dregs of wine or tartar in the manner already described.

<margin>Sharpening the Water of Life with volatile Salt of Tartar.</margin>
After this, take that part of the water which we commanded you to keep aside (namely, the second part of the rectified water) to serve as the sharpness <note>the acidity or potency</note> of the vegetable menstruum <term>Menstruum|A solvent used to dissolve solids; in alchemy, it is the liquid that "opens" the metal or plant</term> (which is nothing other than the most highly rectified Water of Life <note>alcohol</note>). You shall sharpen it in this way, reducing it over the menstruum. Take one ounce of the Vegetable Sulfur you have made and place it in a glass vessel: pour over it three ounces of the water revealed to you above (I suspect the text should read "reserved for you") and, with the vessel well-sealed with its cover, place it in the Water-bath for one natural day <note>24 hours</note>. Afterwards, distill it in the Ash-bath until everything that can ascend has ascended. Then, determine the weight of the Salt remaining in the bottom of the vessel: add to the bottom three parts of its weight of the "Burning Water" <note>high-proof alcohol</note> mentioned above, and place it in our Water-bath for one natural day. Afterwards, distill it in the Ash-bath, and repeat these steps. Then the whole Vegetable Salt is carried through the alembic <note>the still-head</note> with its own water, and a mixture is made. This single, clear water we call the **SIMPLE Menstruum**, and the Vegetable Menstruum, which has the power to dissolve all metals while preserving their form. It is also called the "Simple Resoluble Menstruum" because it can be reduced into a "Resolutive Menstruum" through circulation.

# THE PROCESS

...for the sublimation of our sulfur, as well as for the composition of our aforementioned precious stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>.

<margin>The solution of Quicksilver by means of the vegetable solvent.</margin>
And, my Son, the method is this: that you take one pound of common quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, and place it in a glass vessel, and pour over it the vegetable solvent <term>menstruum; a specialized alchemical solvent</term> so that it floats four fingers deep above it. Place this in a Water-bath <note>original: *Balneo*</note> or in dung <note>original: *fimo*; used as a source of gentle, steady heat</note> for six days, and the whole will be dissolved into a "glorious water."

<margin>A new mixture of dissolved Quicksilver with a solvent so that it may dissolve the Sun <note>Gold</note>.</margin>
Draw off the solvent by means of a gentle bath, and at the bottom of the vessel there will remain for you the "light of pearls" and the "soul of metals." Then take this glorious water, of which there will be one pound, and mix it with two pounds of the "heavenized" (that is, circulated) vegetable solvent, and the whole will become one "soul." With this, you may dissolve all metallic bodies, even the "perfect" ones <note>Gold and Silver</note>, for the creation of our Sulfur. And know, by THE TRUTH AND FAITH OF GOD, that no natural Sulfur of any metal could be sublimated without this water of common quicksilver.

<margin>The calcination of gold through Mercury.</margin>
Now we shall reveal to you the Calcination <term>calcination; the process of reducing a metal to a powder by heating it</term>, by which none of the metals lose their essential form, and the solvent resolves them within a short time. And the mastery of this secret is as follows: Take Gold or Silver, beaten into thin plates. <margin>Amalgam <note>A mixture of mercury with another metal</note>.</margin> Take a small portion of this with an equal amount of common quicksilver, and place it over a slow fire. When it begins to smoke, add the metal plates and stir with a wooden rod; afterward, place it in a vessel <term>garola; a type of crucible or small pot</term> containing cold water. Unless the resulting paste is brittle enough to break like bell-metal <note>a hard, brittle copper-tin alloy</note>, return the mass to the distilling vessel <term>alembicum</term> and allow more of the quicksilver to evaporate, then place it in water again. After it has become hard, as described, place the paste in a vessel <term>galaide; likely a mortar or specialized vessel</term> with a fourth part of common salt, and grind it vigorously until the paste and the Salt all appear as a "Black Salt." Take this Salt and place it in a sublimator if you wish to recover the quicksilver; if not, place it in a vessel <term>garola</term> that can withstand the heat, and apply fire until you see that all the Mercury has evaporated or sublimated. Once this is done, put that Salt into another vessel and pour very hot water over it as you see fit. Stir it with a wooden rod; the Salt will dissolve and turn into a black water. Let this settle, then pour it off gradually until it is all gone, and the lime <term>calx; the powdery remains of the metal</term> will stay at the bottom. Pour more very hot water over it and repeat the process until the water comes away from the lime as clear as when it was poured in. Finally, set the lime out to dry...

Now there are many modes of preparation for our Stone recounted in our *Testament* and in our other volumes, namely: Solution, coagulation, sublimation, distillation, calcination, separation, fusion, inceration <term>inceratio; the process of softening a substance to a waxy consistency</term>, imbibition <term>imbibitio; the repeated addition of liquid to a dry substance</term>, fixation, etc.; the meaning of all of these is "decoction": 

<margin>A single decoction.</margin>

...shining, which is the White Tincture; afterwards, with a greater degree of fire, the matter turns lemon-yellow, and finally reddens into the form of a Ruby.

<margin>Multiplication</margin>
Our Multiplication, truly, is nothing other than the repetition of the composition of our primary work. And thus far speaks Raymund Lully.

<margin>Lully's Method</margin>
Lully's intention is that the solvent <term>menstruum; a specialized alchemical solvent</term> be removed after the first dissolution. For this purpose, he instructs so subtly that by the heat of the Water-bath <note>original: *Balnei*</note>, the solvent ascends with its Sal Ammoniac <note>original: *sale Armeniaco*; ammonium chloride, used to increase the potency of solvents</note>, while in the meantime the muddiness and viscosity of the Mercury and Salt remain at the bottom.

<margin>Concerning the Spirits of Salts</margin>
Because in sublimated Mercury <term>Mercury sublimate; a toxic compound of mercury and chlorine</term> there are also the Spirits of Vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid</note> and Saltpeter <note>Potassium nitrate</note>, he says of this in his *Testament* that those two Spirits cannot be absent. And if the Spirits do not ascend with the solvent, but remain below: then after they have completed their work of the second dissolution, they partly exhale as the fire increases; partly, insofar as they partake with the Mercury, they are converted into it; and partly, as the Stone thus grows, they are cast down into a heterogeneous powder. And this is the reason why Lully, in the practical section of the *Testament* and elsewhere, mentions not only the vegetable solvent but also the mineral one, as has been sufficiently shown from Lully himself in the preceding pages.

<margin>The error of some in explaining Lully</margin>
Some (such as Janus Lacinius <note>A 16th-century Italian editor of alchemical texts</note>), not noticing this, have cautioned that a certain mixture should be made from *aqua fortis* <note>Nitric acid</note> and the vegetable solvent, and that Mercury should be mixed with that mixture. And perhaps that speculation might reach a certain particular tincture <note>A "particular" tincture was thought to transform only a specific amount of metal, rather than the "universal" power of the Stone</note>, but it will not be possible to reach the secret Stone by this method—which Lacinius himself clearly and frankly admits. Nevertheless, I will include Lacinius's opinion, not because I approve of it, but so that if anyone wishes, they may also test him. For besides the fact that Lully is clear enough on his own in the preceding points, Lacinius is not an authority to me: seeing that he never possessed the Stone, but published either collections of other authors (for so he himself names his labors) or his own—and sometimes quite foolish—speculations, not without the corruption of good books (as appears in the *Precious Pearl of Bonus of Ferrara* <note>original: *Pretiosa Margarita Boni Ferrariensis*; a famous alchemical text published by Lacinius in 1546</note>, which he published in Venice). However, I wish to leave the judgment between both opinions, this one and that one, to the fair reader who is well-experienced in both chemical matters and books.

# THE PROCESS OF LULLY ACCORDING TO PART III.
## Following the mind of JANUS LACINIUS of Calabria, whom I nonetheless do not approve of. <note>The author or editor here signals a disagreement with Lacinius’s interpretation of Lully’s work, a common feature in alchemical debates regarding the "true" method.</note>

<margin>The preparation of the Mercurial aqua fortis.</margin>
Make a "strong water" <term>aqua fortis; a powerful acid, typically nitric acid</term> from dried vitriol <note>original: *vitriolo*; iron or copper sulfate</note>, saltpeter <note>original: *Sale nitro*</note>, and cinnabar <note>original: *Cinabrio*; mercury sulfide</note>, using half their weight. Once this is made, repeat the process with one pound of this water and half a pound of fresh cinnabar; do this three times, always adding new cinnabar. Then, rectify <note>purify through redistillation</note> the water by itself so that it is well-purified. Finally, take that clear water and mix it with an equal amount of "sharp vegetable water" <note>original: *aquæ vegetabilis acutæ*; likely distilled vinegar or spirit of wine</note> along with its "earth," whether sublimated or fixed. Take great care during the act of mixing; you must mix them little by little, cautiously and with diligence. Let them stand for a natural day <note>a 24-hour period</note> in a sealed vessel so they may be well-blended together. Then, distill all the water in a Water-bath <note>original: *Balneo*; a Bain-marie</note>, pour it back over the residue, and distill again. Repeat this work until the "mineral spirit" is well-united with the "vegetable spirit," and you see them joined at the bottom of the flask <margin>Ice made from the Mercurial water.</margin> <note>original: *bo-ciæ* or *bocia*</note> in the form of ice. Discard the distilled water, as we have no further use for it. If you wish to multiply this spirit—or ice—multiply it with new waters, always distilling in the Water-bath as you did the first time. However, place one pound of the *aqua fortis* over one ounce of this salt. In this way, you can multiply this ice (or, to speak more correctly, this "fire") as much as you please.

<margin>Conjunction with the Sun or Moon.</margin>
Take, therefore, one pound of this Spirit, or salt, or ice—or "Vegetable Matter" <note>original: *G. Vegetabili*; likely *Glutinum* (Gluten) or *Gummi* (Gum), a specialized Lullian term for a sticky alchemical intermediate</note>, which is the same thing—and grind it with one ounce of "volatile Gold" <note>original: *Solis volatilis*; gold prepared as leaf or in a reactive state</note>, or gold that has been thinned into leaves or dissolved and reduced to the nature of a Spirit by means of its own "menstrual water" <term>menstruum; a specialized alchemical solvent</term> conforming to its nature. When you have the Moon <note>Silver</note> or Sun <note>Gold</note> thus prepared in leaves, you will have it ready to be dissolved and united with the ice noted above, as has been described. Then place both in the Water-bath for eight days, and the whole will be dissolved into a <margin>Circulation.</margin> water the color of gold. Let them circulate together in a twin vessel, which they call a "Pelican" <note>original: *pellicanum*; a circulatory distillation flask with two side-arms that feed the distillate back into the body</note>, for twenty days or thereabouts, and it will congeal into a stone the color of a ruby. Dissolve it in the Water-bath and congeal it in ashes, and it will be the Medicine, one part of which falls upon a hundred parts of Mercury or Silver <note>original: *Lunæ*</note> and turns it into Gold <note>original: *Solem*</note>.

# THE PROCESS OF GEBER THE ARAB, COLLECTED from various places in the *Summa Perfectionis* <note>The *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii* (The Height of the Perfection of Mastery) is one of the most influential alchemical texts of the Middle Ages, traditionally attributed to Geber.</note>, in which GEBER handed it down in a scattered manner.

## And first indeed concerning the
## WHITE TINCTURE.

### First Step.

<margin>Quicksilver is the unique material which [is sought].</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a landscape scene with a building and hills in the background.</image-desc>
IN searching among other mineral things, we have found by our discovery nothing more than Quicksilver <note>original: *Argentum vivum*; literally "living silver"</note> to be more friendly to the natures of [metallic] bodies. By bestowing our labor upon this in our work, we have found it to be the true medicine of alterable things <note>referring to base metals that can be "altered" into gold or silver</note> in its completion, with a true and notably peculiar alteration.

<margin>The nature of Quicksilver.</margin>
For Quicksilver is friendly and agreeable to metals, and is the medium for joining tinctures. It is fixed <note>made stable so it does not evaporate when heated</note>, and it is of a tincture of most exuberant restoration of redness, and of glowing splendor. It is also a perfecter and a preserver against burning. Nevertheless, <margin>Quicksilver is not the Tincture in its own nature.</margin> it is not the perfecter, or the Medicine, in its own nature, but rather that which is produced from it by our artifice. For that matter is not Quicksilver in its own nature, nor in its whole substance, but a part of it; it is a matter which took its origin from that source, and was created from it.

<margin>Preparations to be applied to Mercury.</margin>
But since we have found that it does not change without the administration of an alteration of its nature, we have similarly found that it must necessarily be prepared, since it cannot be mixed in the "deep" <note>original: *in profundo*; referring to the internal, essential level of the metal</note> without that method of preparation. And this is so that its substance may become such that it is mixed in the deep, even unto the depth of the alterable body, without separation forever.

<margin>Sublimation of Mercury is necessary.</margin>
This, however, does not happen except very subtly with a certain and determined preparation in the chapter on sublimation. It is necessary, therefore, that the Stone <note>the *Lapis*, or the raw material for the Philosopher's Stone</note> be taken, and that the work of the first step of sublimation be applied to it with diligent persistence, so that by this it may be cleansed of corrupting impurity. This is the perfection of sublimation: that the stone be refined with it until it reaches the ultimate purity of subtlety. And thus, by the method of separation, you may divide its most pure part and carry it aside.

<margin>The manner in which Quicksilver is sublimated.</margin>
The manner of the sublimation of Quicksilver is as follows: its sublimation is its complete, highest purification from earthiness...

and the removal of its wateriness. For we are excused from the labor of removing its burning <note>original: *adustio*; in alchemy, this refers to the presence of "combustible sulfur" which causes substances to char or blacken under heat</note>, since it does not possess it. We say, therefore, that the ingenuity of separating its superfluous earth lies in mixing it with things with which it has no affinity, and repeating its sublimation from them many times, until you see it become the whitest white, exceeding snow in its whiteness, and as if dead, clinging to the joints <note>original: *spontilibus*; referring to the connection points or "vertebrae" of the aludel pots</note> of the aludel <note>A series of pear-shaped ceramic pots stacked on top of each other used for collecting sublimated vapors</note>. 
<margin>Dregs to be added to the Mercury.</margin>
And of this sort [of mixing materials] are Talc, and the lime <note>original: *calx*; a powder produced by roasting or calcining a substance</note> of eggshells and of white marble; likewise, very finely ground glass and every other kind of prepared substance. For by these it is cleansed, but by other things having an affinity with it—unless they be the bodies of perfection <note>Referring to the "perfect metals" like gold or silver</note>—it is instead corrupted. This is because all such things possess a sulfureity <note>the quality of containing sulfurous impurities</note> which, ascending with it during sublimation, corrupts it. And you can see the proof of this in experience: for if you sublimate it from tin or from lead, you will see it infected with blackness after the sublimation.

Therefore, its sublimation is better through those things with which it does not agree. With those things it *does* agree with, it would be better if they did not have sulfureity. For this reason, sublimation from lime is better than from all other things, because lime has little affinity and possesses no sulfureity.

<margin>Removal of the wateriness of Mercury.</margin>
The method of removing its superfluous wateriness <note>original: *aqueitas*; the volatile, watery moisture that prevents a substance from being "fixed" or stable</note> is this: when it is mixed with the limes from which it is to be sublimated, let it be ground and mixed with them by "imbibition" <note>the process of soaking a dry substance with a liquid until it is absorbed</note> until nothing of the mercury is visible. Afterward, let the wateriness of the imbibition be removed over a very slow fire. As that moisture recedes, the wateriness of the quicksilver also recedes with it; however, let the fire be so gentle that the entire substance of the quicksilver does not ascend because of it. Thus, through the multiple repetition of imbibition with grinding and gentle roasting <note>original: *assatione*</note>, the greater part of its wateriness is destroyed, and the remainder is removed through the repetition of the sublimation. From there, you should fix one part of that which is most pure, and leave another part unfixed.

Mercury can be fixed without being turned into "earth" <note>a dry, non-fusible powder</note>, and it can likewise be fixed with its conversion into earth. It can therefore be fixed without the consumption of its melting humidity <note>original: *humiditas fundens*; the "moisture" that allows a metal to melt into a liquid state</note>: for because of the good adherence of its parts and its strength—

<margin>
The method of fixation through frequent sublimation.
</margin>

...the nature of its composition, if in any way its parts are thickened by fire, it no longer permits itself to be corrupted, nor does it allow itself to be raised further into smoke by the entry of a furious flame into it: because it does not suffer rarefaction, owing to its density and lack of burning <note>original: *adustio*; in alchemy, this refers to the presence of "combustible sulfur" which causes substances to char or blacken under heat</note>, which is completed through the combustible sulfureity it possesses. However, by its successive and repeated sublimation, it is fixed and does not turn into earth; rather, it yields a metallic fusion. The intent of hastening its fixation is that you should exercise your ingenuity to find a way to repeat the sublimation multiple times in a short duration. This is done by using two aludels <note>A series of pear-shaped ceramic pots stacked on top of each other used for collecting sublimated vapors</note> with their double covers, in this order: you must never cease the act of sublimation until it is fixed. 

Therefore, when it has ascended in one, let it be cast into another aludel, and so let it be done by turns. And never let it be allowed to rest idle, clinging to the joints <note>original: *spondilibus*; the connecting ribs or segments of the aludel pots</note> of the aludels, but let it be in a continuous elevation by fire until its rising ceases. For in whatever shorter time you can multiply the repeated sublimations, by so much more quickly and better will it happen that the time of its fixation is shortened. And for this reason, a second method of fixation was invented, which is through the precipitation of the substance to be sublimed toward the heat and harshness of the fire with violence, so that it remains continuously in it until it is fixed. For the harshness of the fire easily destroys and removes its wateriness <note>original: *aqueitas*; the volatile, moist quality of mercury</note>. 

And this shall be done through a long glass vessel, the bottom of which should be made of earth and not glass (because it would shatter into pieces), joined to it skillfully with a good seal. Let the shape of the vessel be of great length, in which it may find a place for cooling, adhering, and resting in its joints due to its length, and not a way of escape; until, by a repeated turn, it is precipitated back to its bottom by the fierce heat of the fire, with many repetitions, until it is fixed. When, therefore, it has adhered to its joints, let it be cast down to the depths of the heat continuously by turns with an iron or stone spatula, until it becomes fixed.

<margin>
The Calcination of Mercury through fixed precipitation.
</margin>

This precipitated and fixed **Quicksilver** <term>Mercury|The metal mercury, often called 'Argentum vivum' (living silver) in these texts</term> should then be placed in a furnace of great heat, in the manner used for preserving limes <note>original: *calcis*; powders produced by roasting or oxidizing a substance</note>. For the calcination of spirits <note>In alchemy, 'spirits' refer to substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that vaporize when heated</note> is done so that as they approach fixation, fire may be administered to them, increasing it successively and little by little so they do not flee, until it happens that they can tolerate the maximum fire. The reason for the invention of the **Calcination of spirits** is so that they may be better fixed and more easily dissolved into water: because every kind of calcined substance is more fixed than one that is not calcined, and is of easier solution.

### The Third Degree

<margin>Cerification for the purpose of the second order</margin>
When you have fixed the <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *Argentum vivum*, literally "living silver"</note>, then repeat the sublimation of the remaining part that was saved and not yet fixed upon the fixed portion, so that it may likewise be fixed. Keep what you will test over the fire: if it yields a good fusion <note>meaning it melts into a liquid state rather than turning into smoke</note>, then you have administered sufficient sublimation to it. But if not, add to it some portion of sublimated mercury and repeat the sublimation until it is done. If it possesses a clear and very white color, and is transparent, then you have cleansed it well; if not, you have not. Therefore, do not be negligent in its preparation, which is done through sublimation; for as the cleansing is, so follows the perfection achieved through it, in its <term>projection</term> <note>the act of casting the alchemical medicine onto base metals to transform them</note> upon any one of the imperfect bodies and upon the raw mercury itself. If, therefore, you have cleansed it correctly by sublimating and have perfected it, there will be a firm and perfect tincture of whiteness, to which there is no equal. This fourth degree <note>Geber appears to be counting stages of refinement here</note>, without the preceding solutions and elevations of the fixed to volatility, is seen to belong to the **second order**. But he who wishes to ascend to the **third order** <note>The "Third Order" refers to the highest level of alchemical medicine, often called the Great Elixir or Philosopher's Stone</note> should act in the following manner immediately after the fixation.

<margin>The method of Solution</margin>
When the matter has been fixed, dissolve that which is soluble from it. That which is not soluble, you should send to <term>calcination</term> <note>heating a substance to a high temperature until it becomes a fine powder</note>, and thereafter repeat the solution upon the same until again that which is soluble from it is dissolved by every means. Thus let that order be maintained until the greater quantity is dissolved.

There are two methods of solution: namely, by warm dung and by boiling water; both of which have one intent and one effect. The method by dung is thus: let the <term>calcined</term> material be placed in a glass ampoule <note>a small glass flask or vial</note>, and pour over it a quantity of distilled vinegar, or something similar, or double its amount. Let its opening be sealed well so that it does not breathe <note>i.e., let no vapors escape</note>, and let it be left to dissolve under warm dung <note>original: *fimum tepidum*; fermented horse dung was used as a natural, steady heat source for gentle digestion</note>. Afterward, let the dissolved part be removed by distillation through a filter; that which is not dissolved, however, should be calcined again. The method which is done by boiling water is faster: it is such that the calcined material is similarly arranged in an ampoule with vinegar, the opening being sealed so it does not breathe. This is to be buried in a cauldron full of water and straw, as in the manner of distillation, and afterward a fire should be lit beneath it until the water boils for an hour. After this, let the solution be distilled and kept separately. That which is not dissolved should be calcined again and dissolved again in the same order, until through repetition the whole is dissolved. After this, mix all the solutions together and <term>coagulate</term> <note>turn the liquid back into a solid form through evaporation or cooling</note> them.

# PROCESS
<note>original: *PROCESSUS*</note>

<margin>Coagulation of the dissolved matter</margin>
The method for the **coagulation** <note>the process of thickening or solidifying a liquid</note> of dissolved things is by using a flask in a bed of ashes <note>an alchemical "ash-bath" used for gentle, even heating</note> buried up to its neck. Maintain a tempered heat until the wateriness vanishes. Then, by roasting it lightly, preserve it in that tempered heat until a greater fire can be administered to it, as its requirements demand.

<margin>Repetition of the solution</margin>
After this, follow the first order of **solution** <note>dissolving a solid into a liquid</note> until everything that is soluble in it is dissolved again. Coagulate it once more, and once more preserve it in the tempered heat until a greater fire can be administered for its perfection.

Reiterate all these orders of preparation upon that material four times, and finally **calcine** <note>to reduce a substance to a powder by heat</note> it in its own way. By sufficiently administering this, you reach the most precious **earth of the Stone**. At this point, if you wish to "tinge" <note>to transform or color a metal, indicating the alchemical change into gold or silver</note> immediately, and if you wish to increase the Stone in both quantity and quality, then proceed to **ceration** <note>the process of softening a substance until it has the consistency of wax, allowing it to melt without evaporating</note> by the following way.

<margin>The use of solution</margin>
The reason for the discovery of "solution" is the **subtilization** <note>making a substance "subtle" or fine so it can penetrate other materials</note> of those things which otherwise have neither fusion <note>the ability to melt</note> nor "ingression" <note>the ability to enter into and transform the body of a metal</note>. For it is necessary that everything which is dissolved takes on the nature of salt or alum, or things similar to them.

Now, it is the nature of these things that they provide a **fusion** before they undergo vitrification <note>turning into glass; alchemists wanted the material to stay liquid and active, not to become a hard, inert glass</note>. Therefore, dissolved **spirits** <note>volatile substances</note> will likewise provide a similar fusion. Since they agree greatly by their nature with metallic bodies and with each other, once fusion is achieved, it is necessary for them to penetrate the bodies through that fusion, and by penetrating, to **transmute** them.

<margin>How the penetrative power is joined to the Stone</margin>
However, one does not arrive at this ability to penetrate and transmute without the **Magistery** <note>the "Mastery" or secret alchemical technique</note>. This consists of the following: after its solution and coagulation, one must administer to it some **purified spirit** that is not "fixed" <note>meaning it is still volatile</note. Let it be sublimated from the material so many times until it remains with it, providing it with a faster fusion and preserving it from vitrification during that fusion. From these things results a good fusion, an "ingression" <note>entry into the metal</note>, and a stable "fixation" <note>resistance to fire</note>.

<margin>Quicksilver is most suitable in creation</margin>
In many things, this "cerative" moisture (which brings about fusion and penetration) is found better, more feasibly, and more closely than in others. Specifically, it is found closely in **Sulfur** and **Arsenic**, but more closely and better in **quicksilver** <note>original: *argento vivo*</note>. But let this not stand

### *The Fourth Degree.*

<margin>
Multiplication of the Stone in power and quantity.

How the fixed stone is produced.
</margin>
Next, take the quantity of the non-fixed <note>volatile; parts that evaporate when heated</note> part that you have saved, and join it with this portion of treated "earth" <note>the solid, stable residue from previous steps</note> through a subtle and ingenious method, mixing them down to the smallest particles. This method involves the "Raising" of the substance by the way of **sublimation** <note>the process of heating a solid until it becomes vapor and then collecting it as it cools back into a solid</note>, until the fixed part rises completely together with the non-fixed part. If this does not happen, repeat the addition of the non-fixed part bit by bit until it is sufficient to lift the whole substance.

<margin>
Repeated fixation.
</margin>
Therefore, when it has been raised, repeat its sublimation until, through this repetition of treatment, the whole becomes **fixed** <note>stable under heat; no longer evaporating</note>. Once the whole is fixed, repeat the process again: drink up <note>original: *combibe*; to soak or saturate the solid with liquid</note> a quantity of the non-fixed part, using the method known to you, until it is raised once more. Let it be fixed again until it allows for an easy **fusion** <note>melting</note> when it is ignited. From the repetition of this preparation degree, a multiplication of the "goodness of alteration" <note>the potency or ability of the medicine to change metals</note> results in the medicine.

<margin>
The power and effect of multiplication.
</margin>
From the variation in the number of times the work is repeated upon the Stone in its degrees, there results a variation in the goodness of the multiplication of its effects. Thus, some medicines may transform a hundred times their own weight, some two hundred times, some three hundred, others a thousand, and some indeed an infinite amount of metal into a true, perfect, **silver-making** <note>original: *Lunificum*; related to Luna, the alchemical name for Silver</note> body.

This is the medicine that transforms every body diminished from perfection, and every kind of **Mercury** <note>original: *Argentum vivum*; "living silver"</note>, into a most perfect Lunar <note>Silver</note> body.

### The First Degree.

<margin>The nature and composition of Sulphur.</margin>
In the division of sulphur, it is necessary to apply great caution. For Sulphur has a homogeneous and very strong composition, and it is uniform in its substance throughout its parts. Therefore, he who seeks to draw the work out from it should not attempt to do so by preparing it on its own. This is because the work is perfected only when mixed; without such a mixture, the Mastery is delayed until one reaches the point of despair.

For if the Sulphur were not joined with the **residue** <note>original: *fœce* (dregs or lees); the solid matter left over after heating</note> of some fixed <note>stable under heat</note> substance, then it would be necessary for the Sulphur to rise up in its entirety during heating without being purified. And if the residue were not mixed in down to the smallest particles, the same thing would happen as if there were no residue at all.

However, if it is **sublimated** <note>the process of turning a solid into vapor by heat and then back to solid</note> with the **calx** <note>the powdery oxide or "ash" left after a metal has been burnt</note> of certain bodies, then it is sublimated well and can be perfectly purified with ease. It is therefore the intention that these residues be provided from the calces of metals.

For in these metallic ashes, the sublimation is an easy operation; but with other substances, it is most difficult. Therefore, there is nothing else that can take their place.

<margin>The proportion of residue to be used.</margin>
The correct proportion of residue is that the quantity of the residue should equal the quantity of the substances to be sublimated. In this, even an unrefined craftsman cannot go wrong. For a craftsman of average skill, setting the weight of the residue at half the weight of the substances to be sublimated happens to be sufficient, and in this he should not err. But for the practiced and most expert artist, even the smallest portion of residue suffices. 

For the smaller the quantity of residue, the greater the abundance of the sublimation must be—provided that as the amount of residue is reduced, the amount of fire is proportionally reduced. For with a small quantity, a small fire should be drawn forth for perfection; with a large quantity, a large fire; and with a greater quantity, a greater fire. The best kind of residue consists of iron scales or "burnt copper" <note>copper oxide</note>. Because these have been deprived of much moisture, they easily soak up the Sulphur and unite with it. But only the experienced practitioner knows the true path of this method.

<vocab>Sulphur, Mastery, Sublimation, Residue/Dregs, Metallic Ashes, Fire, Iron Scales, Burnt Copper, The First Degree</vocab>

<header># GEBER THE ARABIAN</header>

<margin>The Sublimation of Sulphur.</margin>
If, therefore, Sulphur is to be **sublimated** <note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then collecting it as it cools back into a solid; this serves to purify the substance.</note>, it is necessary that it be sublimated using gentle heat. Because it possesses extremely subtle parts joined uniformly with coarse ones, its entire substance would otherwise rise up without any purification; indeed, it would be blackened and scorched.

<margin>What is required for cleansing Sulphur.</margin>
To separate the impure, earthy substance, one must discover two types of ingenuity: namely, the correct proportion of fire, and purification through mixing with **dregs** <note>original: *fecum*; the solid residue or sediment left over from a previous process, used here to "anchor" the impure parts of the sulphur.</note>. This is because mixing with the dregs captures the coarse parts and holds them down at the bottom of the **aludel** <note>original: *aludelis*; a specialized alchemical apparatus consisting of a series of pear-shaped pots used to collect the vapors of sublimation.</note>, preventing them from rising.

<margin>Degrees of fire required for the sublimation of Sulphur.</margin>
It is therefore necessary for the craftsman to apply three degrees of fire to the sublimation. The first should be proportioned so that only the altered, purer, and clearer parts rise, until he clearly sees them being cleansed of their earthy foulness. It is helpful first, with a small amount of fire, to draw out only the "wateriness" from the substances to be sublimated; once this is removed, if anything rises, the fire should not be increased at the start. In this way, the most subtle part—which is the cause of **scorching** <note>original: *adustionis*; the unwanted burning or charring of the substance that ruins the alchemical work.</note>—is removed by the weakest fire and set aside. <margin>First degree of fire.</margin> When little or nothing more rises, the fire beneath it should be strengthened.

<margin>Second degree of fire.</margin>
The second degree is to ensure that whatever pure essence remains in the dregs is sublimated with a greater force of fire—namely, by heating the aludel and the dregs themselves until they glow, which you will be able to see with your own eyes.

The "head" (the top) of the aludel should be emptied very frequently, lest the rising substances accumulate too much and fall back to the bottom, and lest the many repetitions of sublimation keep you occupied for a long time. Furthermore, one should always separate the powder that rises near the opening of the aludel's head from that which is found to have ascended as a fused, dense mass in pieces—clear and transparent near the bottom opening, clinging to the **rims** <note>original: *spondilia*; the joints or edges where the alchemical vessels meet.</note> of the vessel. This latter part has less "scorching" than that which is found to have risen near the top opening.

<margin>Third degree of fire.</margin>
The third degree is to apply the weakest fire, without the dregs, to that which has already been sublimated and purified. This is done so that hardly anything rises; what does rise from it is a most subtle substance that is of no value in this work, as it is the medium through which scorching occurs in sulphurs.

<header>PROCESSUS</header>

<margin>The overall purpose of the sublimation of sulphur.</margin>
The entire purpose of the **sublimation** <note>The process of heating a substance into vapor and collecting it as a solid again to purify it.</note> is therefore this: that by removing its earthiness through the proper administration of fire, and similarly by casting off its most subtle and smoky part (which causes burning and corruption), that part which consists in equality remains for us. This is the part that undergoes a simple **fusion** <note>Melting into a liquid state.</note> over the fire without any burning, and which flees from the fire without catching flame. For that which is sublimated does not ignite directly; rather, it flies away and is thinned out without inflammation, though the melting precedes this. And if it is not found to be in this state, the work should be applied to it until it is found to be so.

## The Second Step.

<margin>Fixation is necessary in purified Sulphur.</margin>
A moderate substance of sulphur, prepared in the manner described, is not a cause for the perfection of bodies or of **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; the metal we now call mercury</term> unless it is **fixed** <note>Alchemical "fixation" refers to making a volatile substance stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates or escapes the fire.</note>. For when it has not been fixed, even if the impression it leaves is not easily removed, it is nonetheless not stably perpetuated. Sulphur is fixed in two ways: through frequent repetition of sublimation, and through **precipitation** <note>In this context, forcing a vaporous substance back down into a solid state through intense heat.</note> by the harshness of fire. This is the same method used for the fixation of quicksilver, and they do not differ from one another except in this: that Sulphur cannot be fixed through this latter method (by precipitation) unless its most thin, flammable parts are first separated from it by a subtle artifice of division. Quicksilver, however, does not require this consideration. And for this, it similarly needs a tempering of heat, just as quicksilver needs in this mode of precipitation. They also differ because sulphur takes a longer time to be fixed than quicksilver, and also because it is raised higher due to its **rarity** <note>Meaning its low density or lightness.</note> than quicksilver. Therefore, it requires a longer vessel than quicksilver for its fixation.

## The Third Step.

For the **second order of Medicines** <note>In the school of Geber, "Medicines" are alchemical agents used to transform base metals. The second order refers to those that change the external qualities but may not be permanent.</note>, this fixed Sulphur is brought to a **Tincture** <note>An alchemical substance capable of "staining" or transforming the color and nature of a metal.</note> through creation. The method of which is this: let purified, non-fixed quicksilver be taken, and let its sublimation be repeated over the fixed sulphur so many times until, remaining in it with its moisture, it provides a good fusion. Because, in truth, a Medicine of the third order is primarily sought—since it does not differ from a medicine of the third order in any way, except through the most subtle modes of preparation...

### The Fourth Step.

<margin>Note: Quicksilver is purified with pure water and common salt. The multiplication of the red Stone.</margin>
It consists in the addition of purified, non-fixed Quicksilver. And the method of this addition is through the repetition of the non-fixed part of the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical work.</note>, joining them through an ingenious method of **sublimation** <note>Heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again.</note>, until it is elevated with it, and once again fixed with it (through sublimation) so that it remains stable. And the more often this order of the completion's abundance is repeated, the more the medicine of this abundance is multiplied, its quality is increased, and its growth in perfection is maximized.

<margin>Repetition of the entire process of making the Stone.</margin>
And indeed, lest we be bitten by the envious <note>A common alchemical trope referring to critics or those who might steal secrets.</note>, we shall tell the full completion of this **Mastery** <term>Magisterium; the successful completion of the alchemical process</term> in a brief, complete, and well-known discourse. Its intent is that the Stone be most perfectly cleansed through the method of sublimation, along with its addition; from there, by ingenious means, let the volatile part of them be fixed; then indeed, let the fixed become volatile, and the volatile become fixed again; and let the fixed be dissolved, and the dissolved become volatile again, and the volatile become fixed again, until it flows and transforms into a certain certain **sun-making** <note>original: "solificum", meaning it has the power to turn metals into gold (Sol).</note> completion. From the repetition of this step in the Medicine, there results a multiplication of the quality of transformation. From the diversity of the work's repetition upon the stone in its degrees, there results a diversity in the multiplication of the quality of transformation: so that among Medicines, some may transmute a body a hundredfold, some twofold hundredfold, some threefold hundredfold, some indeed a thousandfold, and some may transmute a body into an infinite sun-making substance. And in this order is completed the most precious secret, which is above every secret of the sciences of this world, and a treasure in—
