### VI. ANOTHER AND QUITE EXCELLENT method for the red Tincture, set down by Geber in various places, sparingly and in few words.

<margin>Praise of Quicksilver.</margin>
**Quicksilver** <term>Argentum vivum; the metal we now call mercury</term> is fixed and is a **Tincture** <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a potent substance capable of transforming or "dyeing" base metals into gold or silver.</note> of redness, of most exuberant restoration and shining splendor; it does not depart from that which it is mixed with, so long as it remains in its own nature. Therefore, let the Most High be praised, blessed, and glorious, who created it and gave it its substance and the properties of its substance—properties which no other thing in nature happens to possess—so that this perfection might be found within it through the artifice we have discovered as a near potential. For it is this which overcomes fire, and is not overcome by fire: but rests in it amicably, rejoicing in it.

<margin>The excellence of Quicksilver in the red Stone.</margin>
Therefore, strive in all your works so that the Quicksilver prevails in the mixture. And if you are able to achieve perfection through Quicksilver alone, you will be a seeker of the most precious perfection, and of that perfection which surpasses the work of nature. For you will be able to cleanse it inwardly to a degree that Nature herself does not reach.

<margin>The process for eliciting the red Tincture from Mercury.</margin>
It is indeed sometimes (though not always) turned red by itself through **precipitation** <note>original: "præcipitatione"; here referring to the process of a substance settling out of a solution or being transformed through heat in a sealed vessel.</note>. If this should happen, there is no need for it to be tinted by **Sulphur** <note>The active, "combustible" principle in alchemical theory.</note>, but let it be **calcined** <note>Reduced to a powder through dry heat.</note>, dissolved, and **coagulated** <note>Turned from a liquid back into a solid.</note>, and let this be repeated four times or more. Afterward, with non-fixed quicksilver, let it be made volatile, and the volatile be made fixed: and consequently, as was said in the preceding sections.

->End of this Tincture.<-

# VII. THE WHITE TINCTURE FROM AR-
## *senic as described by Geber.*

<margin>The nature of Arsenic.</margin>
Arsenic is a tincture of whiteness. Because, however, in the root of its nature—through the action of nature—many of its inflammable parts have been loosened, the artifice of separation is therefore easy. <note>Geber suggests that arsenic is naturally suited for making silver because its "burning" impurities are easily removed.</note>

### *The first Step.*

<margin>The sublimation of Arsenic.</margin>
The sublimation of arsenic is done just like the sublimation of sulfur: but its better sublimation is from the calxes <term>metallic powders produced by heating</term> of metals.

### *The Second Step.*

<margin>The fixing of it.</margin>
Arsenic is fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixing" means turning a volatile substance into a solid that can withstand heat without evaporating.</note> just like sulfur.

### *The Third and Fourth Step.*

There is one and the same method as that which was observed in sulfur, except that arsenic does not yield a solar <term>gold-making</term> tincture, but only a lunar <term>silver-making</term> one.
Look for the rest in the preceding processes, since the operation is the same in both cases.

->*End of the Tinctures written by Geber.*<-

# VIII. THE PROCESS OF ST. THOMAS AQUIN-
## *as, just as Paracelsus mentions it in the 3rd book "On Long Life," chapter 8.*

<margin>A brief recitation of the process.</margin>
REDUCE Mercury through elevation <term>sublimation</term> for so long until it passes into a fixed crystal. Then digest it into a resolution <term>liquefaction</term> and a coagulation, and join it with gold, so that this itself becomes its ferment. Proceed then according to the precept of Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>, until the end of the Stone. Thus far Paracelsus.

<margin>A true and certain explanation of this process.</margin>
Take one pound of Mercury, sublime it three times with vitriol <term>iron or copper sulfates</term> and common salt: then sublime it just as many times with an equal amount of Venetian glass (always adding new dregs) until the Mercury leaves no blackness behind. This—

# THE PROCESS
<meta>catchword: follows.</meta>

<margin>The solution of the fixed Mercurial Crystal.</margin>
Sublimate mercury alone and by itself many times, until it leaves no dregs behind and it flows like oil in the bottom of the vessel: then the Mercury will have become a transparent stone, like Crystal. When this has been well-pulverized, keep it in a closed vessel in a <term>Water-bath</term> <note>original: "Balneo Mariæ," a double boiler used for gentle heating</note> until it is dissolved into water, which appears almost like wine. Distill this through a glass retort so that as much as can pass through that distillation does pass. Let the residue be pulverized and soaked with its own water, and placed to dissolve in a water-bath as before: afterward, let it be distilled again, and let this whole process be repeated until all the Mercury is converted into water.

## NOTE

<margin>On the goal and effect of obtaining Mercurials. How gold is to be brought to the form of a ferment.</margin>
Without a sharpened vegetable <term>solvent</term> <note>original: "menstruo vegetabili," a liquid used to dissolve solids, often derived from wine or vinegar</note>, I do not believe that Salt or the Moon <note>In alchemy, "the Moon" (Luna) refers to silver.</note> can be dissolved. For I have seen a certain mercurial water, cooked for a long time with the lime <term>powdered oxide</term> of the Sun <note>The "Sun" (Sol) refers to gold.</note>, yet it dissolved nothing of it. Therefore, either (as Lull <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note> teaches) that solvent will be necessary, or it will be necessary that the gold which is used for the ferment be first reduced separately either into a soluble form or into a state of viscosity: for then a similar form can act upon its like, which otherwise would never happen. And this is the reason for joining the ferments, which must be observed in all viscous forms of tinctures: unless one has Mercury joined with the solvent for performing the dissolution of Gold; otherwise, one labors in vain.

<margin>Another way of making Mercury viscous.</margin>
I will add in this place a certain viscosity of sublimated Mercury—not a certain one <note>The author likely means this is an optional or alternative method.</note>, but let whoever wishes use it. Take one ounce of Mercury, three times sublimated, and dissolve it in four ounces of rain water in which, however, two ounces of borax have first been dissolved. Distill in ashes <note>A method of indirect heating where the vessel sits in a bowl of warm ashes.</note>, and the Mercury remains in the bottom: draw it off five more times, and you will find the Mercury flowing like wax and fixed; the longer it remains in the fire, the more beautiful it becomes in fusion. Give the ferment to this, and you will "tinge" <term>transform or dye the metal</term>.

## *End of the Tincture of Blessed Thomas.*

# PARACELSUS’S TINCTURE FROM NO. 9 ALONE.
## *Sulfur: taken from the book "On the Nature of Things"*
### *Books 1 & 5.*

<margin>By what means Sulfur can be mortified.</margin>
The <term>mortification</term> <note>original: "mortificatio," the process of "killing" or stripping away the outward properties of a substance to reach its essence</note> of sulfur occurs when the combustible and foul-smelling "fatness" is removed from it, and it is converted into a fixed substance. This is accomplished as follows: 
Take some weight of common yellow sulfur, reduced to a very fine powder, and three times draw off from it very sharp <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "aquam fortem," literally "strong water," usually referring to nitric acid</note>. Then the sulfur will remain at the bottom, black in color. Let it be washed with common fresh water, distilling it until the water comes off entirely fresh and does not smell of any sulfurous stench.

<margin>Reverberation of Sulfur.</margin>
Therefore, <term>reverberate</term> <note>original: "reverberâ," a process of heating a substance in a furnace where the flames are reflected or "reverberated" back onto the material</note> this sulfur in a closed reverberatory furnace in the manner of Antimony. First it becomes white, then yellow, and finally red like <term>cinnabar</term> <note>a bright red mineral, mercury sulfide</note>. When you have brought it to this state, rejoice, because this is the beginning of your riches. This reverberated sulfur tints any Silver into most excellent gold, and restores the human body to the highest health, beyond what is fitting to write: so great and so distinguished is the virtue of this reverberated and fixed Sulfur.

<margin>Extraction of the Quintessence from fixed Sulfur.</margin>
Take that reverberated Sulfur, and pour <term>Spirit of Wine</term> <note>original: "Spiritum vini," concentrated alcohol or ethanol</note> upon it, with which the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>original: "Essentia Quinta," the "fifth essence" or purest spiritual component of a substance</note> of sulfur may be extracted. After the Spirit of Wine is drawn off, the Quintessence of sulfur appears red and transparent like a Ruby. This is a great and most excellent <term>arcanum</term> <note>a deep secret or hidden mystery; in medicine, a potent "secret" remedy</note> for transmuting white metals, and for coagulating living Mercury into the most fixed Gold. Therefore, hold this Secret as a huge treasure for becoming rich, and you may live deservedly content with this single artifice of transmuting metals.

<margin>Notable point.</margin>
It must be observed, however, that when the aqua fortis is drawn off from the sulfur, it should stand four finger-breadths above the powder, and by repeatedly pouring the aqua fortis back until it is finally dried, this Sulfur of a blackish color is drawn off.

<margin>Use of this Tincture in diseases.</margin>
The dose of this Quintessence extracted in Spirit of Wine, for the most dangerous diseases, is four or six drops, taken daily until health is fully restored. If taken in the springtime, and if one uses it in the stated manner for 28 days, it restores youth. Against the plague, let six drops be taken or...

## THE MOST NOBLE PROCESS OF PARACELSUS, which he set forth in very few words in the *Tincture of the Physicists*, chapter 4.

<margin>
10.
</margin>

<margin>
Paracelsus’s words concerning the Tincture of the Physicists.
</margin>
"I tell you, do not take anything except from the <term>Lion</term> <note>original: "Leone," an alchemical symbol often representing the fixed or solid part of a substance, such as gold or sulfur</note> its rosy blood, and from the <term>Eagle</term> <note>original: "aquila," a symbol for the volatile or spiritual part of a substance, often associated with mercury or sal-ammoniac</note> its white glue. After you have joined these together, coagulate them according to the process of the Ancients. And thus you will have the Tincture of the Physicists, which many have searched for, but very few have found." Thus far says Paracelsus.

<margin>
Explanation of the Paracelsian sentence.
</margin>
Certainly, no commentary will be needed here for one who has understood the preceding processes of <term>Lull</term>, <term>Geber</term>, and <term>Thomas</term> <note>Referring to famous alchemists: Ramon Lull, the 8th-century chemist Jabir ibn Hayyan, and Thomas Aquinas, to whom alchemical works were often attributed</note>. Paracelsus means viscous Mercury, which he here calls "gluey." How that is prepared has already been shown by us earlier.

It is easy to understand what that red blood of the Lion is. For whether you mix the <term>Soul of the Sun</term> <note>original: "Solis animam," referring to the essence or "tincture" of gold</note>, or—what is of easier labor and the same effectiveness—the red, transparent <term>Quintessence</term> of fixed sulfur with the viscosity of Mercury: who does not see that in the <term>coagulation</term> <note>the process of thickening or solidifying</note>, the Mercury (since it has been glorified and refined) is coagulated not into a metal, but into something more noble, especially with a milder fire that does not cause it to melt. I do not believe a process either faster, nobler, or easier than this can be found in the nature of things.

### N O T E.

Theophrastus Paracelsus, in other places in his writings, understands "G L U E" to mean <term>Tartar</term> <note>original: "Tartarum," the potassium bitartrate deposit found in wine casks, often used in alchemical preparations</note>; which Ramon Lull also wished to suggest.

->*The end of this Paracelsian Tincture.*<-

<margin>
The method to be observed by which metals are reduced to Mercury.
</margin>
In this place, it is first necessary that we strictly observe the method by which all metals—but especially the two perfected ones, <term>Gold</term> <note>original: "Sol"</note> and <term>Silver</term> <note>original: "Luna"</note>—may be reduced into living and (if one wishes) running Mercury by themselves, without the addition of any other mercurial substance. This is an artifice that is otherwise quite hidden, yet it is possible and certain. Although there is more than one method for this matter, and perhaps one is better and faster than another, we shall now set forth the one that experience itself has proven to us, as witnessed by our own eyes and hands. That method and procedure is as follows:

<margin>
The method of making the Mercuries of the bodies.
</margin>
First, the metal must be dissolved into a liquid: Silver by means of common <term>strong water</term> <note>original: "aquā fortis," or nitric acid</note>; Gold, however, by means of <term>Royal water</term> <note>original: "aquam Regis," or aqua regia</note>, which is made if one ounce of crushed <term>sal-ammoniac</term> <note>original: "salis armoniaci," ammonium chloride used as a flux and solvent</note> is added to three ounces of common strong water.

After the dissolution, the waters are to be drawn off through an <term>alembic</term> <note>a chemical still or distilling apparatus</note> until an oily consistency remains; they should be poured back and distilled again, and this must be done a third time. Finally, the waters must be driven off with the full force of the fire along with the spirits. To the dry <term>calx</term> <note>original: "Calci," the powdery metallic residue remaining after the metal has been dissolved or burned</note>, pour spirit of wine three or four times, and likewise draw it off through the alembic. Place this calx into a vessel with an equal weight of crushed <term>salt of tartar</term> <note>original: "salis tartari," potassium carbonate</note> <margin>Mixing</margin> (others add a half-part of sal-ammoniac, as I have also done) and pour over it distilled vinegar so that it floats on top. Or, take the metallic calx and add a half-part of sal-ammoniac, and pour <term>oil of tartar</term> <note>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</note> over it so that it floats on top. <margin>Putrefaction.</margin> Leave the matter well-sealed in a <term>Mary’s Bath</term> <note>original: "Balneo Mariæ," a water bath used for gentle, consistent heating</note> to putrefy, or digest, for twenty days. Then remove the vessel and first take away all moisture through distillation. <margin>Sweetening.</margin> Afterward, once the material is dried, pour on hot water so that the salts in it are dissolved. When it has settled at the bottom, pour the liquid through a filter and add more water until all the saltiness is extracted and the calx is <term>sweetened</term> <note>original: "edulcerata," the process of washing a precipitate to remove soluble salts</note>. <margin>Sublimation.</margin> Dry this again, and once dried, <term>sublimate</term> it <note>to heat a substance so it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note> in a glass alembic with great force of fire. Mercury will then show itself: sometimes "living" <note>liquid</note>, if all the salts have been removed; but "dead" <note>in a powdered or crystalline state</note> in the form of common sublimated Mercury, if the salts were not removed. <margin>Revivification.</margin> But if you wish to have running Mercury from that which ascended "dead," mix it with calcined tartar and quicklime, and [distill it] through a retort...

### XII. OF THE MERCURIES extracted from bodies.

<margin>How the Mercury of a body, when not revivified, becomes a Tincture.</margin>
IF you possess the Mercury of a perfected body <note>Gold or Silver</note> not in its "revivified" (liquid) form, but <term>sublimated</term> in the likeness of Mercury: take this **snow of gold** <note>original: "aurinivem," a poetic term for the white or yellow crust produced by sublimation</note> (as <term>Augurellus</term> <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, an Italian alchemist and poet, c. 1441–1524</note> calls it), enclosed in a small glass vessel or vial, and cook it thoroughly in the heat of a <term>Water-Bath</term> <note>original: "Balnei"; a gentle, indirect heat using hot water</note> or in the heat of the strongest <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the process of breaking down matter through warmth and moisture to induce change</note>. Afterward, it is <term>coagulated</term> <note>turned back into a solid</note> in the proper fire and will gradually show the colors required in the Work. By this method, starting from the mere viscosity of the corporal Mercury, you arrive at a white or red <term>Tincture</term> <note>the alchemical 'medicine' or agent of transformation</note> that is highly penetrating and melts very quickly.

Truly, after your <term>Electrum</term> <note>here referring to the alchemical gold-mercury preparation or alloy</note> has been <term>corrupted</term> <note>broken down/mortified</note> in the manner described, and you wish to proceed further to reach the desired end:

### XIII. *Of MERCURIES extracted from bodies.*

<margin>The coagulation of bodily Mercury in the Medicine of ferment.</margin>
After the Mercury of the body has been prepared and resolved into its own viscosity by means of decoction <note>gentle boiling</note>, some of the Philosophers then coagulate it <note>harden it into a solid</note> not only by itself, but with an added **white or red ferment** <term>Ferment: In alchemy, a small amount of "perfect" gold or silver added to the "mercury" to act like leaven in bread, triggering the transformation into a stable solid</term>; they believe that in this way they can more quickly reach the point of coagulation. In adding the ferment, however, more than one method is observed by them, but especially these following.

<margin>Various modes of ferments.</margin>
Some join to it Gold, either in filings, or leaf, or subtly calcined and **reverberated** <note>heated in a furnace where the flame is reflected onto the material</note>. Others, by means of a **vegetable menstruum** <term>Menstruum: A solvent. "Vegetable" suggests it was derived from plants, like high-proof vinegar or alcohol</term>, resolve the calcined Gold and reduce it into a sliminess before it is mixed with the **Quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>, which they afterwards add to the viscous Mercury, and they coagulate them together.

Others **amalgamate** the gold <note>dissolve the gold into liquid mercury</note>. They grind the **amalgam** with **Cinnabar** <term>Cinnabar: Mercury sulfide, a heavy red mineral often used as the primary source of mercury</term> and drive off the mercury in a reverberating furnace; to the remaining lime <note>residue</note> they add new cinnabar, and again drive it off through reverberation. This they repeat so many times until the gold becomes

...of a red color, having some brownness, and they add this gold as a **ferment** <term>Ferment: In alchemy, a small amount of a perfected substance added to a base material to "infect" it with its own qualities, much like yeast in bread</term>.

Others extract the **tincture**, or the **soul** <note>original: "animam"</note>, from gold prepared in this way (or even prepared through frequent solutions), which they cook down with a viscous matter for the required time, until a complete Tincture is reached.

This final method, along with the second, is the best; however, the first and third are weaker.

<margin>Method for extracting the soul of the Sun <note>The "Sun" or "Sol" is the alchemical name for Gold</note>.</margin>Because the extraction of the soul is known to few, we shall also teach the method for it in this place, which is as follows. **First:** take Gold—either a solution made with **oil of salt** <term>Oil of salt: Concentrated hydrochloric acid</term>, or gold calcinated through the **reverberation** <term>Reverberation: A process of heating a substance in a furnace where the flame is "beaten back" onto the material</term> previously described (in the third method), or **leaf gold** very finely ground with **sugar candy** and then carefully washed. Over this, pour the following **Spirit of Wine** <term>Spirit of Wine: High-proof alcohol, used here as a solvent to pull the "essence" out of the metal</term>, and let it digest in a gentle heat until the Spirit of Wine is colored. When this is poured off, pour on new spirit and let it digest until it too is colored. Continue this until all the redness has been extracted from the gold, and the Spirit of Wine is no longer tinted. Mix all the tinted Spirit of Wine together, and draw off the spirit in a **Water Bath** <note>original: "Balneo"; a gentle heating method using hot water to avoid burning the substance</note>. A **red oil** remains at the bottom, which is the **soul of the Sun** <note>Anima Solis</note>. If you drive off all the moisture, it ends in a red powder.

<margin>How the soul ought to be mixed.</margin>If you wish to mix this soul, mix it while it is still in the form of an oil. For in this way, it will be mixed with the **viscous Mercury** inseparably, just as water is mixed with water. The remainder of the Spirit of Wine is easily evaporated with gentle heat; for viscous materials do not rise as easily as the Spirit of Wine, which vanishes first.

<margin>Tartarized spirit of wine.</margin>**Tartarized Spirit of Wine** is prepared thus: Wash finely ground **tartar** <term>Tartar: Potassium bitartrate, the sediment found in wine casks; when purified and heated, it was used to dehydrate and strengthen alcohol</term> and sweeten it with distilled rain water five times, until no acidity is tasted in the water. Over this dried **lime** <note>original: "calci"; referring here to the powdered, processed tartar</note>, pour the spirit of wine so that it may extract as much as it can. Distill this spirit through a **Retort** <term>Retort: A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</term> with a well-secured receiver, and you have it.

# PROCESSUS

...by its entry <note>original: "ingressione"</note>, and is multiplied with difficulty. Then it tinges only very few parts. This, however, is the method.

<margin>A twofold method of coagulation.</margin>
Some cook that **Mercury** <term>Mercury: In this context, not just the liquid metal, but the "spirit" or volatile essence of the substance being worked upon</term> alone without a **ferment** <term>Ferment: A substance, usually a precious metal, added to "ripen" or guide the transformation of the base matter</term>; others, however, join to it a ferment of the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> or **Moon** <note>Silver</note>. If a ferment is added, there is no need for great skill; a simple addition of finely filed, calcinated, or leaf gold as desired (in weight) is sufficient.

<margin>The method of coagulation.</margin>
Both methods are governed in the cooking in this way: the matter is placed in a glass vessel with a round belly and a very long neck. That neck is always kept open. The vessel is buried in sand, so that the sand covers the matter to the height of a finger’s breadth above the belly of the vessel.

<margin>The nature of the fire.</margin>
From the beginning, a slow fire is applied for a few days; afterward, it is increased so much that the hand cannot touch the vessel above the sand. If this fire is continued, within the space of a month you will find the matter red and **precipitated** <term>Precipitated: Here, it refers to the substance settling out of a vaporous state into a solid, heavy powder at the bottom of the glass</term>.

<margin>Fixation.</margin>
From this point, always increase the fire until it can endure even the strongest heat, and the matter becomes a deep red, not fleeing from the fire, but "rejoicing" in it <note>The author uses "gaudens" (rejoicing) to describe a stable substance that no longer evaporates or changes when heated</note>.

<margin>Calcination, solution, and coagulation or waxing.</margin>
**Calcinate** <term>Calcination: Heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term> this **fixed** <term>Fixed: A state where a substance is no longer volatile and will not evaporate when heated</term> matter for several days, as described in the **Geberic process** <note>Referring to the works attributed to Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan), the foundational figure of medieval alchemy</note>. Dissolve it, and then coagulate it again. The more often you repeat this, the better you will perfect it, and you will grant the matter a much easier fusion.

<margin>Multiplication.</margin>
The **Multiplication** <term>Multiplication: The process of increasing the quantity or the transmutative power of the alchemical medicine</term> of it is as follows: add new Mercury of a "perfect body" <note>Mercury derived from or joined with gold or silver</note> in equal weight to this dissolved, coagulated, and fusible Mercury. Regulate it through all the stages as before; it will then return to fixation in a shorter time, and you will find your matter increased in both power and quantity. When you have multiplied it a third time with the Mercury of the body, you will no longer need the Mercury of the body; it is enough to add common mercury that has been **sublimated and revived** <term>Revived: Mercury that has been purified through distillation or chemical extraction from a mineral state back to its liquid form</term>, following the same weight and governance.

<margin>The first method is more excellent.</margin>
Some, however, have used a more subtle method in this same governance, taking a longer time indeed, but achieving a more perfect operation. They enclosed the Mercury of a perfect body—either alone or with a ferment—in a small glass vessel, the mouth of which they stopped with clay, but not with a **hermetic seal** <term>Hermetic seal: A completely airtight closure made by melting the glass neck of the vessel</term>. This was done so that a place might be given for the "wateriness" of the running Mercury to breathe out, yet without any of its more noble matter vanishing.

<margin>Method of the fire.</margin>
They governed this with a slow fire, yet not so slow that the exhalation of the Mercury’s wateriness could not occur. These practitioners saw the matter gradually constricted and wrinkled into a black powder, losing its moisture, and falling <note>original: "decide-"</note> into a dead-like **lime**...

...to settle. For this matter, they did not yet increase the fire, but for a long time they cooked it with the first heat, until, after the succession of colors had passed, they saw a certain most brilliant whiteness <note>original: "albedinem quandam fulgidissimam"</note>.

<margin>The increase of fire</margin>
And when they gradually increased the fire, the matter became fusible <note>capable of being melted</note> once more, in the manner of wax. They used this matter as a **white tincture** <term>White Tincture: An alchemical substance that has the power to transform base metals into silver</term>. But by increasing the fire a little more, they proceeded to a yellow state <note>original: "citrinitatem"</note>, in which the matter began to crumble into powder again. However, as the redness <note>original: "rubore"</note> arose, they managed it with a greater fire, and thus recovered an easy fusion, such that the matter was brittle and red like glass when out of the fire, but in the fire, it behaved like flowing wax.

<margin>The intention of these craftsmen.</margin>
These craftsmen guarded the **radical moisture** <term>Radical Moisture: The essential, life-sustaining fluid inherent in matter, which alchemists sought to preserve while removing "superfluous" water</term> of the **Mercury** from the beginning of the cooking, and they drove out only that moisture which was watery and heterogeneous <note>foreign or impure</note>. From this, a good thickening and a very soft fusion followed. <margin>Advantages of this Process. Multiplication.</margin> This process, however, is very tedious, so much so that it can extend to two or three years. Yet it requires no "solutions" <note>dissolving of the matter</note>, but after the first preparation, it is completed in a single vessel, with only one furnace, and a single regime. Likewise, it involves easier labor in **multiplication** <term>Multiplication: The stage where the potency and quantity of the alchemical Stone is increased</term>: it is enough to add to it an equal part of highly prepared common Mercury, and first manage it with a slow fire until blackness <note>original: "nigredinem"</note> appears; then with a slightly stronger fire until whiteness; and finally with a more intense fire until true redness. And this multiplication proceeds unto infinity. <margin>The management of fire is the sinew of this art.</margin> But because so much depends on the management of the fire, if anyone wishes to proceed by this path, something must be said specifically about that fire. For if it is too much, then all parts of the Mercury—both the homogeneous and the heterogeneous—are raised up <note>evaporated</note>, and no thickening of the parts can occur, but everything vanishes. Then, if it is too slow, even if the Mercury were kept in the fire for a hundred years, no true alteration could follow. <margin>The method of the required fire.</margin> Again, fire tending directly upward is more dangerous, as the more viscous part of the Mercury can easily ascend. Therefore, the Philosophers discovered such a fire which they called **dry vaporous fire** <note>original: "ignem siccum vaporosum"</note>, which either heats the vessel equally from every side or descends from above. For that fire destroys the wateriness and consumes it with its heat, and binds the homogeneous parts more tightly into one, from which a good thickening and coagulation necessarily follow.

<margin>Signs by which the fire is distinguished.</margin>
This fire, when correctly formed, provides a sign of a black powder appearing around the mass and multiplying daily. If the fire is too weak, the matter remains in the same state; if it is greater than what is right, a certain redness appears at the sides of the vessel; and if it happens—

But, the fire must be tempered; otherwise, you will lose the fusion <note>the ability of the substance to melt like wax</note> in the stone. 
And this is concerning the fire.

<margin>The ratio of weight.</margin>
The weight is entirely arbitrary, and it does not matter all that much. For one part of ferment, six, eight, ten, or even twelve parts of Mercury can be used. The less there is of the "body" <note>the solid metallic component</note>, the more penetrating the tincture will be; however, the coagulation <note>the thickening into a solid</note> will be faster.

### Fourth Use
# OF MERCURIES MADE FROM 
## perfect metallic bodies.

<margin>
XV.

The coagulation of corporal Mercury with the simple ferment of the Sun.
</margin>
Take three parts of the Mercury of the Sun <term>Mercury of the Sun: A specialized mercury supposedly extracted from or prepared for gold</term>, and one part of finely filed Gold <note>original: "Auri"</note>, and make an amalgam. 
Place this mass into a vial with a long neck; place it in ashes or sand, so that the sand rises a finger's width above the belly of the flask. The neck of the glass should be stopped with cotton. Give it a fire of the second degree <term>Fire of the second degree: A moderate, steady heat, stronger than a simmer but not yet a glowing heat</term>; and when a full month has passed, you will find a most beautiful red precipitate. In medical matters, this performs nearly the same work in the human body for "incurable" diseases as that which is attributed to the **Philosophers' Stone**. Its dose is from one to three grains.

<margin>Another method, but more suited to Medicine.</margin>
Or: Take the amalgam and place it in a vial whose neck enters the belly to the length of a finger joint. Place this vessel on its side and cover it with sand, yet in such a way that at the top of the belly, a small piece of glass remains uncovered, about the width of half a berry. Give it a fire of the second degree, and it is sublimated <term>Sublimation: The process where a substance is heated into vapor and then collects as a solid on a cooler surface</term>, and part of it is driven back down again from the top by the heat. Every day the neck must be turned around, so that the part which was uncovered is turned to the bottom, and the bottom of the belly stands out above. In this way, it can remain in continuous sublimation until its full precipitation and fixation <term>Fixation: The point where a substance becomes stable under heat and no longer evaporates</term>. In this manner, some of the fusion is also preserved, which might be lost in the previous method. However, this latter method belongs properly to medicine, while the former method is more suited to the use we are primarily treating here. Let us proceed, then.

<margin>The method of augmentation.</margin>
After you have precipitated your Solar or Lunar Mercury with its ferment for the space of a month: then take it out and grind it. Furthermore, add to it a fourth part of purified common Mercury; that is, if the matter weighs three drams <note>original: "drachmas"</note>;

To this, again add a fourth part of itself (based on its current weight), and regulate it for a month. <margin>Reduction of the increase</margin>
Regarding this, if you wish to apply any of it to your own use: take some part, place it in a vial with a long neck in sand, as before, but add nothing more of Mercury. Give it a fire stronger by one degree for a month, or twenty days. Then indeed, coat the vial with good clay <note>a process called "luting," which protects the glass from breaking under high heat</note>; or take a glazed earthen vial made of the best clay: and place it in the fire, so that it may be ignited: just as vessels are held in the fire during the preparation of aqua fortis <term>aqua fortis: literally "strong water," a historical name for nitric acid used to refine and separate metals</term>, until it is completely fixed <note>original: "figatur," meaning the substance becomes stable and no longer evaporates or changes state when heated</note>, and nothing rises in vapor. Increase the remaining matter as you did before.

### PROCESSES OF CERTAIN ANCIENTS.
### From common Mercury, and the Sun or Moon.

<margin>Work from common Mercury, and the Sun or Moon.</margin>
Just as it was stated in the third use of corporal Mercuries, how they are coagulated from a flowing form into a tincture: that is also to be understood in exactly the same way in this place.

For in place of corporal Mercury, some have done similarly in all things with purified common Mercury. Therefore, so that we do not repeat the same things, we refer the reader to the second method of the third use of corporal Mercuries, where we have sufficiently discussed the management, colors, fire, and weight.

<margin>Differences between this work and that which is placed in the third use of corporal Mercuries.</margin>
Now, however, we will only briefly advise in what ways these two processes differ from one another.

First: one uses corporal Mercury <note>mercury supposedly intrinsic to a specific metal</note>; the other uses Mercury drawn out from a "perfect body" <note>the "perfect bodies" are Gold, referred to as the Sun, and Silver, referred to as the Moon</note>.

Second: This process first purifies the Mercury through sublimation <note>turning it into vapor and back to solid to remove impurities</note>; but the other, because he extracts Mercury from the most perfect bodies which are already highly purified by nature, has no need for the labor of purification.

<header>THE PROCESSES</header>

Thirdly: The Mercuries of bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" (corpora) refers to the solid metals, such as gold or silver, from which a specialized mercury has been extracted.</note> are coagulated more quickly because they were once a perfect body; this is in contrast to common Mercury, which was never a body before.

Fourthly: Greater caution is needed in the coagulation of common Mercury; for its watery parts are not as easily separated (being naturally entangled within the Mercury) as they are from the Mercury of a body, to which they have come accidentally through artifice.

Fifthly: So that the Mercury may be dried out more easily, some take equal parts of the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note>; they melt these together, break them down with a file, and mix them with nine parts of Mercury. For the Moon, by its dryness, more easily drinks up the moisture of the Mercury. In other respects, they behave equally.

Seeing the great difficulty in the coagulation of Mercury, and being ignorant of how to regulate the fire from above; and noticing also that there is a certain power in Saturn <note>Lead</note> to coagulate Mercury by its scent and smoke alone: some have devised a way to extract the most subtle and pure spiritual nature, clarified from Saturn. In this way, they might restrain the Mercury with a "double halter" <note>An alchemical metaphor for two different methods of stabilization working together.</note>: that of the ferment, and that of the soul of Saturn. The Process
</margin>

<margin>
Grinding

Place it over the fire of a lamp: and every week uncover the vessel twice, and if anything has risen [to the top], cast it back down to the bottom.

Cooking II.
Cooking III.

### The Soul of Saturn is extracted thus.

<margin>Extraction of the soul of Saturn.</margin>
Pour distilled vinegar over <term>Minium</term> <note>Red lead (lead tetroxide). In alchemy, Saturn is the symbol for lead.</note> so that it stands three or four fingers' breadth above it: digest for twenty-four hours, pour off the vinegar, and do as before: repeat this continually until you have extracted enough of the soul, according to your desire. Afterward, mix all that vinegar together, and draw it off in a <term>Water-bath</term> <note>original: Balneum; a gentle heating method using a vessel of hot water.</note>, and there remains at the bottom an oil, which is sweet, and is the soul of Saturn <note>This "sweet oil" is likely lead acetate, also known as "Sugar of Lead" due to its sweet taste, though it is highly toxic.</note>.

<margin>Various ways of using the soul of Saturn.</margin>
Some use this oil and pour it over an amalgam: others indeed draw off the moisture until the matter becomes like a crystalline substance and can be ground: others dissolve this soul repeatedly and coagulate it again by the removal of the vinegar, until it flows over a very slow fire like wax. And this method seems preferable to the others.

# THE SERIES OF TREATISES OF THIS
## *Chemical Philosophy.*

**I.** A true and unmasked <note>original: "non fucata"; meaning a demonstration without the usual deceptive or overly metaphorical language of alchemy.</note> demonstration of the threefold preparation of Gold and Silver, which is highly necessary for this Art.

**II.** A clear and sincere explanation of the true and correct method for generating the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and silver.</note>, or the Silver-making and Gold-making Salt.

To these are added ten Canons <note>Rules or fundamental principles.</note>, which constitute the Basis of the entire work.

It would truly be the mark of an impudent man, not an honest one (*Illustrious Prince*), to claim the works of others for himself and publish them as his own. Therefore, since I am not the author of this book which I dare to offer to **YOUR SERENE HIGHNESS**, but rather it belongs to another—who dedicated some of its parts to certain men before his departure from the living—I have decided to explain to **YOUR ILLUSTRIOUS HIGHNESS** the reasons for my plan regarding the publishing and offering of this book, lest I be considered a <term>Plagiarist</term> <note>One who steals the writings of others; a serious accusation in the Republic of Letters.</note> or be rightly accused of rashness. Roughly three years ago, while staying at **FRANKENTHAL**, I enjoyed a most pleasant friendship with **JOHANN BARTHOLOMÄUS BURGGRAV**, *Land-Scribe of Neustadt* <note>A local administrative and legal official.</note>, a man most distinguished in learning and piety. He had read my writings, especially the *Apology for Paracelsus against Thomas Erastus* <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583) was a famous physician and theologian who fiercely attacked Paracelsus and the use of chemical medicines.</note>, and other candidates who deny that **Metals**, in whatever way prepared, can benefit human nature. On one occasion, he asked me whether I had read the book of the most learned **GASTON** *Claveus* <note>Gaston de Cloves, a French lawyer and alchemist known for defending alchemy against the attacks of Erastus.</note> against **THOMAS** *Erastus*. When I replied that I had not, he not only offered me the book itself but even gave it to me as a gift—a lasting monument of our friendship—on the condition, however, that I should publish it for the public after reading it; affirming that its first part had hitherto been dedicated to no one. I accepted the condition along with the book and, setting aside all other matters, applied myself seriously to the reading. ...I have added annotations. And since I understood from a serious reading that the author’s intent was not to hide the book in shadows, but to share it with all the <term>sons of knowledge</term> <note>Latin: *scientiae filiis*. When I observed these things, I inquired of every <term>printer</term> <note>Latin: *typographis*.</note> I could reach whether they knew if it had been printed anywhere. When they denied this, I decided it was not right for the excellent labors of such a great man to remain hidden any longer, nor for students of **Chemistry** to be deprived of reading them. 

Truly, this age of ours is full of **impostors** who spare neither Princes nor men of the lowest rank. For I see Kings and Nobles being deceived by these <term>charlatans</term> <note>Latin: *Agyrtis*, a Greek-derived word for wandering quacks or swindlers.</note> who, selling fraudulent and <term>sophistical</term> <note>In this context, "sophisticas" refers to "sophistication" in the old sense: the adulteration or faking of metals to look like gold or silver without possessing their true properties.</note> chemical arts under a pompous appearance, swindle them out of their silver. 

From this, a huge number of both **deceivers** and **fraudulent schemes** arises daily. Because of them, the most praiseworthy art of Chemistry not only suffers harm, is suppressed, and is corrupted—rendering chemists themselves hated by everyone as they waste their lives, time, and resources on vain operations—but grave damage also spills over into the state. Such is the cunning of many that, through simulated experience in chemical matters, feigned friendship, and various promises, they fraudulently fish for secrets from others, claim them as their own, and peddle them around, only for these same "arts" to be bought by others for vast sums of money. ...for [I know] that such scoundrels have sometimes wrestled away handwritten commentaries on **chemistry** <note>Latin: *chymia*. But when I had thought long and hard about whose patronage I should use to win favor and authority for the book, the family of the **Landgraves of Hesse** came to mind, which through all ages has been the *Glory of Germany, the light of the fatherland, the House of the Muses, and the bulwark of Religion*. In that family those most holy Heroes excelled—your father and grandfather, the clearest lights of the Christian world—who did not hesitate to oppose themselves so often to the tyranny of the enemies of the Church. 

Indeed, I saw you as the heir and possessor of your ancestors' virtues, you who perform sacred rites to Mars and Minerva <note>A classical metaphor: "Mars" refers to military skill, while "Minerva" refers to wisdom, the arts, and science.</note> alike, and who easily surpasses all Princes in generosity toward foreigners. *I do not want it to be hidden from you that all the power and efficacy of the whole art consists in two words, namely,* **DISSOLVE AND CONGEAL**. <note>original: "SOLVE & COAGULA." <margin>A twofold solution.</margin>

# ON THE TRIPLE
## PREPARATION
### OF GOLD AND SILVER.

<margin>
The goal of Silver-making <term>Argyropoeia; from the Greek 'argyros' (silver) and 'poiein' (to make)</term> and Gold-making <term>Chrysopoeia; from the Greek 'chrysos' (gold)</term>. What the matter is in the art for receiving the form of gold and silver.
</margin>

The goal and aim of **Silver-making** and **Gold-making** is that silver and gold may be produced. However, it is necessary that some matter be provided which is in its "closest potentiality" <note>An Aristotelian concept meaning a substance that is nearly ready to be transformed into something else.</note> for receiving the form of silver or gold.

1. We have proven through the most evident reasons and certain experiments in our *Apology* <note>Referring to an earlier defensive work by the author.</note> that this matter is **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum," the metal we now call mercury.</note>, both the common kind and that which is implanted within the other metals. There is no need for repetition here, lest it be tedious. The testimonies of most illustrious men and others provide credit that this is most true—they who have seen with their own eyes a great quantity of quicksilver changed into silver and gold by casting into it a small quantity of the **Philosophers’ Stone**.

<margin>
On imprinting the form of the proximate matter.

The substantial form in any body is unique.

Substantial form is the "First Act."

Accidental form is the "Later Act."
</margin>

2. However, this **form**, which is to be imprinted on the proximate matter by the "efficient cause" (about which we shall speak shortly), is not *substantial* but *accidental*; there is a great difference between them. For the **substantial form** constitutes the principal part of a mixed or composite body; it belongs to the category of "substance," and the mixed body receives its name from it. It is unique in each of its bodies, and is properly called the "form."

But the **accidental form** does not constitute a part of the body, nor does it belong to the category of substance, but rather to the others <note>Referring to Aristotle's categories, such as Quantity, Quality, or Relation.</note>; nor does a mixed body receive its name from it. Many accidental forms can happen to one and the same body—such as quantity, quality, and so on. Such a form cannot exist by itself; it is always in some subject. It can be present or absent from that same subject—in reality, in the imagination, or in the intellect—while the substantial form remains unharmed. These include both primary and secondary qualities. That substantial form is the **first act** <note>original: "actus prior." In Scholastic philosophy, this refers to the fundamental existence or essential nature of a thing.</note> of a mixed body; the accidental is the **later act**.

Therefore, when quicksilver and the other metals are changed into silver or gold, their *substantial* form does not perish, but only the *accidental* form. Thus, the composite is not destroyed, but perfected. For the composite or subject is not destroyed unless something else is generated and a new substantial form arises. But since I foresee that many will contradict this opinion...

<summary>This page introduces the theoretical basis for alchemy, arguing that transmutation is possible because it only changes the "accidental" qualities (like color) of mercury into gold, rather than destroying its "substantial" essence. The author identifies quicksilver (mercury) as the primary material for this work.</summary>
<keywords>Argyropoeia, Chrysopoeia, quicksilver, mercury, Philosophers' Stone, substantial form, accidental form, Aristotle, alchemy theory</keywords>

--- Page 440 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical and chemical argument regarding the transformation of metals, specifically focusing on the Aristotelian concept of "forms." It follows the previous page's introduction of quicksilver as the "proximate matter" for creating gold and silver.</meta>

# OF GOLD AND SILVER.
### Dd 4

<margin>This perfection concerns the accidental, not the substantial [form].</margin>
Because two forms cannot exist in the same subject, I ask them: is the **substantial form** <note>The essence of what a thing is.</note> of an unripe grape the same as that of a ripe one, or is it different? I believe they will answer that the substantial form of both is the same, and they will fear to call it "incomplete." And yet, this grape is unripe until it can be perfected by ripeness or **maturation** <note>original: "pepanſi," from the Greek 'pepansis,' meaning the ripening of fruit or the concoction of humors.</note>. Therefore, this perfection does not belong to the substantial form, but to the **accidental** form.

<margin>What kind of corruption it may be called if quicksilver is turned into gold or silver.</margin>
But they will say: "That which was before and now is not, is **corrupted**." Therefore, they argue the prior form which was in the compound has perished, and now another has arisen. Thus they teach that **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver," known today as mercury.</note>, which existed before, is corrupted after it has been changed into silver or gold. To these people I grant that when quicksilver has been changed into silver or gold, a mutation—or if you prefer, a **corruption**—of the prior **accidents** <note>External properties like color, hardness, or state of matter.</note> occurs; the prior accidental form perishes, and a generation of other accidents occurs, and another accidental form arises in the subject. But the substantial form, or the "prior act" within the quicksilver, does not vanish because of this; rather, it persists. And the quicksilver or the compound, which was imperfect, is perfected. 

In this mutation of quicksilver—both the common kind and that which is implanted in metals—into silver or gold, not all the prior accidents perish. <margin>Which properties are specific and common to gold and quicksilver.</margin> For those things which are specific and common to silver, gold, and quicksilver do not perish, but persist. These specific and common accidents, especially between gold and quicksilver, are: that their compound is not corrupted or consumed by fire; that they are entirely free from **combustible oily moisture** <note>In alchemy, the "sulfur" that causes substances to burn; mercury and gold were thought to contain a "fixed" or non-burning moisture.</note> and burning; that their mixture into substantial parts is indissoluble; that they are of the greatest weight; and other such things.

<margin>What the accidental properties of quicksilver are.</margin>
But only certain accidents perish which do not belong to the property of the substantial form, but are accidental: that quicksilver is thin, liquid, volatile, and undefined; for since it was not thick, solid, fixed, and **concocted** <note>ripened or "cooked" by nature's heat</note>, it is now defined and perfected. This, therefore, is constant and settled: that quicksilver, whether the common kind or that which is within imperfect metals, differs from silver or gold only by its **accidental form**, and not by its **substantial form**. Yet this difference is not perceived by the senses through its functions, but by reason through the intellect. Once certain prior accidental forms are emptied—those which do not belong to the property of the substantial form but to the accidental—it can display all the functions of silver and gold, which are: to resist fires and to endure all their tests, according to the nature of each.

Enough regarding the **matter**, which is in its "closest potentiality" for the art.

<summary>The author argues that mercury and gold share the same essential essence (substantial form) and that transmutation is merely the "ripening" of mercury's external properties (accidental form). He lists shared physical properties like density and fire-resistance to prove their underlying unity.</summary>
<keywords>quicksilver, mercury, gold, silver, substantial form, accidental form, maturation, corruption, fire-resistance, density, transmutation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion from page 423 regarding the "forms" of metals. Having previously argued that the transformation of quicksilver into gold involves a change in "accidental" properties rather than the destruction of its core "substantial" essence, the author now turns to the "efficient cause"—the external or internal force that triggers this change.</meta>

# ON THE TRIPLE PREPARATION
### Page 424

...and concerning the form it takes on after it has reached its **posterior act** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "act" or "actuality" is the realized state of a thing's potential.</note>. For I have written many things about these matters in the earlier works I published.

<margin>The efficient cause in this art.</margin>
3. I have decided to treat the **efficient cause** <note>The agent or force that brings about a change.</note> more clearly, so that if anything regarding this has been handed down by us less suitably or truly, it may be supplemented and repaired here.

The efficient cause is that which, by abolishing the **accidental form** <note>Non-essential qualities like color or hardness.</note> from **quicksilver** <note>Mercury.</note>—or from that which is implanted within the metals—perfects it into silver or gold. Most have thought that fire and external heat alone are the efficient cause, because by purging it separates **heterogeneous** <note>Unlike or foreign substances.</note> things and **concocts** <note>A term for "ripening" or "cooking" a substance to perfection.</note> them. The author of this opinion is Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century philosopher and theologian who wrote extensively on alchemy and minerals.</note> in the book *On Minerals*, Book 4, Chapter 7. He thinks that not only from metals, but from every mixed body, three bodies can be elicited, in these words: "From all the aforesaid," he says, "it becomes somewhat clear by what reasoning many **Alchemists** <note>original: "Halchemistarũ"</note> assert that from every **elemented body** <note>A body composed of the four elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note> three bodies can be elicited: namely, oil, glass, and gold. For it is evident from what has often been observed that there is a certain fatty moisture in every elemented thing, which is poured around the parts. Because this is viscous, when the watery moisture vanishes, it distills from the burning roasted body, because it is driven by **roasting** <note>original: "optesin," from the Greek 'optēsis' (ὀπτησις), meaning baking or roasting.</note> from the inner parts to the outer parts, in which it was longer defended from the fire."

<margin>A certain fatty moisture in every elemented thing.</margin>
Furthermore, in every mixed body there is something moist, which is a watery part mixed with a subtle earthy part, so that each holds the other. And this, being very strongly roasted by **sublimating** <note>The process where a solid turns into vapor and then back to solid.</note> itself in the inner pores of the body (whose outer openings are closed by combustion), divides itself, as it were, into two. For the thicker and more watery part floats in the upper parts of the body, and through the strongest fire is poured out by the pouring of glass, and is congealed by cold into glass. But the more pure part, sublimated because of its heat, becomes **saffron-colored** <note>Yellow or gold-colored.</note> and is poured out by the pouring of gold, which is congealed by cold into gold. Perhaps some have experienced this in imperfectly mixed metals, but they have wasted nothing other than oil and effort. This can occur even less in quicksilver. Although **Geber** <note>A Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary 8th-century father of chemistry/alchemy.</note>, in his book *The Sum of Perfection*, handed down that it is coagulated and thickened by long-lasting fire. I think, however, that not even this can be done within three years. If, however, gold were elicited from imperfectly mixed metals, this change would occur through **corruption and generation** <note>A radical change where one substance dies and another is born.</note>. Yet it is not elicited through those, but through **mixture** <note>original: "mistionem," referring to a specific alchemical process of combining elements into a unified whole.</note>, as we proved in the *Apology*, and will confirm again below with most evident reasons.

# ->OF SILVER AND GOLD<-

4. Others have argued that all types of salts, alums, <term>vitriols</term><note>original: "atramentorum"; referring here to metallic sulfates used in industrial and alchemical processes</note>, and lesser minerals are an aid to the heat of the fire. From this, many types of <term>cements</term><note>A "cement" in this context is a dry refining paste used to purify precious metals through heat.</note> and many so-called <term>graduations</term><note>Processes intended to "upgrade" a metal's quality, color, or purity.</note> have been invented using sharp and extremely potent distilled waters <note>Strong acids like nitric or sulfuric acid.</note>. But because all these things are not made of the same "matter" as metals, they do not mix with them any more than fire does on its own. They do not bring the work to perfection; rather, they merely assist the heat so that imperfectly mixed metals are destroyed more quickly and turned into glass. For they consume the moisture and burn away the earthy parts.

However, I would not wish to deny that gold can often be drawn out from pure silver that has been exposed to a "cement" prepared from common salt and what they call <term>alkali</term><note>original: "vitri quam alcali vocant"; likely referring to potassium carbonate or similar salts derived from plant ashes.</note>, and then reduced back into a solid body; this gold settles at the bottom of the vessel or is separated by "sharp water." By repeating the work, the silver is purged and <term>concocted</term><note>Ripened or matured through heat.</note>, and its moisture is refined. Because it is excellently mixed, it cannot be torn away or separated from its own dry, earthy part. This same dry, earthy part, which is white in its current state, is red in its potential; through this "cooking," it becomes red and tints its own moisture into a lemon-yellow color. Truly, however, **these seasonings are more expensive than the fish.** <note>A Latin proverb meaning the cost of the process exceeds the value of the result.</note>

5. There are others, furthermore, who have placed this efficient cause in salts drawn from imperfectly mixed metals. They have attempted to mix these salts with <term>quicksilver</term><note>Mercury.</note> or with those same metals using the same cements and graduations. I would not deny that such a mixture can be made, since all these things share a common matter and fight with opposing qualities. However, I do not think they possess the power to "make silver" or "make gold."

I do confess that gold can be increased in quantity by cooking and refining a <term>malagma</term><note>An amalgam or paste-like mixture.</note> made of gold, silver, and quicksilver, mixed and covered with salt drawn from copper and iron—as I have handed down in my book, *On the Right and True Method of Producing the Philosophic Stone*. But this increase is of such small quantity that the expenses surpass the work. Therefore, if everyone who at this time is fruitlessly spending their labor and money on such things would take my advice, I would counsel them to spare themselves such great labor and expense and to begin to be wise—unless they prefer to remain wretched and beggars even after many years.

<margin>
What the true subject of the efficient cause is.

Silver and gold are the principles of generation.
</margin>

6. The true and natural subject of the silver-making or gold-making efficient cause is silver and gold. In other bodies or things, it is sought or hoped for in vain. Fire is the principle for generating and increasing fire from another body. Silver and gold are the principles for generating and increasing silver and gold within the **proximate matter.** <note>The immediate substance ready to be transformed.</note>

# ->ON THE TRIPLE PREPARATION<-

And universally, just as in the seeds of every species the power of nature serves to propagate itself, so too in silver and gold there is a power to increase themselves, albeit through a different kind of change than what is seen in animals and plants. For in those living things, the <term>efficient cause</term><note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; here, it is the active agent that drives the alchemical process.</note> first corrupts the other things upon which it acts, and finally changes and converts them into that same subject. Silver and gold, however, are mixed into "proximate matter," and they first alter it and then bring it to perfection. This force and faculty, or efficient cause, is a certain property which does not belong to the category of the elements, nor to their primary or secondary qualities, nor does it draw its origin from them; rather, it flows solely from the <term>form</term><note>The "form" refers to the essential nature or "soul" of the metal that gives it its specific identity as gold or silver.</note> of the mixed body itself. It lies beyond the reach of human senses; it cannot be perceived by taste, nor smell, nor touch, nor indeed by any sense, but only by observation and experience that has been truly established by long usage. Thus, it has been discovered through constant observation that fire does not beget a tree, nor an animal, but rather the powers and faculties inherent in every seed are the authors of generation and propagation.

<margin>External fire is an auxiliary efficient cause. The principal cause is silver and gold.</margin>
But if we said long ago that within the souls of these bodies, external fire and heat were the efficient cause, this must be understood as the auxiliary cause, not the principal one. This principal cause must be sought and investigated nowhere else than in the silver and gold themselves. It must be admitted, however, that the subject of the principal efficient cause can neither be perfected, nor bring about perfection, without the support and labor of external heat.

<margin>Why gold and silver in nature do not act upon quicksilver and the remaining metals.</margin>
VII. But it is often asked: since that <term>silver-making</term><note>original: "argentifica"</note> or <term>gold-making</term><note>original: "aurifica"</note> power is inherent in silver and gold, and we have said that perfection is completed by their mixing with the "proximate matter," why do they not perfect other metals or <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> when mixed? For quicksilver mixed with gold in an <term>amalgam</term><note>original: "malagmate"; a mixture of mercury with another metal.</note> does not perfect the quicksilver; instead, the mercury is dissolved into vapor by fire (which nevertheless returns to quicksilver when cooled), while the gold remains. Likewise, lead melted by fire with silver or gold is not perfected into silver or gold; rather, the lead is separated in the test of the <term>cupel</term><note>original: "examine Cineritii"; a refining process where lead is oxidized and absorbed by a porous container made of bone ash, leaving the precious metals behind.</note>, while the silver and gold persist within it. This is not a useless question; indeed, it is one that reveals the entire secret of this art. He who is ignorant of its explanation must necessarily <term>stumble blindly</term><note>original: "cæcutire"</note> in practical work. The solution to the question is this: The "form" in every body is the first and chief efficient agent in which the power, faculty, and property are hidden, and through which it acts. But this form alone is ineffective for acting unless it is equipped with primary and secondary qualities as its instruments—not unlike an artist who can indeed imagine a statue in his mind...

<summary>The author explains that gold and silver possess an internal "seed-like" power to perfect matter, but this power requires external heat as a tool and the correct "instruments" to function. He poses a central alchemical riddle: why precious metals do not naturally transform mercury or lead into gold despite being mixed with them.</summary>

### ->OF THE TRIPLE PREPARATION<-

<margin>
Silver in its unaltered nature does not act upon metals and quicksilver.
</margin>
...is able to [conceive a design], but he cannot carve it into stone and make it visible to the eyes without tools. In the same way, the <term>form</term><note>In Aristotelian terms, the "form" is the essential nature or "soul" of a substance that gives it its specific properties.</note> of silver and gold possesses an inherent silver-making and gold-making power and faculty from its hidden property, but it is ineffective in action unless it is armed with active qualities. Therefore, silver and gold in their unaltered nature do not act on metals or <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: *argentum vivum*, or mercury.</note> when they are mixed with them.

Many have believed that the thickness <note>Meaning the physical density or solid state.</note> of silver and gold is the reason why they cannot exercise that silver-making and gold-making property upon quicksilver and metals. Thus, they thought that if the metals were reduced into a spirit and a thin consistency, gold could be generated from quicksilver and imperfectly mixed metals. For so sang Augurellius <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli (c. 1441–1524), an Italian poet and alchemist whose work *Chrysopoeia* was highly influential.</note> when speaking of metals:

> But if they do not bring forth offspring, and do not veil the rest,
> The cause is in themselves; for there the spirit, hidden
> Deep in the matter, which extends all life,
> Unfolds its powers from itself with difficulty, unless a vivid virtue
> Should bring these things out, lying hidden from the dense mass by the hand of man.

A little later he adds concerning the spirit of gold:

> Finally, even so, detained in the yellow gold,
> The spirit itself desires the hand of the craftsman, who may loosen the chains,
> And who may restore it to power by its own virtue.
> But if someone, hurrying, should ever unfold this
> With certain strengths, and afterwards cook it long over a warm fire:
> Continually he will behold—a thing wonderful to see—life
> Imparted to the gold through the long use of the seed:
> Nor will it fail to produce gold for itself from gold.

<margin>
The thinness of the substance of bodies is not the primary cause but an assistant.
</margin>
<margin>
The nature, reason, and order of mixing.
</margin>
<margin>
The first and principal qualities.
</margin>
Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century polymath often called the "Father of Chemistry."</note> also teaches in many places that the reduction of different bodies into the smallest parts is the cause of mixing and true union. We, however, say with Aristotle that the thinness of the substance of bodies is not the primary cause of mixing, but only an assistant, just as other secondary qualities are not. For this is the order, this is the law of true mixing: First, that there be a mutual and mathematical contact of the bodies to be mixed, and that into very small parts; from this, that they act and <term>suffer</term><note>In natural philosophy, to "suffer" (passio) means to be acted upon or changed by another substance.</note> in turn, and that with equal and opposing forces. But the mixable bodies act and suffer through the <term>primary and principal qualities</term><note>The four basic qualities of Aristotelian physics: hot, moist, cold, and dry.</note>, which are hot, moist, cold, and dry: for the hot acting upon the cold, and the moist upon the dry, destroy one another. For only these principal qualities are able to act and suffer [mutually]...

To be effective in alchemy, these metals must be reduced to a "spirit" so their primary qualities (heat, moisture, etc.) can interact and achieve a true philosophical union.</summary>

### ->OF THE TRIPLE PREPARATION<-

...are mutually suited. The same is not true for secondary qualities, in the number of which are thinness and thickness. Indeed, it is most certain that the thinness of a substance brings great assistance to the primary acting qualities <note>The "primary qualities" in Aristotelian physics are Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness. "Secondary qualities" like density or texture are thought to be derived from these.</note> in their operation.

<margin>Form acts through primary qualities, and these through the later ones.</margin>
But just as the <term>form</term><note>The "form" is the internal blueprint or essence of a substance that dictates what it is.</note> acts through the primary qualities as if through instruments, so these principal qualities act through the later (secondary) ones. Thus, from the balanced conflict of contrary principal qualities within a common matter—which can certainly be divided into very small parts—there results a true mixing and union of different ingredients. Silver and gold themselves are less provided with the forces of heat and dryness than is necessary to overcome the coldness and moisture of <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: *argentum vivum*, or mercury.</note> and other metals.

<margin>The role and duty of Art is to make the extended degrees of the primary qualities more intense.</margin>
They are also of too thick a consistency for their parts to be able to penetrate the parts of those metals. Therefore, the role of the Art <note>In this context, "Art" refers to Alchemy—the human intervention into natural processes.</note> is to take the merely *extended* degrees of heat, dryness, and thinness in silver and gold and render them more *intense*. Thus, equipped with these as if with weapons, the silver-making and gold-making power and faculty can drive away a certain "accidental form" <note>An "accidental form" is a temporary property, like the state of being liquid or impure, as opposed to the "essential form" or true nature of the metal.</note> from the quicksilver and the rest of the metals, and summon a form suitable to silver-making and gold-making. In this way, and by no other means, true silver and gold are made from quicksilver and imperfectly mixed metals with the help of Art.

<margin>What the extension of qualities is.</margin>
The "extension" of qualities in a subject is the acquisition of some accidental form throughout all its parts, which previously was not in that subject or not in all its parts—such as when a cold hand becomes warm everywhere, in all parts or in some.

<margin>What the intension of qualities is.</margin>
"Intension," however, occurs when the degree of an accidental form already actually existing in the whole subject acquires greater power, while the previous level of heat remains the same <note>Essentially, "extension" is spreading a quality across a surface, while "intension" is increasing its concentration or strength.</note>.

<margin>The intensification of the powers of silver and gold.</margin>
Therefore, the powers of silver and gold will be intensified when the heat <note>The original Latin text here reads *coloris* (of color), but given the context of "heat, dryness, and thinness" throughout the page, this is almost certainly a scribal or printer error for *caloris* (of heat).</note>, dryness, and thinness of the substance already existing in their subject receive an increase.

<margin>The effect of intensification.</margin>
And the more intense these qualities are, the more promptly and sharply the silver-making or gold-making form will act upon the "proximate potential matter" <note>Matter that is already close to becoming the target substance, such as purified mercury.</note> and perfect more of its parts into the truest silver or gold.

<margin>Upon what intensification depends.</margin>
This intensification of the degree of qualities in silver or gold depends on their various preparations, which is the whole and principal part of <term>Argyropœia</term><note>The art of making silver; from the Greek *argyros* (silver) and *poiein* (to make).</note> and <term>Chrysopœia</term><note>The art of making gold; from the Greek *chrysos* (gold) and *poiein* (to make).</note>. Upon this, students of the same art must place all their efforts and all their labor.

This is the cause that urged us to prescribe the title to these newly published works: *On the Triple Preparation of Silver and Gold*. I know that many use many different preparations, which, if they are directed toward producing the degrees of intensification of the qualities in silver and gold...

It distinguishes between "extension" (spreading a quality) and "intension" (increasing its strength), identifying the latter as the core secret of making gold and silver.</summary>

# OF GOLD AND SILVER

...may be directed, well indeed. But those methods which rely partly on authority, partly on reason, and partly on experiment, we have decided to explain soon. We shall do so, however, in brief and concise words, so that such great secrets and mysteries of nature are not shared with the unworthy, the impious, and those who mock.

<margin>
The first preparation of silver and gold is the reduction into calx.
</margin>
8. The first preparation is the reduction of silver and gold into <term>calx</term><note>A powder or "ash" produced by heating a metal to a high temperature or reacting it with other substances; essentially an oxide.</note>. <margin>Calcined things become drier, thinner, and hotter.</margin> For whatever things have been calcined turn out hotter, drier, and thinner through this "cooking" process. <margin>The powers of heat, dryness, and thinness are more intense in the stone.</margin> The example is evident in the calx of stone <note>Likely referring to quicklime (calcium oxide) produced by heating limestone.</note>. Therefore, silver and gold—which possessed weaker powers before being reduced to calx and were ineffective for acting—are rendered effective for acting by the more intense heat, dryness, and thinness sought and obtained through this calcination. 

They are calcined, moreover, when an <term>amalgam</term><note>original: *malagma*; a mixture of mercury and another metal.</note> is made from them with <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury.</note> which is squeezed through leather; thus a sphere remains of both [the metal and the mercury] which did not flow out through the pores of the leather. Let something be added to the sphere which is of the nature of quicksilver (for reason does not advise [explaining] all things to the common people) and, once everything is ground and cast into a glass vessel, let them be cooked until, by the force of fire, the quicksilver and that which is of its nature have evaporated <note>original: *expiraverint*; literally "breathed out."</note>, leaving the calx of silver or gold at the bottom of the vessel. 

<margin>
What calcination is.
</margin>
This calcination must be repeated as many times as necessary until the calx has turned into a most fine powder lacking all luster <note>original: *omni luce carentem*; refers to the loss of the metal's characteristic metallic shine.</note>. Finally, <term>sal ammoniac</term><note>original: *sal armoniacus*; ammonium chloride, used in alchemy as a volatile agent to help transform metals.</note>—previously perfectly purified by <term>sublimation</term><note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid on a cool surface, used for purification.</note>—is mixed with their calx and is again sublimated four or more times, so that the calx may acquire an even greater degree of heat, dryness, and thinness. 

But this degree of intensification of qualities and preparation is weaker than the others. For the calx does not entirely cast off its metallic nature; it still tastes <note>original: *redolet*; literally "smells of," but often used to mean "retains the character of."</note> somewhat of its density, and in a melting fire, it would return to a liquid metal body. Therefore, not every kind of quicksilver is useful for silver or gold indiscriminately; rather, only that which is either "cooked" by nature and extracted by art from imperfectly mixed metals, or common mercury which has been rescued from excessive coldness and humidity—that is, having been sublimated often and adhering to the sides of the vessel as if dead, and then rendered "alive" and fluid again. 

The method of acting is to make an amalgam or mixture from three parts of either [type of] quicksilver and one part of silver or gold calx. Then, having been cast into a suitable glass vessel, let them be cooked first with a weak heat, and then with the heat gradually increased. You will then see the mixture take on various colors from time to time, until finally the mixture of silver calx and quicksilver has contracted an ash-colored or whitish hue, while the gold has contracted a red color, and both works have turned into a very fine and <unclear>impalpable</unclear> powder. And it is a wonder that the same quicksilver, from...
