# OF THE TRIPLE PREPARATION

by the mixing of different <term>calxes</term><note>A powder or "ash" produced by heating a metal; an oxide.</note>, they take on a different color toward the end of the "cooking" process. What is even more wonderful is the difference in density and weight between them, as we can see. For golden calx cooked with <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: *argento vivo*; mercury.</note> is denser and heavier than white [silver] calx of the same volume. However, anyone who perceives that the difference in color or weight proceeds first and most directly from the *form* of that silver and gold—rather than from the elements or their qualities—will cease to wonder. It should be noted that quicksilver skillfully drawn out from silver and mixed with golden calx is perfected into gold by a swift cooking. For that which approaches closer to maturity will offer less resistance to the silver calx.

<margin>
Second preparation.
Salt and oil from silver and gold.
</margin>
9. The second preparation is the reduction of silver or golden calx into a <term>fusible salt</term><note>A salt that can be melted into a liquid state.</note>, and from there into an oil. It is drawn out by art alone and by the method usually used for all mixed calcined bodies. <margin>The method for drawing out the salt from silver or golden calx.</margin> First, a <term>lixivium</term><note>original: *lixivium*; a liquid solution produced by leaching or "washing" the calcined metal to extract soluble salts.</note> is made, which, after being purified several times through a filter, is coagulated by gentle heat. That which remains after the watery moisture is exhausted is truly a salt, or possesses the nature of salt; this is detected by its taste, and it dissolves in any cold and humid liquid because it was hardened by dry heat. But just as mixed bodies of different kinds and species are endowed with different and various powers, so too are the salts drawn from them. Therefore, those salts extracted from silver and gold have <margin>Extracted salts are more effective than the calx of the same [metals].</margin> silver-making and gold-making power, but it is far more excellent and effective than the calx of the same metals. For by this preparation, they are delivered from the impure dregs. <margin>The nature of salt.</margin> Indeed, it is the purest earth, and it turns toward and is ennobled by a certain fiery nature. And the more these salts are purified by the filter and coagulated, the greater the powers they obtain. But so that a greater thinness may be granted to them, after many solutions and coagulations, <margin>How salts are reduced into oil.</margin> they are dissolved into an oil of their own accord by being exposed in a cold and humid place. In turn, these oils are coagulated by gentle, dry heat. This work is repeated again and over again until they can no longer be coagulated by dry heat, but persist as fluids—just as walnut or olive oil does not harden when exposed to a hot or cold place. These oils, when mixed with common quicksilver, perfect it into silver or gold in the space of eight days, using first a gentle cooking and then increasing the heat, according to the nature of whichever oil was used. The dosage is learned only through experiment. <margin>The power and faculty of the gold-making oil.</margin> Moreover, there is another power and faculty in this gold-making oil. For if seven ounces of quicksilver, perfectly purified seven times by <term>sublimation</term><note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collecting the solid deposit as it cools.</note>, are mixed with an ounce of the oil, and that which has been raised up and hardened by the force of the fire is frequently pushed back down, finally...

### OF GOLD AND SILVER

<margin>The sign of the oil's perfection.</margin>
...it will be fixed with the oil; and in a burning fire, it will persist as an oil, but once removed from the fire, it hardens like frost. One ounce of this coagulated substance cast into pure silver will perfect it into the purest gold. However, the quantity and dosage of the silver can only be determined by experience. For the more exquisite or negligent the preparation has been, the more or fewer parts of silver it will transform. The sign of perfection for both the oil and the <term>sublimate</term><note>A solid substance produced by heating a material until it vaporizes and then allowing it to condense back into a solid form.</note> fixed with the oil will be this: if a grain of either is thrown onto a metal plate glowing in the fire, it suddenly melts like wax without smoke and enters the internal parts of the plate, tinting it with a silver or golden color, just as oil very quickly penetrates paper. This oil is a "medicine of the second order" that coagulates quicksilver, about which <term>Geber</term><note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a 9th-century scholar; his "Sum of Perfection" was a foundation of European alchemy.</note> speaks in these words in his *Book of the Sum of Perfection*, chapter 26:

> "Quicksilver, since it is fugitive, requires a medicine from some inflammation that suddenly—before its flight—adheres to it in its depths, and is joined to it in its smallest parts, and thickens it, and preserves it in the fire by its fixation, until there comes to it a tolerance for a greater fire consuming its moisture, and converts it by this benefit into a true <term>solific</term><note>original: *solificum*; gold-making (from *Sol*, the Sun/Gold).</note> or <term>lunific</term><note>original: *lunificum*; silver-making (from *Luna*, the Moon/Silver).</note> substance—that is, gold or silver—according to that for which the medicine was prepared. And elsewhere he says: From this it clearly remains that from whatever thing its medicine is drawn, it must necessarily be of the most subtle and pure substance adhering to it by its nature, and of the easiest liquefaction, and thinnest like water, and fixed against the fight of the fire. For this will coagulate it and convert it into the solar or lunar nature."

<margin>What is subtler and purer than oil?</margin>
This oil indeed possesses all these properties and qualities. For what is subtler and purer than oil? What adheres more to <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: *argento vivo*; mercury.</note> than silver and gold—and especially gold? What is of easier liquefaction than the oil itself, which is fluid? What is of a thinner consistency than this oil? What can be more fixed than it, since it has flowed out from silver and gold, which all tolerate the force of fire? Indeed, the writings of <term>Raymond Lull</term><note>A 13th-century philosopher to whom many later alchemical texts were attributed.</note> teach nothing else than the method for making this oil from silver and gold, though by another way. For by distillation, he draws out "waters" from every kind of salt, alum, <term>chalcanthum</term><note>Vitriol or copper sulfate.</note>, and lesser minerals, and even from the metals themselves. By the sharpest power of these waters, he dissolves silver and gold (which have been previously <term>calcined</term><note>Reduced to a powder through heat.</note>), then coagulates them with a gentle fire. He says that the thicker and more effective part of these waters—which he calls the <term>spirit of the quintessence</term><note>The "fifth essence," the purest and most potent part of a substance.</note>—is fixed and united with the silver or gold and turned into oil. To this, he then mixes a sevenfold amount of perfectly purified sublimated quicksilver and, with repeated...

### ON THE TRIPLE PREPARATION

What is laborious for the ignorant and inexperienced is very easy for those who are knowledgeable and practiced. Furthermore, the oil prepared in our manner is free from every other thing or external, suspicious body; it is true <term>potable gold</term><note>Latin: *aurum potabile*; a legendary alchemical medicine consisting of gold dissolved in a liquid, believed to grant longevity.</note>, which is a most suitable remedy for many desperate diseases—if what they report about potable gold is true. <margin>X. The third preparation for extracting the spirit.</margin>

Moreover, this spirit attains such great and admirable powers because through this sublimation it takes on an ethereal and fiery nature, and casts off all impurity and earthy dregs. But the mass of our **Philosopher’s Stone** does not grow by quantity alone; rather, it increases in its strengths and faculties at the same time. This happens if the Philosopher’s Stone, having already been brought to light, is dissolved again into oil, which—after adding new **sublimated quicksilver**—is then carried up into a spirit by a violent and headlong fire, and is then gradually fixed again by the previous degrees of heat. And the more often this work is repeated, the more increase in mass and power it acquires. In this order of **solution, sublimation, and fixation**, **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy; his works emphasize the systematic repetition of processes.</note> says the secret is completed—a secret which is above every secret of the sciences of the whole world, and is an incomparable treasure.

### XII. 
It also remains for us to prove, by the most evident demonstrations, that the change of **quicksilver**—both the common kind and that which is implanted in metals—occurs through composition alone, and not by other types of change. We shall discuss this same composition a little more fully than in our previously published works. For there are many things that can be said against this view. 

First, every change is either in **substance** (called arising and passing away, or generation and corruption), or in **quality** (called alteration), or in **place** (which is properly motion, not change). Therefore, the change of quicksilver and the remaining metals into silver or gold must occur under at least one of these first three types of change, and not through composition. 

Furthermore, since we have said that gold reduced to **lime** <term>Calx</term><note>A powder produced by heating a metal; the "ash" of the metal.</note> can return to gold again through melting, this type of change would be **alteration**. But when that lime is increased by the addition of quicksilver, it would be **accretion** <note>Growth in size by adding more of the same material.</note>. Then, when gold is turned into lime, lime into salt, salt into oil, oil into spirit, and the spirit back into lime, all these changes would be said to be contained under the category of **generation and corruption**. 

To these and similar objections, we respond based on the authority of **Aristotle** and all other philosophers: this is **composition** <note>Original: *mixtio*.</note>, and it is contained under the genus of change, yet differs from the other species. For this to be understood more clearly, it must be noted that these specific conditions meet and concur in "mixables" and the act of mixing, which do not all meet or concur in other types of change. 

First, the things that are being mixed must be actual and separate by themselves, existing before they are mixed; from this, it follows that they must share a common matter. Second, as they touch and are mixed, they must act and be acted upon by one another through their primary qualities...

...opposing qualities. Likewise, in a mixture, neither component is corrupted or perishes, nor do they destroy one another; instead, each is altered, and the forces of both the **agent** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the 'agent' is the active force that causes change, while the 'patient' is the matter being acted upon.</note> and the **patient** are broken down on both sides and reduced to a certain balanced temperament. From this, the form of silver and gold may spring forth; the agent perfects the subject, and the patient undergoes the perfection. Finally, from these altered components, a body of a single form arises, reflecting the nature of both, which nonetheless is not strictly the previous subject of either the agent or the patient, but a certain "third thing." Therefore, Aristotle defines mixture as the union of altered mixable things.

<margin>
What mixture is to Aristotle.
</margin>

All these points must be understood regarding true mixture. Although Aristotle seems to have spoken about the mixture of simple bodies (from which a compound body arises), it is manifest that these rules have their greatest application in the mixture of our **silver-making** and **gold-making seed**, and of **quicksilver**, and of metals—which are already mixed bodies. First, all these things are actually separated by themselves and exist independently before their mixture.

<margin>
The common matter of all metals.
</margin>

They also share a common matter. For all things are essentially quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note>, but one is more perfect than another; indeed, we have proved that they differ only by accidental forms. They also struggle with contrary qualities. For the **seed** is hot and dry, while quicksilver and metals are cold and moist—if not in actuality, then at least in potentiality, as physicians say of medicines. Therefore, when they touch and are mixed, they act and suffer upon each other. They are also contrary in the thinness and thickness of their essence: the seed is thin, so that it may have the power of entering the parts of the quicksilver and metals, while the metals are very thick, so that in this quality they may retain the nature of metal.

Furthermore, in this mixture, neither is corrupted, nor do they perish or destroy each other, but each is altered. For after a perfect mixture, the **tincture** <note>A 'tincture' is the concentrated essence or 'seed' used to transform base metals into gold or silver.</note> of the silver-making and gold-making seed is visible in the changed quicksilver and metals; yet this changed matter remains quicksilver just as it was before the mixture, but now it is defined and **concocted** <term>concocted</term><note>The term 'concoction' (concoctio) refers to a process of ripening or perfecting through heat, similar to digestion or ripening fruit.</note>. Even metals changed into silver or gold remain metals, nor does the "genus" or category of metal perish in those changed things. Furthermore, the forces and faculties are broken down—both the active forces of the seed or tincture, and the passive and resisting forces of the quicksilver and metals—but the seed perfects by acting, and the metal is perfected by suffering the action.

Finally, what arises from this action and passion is a **mixed body**, and it is not the seed, nor the quicksilver, nor the metal as it was before the mixture; rather, it is a certain third thing, namely silver or gold, which possesses a unique substantial and accidental form: that is, a silver or golden form. And this third body in a certain way reflects the nature of both. These conditions, however, are not found in other types of change...

<meta>This page continues the technical philosophical argument from page 435, where the author uses Aristotelian physics to distinguish between "true mixture"—which is necessary for alchemical transmutation—and other types of physical change like simple burning or biological growth.</meta>

<page-num>436</page-num>

### OF THE TRIPLE PREPARATION

...experience demonstrates they agree. For those things which generate and corrupt, and those which are generated and corrupted, can indeed exist independently by themselves in actuality before the generation and corruption—such as fire and wood. Yet, those things do not share a **common matter**, and the same is true for animals and the food which is changed into them. When they touch one another, the fire acts upon the wood and the other agents act upon the food, and they suffer nothing in return; the wood and the food, however, only suffer the action, and they do not resist or react.

But if we were to allow for some **re-action** <note>original: *repassio*; in Aristotelian physics, this is when the object being acted upon "fights back" or affects the agent in return.</note> in those agents, it would only be introduced during the time they are acting. Once the reaction ceases, they return to their original strengths; just as the "heat" of an animal suffers something while acting upon food, but once the digestion <note>original: *coctio*; literally "cooking," the term used for internal digestion in ancient medicine.</note> is completed, it resumes its original power. 

Furthermore, that which is corrupted perishes entirely, and from a **Being**, it becomes a **non-Being**. Likewise, that which is generated did not exist before, and from a non-Being, it becomes a Being. For the wood which becomes fire through burning is corrupted, and fire is generated. There occurs, as they say, a **resolution of all accidents to prime matter** <note>This means all the specific qualities of the wood (its brown color, its hardness, its smell) are stripped away until only the formless "first matter" remains to be shaped into fire.</note>, and no quality is seen in the newly generated thing that was in the corrupted thing before it perished. Therefore, we do not say that wood is "mixed" with fire. 

Nor in either generation or corruption are the powers or qualities of the generator or corruptor (and the corrupted and generated) broken down on both sides; rather, the former remain, while the latter perish. Nor does a "third thing" arise from the action of the corrupting and generating forces that smells of the nature of both. Instead, either the corrupted is changed entirely into the generator—as wood into fire and food into the body of an animal—or, if the forces are equal, both are destroyed and a third thing is generated that is foreign to the nature of both. This is seen in simple bodies when, from water and fire, they are resolved into smoke and ashes, and air is formed, or in compound bodies when they are resolved by fire. For these, once resolved, perish, and nothing of the previous qualities remains.

The same reasoning for this difference applies to that species of change called **augmentation** or **increase** (and in animals and plants, **nourishment**), as distinct from the species of change called **mixture**, insofar as one looks at the change of that which is nourished. For something is corrupted and it is called a "partial generation," but that which is increased, nourished, or diminished remains the same body after the growth, nourishment, or reduction as that which existed before.

<margin>
The difference between alteration and mixture.
</margin>

The difference between **alteration** and **mixture** is that the qualities that undergo alteration are **accidents** <note>Qualities like color or temperature that cannot exist without a physical object to "hold" them.</note> and can never exist separately by themselves, but always cling to substances; therefore, they are not "mixed."

<margin>
Mixture of substances; alteration of accidents.
</margin>

But the substances that are mixed are separate and exist independently, such as **silver-making** or **gold-making seed**, and **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>, and metals that are imperfectly mixed.

<margin>
What true mixture is.
</margin>

For true mixture is cor- <meta>catchword: est cor- (continues as "is the union...")</meta>

This is partly because the calx, through various alterations, possesses a different nature, power, and quality than unaltered silver and gold; and specifically because the quicksilver is not destroyed in the mixture with this calx, but is instead perfected. From the mixture of both, a certain "third thing" results, which is neither calx nor quicksilver, but a powder that will melt into silver or gold through fusion. Furthermore, this same powder, by a longer and more vehement digestion <note>original: *coctione*; literally "cooking," referring to the application of steady heat to mature a substance.</note>, could become calx again before it is melted. Indeed, for all the same reasons we mentioned regarding the growth in quantity alone of both the calx and the oil, or the Philosopher's Stone and the gold-making salt in both quantity and power, these things pertain more to mixture than to accretion. And as for the change of quicksilver and other metals into silver or gold by means of the oil of gold or the Philosopher’s Stone, it is more truly and conspicuously said to happen through mixture. For the oil and the Philosopher’s Stone are further removed from the nature of silver and gold than the calx is.

<margin>
Oil and the Philosopher’s Stone are further from the nature of silver and gold than calx.
</margin>
But if we must consider the nature of the change in those things being mixed before they are actually joined, we must concede that the change of silver or gold into calx, oil, or the Philosopher’s Stone is merely an alteration <note>An "alteration" (*alteratio*) in natural philosophy is a change in quality (like color or temperature) that does not change the essential identity of the substance.</note>. In the same way, if the change of quicksilver and the rest of the metals into silver and gold is considered by the mind as something happening separately and without mixture, it would be only an alteration. But after the mixture is perfected, it is not merely an alteration of each part, but a union of different altered things under a single form of the mixture.

# ON THE TRIPLE PREPARATION

...by mass or weight, but by the effective power of force. This must be explained more clearly through a demonstration. No one doubts that physical bodies can be weighed on a balance, and that the judgment of the eyes can discern those which weigh more or less. But the primary qualities—namely hot, cold, moist, and dry—which exist within those same bodies, are impossible to weigh on a scale. Rather, their magnitude is judged solely by their power and effectiveness. 

Therefore, while one can weigh the physical body of both the "efficient cause" <note>The "agent" or the thing that triggers a change.</note> (that is, silver and gold, or what has been altered from them) and the "patient" <note>The substance that receives the action or is changed.</note> (that is, quicksilver and metals) on a scale, their qualities cannot be weighed at all. Furthermore, when these same subjects of the efficient and patient causes are mixed, it is not necessary for them to be of the same mass and weight. For even when the four substances of simple bodies—that is, the elements—are mixed so that a composite results from them, they are not of equal weight or mass. For there is more of the "earthy" substance in gold, which is known by its heaviness, than of water; there is less of the "airy" substance than of these, and less of the "fiery" than of the rest. 

But for both simple bodies and for mixable things that are mixed in turn, it is necessary that the contrary qualities be equal in degree, so that these same subjects may be reduced to a temperament <term>temperament: the specific balance of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that defines a substance's nature</term>. For example, if calx, oil, or the philosopher's stone are hot, dry, and thin in one degree, then the common quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, or that which is innate in metals, must also be cold, moist, and thick in one degree. If the former are stronger through many intense degrees of heat, dryness, and thinness, then it is necessary that the latter fight back with an equal number of degrees of contrary qualities. This

# OF GOLD AND SILVER

...while there is one [degree] of contrary qualities. One ounce of calx <term>calx: the powdery residue or "ash" left after a metal has been roasted or "calcined"</term> must be mixed with three ounces of quicksilver <note>original: "Argenti vivi"</note>. For there will be as many degrees of the active qualities in a single ounce of the acting subject as there are degrees of the passive qualities in three ounces of the receiving subject. But if there were a hundred, or a thousand, or more or fewer degrees of active qualities in a single ounce of the acting subject, then this single ounce would have to be mixed with a hundred, or a thousand, or more or fewer ounces of quicksilver. In this way, therefore, the equality of the contrary qualities must be estimated. However, no certain rule can be handed down for this proportion: it can be determined by experience alone and the judgment of the eyes. Nevertheless, because we have said that calx, oil, or the Philosopher’s Stone prevail with intense qualities of heat, dryness, and thinness, one must not think that they themselves have fallen away from a proper temperament. For that was said comparatively, if they are compared to the qualities of quicksilver and of imperfectly mixed metals. Otherwise, accepted absolutely and simply, those substances are most temperate, and all their qualities and powers are equal: for that reason, they are not dissolved by fire. Base metals, however, are subject to dissolution because of their imbalance <note>original: "intemperiem"</note>, unless they are reduced to the temperament of silver or gold and perfected by the benefit of mixing with them.

## XIV

<margin>Whether a silver-making or gold-making power can be drawn out from imperfectly mixed metals.</margin>
This may be asked: whether from imperfectly mixed metals <note>i.e., base metals like lead, tin, or copper</note> it is possible to draw out calx, salt, and oil, and from that oil a spirit be sublimated and fixed, just as we said is done from silver and gold. And whether these same things, when quicksilver and imperfectly mixed metals are added, can reduce them to a temperament and perfect them. Certainly, it is certain that those things can be drawn out by the same art by which they are drawn from silver and gold. But to reduce and perfect imperfect things to a state of temperament is impossible. 

<margin>The silver-making and gold-making power or property is implanted in silver and gold alone.</margin>
The cause is that the silver-making and gold-making <note>original: "argentifica & aurifica"</note> power or property is implanted by nature in silver and gold alone, which proceeds most directly from their unique form. I see that few or none have noticed these things which we have discussed regarding mixture; yet if these are ignored or passed over, it will not be easy to wash away the arguments of the Adversaries who attack this art, and those who set their hand to the practical work will necessarily walk like the blind. For those arguments which are brought against this art rely on a likeness to the changes seen in animals and plants, which are corrupted, generated, increase, or are altered. 

<margin>Altered metals are mixed and united with the subject of their efficient cause.</margin>
But quicksilver, or imperfectly mixed metals, are neither corrupted, nor generated, nor increased; rather, having been altered, they are mixed and united with the subject of the efficient and perfecting cause,

# OF THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE.

<margin>It requires easy labors and small expenses.</margin> ...or what I call the silver-making or gold-making salt <note>original: "salem argentificum aut aurificum"</note> have been or will be spent by men in good faith. Wherefore, as we said in our *Apology*, in the investigation of the craft of this salt, all other things having been cast aside, students of gold-making <note>original: "Chrysopejæ"</note> ought to bestow all their effort.

<margin>Why the Philosophical Stone is called gold-making salt.</margin> But lest we seem to labor in vain in the method of investigating and perfecting it, we must ask more closely why we name it "gold-making salt," and why, being endowed with this gold-making path, it perfects common quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum vulgare"</note>—or that which is within metals—into the truest gold. This, therefore, is the reason and cause.

<margin>From mixed bodies, many substances are drawn forth by art.</margin> In every mixed body, insofar as the method of mixing alone is considered, many and various substances are drawn forth by the ministry of art. These are generally divided into two: namely, the moist <note>original: "humidam"</note> and the dry <note>original: "siccam"</note>, because their matter consists primarily of water and earth, although they also consist of the substances of fire and air.

<margin>A mixed body consists of the moist and the dry.</margin> But the moist substance, like water, becomes thin and is raised into vapor or exhalation when fire acts upon it; the dry substance, however, like earth, remains and is fixed.

<margin>The moist is twofold: watery and oily.</margin> Again, both substances are distributed in two ways. For that which is moist is either watery, reflecting the qualities of water—namely coldness and moisture—or it is aerial and oily, reflecting the qualities of air—namely moisture and heat. Furthermore, both are distinguished by thinness and thickness: for that which possesses more earth is thicker, and that which has less is thinner. For the watery substance is not pure, but also consists of the substances of the other elements, namely air and fire.

<margin>The dry is twofold: pure, like salt; and impure, like dross.</margin> The dry is also separated into the pure and thin, and the impure and thick. For the pure and subtle part obtains the nature and name of "salt," reflecting partly the quality of earth (dryness) and partly that of fire (heat). The impure and thick part is like the dross <note>original: "fæx"; refers to the dregs or sediment left after processing</note> of the remaining substances, which is changed into glass when the heat of the fire is intense.

<margin>Heterogeneous bodies and those of weaker mixture are easily separated into various substances.</margin> We see that all these various substances are most easily separated in reality from bodies of a weaker mixture and those which consist of heterogeneous <note>made of different kinds of parts</note> parts, such as wood; but they are separated with great difficulty from bodies of a uniform mixture and those which consist of similar parts. For when wood is burned, a certain "alimentary humor" <note>the sap or natural moisture of the plant</note> sweats out, which is watery and thin. Once the flame is extinguished, the charcoal contains a substance that is partly watery and partly oily, though both are thicker. When these substances have been separated, the remainder is ash, from which salt is drawn out and filtered by means of a lye-solution <term>lixivium: a liquid produced by leaching wood ashes, used here to extract soluble salts</term>. For as the heat acts, the water of the lye goes off into vapor, and that which settles in the vessels is found by taste to be salty. But when the salt has been drawn out, the ash which remains is that which is melted into glass by the action of the fire's heat. This ash, through...

# THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE

<margin>Salt drawn from copper and iron changes silver into gold. The Practice.</margin>
...[they are able], by the power of salts artfully drawn out of copper and iron, to purge silver, to define its indefinite moisture, and to perfect it into the truest gold? For an **amalgam** <term>amalgam: *malagma*, a mixture or paste, usually of a metal with mercury</term> is prepared from gold and silver with refined **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo", mercury</note>, and that part of the quicksilver which flows through is pressed out in leather, leaving behind a solid ball. With these salts and **chrysocolla** <term>chrysocolla: likely borax or a similar salt used as a flux in soldering and smelting</term> added, the mass is wrapped in an earthenware vessel. It is concocted here first with a weak heat, then with the heat gradually increased, and finally it is melted with a more vehement fire. That which settles at the bottom of the earthenware vessel is called the **regulus** <term>regulus: the "little king," a pure metallic button found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</term>; it is a solid mass which, when exposed to the royal test of **cementation** <note>original: "cæmenti examini". Cementation was a dry refining process used to separate gold from silver and base metals using heat and salts.</note>, is purged, and what remains is entirely gold. Thus silver is changed and perfected into gold. Nor does the cause of this perfection arise from anywhere else than from the quality of the salts of copper and iron, even though the gold and quicksilver also assist. However, these salts are to be esteemed as nothing if they are compared with our **gold-making salt**, about whose power and faculty I shall say more a little later.

<margin>Nature, unless aided by art, cannot provide the stone.</margin>
<margin>Nature is the teacher of this art.</margin>
<margin>The order of things to be discussed.</margin>
Now, therefore, we shall approach the account of this gold-making salt, or gold-making stone, or the **Philosophers' Stone**. For Nature alone, unless aided by **Art** <note>In this context, "Art" refers to alchemy and human technological skill.</note>, has denied us the possession of it. Indeed, this could be more solidly demonstrated by one skilled in the art who might teach it in person than it could be confirmed by reasons. For this art is among those which do not command faith except by the testimony of the eyes and the other senses, when the effects of the gold-making salt are demonstrated in actual fact. But since there are few who have learned the precepts of the art, fewer who have handed it down truly and openly in writing, and very few or none who wish to demonstrate it in actual practice, teachers must be summoned from elsewhere—teachers who may not only teach the precepts of the art but also show how to truly discern and judge all those things which have been handed down in writing by most authors. That teacher is **Nature**. By dwelling upon the contemplation of her power and her works, we shall never stray from the right path, especially in the investigation and perfection of our gold-making salt. Yet Nature herself requires the hand of the craftsman to supply her with material, while she herself performs the work. First, therefore, we shall focus on the works of Nature, by contemplating generally the causes, the order, and the method of Nature alone in the procreation of our bodies. Then, we shall state in which things we can imitate Nature and in which we cannot. From there, we shall declare the parts of the art, and finally, the method and manner of operating. These are the things I have proposed to treat in order.

# ON THE METHOD OF GENERATION
### PAGE 444

<margin>
**Matter** and the **efficient cause** are most especially desired in Art.
</margin>
...[physi]cal <note>original: "cam"; likely the end of *physicam*, "physical matters"</note>, since these things must be drawn from physical sources, and we have touched upon certain of them in our **Apology** <note>original: "Apologia nostra"; likely referring to a previously published defense of the author's theories</note>. I will only repeat this: that the **Matter** from which something is made, and the **Efficient Cause** by which it is made, are most desired. The former is passive, so that it may receive form; the latter acts and carves form into it, just as a sculptor carves stone or a seal impresses a figure into wax. Therefore, we will not linger longer on the knowledge of natural causes, but we will contemplate the order and manner of nature's acting more closely: for these things are of the greatest service to our work.

<margin>
The order and manner of nature's acting. **Univocal** and **equivocal** generation. The Heavens and the stars, so that they may produce seed.
</margin>
Looking, therefore, most sharply at the order of nature—which she preserves in all this diversity of things which she procreates—we see first that she herself, in **univocal generations** <term>univocal generations: *univocis generationibus*; generation where the offspring is of the same species as the parent, such as a plant producing a seed for the same plant</term>, produces seed from something corrupted. However, in **equivocal generations** <term>equivocal generations: *aequivocis*; "spontaneous generation" where living things were thought to arise from decaying matter of a different kind, such as insects from rotting meat</term>, she produces a body that takes the place of seed, and finally she perfects both. And this is the inviolable order of Nature. For most plants and perfect animals first bring forth seed, which they then perfect. The heavens and the stars corrupt and putrefy some composite body: and from that putrefaction a certain moist body is produced, which is like a **seminary** <note>original: "seminarium", a nursery or seedbed</note>, in which there is a certain proportion of celestial heat, by which that very thing is perfected. But also of metals and minerals, and of all things that are birthed in the veins of the earth, the proximate matter is produced from the corruption of another preceding thing, which is afterwards perfected by the **efficient cause**.

<margin>
The difference of generation and corruption from **perfection**.
</margin>
There are, however, species of birth and destruction—or **generation** and **corruption**—that are far different from the species of **perfection** <note>In alchemy, "perfection" refers to the final stage of making a substance "noble" or complete, such as the transition from a base metal to gold</note>, which must be especially noticed, and which reveals the whole secret of this work. In every generation, whose companion is perpetual and inseparable corruption, the body from which the seed is produced is not changed entirely into seed, but only the purer portion. Plants and animals bring forth their seeds from food: for every seed is a useful **excrement** <term>excrement: *excrementum*; in early science, any substance separated or secreted by the body, not necessarily waste</term> of food. So too, the body from whose corruption animals are birthed is not changed entirely into the nursery of animals, but only a certain portion. And when fire is generated from wood, the whole substance of the wood is not turned into fire, but only the aerial portion: the watery substance vanishes, and the earthy settles as ash.

<margin>
What seed is. Generation is from non-being to being. Resolution to the **primary matter**.
</margin>
Furthermore, there is the generation of a **substance** which previously was not, or from non-being to being. In the corruption of a mixed body, there occurs a **resolution** <note>the breaking down of a substance into its base components</note> of substances to the **primary matter** <term>primary matter: *materia prima*; the formless, fundamental base material of the universe from which the four elements arise</term>, that is, to the **elements** from which the mixed body was composed; but in generation, a mixing of those same separated elements occurs. But when the seed, or that which takes the place of the seed, is perfected, nothing is lost from the quantity of the seed; indeed, it is usually increased. For when an egg is hatched, once the shell is broken, it leaves nothing in the shell, but the whole...

It navigates the philosophical debate between Jean Fernel and Julius Scaliger regarding whether "form" (the essence of a thing) exists within the seed or enters it from the outside.</meta>

# OF THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE
### PAGE 445

<margin>
What occurs in **perfection**, and what does not.
</margin>
...then it is found changed into a chick. When the offspring of animals are brought to **perfection** <term>perfection: *perfectione*; in this context, the state of being fully formed or completed</term>, none of their substance is lost; rather, they are increased. When the substance of a seed is perfected, it remains the same as it was before, and there is no change from "Non-Being" to "Being." In the process of perfection, no dissolution or separation of substances occurs; instead, all parts persist without loss, even though they are changed—just as in an egg when a chick is formed from it. In short, **generation**, **corruption**, and **perfection** are all directed toward different ends.

<margin>
Objections.
</margin>
I know that many will rise up against this opinion, for they will deny that the seed is "perfected." Instead, they will argue that the seed is **corrupted** <term>corruption: *corrumpi*; the philosophical idea that for a new form to arise, the old form must be destroyed</term>, and the animal is generated from that corrupted seed. For when an animal is generated, it did not exist before, and the seed which existed previously is destroyed and is no longer there. From this arises that most famous debated question: whether the **soul** of a dog—which is its **form**—exists within the seed. Does it exist there in *actuality*, or only in *potential*? Is the form of the seed and the form of the animal born from it the same? Or is there one form for the seed and another for the dog that arises from it? 

<margin>
The opinion of **Fernelius**.
</margin>
**Fernelius of Amiens** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a highly influential French physician and philosopher</note>, that greatest philosopher and physician, speaking through the character of **Eudoxus** while disputing against **Brutus** in the first book of *On the Hidden Causes of Things* <note>original: "de abditis rerum causis"</note>, contends with many reasons and arguments that not even the smallest bit of "form" pre-exists in the matter. Instead, he argues that when the matter has reached its highest state of preparation, the form enters immediately and in an instant from the outside, as if by some inevitable necessity.

<margin>
The opinion of **Jul. Scaliger**.
</margin>
**Julius Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a celebrated Italian scholar known for his scientific and philosophical commentaries</note>, a most subtle philosopher, argues that this opinion is overly ambitious. With most evident reasons and by the authority of **Aristotle**, he seems to confirm that the soul or form of a dog is *actually* in the canine seed. He argues that the canine seed is simply an "imperfect dog," and that the seed is perfected by the soul or form of the dog, which is the principal part of the dog's substance, acting as the **efficient cause**.

<margin>
How **Form** is perceived.
</margin>
He argues that this "dog-form" or soul is not perceived by the functions of the senses, but by the reason through the intellect. Likewise, the form of a bird is actually in the egg, but the egg is simply an "imperfect bird." The egg is not destroyed while the hen sits upon it; rather, it is perfected. This is the same for all other seeds. 

<margin>
The **Author's** opinion.
</margin>
If I may interpose my own view among such clashing opinions of most famous men, I would think it necessary to say 

<margin>
How **Form** is to be considered.
</margin>
that **form** must be considered as either a **prior act** or a **posterior act**.

The **prior act** constitutes the form itself; for "act" is form, which cannot be called "begun" or "imperfect," since physical substances do not admit of being "more" or "less" <note>This refers to the Aristotelian principle that a thing is either entirely a specific substance or it is not; you cannot be "more human" or "less human" in essence</note>, as is confirmed in the study of physics.

<margin>How the **form** is made in the seed.</margin>
...the later **act** <term>act: *actus*; in Aristotelian philosophy, 'act' refers to the fulfillment or realization of a potential</term> of the **form** <term>form: *forma*; the internal principle that gives a thing its specific identity</term> carries out actions and functions. A puppy does not yet reproduce, yet it is a dog in "act" <note>original: "actu"</note>; but when it has reached perfection in age, it will produce seed. Thus, we must say that in the seed, the form exists in the **first act**, but not at all in the **later act**. However, only when the seed has been perfected is the later act added; but the form is not "imperfect" because of this—rather, it is the seed or the composite that is developing. 

As for the objection that when a dog is produced from seed, it is a **generation** <term>generation: *generatio*; the process of bringing something into being</term> (since there was no dog before, and the seed ceases to be seed once it was there), it is to be explained thus: the **substance** of the dog is not "generated," but rather an **accident** <term>accident: *accidens*; a property or quality that does not change the core essence of a thing</term>, or the "later act" of the dog's substance, which is not a true generation. For that later act is a property and an accident which was not yet in the seed before the dog existed, but it cannot be called a "substance" because it is added to a substance and cannot exist by itself. Thus, when a dog grows, the form or the matter of the dog does not grow, but the dog as a whole grows. This question is indeed of great importance, even in our proposed business regarding **our gold-making salt**, as we shall soon add. For even if it is numbered among **equivocal generations**, it must nonetheless be judged in the same way as **univocal** ones.

<margin>How the soul of man is infused into him.</margin>
However, all men agree and unite on one point: that the **rational soul** of man was not previously in the seed in act, but is created by God and infused into the fetus from the outside, and that it is immortal. This opinion is most true and beyond all controversy.

<margin>Three orders of Generations.</margin>
Therefore, Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a famous Renaissance scholar and physician</note> establishes three orders of generations: 
1. One is **univocal** <term>univocal: *univoca*; where parents produce offspring like themselves</term>, whose parents are the efficient causes and produce things similar to themselves.
2. Another is **equivocal** <term>aequivoca*; where life was thought to arise from non-living matter or celestial influence</term>, whose parent is the heavens and the stars, and they do not produce things similar to themselves.
3. And finally, the **rational soul** of man, whose creator is God alone. When this is infused, the other souls that were in the seed—namely the **vegetative** and **sensitive** souls—are abolished, and this single soul remains, according to the opinion of the theologians.

<margin>Definition of **Perfection**.</margin>
<margin>Distinction.</margin>
Hence, **perfection** can be defined as the promotion of that which already exists in the nature of things and in the "first act" to the "later act," just as when a dog is made from dog-seed. Every perfection is said to be either **simple** or **comparative**. Thus, seed, spoken of simply, is perfect; but comparatively, it is imperfect. 

Again, comparative perfection exists either between substances, or between substances and accidents, or between accidents themselves. For example, in the **simple bodies** <note>the four elements</note>, the substance of **Fire** is more perfect than the substance of **Air**, because there is more "action" in fire; likewise Air is more perfect than Water, and Water is more perfect than Earth. In **mixed bodies**, man is more perfect than the beast; the beast is more perfect than the plant; the plant is more perfect than inanimate bodies. But also, every substance is more perfect than an accid...

# ON THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE
### PAGE 447

...than the producer <note>original: "reproducente"; completing the word from the previous page's catchword "ripro-"</note>, is more perfect, and some accidents are more perfect than others: Heat is more perfect than cold, cold than the moist, and the moist more perfect than the dry. <margin>The goal of perfection.</margin> Now, the goal and aim of perfection is twofold: one is to acquire a perfect power of acting <term>acting: *agendi*; the ability to initiate change or perform a function</term> which it did not previously possess, such as when an animal becomes capable of generating seed. The other is to possess a perfect power of being acted upon <term>being acted upon: *patiendi*; in Aristotelian philosophy, 'passion' refers to the capacity of a thing to be changed by an external force</term>, just as a man of mature age is more capable of enduring labor than an infant. However, this potential for being acted upon belongs more properly to inanimate bodies than to animate ones; for living things perform the duty of acting rather than being acted upon, while inanimate things are defined and characterized by being acted upon rather than acting.

<margin>Degrees of perfection.</margin> There are also degrees of perfection: for a man of mature age reproduces, but neither an infant nor one worn out by old age does so. Yet we do not place these degrees of perfection in the **form** <term>form: *forma*; the internal blueprint or soul of a thing</term> itself; for the soul of an infant does not, in itself, act more or less than the soul of a man. Rather, it acts more sharply or more dully through the **later act** <term>later act: *actus posterior*; the full expression or active operation of a nature</term>, which is a property and an **accident** <term>accident: *accidens*; a characteristic that can change without altering the core essence of the subject</term>. All these things must be very carefully noted.

<margin>The manner of perfection.</margin> Indeed, the manner in which perfection arises from a seed already produced by nature is explained by **concoction** <term>concoction: *concoctio*; a ripening or "cooking" process driven by internal heat</term>. For according to Aristotle, concoction is a perfection brought about by natural heat from passive opposites; these passive qualities are the underlying matter of each thing, such as the seed. <margin>Three species of concoction.</margin> There are three species of this concoction: **Pepansis** <note>original: "Pepansis"</note> or ripening, which is the concoction of the moisture existing and undefined within the moist seed, performed by natural heat. **Ephesis** <note>original: "Ephesis"</note>, or boiling <term>boiling: *elixatio*; cooking or refining through moist heat</term>, which is the concoction of the boundless moisture in the moist seed by means of moist heat.

**Optesis** <note>original: "Optesis"</note>, or roasting <term>roasting: *assatio*; refining through dry heat</term>, which is the concoction of that same boundless moisture by dry heat. All these concoctions occur both by nature and by art; however, ripening belongs more to nature, while the others belong to art. These terms are used either literally or metaphorically; whoever desires more on this should consult Aristotle’s *Meteorology*, Book IV. <margin>The natural manner of concocting.</margin> This manner of acting, perfecting, and concocting the seeds of plants and animals is known to nature alone. For the instrument of that nature (or soul) is the **natural heat** <term>natural heat: *calor naturalis*; an innate vital heat that alchemists believed mirrored the influence of the stars</term> which corresponds in proportion to the element of the stars, which art cannot imitate. However, things are different in inanimate bodies, which possess only the logic of mixture—as in the seed of our **gold-making salt** <term>gold-making salt: *salis nostri aurifici*; likely a reference to the "Salt of the Philosophers," a key reagent in the Great Work</term> and in the perfecting of metals, as we demonstrated in the *Apology*, and as will hereafter be more clear, God willing.

These things having been so explained regarding the works which nature produces from itself without the help of any art, we must next ask whether account must be taken of all of them, both in our gold-making salt as well as in...

# ON THE METHOD OF GENERATION
## PAGE 448

...in the procreation of gold <note>original: "auri-ri procreatione"; completing the word from the previous page's catchword</note>, which is not achieved by nature alone, but by art acting as an assistant and provider to nature. We must consider in which aspects art imitates nature, and in which it does not. In these matters, Art follows in the footsteps of Nature. Just as Nature performs nothing without matter or a subject, neither does art.

<margin>In which ways art imitates nature. Matter.</margin>
For in every work, whether of nature or of art, **Matter** is sought first. This Matter is either "remote" <note>primary raw materials</note> or "proximate," which is the **seed**, or that which takes the place of the seed. But the remote must be reduced to the proximate; which is to say that, according to the order of nature, the seed must be generated first. Likewise, art does not seek just any matter, but the proximate matter—that is, the seed of the **gold-making salt** <term>gold-making salt: *sal aurificus*; a prepared chemical substance, often identified with the Philosopher's Stone in its salt form, used to "tinge" or transform metals</term>, or of the **Philosopher’s Stone**, as well as the gold to be perfected. Nor is the seed sufficient, for an **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: the primary agent or force that brings something into being</term> is required, which either carves the form into the matter (that is, generates the seed in which the form resides) or perfects the seed itself. Thus, once the seed of the gold-making salt or of gold has been sought, art investigates the proper natural efficient cause that may perfect it. The goal of nature is the **form**, or the perfection of the resulting offspring; such is also the goal of art. Nature’s method in perfecting the seed consists of **concoction** <note>original: *Pepansis*; the ripening or maturing of a substance through internal heat</note>, **seething** <note>original: *Ephesis*; a form of boiling or cooking in liquid</note>, and **roasting** <note>original: *Optesis*; cooking by dry heat</note>. The method of art employs types of seething and roasting.

<margin>In which ways art does not imitate nature.</margin>
Yet in these things, Art cannot imitate Nature: for Nature, when about to produce gold, brings forth its own matter within the mines, which is the seed of gold—which, according to the opinion of **Aristotle**, is a vapor mixed with a subtle, earthy substance. This vapor (or whatever else it may be, for authors do not agree on the matter) is either the subject or it is not the seed, nor can it be, for the purpose of producing gold from it. Instead, art possesses another seed drawn from the bosom of nature. Nature generates the seed and then perfects it; Art can neither generate nor perfect it alone, but can only assist so that it may be perfected. For Nature is the primary efficient cause, and art is merely the assistant. According to the decree of Aristotle, the efficient cause in Nature for perfecting metals is the **cold and the dry**. The efficient cause of Art is **heat**. Nature never produced the gold-making salt alone, nor could it do so, because it does not employ fiery heat. Art assists nature so that the gold-making salt may be produced by a natural efficient cause.

Nature generates gold in the mines over a long span of time; but as for the other metals and **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: *argentum vivum*; mercury, considered in alchemy to be the metallic "seed" or "womb" of all metals</term>, which are the seed of gold, nature—or rather, that which has its origin in a natural thing, namely the fusible gold-making salt—perfects them in a moment through **projection** <term>projection: *projectio*; the final alchemical act of casting the Stone or "salt" onto molten base metal to instantly transform it into gold</term>, with the aid of fire, which is also natural. However, the assistance of Art was necessary in the preparation of that gold-making salt.

The tasks of Art, therefore, are to investigate the seed, both for our salt...

Yet the generosity of nature has offered both to us of her own accord, and we have them in our hands. <margin>What the seed of the stone and of gold is.</margin> For gold and its own quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note>, as I will soon set forth, are the seed of the gold-making salt; and quicksilver and the remaining metals are the seed of gold. But nature has left those seeds of the gold-making salt and of gold imperfect, nor has she proceeded further; rather, art assists the same nature so that they may be perfected. <margin>Nature’s generosity</margin> Nor has nature provided the efficient cause with less generosity—indeed, she has been quite lavish—than she has the seeds. For this efficient cause is fire and external heat, which must be administered in a certain proportion and by determined degrees of heat throughout the progress of the work. In all the smallest bodies, which are perfected by mixture alone, the general efficient cause is fire. And this fire is natural, and not to be sought further afield, but we have it, like the seeds, even in our hands. Therefore, we should not complain about the generosity of nature, which has produced the seed and the efficient cause, but rather about our own shameful ignorance if we do not know how to perfect that same seed. <margin>The goal of perfection varies.</margin> But just as the goal and purpose of perfection—or the "second act," which comes from nature alone—varies once the seed has already arisen, so too is the goal diverse in perfecting our seed of the gold-making salt or the seed of gold. For the goal of perfecting the seed into the gold-making salt is that we may provide it with the faculty of acting. Gold, which is part of the same seed, is imperfect; it does not act upon quicksilver or the metals, nor does it perfect them, except finally when it has been perfected into the gold-making salt. However, the goal of perfecting quicksilver and the remaining metals into gold is so that they may obtain the "power of suffering" <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "suffering" (*passio*) refers to the capacity of a substance to be acted upon or transformed by an external agent.</note>. The general methods by which these seeds are perfected are, namely, <term>Ephesis</term> and <term>Optesis</term>, which are named not literally, but by metaphor and analogy, as I have said. <note>These Greek terms refer to "boiling" (*ephesis*) and "roasting" (*optesis*), used here to describe the moist and dry stages of alchemical heating.</note>

For the indefinite and undetermined moisture of these seeds is diminished by concoction—partly by moist heat and partly by dry heat—and through the help of art, they acquire their "second act" <note>The final, realized state of a substance.</note> for themselves. There is, however, far more art required in perfecting the seed of the gold-making salt than in perfecting metals or quicksilver into gold. <margin>Metals are perfected through the Stone by projection alone, with the help of fire.</margin> For these latter are perfected into the purest gold immediately by the action of fire, through the mere **projection** <note>The act of throwing a small amount of the Philosopher's Stone onto a molten base metal to transform it.</note> of the same gold-making salt. ...-nished, it is digested and brought to its end, and thus it passes into gold.

But the seed of our gold-making salt requires longer labor and a span of time to be perfected. Concerning the method of procedure, I shall speak a little more fully later, God willing, when I reveal the complete practice. But why gold is the seed of our gold-making salt—not alone, but as a part of it—and why quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note> is mixed with it, must now be discussed.

<margin>Why it is joined to gold in the work.</margin> Truly, gold must be the primary part of the seed, since we have proved that one end of *Chrysopoeia* <note>original: *Chrysopœjæ*; the art of making gold</note> is the transformation of gold into salt; this is urged by the authority of all who have truly and seriously engaged in this art, and confirmed by reason. However, that gold alone is not the matter of our seed is evident from the fact that, by itself, it can neither be corrupted <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to the breakdown of a substance's form so it can be reborn in a higher state.</note> nor further perfected by any art.

<margin>Every birth begins from the moist and ends in the dry.</margin> Then indeed, because every birth takes its beginning from the moist and ends in the dry: as we see that all seeds of animals are first moist and then dry, and experience itself teaches that the same happens with fruits. Since gold is actually dry in its current state, and cannot attain greater perfection within the nature of gold, our predecessors judged—and rightly so—that gold must first be dissolved into a liquid, so that it may then be acted upon by an agent to be perfected. For although the matter of gold is simply perfect, it is nevertheless imperfect when compared to that same matter once it has been changed into a liquid; for by this dissolution, there occurs an expansion of the substance’s subtlety and thinness, and an intensification of the acting qualities.

<margin>Gold in its own nature is not yet a part of the gold-making seed.</margin> Therefore, gold in its natural state is not yet part of our gold-making seed, but becomes so only after it has been changed into a moist substance. But neither is this dissolved substance of gold the whole matter of the seed, as I said, but only a part; it cannot be changed into a liquid, nor be perfected once changed, without the mixture of another moisture. This is no different than a grain of wheat sown in the earth, which can neither put forth a moist sprout nor perfect and propagate itself without the mixture of the surrounding moisture. Therefore, the moisture which dissolves gold into a moist substance is the other substantial part of our gold-making seed, and both mixed together are the seed itself, which needs only digestion <note>original: *concoctione*; the process of "cooking" or maturing through heat</note> to be perfected. But while the professors of this art agree with one voice that the substance of gold dissolved into a liquid is one part of the seed, they conversely differ most greatly regarding the other part of the same seed—namely, what that substance is which has the power to dissolve gold.

<margin>Diverse opinions of the Philosophers.</margin> Some have prolifically claimed that these are waters distilled by art from minerals, others from animals, others from vegetables, and others from a mixture of all these. And many things written here and there by Raymond Lull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher; many alchemical texts were attributed to him in the Renaissance.</note> seem to say nothing else, provided that...

# OF THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE

...whether the author of these things is <term>Lullius</term> <note>original: "Lullius"; referring to Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316), a famous philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical works were falsely attributed.</note>, or rather they are ascribed to him, they cannot at all agree with those and others of this same opinion. For the moisture that dissolves gold should not be corrupted or changed from the fluid nature of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi"; literally "living silver" or mercury.</note>; it does not wet, nor does it cling to other bodies, nor is it mixed or united—and it is finally fixed with a true union and fixation—except with gold; and together with gold, it is perfected into the <term>gold-making salt</term> <note>original: "salem aurificum"; another name for the Philosopher's Stone in its finalized, stable form.</note>. 

But those sharp distilled waters <note>likely referring to strong acids like *aqua regia*, which was known to dissolve gold but was viewed by some as too corrosive for true "philosophical" work.</note> have stripped away the fluid nature of <term>quicksilver</term>; they wet what they touch, just like water and oil, and they do not cling or mix through a true mixture, nor are they fixed by any art with gold, nor are they perfected into the <term>gold-making salt</term> with gold; indeed, in the testing [by fire], they are separated, burnt away, and vanish into smoke. 

Therefore, those judged more correctly who declared that fluid <term>quicksilver</term> is the other part of the <term>philosophical seed</term>, which truly dissolves gold into <term>quicksilver</term> [itself], and is united to it, and together 

<margin>Opinions on Mercury</margin> 

with it is perfected into the <term>gold-making salt</term>: for they are of one nature. For gold melted by fire appears to be fluid <term>quicksilver</term>, while this [quicksilver], when removed from the fire, appears as liquified gold. 

But even those who assert that <term>quicksilver</term> is the other part of the seed, and pronounce that it has the power of dissolving gold and being united with it, also seem to disagree among themselves as to which <term>quicksilver</term> it might be: whether the common kind, or that which is skillfully drawn out of metals, and from which metal most of all—whether from lead, or from tin, or from bismuth (which they call <term>icy tin</term> <note>original: "stannum glaciale"; a common early modern name for bismuth because of its crystalline, brittle structure.</note>), or from <term>antimony</term> <note>original: "stibio"</note>, or any of the others. 

<margin>Defects of common Mercury.</margin> 

For those who deny that common <term>quicksilver</term> is part of our seed assert that it has a colder quality, because of which it does not have the power to dissolve gold; its moisture, moreover, is too undefined, volatile, and spiritual, because of which it cannot be fixed with it.

But <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "Argento"</note> skillfully drawn out from the other [metals] possesses a greater digestion from nature.

Those who assert that no other liquor is more effective for dissolving gold than <term>quicksilver</term> are moved by this reason: that gold must be dissolved by <term>Ephesus</term> <note>likely a term for a specific alchemical process of "release" or digestion.</note> or <term>boiling</term> <note>original: "elixatione"; a slow decoction or cooking process in a moist heat.</note>, just as meat is boiled in water: for quicksilver is compared to water, because it contains a great quantity of moisture, which is the efficient cause of the dissolution. 

<margin>Why Mercury should not be sublimated from minerals.</margin> 

For this reason, it should not be altered from dry minerals through <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: "sublimationem"; the process of heating a substance to vaporize it, then cooling it back into a solid form.</note>: this opinion is stubbornly defended by <term>Bernard of Trevisan</term> <note>original: "Aernardus Treviensis"; an influential 15th-century alchemist known for his "Parable" and letters on the Stone.</note>, in the letter sent to <term>Thomas of Bologna</term>, physician to King <term>Charles VIII</term> <note>original: "Caroli octavi"; King of France (r. 1483–1498). The letter mentioned is a famous alchemical text discussing the nature of the Stone.</note>.

Nor are authorities of the most learned philosophers lacking to others, but I will not dwell longer on discussing these various and conflicting opinions.

# ON THE METHOD OF GENERATION

...is the plan. All these things are of one genus and species, differing among themselves only in **accidents** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are properties (like color or temperature) that can change without altering the essential nature of a substance.</note>. But so that it may be shown with certainty which liquid will be more effective for dissolving gold, the causes of the **solidification** <note>original: "concretionis"; the process of a substance becoming solid or dense.</note> of gold must be examined: for the causes of its dissolution are the opposites. Yet from the doctrine of **Aristotle** <note>The author refers to the classical theory that metals are formed from vapors trapped and hardened within the earth by cold and dryness.</note> we have learned,

<margin>Causes of the solidification of gold.</margin>
that the cause of solidification is partly the dryness of the earth which is within the moisture of the gold and binds it together, and partly external cold and dryness, which thicken and force the vapors (which are the immediate matter of metals) within the rocks: Therefore, internal

<margin>Causes of the dissolution of gold.</margin>
moisture, and external moisture and heat, will be the efficient causes of the dissolution of gold into a moist substance. Now this external moisture must be of the same nature as the moisture of the gold, such as the moisture of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury.</note>, so that when it overcomes the other in quantity, it can dissolve the dryness of the gold. But the less cold this moisture of quicksilver is, the more readily it will dissolve the gold. Therefore, I would not wish to reject the opinion of those who are accustomed to draw out quicksilver from lead, tin, **bismuth**, or **antimony** <note>original: "stibio"; a metallic element often used in alchemical preparations to "purify" gold or create specialized mercuries.</note>, for it is less cold than common quicksilver, and is a little more digested and refined: And I hear that many use these for the dissolution of gold, and have perfected the work from a mixture of both, as if from a true seed: but I should not be blamed if I say that common quicksilver is the other part of the seed, provided that it has first been mixed and truly united with a small portion of gold, for then it is called, by metaphor—

<margin>Animated quicksilver.</margin>
—**animated quicksilver**, not because it possesses a soul, for it is inanimate, but because just as a soul makes a living creature warm as long as it is in the body, so gold wards off and tempers the coldness of the quicksilver when it is truly mixed with it.

<margin>What the gold-making salt is.</margin>
For the smallest portion of the **Philosopher's Stone**, or the **gold-making salt** <note>original: "salis aurifici"; the finalized alchemical agent.</note> (which is nothing other than gold cooked far longer than natural gold), rescues and tempers infinite parts of quicksilver from excessive coldness. One should rely on this animated quicksilver rather than that which is drawn out from metals by art: for the latter is extracted from metals only with great artistic skill, and many labors and expenses. But we have a vast abundance of common quicksilver, and it can be easily purified and mixed with gold, and united to it, as I shall soon say. Therefore, to bring this question to a close: Quicksilver drawn out by art from lead, tin, or antimony, or common quicksilver prepared and animated (let it be permitted now and hereafter to use technical terms, so that all things may be spoken more meaningfully),

<margin>The other part of the gold-making seed.</margin>
is the other part of the seed of our gold-making salt, and both mixed together are the true seed of the same, though imperfect. It remains that the [method] of perfecting each imperfect seed...

# ON THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE

...should I explain the method or practice clearly and concisely, which is proper to this art, and which the title of this Letter sets forth? Truly, each seed must be prepared separately, and then mixed, before the mixture is subjected to the perfecting cause, namely external heat. This preparation is a certain disposition and ability to receive the degrees of perfection, or the <note>original: "interitum"; referring to the alchemical death or breakdown of the original forms</note> destruction of both forms, so that heterogeneous things may be separated, and each seed purified: no differently than skilled farmers are accustomed to first clean and select seeds before casting them into the earth.

Furthermore, the predecessors of this art called these seeds by the barbaric term ***Rebis*** <note>From the Latin 'res bis', meaning 'a double thing', signifying the union of two opposites into one.</note>, as I have already said in the *Apologia*. Gold acts as the masculine seed, hotter and drier; <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note> as the feminine, colder and more moist. They called the former "sulphur" and the latter by the same name <note>The author is referring to the "Mercury of the Philosophers" which was often described using the same terminology as its counterpart.</note>, from whose embrace the <term>philosophical stone</term> <note>The legendary substance sought by alchemists to transform base metals into gold and grant long life.</note>, or our gold-making salt, is perfected. First, I will speak of the preparation of the feminine seed, and of its animation: nor will I fear, in so serious a matter, to depart a little from Latin usage, so that everything may be understood more significantly and easily.

->The Practice of the Work.<-

Mercury (☿)</margin>

# ON THE METHOD OF PROCREATION

<margin>Dissolution of the compound.</margin> ...finally, let the whole <term>amalgam</term> <note>original: "malagma"; a soft paste made by alloying a metal with mercury.</note> flow through the leather by squeezing, and let the gold be truly mixed and united with the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note>. Therefore, when the whole amalgam has been composed of twelve ounces or more of quicksilver and a single ounce of gold, and strained through linen, enclose it in a glass vessel having the shape of an egg, of which the amalgam should occupy a third part; let the remaining parts of the glass be empty, and let the vessel be sealed with glass. Then cook and dissolve it with a faint, weak, and uniform heat in a suitable furnace for forty days, within which you will find a blackness rising to the surface, which is a sign of the perfect dissolution of the gold into the quicksilver. Open the vessel, and squeeze the amalgam wrapped in leather; if it all flows out, well and good; if not, weigh what did not flow out on scales, and if it weighs an ounce, as I suspect, add nine ounces of fresh, prepared quicksilver.

<margin>Repetition of the dissolution.</margin> Grind and wash it, and again enclose it in a glass jar, and with the glass sealed, cook it again as before, until you see blackness rising to the surface, which will happen in a shorter time; from here, with the glass vessel opened, let the amalgam wrapped in leather be strained by squeezing. And let these works be repeated again and again, until the whole amalgam has flowed out, squeezed through the pores of the leather. In this way, the gold will be cut into very tiny parts; however, both are not yet truly mixed and united. Moreover, the amalgam that has flowed out must be ground, washed, and strained through leather more often, so that the whole may be more easily carried into vapor.

<margin>Distillation of the amalgam.</margin> Therefore, put it into a crooked glass vessel <note>likely a retort, a flask with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>, fortified with tenacious clay <note>a process called "lorication," where a vessel is coated in clay to protect it from the direct heat of the fire</note>, and distill it up to the middle part, first with slow heat, then increased, and finally with violent and fiery heat, so that the gold may breathe out together with the quicksilver, and glide down into the receiving vessel into fluid quicksilver. For gold and quicksilver possess the greatest similarity, both in matter and form; and when the gold has been rarefied into very tiny parts like quicksilver, it is necessary for it to be united to the quantity of quicksilver, <margin>Caution.</margin> so that one is not pulled away from the other, but by the action of the fire they are carried upward together into vapor. But if by chance some of the gold should remain at the bottom of the vessel, the same works as above must be repeated, adding new quicksilver, and these things as many times until the whole has been distilled, unless perhaps some dregs have settled, which are useless and should be thrown away.

<margin>The feminine seed.</margin> This is the true feminine and metaphorically animated seed, which has the power of dissolving gold: it is the second part of the seed of our gold-making salt. This is the quicksilver which we called "our own" in the *Apologia*.

<margin>Azoth.</margin>

It is drawn out by the same principle by which meat is dissolved and changed into broth by boiling. It is, finally, that by whose benefit we have said common quicksilver more freely unites with the <term>calx</term> <note>A fine powder produced by heating a metal; an oxide.</note> of gold than water is mixed with water. This same **animated quicksilver** is increased infinitely if it is mixed again with gold and new quicksilver by the art we have described.
<margin>The Menstruum and the vinegar of the Philosophers.</margin>

Pour the distilled water back over it and distill again, repeating this seven times. Thus, you will have the true calx of gold, so that it may be mixed with the **animated quicksilver**.
