->### OF THE METHOD OF PROCREATION<-

For, (says **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a 13th-century author whose works were the foundation of European alchemy.</note>) substances that are truly **calcined** <note>original: "calcinata"; reduced to a powder through heat.</note> approach the nature of salt: and the thinner the substance is before its conjunction with the **feminine seed** <note>The "animated quicksilver" described on the previous page.</note>, the more easily and quickly it will be dissolved into **quicksilver**, and hence, by cooking, it will be reduced even more easily and more quickly into powder.

These prepared seeds must first be mixed mathematically and through contiguous parts, then, after the preparation is complete, mixed naturally and through contiguous parts in a true union:
<margin>The law of mixing.</margin>
for this is the law and the order of all things that are finally truly mixed: first, the parts must touch each other, with their prior forms remaining whole in the mixture, and then they are altered, and finally they are united.
<margin>The conjunction of mathematical practice.</margin>
This mathematical and prior conjunction is performed as follows. Cast this **calx** <note>original: "calcem"; a fine powder of metal.</note> of gold into a ceramic vessel of the kind goldsmiths use to melt gold, and cover it with another small vessel so that no coals or anything else may fall inside. Bury it on all sides with lit coals until the vessel is red-hot and glows fiercely, yet take care that the calx of gold does not melt. Into another ceramic vessel, cast eight ounces of **animated quicksilver**, and let the vessel be surrounded by coals. Cook it until the quicksilver begins to evaporate: immediately cast the glowing calx of gold into the animated quicksilver and stir it with a rod. Move it until you perceive by touch that both are mixed and **amalgamated** <note>original: "amalgamatum"; the process of mercury bonding with another metal.</note> through very small parts. Then, cast this **amalgam** <note>original: "malagma"</note> into a wooden vessel filled with water. From there, grind the amalgam and wash it again, and dry it so that all moisture vanishes. Then, press it while wrapped in leather. The globe that remains is the seed of our future gold-making salt, mixed from the masculine and feminine with the just proportion of each: about which many have doubted and held diverse opinions, but with nature as our guide, one never wanders astray.

<margin>Weights.</margin>
For the calx of gold retains exactly as much of the animated seed as is necessary; whatever is superfluous flows out through the pores of the leather.
You will see that this globe weighs four ounces, more or less. Therefore, there is one ounce of the golden calx and three ounces of animated quicksilver, or thereabouts. However, even if more than three ounces of animated quicksilver were mixed, even up to five, there would be no danger; the seed would simply dissolve more quickly, but would grow together and **coagulate** <note>thicken into a solid.</note> more slowly. The seeds thus prepared and mixed in the just proportion of nature, before they are subjected to the cause that brings them to perfection, 
<margin>The Place.</margin>

The seeds of animals are not perfected except in the **matrix** <note>The womb.</note>; eggs are perfected in the shell, and the fruits of the earth are produced in the soil; if they are outside these places, they are corrupted. ## OF THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE

<margin>The sealing of the vessel.</margin>
Our vessel is a glass egg, which is to say, a small vessel blown into the shape of an egg. Within this, the twin globe <note>The combined "masculine" and "feminine" seeds described on the previous page.</note> is to be placed in such proportion that the globe occupies one-third of the glass vessel, and the remaining parts are left empty. These empty spaces contain the vapors of the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury.</note>, should any happen to rise, so that the vessel does not burst. Indeed, the mouth of the vessel must be obstructed with glass—just as animal fetuses in the womb, or the white and yolk of an egg, are enclosed by a shell so that nothing may breathe out. For in the seed of the **animated quicksilver** <note>Mercury that has been "prepared" or "vivified" for the work.</note> there is a certain vapor and spirit of such thinness and subtlety that, if it should escape, it would vanish from the sight of the eyes. This spirit is the other cause of completion, working alongside external heat; if it flies away, the work is lost, just as if an eggshell is pierced, the chick fetus perishes. Its flight and evaporation cannot be restrained by any **iron lute** <note>original: "luto aliquo ferreo"; a strong sealant paste made of clay, iron filings, and other binders used to seal alchemical joints.</note>, no matter how thick, compact, and solid, but only by glass, which is the densest material and lacks pores. Many, however, have thought that our gold-making salt should be perfected by the same way and method by which they draw out salts from all mixed bodies using fiery heat—namely, by distracting those bodies into various substances through fire, just as we said above that salt is drawn from wood by lye after it has been turned to ashes.

Therefore, they draw out sharp waters <note>Acids, such as aqua regia or nitric acid.</note> from various bodies, by the power of which they dissolve gold into a liquor; they then pour this distilled liquid back over the dissolved material, thicken it with a lingering heat, and believe that what remains is our gold-making salt.

<margin>The various and vain works of the sophists.</margin>
<margin>The goal of gold-making.</margin>
They also act upon infinite other bodies, all of which are varied, useless, and **sophistical** <note>original: "sophistica"; in alchemy, "sophists" were those who used false or purely chemical methods rather than true philosophical alchemy.</note>, and possess more of opinion than of truth. When Nature has first produced a seed, she does not distract it into various substances, but perfects it; she takes nothing away from the seed, but completes the whole. This is more clear in an egg, which is the seed of the chick, and the chick is imperfect. Thus, by imitating the works of nature, once the seed of our gold-making salt has been established—whatever and of what kind it may be—it must not be secreted or divided into various substances, but perfected by **concoction** <note>original: "concoctione"; a slow, steady heating process akin to digestion.</note> alone, and the whole changed into the nature of a fusible salt. This is the goal of all **Chrysopoeia** <note>original: "Chrysopœiæ"; the art of making gold.</note> in producing the efficient cause, which perfects quicksilver and the other imperfect metals into gold, with the help of fiery heat.

<margin>The 6 stages of perfecting the stone.</margin>
The stages for perfecting this, our gold-making salt, are six in number: **Dissolution**, **Coagulation** (or thickening), **Prior Fixation**, **Posterior Fixation**, **Calcination**, and **Inceration** <note>original: "inceratio"; the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency so it can "penetrate" other metals.</note>. I have said there are several stages.

For since I have defined perfection as the promotion of a seed already born to the final act of its form: it is not immediately per—

# OF THE MANNER OF PRODUCTION

<margin>An analogy.</margin>
<margin>External heat.</margin>
<margin>The vessel must not be moved during the decoction.</margin>
That completion is perfected as a primary act or form; and while the primary substance does not admit of degrees, the subsequent acts—that is, the qualities—do. In this way, fruits born of a tree admit degrees of perfection before they reach full maturity. For in the intervening time, they are more perfect than they were before, and so on, until they reach extreme ripeness. We must judge the perfection of our **gold-making seed** <note>original: "semine nostro aurifico"</note> in the very same way. Since external heat is the efficient cause of this perfection, and there are six degrees of the same, the first five degrees follow a progressive path of heat. The last is a reiteration of these five degrees. Furthermore, while the seed is being perfected, it must not be moved from its place, nor should anything be pulled apart—as is commonly done in **sophistical works** <note>Deceptive or "false" alchemy that seeks shortcuts rather than the true natural process.</note>—but it must be committed solely to the five degrees of heat.

### Degrees of Operations

#### Dissolution

<margin>The first degree of perfection. 412.</margin>
<margin>The sign of solution.</margin>
<margin>An analogy.</margin>
**Dissolution**, therefore, is the first degree of perfection. It is the reduction of the **Golden Lime** <note>original: "Calcis aureae"; gold that has been calcined or reduced to a fine powder</note>—which is one part of the seed—into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>. This is achieved by the heat of the first degree, as well as by the power of the spirit and vapor inherent within the quicksilver, just as we see happening in the seeds of animals, in eggs, and in grains of wheat when they are sown. For by this degree of heat, the globe of **malagma** <note>original: "malagmatis"; a softened mass or paste-like mixture of the alchemical ingredients</note>, which was at first somewhat hard, softens and dissolves. Once the solution is completed, the entire contents of the glass vessel appear as a thick and, as it were, putrid quicksilver. The sign of perfect dissolution is **blackness** <note>Known in alchemy as the "nigredo" stage, symbolizing the death of the old form before rebirth.</note>, appearing most prominently on the surface. For the heat, acting upon the moisture, produces this blackness. This dissolution is completed in the space of about forty days. This same dissolution is a kind of **epsefis** <note>original: "Epsefis"; from the Greek ἕψησις, meaning boiling or decoction.</note> or a species of **elixation** <note>The process of boiling a substance in a liquid to extract its essence.</note>. Just as meat is dissolved into broth by elixation through heat existing in a watery moisture, so gold is dissolved by heat acting in the moisture—namely, the quicksilver.

#### Coagulation

<margin>The second degree of perfection.</margin>
Next follows **coagulation** or thickening, which is the inspissation <note>thickening</note>, hardening, and drying of the seed that was dissolved into fluid quicksilver. This is achieved by the power of the second degree of heat as the efficient cause, and by the power of the "earthiness" inherent in the **Golden Lime**, the property of which is to dry and to bind.

<margin>The property of the Golden Lime.</margin>
For at first, when the moist quicksilver exceeded the dry portion of that same Golden Lime in quantity, it was necessary for the dry part to yield and be dissolved into a somewhat thick and putrid consistency of quicksilver. But as the heat is increased, that most subtle vapor of the quicksilver vanishes, as it were, into the air through the empty parts of the vessel, and

# OF THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE

...it is necessary for the moisture to be forced together and thickened, in no different a way than oil is thickened by long-lasting heat as the subtle spirit departs.

<margin>40. The days of dissolution, and likewise of coagulation.</margin>
Now, the dryness of the **golden lime** <note>original: "calcis aureæ"; gold reduced to a fine powder through calcination</note>, drinking in the moisture of the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury</note>, greatly assists and constrains it. Thus, by these same causes—the viscous and moist liquid—stones are first formed in the bodies of animals by the dry earthy material that exists within the moisture, with external heat acting as the efficient cause. In the same way, we observe that the dissolved seed is gradually thickened and made dense, and bound and forced into a solid stone; this usually happens within a space of forty days. Meanwhile, the seed will maintain a black color, and this blackness will even deepen. This concoction is a type of *optesis* <note>original: "optesis"; a Greek term for roasting or baking by dry heat</note>, or roasting, as are the subsequent stages that follow.

### The First Fixation

<margin>
The third degree of perfection.
What fixation is.
Fixation lasts 40 days.
</margin>
Since this moisture of our seed is not yet defined or unified by this cooking, but is instead volatile, it must be defined and **fixed** <note>Stabilized so that it no longer evaporates when exposed to fire</note> by heat of the third degree. Therefore, fixation follows. Fixation, according to the author **Geber** <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational 8th-century figure in alchemy</note>, is the appropriate adaptation of a thing fleeing from fire to endure the same. The purpose of this, he says, is so that every alteration and every **tincture** <note>The power of the alchemical agent to change the color and nature of a metal</note> may be made permanent in the thing altered, and not be changed. It can also be defined as the mastery of the undefined and indeterminate moisture existing in the seed, accomplished by the power of heat of the third degree, with the dryness inherent in the earthy part of the seed also acting as an agent. This fixation is also completed within a space of forty days.

During this cooking, various colors are seen, which eventually all end in a brilliant and snowy white; and this **whiteness** <note>original: "albedo"; a major milestone in the alchemical Great Work</note> is the true sign of fixation.

In this color, they say, the body, spirit, and soul are truly united and fixed. This is nothing other than the equal proportion, union, and fixed perfection of all the elements of the seed.

This perfected seed is called the <term>silver-maker</term> <note>original: "argentificum"</note> because, when projected into quicksilver, it halts, fixes, and perfects it into the truest silver. But this is called the "first fixation"; though it may be considered perfect in a simple and absolute sense, when compared to the fixation of our **gold-maker**, it is still undefined and imperfect, and does not yet deserve the name of "salt" or "stone."

### The Second Fixation

<margin>The fourth degree of perfection.</margin>
Therefore, once the first fixation is finished, the second fixation follows in order. This is the perfect and absolute cooking and mastery of the innate and undefined moisture within the moisture of the seed, as if by the heat of the fourth...

-># ON THE METHOD OF PRODUCTION<-

<header>ON THE METHOD OF PRODUCTION</header>

...the fourth degree having been reached. By this heat, the seed does not take on various colors [all at once], but the **whiteness** <note>original: "albedo"; the stage of the alchemical work where the material becomes pure white</note> is first changed into a lemon-yellow and then a deeper yellow, and from there gradually into red.

<margin>
From where the various colors come.
</margin>

For from the various **concoctions** <note>original: "concoctio"; a process of ripening or "cooking" through heat, similar to digestion</note> of the moisture, various colors emerge: but when it has first been concocted, whiteness appears. By the force of fire, this is changed into yellow, and from yellow finally into red. This is clearly seen in **realgar** <note>original: "sandaracha"; a red arsenic sulfide mineral</note> and **ochre** <note>original: "ochra"</note> when they are concocted. For the subtle, most pure earthy part within the seed, when it is concocted and not scorched, is white in its current state but red in its potential. Through more vehement concoction, it becomes red, staining all its own moisture with that color. This white seed persists as a solid mass for a very long time, and finally, through continuous concoction, it is gradually broken down and changed into a red powder.

<margin>
2. Fixation of 240 days.
</margin>

Moreover, this fourth degree of concoction is completed in two hundred and forty days. One need not be fearful of the degree of heat at this stage, since the seed is already **fixed** <note>made stable and non-volatile</note> after the white stage. Previously, before that perfect whiteness, there was danger in managing the heat because the two seeds <note>referring to the "male" and "female" principles, usually sulfur and mercury</note> were not yet fixed and united.

### Calcination

<margin>
The fifth degree of perfection.
</margin>

Even if the moisture of this seed has been overcome by these four degrees of heat, it is not yet entirely so, nor in such a way that it fully obtains the nature of salt. For the nature of salt is extremely dry and devoid of all moisture; salt is, in essence, pure earth.

<margin>
What the nature of salt is.
</margin>

It is also the nature of salt to be dissolved by cold moisture, because it was hardened by dry heat. Unless, therefore, the moisture is entirely overcome, the substance will not truly obtain the nature of salt, nor will it dissolve in a watery liquid. This dissolution is necessary, for our **golden salt** <note>original: "sal noster aurificus"; the Philosopher's Stone in its final, medicinal form</note>—being the highest medicine for human bodies—must be soluble in any liquid when it is given to a sick person to swallow.

<margin>
The medicinal virtue of the golden lime.
</margin>

Furthermore, that powder cooked in the fourth degree still contains some unknown impurity and earthy matter mixed in, which does not belong to its true nature or the proper proportion of salt; this must be removed from the red powder. This most perfect and absolute cooking of the red powder, and its liberation from the earthy dross, is achieved by **calcination** <note>the process of reducing a substance to a fine powder or ash through high heat</note> and by the heat of the fifth and final degree.

<margin>
What calcination is.
</margin>

For Calcination, according to the definition of **Geber** <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry"</note>, is the pulverization of a dry thing by fire, through the removal of the moisture that holds the parts together. It seems more correct to say it is achieved through the absolute concoction of the undefined moisture.

<margin>
The cause of calcination.
</margin>

Geber adds that the purpose of calcination is so that the powder may be more perfectly fixed and more easily dissolved into water. Experience shows that every kind of calcined material is more stable and easier to dissolve than those that have not been calcined.

# OF THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE

<header>OF THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE</header>

...experience teaches: since a body thinned into slender and very small parts is more easily mixed with water. Therefore, when this has been accomplished by external heat, it will be more easily dissolved into water. By this **calcination** <note>original: "calcinatio"; the process of reducing a solid to a fine powder through prolonged heating</note>, that powder swells in the manner of a **ferment** <note>a substance that causes "rising" or transformation, similar to yeast in bread</note>, on account of the long-lasting fiery heat by whose power it is reduced into very small parts. A certain impure earth settles at the bottom of the vessel and is truly separated from the red powder, which must be discarded:

<margin>
Damned earth.
</margin>

for it is not of the nature of the salt. They call this same earth vile, **damned**, and cursed <note>original: "vilem, damnatam, & vituperatam"; in alchemy, the "terra damnata" is the inert, useless byproduct left after the essence has been extracted</note>, and it is like the useless dregs of the remaining effective substances. It is of the genus of earth which, by excellent heat, is changed and melted into glass. 

<margin>
The vessel for calcination, and its duration.
</margin>

This calcination must be completed in an earthen vessel over the space of eight days: thus you will have the truest red **gold-making salt** <note>original: "salem aurificum"; the philosophical salt capable of transmuting metals into gold</note>, whose color will be like scorched blood, and it will dissolve in any liquid. For everything truly calcined, as we have said, approaches the nature of salt: and therefore it is necessary that they follow one another in their properties. It is the nature of salts that they are dissolved by an aqueous liquid.

->Ceration<-

<margin>
The sixth degree of perfection.
</margin>

Though these things are so, our salt has not yet achieved absolute and finished perfection. That perfection consists in its being easily and quickly melted by fire, just like **wax** <note>original: "cera"; the stage of "ceration" (ceratio) makes the brittle stone soft and flowable so it can "melt" into other metals</note>, and that it be of the thinnest consistency in fusion, like water. 

<margin>
The necessity of ceration.
</margin>

Otherwise, it will not obtain the power of penetrating and entering the densest parts of **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury</note> or of other metals; therefore, if it were cast upon them, it would not complete the transformation. Yet, our gold-making salt, having been hardened and altered by such long **concoction** <note>ripening through heat</note>, lacks this property of sudden melting; therefore, it must be restored to it. 

<margin>
A doubt.
</margin>

It ought not to seem strange that I said before that our gold-making salt is dissolved in any liquid, and here also that it is melted by heat—which seems to be said against the rules of **Aristotle** <note>The author is navigating a contradiction in classical physics (Meteorology, Book IV), where substances usually behave as either "water-like" or "earth-like," but not both</note>. For those things, he says, which are hardened by dry heat are dissolved by cold moisture, such as salts; 

<margin>
The solution.
</margin>

but those things which are "cooked" by cold are dissolved by heat, such as metals. But experience teaches that common salt is not only dissolved in an aqueous liquid, but also in fire. For if salt, like silver, is melted in a pottery vessel, you will see it dissolved like pure water, and if cast into a small channel, it hardens by cold like a metal: this also happens in other salts. But if they are purified more often by solution in water, filtration, and coagulation, they will finally be melted by a light heat, like wax.

By the same reasoning, certain men have thought that a very rapid fusion must be prepared for our gold-making powder: certainly, it is necessary that our salt, lacking fusion, be dissolved by moisture, but...

# ON THE METHOD OF PROCREATION

<margin>The ceration of the sophists.</margin>
...not in a watery liquid, for our salt does not require a simple and easy melting to be fully perfected, but rather a moisture that is joined to it at its center and fixed with it, to protect it from **vitrification** <note>original: "vitrificatione"; the process of turning into glass, which would make the stone brittle and useless</note>. A watery liquid cannot provide this, for by no art could it be fixed with our salt; therefore, it must be both dissolved and "waxed" <note>original: "incerandus"; the process of **ceration**, making a substance fluid like wax when heated</note> at the same time. For ceration is the final stage of perfection which **Geber** <note>an 8th-century alchemist, often called the father of chemistry, whose Latin-translated works were foundational to European alchemy</note> defines as the softening of a hard, non-fusible thing toward liquefaction. He says the reason for this discovery is so that a substance which lacked the ability to melt because it was deprived of its moisture might be softened into a body capable of alteration, so that it might flow. He argues that those who think ceration is done with oils and liquid waters err and hallucinate greatly; instead, it must be performed using spirits.

<margin>The method of ceration.</margin>
He calls **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> "spirits," and truly this dissolution and ceration is provided to our powder and salt by a mixture of "animated" quicksilver <note>mercury that has been chemically prepared or "awakened" for use in the Great Work</note>. This is the method: mix a denarius—or twenty-four grains—of the powder with four denarii of animated quicksilver to make a **malagma** <note>a soft, dough-like paste or amalgam</note>. Enclose this in a glass vessel blown in the shape of an egg, seal the glass, and cook it with the four prior degrees of fire in the same order that the powder was originally worked. Within thirty days, all the colors will manifest themselves which previously took nine months to appear. Repeat the same work seven times, adding four parts of animated quicksilver to the powder each time.

<margin>
Colors in ceration.
The sevenfold repetition and the shortening of the work.
</margin>
The repeated work is completed in a shorter time than the first time. For that which is already salt is dissolved more quickly than that which is not yet salt but has the potential to be. In this way, you will possess the most perfect **gold-making salt**, or the **Philosopher’s Stone**: most fixed, as fusible as wax, as thin as water, penetrating, dyeing, transmuting, and perfecting all quicksilver—both common mercury and that which is found within metallic bodies—into the truest gold.

<margin>The sign of perfect ceration.</margin>
The sign of the salt’s perfection will be this: if a grain of it is cast upon a glowing hot silver plate, it will melt immediately and penetrate the inner parts of the silver, spreading itself widely in every direction like oil, and will stain it with a golden color both inside and on the surface, without any evaporation into vapor.

As for what remains after the twenty-four grains are removed, you shall perfect it by the same reasoning and the same method described above.

At first, only twenty-four grains are removed because the quantity is increased with each reiteration of the work by the addition and mixing of new quicksilver. Even if many more than twenty-four grains were harvested from the mass, toward the end...

[...lest] the mass of the seventh repetition be greater than what could submit itself to digestion.

### Multiplication.

<margin>Multiplication.</margin>
Even though substances themselves are neither intensified nor diminished, their qualities act as if through instruments; and since qualities can be intensified and diminished, our **fusible salt** <note>a salt that melts like wax; the near-final form of the Philosopher's Stone</note> acts more sharply or more dully through them. Therefore, our predecessors investigated with admirable art how to increase our gold-making salt—or the fusible philosopher's stone—both in quantity and in its strength or power to act.

<margin>A twofold method of multiplying.</margin>
There are two ways or methods for this increase.

One is to take an ounce of the already perfected salt and mix it with twelve ounces of **animated quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi animati"; mercury that has been "awakened" or chemically prepared for use in the Great Work</note>, then dissolve and distill it. From this, four ounces of this animated quicksilver should be mixed with one ounce of our perfected salt and digested with four degrees of heat. The second method is more direct: cast a small portion of our perfected salt into common quicksilver. From this gold, which we call **philosophical gold**, extract the quicksilver with great skill. Mix one ounce of that with one ounce of our perfected salt and digest it with four degrees of heat. In a very short time, you will see all the colors that you first saw when making our gold-making salt. For intensification is a degree of quality more deeply rooted in the same part of the subject. By this repetition, the entire salt is rendered **fiery**, possessing an extremely thin and subtle consistency. For fire and things that are fiery possess more power in their actions; the thinner they are, the more readily and quickly they penetrate and enter the inner parts. Therefore, the more often you repeat this, the more increase in both quantity and power will be added to the resulting powder. This method of acting is prescribed in these ancient verses:

> *If you dissolve the fixed, and make the dissolved fly,* <note>original: "Si fixum solvas, faciasq; volare solutum"; refers to making a solid substance volatile or gaseous</note>
> *And fix the bird, I shall make you live safely:* <note>original: "Et volucrem figas"; turning a volatile vapor back into a solid</note>
> *Separate the joined, then rejoin the separated,*
> *Melt the hardened, harden the melted, and I shall call you blessed.*
> *Say that **Arsenic** <note>original: "Arsenicum"; in alchemy, this often refers to a volatile "soul" of a metal rather than just the modern element</note> is the soul, but the spirit remains.*
> *Quicksilver is the spirit, and **calx** <note>original: "calx"; the powdery remains after a metal is burned or oxidized, representing the "body"</note> is said to be the body.*

By "the fixed" is understood gold; its dissolution is performed through common quicksilver, or another substance reduced from a metal into quicksilver...

-># ON THE METHOD OF PROCREATION<-

Once drawn out, the dissolved part flies away; however, when both are distilled by the force of fire into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>, they fall into the receiving vessel. That which is volatile is **fixed** <note>made stable and solid so it no longer evaporates when heated</note> when four parts of it are mixed with one part of **gold calx** <term>calx: a metal reduced to a fine powder or oxide through heating</term> and are joined by the process of "cooking." Those things which were joined are separated when the solid parts of the gold are dissolved; they are joined again when the dissolved parts are fixed. **Arsenic** <note>In this context, not the modern poison, but a "philosophical arsenic" representing a volatile, soul-like spirit</note> is the "soul"—that is, gold converted into quicksilver, whether it be common quicksilver or that drawn out from other metals by the alchemical art. **Calx** is gold reduced to a powder. This is not far from the teachings of those who say that **Azoth** <term>Azoth: the universal solvent or "mercury of the philosophers" believed to be the essential agent of transformation</term> and fire are sufficient for this work. For Azoth is also gold dissolved into a somewhat thick quicksilver; when this is cooked and fixed by a tempered heat, it becomes our "stone," or rather, our **fixed and fusible gold-making salt**. Indeed, from what we have said, anyone will be able to easily understand whatever the ancient writers expressed in riddles.

<margin>A summary of the work from Geber.</margin>
Finally, Geber <note>A Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary father of chemistry, though the text cited here (The Sum of Perfection) is likely by a 13th-century European author using his name</note> summarizes the above method in a few words in chapters 30 and 43 of his book, *The Sum of Perfection*. He says: "This is the sum of the intention of the whole work: that the 'stone' known in these chapters be taken along with its additive—that is, gold converted into oil or quicksilver—and let it be refined until both reach the highest purity. Finally, let both become a **fixed volatile** <note>a paradox describing a substance that is pure and spiritual (volatile) but stable under heat (fixed)</note>. In this order, the secret is completed, which is most precious, and which is an incomparable treasure above every secret of the sciences of this world."

<margin>The powers of the stone.</margin>
How great the powers and faculties of our gold-making salt are can only be demonstrated by experience. A single grain of the powder is cast into corrected and purified quicksilver; at first, this mercury is not turned into metal, but into a powder. The strength of this powder is then diminished, and a final portion of this powder is cast into more quicksilver. This "projection" <note>the act of casting the alchemical medicine onto a base metal to transform it</note> from the resulting powder is repeated until it is no longer a powder that is produced, but a fused metal. For in the mixture, the fiery qualities—hot and dry—of our gold-making powder struggle against the cold and moist qualities of the quicksilver. Only through a specific proportion of these active and passive qualities is the quicksilver (whether common or derived from metals) tempered and perfected into gold.

<margin>A doubt.</margin>
Perhaps many who hear us profess that common quicksilver—no matter how "animated" or prepared—is one half of the "seed" <note>the "feminine" reproductive element in alchemical generation</note> will have their doubts. This is because gold is only carried upward with it into a "sublime" state with great difficulty, and because common mercury possesses an excessively undefined and limitless humidity. Lastly, they may argue that if this mercury constitutes the other half of the seed, the perfection of both seeds will be delayed for a very long time. Therefore, either...

->### THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE<-

Many will judge that **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> drawn out from tin, lead, or the **regulus** <term>regulus: the metallic part of a mineral that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</term> of **antimony** <note>original: "stibium"</note> (for so they call that which settles at the bottom during the purification process) is superior and more direct. I shall not oppose their opinion much; indeed, I readily subscribe to it, especially if the quicksilver is extracted from the regulus of antimony. For it possesses the greatest similarity of its entire substance to gold. However, it must be noted that the degrees of the initial heat must be intensified or reduced according to the different temperament of the quicksilver used.

<margin>The aim of the art.</margin>
The aim of the art is to unite the moist with the dry and to **fix** <note>to make a substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated</note> both with a firm and solid fixation. Hence, in the observation of every external degree of heat, the law is this: that the heat must be equal and tempered, so that it may be able to transform both mixed seeds, but not to thin them out into vapor. Therefore, if common "animated" quicksilver is mixed with gold, the degree of heat must be reduced at the start of the work, for it is more indefinite and volatile; but if quicksilver drawn out by the art from other metals is mixed with that same gold, a slightly more intense degree of heat must be applied.

For quicksilver of this kind, since it is thicker and more "digested" <note>matured or refined through heat</note> by nature, tolerates a greater force of fire and does not fly away into smoke from the heat of the fire as easily as the common variety.

<margin>Mercury from lead, tin, and the regulus of antimony, and how it is to be drawn out.</margin>
This quicksilver is extracted from lead, tin, and the regulus of antimony by the same way and method that **Geber** <note>Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> teaches in the sublimation of **marcasite** <term>marcasite: in this context, a mineral or metallic ore used to provide the "spirit" of the metal</term>. By the force of an excellent fire, a certain dry vapor is carried upward, which is thickened and solidified on the cold sides of the vessel. This, being removed and macerated in **oil of tartar** <term>oil of tartar: a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, often used as a solvent or cleaning agent</term>, then washed and ground, emerges as fluid quicksilver, as if liberated and purged from its earthy dregs.

<margin>The silence of the ancients.</margin>
All those ancient professors of this art passed over this method of drawing out quicksilver in silence, and never handed it down in their writings—and they did so deliberately. For it is the secret of the entire art and the gateway to what follows. It is certain that they revealed the later stages very openly, but kept these prior matters hidden.

This, therefore, is the clear, right, true, and direct method for preparing our **gold-making salt**, or the **Philosophers' Stone**, whose power and faculty is to perfect quicksilver, as well as the remaining metals, into the truest gold. <margin>True potable gold</margin> It is also true **potable gold** <note>original: "aurum potabile"; a medicinal liquid gold</note>, which may be dissolved in any liquor; and, as they say, it is the most excellent and most suitable remedy for driving away desperate diseases.

I have always thought it safer to insist upon this gold-making salt above all else.

<margin>Objections.</margin>
But there will not be a few who will argue that gold without quicksilver...

# ON THE METHOD OF PRODUCING
<meta>catchword: from gold</meta>

...dissolved, and they will affirm that they have accomplished something even without this **gold-making salt** <note>original: "sale aurifico"</note> or **Philosophers' Stone** through their own experience, and indeed in a shorter space of time. 

<margin>Response.</margin>
To these I respond: I do not deny that certain salts can be turned into water and a liquid consistency by art, and more quickly than gold is dissolved by **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivo"; mercury</note>. By the sharp force and power of these waters, gold appears dissolved into a certain liquor, but it is not *truly* dissolved, nor does it shed its metallic nature. It is only seen as dissolved so long as it remains held in that salty liquor, 

<margin>Note.</margin>
which is not truly mixed with the gold, nor united to it. For dissimilar natures do not truly mix. Therefore, when that salty liquor is driven off by a violent fire, it thins into vapor and is carried upward, while the gold settles at the bottom of the vessel as a **fixed** <note>stable and resistant to evaporation</note> yellow or saffron-colored powder. When **borax** <term>Chrysocollâ: a flux used in soldering and refining gold</term> is added, this powder melts and returns to gold again without any loss of substance. 

But quicksilver, which we have called the "other part of the seed," truly dissolves the gold, is united to it, 

<margin>The sympathy and apathy of gold and mercury.</margin>
and is **fixed** with it forever. For they are of the same form, but not of the same temperament, or rather, not of the same degree of perfection. Once this dissolution and the fixation of both are completed, our powder or **gold-making salt** cannot thereafter return to gold, unless it is **projected** <term>projection: the act of casting an alchemical substance upon a base metal to transmute it</term> in a certain proportion onto other metals or quicksilver. For this salt is the true **tincture** <note>a concentrated essence capable of transforming other bodies</note> and the **most fixed oil**, possessing a most subtle essence. 

In the meantime, I also do not deny that gold dissolved into this watery liquor by the force of sharp waters can perfect quicksilver and silver into the purest gold. However, they have not handed down the cause of this effect; through their ignorance of what they do, they do not understand it, and they cannot correct an error. It is necessary for us to provide this explanation, even though it may seem to step beyond the purpose of our current discourse. But just as a ball thrown with great force cannot be called back, so my pen is so inclined that it cannot easily be pulled away until it has touched upon everything pertaining to this matter. Perhaps those who read these things, whether before or after my death, will be mindful of us. 

<margin>The cause of the perfection of quicksilver.</margin>
This is the cause: for quicksilver to be perfected, it needs only **concoction** <note>original: "concoctione"; a process of ripening or maturing through heat, like fruit ripening on a tree</note>. It is, as we have said, gold that is imperfect and immature. External fiery heat alone cannot accomplish this concoction, for it does not mix with or adhere to the quicksilver; it is necessary for something to adhere to it so that it may be held while it is being ripened, lest it flee in flight by the force of the fire. Again, gold—even if it adheres to the quicksilver—cannot hold it by itself, both because its consistency is too thick for it to enter the inner parts of the mercury, and because gold’s melting point is slower; it is not held but vanishes by the violence of the fire. But even if the quicksilver...

# THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE

<margin>The cause of cooking. Lully's opinion.</margin>
...it would be held by the gold, yet it would not be **cooked** <note>original: "concoqueretur"; the alchemical process of maturation or digestion through heat</note> by it. For the cause of **cooking** <note>original: "concoctionis"</note> is heat and a fiery quality, yet fiery qualities are not innate to gold by which it might tame, define, and overcome the indefinite moisture of **quicksilver** <term>argenti vivi: mercury</term>. But when gold is thought to be dissolved into a liquid by these salty liquors, even if it is not truly dissolved nor mixed, it can nevertheless perform these things—not in the same way as our **gold-making salt** <note>original: "sal noster aurificus"</note> or the **Philosophers' Stone**, which alone of its own power, needing no other help except perhaps the aid of fiery heat, brings the work to completion. Rather, gold is assisted (even if it has not shed its metallic nature) by those sharp liquors, by which the dissolved substance is made of the thinnest consistency and easiest melting, like wax, as long as they are mixed with it. For these liquors do not immediately fly away except by a more vehement fiery heat, although some, like **Lully** <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316), a major figure in medieval alchemy and logic</note>, have believed that they are forever **fixed** <note>original: "figi"; rendered stable and non-volatile</note> together with the gold—a thing I could not bring myself to believe. But their fixation is sufficient to retain the quicksilver in the struggle of the fire, until it reaches the nature of the **body** <note>the solid, metallic state</note>. Furthermore, since these liquors are nothing other than salts and possess the nature of salt, they cook the moisture of the quicksilver separately by their own fiery qualities, define it, and finally overcome it entirely.

Silver also, in order to be perfected, requires only purification and cooking.

Yet these salty liquors provide both: indeed, the power of salts is wondrous in this whole work. But silver, since it is more dry, requires mixing and union with quicksilver, as if with a glue, by whose benefit it may undergo and endure all the **tests of gold** <note>original: "auri examina"; the rigorous refining processes like cupellation or the touchstone that prove a metal's purity</note>.

<margin>An easy method of reducing gold into a liquid</margin>
For because the moisture of gold is pure, viscous, and intensely **cooked** by nature, it cannot be drawn away from its dryness by any art. The method of turning gold into a liquid is manifold, and you will find it prescribed and publicized everywhere among authors; but this one is easy among all the others. Let gold be reduced to **calx** <term>calcem: a fine powder produced by heating or dissolving a metal; an oxide</term>, by that way and method which we spoke of above in its preparation. Next, let the calx be dissolved in **aqua regia** <term>regia aqua: "royal water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</term>—that is, sharp water distilled from saltpeter and **vitriol** <term>calchanto: a sulfate mineral, often copper or iron sulfate</term>—into which **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniacus: ammonium chloride</term>, best purified by **sublimation** <note>a process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</note>, is then poured and dissolved in the same aqua regia in a warm place. From here, distill the thinner watery liquor by distillation through warm water, which they commonly call the **Bain-Marie** <term>Balneum Mariae: a water bath used for gentle, even heating</term> or "Bath of Mary." Repeat this same distillation seven times, until you see a **red oil** remaining in the very bottom of the vessel. This oil is dissolved by light heat, but once removed from the fire, it congeals and thickens like gum in a cold place. To this gum, mix four...

# ON THE METHOD OF PRODUCING THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE

<margin>The use of the oil of gold.</margin>
...parts of **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniacus: ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to aid in the sublimation and dissolution of metals</term>, likewise most excellently refined and purified by very frequent repetitions of **sublimation** <note>the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</note>, and let it be dissolved into water. Then, cook it over a slow and weak fire into a thick consistency; afterward, dissolve it in a damp place, and then dry it out again. Repeat this same work over and over, by congealing and dissolving, until at last it no longer hardens in dry, weak heat, but remains and persists perpetually in that same heat like a thick oil.

Take one ounce of this oil and mix it with four ounces of **quicksilver** <term>argenti vivi: mercury</term> which has been most excellently cleansed and purged of impurities by the best possible method. Once placed in a suitable glass vessel, cook it for the space of eight days, gradually increasing the level of heat until at last you have applied the most vehement heat of the fourth and final grade <note>alchemists typically used four "grades" or intensities of fire, ranging from a gentle lamp to the heat of a blast furnace</note>, and you see a red, or at least a saffron-colored, powder. When this powder is finally taken out, you shall melt it with **chrysocolla** <term>gold-solder or borax; a flux used to help metals flow during melting</term> into true gold.

In truth, this will be done even more quickly and better if a globe made of gold and quicksilver <note>an amalgam</note>, prepared by the method we taught above, is ground together with a small portion of this oil smeared upon it, and finally cooked as indicated in the previous practice.

Lastly, you will carry out this same work even more successfully and safely if you compose and press out a globe from gold, silver, and quicksilver, and mix a small portion of this same golden oil into this globe, grinding the mixture, and finally, as has often been said, cooking it by gradually increasing the stages of the fires.

Truly, however, these "oils of gold" prepared by means of **sharp waters** <note>original: "aquas acres"; corrosive acids such as aqua fortis or aqua regia used to dissolve metals</note>, even if they seem to be of great importance, are to be considered as nothing if they are compared with that **gold-making salt** <note>original: "sale illo nostro aurifico"</note> of ours, or the **Philosophers' Stone**.

# THE PRINTER
## TO THE READER, GREETINGS <note>original: "Lectori S." — S. is an abbreviation for *Salutem*, a standard Latin greeting wishing health and prosperity.</note>

If you take these rules in good part, however brief they may be, you will incite and entice that same friend to share greater things hereafter. # CANONS OR <note>original: "CANONES SEV"</note>

## THE TEN RULES, CONCERNING THE

### Philosopher’s Stone.

> Which, if rightly understood, will open no small path to the adopted goal for the **son of the art.** <note>The "son of the art" (filius artis) is a traditional alchemical term for a dedicated student or initiate of alchemy.</note>

->The First Rule.<-

The Stone which is sought is one, a unique medicine, nor can there be many.

->The Second Rule.<-

The matter of the thing, or of the one Stone, is likewise unique and not manifold; nor is that immediate power found in any other thing in the whole world, nor is that secret found in any other thing, nor does it have its like in the entire world.

->The Third Rule.<-

Yet it contains within itself several things, especially two **hypostatic** <term>hypostaticas: from the Greek 'hypostasis,' referring here to the fundamental or essential underlying substances that make up a single reality</term> ones: the Lower and the Upper; indeed, from different perspectives, it contains three, four, and five.

->The Fourth Rule.<-

That Thing also, in its own respect, is All things, and contains All things, and is above all **sublunary** <term>sublunaria: the earthly realm "below the moon," which was believed to be subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens</term> things. And likewise, from another perspective, it is Nothing, because it is **Hyle** <term>Hyle: a Greek term for "prime matter," the raw, formless substance of the universe</term>, or from **Chaos** <note>original: "de Chao"</note> and the seed of the world, possessing much blessing.

->The Fifth Rule.<-

That unique matter is the **First Matter** <term>Materia prima: the original, undifferentiated substance from which all metals and minerals were thought to originate</term> of all Metals—not those already made, but those yet to be made—wherefore it is neither animal, nor vegetable, nor mineral, but **Catholic** <term>Catholica: used here in its literal sense of "universal" or "general," rather than a religious designation</term> and universal, and by no means specific. And it is Earthy Water, and Watery Earth, in the womb of the Earth, mixed with the Earth, with which the Spirit and **Fifth Essence** <term>Quinta Essentia: the "Quintessence," the purest and most subtle element that permeates the other four (earth, air, fire, water)</term>—or Celestial influence—mixes itself.

->The Sixth Rule.<-

In external form, however, it agrees with minerals, and is discerned from ores; for which reason it is Natural, not Artificial, since it is prepared by Nature herself.

HEADER: TEN CANONS CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHER’S STONE. <note>original: "CANONES DECEM DE LAPI. PHIL."</note>

### Rule Seven.

And just as there is a single stone and a single matter, so also there is a single preparation, which completely imitates Nature as much as possible: And indeed, the operation of Nature ought to be the standard for artificial methods.

### Rule Eight.

And just as Nature raises a certain vapor from that matter—which vapor, enclosed within the mines and arriving in a pure place, is congealed and fixed into a pure metal by a pure, sulfurous mineral virtue over a long period of time—so also this preparation is divided into two parts. The first of these is **natural** <note>The original OCR reads "natulis," likely a contraction or error for "naturalis" (natural).</note> in its own respect, and artificial in another way. In this stage, that purified spirit, that truly permanent water, is congealed and fixed with its own body, which has been reduced into a **Fifth Essence** <term>Quinta Essentia: the Quintessence, or the purest, most concentrated spiritual essence of a substance</term>, so that what the Philosophers say is true: *The whole work consists in solution and congelation.* Yet one work can be expanded into many, from different perspectives.

### Rule Nine.

Nature, however, must be assisted, both by administering external fire (while nevertheless stirring up the internal one) and by administering the **Mercury of the Philosophers** <term>Mercurio Physicorum: not common mercury, but a specialized alchemical substance used as a universal solvent or catalyst</term>, either perfected in the moist or more than perfected in the dry: a ferment converting the whole mass into its own nature.

### Rule Ten.

And yet, before fermentation, it is truly **Catholic** <note>original: "Catholica," used here in its original Greek sense of "universal" or "all-encompassing" rather than a religious denomination.</note> and universal, and it acts universally and broadly upon all **sublunary** <term>sublunaria: the earthly realm "below the moon," which was believed to be subject to change and decay</term> things. After fermentation, however, it becomes specific to the metallic nature.

# E P I L O G U E OF THE
## *Whole matter herein.* <note>The original heading "T O- tius" is a split word for "totius" meaning "of the whole."</note>

There is only one stone, one matter, which is the first source of all metals, and indeed a single preparation; if anyone should stray from this, they will not reach the goal. It is divided into two operations, namely **Solution** <term>Solutio: the alchemical process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state, often described as "opening" the matter to release its internal spirit</term> and **Congelation** <term>Congelatio: the process of thickening or solidifying the matter, "fixing" the spirit into a stable, physical form</term>. And it is truly universal before **fermentation** <term>Fermentatio: the final stage where the "Stone" is given a specific direction—like leaven in bread—allowing it to transform other metals into gold or silver</term>, but specific after it.

> Blessed, therefore, be that thing, and blessed be its operation, through Jesus Christ. Amen.

# TO THE READER.

...[so that she] stains [with a permanent quality]: I can rightly affirm that such a man has the doors of nature open to investigate further and higher secrets, and to acquire them with God's blessing. Furthermore, I offer these present Treatises, written from my own experience, to the sons of science, so that while they are engaged with every thought and movement of the mind in inquiring into the hidden operations of nature, they may from there perceive and know the truth of things and nature itself. In this thing alone the perfection of the entire most holy philosophical art consists, provided they proceed along the **Royal Road** <term>Royal Road: Latin "via Regia," referring to the direct and true path of alchemical transformation dictated by nature's own laws, rather than the "short-cuts" or artificial methods used by frauds</term> which nature prescribes in all its operations. 

Therefore, I wish to warn the **Honest Reader** <note>original: "Candidum Lectorem"; literally the "white" or "shining" reader, a standard term for an unbiased or well-intentioned student</note> here to understand my writings not so much from the "bark" or surface of the words, but from the powers of nature, lest he later deplore time, labor, and expense spent in vain. Let him consider that this is the science of the **Wise** <term>Wise: Latin "Sophorum," a term used specifically for "Adepts"—those who have mastered the alchemical art</term>, not of the unskilled. And the meaning of the Philosophers is far different than what can be perceived by either boastful **Thrasos** <note>original: "Thrafones"; a reference to Thraso, a character in Roman comedy representing a swaggering, arrogant soldier</note>, or mocking scholars, or those who are vicious against their own conscience (who, while they cannot rise through virtues, attempt to do so through crimes and slanders against honorable men), or the unskilled charlatans who, with their **whitenings** <term>Whitenings: Latin "dealbationibus," a stage in alchemy where a substance turns white (albedo); frauds often used superficial silvering to mimic this effect</term> and **reddenings** <term>Reddenings: Latin "Rubefactionibus," the final "red work" (rubedo) of the philosopher's stone; a process often faked by using pigments or dyes to deceive investors</term>, have deceived almost the whole world, to the most unworthy defamation of the most praised chemical science. 

Men of this sort, that most holy science will never admit into its inner chambers. For it is a gift of GOD. Therefore, she <note>Nature or Alchemy is often personified as a female figure</note> deservedly drives those who are estranged from GOD far away from her secrets. ## TREATISE I.

### *Concerning Nature, what it truly is, and what kind of seekers it ought to have.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'M' featuring ornate scrollwork and foliage patterns.</image-desc>

MANY wise and most learned men, many centuries ago—indeed, as Hermes <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure often cited as the founder of alchemy.</note> bears witness, even before the flood—wrote much about the making of the **Philosopher's Stone**, and left so many writings to us that, unless nature performed believable wonders for us daily, hardly anyone would now believe that **NATURE** is real. This is because in past centuries there were not so many "inventors" of things; nor did our predecessors consider anything else besides nature itself and the possibilities of nature. 

And although they remained only on the simple path of nature, they nevertheless discovered things which we, though now occupied with so many things, could hardly have imagined with our own wits. This happens because the nature and the generation of things in the world now seem common and simple to us. Therefore, we direct our intellects not toward known things, but toward such things that cannot, or can hardly, be done. 

For this reason, it also happens to us that it is easier to devise subtle things—and we can imagine things that the Philosophers themselves did not know—than it is to arrive at the true course of nature and the sense of the Philosophers. Human nature is so composed that it neglects those things it already knows and always seeks others; much more so for human intellects, to which nature is subject. 

For example: you see any craftsman, when he has already reached the highest perfection of his craft, seek other things, or misuse his skill, or give it up entirely. Thus noble nature also acts, continuing right into the very <term>Iliadum: A term used by the Swiss physician Paracelsus to describe the ultimate limit, the final point of development, or the "first matter" of a thing.</term>, that is, the ultimate boundary, and then it ceases. For a certain permission was granted to nature from the beginning, so that through its complete course it might reach better things and have full rest, toward which it strives with every effort, and rejoices in its end,

# ON THE IMPOSSIBILITY OF NATURE.

no differently than an ant in its old age, for whom nature creates wings as it nears its end: so indeed have our wits progressed so far, especially in the **Philosophical Art**, or the practice of the **Stone**, that we have now almost reached a monumental achievement <note>original: "Iliadū"; likely a reference to the "Iliad in a nutshell," a Latin proverb for something of great magnitude contained in a small space, or a work of immense complexity.</note>. For the art of Chemistry has now discovered such subtleties that hardly any greater can be found; and it differs as much from the Art of the ancient Philosophers as a **Clockmaker** differs from a simple **Blacksmith**. And although both work with iron, nevertheless neither would understand the other’s labors, even though both are Masters in their own craft. If the Father of Philosophers, **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>, were to come back to life today, along with the subtle-minded **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in early chemistry/alchemy.</note> and the most profound **RAYMOND LULLY** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan polymath and philosopher whose name was often attached to alchemical texts.</note>, they would not be regarded as Philosophers by our modern Chemists, but rather as mere disciples. They would not know the many distillations, the many circulations, the many calcinations, and the many other innumerable works of the Artists used today, which the men of this century have discovered and devised from their writings. Only one thing is lacking to us: that we might know that which they themselves accomplished, namely the **Philosopher's Stone** or the **Physical Tincture**. While we seek that, we find other things; and if human procreation were not so common, and nature did not maintain its own right in that matter, we would by now hardly avoid going astray.

But to return to the purpose: I promised in this first Treatise to explain nature, lest a vain imagination deflect us from the simple and true path. Therefore, I say that **NATURE** is one, true, simple, and whole in its being, which God made before the ages, and into which He enclosed a spirit. Know, however, that the boundary of nature is God, who is also the beginning of nature; for indeed, no beginning is finished except in that in which it begins. I have said it is only one, through which God does all things—not because God would not know how to operate without it (since He Himself made nature and is omnipotent), but because it so pleased Him, and so He did it. All things proceed from that one nature, nor is there anything in the world outside of nature. And although sometimes "monsters" or failed births occur, this is not a fault of nature, but a defect of either the **Craftsman** <note>The alchemist or worker.</note> or the **location**.

This Nature is divided into four places <note>The four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>, in which it operates all these things that appear and are in shadow; for indeed, things are in shadow rather than truly appearing as they are. It is changed into male and female, and is compared to **Mercury**, because it joins itself to various places; and according to the locations of the earth, it produces good or bad things, though there are no truly bad places in the earth, however it may seem to us. The qualities, however, are only four, and these are in all things; they do not agree, but one always exceeds the other. Nature herself is not visible, although she acts visibly, for she is a **volatile spirit** <note>original: "spiritus volatilis"; in alchemy, a spirit that can easily escape or be transformed by heat.</note> who performs her office within bodies. She has her place and seat in the divine will. For us, in this place, she is of no use for anything else except that we might know her "places," which may be more suitable or closer to her—that is, so that we may know how to join...

Searchers of nature <term>Scrutatores naturæ</term> <note>These are the investigators or students of the natural world, specifically alchemists here.</note> ought to be such as nature herself is: truthful, simple, patient, steadfast, etc., and most importantly, pious, God-fearing, and not harming their neighbor.

But if you strive for something more excellent than Nature, observe in what and through what it is improved, and this will always occur within its own likeness. For example, if you desire to advance a metal (which is our intention) in virtue further than nature has done, it is necessary to take the Metallic nature, and this in male and female; otherwise you will accomplish nothing. For if you intend to create a metal from herbs, you will labor in vain, just as you would if you tried to produce wood from a dog or a beast.

# TREATISE II.

->*On the operation of nature in our purpose and on the Seed.*<- <note>original: "Spermate"; used here in the alchemical sense of a "seed" or "generative principle" rather than its modern biological meaning.</note>

I have already said that Nature is true, unique, appearing everywhere continuously, which is known from the things produced, namely woods, herbs, etc. I have also said that the searcher of nature <term>Scrutatorem naturæ</term> must be truthful, simple, patient, and constant, applying his mind to at least one thing, etc. 

Now we must begin concerning the act of nature: Just as nature exists in the will of God, and God created her or set her over every imagination, so nature made for herself a seed <term>semen</term>, that is, her will within the Elements. She is indeed one, and yet she brings forth diverse things, but she performs nothing without the Seed <term>Spermate</term>. Whatever the Seed wills, nature performs, for it is like the instrument of some Craftsman. 

Therefore, the Seed of each thing is better and more useful to the Craftsman than nature herself. For from nature without the Seed, you will accomplish as much as a Goldsmith could without fire, gold, or silver, or a Farmer without grain or seed. Once the Seed is obtained, nature will be ready at hand, whether for evil or for good. She works in the Seed as God works in the free will of man— <note>The text cuts off here at the word "homine" (man) and will continue on the next page.</note>

The **Seed**, therefore, is the **Elixir** <note>The supreme medicinal or transformative substance.</note> of any thing, or the **fifth essence** <term>Quintessence</term>, or the most perfect boiling and digestion of a thing, or the **Balsam of Sulfur**, which is the same as the **Radical Moisture** <term>Humidum Radicale</term> in Metals. The four Elements generate the Seed by the will of God and the imagination of nature. For just as the Seed of a man has its center, or the vessel of its seed in the kidneys, so the four Elements, by unceasing motion (each according to its own quality), project the Seed into the center of the earth where it is digested and sent outward by motion. Truly, the center of the earth is a certain empty place where nothing can rest. 

<margin>+ Excentrics</margin> Into the center (so to speak), or the margin and circumference of the center, the four Elements project their qualities, just as a man emits his seed into the womb of a woman, in which nothing of the Seed remains; but after the Matrix <note>The womb or generative environment.</note> receives the required portion, it casts the rest outward. Similarly it happens in the center of the earth, that the **Magnetic force** of some part of a place attracts a thing to itself that is suitable for bringing forth something; the rest is cast out into stones and other waste matter <note>original: "excrementa"; referring to non-generative byproducts.</note>. For all things have their origin from that source, nor is anything born in the whole world except through this source.

For example: let there be on some flat table a small vessel of Water, placed in the middle of the Table, and all around let various things be placed, and various colors, likewise Salt, etc., each separately. Let the Water afterwards be poured into the middle; you will see that Water flowing here and there, and while one stream touches a red color, it will become red from it; if it touches salt, it will borrow the taste of salt, and so for the rest. For Water does not change the places, but the diversity of the places changes the Water. In a similar way, from the center of the earth, the Seed projected into the center by the four elements passes to various places, and according to the nature of the place the thing is "natured" <note>That is, it takes on the specific characteristics of that environment.</note>. If it arrives at a pure place of earth and Water, a pure thing is made. The Seed of all things is one and the same, and yet it generates various things, as appears from the following example:

The Seed of a man is a noble seed, and at least it is created for the generation of a man; nevertheless, if a man should misuse it (which is within his free will), an abortion is born. For if, against the gravest prohibitions of God, a man were to enter a cow or another beast, the beast would easily conceive the seed of the man; because nature does not...

## TREATISE III.

->*On the true first matter of Metals.*<-

The first matter of Metals is twofold, but one without the other does not create a Metal. The first and principal is the **moisture of air** mixed with heat; this the Philosophers have named **Mercury**, which is governed by the rays of the Sun and Moon <note>original: "Solis & Lunae"; alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver, or the masculine and feminine principles.</note> in the Philosophical sea. The second is the **dry heat of the earth**, which they have called **Sulfur**. 

But because all true Philosophers have greatly hidden this, we shall explain it a little more clearly—especially the **weight**, for if that is ignored, all things are destroyed. From this it happens that many produce failures <note>original: "abortus"</note> from a good starting material. For there are those who take the whole body for the matter, or the seed, or the sperm; others take only a fragment; and all these turn aside from the right path. For example, if someone were to take a man's foot and a woman's hand and wished to create a human from this mixture, it would not be possible. For there is in every body a center and a place, or a point of the seed or sperm—and it is always the 1/8200th part even in <unclear>in</unclear> a single grain of Wheat. # ON THE FIRST MATTER OF METALS.

...the grain or body is turned into seed, but there is only a certain necessary spark in the body, which is guarded by its body from all excessive heat and cold, etc. If you have ears and senses, pay attention here and you will be safe—not only from those who are ignorant of the place of the Seed <note>original: "Spermatis"</note> and strive to reduce the entire grain into seed, but also from all those who occupy themselves in the vain dissolution of Metals and wish to dissolve Metals entirely so that, afterward, from their mutual mixture, they might create a new Metal. But if these people would consider the process of nature, they would see that the matter stands far differently. For no Metal is so pure that it does not also have its own impurities, though one may have fewer or more than another. But you, friend reader, will first observe the "point of nature," as was said above, and that is enough for you. However, keep this caution for yourself: do not seek that point in the metals of the common people <note>original: "Metallis vulgi"; referring to ordinary, commercially traded metals</note>, in which it is not present. For these metals, especially the common gold <note>original: "aurum vulgi"</note>, are dead; but ours are living, possessing a spirit, and these must certainly be taken. For know that the life of Metals is fire while they are still in their mines, and their death is also fire—namely, the fire of fusion <note>The act of melting metal into ingots kills its "growth" or "vitality" according to alchemical theory.</note>. But the First Matter of metals is a certain moisture mixed with warm air, and it is in the form of a fatty water adhering to every thing, whether pure or impure; yet it is more abundant in one place than in another, which happens because the earth is more open and porous in one place, having an attractive power, than in another. It sometimes comes into the light by itself, dressed in a certain garment <note>original: "induta veste aliqua"; a metaphor for the external appearance or matrix of the mineral</note>, especially in places where it has nothing to adhere to. It is recognized in this way: because every thing is composed of three principles, but in the matter of Metals, there is only one without conjunction—except for its garment, or rather its shadow, which is **Sulphur** <term>Sulphur: In this context, not the chemical element, but the active, combustible principle of "soul" within minerals.</term>, etc.

## TREATISE IV.

### How Metals are generated in the bowels of the earth?

Metals are produced in this manner: after the four Elements project their virtues into the center of the earth, the **Archæus** <term>Archæus: The "inner craftsman" or vital formative force of nature that directs the growth of minerals and living things.</term>, by distilling, sublimates them by the heat of perpetual motion toward the surface of the earth. For the earth is porous, and the wind <note>original: "ventus"; here referring to a vaporous or gaseous state</note>, by trickling through the pores of the earth, is resolved into water, from which all things are born. Let the sons of learning therefore know that the seed of Metals is no different from the seed of all things—namely, a moist vapor. Therefore, Artists seek in vain the reduction of Metals into the "First Matter," which is only a vapor. The Philosophers did not understand such a reduction...

### TREATISE IV.

...first matter, but only the second matter, as Bernard of Treviso <note>original: "Bernhardus Trevisanus"; a 15th-century Italian alchemist whose works emphasize the use of "living" mercury.</note> argues excellently, although not so clearly because he speaks of the four elements; nonetheless, he intended to say this, and spoke only with the "sons of the art" <note>A traditional term for initiated alchemists or those deemed worthy of secret knowledge.</note>.

But I, in order to reveal the theory more clearly, wished to caution and warn everyone here to cease so many dissolutions, so many circulations, so many calcinations <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile parts or oxidize it into a powder.</note>, and repetitions. For such things are sought in vain in a hard substance, since it is soft of its own nature everywhere. Let not the first, but only the second matter be sought—such a matter, surely, that as soon as it is conceived, it cannot be changed into another form. 

But if you ask how a metal might be reduced to such a matter, I follow the intention of the philosophers in this: I desire this above all else, that the "sons of art" understand the sense of the writers, not the syllables; and that where nature ceases—namely in metallic things, in the perfect bodies before our eyes—there the art must begin.

But to return to the point (since our intention here is not only about the Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note>), let us now discuss the matter of metals. A little while ago, I said that all things are born from liquid air or vapor, which the elements drop into the belly of the earth through perpetual motion. After the Archæus <note>Archæus: In alchemical theory, the internal "master chemist" or vital force of nature that directs the growth and transformation of substances.</note> of nature has received this, it sublimates <note>The process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then cools back into a solid; here used to describe the movement of vapors through the earth.</note> it through the pores, and distributes it to each place with its own wisdom (as we have related in the preceding pages); and thus, by the variety of places, various things also come forth and are born. 

There are those who believe that Saturn <note>Saturn: Alchemical name for Lead.</note> has one seed, and gold another; and so on for the remaining metals. But these ideas are vain. There is only one single seed; the same is found in Saturn as is found in gold, the same in the Moon <note>Luna: Alchemical name for Silver.</note> as in Mars <note>Mars: Alchemical name for Iron.</note>, and so forth. But the location in the earth was different, if you understand me correctly.

Although nature ceased sooner in the Moon than in the Sun <note>Sol: Alchemical name for Gold.</note>, and so with the others. For when that vapor is sublimated from the center of the earth, it passes through places that are either dry or hot. If, therefore, the vapor passes through hot and pure places, where the "fatness" of Sulfur <note>original: "pinguedo Sulphuris"; refers to the oily, combustible principle of matter in the sulfur-mercury theory.</note> clings to the walls, that vapor—which the philosophers have called the Mercury of the Philosophers <note>original: "Mercurium Philosophorum"</note>—adapts itself and joins with that fatness, which it afterward sublimates with itself; and then it becomes an unctuousness. Leaving behind the name of "vapor," it takes the name of "Fatness" <note>original: "Pinguedinis"</note>. 

This fatness, coming afterward by sublimating to other places which the preceding vapor has already purged, where there is subtle, pure, and moist earth, fills its pores and joins with it, and thus becomes the Sun <note>Gold</note>. But if that fatness comes to impure and cold places, it becomes Saturn <note>Lead</note>. If, however, such earth is mixed with Sulfur, it becomes Venus <note>Copper</note>, and so on. For the more purified a place is, the more beautiful the metals it produces. For it must be known that this vapor continually issues from the center to the surface, and by going, it purifies the places; hence it happens that today there are found mi-

...generated in places where a thousand years ago there were none. For in its progress, nature always refines what is crude and impure, gradually drawing it along. This is the repetition and circulation of nature: it is sublimated <note>original: "sublimatur"; in alchemy, the process of heating a substance so it rises as vapor and then cools back into a solid, used here to describe the earth's natural refining process.</note> for as long as it takes to produce new things, until the place is perfectly purified. The more it is purified, the nobler the things it produces. In winter, however, when the cold air constricts the earth, that oily vapor is also congealed; then, when spring returns, it is mixed with earth and water and becomes Magnesia <note>original: "Magnesia"; here referring to a primordial "mother" substance or magnetic agent that attracts celestial influences, rather than the modern chemical element.</note>. This draws to itself a Mercury of the air <note>original: "Mercurium aeris"; a vital, spiritual essence believed to be carried in the atmosphere.</note> similar to it, which gives life to all things through the rays of the Sun, Moon, and Stars, and thus it brings forth grass, flowers, and the like. For Nature does not rest for a single moment. Metals, indeed, are procreated in this way: the earth is purged by a long distillation, and afterwards, they are generated by the arrival of a rich oiliness <note>original: "pinguedinis"; often used in alchemy to describe the sulfurous, combustible, or "fatty" principle of a substance.</note>; they do not arise in any other way, despite the vain opinion of those who interpret the writings of certain philosophers incorrectly.
