### FIRST PART ###

[...that he might pro]ve, and we should not presume to cast a bridle upon His will; for here is truth, wisdom, and justice, distributing to each according to his due through the Holy Spirit, just as it was poured out upon the Apostles. For this reason also, we are commanded to ask for our daily bread every day in the Lord’s Prayer <note>original: "oratione Dominica"</note>, for we do not know what we ought to ask from God, and quite often we ask for those things which will result in our ruin, although these are sometimes granted to us so that we may be tested by them. Therefore, only the help of the Holy Spirit, prosperous health, and the benefits of peace are to be sought from God; for from Him descends all knowledge and wisdom, both natural and spiritual. 

But Christ desired the salvation of men quite ardently; hence He says His kingdom is not of this world, and that He came into the world for this purpose: to lead saved men back to the celestial kingdom and to rescue them from the darkness of ignorance and earthly riches, until at last He might lead some there. To that end, He gave us that Lord’s Prayer as we call it, and taught how we ought to direct our prayers to God the Father, whose children we are through adoption, whereas before this we walked before Him under the ceremonies of the Law in fear and servile dread. 

Beyond these things, I think it is not hidden from you that the natural arises from the supernatural, and that the kingdom of God is from eternity, from which the temporal kingdom flows. For was not the first heaven and the firmament prepared, after this the Element <note>referring to the primal substance of creation</note>, and last of all the earth? After this, man was established—a new creature and a microcosm <term>microcosm: a "little world"; the philosophical idea that the human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the macrocosm)</term>. For God first begins in man on the earth as if in the center of a circle, just as He had previously taken His beginning from a greater center. After this, life and a soul were instilled into the body of man—an eternal and immortal life and soul. For this is super-celestial, and like a divine starry heaven <note>original: "coelum divinum sidereum"</note>, like the essential spirit of all natural living creatures. 

But finally, the elemental body was formed, as if into a single body, the center of the earth, designated by Christ as the "salt of the earth" <note>original: "salis terrae"; a reference to Matthew 5:13</note>. For salt preserves all things from rot, just as it is known from the natural ocean of the world what contagion would be born from such rot unless God preserved it with that salt—especially if it were to lie entirely devoid of motion. To salt are also compared the pastors and ministers of the Word, who preserve the members of the faith committed to them from rot, through the preaching of the divine Word and the Holy Spirit in this ocean of the world. Also, Adam, the first father of us all, possessed universal knowledge...

### THE HIDDEN PHILOSOPHY OF AURELIA ###

...[possess]ed <note>The word fragment "bat" likely concludes a verb such as "possidebat" (he possessed) from the previous page.</note> knowledge of all creatures, while we, his descendants, possess and know only certain fragments. We recognize that our knowledge is imperfect, just as in the final days, many men will be gathered together in many places in the stead of the single Adam. It is said that all arts shall be fully revealed before the supreme judgment of the world. However, to no man is such great knowledge and science given as was granted to our first parent, Adam, and given to Christ, that "New Adam." He bestows this knowledge also upon His bride <note>original: "sponsæ suæ"; in this context, the "bride" refers to the collective body of believers or the Church.</note>—that is, many individuals gathered into one—until we enter into eternal life, in which all things shall be made new and revealed, and to each, a due reward shall be given. For in this world, we are subject to the various troubles and cares of temptations because of the stain of sin, through which great disadvantages are brought upon the human race by the Enemy. For we, having lost the image of God, always act contrary to His will. 

Besides these things, you should also consider that saying of the Savior, in which He commands us to seek those treasures that are subject neither to decay nor to the greed of thieves and robbers. Instead, let them be spiritual treasures, sustaining the consciences of men in the final waves of temptation. When the spirit and body, convulsed with terror and trembling, seek the help of human aid in vain, at that moment in time, heavenly armor <note>original: "armatura cœlestis"</note> must be sought with the greatest effort. Then, the fading and fragile power of those cardinal worldly virtues in which we boasted while the "time of grace" flourished—namely beauty, wisdom, wealth, and power—becomes apparent when compared to the divine glory, which is to be sought in Christ alone and in His word. 

But if, during the time of this our pilgrimage, being vigilant and devoted to prayer, we testify to our faith, charity, hope, modesty, humility, and patience, as the bride of Christ, so that we may be conformed to our bridegroom, Christ the Savior, we shall ascend into the bosom of Abraham and Isaac <note>original: "in sinum Abrahæ & Isaaci"</note> by the ladder of Jacob. And we shall see the glory and the rock of faith <note>original: "petram fidei"</note>, and the disciple beloved by the Lord, John, who like a soaring eagle turns his eyes toward the sun—that is, the glory and brightness of God, which was hidden and concealed even from Jacob. Indeed, these three disciples perceived a taste and a certain ray of this glory on Mount Tabor <note>A reference to the Transfiguration, where Peter, James, and John saw Jesus revealed in divine splendor.</note>. Truly, all these things have been written to the end that, by their example, having despised worldly riches and following only the divine word and His command, we might implore the help of the Holy Spirit, and in faith, charity, hope, humility, and patience live before

# PART ONE #

...[let us] walk with God, perceiving in the same way a certain taste of this heavenly Jerusalem and Paradise. For we learn these things from the word of God alone, and not truly from the allurements of this world, for He alone is just and merciful. Therefore, he who desires the restoration of the divine image within himself should study works of mercy and charity, since we, being many, are one body in Christ, and His unique bride. I wanted to propose all these necessary things to you, although you also drink daily from the hearing of the word of God, so that, attending to these with more burning care, you may certainly determine—according to that saying of Paul—that godliness is a great gain <note>original: "magnum esse vectigal"; referencing 1 Timothy 6:6, "godliness with contentment is great gain."</note> if one does not crave greater things. For we bring nothing into this world, nor do we carry anything out from the goods of fortune when we depart from it. 

But if God has bestowed the necessities of life and food, it is right that we live content with those gifts. For those who anxiously seek those worldly riches fall into temptations and the snares of desires, until they are plunged by them into extreme ruin. For greed <note>original: "Avaritia"</note> is the root of all evils, and those who have lusted after it have strayed from the faith, submerged in deep calamities. Flee all these things, O man of God, with your greatest effort, and follow righteousness, piety, faith, patience, and humility, fighting the good fight; and lay hold of that eternal life for which you were created, and which you professed before many. 

Moreover, command the rich of this age not to be puffed up with pride, nor to hope in uncertain riches, but to place their hope in the living God, who supplies all things, so that they may do good to others, being rich and abundant in good works, and acquire treasures as a good foundation and the attainment of eternal life. This is the sum and the argument of our whole response, so extensively enumerated thus far, by which I might somewhat soothe that desire of yours for earthly riches; for these words were brought forth from the heavenly center of that Sun of Justice <note>The "Sun of Justice" (*Sol Iustitiae*) is a biblical title for Christ, often used in both theological and alchemical texts to represent the source of spiritual illumination and perfection.</note>, and by the rays of the Holy Spirit through that chosen vessel of God <note>original: "vas illud electum"; a traditional title for the Apostle Paul, referring to Acts 9:15.</note>. Moreover, the heavenly life and blessedness far precede that earthly life, which it also befits us to emulate in this flesh, so that we may be made spiritual flesh, which abstains from all the allurements of this world, waging a continuous war with the enemies of God under the yoke of the spirit.

->ADOLPHUS<-

Great wonder comes upon me when I see you longing for those spiritual mysteries and heavenly teachings, although few initiates <term>initiates: "mystae", those initiated into sacred or secret mysteries</term> of this world are accustomed to turn their minds to them, so truly...

->THE OCCULT PHILOSOPHY OF AURELIA<-

...[Truly,] you have delivered all these things so far at such length and somewhat obscurely, so that anyone might more easily be inflamed with the love of gold than with the love of divine scripture. I, however, have heard all these things so far with great pleasure; I am hearing many things for which I have had no concern until now, just as we, being by nature more prone to evil, are less attentive to right words or deeds.

### THE ELDER <note>original: "SENIOR"; likely a reference to the character of the wise teacher, common in alchemical dialogues such as those attributed to Senior Zadith.</note>

For that reason, we must pay all the more attention here, because even this natural work <note>Refers to the alchemical *Opus*, or Great Work.</note> is most full of divine glory in its images and parables, quite apart from the abundance of earthly riches it offers. Truly, as I look upon the lives of men, a weariness of most of them takes hold of me; for few are worthy for this mystery to be revealed to them. In my own youth, I was destitute of all things and held in mockery by everyone; at last, I was taken in with difficulty by a certain good man. Tossed about until now with great care, anxiety, and the various troubles of many afflictions, I have only barely emerged. 

Perceiving from these experiences the blindness of men in spiritual matters, I offer my ears and eyes obediently to Christ the Savior, entreating Him with an ardent vow that He might rescue both me and others from that worldly blindness. Of this kind also is what we see in many of the learned: we see them abounding in riches yet holding almost everyone else in contempt, puffed up with excessive ambition and pride. Yet, at that final point of life <note>original: "extremo illo vitæ articulo"; referring to the moment of death.</note>, those riches and that ambition can bring them no help, and their strength is so diminished that it is scarcely sufficient even to drive away flies. 

Was it truly for that ambition, pride, and idleness alone that we were sent into this light by God—born merely to consume the fruits of the earth? <note>original: "fruges consumere nati"; a classical idiom for those who live unproductively.</note> Should we not rather direct all our care and concern toward acquiring that divine wisdom? That wisdom is poorly cast out by most, and not welcomed with hospitality as it once was by Abraham, Lot, and the Virgin Mother of God <note>original: "Deipara virgine"</note>. For wisdom turned aside to visit them, and prepared for itself a firm dwelling in their hearts. 

This wisdom, moreover, is the spirit of God—indeed, it is God Himself. From this it is clear what the Word of God is that intends to dwell in us; for this is that perfect wisdom. However, it does not dwell in those who are proud and exalted in spirit, or those who do not seek wisdom. For wisdom seeks and investigates those whom she loves—namely, the pious and those who obey reason—and this piety is the beginning of wisdom. From this foundation, the different states of the human race have been established, both in spiritual and bodily matters: such as Theology, Jurisprudence, Medicine, the Mechanical arts, and those called the Liberal arts. In this way—

<summary>The Elder explains that the alchemical "natural work" is a reflection of divine glory and laments the pride and spiritual blindness of the wealthy and learned. He argues that true wisdom is the Spirit of God which only dwells in the humble and pious, forming the basis for all human disciplines.</summary>

# PART ONE

...[explanation], so that all the manual arts <note>original: "artes manuariæ"; refers to crafts and physical labor, including alchemy.</note> are brought back to a good and just order through those seven <note>Likely referring to the seven stages of the alchemical process or the seven planetary metals.</note>, where good is separated from evil and truth is distinguished from falsehood. For it is God's will that, once evil is separated from good, the true light may shine within us. Since that fall of the first Adam, all things were subverted and disturbed through the wrath and cunning of the devil; but the New Adam <note>A common theological and alchemical title for Christ, signifying the restoration of humanity.</note> separates us—as if we were that regenerated Eve—from every stain, discerns good from evil, and restores a new life and a new world through Himself and His holy word. This is done so that hereafter the body and spirit may never be separated from one another, but may remain firm in the image of God. For this is the will of God, and in this way, He remains with us until the end of the world.

Truly, to the stubborn world, He presents that Jewish blindness and darkness <note>A common period trope used to describe those who adhere strictly to the "letter" of old laws or material reality, failing to see the "spirit" or the new light.</note>—those who insist on following the footsteps of that old Adam and do not, through faith in Holy Baptism, deliver him to death and suppress him. For this is the sacred operation of the Holy Spirit through the Word in faith; without the Word, however, there is nothing, for it is the very Word of God. But whoever does not believe the Word remains stuck in the darkness of death with that Adam and has no hope of eternal life, for they cannot persist in faith without a foundation. Such a person is a Heathen and marked by heretical depravity, stumbling at the cornerstone <note>A biblical reference to Christ (Psalm 118:22), here linked to the testimony of St. John.</note> pointed out by Saint John.

For God, in His immense mercy, has set before us many means by which, according to His will, we might be preserved from many temptations and evils, and might avoid the cursed spirit and perverse doctrine that procures the subversion of both soul and body. To this is also added the office of the political magistrate, through which the magistrate strikes back the violence and audacity of the wicked from the necks of the godly, procures harmony and peace, drives away all frauds and deceits, and grants to each person their right—not according to the whims and will of men, but according to the norm of justice and the divine will. 

The same is to be felt regarding the physician and the medical faculty, who drive away and repel all types of diseases and infirmities. For that malignant spirit sends all kinds of evils, temptations, and afflictions upon the human race—such as frauds, malice, enmities, hatreds, lies, adversities, slanders, poverty, persecutions, inconstancy, and other various species of temptations, all warring against faith, hope, and charity. This can also be seen in the Apostles John, Peter, and James, who, while Christ the Savior was being led away captive from the garden, provided a manifest example of human frailty and inconstancy.

# THE HIDDEN GOLDEN DAWN OF PHILOSOPHY
<note>original: "AURELIÆ OCCULTÆ PHILOSOPH."; Aurelia is a Latinized form often referring to "golden" or "splendid," likely hinting at the alchemical Great Work.</note>

[The Divine] Word, therefore, must be pursued with the greatest zeal, fixed in our minds, and confirmed by the seal of the sacraments, so that upon our departure from this life we may seal our faith and, against the power of the gates of hell, enter into eternal life. 

Lest these things, which I have spoken so at length, weary you, throw away the care for worldly wealth—following the example of Tobit <note>A biblical figure known for his piety and for instructing his son to give alms and trust in God rather than riches.</note>—and be content with your necessary daily food. Lean all your hope upon God and distribute alms to the poor, leaving the care of all other things to God alone. 

Truly, so that you may more fully achieve the unravelling and understanding of these sayings, I offer you this gift, through which these words will be more fully and abundantly declared to you. May you obtain a reward and a most generous treasure, so that you may progress more happily in the novelty of life and the diligence of your studies for the benefit of your neighbor and the glory of the Divine Name. 

This is truly such a treasure (provided that, with God’s help, you perceive its knowledge) which is found in no books of the learned, nor in the boxes of the apothecaries <note>original: "unguentariorum"; literally "perfumers" or "makers of ointments," referring to those who prepare medicinal or chemical compounds.</note>. It is hidden from the eyes of usurers, money-lenders, and Euclios <note>A reference to the character "Euclio" from Plautus’s play *Aulularia*, a classic archetype of a paranoid miser.</note>, nor can it be purchased by any man for any price. For this is our water and fire, yielding benefit and profit to the good, but clearly resulting in ruin for the wicked whenever the wicked abuse it for worldly pleasures and sloth; for worldly men do not embrace those things which are usually sought with great labor. 

If, therefore, you are humble, patient, modest, and of a calm mind, you will achieve this treasure of true tranquility and opulence, and you will be able to serve God and your neighbor usefully. First of all, I shall present to you that Egyptian priest and King, Hermes, and his Emerald Tablet <note>The *Tabula Smaragdina*, a foundational text of Hermeticism and alchemy.</note>. To him I shall join as companions the writings of Brother Basil <note>Basilius Valentinus, a legendary alchemist and monk.</note>, Count Bernard <note>Bernard Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemical author.</note>, the writings of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus Paracelsus, the famous Swiss physician and occultist.</note>, and the Tincture of the Physicians <note>original: "tincturam Physicorum"; a reference to the universal medicine or the Elixir.</note>, provided that you first declare more openly what your opinion is on this matter.

->ADOLPHUS.<-

Behold, at last, the finishing touch <note>original: "colophon"; historically the final inscription in a book, here used to mean the ultimate goal or crowning achievement.</note> of my desire, which I have waited for with such greed and heat until now. I truly and solemnly promise that I will use this treasure for the benefit and profit of my neighbor and the glory of the divine name, and that I will communicate it [to others]. I shall establish all my actions toward that end, so that I may show others what becomes of use, and so that my mind or spirit, contaminated by vices or crimes, may not become a scandal to others, so far as is ever possible in this fragility of human flesh.

### T H E  E L D E R.

Rest assured that even a person who enjoys only a modest abundance of wealth can effectively perform works of mercy <note>Traditional acts of charity and compassion performed for the benefit of others.</note>; indeed, beneficence that flows from a slender stream of resources is even more greatly approved by God. Truly, however, since I believe I have seen the purity of your soul clearly enough, I hand over to you, at the conclusion of this conversation of ours, this mystery wrapped in the veil of parables. It will be your duty to watch over the reading of these words, and others which relate the secrets of this mystery, with more attentive study. Observe with the greatest care this present short commentary written by me for your use; commit the care of all other things to God, the Best and Greatest.

### A D O L P H V S.

Indeed, venerable elder, I offer you immense thanks—as many as I can conceive in my mind—for such a precious gift and for the faithful instruction I have received from you thus far. Meanwhile, I solemnly promise that I shall, through diligent reading, convert these teachings into my very lifeblood <note>original: "in succum sanguineum"; an idiom meaning to internalize knowledge so deeply that it becomes part of one's vital nature.</note>. I shall implore God’s help with burning prayers, and I will so arrange all the actions of my life that I may provide an example of virtue to others. Truly, I dedicate, consecrate, and offer all my studies and efforts to your interests.

### T H E  E L D E R.

Would that all these things might come to pass by the helping kindness of God. But if the Best and Greatest God should grant you the knowledge of this mystery, be grateful, rendering praise and glory to God alone, according to that saying in Jeremiah 9 <note>Referencing Jeremiah 9:23–24.</note>: *Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man trust in his riches; but let him who glories, glory in this alone: that he knows that I am the Lord, who is merciful and just,* says the Lord, your God.

<meta>Continuity: This page continues "Part Two" of the work, moving from the symbolic frontispiece and introductory maxims of the previous page into a practical and philosophical discourse on the ease of the alchemical art for those who understand its "parables." <page-num>563</page-num>
<header>PART TWO.</header>

This art and mystery is handed down to no one with the barriers so removed and more openly than in parables, which must indeed be exactly considered and weighed; besides which, the books and commentaries of other Philosophers are also to be understood. However, to thoroughly attain this art of ours, very little labor and study, and few and small expenses and instruments are required. For this art can be learned in even twelve hours, and in the space of eight days it can be brought into work and effect, since it has its own principle within itself—whereas in other arts a period of six or seven years may be required for them to achieve their result. Yet some have spent thirty or forty years with great expense, never reaching the end of this mastery. Those craftsmen, however, to whom the end is known and understood, strive with all their might to hide and cover this craftsmanship, which the followers of this world are usually amazed by. But truly all these things are placed in the mercy of God, and for this work of ours only Azoth <term>Azoth: Considered by alchemists to be the "Universal Solvent" or the essential "mercury" of the philosophers; the beginning and end of the Great Work.</term> and fire are required, which is nothing other than to wash, cook, dissolve, putrefy, coagulate, and fix <note>original: "lavare, coquere, solvere, putrificare, coagulare & fixare." These are the standard stages of the alchemical process: cleansing, heating, breaking down, rotting/fermenting, thickening, and finally making the substance resistant to fire.</note>. All these things can be performed by the poor and needy as well as by the rich; nor is it even necessary that this craftsmanship be handed down in writing for the sake of preserving the memory, but it can be known by the living tradition of the voice itself. But I cannot declare these things to you more plainly and clearly because of the unjust power of some, but this at least I say and command: for this craftsmanship, use lunar water, or the water of silver, in which the rays of the sun are joined. And this operation is truly suited to women, as the ancients used to say <note>original: "verè mulieribus... convenit." A common alchemical trope (opus mulierum) suggesting that once the secret is known, the process is as simple and routine as domestic chores like washing laundry or cooking.</note>, although so many and such great volumes have been written about it by various people, and such a great number of commoners as well as nobles investigate it with great expense and labor—in vain and fruitless labor, to be sure, for nature has drawn a bar across the inside. <margin>9</margin> After this, certain parables along with the Emerald Tablet of Hermes, the most excellent Philosopher, are proposed to you for greater and fuller knowledge.

But if you have brought the operation to an end, and have cast it from its high state into the "sifted earth" (which in our art is compared to muddy earth), purge and free it from that; then it will shine with a far more splendid ray. But if you see it somewhat sad and changed, wash it in the bath of beauty, and adorn it with the garment of permanent brightness and the raw earth in which it wonderfully rejoices. Let it remain in that clothing for a time appropriate to it; then let it remain in it perpetually, by which you may also cast chains upon it according to your will. This is the **mystery of the universal Moon**, which if you have achieved, all the secrets of the art will be revealed to you.

## THE SYMBOL OF BROTHER BASIL
## Valentinus.

The stone is the least precious of all, from which the fugitive fire is extracted; but from this fire the stone itself is constructed, with a white and red color, and yet it is not a stone. In this stone nature works and produces a clear fountain which suffocates and absorbs its fixed father in the waters, until a soul is finally returned to him, and the fugitive mother becomes like him in the kingdom.

If indeed it shall have remained unharmed in the fire, it consumes the greatest sicknesses of men, beasts, and metals.

Indeed, after those ancient **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists or "philosophers by fire."</note> recognized this sign, they searched with the greatest zeal for the center of the middle tree in the **earthly Paradise** <note>original: "Paradiso terrestri"; a common alchemical metaphor for the balanced state of the First Matter before it is corrupted or divided.</note> within this mystery, entering through five contentious gates. 

The **first** of these was the knowledge of the true matter, for in this the first and most fierce battle arises. The **second** is the preparation, according to which the matter must be prepared so that they might find the **sparks of the eagle** and the **blood of the lion** <note>original: "favillas aquilæ & leonis sanguinem"; symbolic terms for volatile Mercury (the eagle) and fixed Sulfur (the lion).</note>; under this gate a sharp battle breaks forth, for the water and the blood are acquired, as well as a luminous spiritual body. The **third gate** is the fire, leading toward maturity. The **fourth** is multiplication and augmentation; in this, weight is necessarily required. The **fifth** and final gate is **projection** <note>The final stage where the Philosopher's Stone is cast upon "base" metals to transform them into gold.</note> into metal. 

Glorious, truly wealthy, and sublime is he who occupies the fourth gate, for he acquires the **universal medicine** <note>original: "universalem medicinam"; a substance believed to cure all diseases and prolong life, identical to the Philosopher's Stone.</note> for all illnesses. This is that great character of the **Book of Nature** from which the entire **Alphabet** <note>The "Alphabet of Nature" is a concept suggesting that the physical world is a language written by God, which the alchemist learns to read and manipulate.</note> arises. The fifth gate, however, serves only the metals. 

This mystery, existing from the very cradle of the world and the creation of **Adam**, is the most ancient of all things. It is a science inspired by God—the Best and Greatest—into nature through the **Word** <note>original: "verbū inspiratū"; referencing the Logos or the divine creative command.</note>; it is a wonderful power, a blessed fire of life, a transparent **carbuncle** <note>A term for a deep red gemstone, often used to describe the glowing appearance of the finished Philosopher's Stone.</note>, red gold, and the divine blessing of this life. Truly, because of the malice of men, this mystery of nature is granted to few, even though it turns and lives daily before the eyes of the whole world, as is clear from the following parable.

### FIRST MATTER.

I am the poisonous dragon, present everywhere, and to be acquired for the smallest price. He who investigates rightly will discover within me that upon which I rest, and that which rests above me. My water and fire destroy and compose; from my body you shall extract the **green and red lions** <note>original: "viridem & rubrum leonem"; symbolic names for the acidic starting liquid (green) and the perfected, fixed state (red).</note>. But if you do not know me exactly, you will consume your five senses with my fire. A premature poison issues from my nostrils, which has brought death to very many. Therefore, separate the **thick from the subtle** <note>original: "Crassum itaque à subtili"; a famous instruction from the *Emerald Tablet* of Hermes Trismegistus, referring to the distillation of pure spirit from dross.</note> with art, unless you rejoice in extreme poverty. I bestow upon you the powers of males and females alike, and even of the heavens and the earth. Truly, the mysteries of my art must be handled with courage and greatness of soul, if you desire to overcome the force of my fire, a task in which very many have suffered the loss of both their property and their labors. I am the **Egg of Nature** <note>original: "Ovum naturæ"; a metaphor for the alchemical vessel and the potential within the matter.</note> known to the wise alone, who, being pious and modest, generate the **microcosm** <term>Microcosm: the "world in miniature," representing the belief that the human being or the alchemical work mirrors the entire universe.</term> from me. I am prepared for men by God the Best and Greatest, though given to very few (even as very many desire me in vain): so that they may do good to the poor from my treasure, and not bind their souls to perishable gold. I am called by the name of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii nomine"; referring here to "Philosophical Mercury," the living spirit of matter, not common quicksilver.</note> by the Philosophers; my husband is gold (the Philosophical kind). I am the ancient dragon, present in all parts of the earth; I am father and mother, youth and old man, the strongest and the weak, death and restoration, visible and invisible, hard, soft, descending into the earth and ascending to heaven, the highest and the lowest, the lightest and the heaviest. In me the order of nature is often inverted: containing the natural light in color, number, weight, and measure; I am dark and bright, proceeding from heaven and earth, well-known and yet existing as nothing at all. All colors shine forth in me, and all metals through the rays of the sun: I am the **Solar Carbuncle** <note>original: "Carbunculus solaris"; a mythical glowing gemstone, here signifying the perfected Philosopher's Stone.</note>, the most noble clarified earth, through which you will be able to transmute copper, iron, tin, or lead into gold.

## THE OPERATION OF THE PHILOSOPHICAL
### Mystery.

I am a weak and infirm old man, surnamed "Dragon." For this reason I am shut in a **cage** <note>The "cage" or "prison" is a common alchemical metaphor for the sealed glass flask (alembic) where the matter is heated.</note>, so that I may be redeemed by a royal crown, and enrich my family with wealth. Though I exist now for the first time as a **fugitive servant** <note>original: "servus fugitivus"; a term for volatile Mercury that escapes as vapor.</note>, after these things we shall truly possess all the treasures of the kingdom. A fiery sword afflicts me with great torments, and death breaks my flesh and bones until six weeks have passed; would that I could truly overcome my enemies! My soul and my spirit leave me; I am a fierce poison, likened to a **black crow** <note>original: "corvo nigro"; the "nigredo" or blackening stage, representing the death and decay of the old form before rebirth.</note>, for this is the reward of malice. I lie in dust and earth—would that from three, one might be made! O soul and spirit, do not truly desert me, so that [I may see] the light of day again...

### THIRD FIGURE.

<image-desc>A circular woodcut emblem depicts a crowned king standing centrally. He holds a personified sun with a face and rays in his right hand and a crescent moon in his left hand. **Ten men**, throwing this **Hero** <note>original: "Heroem"; referring back to the "hero of peace" or the Stone in its transitional state.</note> to the ground, strip him of life; yet he forgives and pardons them for this outrage, since after this, brought back to life, he rejoices in **eternal life**. As the darkness of the **Moon and Sun** <note>original: "Lunae & Solis"; this refers to the *nigredo* or "blackness," a stage of symbolic death where the light of the metals is extinguished before purification.</note> rushes in, this **shepherd** falls; yet he cannot be separated or divided, since he is not like the **first earth** <note>original: "terrae primae"; likely referring to the crude, unrefined "prime matter" that has not yet been spiritualized.</note>. 

His enemies likewise will fall in death along with him, if only they wish to become sharers of his **glory and honor**. Moreover, by pure grace, the **Iris** <note>original: "Iris"; the rainbow, which in alchemy signifies the *cauda pavonis* or "Peacock's Tail," a stage where many colors appear in the vessel, signaling that the "blackness" is ending.</note> appears when the **King** favors them, and then his praises and honors must be sung.

# THE UNIVERSAL WORK
## *Of the Philosophers.*

That **Old Man** is the first principle revealed through the Hermetic art; he is **Sulfur**, **Salt**, and **Mercury**, the lower just as the upper, the star of the **Sun**, abundant in colors, fire, air, water, and earth. He is descended from the lineage of **Diana** and **Apollo** <note>Diana and Apollo represent the Moon (Silver) and the Sun (Gold).</note>; the masculine denotes fire and air, while the feminine denotes earth and water. He is both heavy and light in weight, stable, constant, and fleeting. Strip him of his earthly garment and prepare him naked; enclose him in a warm bath and cook him with the heat of vapors day and night until the **sevenfold star** appears, running its course through the sphere, and let him be suffocated in the water.

The **Black Crow** <note>The Crow represents *Nigredo*, the first stage of "blackness" or putrefaction in the alchemical process.</note> is the first bird; it flies around corpses until the **White Dove** <note>The Dove represents *Albedo*, the second stage of purification or "whitening."</note> comes forth, followed by the **Red Bird** <note>The Red Bird represents *Rubedo*, the final stage of "reddening" and perfection.</note>. Spiritually, therefore, first extinguish the crow so that all colors may emerge. The **Unicorn** <note>An emblem of purity and the spirit; in alchemy, it often represents the volatile spirit or Mercury.</note> indeed rests; while the bodily **Moon** exists, she prepares the way for the **King**, and white silver emerges. The **King** follows this—red, still solitary, but most pure. If you lead him through all the kingdoms together with his own mother, his value will be multiplied tenfold, and he will provide infinite riches and benefits to his brothers. Happy, and thrice and four times blessed is he who has attained full knowledge of this art.

I cannot describe his brightness and purity in words, and as if overcome by a dream, I finally cried out: "Deliver me, O Lord God, from all evil!"

The man approached me and said, "Adolphus, follow me; I will show you those things prepared for you, so that you may pass from darkness into light." I said, "I do not know who you are; may the Spirit of the Lord of heaven and earth guide me." But he said, "Follow me, for since you love both me and my master, you are loved back by me with a reciprocal love, and you shall celebrate that eternal Lord with the highest praise."

Having said this, we finally entered the inner parts of the cave. Considering all those things more carefully, I saw in his crown a very bright red star, whose rays penetrated my whole body and my heart. His garment was of white linen, sprinkled with multicolored flowers, with a green color shining through from within. Furthermore, a certain ever-moving vapor ascended from his heart to his brain and back again. Finally, he struck the wall with his hand with a great crash and vanished from my sight. At this, great darkness, solitude, and fear again occupied my soul. 

But when the sun rose, I lit a wax candle to search the interior of the cave. I saw the wall that had been struck and found a lead chest <note>In alchemy, lead is the metal of the planet Saturn. Finding a lead chest often symbolizes the beginning of the "Great Work," where the base material is first identified.</note>. When I opened it, I saw a book with leaves made of beech-wood, in which a parabolic <note>A "parabolic figure" refers to a symbolic or allegorical illustration meant to convey a deeper spiritual or chemical truth.</note> figure of the "Old Adam" was noted. I turned this over in my hand day and night until at last, through a single word, that secret was revealed to me, from which I came to know many wonders deeply. I looked toward the South, where those hot Lions are, and toward the regions subject to the Pole in the North, where the bears wander. I sang the name of the Lord with the highest praise and recognized the mystery of that sealed "Book of Nature"—an absolute secret which I will set down in this place, just as it had been added before.

## TO THE VERY REVEREND 
## AND MOST NOBLE LORD, WOLF-
## gang von Heussenstamm: Canon of the Cathedral Church 
## of Mainz: and most worthy Dean of the Noble 
## Chapter of Saint Alban in that same place: 
## his gracious Patron.

*Just as not every land brings forth all things for us,*
*But each earth flourishes with its own gift:*
*So also we men cannot all do everything,*
*But each one rejoices, enriched by his own talents.*
*To this man, by the nod of the Gods, friendly Fortune smiles;*
*One possesses the riches of the body, another those of the mind.*
*Rare is the man on earth to whom the Gods grant everything;*
*Rare is the man whom they heap with most things at once.*
*Such a one you are, HEUSSENSTAMM, the glory of the Aonian sisters* <note>original: "Aonidum... sororum." A classical reference to the Muses, who were said to dwell on the Aonian mount (Helicon).</note>,
*Whom the honor of mind, fate, and body adorns.*
*Who, although you are descended from an ancient lineage of ancestors,*
*Yet surpass your race with a still nobler mind.*
*For in you heroic virtue, the grace of the tongue,*
*And the wit of genius and judgment compete.*
*Happy Mainz* <note>original: "Maguntia."</note> *raises up this honor to the heavens,*
*And august Austria boasts of your grandfathers.*
*The time will come for singing your name and your praises,*
*Provided that the work of history I am composing now rises up.*
*Meanwhile, receive with a joyful face these present remains,*
*Which I offer to you, so they do not perish.*

# THE LIFE
## OF ARNALD OF VIL-
### L A N O V A.

*Arnald of Villanova, a distinguished Philosopher and excellent Physician—and if a cultivation of more humane letters* <note>original: "literarum... humaniorum." This refers to the study of classical literature and the humanities, which the author suggests would have made Arnald equal to the greatest ancient Greek or Roman scholars.</note> *had been added, he would even be compared to the ancients—was French by nationality, as Symphorien Champier* <note>original: "Symphorianus Campegius." A prominent French physician and humanist (1472–1539) who wrote about the history of medicine.</note> *testifies. For he was born in the Province of Narbonne, in a certain town called Villanova, around the year of Christ 1300* <note>While the text provides this date, modern historians usually place Arnald's birth earlier, around 1240, and his death in 1311.</note>*, at almost the same time when Peter of Abano, called "the Reconciler,"* <note>original: "Petrus Aponensis, dictus Conciliator." An Italian physician and philosopher known for trying to reconcile the differences between various medical and philosophical schools.</note> *and Raymond Lully flourished. He left behind many works in Theology and Philosophy, and even more in the Medical art. In Alchemy he was so great a Master that he stood as the teacher of Raymond Lully in that art, and he even made gold plates that were not inferior to the most perfect gold. For he so searched into the secrets of nature that almost no one after his own age has penetrated deeper. For this reason, he was held in great honor by Frederick, King of Sicily: by whom, when he had been sent to heal the Roman Pontiff* <note>The Pope.</note>*, he finally died on that journey and was buried at Genoa. The chemical works of Arnald which have reached our age are roughly these: The Rosary of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Rosarius Philosophorum."</note>*; The New Light* <note>original: "Lumen novum."</note>*; The Flower of Flowers* <note>original: "Flos Florum."</note>*; and The Mirror of Alchemy* <note>original: "Speculum Alchimiae."</note>*; of which this last one has never before been*

# THE MIRROR OF ALCHEMY,

## BY ARNALD OF VILLANOVA,

In order that we may arrive at perfect knowledge, it is first necessary to know that there are three Stones and three Salts from which our entire mastery <note>original: "magisterium." In alchemy, this refers to the "Great Work" or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> consists: namely, the mineral, the vegetable, and the animal. There are likewise three waters: namely, those of Mercury, the Sun <note>original: "Solis." In alchemical symbolism, the Sun represents Gold.</note>, and the Moon <note>original: "Lunae." In alchemical symbolism, the Moon represents Silver.</note>. And Mercury is the mineral; the Moon is the vegetable, because it receives only two virtues, namely whiteness and constriction; and the Sun is the animal, because it receives three: namely, whiteness, constriction, and redness. For this reason, the Sun is called the "great animal": and salt and silver <note>original: "argentū." While this usually means silver, in this context it may refer to the metallic "money" or essence derived from the solar/gold work.</note> are made from it; and the Moon is called a plant, and alkali salt <note>original: "Sal alchali." An alkaline substance, often derived from plant ashes, essential in early chemical processes.</note> is made from it; and Mercury is called the mineral stone, and mineral salt is made from it—that is, common salt. 

Therefore, you should know, dearest son, that this science is nothing other than the perfect inspiration of God: because the entire mastery consists of one single thing. And so we shall show you through the sayings of the Philosophers: and likewise, according to what we have seen and touched with great labor and with great industry, we have known that single thing to be perfect for the White and for the Red <note>original: "ad album & ad rubeum." These refer to the "Albedo" (the silver-making stage) and "Rubedo" (the final gold-making stage) of the alchemical process.</note>. And we have been unable to find any other thing where perfection might reside, regarding either the true transformation of bodies or their perfect preparation, which would not happen to be entirely corrupted and blackened. 

But we have found that single thing to be perfect, which, after it has been brought to a true fusion by our mastery, leads everything it touches to the truest completion, without any loss, according to how the material was prepared. For when it is perfected for the White, it is not yet complete regarding the truest perfection. Nevertheless, it leads everything it touches to the Lunar completion <note>Meaning it transforms base metals into silver.</note>; but because the Moon is not entirely perfect in every judgment, we say that the medicine, when prepared for the White, is not perfect in its truest completion. But when it is prepared for the Red, then we say it is perfect in every judgment. And the white medicine and the red medicine are not different, except that to the preparation of this kind of non-burning medicine is added our sulfur <note>original: "sulphuris nostri." Alchemists distinguished between common brimstone and their "Philosophical Sulfur," which was a refined principle of combustibility and color.</note>, by means of fixing and <term>calcining</term> <note>calcining: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the air to change its properties or reduce it to a powder.</note> with clever industry, and with much repetition by one who administers it perfectly, and by means of 

<summary>Arnald of Villanova introduces the "Mirror of Alchemy," classifying the primary materials of the Great Work into three categories—mineral, vegetable, and animal—and asserting that true transmutation depends on a single, divinely inspired substance.</summary>

<margin>Whether quicksilver adheres to bodies.</margin>
There are some who think that common quicksilver adheres to bodies, and that <term>Geber<note>An influential 8th-century Arab alchemist (Jabir ibn Hayyan) whose writings formed the foundation of medieval European alchemy.</note></term> is to be understood in that place where he says:

For common quicksilver does not adhere to bodies: rather, the bodies adhere to the Mercury itself. And this is certain through experience, because if common quicksilver is joined with any body, the quicksilver remains in its own nature, or it departs, and the body returns to its own nature. And for that reason, common quicksilver does not adhere to bodies: and because of this, many are deceived in working with it.

### THE FIRST DISPOSITION OF THE MIRROR.

<margin>
The first disposition, or sublimation.
</margin>
Take the body, which I showed to you above, and fit thin plates together: then place them in our philosophical vessel, and close the mouth of the vessel well, so that it cannot breathe: and roast it with a gentle fire, until it is broken apart: and keep it in the fire in the usual manner, until the whole substance is <term>fixed<note>original: "fixa." A substance is "fixed" when it can endure the fire without evaporating or sublimating.</note></term>, and so that nothing ascends which can be seen: then the true <term>putrefaction<note>The stage where the material breaks down and turns black, considered a necessary death before the "rebirth" of the metal.</note></term> will be completed. And know that this is the first disposition, which is called <term>Sublimated<note>original: "Sublimatus." While sublimation usually means turning a solid to vapor, here it refers to the purification of the substance.</note></term>; just as <term>Geber<note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous authority in medieval alchemy.</note></term> said. Since the sum of the intention of the whole work is that it be summarized in known chapters: then indeed, with the insistence of the work, let it be persisted upon the work of the first degree of sublimation: and through this, let it be cleansed from corrupting impurity: and it is, namely, the perfection of sublimation: and with it let the <term>Stone<note>The Philosophers' Stone.</note></term> be most perfectly sublimated, until it reaches the ultimate purity of sublimation. Hence know, My Son: that in sublimation alone the whole mastery is completed. Therefore, sublimate the subtle from the thick gently, with great ingenuity; it ascends from the earth to the heaven: and again it descends to the earth: and according to how you have cleansed our matter, pure or impure, so you shall find in the end. For if it were <term>quicksilver<note>original: "arg. vivum" (argentum vivum). Common mercury.</note></term> of good substance, and sulfur [that is] not pure and burning, where the whole perfection lies, it will convert the imperfect body. And I will give you an example. If, however, it were quicksilver of good substance, and sulfur not pure and burning, it will convert it into bronze. And if it were bad, porous, unclean, earthy quicksilver: and sulfur not clean, and entirely imperfect, iron will be made from it. Tin, however, seems to have good quicksilver: but bad sulfur, and not well fixed, nor well mixed. Lead, however, [has] bad quicksilver, and thick, and heavy and earthy: sulfur also bad, of bad taste and stinking, and weak. Whence it is not well congealed. Whence know, son, that all perfection consists in philosophical sulfur. Because

Philosophical Sulfur.

...supereminently: But the other is foreign to its nature and incorruptible, because this is removed only with great labor; yet the other <note>meaning the radical or essential sulphurity</note> cannot be removed by any ingenuity of art. This is because **combustible sulphurity** <note>original: "sulphureitas combustibilis"</note> or "foreign sulphurity"—which are the same thing—is destroyed by the calcination of fire. He who is experienced in the art knows this to be true. However, the **radical sulphurity** <note>The essential "sulfur" that gives a metal its identity.</note> is not destroyed at all, for it belongs to their perfection.

For according to the Philosopher <note>Usually referring to Aristotle, the ultimate authority for medieval scholars.</note>, if **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: mercury</term> is pure, it will coagulate by the power of **philosophical sulphur** into the truest **silver**; and this is the best means for Alchemists to artistically create an **elixir** for **silver**. But if there should be an **excellent sulphur** with redness—clear, pure, and clean—it will coagulate the **quicksilver** into the truest **gold**, provided that the power of a non-burning "fire-likeness" is within it. This is the best means for the **elixir** for **gold** to be made from it.

Wherefore you should know, my son, that the Philosopher first handed down the recipe for **white sulphur** for **silver**, and afterwards **red sulphur** for **gold**. This is because nothing can become **gold** unless it was first **silver**. No thing can pass from the first state to the third unless it has first been in the second. Since there is no passage from one extreme to another except through the middle, it is impossible to move from **black** to a perfect **yellow** <note>original: "citrinum," the golden-yellow color of the "Citrinitas" stage.</note> unless the material has first been **white**. For **yellow** is composed of much **white** and a very little **red**. 

Neither can a transition be made from **yellow** back to **white** unless it has first been **black**. Since **gold** cannot be turned into **silver** unless it has first been destroyed, corrupted, and turned **black**; for a better thing cannot be made into a worse thing except through its own corruption. Indeed, the corruption of one thing is the generation of another. 

And so that you may better understand the sayings of the philosophers, we tell you: he who knows how to convert **gold** into **silver** also knows how to convert **silver** into **gold**. This is because their non-burning **sulphur**, which is **white** for **silver**, can—through a greater "digestion" or ripening by fire—become **red sulphur** for **gold**. For **yellowing** <term>yellowing: citrinatio</term> is nothing other than complete digestion and the removal of **blackness**. 

Heat acting upon moisture generates first **blackness**; then in the yellowing stage, **whiteness**; then in the white, **yellowing**; and finally in the yellow, **redness**. This is seen clearly in the boiling of **lead**: for first it is turned into **black ash**, then into **white**, then into **yellow**, and ultimately into **red lead** <note>original: "minium rubeum," a bright red pigment made from lead.</note>. Behold, by God, I have taught you, my son, the entire operation! 

And thus **white** and **red sulphur** are obtained from only one matter of metals, fully purified, though cooked and digested in different ways. Therefore Plato says that in all **silver** there is **white sulphur**, just as in all **gold** there is **red sulphur**. But such **sulphur** is not found upon the earth, as Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher (Ibn Sina).</note> says, except for that which exists within these metallic bodies. And therefore these bodies must be subtly...

The names of the seven dispositions.
Distillation, Descension

MASTER: There are seven dispositions of this mastery: the first is called Sublimation <note>the process of turning a solid into vapor and back to solid to purify it</note>, the second is Calcination <note>heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder</note>, the third is Solution <note>dissolving a solid into a liquid</note>, the fourth is Ablution <note>washing or cleansing the matter</note>, the fifth is Ceration <note>softening a substance until it has a wax-like consistency</note>, the sixth is Coagulation <note>solidifying a liquid</note>, and the seventh is Fixation <note>making a substance stable and resistant to the fire</note>; and these are our operations. For when our water in the washing of the earth rises on high, they then called it distillation; and when it descends upon the earth, they then called it descension. Thus they established nine operations so that the science might be more obscure. There was also a certain man who said: "Our water washes the filth from our earth, and our **Sun** <note>gold or the masculine principle</note> is the helper; and little by little with these, you shall change all blackness." Water of life and perpetual water.

For this reason, Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and influential figure in early alchemy</note> says in his book:

You asked if you would wet your finger if you touched it: I say no; nor can it be touched without harm once our water is made. Likewise, if you were to bathe a man in it, or give it to him to drink, he would die immediately. For this reason, many Philosophers called it poisonous water and stinking water, and said it was a toxin <note>original: "toxicum"</note>; and they spoke the truth to those who understand. DISCIPLE: Master, I have understood everything you said. But tell me, when <term>Chibrit</term> <note>Arabic term for Sulphur, specifically the "Philosophical Sulphur"</note> is dissolved in the <term>Lion</term> <note>A common alchemical metaphor for a powerful solvent, often called the "Green Lion" or "Philosophical Mercury"</note>, should we increase the fire during its coagulation, or decrease it? <margin>On the management of fire.</margin> MASTER: Son, know that when our matter is dissolved and we must coagulate it, we must decrease the heat of the Sun <note>Refers to the specific degree of heat in the alchemical furnace</note>, so that it may be dissolved even better a second time. And know that many laborers in this science are deceived in this: because once the solution of the Stone is made, they coagulate it with a stronger heat of the Sun; and they do this in every boiling. For this reason, it happens that the matter hardens at the end; and when it is necessary, it cannot be dissolved except with great labor; and thus it is <term>vitrified</term> <note>Turned into glass. In alchemy, vitrification was considered a failure because glass is "dead" and cannot be further transformed</note>. Therefore, so that no one can curse me, I say that the entire operation consists in the management of the fire: for he who knows how to rule the fire will reach perfection. Wherefore he who rules his matter with a slow fire can reach perfection without any doubt; for there is no need to fear that the matter will be vitrified, nor that the spirit, which is most subtle, will depart. For this reason the Philosopher said:

> *Flee what is too close, and do not weary the animals; for the spirit is ready to flee because it has been beaten unskillfully.* <note>original: "propinquum fuge, & animalia noli fatigare: spiritus autem promptus est ad fugiendum, quoniam verberatus est indoctè." The "animals" and "beating" are metaphors for the volatile substances and the application of heat.</note>

O untamed laborers: why do you desire the heat of the fire so much? For with violent fire the matter is destroyed and vitrified. For this reason all the Philosophers said:

> *Take care to avoid vitrification: because it is not the nature of our Stone to be vitrified:*

therefore, roast gently in all its boilings, and you shall have the knowledge; if you do otherwise, you will not rejoice in your work. Wherefore Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous authority in medieval alchemy</note> placed all perfection in sublimation alone: but there are few who well understand what sublimation is. <margin>What is sublimation.</margin> Sublimation is nothing other than to separate the subtle parts from the gross parts: and this must be done with a slow fire. For if we performed the separation with a violent fire, the gross parts would ascend with the subtle parts; and therefore it would not be sublimation, but rather destruction. See what Geber says in the last chapter:

> *And by the manner of that separation, you shall divide the purest part.* <note>original: "Et per separationis illius modum, purissimam partē dividas."</note>

Likewise Geber:

> *Since the sum of the intention is nothing else but that the Stone known in the chapters be taken: then indeed, with the urgency of the work, let the work of the first degree of sublimation be applied continuously upon it: and by this let it be cleansed from corrupting impurity: and that is, namely, the perfection of sublimation: and with it, without any addition, understand the word: Let it be sublimated.*

...the Stone, until in the final sublimation it reaches purity. Now therefore, my Son, it has been sufficiently demonstrated that in sublimation alone, and in the fire alone, lies the total perfection of this <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterii"; refers to the completion of the Great Work</note>. Do not be stiff-necked, therefore, nor fanciful in your understanding. I want you to act in such a way that you imagine how <term>bodies</term> <note>In alchemical texts, "bodies" almost always refers to metals</note> are generated in the bowels of the earth, and by what heat their <term>cooking</term> <note>original: "decoctio"; the process of "ripening" metals through heat over time</note> is achieved: and whether that heat is gentle or violent.

Wherefore we say that metallic bodies are generated from four substances: namely, from two types of quicksilver <note>original: "arg. vivo"</note> and from two types of sulphur. The first type is from quicksilver that is good, pure, clear, clean, and also fixed. The second is from sulphur that is fixed, pure, clean, and clear; and in this way, perfect bodies <note>Gold and silver</note> are generated. However, imperfect bodies are generated from good quicksilver in some quantity mixed with bad and earthy quicksilver in great quantity, and from good sulphur in some quantity mixed with bad, earthy, and oily sulphur in great quantity. Thus are the imperfect bodies generated, some more so, some less.

Now therefore we have shown the principle of nature and from what they are reborn; and because of this, you can recognize from what cause our matter ought to be drawn out. Regarding the cooking, I say that nature performs its cooking plainly and gradually, and not with violence; for nature performs the entire cooking through the most tempered heat of the Sun in the bowels of the earth. The heat of the Sun is not violent; rather, it is tempered. Therefore, look and consider whether you ought to make your own cooking violent. And I say that you should not, because the heat of [artificial] fire is stronger than that of the Sun. For this reason, the Philosophers said: *smoothly with a slow fire* <note>original: "suaviter cum igne lento"</note>.

Wherefore you should know that all who practice this science are deceived in the <term>governance</term> <note>original: "regimine"; the systematic control of the furnace</note> of the fire more than in any other thing, because they do not know moderation. Many there are who know the Stone, but are ignorant of the governance of the fire. Therefore, my son, do not be negligent in learning the governance of the Sun, for therein lies the whole secret. We have now said enough; but now let us pass on to the Seventh Disposition.

## THE EIGHTH DISPOSITION OF THE MIRROR.

<margin>From where sulphur is extracted,</margin>
From this, my dearest son, you may draw the greatest secret: that quicksilver receives into itself that which was of its own nature, but rejects what is foreign; for its nature rejoices more in its own kind than in the strange. From this, it is clearly known from what things the matter is drawn: for we say those bodies shine more and are of greater perfection which contain a greater quantity of quicksilver, and those less which contain less. But because we said before that <term>sulphur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulphur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle, while Mercury represents the passive, feminine, and fluid principle.</note> is the matter of the Philosophers, we wish to demonstrate from what thing it may be extracted, so that you may know we have spoken the truth. Thus, white and red sulphur are obtained entirely from the one matter of metals, fully purified, though boiled and digested in a different manner. Therefore Plato says: *that in every silver there is white sulphur, just as in every gold there is red sulphur; and yet not every white sulphur is red.* Likewise, such sulphur is not found upon the earth, as Avicenna says, except that which resides within these bodies. And therefore we prepare these bodies subtly, so that from that matter we may have white or red sulphur upon the earth, from which gold or silver was made beneath the earth. Our mastery <note>The "mastery" refers to the Alchemical Great Work or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> perfects the imperfect body through the perfect body, without the administration of any foreign thing. However, all bituminous sulfur <note>original: "sulphur bituminosum"; this refers to impure, oily, or combustible sulfur which alchemists believed caused metals to be "burnt" or corrupted.</note> is foreign to quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, because it is inherently corrupt. On the contrary, that substance into which it is to be converted by our mastery—namely, gold and silver—is not foreign to it. Therefore, make use of venerable nature; for it is not improved except within its own nature. Do not introduce anything alien into it, neither powder nor any other thing; for diverse natures do not improve our Stone, and nothing enters into it except what was born from it. Therefore, it is necessary to gather the medicine for bodies from physical things, because it is necessary that this medicine agree with them in nature. Because of this, there is no body worthier or purer than the Sun <note>Gold</note>, or its shadow <note>Silver; often referred to as the "lesser light" or the "shadow" because it reflects the sun's light.</note>, without which no "tinging" <note>The ability to "stain" or transform the color and nature of a base metal into a noble one.</note> quicksilver is generated. Anyone who strives to "tinge" without quicksilver proceeds blindly to the practice, like a donkey going to a banquet <note>original: "sicut asinus ad cænam"; a common medieval proverb used to describe someone attempting a task for which they are entirely unsuited or unprepared.</note>. For golden gold and silvery silver provide the color; and also, he who knows how to "tinge" quicksilver with the Sun and Moon reaches the secret which is called "white sulfur." And when it is made red, it will be "sulfur for gold" <note>Alchemists sought "White Sulphur" to make Silver and "Red Sulphur" to make Gold.</note>. Therefore, from these two prepared bodies, our medicine is drawn out with its sulfur and arsenic <note>In alchemy, "arsenic" often referred to a "spirit" or a volatile principle rather than just the modern chemical element.</note>. It is necessary that the Philosopher's Stone be drawn from the nature of the two bodies before the Elixir is completed from it. This is because the Elixir must be more purified and "digested" <note>matured or refined through prolonged heat</note> than gold or silver themselves. This is so that it may entirely convert things from a state of diminished perfection into gold or silver, which gold and silver alone cannot do. For if they gave away their own perfection to another, they themselves would become imperfect. They cannot "tinge" except as far as they themselves extend: for nothing whitens except according to its own whiteness, and nothing reddens except according to its own redness. Therefore, we perform our works upon our Stone so that its tincture may be improved far beyond what it is in its own nature. Thus we say that the work of the Philosophers is nothing else but to dissolve our Stone into our quicksilver, so that it may be reduced to its first matter <note>original: "primam materiam"; the underlying substance from which all metals were thought to originate.</note>.

<margin>Species cannot be transmuted, but individuals of the species [can].</margin>
Wherefore the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, the ultimate authority for medieval scientists.</note> in the fourth book of *Meteorology* <note>original: "metheororum"; alchemists frequently cited a specific passage from this work to justify their science, even though Aristotle’s actual views on the matter were skeptical.</note> of this art mocks the Sophists <note>Those who use deceptive or false logic.</note>, saying: *Let the practitioners of Alchemy know that species cannot be transmuted, unless they are reduced to their first matter.* And later he adds: *Which first matter is indeed quicksilver, since it is the element of all ductile metals; for then they are well changed into a form other than they were before.* Indeed, it is not the "species" <note>The abstract essence or category of a metal.</note> that changes, but the individuals of the species <note>The specific, physical piece of metal at hand.</note>, because these individuals are subject to perceptible actions...

they are convertible within themselves. But Species, since they are Universal, are not subject to the actions of the senses, and therefore in themselves they are incorruptible. The species of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, which is "silverness," is not changed into the species of gold, which is "goldness," nor vice versa. This is because species cannot truly be changed; however, the individuals belonging to those species can be, provided they are reduced to their <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: "materiam primam"; the fundamental, formless substance from which all things are made according to Aristotelian physics.</note>. For when the form of that individual is destroyed and resolved into prime matter, another form is easily and even necessarily introduced. This is because the "corruption" <note>destruction or breakdown</note> of one thing is the "generation" of another. Likewise, matter can in no way be destroyed without remaining under some form. Therefore, once one form is destroyed, another is immediately introduced, prepared for this operation or another.

And for this reason, the Philosopher <note>Usually a reference to Aristotle, the primary authority on natural physics in the Middle Ages.</note> says: *You have need to labor first in the solution and sublimation of the two Luminaries.* <note>The "two Luminaries" are the Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver).</note> For the first step of the operation is that it becomes quicksilver; and in this work, he declares what the Stone is, since the beginning of his work is the dissolution of the Stone itself. The dissolution of the body is the freezing <note>original: "congelatione"; the process of making a liquid solid or fixed.</note> of the Spirit, and the freezing of the Spirit is the dissolution of the body. Then the body is mixed with the Spirit, and the Spirit with the body, and they are never separated for eternity, because each of them acts upon its companion which is similar to itself. Therefore, do not wander from this path: for whatever a man sows, that shall he reap. For if anyone is wise, he is always seeking to reach perfection, because he always contains his own seed within himself.

Because of this, Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath whose writings on medicine and alchemy were highly influential in Europe.</note> says: *If I did not see gold and silver, I would say for certain that Alchemy was not true. But since I see gold and silver, I know most certainly* <margin>The Stone does not have movement by itself to become the Elixir.</margin> *that the science is true.* Therefore, although this Stone already naturally contains the "tincture" <note>The power to change the color and quality of a metal.</note> within itself—because it was perfectly created in the body of the earth—nevertheless, it does not have movement by itself to become a complete <term>Elixir</term> <note>The perfected substance capable of transmuting base metals and healing the body.</note> unless it is moved by art and operation. Thus, various arts have been invented by different Philosophers so that you may complete through craftsmanship that which was left unfinished by nature.

Therefore, do not be foolish in understanding our matter; for nothing is found in the result that was not already in the source, and one cannot give what they do not have. I tell you this so that you cannot blaspheme us: this will never happen until the Sun and Moon, joined in one body, are projected <note>The act of "projection" involves throwing the finished Elixir onto molten base metal to transform it.</note> upon the "diminished" <note>imperfect or base</note> bodies. For if they are joined with lead, it will be lead; and if with iron, it will be iron; and if with other bodies, it will be similar to them. O Son, incline your ears to this: if it is joined with these two "rays" <note>referring again to Gold and Silver</note>, it becomes the perfect Elixir. One must not work, therefore, except with this most noble matter, for things do not come to be except according to their nature. He who seeks from nature what is not in her finds only foolishness and the loss of time. I tell you, however: do not eat of the son whose mother suffers her menses <note>An alchemical metaphor warning against using impure "mercurial" starts or corrupted base materials before they have been purified.</note>, because

...because it will be leprous <note>In alchemical texts, "leprosy" refers to impurities or corruption within a metal that prevent it from being perfected into gold.</note>: and both you and your work will be frustrated. Eat of the fatter meat, and you shall have what you desire. Therefore, make an ointment from sulfur, arsenic, and quicksilver, and you will have what you desire. For that which has a red head, white feet, and truly black eyes, is the mastery <note>original: "magisterium"; the completed alchemical process or the Elixir itself. These colors—black, white, and red—represent the three main stages of the work: Nigredo, Albedo, and Rubedo.</note>. Our medicine is composed solely from nature: and this is true. I will provide an example for you: it is certain that every thing is made of that into which it is resolved. For instance, ice—by means of heat—is converted into water; therefore, it was previously water. In the same way, our Stone is resolved into our quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," or mercury.</note> through the philosophical mastery; therefore, it was previously quicksilver. Now, the method of converting it into quicksilver is the conversion of natures back to their first root.

To convert nature, however, is to rotate the Elements in a circle. Because of their natural suitability for one another, the Elements are <margin>How the Stone is converted into quicksilver.</margin> converted into each other; thus, they are generated and destroyed, and transformed into one another. Therefore, convert the Elements, and you will find what you seek. For our operation is nothing other than the change of natures, and an admirable connection of the hot with the cold, and the moist with the dry.

However, the dry is not converted into the moist unless it first becomes cold; nor is the cold converted into the hot unless it first becomes moist. This is because there is no passage from one extreme to another except through a middle state. Earth is not turned into air unless it is first turned into water; nor is fire converted into water unless it is first turned into air. Water and air are the middle Elements; Fire and Earth are the extreme Elements. Air, therefore, is close to fire, just as water is close to earth. For this reason, water is the opposite of fire, and earth is the opposite of air. This is because water is cold and moist, while fire is hot and dry; earth is cold and dry, while air is hot and moist.

Thus, air and water share the quality of moisture, and so each is immediately converted into the other. Likewise, fire and earth share the quality of dryness, and are therefore immediately converted into one another and are only separated with difficulty. Conversely, air and earth, or fire and water, cannot be turned into one another unless fire <margin>Four ways of converting the Elements among themselves.</margin> is first converted into air and earth into water. In this way, the dry is converted into the cold, the cold into the moist, and the moist into the hot; then you shall possess the mastery. There are four principal methods of the <term>regimen</term> <note>original: "regiminis"; the controlled sequence of alchemical operations, often involving specific temperatures.</note> for converting the Elements into one another: namely, to dissolve the coarse into the simple; to wash the dark into the bright; to reduce the moist into the dry; and to fix the volatile upon its own body.

Now, therefore, I have demonstrated the whole operation and the entire doctrine to you, my son. But because we wish to show it even more clearly to you, we say that all perfection lies in the solution <note>The process of dissolving a solid body into a liquid or "mercurial" state.</note>. Thus said <term>Morigines</term> <note>Likely Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit-alchemist of the 7th or 8th century, famous for his dialogues on the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, who spoke thus: "This mastery...
