For who was ever endowed with such sharp senses that they could comprehend—whether with eyes, or tongue, or the remaining organs of sense—matter without form, or form without matter? But, you will say, where the senses grow dull, there one must come to reason: clearly that is the same as saying: where the light of truth does not shine, there one must flee to the side-paths of lies. From this emerges a manifest distinction between *Hermetic and Peripatetic Physics*. For just as the former is given to faithful men from above by the Father of Lights—namely, by **GOD**—so the latter is whispered to the crowd of the unfaithful—namely, *Aristotle* and his followers—by the father of darkness and lies, that is, a *cacodaemon* <term>Cacodaemon: An evil spirit or demon; the opposite of an "agathodaemon" or good spirit.</term>. It is truly a cause for grief that so elegant and beautiful a building of physics is built upon such a weak and feeble *Peripatetic* foundation; because it is built on false and adulterated principles, it must also be corrupted and depraved. For once one absurdity is granted, innumerable false conclusions follow. This, alas, students of *Natural Philosophy* experience to their own great loss; disputing about physical causes, they are tossed by perpetual waves of uncertainty, so much so that they find no place where they can safely plant a foot. # ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICIAN’S STONE.

[God] alone, from the inexhaustible and infinite treasury of His kindness, most generously bestows upon those who ask and are faithful the spirit of discernment between truth and falsehood, so that they may deliver a right and blameless judgment on any question proposed. ## CHAPTER I.

...will [perish]. <note>The text likely completes a thought from the previous page: "their paganism will perish."</note> Return to your senses, O pagan philosophers! Cast off that true paganism in philosophy, which is an abomination to God and all good men, and put on true Christianity. Do not profess this with your mouth only, but show it in your deeds and reality, and consider that an account must be given for every idle word. For what greater vanity is there than to follow and defend the delusions of the pagans? These writings overflow with so many obvious trifles and lies that one can hardly find a single page that does not contain as many errors as it does lines and words—so much so that a single strike of the pen <note>original: "litura," referring to the act of erasing or crossing out text</note> would be enough to correct them all by wiping them away. 

I wanted to treat this subject of **divine inspiration** as the principal head of our art at some length from the start, so that the minds of my readers, enticed by the example of **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many ancient alchemical and philosophical works are attributed</note>, might be better prepared at the very threshold to investigate and understand what follows.

However, just as the mercy of the heavens and the influence of the stars are not enough for a gardener to nourish and raise his plants unless he also diligently cultivates the soil, so too will a philosopher rarely, if ever, be found worthy of divine inspiration unless he brings a mind prepared and equipped in the proper manner. This preparation is perfected primarily in two workshops: the **Oratory** <note>a place dedicated to prayer; from the Latin "oratorium"</note> and the **Laboratory** <note>a place dedicated to manual work; from the Latin "laboratorium"</note>. Each of these uses its own specific instruments. 

In the **Oratory**, the primary tools are: prayers, petitions, vows, groans, and unutterable sighs directed toward God, the Best and Greatest. Also required are study, diligence, industry, persistence, research, and frequent meditation on the **Book of Scripture** <note>the Bible</note> and the **Book of Nature**. 

In the **Laboratory**, the tools generally consist of charcoal, a furnace, tongs, vessels, bellows, and countless other things of this kind that would be too tedious to list one by one. With these few things properly arranged in the laboratory, and with the fire piously kindled both in the philosophical furnace and in the craftsman's own heart, only then should he implore God's help. He must not cease his work until he achieves his desire and experiences the certain blessing of God—just like Hermes himself. After various labors, Hermes freely and honestly admitted that divine grace had come to him, saying: 

> "I did not spare my soul from labor, and I obtained this knowledge only through the inspiration of the living God, who deigned to reveal it to me, His servant."

->ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICAL STONE<- <note>original: "DE LAPIDIS PHISICI SECRETO." The "Physical Stone" refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of alchemical practice.</note>

## COMMENTARY. <note>original: "SCHOLIUM." In early modern texts, a scholium is an explanatory note or commentary on a primary text.</note>

God distinguished man from the rest of the living creatures so that, being endowed with reason, he might preside over all other created things and bring everything under his dominion. This gift of reason is nothing other than a small portion or a certain spark of divinity—an invisible spirit, or the "breath of life" which God breathed into the face of man, and so "man became a living soul" (Genesis 2). God wills that we walk piously and wisely in this light of reason, and that we meditate day and night upon His law, which is revealed to us both through Holy Scripture and through Nature and the Created World.

Indeed, **Adam**, the **First-Formed** <note>original: "Protoplastus," a Greek-derived term for Adam as the first created human</note>, was perfectly adorned in that light before the Fall; he shone among all other creatures like the Sun among the stars, and contemplated all the wonders of God as if in a most clear mirror. But because this light of reason in his descendants greatly failed from its original perfection and clarity after the transgression of the law, **Jesus Christ**, the Son of God, offered himself of his own accord for its restoration. For us, his faithful, he has become a life-giving, spiritual, and heavenly soul. With this soul within us acting as a guiding middle nature, and with the sacred breath of grace and divine gifts cooperating at the same time, we rise again from the sleep of ignorance, wickedness, and "dead philosophy." Running out into the vast field of knowledge, sincerity, and "living philosophy," and exercising ourselves there strenuously and constantly, we can rightly boast that we walk faithfully in the restored Light of reason and in the ways of the Lord, as befits wise men. For if we walk in this light, we will by no means resist the divine will. Moreover, according to the opinion of **Hermes**, God permitted man this freedom or choice to philosophize. On the other hand, it is in no way the will of God that a man should pollute himself with the vices of sin, or seize upon any opportunity for wrongdoing that is offered. For He is the most fierce enemy of sin, and no one who is subject to the dominion of sin and fails to restrain his overly loosened reins will escape unpunished.

# CHAPTER I.

## COMMENTARY. <note>original: "SCHOLIVM"</note>

If anyone doubts whether **Hermetic Philosophy** <term>Hermetic Philosophy: A tradition of spiritual and scientific thought attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus, often associated with alchemy and the pursuit of divine wisdom.</term> is consistent with Christianity or not, the words just recounted will soon shake off the burden of that doubt. For what greater affinity or kinship could there be, or what could come closer to the true mark of a Christian man, than what is perceived from these words of Hermes? For we have a command to love GOD with all our soul and all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves. The Author loves GOD with such reverence and fear that, unless he remains constant in His love and fear, he dreads becoming guilty of the judgment of eternal damnation. Furthermore, he pursues his neighbor with a faithful love no different than he has for himself, in that he greatly desires to make him a common partner in his knowledge. Certainly, he would never have taken this into his mind unless the terror of the final judgment and the love of GOD and the faithful few had swayed his soul.

But you will perhaps ask: what is the cause of this tenacity in revealing this secret? It is surely the impiety of men, the vast majority of whom are unworthy to be admitted into the sanctuary of Philosophy. It is because of these, he says, that he would have disclosed nothing. But because out of such a great multitude of impious and wicked men, GOD has always left a "seed of Philosophical piety" in some—however few they may be—he says that for the sake of these few, he will sacredly observe the **law of retaliation** <term>lex talionis: Traditionally the law of "an eye for an eye," but here used to mean a reciprocal duty to pass on the gift of knowledge to others as it was given by God.</term>. To these, he will hand down the same knowledge which he obtained through divine revelation, committed to writing in such a way that nonetheless, only the worthy **sons of doctrine** <note>original: "doctrinæ filii," a term for initiated students of alchemy</note>—to whom, as we shall soon hear, he addresses this discourse—will be able to draw the true meaning from it.

# ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICIAN’S STONE <note>original: "DE LAPIDIS PHISICI SECRETO" – The "Physician's Stone" is another name for the Philosopher's Stone, emphasizing its power to heal the body as well as transmute metals.</note>

they attempt to push themselves into this art, even though they are by their very nature poorly suited for it. For they eventually experience the same outcome that many monks are accustomed to experiencing: who, while they are still boys and not yet firm in their natural inclinations, enter into monasteries out of a certain ill-advised zeal. However, when they reach adulthood and return to their true character, they are carried away toward very different studies. Hence, hating the monastic life, they bid farewell to the monasteries; they go out, they depart, they break away, they escape. And thus, quite often, a monk becomes an adulterer, the tonsured man becomes a braggart, and the religious man becomes a stable-boy. <note>The author uses a Latin wordplay here: "ex monacho mæchus, ex raſo Thraſo; ex relligioſo agaſo," contrasting the holy titles with lowly or scandalous occupations.</note> Those who attempt to insinuate themselves into this most profound science beyond the powers of their own talent and nature run into the same pit of disgrace. For after various labors, undertaken and paid for in vain, and despairing of reaching the highest peak of the art, they are finally transformed by a wondrous metamorphosis from **Philosophers** <term>Philosophers: In this context, true practitioners of alchemy who seek wisdom and the transformation of nature.</term> into sophists, and from doctors into **medical hacks** <term>medicaſtri: Charlatans or "quacks" who practice medicine without true knowledge or skill.</term>.

Today, a huge number of these people are encountered everywhere. Having built many different little furnaces, they spend their days and nights cooking, distilling, extracting—or rather, pilfering coins, namely from their own and others' pockets—refining, thickening, and mixing the highest things with the lowest. They gather for themselves a great heap of so-called **Chemical** <term>Chymicorum: Here referring to "vulgar" chemistry—mere laboratory experimentation without the spiritual or philosophical depth of true alchemy.</term> medicines, and they seem to themselves to be very wise in that vain labor. And unless manifest experience cried out against them, they would surely persuade many people, even the learned and erudite, with their chatter, that their foul dung is nothing but sweet and pleasant figs. Furthermore, from the common **Chemists** <term>Chymicis</term> who are not even learned, they become surgeons, bath-attendants, and traveling peddlers. From the wretched and desperate **Alchemists** <term>Alchymiſtis</term>, they become impostors, thieves, and gallows-birds; many of whom in our own age have ended their lives miserably, hung and suffocated on the gallows. Therefore:

->*You shall say or do nothing against the grain.*<-
<note>original: "Tu nihil invita dices faciesvè minerva" – A famous line from the poet Horace meaning that one should not attempt anything that goes against their natural abilities or "Minerva’s" (wisdom's) favor.</note>

I have frequently observed in conversations held with men of this sort that they neglect all reading and meditation on Philosophical writings, and have only money in their mouths: they speak of money, they dream of money, they stay awake for money. Some of them are gripped by such a greed for scraping together gold and silver that they do not resemble men, but rather famished wolves who, emaciated by a fast of eight or more days, seek to swallow down any food offered from the hunt with a most burning stomach. Such ravenous wolves and **Gold-eaters** <term>Chryſophagi: From the Greek, meaning "those who devour gold."</term> are to be kept far away from the art, seeing as the voluntary poverty of the Philosophers does not recognize them as genuine disciples, but as bastards to be banished far from the kingdom of Philosophy into exile, <unclear>nor</unclear> are they to be recalled forever, unless perhaps they repent. For Nature laughs...

# CHAPTER I.

Nature (says the most learned Severinus <note>Petrus Severinus (1540–1602) was a Danish physician and influential follower of Paracelsus who sought to link medicine with Hermetic philosophy.</note>) hates greedy hopes. Indeed, ignorance in a Philosopher is much more tolerable than greed; likewise, a lack of knowledge is more tolerable than a lack of restraint and luxury. For it is fitting for a Philosopher to be a man of piety, integrity, and consistency in his words and deeds, possessing a firm faith in God, being prudent, and greedy for nothing except for wisdom.

Having established these qualities, which are found especially in a true craftsman, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the father of alchemy and the author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> now begins the description of the **Great Work** <term>Great Work: Often called the *Opus Magnum*, this refers to the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</term>, which he calls the "science of the elements." But lest anyone think he is speaking of the elements as they are commonly understood in the schools of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who taught that the physical world was composed of four material elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</term>—who say an element is a simple body from which everything is first formed—he adds these two words: *not bodily, nor imprudently.* If it is not bodily nor imprudently, then it is **spiritually and wisely** <note>original Greek: "πνευματικῶς καὶ σοφικῶς"</note>. Chemical Philosophers always use this freedom in teaching, inventing technical terms according to their own judgment. For some have said the principles of the art are the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire, as our Hermes does here; but others have established only three principles: soul, spirit, and body, as the same Hermes does elsewhere; or salt, sulfur, and mercury, as Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> does; others say two: the active and the passive, the male and the female, or sulfur and mercury; others say only one: namely, Philosophical Water. But leaving aside the multitude of names, which is almost infinite, let those eager for the art instead turn themselves to investigating and knowing that one single subject, about which the Philosopher says in this verse: *Whatever the wise seek is found in Mercury.* <note>original Latin: "Est in Mercurio quicquid quærunt Sapientes."</note> Because the core of the matter turns primarily on the student of the art having this **Mercury of the Philosophers** <term>Mercury of the Philosophers: A foundational substance in alchemy, distinct from common liquid mercury (quicksilver); it represents the "prime matter" or universal spirit contained within matter.</term> well-examined before all else, I will present here some hieroglyphic figures for his benefit; in these, I will outline the various properties and conditions of Mercury with as much clarity and brevity as possible.

This circle signifies nothing other than the true and unique Mercury of the Philosophers, the first matter <term>first matter: Also known as *materia prima*, this is the formless, primordial substance from which all things are created</term>, the primordial Philosophical water, simple and one without division. ### 2.
### Double Circle.

<image-desc>A diagram of two concentric circles.</image-desc>

The double description of the circle indicates that doubled Mercury of Bernard of Trevisan <note>Bernhardus Trevisanus (1406–1490) was a famous Italian alchemist. He taught that the "Mercury" of the Wise was actually a combination of two principles found within a single substance.</note>, namely the active and the passive: or sulfur and Mercury. For the more apparent a thing is, the more corporeal <term>corporeal: Having a physical, solid body.</term> it is; but the more hidden and concealed, the more spiritual, perfect, and noble it exists. The smaller hidden part acts upon the larger and assimilates it to itself.

The meaning of these three triangles is the same in both cases. For just as the body and the soul—or salt and sulfur—cannot be joined to one another and united in their smallest parts except through the mediation of the spirit and Mercury, so too the Moon and the Sun <note>In alchemy, Luna (the Moon) and Sol (the Sun) represent Silver and Gold, or the feminine and masculine principles.</note> cannot produce offspring like themselves except through the mediation of Mercury. # CHAPTER I.

...seen by many until now, but understood by barely one in a thousand.

<image-desc>An alchemical diagram consisting of a circle containing an equilateral triangle. Inside the triangle is a square, and within the square is a smaller circle with a central point.</image-desc>

Having thus recognized the <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>original Latin: "Philosophorum Mercurio." This is not common quicksilver, but a specialized substance the alchemists believed was the "soul" of matter.</note>, Hermes indicates the hidden method of operation in the following words. "It does nothing," he says, (namely Mercury) "unless it is composed." He adds this reason: because it is not perfected until its colors are fully realized. But what else does the author imply by the significance of the colors, other than the completion of the entire work from the beginning to the very end? For a transition is not made from one extreme to another except through the middle. Therefore, the work must begin from the first of the colors; that is, Mercury, though perfect in itself, does nothing and is of no use in the <term>Alchemical work</term> unless it is <term>mortified</term> <note>In alchemy, "mortification" refers to the process of breaking down a substance, often through heat or acid, so it can be "reborn" in a more perfect form.</note>. For unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies <note>A reference to the biblical verse John 12:24.</note>, it bears no fruit, but remains alone. In the same way, Mercury, when cast into its own earth, receives a new vigor of generation.

For it is known even to farmers that any seeds, although they may appear dried up and half-dead, will be resuscitated into fertile vigor if they are committed again to their own earth. According to the destined condition and internal natural knowledge of any seed, they happily lead the entire work of <term>regeneration</term> to its conclusion. For the earth of the <term>matrix</term>—or the womb—serves as the suitable vessel for the thing to be generated. And our earth is still a <term>virgin</term> <note>original: "terra nostra adhuc virgo." This refers to "Virgin Earth," or matter that has been purified of all "superfluous" qualities but has not yet been "impregnated" by the alchemical seed.</note>, which, having been defiled by the intimacy of no man, conceives in a certain heavenly manner. For since it is pure and free from every stain and blemish, it also yearns to conceive a similar seed, pure and immaculate. For whatever it has sown, this also shall it reap. 

But although that which is sown is perfect in itself and by its own nature, it does not remain in that simple state of perfection, but is dissolved and corrupted through our process of <term>putrefaction</term> <note>The stage of "blackness" or *nigredo*, where the matter rots to release its essence.</note>. This corruption, however, is not for the destruction of the species, but for its preservation and for the bringing about of a greater perfection within it. We read concerning the three **Magi** <note>The Three Wise Men or Kings from the biblical Nativity story.</note> who came from the East to Christ, that they were three kings, and were without a doubt sufficiently powerful and wealthy. Although these men possessed kingdoms ample and splendid enough for the simple sustaining of this life...

## HERMES.

> *Know, sons of the wise, that the <term>water of the ancient philosophers</term> <note>original: "priscorum Philosophorum aqua." This refers to the primary liquid substance or solvent used in the work.</note> is a division, which divides itself into four other things. One into two, and three into one: the third part of which belongs to color—namely, of the moisture with the coagulating agent—while two-thirds are the weights of the wise.*

## COMMENTARY <note>original: "SCHOLIVM"</note>

What the author previously called the "science of the elements," he now names the "water of the philosophers." He says this must be divided into four parts: specifically, one part into two, while three parts are to be added to one. From all these joined together, seven parts result, as if scattered throughout the context of the words. For one and two make three; three and one make four. If you add this four to the previous three, you complete the <term>seven</term> <note>original: "septenarium." The number seven was considered sacred and represented the seven planets and the seven stages of transformation.</note>. Furthermore, he divides the differences of the colors into two-thirds—that is, into three red spirits and three white. It is certain that these spirits, having first arisen from the single water of the philosophers, can be resolved back into the same. Thus, that number seven is similarly drawn out through the addition of the unit, which the water supplies. In these numbers, the author seems to suggest (not obscurely) that the "weights of the wise" are silently hidden, especially in the seven—a number held sacred in antiquity, as much wisdom was thought to be stored within it. But you must contemplate its force and virtue with the eyes of the mind. For the common eye, as <term>John Dee of London</term> <note>John Dee (1527–1608/09) was a famous English mathematician, astronomer, and advisor to Queen Elizabeth I, deeply involved in alchemical studies.</note> testifies, will be clouded and will greatly doubt.

### H E R M E S.

<margin>5 {</margin>Take of the <term>moisture</term> <note>original: "humore." Likely referring to the "mercurial water" or the liquid state of the matter.</note> one ounce and a half; and of the <term>southern redness</term> <note>original: "rubore meridionali." A symbolic term for the "Soul of the Sun" or the fixed sulfur/gold aspect.</note>, that is the soul of the Sun, a fourth part, which is half an ounce; and of the lemon-yellow <term>Seyre</term> <note>original: "Seyre citrino." "Seyre" is an obscure alchemical term often referring to a specific mineral or state of sulfur.</note>, likewise half an ounce; and of <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmento." A yellow arsenic sulfide mineral, used here symbolically for its color and volatile properties.</note> a half, which together make eight—that is, three ounces. Know that the <term>vine of the wise</term> <note>original: "vitis sapientum." A metaphor for the alchemical process that "grows" and "produces wine" (the elixir).</note> is extracted in three, and its wine is completed at the end of thirty.

### S C H O L I V M.

Hermes continues to further explain the weights used by the wise, citing them under various names. For the "moisture," the "southern redness," the "soul of the Sun," the "yellow Seyre," the "orpiment," the "vine of the wise," and the "wine" signify nothing other than the **water of Mercury** distilled seven times: which, after the eighth distillation, is turned into the "ash of a virgin" or a most subtle powder. Because of its purity and perfection, this powder resists fire. Therefore, do not be surprised that eight parts and three ounces are equated: for the number three (which is also repeated through the number thirty) is just as much a mark of perfection as the number eight, according to that well-known saying: *Everything in three is perfect.* <note>original: "Omne trinum perfectum." A common Latin proverb suggesting that the number three represents completion or the divine.</note>

### H E R M E S.

<margin>2 {</margin>*Understand, therefore, the operation; the <term>cooking</term> <note>original: "decoctio." The application of heat to break down and refine the substance.</note> diminishes it, but the <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tinctura." The final medicinal or transformative power of the Stone.</note> increases it, because the Moon is diminished after fifteen days, and in the third she is increased. This, therefore, is the beginning and the end.*
<margin>5 {</margin>

### S C H O L I V M.

There are those who divide the operation of the Stone into two parts: the "former" and the "latter." The former part, which Hermes expresses by the name of "cooking," diminishes the Stone; that is, it dissolves and destroys the Stone while it exists in its simple and natural state of perfection. Once it is dissolved and "corrupted," it is restored to its former splendor of perfection through the medium of regeneration. When this is finished, the latter part of the operation begins, by which the power of the Stone is multiplied infinitely with a massive return on the investment.

The author confirms this by the example of the **Moon**, which after fifteen days (that is, its fullness) is diminished, and in the "third"—namely the <term>quadrate</term> <note>original: "quadrato." Referring to the moon's quarter phases, marking a point of transition and growth.</note>—it takes on growth again. In these few words, the whole work is contained, and both the beginning and the end are revealed clearly enough <note>original: "τῷ φρονοῦντι" - "to the one who is wise/understanding."</note>. But it should not seem strange that such a difficult and great secret can be explained with such brevity of speech; for some are found who, because of simplicity—

### COMMENTARY.

<note>original: "SCHOLIVM." A traditional term for an explanatory note or commentary on a primary text.</note>

For just as you see in the firmament above, those astral bodies differ only in this: that some surpass others in magnitude and in the clarity of their light and splendor; [all...]

# CHAPTER I.

All things in the universe consist of one and the same matter: most pure, diaphanous, and translucent. Thus, all bodies in this lower world seem to differ greatly from one another in their external appearance; yet, when all are considered from within, they proceed from one and the same principle, or "first thing." That internal principle is nothing other than—according to Solomon in the <term>Book of Wisdom</term> <note>original: "Sap. cap. 11." Referring to the Wisdom of Solomon 11:17.</note>, chapter 11—a certain invisible matter from which the world was created; or, according to John the Evangelist, chapter 1, it is the **WORD**, through which all things were made, and without which nothing was made that has been made.

But you will say: if the **Word** is the principle of all things, and if, according to the testimony of Scripture, that same Word shall never perish but remain for eternity, then one should not seek or investigate it within these <term>sublunary</term> <note>Meaning "below the moon"—the earthly realm subject to change and decay, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note> and corruptible bodies, all of which die, perish, and pass away. To this objection, I shall respond to you succinctly and briefly: all things indeed that were created through the Word were "very good"—that is, they were adorned by God with the highest perfection of blessedness. But because the earth was also cursed on account of the transgression of Adam, death entered into the world, so that there is now nothing in the whole world that does not exist stripped and bereaved of that primitive perfection, and consequently made subject to death. 

However, the Almighty had mercy on His creature; to free it from death and restore it to the kingdom of life, He sent into the world that same **Word**, which is the Light and Life of the world. Thus, for a second time, He regenerated the world through this **WORD**. For the one giver of life and regenerator always remains the same **GOD**, outside of whom there is no hope of salvation. 

Through this regeneration, a "new creature" has been made: for the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have been made new. <note>original: "2. Cor. 5." Referring to 2 Corinthians 5:17.</note> Therefore, we must consider this **Word** not according to the "old creature," but according to the "new." For we now know no one according to the flesh (that is, the old creature), but according to the spirit (that is, the new creature). Just as Christ dwells within those who are reborn in an invisible manner and is not manifested in this world, but only in the next, so the **WORD** of regeneration adheres invisibly to all things. However, it is not manifested in elemental and coarse bodies unless they are reduced into the <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: "essentiam quintam." The "fifth essence," a pure, spiritual substance hidden within the four physical elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note>, or the celestial and astral nature. This **Word** of regeneration is that "Seed of Promise," or the <term>Heaven of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "cœlum Philosophorum." A metaphorical term for the purified state of matter in the alchemical Great Work.</note>, most brilliant with the infinite lights of the stars, to which Abraham was led out to look upon and contemplate. On which account, whoever looks upon this heaven...

-># ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICAL STONE<-

...our <note>The text likely refers to the "Stone" or the "subject" being discussed.</note>, which indeed, by reason of the **lesser** and **greater world**, can be considered as a twofold savior (although the same **GOD** works all things in all). Whoever wishes to behold this should cast aside <term>Adamite</term> <note>Relating to the "Old Adam"—the fallen, carnal nature of humanity after the exile from Eden.</note> things—that is, carnal things. For those who are too dull-witted judge only by the sight of external and corruptible things. Instead, let him receive spiritual organs of sight from the "new creature." Through these, he will easily recognize that for the whole world—both the created and the regenerated—there is only one author, one maker and effecter of all things, and one principle. This is the "first being," which is never separated from nature, but rather purges nature from corruption and blemish, revives it, and restores it to its former liberty of perfection.

Do not wonder, however, that things subject to death strip off the form of the "old creature" and seem to be reduced almost to nothing. For death is the beginning of life: only the old or **Adamite** body dies. But the Spirit of the new re-creation fashions for itself a new body, much more noble and glorious than the old. *For that which is sown is not made alive unless it first dies.* It is sown in corruption, and rises in incorruption: it is sown in dishonor, and rises in glory: it is sown in weakness, and rises in power. *1 Corinthians 15.*

And all these things, as **Hermes** <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> testifies in the **Emerald Tablet** <note>original: "Smaragdina tabula." A foundational alchemical text said to contain the secret of the "one thing" from which the universe was made.</note>, are done by one, through the meditation of one. For the same **GOD** who said, *you shall die the death*, also said, *you shall be saved*. Therefore, death and life have obtained their effective power and authority of operating through the same **WORD OF GOD**. For every word proceeding from the mouth of **GOD** is essential. It is not a vain and vanishing spirit or breath, as many ignorant and impious people hold in their most destructive opinion born of unbelief.

*My words*, says **Christ** our Savior himself, *are spirit and life*—that is, the substantial and essential seed of the new creature. And whoever believes in this is saved, and is essentially united and joined with Christ, so that the head and the members—that is, Christ and the Church—are two in one flesh. But he who does not believe remains in sin; and because the wages of sin is death, every unbeliever, already judged by the **WORD**, is condemned and dies an eternal death.

Therefore, just as the salvation of man depends solely on the knowledge of **Christ** and true faith in him—seeing as he is the one and only Savior of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "small world"—the human being, viewed as a reflection of the entire universe.</note>—so too for the Philosopher, the knowledge of the **macrocosmic Savior** <note>The savior of the "great world" (the universe). In alchemy, this is the Philosopher's Stone, which "redeems" base matter into gold.</note> is highly necessary. This is the "Heaven of the Philosophers" or the "Word of regeneration," which is but one thing diffused through the whole world, found everywhere in all things: in the bodies of animals, humans, beasts, plants, trees, shrubs, metals, minerals, and stones. Therefore, if you once recognize this one thing, and within...

## H E R M E S.

<margin>☛ 9</margin>
> *Therefore, guard the quick-silver <note>Latin: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury.</note>, which is produced in the innermost chambers where it has been coagulated. For it is the quick-silver itself, which is said to be from the residual earth.*

## C O M M E N T A R Y.

It is well established among the Chemical Philosophers that quick-silver is the "first matter" or the first being of all metals. But beware of thinking that it is common silver, or the mercury sold in the marketplace, which they also call litharge <term>lithargyrum</term> <note>Lead oxide, often associated with the dross or byproducts of refining common metals.</note>. It is indeed silver, but not the common sort. For the common kind is dead and, by itself, less fit for the physical work; but this is **living**, philosophical—that is, rightly prepared by nature with the assistance of art. It is Mercury, not of the common folk, but of the Philosophers: fiery, vital, and flowing, which is mixed with all bodies and again separated from them. The place in which this quick-silver is generated is indicated by these words: *it is made*, says the author, *in the innermost chambers, in which it has been coagulated.* Elsewhere, it is a common saying among the Philosophers that in those places where metals grow, no metals are actually found <note>This paradox suggests that the "growing" or living state of a metal is distinct from its "found" or dead state in a mine.</note>.

Therefore, the place will be all the more difficult to find as it is more hidden and concealed in the mines of the earth. But here you will note a distinction between common metallic mines and hidden philosophical mines. In the former they are found, but do not grow; in the latter, however, they grow but are not found. Read about these in the *Mineral Economy* <note>Original: "oeconomiam mineralem," a work by Paracelsus (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals in medicine.</note> of **Paracelsus**, who treats the cause of this difference extensively there. This very quick-silver, residual from the Philosophical earth, if you know it rightly, must be carefully guarded. If perhaps there is a fear that it might contract a blemish over a long period of time, you can imitate the example of the Roman Church: in which the navel strings of infants are burned to ashes, so that they can be preserved for a long time—specifically until the "day of ashes" <note>Original: "diem... cinerum," referring to Ash Wednesday.</note>, which is Mercury's day <note>In Latin, Wednesday is "dies Mercurii"; in French, it is "Mercredi." The author is making a linguistic and symbolic connection between the "ashes" of the church and the chemical "ashes" (calcined state) of Mercury.</note> (in French, *of the ashes*). If in the same way you burn your quick-silver by the force of fire and convert it into ash, it will better resist the voracity of time and will be preserved for infinite years. It is certainly worthy of being diligently guarded. For it is an incomparable treasure, and a thing more precious than gold itself; for this reason, it is also preferred far above gold by the Philosophers. Indeed, in the *Rosary of the Philosophers* <note>Original: "Ros. Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical text illustrating the stages of the Great Work.</note>, gold is imagined to address Mercury thus: *“Do you,”* it says, *“prefer yourself to me, though I am the Lord...?”*

## SCHOLIVM. <note>A commentary or explanatory note.</note>

The speech of the Philosophers is covered with parables, riddles, and a thousand layers of metaphors <note>original: "troporum involucris," literally "wrappings of tropes"</note>; it ought not to be immediately open to just anyone at first glance. Nor are all things suitable for all people. The cause of the more obscure language in Chemical writings has been partly explained above, and will be partly explained in what follows. But if anyone, impatient with long meditation and inquiry, desires a swifter way to escape from this Chemical labyrinth: behold the faithful counsel of the author, who commands one to seek the meaning of his words from God. For GOD by no means overlooks the wicked counsels of the ungodly: nor, in turn, does He deny His rewards to the pious and wise. It befits a true disciple of the art to flee from evil and pursue good; he who is instructed and properly fortified with such weapons of piety can approach this sacred study without fear, and will without doubt obtain his wish.

->*For it is granted only to the sacred to know these sacred things.*<-

For wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul, nor will she dwell in a body subject to sins. <note>A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 1:4.</note> And although the author has said much about the most noble secret, and has omitted nothing of all those things which are necessary to know in this science: yet he openly confesses that this mystery has been revealed only to the intelligent. From which it follows that those who are of a dull and slow wit and a malicious mind are completely excluded from this secret. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee from deceit, and will withdraw itself from thoughts that are without understanding. <note>Wisdom of Solomon 1:5.</note>

§ ->COMMENTARY.<-

The reason why students of Chemistry are called *investigators* of rumor by Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts are attributed.</note> seems to be this: alchemy has experienced both types of reputation—the good and the bad, praise and reproach—inasmuch as various rumors about it are spread throughout the whole world. For there are those who extol it with praise even to the heavens, declaring no art to be more useful to the human race after Sacred Theology. Others, conversely, do not blush to blasphemously claim it was invented by Pluto <note>The Roman god of the underworld.</note> and brought forth from the depths for the destruction of mankind. Therefore, they contend not only that the art should be abolished, but that the practitioners themselves should be wickedly and cruelly eliminated—forgetting, evidently, what the Poet sings in a certain place:

> *The ignorant man carps at what he does not grasp;*
> *But the learned man smiles at such great mysteries.*
> *Thus both proceed: but one is a fool,*
> ->*The other envious.*<-

And so this most innocent art, flying everywhere through the mouths of men, is blamed by some and praised by others; so much so that it deserves to be called "most famous," and its disciples may not ineptly be called "seekers of rumor" or "investigators of the famous art." 

Now, the Mountain of the Philosophers, upon which the vulture sits, is of the greatest height. In its lowest part, it is surrounded and well-fortified on all sides by a very strong wall of fire; it has only a single door through which the practitioner is allowed to enter and exit. At this threshold of the mountain is situated a sleepless Dragon, named <term>all-seeing <note>original Greek: παντώφθαλμος (pantophthalmos)</note></term>. For in both the front and back parts of its body, it is full of eyes; it sleeps with some eyes closed and others open, so intent is it on its constant watch in guarding the door of the mountain. It watches lest by chance an unworthy person enters and ascends with unwashed hands <note>An idiom meaning "unprepared" or "without proper reverence/purification."</note> to the peak or highest summit where the Philosopher’s Stone is placed. If that Stone is once taken away by anyone, in the moment of a single hour another immediately grows in its place; thus, in twelve hours or a single day, one may pluck the multiplied stone twelve times. But it is impossible for anyone to enter through this door unless the Dragon, with all its eyes closed, falls deeply asleep, seized by a sweet and peaceful slumber. This is the task, this is the labor <note>A reference to Virgil’s Aeneid (Hoc opus, hic labor est), describing the difficulty of returning from the underworld.</note>: to find the way, specifically...

And although mention is made here of only one crow, nevertheless three will meet you on this **Mountain of the Philosophers**. The **Black**, which is the "head" of the art; the **White**, which is the "middle"; and the **Red**, which imposes the end of all things. For the ultimate desire of nature is in our "redness" <note>This refers to the three main stages of the Great Work: *Nigredo* (blackening/decomposition), *Albedo* (whitening/purification), and *Rubedo* (reddening/perfection).</note>. Nor should you wonder that we establish so many differences or varieties of colors in crows, although only black ones are commonly known. I confess indeed that black ones are the most common; yet after these, not infrequently have I seen with my own eyes even white ones in the courts of princes and kings, as at **Dresden in Meissen** in the garden of the Imperial Elector, and elsewhere. 

Finally, red crows are truly very rare, of which I remember seeing only two in that great aviary of our **Most Christian King** <note>A traditional title for the King of France.</note>, which is built in the royal garden at a certain village they commonly call <term>Fontainebleau</term> <note>original: *fontem bellum*; literally "Fair Fountain."</note>; however, even these were not entirely red, but only variegated with red feathers. But entirely red ones, as I said, very rarely show themselves to human sight, nor, to confess the truth frankly, have they ever been seen by me until now, unless perhaps without my knowledge. Nevertheless, I can not only prove that they truly exist by the testimony of men most worthy of trust, but reason itself dictates it. These three crows, then, as I also warned before, will show you the way by their voice or cry. But their voices are so subtle and delicate that they are [heard] not by the external senses, but rather by the internal and mental...

## SCHOLIUM.
<note>A "Scholium" is a marginal or explanatory note, common in academic and alchemical texts to clarify the primary author's meaning.</note>

The author frequently warns his disciples that they should acknowledge this singular gift of **GOD** with due reverence, and that they should drive away and exclude all the fatuous and foolish from the same. Furthermore, he relates certain properties of the stone, calling it "hidden"—that is, known to few; "venerable"—that is, to be held in the highest price; "bright in color"—that is, most deeply red. For redness is the most certain sign of ultimate perfection. He calls it a "sublime mind"—that is, a <term>sublimated</term> <note>In alchemy, sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collecting the purified solid that forms upon cooling.</note> and exalted spirit. He calls it an "open sea"—that is, the <term>mercurial water</term> <note>original: *aquam mercurialem*; a fundamental alchemical solvent, often called the "Universal Solvent" or "First Matter," believed to be stable even when exposed to fire.</note> which is perennial, fixed, and permanent in the fire. The stone contains all these properties within itself, which no one can know exactly before its completion; but then they finally burst forth when it stands prepared. This is no different than in a pear tree: it is unknown what kind of fruit it will put forth until at last you see clearly with your eyes that it has produced pears—not apples, nor plums, nor cherries, nor fruit of another kind. Therefore, because Hermes knew all these powers and properties in the stone by his own experience, he also liberally communicates them by teaching.

### SCHOLIUM.

<note>original: *Scholium*; a marginal note or explanatory commentary.</note>

There are three species of concoction: The first is produced by external fiery heat in a moist medium, and is called **boiling** <note>original: *elixatio*.</note>. The second is perfected by external heat in a dry medium, and is called, in a single word, **roasting** <note>original: *assatio*.</note>. The third, however, is produced by internal, natural heat in a moist medium, and is called by the Greeks **ripening** <note>original: *πέπανσις* (pepansis); the natural process of fruit maturing or digestion.</note>. It is now asked which species the author is speaking of here—whether the first or the third—since both are produced by heat in moisture. But a distinction must be observed between the two: the former is produced by external fiery heat, while the third is produced by internal natural heat. If the matter stood by my vote alone, I would certainly decree that both the first and third species should be admitted to this work. For nature is the internal principle of generation; yet it does not operate until some external aid is added to excite that internal principle. Therefore, the heat to be employed in this art is twofold: External, which excites, and Internal, which perfects. This is according to these short verses:

> *Master, you shall first of all imitate nature in your art.*
> *External fire only excites this mass;*
> *But the internal heat, with ethereal warmth, perfects all things.*

Which I have chosen to translate into our French tongue thus:

> *Worker, above all take care,*
> *That art imitates nature.*
> *The external fire of charcoal*
> *Renders the matter altered [prepared];*
> *But the internal and ethereal*
> *Will make your work good.*

Nevertheless, both must take place in moisture. For all generation naturally occurs in a "moist heat," which Hermes calls "fire."

moist: as if to say: I wish a twofold heat of fire, external
and internal, to be applied here. For we see from daily
experience that when the heat of the Sun follows a fruitful rain,
herbs, trees of every kind, and fruits are more and more
drawn toward generation; otherwise, in a dry time, with the Dog Star
<note>original: *Sirio*; referring to Sirius, the "Dog Star," which was believed to cause the parching heat of midsummer.</note> scorching the fields too much, they wither away as if juiceless and
bloodless. Therefore, Hermes wishes the Stone to be prepared with
this twofold heat of cooking: in which it is increased, that is,
raised to the final perfection of maturity, and is continually
preserved by this kind of fire until the root appears—that is,
the seed of the metals. For we have found in almost all
plants and trees that after the cycle of generation is
complete, they finally bring forth seed, as the principal author for
propagating and preserving their species. Nature follows this
same process in the procreation of metals which, after their
total generation is finished, finally, with the help of
Art, also produces their seed. This alone is the true
**Mercury of the Philosophers**, into which all metals are
resolved before a mutual transmutation of one into another
can occur. This is according to that saying of Aristotle in *Meteorology*,
chapter 4, where he says: *It is impossible for one species of metals
to be transmuted into another, unless they are first reduced into
their first matter.* <note>original: *materia prima*; the primitive, formless substance from which all things are made.</note> Therefore, all those err who attempt to reduce metals
into crude Mercury, and not into the root, as Hermes says, or into
their seed—which is the first and last living thing in metals,
just as the heart is in animals. For Nature always moves
forward; she never goes backward. Just as the Sun, in its
circular course, proceeds from one eastern region of the sky to the
other western region—and never retreats except by a miracle—
so also must the generation of all things be judged.
The author seems to confirm this further with these words: *Next,
he says, extract the redness and the light part from it, until a
third part remains.* Concerning the redness and the number three
enough has been said abundantly above, so that it is not
necessary to repeat the same things so often.

# CHAPTER I. <term>SCHOLIUM</term>
<note>Scholium: A marginal note or explanatory commentary on a text, common in ancient and early modern scholarly works.</note>

->**COMMENTARY**<-

Here the author anticipates the objection of certain people who accuse the Philosophers of envy. To clear them of this charge, he establishes a distinction between those they might envy and those they do not. They do not feel envy, he says, toward those who are well-mannered and religious, nor toward those who are legitimate or wise. For why should they envy such men, since knowledge is their rightful possession? Indeed, no knowledge is true and good unless it is inspired by GOD, as has been demonstrated at length above. But whoever attempts to resist God with their envy will find their effort is in vain. For a <term>Theodidactus</term> <note>original: *Theodidactus*; literally "one taught by God." In this context, it refers to an alchemist who receives knowledge through divine revelation rather than human schooling.</note> does not so highly value human instruction; he recognizes another Master far superior and more learned than these dusty <term>hypodidascali</term> <note>original: *hypodidascali*; literally "under-teachers" or "schoolmasters." The author uses this as a derogatory term for pedantic academics who prioritize grammar over spiritual or scientific truth.</note>, however much they may shout against us and our doctrine.

For we know their quibbles, as they claim to be "amazed" that we are admitted to ranks of honor and dignity when we can barely speak a word or two in Latin. As if, indeed, the dignity of the arts and sciences depended upon "Latinity," and as if no one should be considered learned unless he has mastered the purity and elegance of the Latin tongue <term>to the fingernail</term>. <note>original: *ad unguem*; a Latin idiom meaning "to perfection" or "highly polished," referring to a sculptor finishing a statue by feeling for any imperfections with their nail.</note> O miserable censors, you seek your glory in this: that whatever you attempt to say, you say it purely, cleanly, elegantly, ornately, famously, properly, knowingly, politely, justly, charmingly, diligently, and weightily. But Isaiah predicted this of you long ago in chapter 33, saying:

> Where is the man of letters? Where is the one who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of the little ones? You shall not see an impudent people, a people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of his tongue: in which there is no wisdom.

Thus far the prophet. For you are more concerned with the **bark** <note>The "bark" (cortex) refers to the outer appearance or literal words, while the "marrow" (medulla) refers to the hidden essence or truth.</note> than with the **marrow** of things, and thus you prefer the shadow to the essence, the fleeting and momentary to the stable and eternal. We, however, are more delighted by the doctrine of truth, which agrees with the laws of Christ—who is Truth itself—and the laws of Nature essentially or *really*, rather than merely verbally or *literally*, if I may speak so. To attain this truth, we strive with all our might, caring nothing for whatever language it may be found in: whether it be Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, Greek, French, or Italian—it is all the same to us. For it is enough for us to hold the matter perfectly and exactly as it is; we gladly leave to you that superficial and external **pomp of words**. What you finally report back from such things, the outcome clearly shows. Because you **sell smoke** <note>original: *fumum venditis*; a Roman idiom for peddling empty promises or vanities that have no substance.</note>, smoke also—that is, the foulest breath and a boastful, petulant, and proud tongue—brings most of you to ruin.

### S C H O L I V M.

<note>Scholium: A scholarly commentary or explanatory note.</note>

The author does three things here primarily: First, he recounts many and various names for the Stone, among which he clearly hints that one alone, known only to the wise, is sufficient. What sort of name that might be has been explained more than enough in the preceding sections. Second, he twice exhorts the sons of wisdom not to permit the unworthy, the greedy, the illiberal, the foolish, the ignorant, or the unfit to enter into the sanctuary of science. Third and finally, he teaches that one must preserve within the stone "the sea, the fire, and the volatile of heaven" until the moment of completion. By "the sea," he understands the moisture of Mercury. For no generation occurs in a dry state, but rather in a moist one, as we noted a little earlier. Therefore, the Mercury must be preserved in a liquid form, yet without its own corruption. For as Raymund <insert>t</insert> <note>Referring to Ramon Llull (Raymundus Lullus), a major medieval alchemical authority. The sentence continues on the next page.</note> says, "hard things..."

<page-num>709</page-num>
# CHAPTER I.

Raymundus Lullius <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315) was a Majorcan polymath and philosopher whose name was frequently associated with later alchemical texts.</note> says that things do not receive celestial virtue, nor do they obey the heavens, if they are not receptive. Just as a seal does not impress its image into a hard stone, but rather into soft wax, so our **matter** is made ready to receive the influence of the superior bodies through its softness or rareness. Consequently, by this very means, it is compelled to obey the motion of the sun. So far his words. By the "fire" and the "volatile of heaven," however, a double fire is understood: the **external** and the **internal**. Both of these must be continually fostered and preserved until the end of the work, according to these verses by Augurelli, the Chemical Poet: <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli (1441–1524), author of the famous alchemical poem *Chrysopoeia*.</note>

> *Therefore, do not let the lukewarm fire be removed from here:*
> *And stir the inward procreative power as the outward force approaches:*
> *Just as a bird sits upon its warm eggs with constant care,*
> *And focuses its strength on the chicks that are to be born.*
> *Remember to always keep this custom in such a way*
> *That it lasts while the orb of Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> turns itself around.*
> *But if you stop, that fiery power which feeds the offspring*
> *With its fuel will die away; it will cease to act,*
> *And suddenly, with the first failing of the fire,*
> *Everything will collapse, and you shall not repair it by any art*
> *Ever again, and in vain will you try to prop up the ruin.*

->HERMES.<-

<margin>a</margin>
No one has ever bestowed <gloss>12</gloss> anything upon me to whom I have not returned what he himself gave, nor have I ceased to honor him, and I have placed a most excellent meaning <note>original: *significationem*</note> upon this. 1

->COMMENTARY<-

In these few words, Hermes treats a certain mark of a true son of the doctrine: and that is **generosity** <note>original: *liberalitas*</note>. If he notices this in someone, he immediately conceives a good hope for him. By the "law of reciprocity" <note>original: *legem talionis*, usually meaning "an eye for an eye," but here used to describe returning kindness for kindness</note>, he himself, out of a generous spirit, kindly returns everything which he had previously received. Furthermore, he does not deprive such a person of his due honor, but cherishes him lovingly and holds him in reverence. For this most becomes a true and sincere Philosopher: the more humane he is, the more learned he will be proclaimed to be, and he will deserve greater praise among all men.

With its help, you shall come from darkness to light, from the desert to a dwelling place, and from narrowness to expansion.*

### COMMENTARY <note>original: *SCHOLIVM*</note>

The three principal colors of the stone were discussed above. However, the author here mentions several more, though he instructs that out of all of them, only one is truly to be recognized, and once known, it must be kept secret. It is easily gathered that this unique color is the **red** <note>original: *rubicundus*</note>. For the more precious and excellent a thing is, the more quickly it is chosen. Indeed, the red color easily snatches the palm of praise and excellence from all others, so much so that nothing more noble or perfect can be imagined under the Sun. If you attain this, you shall keep it secret according to the author’s warning. Finally, Hermes recounts the extraordinary gifts and virtues of the stone, which all may enjoy who, by the grant of Almighty GOD, have come into its possession.

For he says it is the highest preventative against any of the most grievous ailments of the body: it drives away sadness, much like that medicine in Homer called *Nepenthe* <note>In the *Odyssey*, Helen of Troy uses a drug called Nepenthe to banish grief and bring forgetfulness of all ills.</note>, which Helen used to shake off sorrow of the soul and to induce cheerfulness and joy. It repairs the loss of goods and inconveniences, and promptly delivers one from all hardships and adversities. Furthermore, it elevates its owners from an obscure position to the greatest dignities and honors. It comforts the desperate, and those wandering here and there throughout the world, restoring them to their ancestral hearths; and having rescued them from adverse circumstances and every kind of calamity, it blesses them with such a happy lot that hereafter they may spend the remainder of their lives in tranquility and peace, according to the heart's desire.

## HERMES.

### COMMENTARY <note>original: *SCHOLIVM*</note>

It is commonly known that Philosophy is nothing other than the study of wisdom. In this study, he who desires to make praiseworthy progress must, above all else, exercise himself in the fear of GOD. The cultivators of this microcosmic garden ought to be all professors of the liberal arts and of Jurisprudence <note>The study and theory of Law</note>. For just as *Adam*, before the Fall, possessed the knowledge of all arts perfectly without a teacher, and was just and perfect: so the man of the new creature, after regeneration in *Christ*, will be able—from *Christ* and through *Christ*—to perfectly acquire for himself the knowledge of all things and arts, and all justice, equity, and right judgment, without any teacher and without any body or code of law. For He alone is that **LORD** who gives wisdom: and from His mouth come prudence and knowledge. Proverbs 2. ### ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICAL STONE

...ians, <note>This is the conclusion of a word from the previous page, likely *profanians* (the profane) or *unbelievers*.</note> it cannot bear its splendor: for the light reveals those who are base. Therefore, all those endowments of which the woman <note>In alchemical allegory, the "woman" often represents the lunar, passive, or mercurial principle of matter.</note> stands stripped and despoiled must be restored to her through the benefit of the living fire—that is, the male. The polluted and stained redness <note>original: *rubedo*; refers to the final stage of the work, which here must be purified from its initial "rust" or "leprosy."</note> must be reduced to its pristine clarity, purity, and integrity. The work of purification must be continued for so long until the female, receiving the power of her male, is so strengthened that she can sustain cold, heat, and all external injuries, undergo every trial, and finally enjoy and rest quietly in the natural bed of unity with the man.

Just as God rested from the work of creation on the seventh day—which day is called the Sabbath in the books of Moses, that is, the day of rest—so Saturn <note>original: *Saturnus*; in alchemy, Saturn represents the "lead" or the dark, heavy "prime matter" at the beginning of the work, but here he acts as the finisher who brings the matter to rest.</note> puts the final hand to the work of our magnesia <term>Magnesia: a term used by alchemists to describe the crude, transformative substance that contains the "seed" of the Stone.</term>, and from that seventh day of the Philosophers, he also rests. However, by resting, he does not entirely desert the work he has produced; just as God never withdraws from His creatures after the work of creation is finished, both are said only to "rest." Both God and our Saturn rest because they add no further new species beyond those which one had produced by creating and the other by generating during those seven days.

Indeed, just as God enclosed the entire treasure of His divinity—which He had kept hidden within Himself as the Archetype <note>The "Archetype" refers to the original pattern or "idea" in the mind of God before the world was made.</note> from the infinite eternity of ages—within the number of seven days, and manifested it to us through this wonderful craftsmanship of creation in His creatures, representing it so perfectly and graphically that there is no part of the Creator so small that some likeness of it cannot be found in His creatures; in the same way, Saturn, secretly carrying the likenesses of metallic bodies within himself, finally brings forth all bodies unfolded into the light through the same number of seven days when the work is finished.

That neither God nor Saturn is idle is clearly demonstrated by the continued multiplication of all things. Without God, and without Saturn—who acts as the second dispenser and governor of natural things under God—this multiplication would otherwise grow weak, powerless, and ineffective. 

A great force and power, and a supreme secret, lies hidden in this septenary <note>The number seven.</note> of days. When viewed magically and through its internal anatomy, being divided into its parts or members, it represents in a certain way a universal and essential name for both the Creator and the creature. Thus, a single septenary fully embraces all the force and virtue of the other numbers. For the septenary is composed of the ternary <note>The number three, often representing the Trinity or Spirit.</note> and the quaternary <note>The number four, representing the elements or the physical world.</note>, whose characters are commonly expressed as 3 and 4; as if you were to say three times four, which makes twelve <note>The text suggests a mystical multiplication where the spiritual (3) and physical (4) components of the 7 days interact to govern the 12 signs of the zodiac or stages of the work.</note>:

Twelve, however, is resolved among four: which, through these digits 3 and 4, return to the number seven. From this conversion, it is gathered that the same God in creation, and the same Saturn in the generation of things, is 7, 12, and 84—that is, the beginning, middle, and end; or "all in all." <note>original: *omnia in omnibus*; a biblical reference to God's ultimate sovereignty.</note>

We see, moreover, that the same sevenfold consists of a doubled triad and a single unity joining those two triads to each other. For that one day of Saturn is the one which, collected and bound together from all the other days as if into one bundle, produces the day of rest or the Sabbath: so that in the progression of generations, nothing more is repeated besides that one day numbered seven times, and thus it is consequently multiplied through itself even unto infinity. 

We must also observe the twofold distinction of these triads, of which one is celestial and the other elementary. The celestial refers to three pure and perfect principles; the elementary, however, to three impure and imperfect ones. These are reduced through the connective unity into one perfect sevenfold, complete in all its numbers, as can be seen from these circles and the symbols of the planets:

### SCHOLIUM.

The life of a coal is fire; when it is removed, it becomes like a dead body. Not only in coal, but in all other things fire excites, fosters, and preserves life. Indeed, the essence of life is nothing other than pure, clear fire: not that thick and corrupting elementary fire, but that subtle, heavenly, and generating fire of all things, which, according to the testimony of Aristotle, corresponds to the element of the stars.

This [fire], extinguished in metals because of the thickness of the bodily mass, must be resurrected by the Philosophical, oily, and sulfurous water: which happens, as the author wishes, in the space of thirty days. The certain number of days, previously wrapped in silence, is here expressed in manifest words. But although an open assignment of days is made here, the industry of the craftsman is of great value in this work. For here he can establish the regimen of the work in various ways: both by reason of the material he takes (where one exists closer to perfection than another), and by reason of the fire, in whose just and equal moderation the whole secret and science consists. If therefore you skillfully perform all things necessary for this matter, you will be adorned with a royal diadem: by which formerly all Philosophers shone conspicuously above others ignorant of this doctrine.

# CHAPTER II.

...of political princes <note>original: *principum politicorum*</note>, who have sought and seized the external glory of power and riches; whereas most philosophers have preferred to live quietly in voluntary poverty, rather than submit their necks to the troublesome and destructive yoke of wealth. Hence the philosopher Anacreon <note>Though known historically as a poet, in alchemical literature Anacreon is often cited as a figure of philosophical detachment.</note> returned all the money offered to him as a gift to the tyrant Polycrates, because he felt more trouble in guarding it than pleasure in possessing it. In this, the Hermeticists <note>Followers of Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> seem to imitate the example of our Savior and Lord, who confessed in open words before Pilate that his kingdom was not of this world. For such philosophers, being the greatest despisers of worldly delights, seek the highest pleasure from the study of wisdom alone and from investigating divine matters; they are like the obedient disciples of the Wise One, who says in Proverbs 8:
> Love instruction more than gold: for its fruit is better than gold and precious stones, and its yield is better than choice silver.

Oh, if only the present age would consider this! Then surely so many would not labor under that "accursed hunger for gold" <note>original: *sacra auri fame*; a reference to Virgil's *Aeneid* regarding the corrupting power of greed.</note>. These people, after scraping together a great force of gold through right and wrong, afterwards—proh dolor!—misuse it for impious and wicked purposes, and thus from their own coins they prepare hell and eternal punishment of the soul for themselves.

After the Philosopher, therefore, once the work is finished, has gained that royal honor and glory, he rests (says the author) above the well, away from that <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: *auripigmentum*; literally "gold pigment," a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral which alchemists used as a symbolic starting material or a stage in the color changes of the Work.</note> which lacks moisture. The "Well" is the Fountain of the Philosophers, from which they draw their own orpiment that lacks moisture—that is, their own water which flows, indeed, but does not wet the hands. This they digest and cook with several fires for so long until all superfluous moisture is separated from it and it is utterly dried out. It is surely believable that the craftsman is affected by no slight, but by the greatest and most incredible pleasure; he who is finally master of his wish now experiences in reality, looks upon with his eyes, and usefully and fruitfully enjoys all that he has sought and expected for so long a time with wavering hope and the highest desire.

# ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICIAN’S STONE

...the philosopher, a circular conversion <note>original: *circulariter conversiva*</note>; this is because one element shares a symbolic bond with another. For **Earth**, which is dry and cold, shares one quality with **Water**, which is cold and moist. **Air**, however, being moist and hot, shares a quality with **Fire**, which is hot and dry: and thus, consequently, Earth shares dryness with Fire. But there is only one true and primary element of the stone, namely Earth <note>original: *terra*</note>, which, once burned and refined through philosophical calcination <note>original: *calcinatione philosophicâ*; the process of reducing a substance to a fine powder through heat</note>, is afterwards dissolved in a humid place into a liquor or a cloudy, thick, and heavy water. This, having been made more subtle through sublimation, passes into Air or Oil: which, by the continuation of the sublimation, is rendered entirely Fiery. But so that its superfluous moisture may be utterly consumed, this oil must finally be reduced by the strongest fire into ash or a reddish earth. And thus the **Dragon** has devoured its own tail <note>A reference to the *Ouroboros*, the serpent eating its own tail, symbolizing the eternal cycle of nature and the completion of the alchemical work</note>: and the **Pelican** has restored life to its dead young with its own blood, shed from its breast <note>The Pelican is a common alchemical symbol for the vessel and the "Red Stage" of the work, representing sacrifice and revitalization</note>.

For this blood of the Pelican is that red spirit of which the author speaks here. Regarding its color, it is not only blood that is reddish; indeed, even in the human body, you will find no part (though it is undeservedly excluded from the number of parts by the crowd of Galenic physicians <note>Followers of Galen, whose traditional medical theories were often challenged by alchemists like Paracelsus</note>) which abounds more in spirits than blood itself, so much so that it is called by certain doctors the primary seat of life. Furthermore, the author warns that the elements must be joined together sparingly. For the laws of nature are inviolable; so much so that they must be observed exactly and precisely:

->*Beyond or short of which, the right path cannot exist.*<-
<note>original: *Quas ultrà citràq; nequit consistere rectum*; a quote from the Roman poet Horace, suggesting that truth and virtue lie in a precise middle ground.</note>

But let no one feel more scrupulous than is fitting regarding the joining of the elements: nothing is joined with them except what was previously separated. Thus, there is one author of the separation and the joining, and one and the same efficient cause: which is nothing other than the <term>Archeus</term> <note>The "internal chemist" or vital force that Paracelsians believed directed the functions of life and nature</note> of the earth, who is present in the "mines of the Philosophers" with his continuous labor. He is served by the <term>Gnomes</term> <note>Elemental spirits of the Earth; here they represent the hidden, natural intelligence that governs the growth of minerals</note>, who know by innate knowledge what must be separated or joined, and what must be added or taken away. Thus, they have no need for those "know-it-all" consultants who, with their crude and foolish external operations, try to sell dregs for Earth, phlegm for Water, a thicker and subtler liquor for Air, and the most subtle for Fire. These people confound, mix, and macerate things for so long that eventually—either from the sharp power of their own penetration or from the violence of the external fire—the vessels break and everything vanishes into ash and embers, or into smoke

## CHAPTER II.

...at last they vanish. And indeed, such operations are rightly suited to thick and stupid minds. But the **Philosophers**, investigating something more subtle and worthy of their contemplation, leave behind that external bark and apply themselves to extracting the alone external and invisible nucleus of the elements. Because those ignorant sycophants do not perceive this, they rise up against the philosophers and attack them like rabid dogs, biting, slandering, and accusing them; they even place themselves far above them. For what, they say, does that <term>little doctor</term><note>original: *doctorculus*; a mocking diminutive for a scholar who lacks practical experience</note> know, who has spent almost his whole life only in schools and learning letters? He who does not yet know how to properly seal a glass or any vessel, nor has ever dirtied his hands with the handling of charcoal? They claim that much greater labor and sweat are needed before the works of the (so-called) most subtle and ingenious Alchemists can be learned. 

<margin>☞</margin> I once saw such a "square-shaped <term>Polyphemus</term>" <note>A reference to the one-eyed giant from the *Odyssey*, used here to describe a crude, narrow-minded, or monstrous individual</note> in our most great city of the Parisians. He was Greek by nation—and without doubt, always a liar, an evil beast, and a lazy glutton <note>original: *mendax, mala bestia, venter piger*; a Latin rendering of the famous Cretan paradox from Titus 1:12</note>—who did not fear to bark at a certain most learned man, a great philosopher, <term>kabbalist</term> <note>a student of Jewish mysticism and hidden meanings</note>, mage, and one most skilled in hidden things. This Greek not only made himself equal to the man, saying: "As great a philosopher as you are in the Latin tongue, so great am I in my Greek"; but out of contempt he also babbled that the scholar was only cleverly experienced in medical matters, while most impudently lying that in <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: *Chymicis*</note> the man was not even to be compared to himself. 

<margin>☞</margin> The same thing happened to me once in Switzerland, at <term>Augst</term> <note>original: *Augustæ Rauracorum*; an ancient Roman site near Basel</note>. While dining at a certain inn, I conferred with a German man, otherwise very well-lettered. When he found himself unable to answer my objections regarding the Chemical art, and began to blush with shame in the presence of other young physicians who were his friends, he sought to defend the honor of his authority with this quarrelsome insolence: "You," he said, "as I understand from your speech, are utterly ignorant of Chemical matters, nor have you ever even touched a piece of charcoal." 

But I—knowing already from his own confession that he had labored long and gained not the slightest benefit from it—replied simply: "Nor have I incurred so many useless expenses as many are accustomed to do." But if that wretched man had known how little the true seekers of Chemistry care for those dead coals, and how at that very time my lips had been touched and colored by a **living coal** <note>A reference to Isaiah 6:6-7, symbolizing divine purification and the gift of true speech</note> brought to me from the **Philosophical altar** by angelic or rather divine inspiration, he might perhaps have sought my friendship with greater verbal kindness, and not shown himself so difficult toward me.

But that is an ancient calamity among men: that virtue and truth, by suffering violence, are always suppressed; while vice and falsehood, like scum boiling up in this filthy pot of the world, always seek the top. Who then among the philosophers should instruct or rebuke such impious mockers, unless he perhaps wishes to do himself an injury and contract a stain?
