### SCHOLIUM <note>A scholium is a formal explanatory note or commentary on a text.</note>

The listing of so many and such various names serves no other purpose than the knowledge of the true matter of the Stone. It is not that any one of these names—which are partly known, partly unknown and foreign—discloses the matter truly and without deception: but rather that only the ingenious sons of the wise, from all these collected together, may at last be able to draw out the infallible truth of the matter.

Among all things, however, quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note> seems to be chosen first. For <term>George Ripley</term> <note>original: *Riplæus Anglus*; a famous 15th-century English canon and influential alchemical writer</note>, a most sharp philosopher, says: "Philosophers call it quicksilver, and not the common kind, without which nothing that exists can be." If, therefore, nothing exists under the sun in which quicksilver is not found, the author did not wish to call it by the names of all things without reason: concerning which single subject many indeed spend much labor, vain and useless, and searching for a long time, find nothing; but they entangle themselves more and more in labyrinths.

## CHAPTER II.

...chains, so much so that at last they lose all opportunity of escaping from them. For "excessive haste," says the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle, though the proverb "haste is from the Devil" is often attributed to various medieval sources</note>, "is on the part of the Devil"; and this indeed offers them no small occasion for error. For they rush into the art with a certain headlong momentum, driven by an insatiable desire and greed for possession. And while they attempt to handle the sacred mysteries of philosophy—which it is a sin to desecrate or pollute—with "unwashed hands" <note>a classical idiom meaning to approach a sacred or complex task without proper preparation or reverence</note>, and try to set their hand to the work while the matter is still unknown to them, they fall into such great confusion by an inverted order—or as they say in the schools, by *hysteron proteron* <note>original: ὕστερον πρότερον; a Greek logical term for "the latter before the former," or putting the cart before the horse</note>—that they never achieve anything worthy of praise from this path. 

Since, therefore, a perfect and solid knowledge of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argenti vivi*; literally "living silver," the liquid metal mercury</note> is most greatly necessary before anything is attempted in this art, and no closer or easier way is given to reach a knowledge of it than that which is taken from the contemplation of its powers and faculties, I share this faithful counsel with all disciples of this profound philosophy: that first of all, they should most diligently consider, weigh, ruminate upon, and turn over in their minds those virtues and gifts of quicksilver—or <term>philosophical mercury</term>—attributed to it here and there by the philosophers in their writings. For through these, as if by a guiding hand and with the help of divine mercy, they will without any doubt reach the innermost knowledge of the thing itself.

->COMMENTARY<-

<margin>hook mark</margin>
The author here distinguishes between a true or philosophical tincture and a fictitious or sophistic <note>fake or deceptive</note> one. The true one is made from fixed and incombustible sulfur, for which reason bodies are also rendered fixed and incombustible. For every transformation follows the nature of the transformer, and not the thing transformed. It is necessary, therefore, that the best sulfur be chosen for this work. The common variety is unsuitable because it infects, blackens, and corrupts; moreover, it has a double superfluity: namely, an inflammable substance and an earthy dross. Therefore, another must be sought out, which is a simple and living fire, and which revives dead bodies, and brings them to the highest perfection and ultimate maturity. Such a thing, says Avi— <note>likely referring to Avicenna, the famous Persian physician and philosopher</note>

# ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICAL STONE

...[Avi]cenna <note>original: *cenna*; likely referring to Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical works were foundational in the West</note>, it is found nowhere else upon the earth except in the bodies of the sun and the moon <note>alchemical code for gold and silver</note>. In the Sun indeed, it exists in perfection, because it is more thoroughly digested and decocted <note>refined through heat or "ripened"</note>. If a tincture is prepared with this sulfur, and is led from the lowest degree of obscurity through the middle stage—linked like a chain—all the way to the supreme splendor of dignity and spirituality, it tints any body melted by the fire and adheres so firmly to these bodies that it is never again separated from them for eternity; for in this way, the tinter and the tinted have been made into one single tincture. But a false <note>original: *sophistica*; referring to counterfeit or "sophistic" alchemy that mimics true results through superficial means</note> tincture, which is fashioned from intermediate minerals—from burning sulfur, arsenic, alum, and the like—can protect neither the bodies upon which it is cast nor its own substance from the violence of fire; instead, it flees together with the bodies and flies away from the fire into the breezes.

->HERMES.<-

> <margin>3</margin>"Son, the sought-after arrangement of the philosophers is one: in our egg. However, this is by no means found in a hen's egg. Lest such great divine wisdom be extinguished in a hen's egg, the composition is fitted together and composed from the four elements."
> <margin>3</margin>

->COMMENTARY.<-

Various descriptions of the <term>Philosophical Egg</term> <note>original: *ovi philosophici*; a central metaphor for the vessel and the matter of the Great Work, representing a microcosm of the universe</note> are held here and there among the philosophers. Some of them divide its substance into four parts, according to the number of the four elements, as our Hermes does here: and thus the shell is earth; the white is water; the thinner membrane is air; and the yolk is fire. Others cut it into three parts: the yolk, which they compare to <term>sulfur</term>; the white, which they present as similar to <term>mercury</term>; and the shell, which they intend to signify <term>salt</term> <note>these three—Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt—are the 'Tria Prima' or three primary principles of Paracelsian alchemy</note>. There are, moreover, still others who wish the yellow of the egg to represent the three red planets: namely, Mars, the Sun, and Venus; and the white to represent the four white planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, and the Moon. They claim the surrounding shell is like the eighth heaven <note>the sphere of the fixed stars in the pre-Copernican cosmos</note>, adorned with earth or incombustible ash as if with fixed stars. This last part, some say, must be struck with a fiery sword and divided into two parts; so the author most truly feels that an egg of this kind is by no means that of a hen. Indeed, one might more rightly say it is of a cock rather than a hen. For if the story is true—in which a decrepit cock reaching its seventh or ninth year of age is said to lay an egg from which is born the <term>basilisk</term> <note>original: *basiliscus*; a legendary creature whose gaze could kill; here used as a metaphor for the transformative power of the Stone</note>, a most poisonous serpent that kills a man by sight alone—then surely this egg, as the "first matter" of the basilisk, will not be so very far distant

## CHAPTER II.

...from the poison of the wise, both deadly, or the Dragon's water <note>original: *aqua Draconis*; a highly corrosive alchemical solvent</note>, stinking and menstrual. However that may be, we certainly detect a manifest agreement in the effect, so that there is less doubt regarding the similar and identical essence of both.

This is without doubt that cock which a certain man vowed he would offer to Asclepius <note>the ancient Greek god of medicine and healing; the "cock" refers to a famous final request by Socrates, here reinterpreted as a symbol for the alchemical spirit</note>, if he remained free from diseases for a year. Therefore, when both ancient and certain modern philosophers saw this similarity and conspiracy <note>meaning a correspondence or "breathing together"</note> of the egg with the stone, they introduced its example not ineptly in describing the Physical Secret <note>original: *arcano Physico*; the hidden workings of nature or the "Great Work"</note>. Furthermore, there are other reasons by which the example of the egg is approved. For just as an egg of the best nourishment generates good and praiseworthy blood, greatly strengthens the vital powers and spirits, and the white of the egg especially protects the face from the burning of the sun: So also the mercury of the wise <note>original: *mercurius sapientum*; the refined foundational substance of alchemy, not common quicksilver</note>, if prepared and exalted in the proper way and taken in a small quantity, not only feeds and nourishes the human body, but also preserves it from all diseases. And furthermore, it protects metallic bodies against all the force of fire: so much so that they delight in it as if in a familiar and friendly food, and in it—if I may speak with the philosophers—they are improved. 

We see, moreover, that the egg is entirely devoid of life and is a dead body; but from the natural heat of the brooding hen it receives life, and in a certain and defined space of time, it hatches a living chick, adorned with feathers, head, wings, feet, and all necessary organs. It is not otherwise with our stone <note>original: *lapis noster*; the Philosopher's Stone</note>, which in its thick body shows no vital evidence before it is dissolved in its own Stygian water <note>original: *aqua stygia*; a potent acidic solvent, named after the mythological river of the underworld</note>, and is digested for the proper time in the same water as if in its own womb <note>original: *matrice*</note>, which provides it with suitable and moderate heat. When this time has passed, it is turned into a life-giving and spiritual homunculus <note>original: *homunculum*; literally "little man," here referring to the "living" essence of the completed elixir</note>, or a most excellent medicine. This medicine excels with the energies of so many virtues that it miraculously heals all infirmities of the body; it removes and perfectly cures leprosy, quartan fever <note>original: *quartanam*; a form of malaria where fever recurs every four days</note>, the falling sickness <note>original: *morbum caducum*; epilepsy</note>, apoplexy <note>a stroke</note>, and all diseases which the common crowd of doctors wrongly judges incurable. Is this not to raise the dead, and to snatch those soon to perish from the jaws of death? For whether you look at the egg deprived of life, or the imperfect and as it were dead metals, or the languishing and dying sick, everywhere you will recognize the truth of what has been said. 

But here occurs the need to refute the error of those who deny that one species can be transmuted <note>original: *transmutari*; transformed in essence from one thing to another</note> into another, being ignorant of that distinction between perfect and imperfect species. For whatever is still in motion toward the form to which it is ultimately ordered, ought to be called im[perfect]...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 727 regarding the analogy between the "Philosophical Egg" and the development of the Philosopher's Stone. ...perfect: however, when it is at the end of its movement, it ought to be called perfect. For an egg, by reason of the chick, is called imperfect: but truly when the form of the chick has been introduced into the egg—towards which nature in the egg tends as if toward its ultimate limit—then the chick will be perfect: and the species, which before was incomplete or imperfect in the egg, will now be called perfect in the chick.

In this same way, gold, when it has already arrived at the end of its movement and is thus formed according to the first and true intention of Nature, is alone called perfect. Since the remaining metals are in motion toward the form of gold <note>Alchemists believed that all base metals "strive" to become gold over geological time; the alchemist simply accelerates this natural process</note>, they are called imperfect: although they may have diverse forms relative to one another through which they persist and are limited, and are in a certain way perfect within their own species; nevertheless, they are not at the final limit of movement, in which lies the ultimate perfection.

## C O M M E N T A R Y . <note>original: *Scholium*; a marginal note or explanatory commentary on a classical text</note>

Here the author again uses the analogy taken from the egg: by which he wishes to infer that, just as a hen's egg contains within itself everything necessary for generating a chick, so also the Egg of the Philosophers—or our mercury <note>referring to "Philosophical Mercury," the refined foundational substance of the Work, not common quicksilver</note>—has within itself whatever is necessary for it. In the egg, he says, is spirituality and a collection of elements, two things he calls the "greatest aid" and "closeness in nature." By *spirituality*, however, he understands the formative faculty, the "worker spirit" <note>original: *spiritum opificem*; the divine or natural force that shapes matter from within</note>, and the primary author of the chick to be born. For this spirit, out of the coordination of elements which it uses as instruments, arranges all the members—of both the poultry bird and the Hermetic bird <note>the "Hermetic bird" or "Bird of Hermes" is a symbol for the volatile spirit being "fixed" or stabilized into the Philosopher's Stone</note>—by its natural and innate knowledge, and finally brings into this light the Philosophic fetus, perfectly crafted and complete in all its parts <note>original: *omnibus numeris absolutum*; an idiom meaning "perfect in every detail"</note>. This result the author, in respect to the elementary craftsmanship, says is "earth": but that Earth is Gold, that is, the completed work. Furthermore, if we examine the literal anatomy of the word (E G G) <note>original: *O V U M*; the author implies that the very structure of the word or the physical egg contains a map of the universe</note> a little more accurately, we will find in it everything necessary for metallic philosophy. For metals are made from twin principles: namely, from three "near" principles, which are Salt, Mercury, and Sulphur; and from four "remote" ones, which are the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire. To philosophize first, then, concerning the near principles...

### CHAPTER II.

The letter **O** is the Salt of the Philosophers <note>original: *Philosophorum sal*</note>, or the Sun: which first fashions the body that the craftsman can handle and adapt into whatever form he wishes, according to the prescriptions of nature. For without salt, the remaining two principles—namely **Mercury** and **Sulphur**—will never be coagulated, because of the excessive spirituality with which they are endowed. Salt, therefore, has this property: it makes subtle things gross, the incorporeal corporeal, and the hidden manifest. Hence the Philosopher says in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts</note>: "make bodies not-bodies, and the incorporeal, bodies." Likewise: "take the hidden and honorable secret, which is white magnesia <note>original: *magnesies alba*; in alchemy, this refers to a symbolic 'lead' or 'mother' of the stone, not modern magnesium</note>, and that which is mixed with the living; but do not take it unless it is pure and clean, and place it in its own vessel, and pray to GOD that He grant you the sight of this greatest stone."

Now, as for those two **V**s, they both have the same meaning; and through this position **X**, as you see, they join into one letter—namely into **X**, which among the Latins signifies the number ten <note>original: *denarius numerus*</note>. Its character is otherwise expressed by these two marks **IO**: as if you were to say, *one circle*, or a single revolution of a circle. For **I** is the manifest character of unity, while **O** is the character of the circle. Thus, by this cross **X** or the number ten, nothing else is indicated than the Mercury of the Philosophers himself, concerning whom enough has been treated above in our hieroglyphs.

The letter **M**, however, because it is equivalent to the number one thousand, in which there is the ultimate perfection of all other numbers, will deservedly hold the place of **Sulphur**. For Sulphur is fire, the quintessence <term>quintessence: the 'fifth essence' or purest part of a substance, beyond the four physical elements</term>, and the spirit which gives life to all things and alters them; it causes every seed to sprout, every light to ignite, and all fruit to flower. Because it possesses and embraces all things within itself, it also administers all these functions in the natural economy of things. Let these things said regarding the three "proximate" principles suffice.

We shall now add a few things concerning the "remote" principles, where we see that the **EGG** <note>original: *OVVM*; the author uses the archaic spelling with two Vs to facilitate the letter symbolism</note> is composed of four letters. The first letter, **O**, represents the earth. For the Philosophical Earth must be round and circular, so that the heavens, by their motion around it, may be able to work upon it and send their power into it. Unless the earth were round, the Sun and other planets would not be able to exercise their operations around it; rather, their course would either be hindered in its circuit or cast down by a swifter motion, as Paracelsus teaches in his *Dawn* <note>original: *Aurora*, a foundational work by the Swiss physician and alchemist Paracelsus</note>.

The two following letters, **VV**, represent water and air. The first **V**, because it is a consonant—a duller letter—denotes the more imperfect, thicker, and darker quality of water. The second **V**, being a vowel—that is, a more resonant and clear letter—signifies the more perfect, subtle, and clear property of the air.

# ON THE DECREE OF THE PHILOSOPHICAL STONE

For the **Air of the Philosophers** <note>original: *aër Philosophorum*</note> is their **oil**: which imprints a constant, fixed, and stable tincture <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a substance capable of penetrating and permanently changing the color and nature of a metal</note>. **Water**, however, even if it colors by moistening, that tincture is nevertheless wiped away in a brief moment. Finally, the last letter **M** clearly depicts **Fire** for us. For just as **M**, the number one thousand <note>original: *millenarius numerus*; the Roman numeral M stands for 1,000</note>, contains all things: so too does fire finally transform all things into itself, and thus renders all things fiery—that is, spiritual and celestial. 

If, therefore, those **three near principles**—Salt, Mercury, and Sulphur—and these **four remote principles**—namely Earth, Water, Air, and Fire—are reduced into one body by our secret art, they will clearly show us the **seven-fold number of metals**, or that true **Philosophical** or **Magical Electrum** <term>Electrum: historically an alloy of gold and silver, but in alchemy, it refers to a "perfect" metal containing the virtues of all seven planetary metals</term>: in which all mineral nature was shown clearly enough above to rest and keep its Sabbath <note>original: *sabbatizare*; a reference to the work reaching a state of divine rest or completion</note>. From all of this, it is openly proved: that the **Egg** is sufficient unto itself to produce the philosophical birth; and it has no need for the additions of "Alchemists," of external washes, or of senseless men.

The Son said to Hermes: What are the **Sulphurs** suitable for our work—are they celestial, or are they earthly? And he replied: Some are celestial, while others are truly earthly.

### SCHOLIUM.
<note>A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary on a text</note>

There follows here a brief Dialogue, in which the speakers are a father and a son. By the question proposed, the Son desires to know from the father whether the **sulphurs** in our work are celestial or truly earthly. Responding to this, the father says: they are not all of one kind, or of the same genus; rather, some are celestial and some are earthly. In the meantime, however, it remains an acknowledged fact: that both are **sulphurs**. By **celestial sulphurs**, I understand the **Sun** <note>original: *Solem*; representing Gold or the fixed principle</note>; by the **earthly**, I understand the **Moon** <note>original: *Lunam*; representing Silver or the volatile principle</note>. 

For the **Sun** is a hot, fixed, red, and unburnable body, which perfects the **Moon**—his cold, volatile, white, and combustible female—and raises and exalts her to the throne of his glory. However, for this to happen, that which fights with the fire must be mixed with the fire that suits them; they battle, and then a constant friendship is made: as will be said shortly in what follows, and at greater length.

# CHAPTER II. COMMENTARY.

The son proposes another question, asking whether celestial things are governed, nourished, and given life by the celestial, and earthly or inferior things by the earthly. For the heart is the principle of vital function in man; here, it holds the place of life—that is, of the **formal virtues** <note>In ancient philosophy, a "formal virtue" or "formal power" is the inner force that gives a thing its specific shape and identity</note> which are to be distributed into all worldly things. But the father responds that the matter is not as the son supposes, but stands quite differently. For the heaven, he says, is the **male** to the earth, and the earth is indeed the **female** to the heaven. 

On this point, I believe the Platonists agree perfectly with **Hermes**; they understand the heaven to be sprinkled with the seeds of all forms, both those already born and those yet to be born. They believe its soul encompasses the **seminal reasons** <note>original: *seminales rationes*; these are the "blueprints" or "seeds" of all things that exist in the divine mind or the world soul</note>, which a single divine mind carries as if in its own bosom. Whatever is contained within the universe of the world, God has subjected to be preserved by the heavens and the elements, and to be continued by constant birth. Thus, nothing can now be produced from seed or preserved once born without the heavens—unless God, setting aside these "ministers" as it were, should effect something directly from Himself by a miracle. 

Furthermore, whatever things come forth spontaneously without seed—such as many plants, living creatures, all metals, and all stones—take their forms and properties from the heaven alone. The heaven is always present, and it imparts form to all matter prepared with suitable readiness, giving exactly what that matter deserves. This celestial cause is the most excellent and noble **exemplar of all forms**, whose virtue, diffused through all things, penetrates everywhere. Plato called this the **Soul of the World** <note>original: *mundianimam*</note>, another called it the **Giver of Forms**, and Aristotle called it **Universal Nature**. The Earth, however, is the subject and receptacle of all celestial rays and influences. Fertilized by the heaven, she is capable of giving birth to all things from herself; she is receptive to all fruitfulness and, like a **first parent**, is the sprout-producer, center, foundation, and **mother of all**.

It is as if you were to say: "The wise man commands all men." For the middle state is better than that where every nature is united with its own companion. We find in the virtue of wisdom that the middle state is joined together. But the Son asked: "But Father, what among those is the middle state?" He responded:

### COMMENTARY.

If, therefore, heaven and earth are to be joined in a certain magical marriage: it is asked, which is more excellent in the art: heaven or earth? The answer is: Neither performs anything alone unless both are joined together at the same time. Since, however, heaven is in its substance so simple, pure, and devoid of all change—so much so that for this reason it is called <term>ἀσύμβλητον</term> <note>original Greek: *asymbleton*, meaning incomparable or incapable of being mixed</note> by **Aristotle**—a doubt arises here for many: how can any portion or particle of it, sent down here to us, be mixed with our earth, which is coarse, impure, and subject to various changes? But **Hermes** removes this doubt from your mind with these words: *For a middle ground,* he says, *is proposed in the teachings.* What this "middle ground" truly is, he explains again in what follows, where he says: *For every nature there are three things [derived] from two: first, useful water; then, an ointment; and below, the dregs remain.* It is the same as if he were to say: Heaven and earth cannot be joined to one another without a medium—no differently than soul and body (as is said elsewhere) cannot be united into one body without the spirit. 

The spirit, therefore, is the legitimate mediator of every true marriage, both natural and supernatural. For heaven, due to its most simple nature and highest perfection, is like the soul. Therefore, so that heaven (or the soul) may be coupled with earth (or the natural body) in the "bed of union," the spirit must necessarily intervene. This spirit shares in the nature of both, and for that reason is called "middle" <note>original: *mediocris*, here meaning a mediating substance that stands between two extremes</note> by **Hermes**—that is, not too simple and pure, nor too coarse and impure—so that by its right and authority of intercession, it may make this union firm and established. Concerning this spirit, **Marsilio Ficino** <note>A famous 15th-century Italian scholar and priest who led the revival of Neoplatonism</note> speaks thus in Book 3, Chapter 3, of *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens*: *This spirit,* he says, *is an extremely thin body, as if it were not a body and were already a soul; likewise, as if it were not a soul and were already a body. In its power there is the least of earthly nature, more of the watery, more still of the airy, and again, the greatest amount of the fiery and the stellar.* Thus far he speaks.

Here also our **Hermes** mentions three things: water, ointment, and dregs. Now, he declares the Sun <note>In alchemical terms, the "Sun" often refers to gold or the perfected masculine principle</note> to be the "useful water"; he says the "dregs" reside at the bottom as if useless; but the "ointment," wavering toward both, he leaves in the middle. Therefore, the ointment is that spirit which remains in the middle; the water (or soul) is in the heaven, and the body (or earth) is at the bottom.

Again, the purified <note>original: *defaecata*, literally "cleansed of dregs"</note> soul alone ascends into heaven, because it had previously descended from heaven, according to that [verse] in **John 3**: *No one ascends into heaven...*

<header>CHAPTER II.</header>

...into heaven, except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is from heaven <note>original: "filius hominis, qui est de cœlo". This is a paraphrase of John 3:13.</note>—namely, the mediator and savior of the human race, our Lord JESUS CHRIST. By his saving spirit, he illuminates man within the dark prison of this body and dyes him for eternal life. For he is the true light of the world, a single tiny drop of which converts the shadows of the entire world into pure light, seven times brighter than the Sun itself. As the Poet sings, no less truly than elegantly and piously:

->from whose light every light<-
> shines, without whom bright things grow dark; from whom
> darkness glows, even the image of the unpleasant night. <note>original: "cuius de lumine lumen / Omne micat..." These lines describe the divine source of all visibility, both physical and spiritual.</note>

And King Solomon says in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 7: He is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of the majesty of GOD, who renews all things, and passes into holy souls through the nations, making them friends of GOD and prophets. He is found to be more beautiful than the Sun, and when compared to the light, he is superior to every arrangement of the stars. Therefore, just as Christ enkindles, illustrates, and purifies the hearts of men with his nourishing and divine light through the saving fire of the most holy spirit: so also the <term>Light of Nature</term> <note>original: "lumen Naturæ". In Hermetic philosophy, this refers to the divine spark or inherent intelligence within the physical world that allows for growth, healing, and alchemical transformation.</note> not only illuminates, cherishes, and preserves all these lower, worldly, and natural things; but when the separation of the elements occurs, it also performs wonders. This is seen not only in the refining of metals, but it also possesses the greatest power in polishing and exalting stones, which, through the revolution of many ages, it perfectly converts into a celestial and crystalline clarity.

Air, he says, is born from water, and is not separated from it; from both of these consists the life of every single thing. For we see not infrequently that from stagnant, stinking, and putrefying waters the air is immediately infected. This air, from such great corruption, infects the entire neighboring earth and brings on all kinds of burning fevers, pestilences, and other similar horrendous afflictions which can be cured by doctors with no known remedy. When certain doctors of sharper wit noticed this, they judged that this evil must be helped only by the removal of the cause <note>original: "causæ ablatione". This refers to the medical principle of removing the source of a disease rather than just treating symptoms.</note>. Therefore, they purified the air contaminated with poisonous and noxious vapors by a great fire of wood, and they cleansed it so exquisitely that, once those pestilential and most harmful breaths were utterly removed, they rendered the substance of the air serene, clear, excellent, and most healthy. The same occurs in our **Philosophical Heaven**, which in its first resolution or **putrefaction** <note>In alchemy, putrefaction or "nigredo" is the first stage of the Great Work, where the matter is broken down and turns black.</note> is so horribly defiled that, like a most poisonous **Dragon**, it infects everything by its touch. Whence it is also said to dwell in a dark house: to possess within itself blackness, smoke, dregs, and death itself. As long, therefore, as the heaven remains thus infected, it cannot return to its former nature—simple, pure, fixed, and perennial.

Wherefore the author commands that the **Dragon** should ascend into the air through blackness: which will hardly happen on account of its thick and heavy bodily mass. It will not tend upward before it is resolved by the force and power of fire in the **Philosophical glass** <note>The "glass" refers to the alchemical flask or "aludel" used for heating substances.</note> into an airy and vaporous substance. Thus dissolved, it will be exactly purified by the frequent ventilation of the air and will recover the primeval nature of heaven. If the craftsmen achieve this end, singing a hymn first of all to GOD, they will exult piously with joy.

However, it must be carefully noted meanwhile, both here and elsewhere, that from the **sulphurs** <term>Sulphur: In alchemy, this represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle of a substance, often associated with the soul.</term> of which the Philosophers speak, only those are to be chosen which are closer to their first principles. For just as—according to the testimony of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician often cited by alchemists for his theories on natural heat and bodily humors.</note>—newborn infants, only recently weaned from the breasts of nature, abound more in natural heat than adults; so too among the "sulphurs" of things (whose differences extend far and wide), only those are nobler and more excellent which are nearer to their primitive or **mercurial** origin than those which have receded further from it. Those which are "near" are extracted from **Mercury**, gold, and silver. Those "farther away" come from the remaining metals. But the "farthest removed" are those drawn from other minerals, and from all animals and vegetables.

### SCHOLIUM <note>A scholium is a marginal note or explanatory commentary on a text.</note>

<margin>3.</margin>
What we today call the "study of philosophy" was, among the most ancient philosophers, called the "study of wisdom." It is said that **Pythagoras** was the first to refuse such a splendid and magnificent title as "Wise Man" <note>original Latin: "sapiens"</note>; out of a particular modesty, he preferred to be addressed as a "lover of wisdom," or a **Philosopher**. This is supported by **Theodorus Zwinger** <note>A prominent 16th-century Swiss scholar and physician.</note>, that great light of Germany, in the third volume of his *Theater of Human Life*: "Only God," he says, "is Wise. The Philosopher is a lover and imitator of Him, both in understanding and in acting. He loves, so that he may possess; he imitates, so that he may express." The "starred" or "reborn" poet **Marcello Palingenio** <note>Author of the "Zodiacus Vitae," a famous 16th-century poem mixing science, philosophy, and satire.</note> also sings of this sentiment in these verses:

> Can be found on earth: he only seems wise
> Who is less foolish than others, though he may still be ignorant.
> Without a doubt, wisdom belongs to the gods alone.*

Therefore, when **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical and philosophical works were attributed.</note> says here that all the wisdoms in the world are subject to his own wisdom, it must be understood to refer to all kinds of sciences, arts, or disciplines. As we demonstrated above in Chapter 1, the unique **Hermetic Philosophy** <term>Hermetic Philosophy: A philosophical and esoteric tradition based on writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, emphasizing the connection between the earthly and the divine.</term> encompasses all of these within itself. **Theophrastus Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note>, that great thunderbolt of philosophers and physicians, derived his doctrine—contained in commentaries across several hundred books—from this same foundation of Hermetic Philosophy. Out of his "philosophical liberty," he frequently granted the name of "Philosophy" to **Chemistry** *preeminently* <note>original: "κατ’ ἐξοχὴν" (kat' exochēn), meaning 'par excellence' or 'in the highest degree'.</note>. For this reason, he is unfairly accused by some of **disorder** <note>original: "ἀταξίας" (ataxias), referring to a lack of systematic arrangement.</note> and confusion in his teaching of the arts. But if such critics had correctly understood Paracelsus's intention, they undoubtedly would not have risen against him with such hasty condemnation.

**Jacob Zwinger** <note>Jacob Zwinger (1569–1610) was a physician from Basel and the son of the famous scholar Theodor Zwinger.</note>, son of Theodor—otherwise a most learned man and quite skillfully and successfully well-versed in both Hermetic and **Peripatetic** <term>Peripatetic: Referring to the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle.</term> philosophy—says that Paracelsus handed down these arts too confusedly and without distinction, and that he included nearly all of them under the single heading of Chemistry. Zwinger argued that each art should have been considered according to its own different perspective. He says that Chemistry has its own peculiar principles, and likewise Physics, Astronomy, Theology, and the other arts each have their own principles distinct from the others.

But even granted that this is so: how, I ask, could anyone ignorant of Chemistry solidly investigate the principles of **Physics** <note>In this context, 'Physics' refers to the study of natural philosophy and the physical world.</note>?
<margin>{</margin> According to the common opinion of those who philosophize, these principles are merely the dreams of men, insofar as they lack any foundation of certainty. Neither what they are, nor of what sort they are, can be truly or perfectly known unless the Chemist intervenes to demonstrate their certainty to the eye. 

**Astronomers** also frequently wander so far from the true mark in their prognostications and divinations that the trust placed in them has begun to be greatly endangered in our century. This happens for no other reason than that those unskilled in Chemistry attempt to predict the future only from the powers, positions, and constellations of the stars fixed in the upper firmament and located very far away from here. In this, however, they are shamefully deceived. For a much more certain method of forecasting is taken from that **Astronomy** whose principles are so established by chemical demonstration that only a senseless person or one captured by madness would dare to deny them. For the Chemist contemplates "stars" that are not far distant from here, but lie right before his feet; indeed, he not only handles them with his hands, but he also drives the course of unfortunate and malignant influences here and there as he wishes. He guards against every evil in time and drives it away by his ingenious art. 

As for **Theology**, if perhaps...

## CHAPTER II.

If by chance some unbeliever, unskilled and ignorant of sacred literature—as most of the heathens were in former times—should deny **God**, the Chemist <note>The author uses "Chymicus," which in this era referred to both chemists and alchemists, who sought to understand the divine through the study of matter.</note> will demonstrate the power, majesty, and glory of the divine spirit so clearly and without any shred of hesitation, that the person would be compelled, as if by force, to confess the existence of some **God**, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Opt. Max." (Optimus Maximus), a title originally for Jupiter, later adapted by Christians for God.</note>, whose power and magnificence are infinite and immeasurable. Consequently, the same judgment should be held regarding almost all other kinds of disciplines.

Since this is the case, no one will deny that the dignity and excellence of Chemistry are indeed greatest. For she is the torch and the light by whose splendor the truth of the arts and sciences—which otherwise, through the fault of false teachers, lies submerged in a deep and dark sea of lies—begins to struggle free and shine clearly. And just as nothing is found, according to the testimony of the royal Psalmist <note>A reference to King David; see Psalm 19:6, "there is nothing hid from the heat thereof."</note>, that can hide itself from the heat of the Sun; so there is no art or science founded upon such ambiguous and deceptive principles that it cannot be tested by the science of Chemistry, as if by a Lydian stone <term>Lydian stone: A touchstone (basanite) used since antiquity to test the purity of gold and silver by the color of the streak they leave behind.</term>: and its abstruse and hidden truth is finally called back into the light. Rightly, therefore, should the remaining sciences recognize this one as their mistress and Queen, and as is fitting, serve and minister to her as handmaidens.

Many wonder why Chemical authors have produced their art in such a varied style of writing: borrowing terms or vocabulary for the art now from the Physicists, now from Astronomers, Geometricians, Arithmeticians, Physicians, Theologians, and so on. If you do not know the reason, I will tell you. Chemistry, in itself simple, perfect, circular, universal, most ample, most magnificent, and royal—standing alone upon the supreme throne of the arts—uses the labor and ministry of the other arts or sciences as a queen uses her servants and followers. From this, even those arts themselves, with a wonderful consensus and conspiracy <note>In the Latin sense of "breathing together" or harmony.</note>, run together and flow from every side most readily into the service of this, their one mistress. But those who are of a coarse and dull wit will scarcely scent this harmony in the arts, nor will they busy themselves to grasp it, no matter how much they are forewarned; whence also they will not restrain themselves from disparaging good men. But for those

They will not only refrain from depriving the most noble art of Chemistry of the praise due to its eminence and dignity, but they will even approve the methods of such great men as something laudable and adopted for a weighty reason.

Next, let him be pious and upright. For nothing is more useful to a man than piety and integrity, by which he commends himself to both **God** and men. Furthermore, let him be endowed with a sharp and profound intellect, without which he will hardly be able to extricate himself from those tangled and rugged snares of the Philosophical labyrinth. Let him also frequently practice humanity and courtesy toward men in his speech and greetings. Finally, let him not rashly spread among the common people the secrets entrusted to him by **God** or by his teachers, unless he wishes to provoke the divine wrath and petulantly throw himself into the most immediate danger of his life.

For through this medium, as if by **Jacob’s ladder** <note>original: "scalam Jacobi"; a biblical reference to a ladder between heaven and earth, used here to describe the circulation of substances in a vessel.</note>, there occurs in the world's great **alembic** <term>alembic: A distilling apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used here metaphorically for the earth and atmosphere.</term> a continuous ascent and descent of the elements, and the conversion of one into another: so that the lower things are joined with the higher in a most tight bond of marriage, and finally the former are perfected by the latter. This marriage is rightly called **Gamathæa** <note>A term used by Paracelsus to describe the union of celestial influences with terrestrial matter, or a "marriage" of spirit and body.</note> by **Paracelsus** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals in medicine.</note>, the great leader of Philosophers. Through the continuation of digestion, these are strengthened day by day and, as it were, come back to life, reaching the highest light of perfection through many purifications. This light, by the power of its own brightness, wipes away and deletes all stains and blackness or darkness in the bodies, just as the Sun scatters and drives away the clouds. It brings upon them a most glowing and splendid color; once this color is introduced, the craftsman will have his work perfected, and he will be worthy of being treated with royal honors. But unless he attains this goal, he has labored in all things in vain.

Therefore, it will go well for the one who works well; Kings will favor him and adorn him with the greatest dignities. <meta>This page continues the technical explanation of the "Great Work" of alchemy. Having established the spiritual requirements of the seeker on the previous page, the author now provides a practical, botanical analogy—the life cycle of the juniper tree—to explain the four stages of alchemical transformation.</meta>

# ON THE DECREE OF THE PHYSICAL STONE
<meta>catchword: follow-</meta>

As an example, we shall propose the preparation of juniper berry oil: an undertaking which one would hardly attempt unless, first of all, they had established a small bush or juniper tree to grow from the seed in the earth. In its first year, this tree is sterile, producing only the trunk, small branches, and leaves; all of these, being the thicker parts, take the place of **earth** <note>In alchemy, "Earth" represents the solid, unrefined state of matter.</note>. And this is the first operation of the **Stone** <term>Stone: The "Philosopher's Stone" or "Physical Stone," the ultimate goal of alchemy, capable of perfecting both metals and the human body.</term>, which is called its **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrefactio"; the stage where matter breaks down, often associated with the color black.</note> or its dissolution into earth. In the following second year, Nature continues to work upon the little bush, and with no other cultivation added or outside help—except for the natural heat of the Sun alone—the juniper begins to bear ash-colored flowers, as if inclining toward a white color. By their tenderness and softness, these represent **Philosophical Water**, or the Stone resolved into the element of water. Thus in the third year, the strength of Nature grows and increases more and more in the juniper tree, which in its third annual revolution (for it is the year that produces, not the field) changes those flowers into whitening berries, according to that axiom of the Philosophers: **The corruption of one is the generation of another** <note>original: "Corruptio unius est generatio alterius"; a fundamental Aristotelian and alchemical principle suggesting that for something new to be born, the old form must pass away.</note>. Berries of this sort already contain within themselves a certain oily fatness, but it is still crude and not yet sufficiently **digested** <term>digested: In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow heating of a substance to mature or ripen it.</term>. For this reason, they are compared to **Air**. In the fourth and final year, those glowing berries turn into black berries; this color is the sign of completed and perfect maturity within them, beyond which Nature, without the aid of **Art** <note>In this context, "Art" refers to the skill and intervention of the alchemist.</note>, can work no further. For through the duration of the digestion time up to this point, they have been so exquisitely cooked and ripened by the fire of Nature that, having been made partakers of a fiery nature, they have turned entirely into **Fire**. They have reached a point where they cannot ascend higher into the order of the elements by themselves, unless they are assisted by Art. However, because a corporeal thickness is still mixed into these berries, it greatly hinders the spiritual and fiery essence of the medicine, so that by penetrating too slowly, it cannot freely exert its powers in the body of the sick person. Therefore, by applying the aid of Art, that corporeal and useless substance must be separated from it, so that only the interior and purer force of Nature—which alone, according to **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine." Alchemists often cited him to claim that Nature is the true healer.</note>, is the healer of diseases—is left behind in a subtle, penetrating, and helpful oil. This oil, prepared by **chemical art** <note>original: "Chymico artificio"</note>, no longer contains any thickness within it, nor does it have a fiery or corrupting nature, but rather an ethereal and celestial one, most pure and most subtle. In this way, it will **tint** <term>tint: "Tingere" or "Tincture" refers to the alchemical power to transform the inner nature of a substance (or body) through its penetrating quality.</term> the human body toward the highest health, and will remain with it in that state for a long time. Whoever, therefore, desires to establish exactly the division and composition of the elements in the Great Work of the Philosophers: let them place this example of juniper oil before their eyes: [how] nature [would] follow...

> <margin>4.</margin> O <gloss>19</gloss> Blessed watery form of the sea <note>original: "pontica"; in alchemy, "Pontic water" refers to a sharp, bitter solvent believed to be the "mercury of the philosophers."</note>, you who dissolve the elements. ### COMMENTARY.

**G**reat is the force and power within the **Philosophical Water** <term>Philosophical Water: Also called "Mercurial Water," this is the specialized solvent used by alchemists to break down metals into their "first matter" without destroying their internal essence.</term>, so much so that it is rightly called "blessed." Indeed, it can hardly be praised enough or celebrated with sufficient words of honor. For just as spring water washes away external filth from things, so this water not only dissolves the elements but also removes the internal impurities of bodies. When joined with **Philosophical Vinegar**, it draws out from them **incombustible sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur incombustibile"; a spiritualized form of sulfur that is pure and cannot be destroyed by fire, representing the fixed principle of the Stone.</note>, which, through the process of **projection** <term>Projection: The final act of alchemy where the finished Philosopher's Stone is thrown upon base metals to instantly transmute them into gold or silver.</term>, dyes imperfect metals into gold and silver.

This water is the key to the art; the more often bodies are "opened"—that is, dissolved—by it, the more they are thereafter coagulated, and the more noble, excellent, and perfect they become. Thus, no trace of death, blackness, or imperfection remains within them.

The preparation of this water is known to only a few, because of the ingenious subtlety of the craftsmanship required; those common Alchemists do not employ it at all in their distilled waters.

For whatever is attempted in this art without the support of Nature acting alongside it is a vain and fruitless work. Indeed, the preparation of **strong waters** <note>original: "aquarum fortium"; mineral acids like nitric acid</note>, **royal waters** <note>original: "regiarum"; *aqua regia*, a mixture of acids capable of dissolving gold</note>, and other similar liquids that possess a sharpness and the ability to dissolve (or rather, to corrode), and which are therefore used by goldsmiths, is so foreign to true Chemistry that there is a greater resemblance between the colors of an African and a Dane than between that sophisticated <note>In this context, "sophisticated" means "imitation" or "artificial."</note> preparation and the true one. We therefore judge that the right and true method of preparation must be learned plainly not from human masters, but from Nature herself. For we see her sending to us, from the deep abysses of the mountains, streams of water endowed with the most excellent virtues and gifts of every kind, suited for both Chemistry and medicine. Nature alone completes the preparation of these waters without any advisor. A spring of this kind is found in Hungary,

### ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICAL STONE <note>original: "DE LAPIDIS PHYSICI SECRETO"; the "Physical Stone" refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work.</note>

...whose water has the power to transmute all iron into copper. There are others besides, in which if wood is kept for a certain time, it hardens and turns into stone. Ovid is the authority that a nearly similar river is found in Thrace as well, in these verses:

> *The Cicones have a river which, when drunk, turns the entrails to stone,*
> *And covers things touched by it with marble.* <note>Quoted from Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book XV. The Cicones were a Thracian tribe.</note>

Besides the thermal baths and infinite mineral springs <note>original: "acidulas"; literally "little acids," referring to carbonated or mineral-rich waters</note> which occur everywhere in our France and all of Europe, recently in Upper Germany—namely in Meissen, near the city of Schneeberg <note>Schneeberg was a major silver and cobalt mining center in the 16th century.</note>—as was written to me by a certain German friend, mineral springs were discovered by chance by a certain sick woman through the benefit of a dream. Their effects in curing many most serious diseases are being greatly praised. To the preparation of these and similar waters, no pharmacist ever approached, no wretched alchemist; and yet, skillful and wise Nature, by her simple operation, has produced a work far more artful and ingenious than the entire troop of perfume-sellers <term>seplasiariorum: originally sellers of ointments in Capua, used here as a pejorative for charlatans who sell superficial chemical mixtures</term> and sophists could ever offer with their pompous and "bubbly" recipes and processes, as they call them. The Philosophers say: fire and **azoth** <term>Azoth: The universal alchemical solvent, believed to be the "Alpha and Omega" of the work, often associated with the spirit of mercury.</term> are sufficient for you. 

Learn, therefore, first from Nature the preparation of *azoth*, or that Philosophical water. Afterward, cook this prepared water—whether produced artificially or with Nature’s help—by a simple operation, in imitation of Nature herself, in fire alone; let it not weary you, and thus you will undoubtedly achieve the desired end. This operation or cooking is indeed simple and straightforward <note>original: "linearis"; implying a direct, single-track process rather than one with many complex diversions</note>, yet it is not to be performed in a crude or unrefined manner. Therefore, I said before that it is indeed simple, but hidden and known to few—that is, it requires ingenuity. He who is strong in intellect, investigating it diligently and faithfully while despising all the windings of sophisticated processes, will not be frustrated; rather, by this very opportunity, he will enter deeply into the most profound secrets and inner chambers of Nature.

# CHAPTER
## THREE.
### H E R M E S.

<gloss>1.</gloss> *Know, my son, that the* Philosophers *bind [the substances] with strengthened bonds to withstand the fire, because the spirits—once the bodies have been purified—long to be inside them and rejoice in them. Once they possess them, they bring them to life and dwell within them; the bodies then hold them fast, and they are never separated from them again.*

### C O M M E N T A R Y.

For spirits to be perfectly united with bodies and joined to one another by the tightest bond of alliance, the bodies must first be cleansed and washed with azoth and fire. <note>original: "azoth"; a term for the "universal solvent" or the essential mercury of the philosophers.</note> This washing is the end of the "blackness" <note>referring to *nigredo*, the initial stage of decomposition and purification in alchemy</note> or the purification, until the white becomes perfectly white and the red becomes fully red. When the bodies are cleansed in this way, the spirits are drawn by a natural inclination into love for them; inflamed with passion, they suddenly mingle with the bodies, and thus both are bound together by such an unbreakable bond of fellowship that they are never separated again.

But do not think this union is accidental; rather, because such a close affinity exists between bodies and spirits, they easily enter into this everlasting and indissoluble treaty of friendship. For both have proceeded from one source and principle. Yet the spirits are prior to the bodies, and hence more noble and excellent; it is they who created the bodies—or, as Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was an influential Italian Renaissance philosopher who translated the *Corpus Hermeticum* into Latin.</note> puts it, "suitable baits" <note>original: "escas"; literally "food" or "bait."</note> for themselves by which they might be enticed—and they always dwell gladly within them.

### 2. H E R M E S.

*Then the dead elements are brought to life: and the composite bodies provide color, and they are transformed, and they perform wondrous, permanent works, as the* Philosopher *says.*

### C O M M E N T A R Y.

A house, as Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who advocated for chemical medicine.</note> says, always remains dead by itself; only the inhabitants truly live. In the same way, the bodies of metals are the dwellings of their own spirits. When these spirits are received by the bodies, they gradually thin out and correct their earthly corpulence <note>the heavy, impure physical density of the metal</note>, and by their power of bringing life, they [infuse] life into them...

...awaken those who sleep. Now, this is the property of our medicine into which the bodies have been reduced: that one part of it first tints ten parts of an imperfect body; then a hundred; thirdly a thousand; fourthly ten thousand, and thus the progress continues unto infinity. From this, the supreme efficacy of that word shines forth clearly, with which the Creator addressed the whole creation, saying: *Increase and multiply.* <note>original Latin: "Crescite & multiplicamini," the biblical command from Genesis</note> For the more the medicine is dissolved, the more it increases in virtue and power; whereas otherwise, without dissolution, it would remain in its simple state of perfection. 

Therefore, the fountains of heaven and of divine mercy are open, which can be exhausted by no human ingenuity; and nothing else is desired from us than that we employ the proper vessels to receive such healing and divine water which flows from those fountains. For they shall not fail as long as this age of the world lasts; but when this age passes away and ceases, GOD will draw the streams of all fountains back into Himself once more, nor will He permit them to emanate or flow out any longer. In this way, Christ is the inexhaustible fountain of grace toward the human race; the more often we drink from Him in this age, the more we grow in hope, faith, and charity toward Him.

We must, therefore, diligently endeavor, through the constant and fervent exercise of piety and the sacred fire of penance, that our hearts—being dissolved and, as it were, opened—may daily draw such healing and life-giving water from this fountain. For whoever in this age of grace does not, like the wise virgins, <note>referring to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25, who kept their lamps filled with oil</note> procure for themselves a treasure and sufficient supply of this water to attain eternal life, will hope in vain to purchase it in the next world alongside those foolish virgins.

## CHAPTER III.

...it happened that those who hear the name of water might have falsely convinced themselves that he was speaking of common water, or of some artificial graduals, tinctures, solvents, or similar things. For many are still found today who try to extract waters not only from metals and mineral intermediates, but even from stones, flints, and six hundred similar things: which they use incorrectly for their sophistical masteries <term>magisteria: the specialized techniques or "masterworks" of alchemy</term>.

The author, therefore, with deliberate effort, wished to mention not simply "water," but the "aqueous form." Yet there is a very large number of those—even among those who today in the Academies <note>original: "Academiis," referring to formal universities or schools of the period</note> arrogantly claim the title of *Philosophy* for themselves alone—who have not even seen this essential form of water, of which the author speaks, even through a lattice <note>original Latin: "per transennam," a classical idiom meaning to see something only in passing, or through a screen, rather than clearly</note>. Indeed, they have not even glimpsed it from afar, as nearly all of them falsely believe it to be inscrutable; they freely admit it is entirely unknown to them. And nonetheless, they wish to be seen as the highest and most excellent *Philosophers*. I, on the contrary, judge that it must be determined regarding them as follows: that whoever is ignorant of substantial form must also necessarily be ignorant of the principles of natural science. Therefore, how great their knowledge is in this part of Philosophy, I now leave for others to judge.

In one thing both the alchemical and Academic sophists <term>sophistae: here used in the derogatory sense of "sham" scholars who prefer abstract theory over practical truth</term> commit an error. For when the truth of the matter should have been sought from the essential Book of Nature, as if from a light showing the certain and true path to the fountain of natural science: they, having neglected this light, have fallen away toward the empty and frivolous opinions of the heathens and sophists, from which they have been able to draw no certainty so far, nor will they ever draw any in the future. And thus they have abandoned the fountain or vein of living waters, and have dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns, which are not able to hold waters. <note>original: "Ierem. cap. 2," referring to the biblical book of Jeremiah 2:13</note> If you do not know the fountain from which that life-giving nectar of the gods and Ambrosia, or the living waters, flow forth: behold, I pray, what *Esther, chapter 10* says in her book: "A small fountain," she says, "it is, which grew into a river and was turned into light and the Sun, and overflowed into many waters." <note>This refers to the apocryphal additions to the Book of Esther, often interpreted allegorically by alchemists.</note> Prick up your ears here, *Chymiophyte* <term>Chymiophyte: literally a "chemistry-plant," used here to address a budding student of the chemical arts</term>. But if you are less capable of such great mysteries, which are briefly contained in these listed words, hear *Bernard Trevisan* <note>original: "Bernhardum Trevisanum," a famous 15th-century alchemist known for his allegorical descriptions of the chemical process</note> speaking more at length about this fountain as follows:

> *The fountain,* he says, *is of a very wonderful and terrible power, beyond all other fountains of the whole world. Moreover, it belongs to the King of this country alone, whom the fountain knows very well, and he knows the fountain: furthermore, this fountain shines clear as silver, and is of a celestial color. Thus far he speaks.*

This is as Bernhard <note>Bernhard of Trevis (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist noted for his allegories of the "King" and the "Fountain"</note> explains it: The Fountain attracts the King to itself, and after one hundred and thirty days, the King finally emerges splendid, shining, and crowned with a royal diadem. ### 4 HERMES.

*Our most precious Stone, though cast out into the dung, is most dear, cheap, and cheapest of all; for it is necessary for us to mortify and venerate two quicksilvers together: namely, the quicksilver of orpiment <term>auripigmentum: a gold-colored arsenic mineral often used in alchemical experiments</term>, and the eastern quicksilver of magnesia <term>magnesia: in this context, a mystical "mother" substance or a specific mineral used as a primary matter</term>.*

### COMMENTARY

The Stone is said to be precious and cheap at the same time because of the double quicksilver <note>mercury</note> from which it is composed. For first, quicksilver is a cheap and rejected thing, which is found in all places: in dung, on public roads, in the plains, in mountains and valleys. And man cannot live for even a moment of an hour without it; indeed, all living things—both animals and vegetables, such as herbs, plants, and trees—stand in need of it. For it protects all things from corruption, and even all minerals without exception. Do you wish to know what it is? It is not gold, nor silver, nor a gem, nor any precious stone; for all these cost a great price and are not to be numbered among those things that are cheap and meager. Behold, I shall tell you: it is SALT. Yet it is not that common salt with which culinary foods are seasoned, although it shares one quality with it—namely, that of dissolving. Rather, it is the salt of stone <note>original: "sal petræ," usually translated as saltpeter (potassium nitrate), but here used to mean the "salt of the rock" or the foundational salt of the Work</note>. Of the Stone, I say: by which running mercury is transmuted into the best and most perfect metal, and flint into the hardest adamant <note>a legendary stone of indestructible hardness, often identified with diamond</note>. Few (I know) will give credit to my words; but if they were taught by experience, just as the Philosophers are, they would know how this kind of salt of stone is found in all things, and how it can be skillfully extracted from all of them. Then, as eyewitnesses, they would undoubtedly not deny their own faith, and they would not so lightly cast away such a precious salt—which is despised only by the ignorant and therefore called "cheap" by the philosophers—along with filth, rubbish, and dung. Instead, with greater reverence and industry, they would collect it from all corners of the world. Nor do I look here...

<header>CHAPTER III.</header>

The author’s plan, following a certain just and honest "envy" <note>In alchemical literature, "envy" (invidia) refers to the traditional practice of hiding secrets from the unworthy or the uninitiated</note>, was to call it **orpiment** <term>orpiment: a yellow arsenic mineral, used here as a code name to hide the true substance</term> so that it would not become known to the common masses indiscriminately. For in this matter, I have decided that I must gratify not the author's secrecy, but rather those students eager for learning: whom it has been my plan—and always shall be—to help with all my strength in their fair and good endeavors. 

For why should I persuade a student to seek a thing in Rome or Prague, here or there, at the greatest expense of resources, when it can nonetheless be found everywhere and in all places? I shall explain the matter with an example. If some sick person could be cured solely by the sight of the rays of the sun or moon, but I, the physician called into consultation, were to persuade the patient to travel to Italy to see the Sun or the Moon and receive their rays there: would this not be foolish advice, since the same Sun and the same Moon rise every single day throughout the whole year here in France just as well as in Italy? In the same way, many who are about to perform penance undertake a journey to Italy and Spain in vain. 

For they could buy that penance at home for a lower price and with less labor from the **Sun of Justice** <note>original: "sole justitiæ"</note>, our only Savior and Lord Jesus Christ, who promised us the forgiveness of sins for free through faith alone. But let it suffice to have said this much concerning the common and most cheap quicksilver <note>mercury</note>. Now we shall attach a few words concerning the precious and most dear variety: which the author calls the **oriental quicksilver of magnesia**. 

But he is not speaking of the quicksilver that is seen by the eye, nor of the magnesia known to the common people. Rather, by **quicksilver**, you should understand the "radical humidity" <term>radical humidity: the fundamental, internal moisture of a substance that allows it to be transformed without being destroyed by fire</term> of that mixture, which is the radical humidity of our Stone. And by **magnesia**, he understands the entire mixture from which that humidity is extracted, which is called our quicksilver. 

This humidity indeed runs in the fire, and in that same fire, it dissolves the whole compound, congeals it, turns it black, turns it white, turns it red, and perfects it—that is, it does "all things in all things." From this, it is a most precious treasure to the one who knows it and possesses it. Moreover, it is rightly called **Magnesia**. For great is its power and faculty, which, like a **universal magnet**, attracts all things to its own center—whatever the entire circuit of both the higher and lower worlds encompasses. So much so that, by the benefit of this substance, it is permitted to comprehend the entire world within a body of the smallest quantity, scarcely larger than the point of a needle. But a greater secret lies hidden in this precious magnesia than in the common quicksilver. Therefore, the Philosophers have hidden it in 
-> marvelous ways, and it is not permitted for us to say or <-
-> reveal more about it. <-

<header>ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICAL STONE</header>

# HERMES.
->.5.<-

O Nature, greatest of natures, the creator who contains and separates the intermediaries of natures; she who comes with light and was born with light, and whom the dark cloud brought forth, she who is the mother of all.

## COMMENTARY.
<note>original: "SCHOLIVM"</note>

There is one universal nature, which is defined by Aristotle as the principle of motion and rest. Or it is, as Hermes speaks here, the creator of all natures—that is, the producer of all things. And for this reason, because she procreates and gives birth to all things, she is called by the names of all things by the Philosophers. For God, the supreme maker of things and architect of the entire world, placed this one and only Nature in charge of governing natural things. She nourishes and preserves them with her fiery and perennial vigor, which the Creator of things instilled in her at the first creation. This same Nature is a certain **green line** <term>green line: often interpreted in alchemy as "Viriditas" or the life-force that connects the celestial and terrestrial realms</term> which circles the universe. This is the sole cause why, with each revolution of the years—specifically at the beginning of spring—all species of things turn green again and receive a new power of germinating and proliferating, through which they grow and multiply. This ensures that the species themselves do not perish, for if they did, a vacuum would be created in Nature, which would be the greatest of outrages. Hence Virgil rightly sings:

> *In spring the lands swell and crave the generative seeds:*
> *Then the pathless thickets resound with tuneful birds,*
> *And the herds seek out Venus <note>original: "Venerem" (referring to the goddess of love/desire)</note> again on appointed days.*

->Also Ovid:<-

> *Then come the charming suns, and the unknown swallow appears,*
> *And fashions her shining work beneath the high beam.*
> *And the grass which lay hidden, buried in the furrows of the grain,*
> *Thrusts its soft tip out from the warm earth.*

Nature operates upon these lower realms through the rays of the Sun, the Moon, and the remaining stars, which Hermes understands under the term "light." For by their irradiation or illumination, various gifts of virtues are infused into elementary things, according to the various and diverse species of things. The question arises here: does the Chemist also require the labor and aid of Nature in elaborating his secrets and masteries? But the answer is easy for those who know that **Chemistry** <note>original: "Chymia"</note> is an art similar to agriculture, in which Nature claims one part for herself, and the farmer claims the other, as the external operator and craftsman. For just as the farmer is principally occupied only with preparing the field and sowing: the rest

## HERMES.

> *When, however, we join the crowned king to our red daughter, and she conceives under a light fire that is not yet harmful, she will bring forth a son, joined and pre-eminent, whom she feeds with a permanent little flame, and he lives by our fire.*

## COMMENTARY.
<note>original: "SCHOLIVM"</note>

The Queen, or the red daughter of the Philosophers, is the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"</note>. Do not be surprised that she, who elsewhere is the head and splendor of whiteness, is now called "red." For the metallic or **Philosophical Moon** <note>A refined form of silver or a specific state of the alchemical matter</note> is also masculine in nature; when she is betrothed to the **Sun** <note>original: "Sol"</note>, the crowned king, she conceives and gives birth to a son whom the philosophers call their **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>. 

This son is wonderful in every way: his parents, who just recently were his nurses and nourishers, are now themselves nourished and fed by him. For as he is of a versatile wit and imbued with marvelous arts, he knows how to prepare, among other things, the most pleasing feasts and banquets of every kind. He does this not by any common way of cooking, but rather he cooks and prepares them at the most moderate heat of a life-giving and heavenly fire. 

When these are prepared and placed on the **round table of the Philosophers** <note>A symbolic representation of the alchemical vessel or the completed cycle of the work</note>—which holds no more than ten or at most twelve persons—the father, mother, and his other relatives sit down and celebrate a truly philosophical banquet for a whole week. They admit no other food except the **Mercurial** kind—that is, what the son offers them—nor do they allow anyone from a foreign family, who is not joined to them by the closest bond of blood, to sit with them. 

But if, as often happens, the food placed on the table should chance to grow cold, the King, by the mere gaze of his eyes (which shine like a most glowing fire), makes them grow warm again in an instant. Once warmed, they become sweet and delicate to the taste; the family refreshes themselves in a wonderful manner and eats until they are satisfied, so that for a long time they no longer thirst or hunger. Concerning a cook of this kind, such as this [our]—

## COMMENTARY.
<note>original: "SCHOLIVM"</note>

Everything that lives, lives because of the fire enclosed within; therefore, sulfur also contains a fire hidden within itself, which, when excited by an external fire, begins to live a manifest life: and so, that which was previously hidden in the sulfur now exists as something revealed. Moreover, the duty of fire is not only to give life, but also to purify, and to separate heterogeneous <note>substances of a different nature or kind</note> parts for as long as it takes until, once the dregs are finally separated, there appears a most pure and very red tincture, which represents flesh in its heat—specifically, flesh recently slaughtered and still sprinkled with blood, or gore. This is that **blood of the Green Lion**, of which mention is made here and there among the philosophers. But it is called "green" not because of an external green color, but because of the **greenness of life** <term>greenness: or "viriditas," a term for the vital life-force or "sap" that animates nature</term>, according to this verse:

> *Greenness is the joy of life; a dark*
> *Color suits sorrow, etc.*
<note>original: "Læta viror vitæ est, mœrori convenit ater Color, &c."</note>

Hence, also, only that tincture which is similar to fresh, red flesh still wet with blood is said to have reached the degree of perfection. For flesh of this kind, which is nothing other than blood just now coagulated, still abounds with the perfect and full vigor and greenness of the spirits: not unlike the blood of the Green Lion, which, on account of its greenness, flows entirely with an abundance of vital spirits.

Until now, many have been occupied in that error of thinking that "greenness" must be sought in the **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine: distilled alcohol or ethanol</term>, or in wine itself, distilled several times, as is commonly done.
