# CHAPTER III.

<meta>catchword: HER-</meta>

...vines, which appeared green with leaves, flowers, and unripe grapes. From this external greenness, they believed that the "Green Lion" <note>original: "Leonem philosophorum viridem"</note> of the philosophers was so named; but they were shamefully deceived in this, and wandered very far from a true understanding of the Green and Red Lion.

For just as the lion, the strongest of animals, encompasses the strength of all other animals within itself, so the most excellent tincture of the philosophers <term>tincture: in alchemy, a potent substance capable of transforming or "coloring" other matter, often the goal of the Great Work</term> contains within itself the tinctures of all things. This is by no means to be sought in the fragile wood of the vine, or in anything that comes from it. For how can an incorruptible, fixed, and incombustible tincture be drawn from a corruptible and combustible thing? Can grapes be gathered from thorns, or figs from thistles? Like generates and procreates its like. Hence, as Horace <note>A Roman lyric poet (65–8 BC)</note> testifies, only the brave are born from the brave <note>original: "fortes solùm creantur fortibus"</note>. And since, according to Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note>, in our stone or tincture resides the "strength of all strengths" <note>original: "omnis fortitudinis fortitudo fortis"</note>, anyone can guess that it must be extracted from a thing far nobler and more perfect than the wood or fruit of a vine.

But as to what that thing might be, the author seems to indicate clearly with these words, where he says:

> and its tincture remains red from the fire;

likewise:

> Our son the born king takes his tincture from the fire.

From this it is plainly evident: fire is that "strong strength," or the true greenness of the Lion. For whatever tincture flees from the fire must be judged imperfect and immature, and consequently must be nourished longer in the fire until it is perfected. But if, when nourished in the fire, it retains its old and former shape, or rather becomes corrupted and turns for the worse, it must be utterly excluded as a thing foreign to the Great Work of the philosophers, and sent far away from here to Anticyra <note>original: "Anticyras" — A Greek city famous in antiquity for producing hellebore, a plant used to treat madness; the author implies those who pursue the wrong materials are insane.</note>. For just as among men, some are found who, through long use and habit, can take poison—otherwise contrary and hostile to the human body—without harm, and can simmer and digest it in the stomach like some familiar food: so also our stone, in which death and darkness (that is, imperfection and impurity) dominated from the beginning, is gradually cooked in the fire. Day by day it is assimilated more and more to the nature of fire, and at last it is totally turned into fire. Like a salamander <note>In alchemical lore, the salamander was a mythical creature that lived in and consumed fire.</note> in the fire, it lives in a firm womb as if in its own proper element, and in that alone it joys and delights. With the passage of time, it passes into the quintessence <term>quintessence: the "fifth essence" or purest form of a substance, beyond the four physical elements</term> and the medicinal tincture, as much for metallic as for human

->bodies.<-

### HERMES.

> *The dragon, who watches the openings, flees the rays of the sun, and our dead son shall live; the king will come from the fire and shall rejoice in marriage, and hidden things shall be revealed, and the virgin's milk shall be whitened. The son, now brought to life, becomes a warrior of fire, and pre-eminent in tinctures. For the son is a benefit and possesses philosophy.*

### SCHOLIUM.

The Dragon <note>A common alchemical symbol for raw, volatile matter or the "First Matter" of the work</note> signifies the earth, and it is the "black blacker than black" <note>original: "nigrum nigrius nigro," referring to the *nigredo* or blackening stage, the first phase of the Great Work</note>. Now, serpents and dragons delight more in subterranean places, stony areas, and dark caves than in the light of the sun or the openness of day. Therefore, when the sun shines, they flee and seek their hiding places, lest they be too tormented by such a clear brilliance of light, which they cannot bear. 

Therefore, let the dragon be enclosed in a vessel well-fortified and closed, having only a single hole, small and round, through which the rays of the sun can enter; let it be exposed to the sun for a philosophical month <term>philosophical month: a specific duration in alchemical practice, often forty days, representing a complete cycle of transformation</term>. In this space of time, its limbs being utterly dissolved, it will die; and by its lethal stench, it will also infect the approaching son of the king and deliver him to death. 

Therefore, both having been put to death <note>original: "mortificati"</note> and placed into another clean glass, let them be set in the sun for another philosophical month; or if it be winter time and the heat of the sun is weaker, you shall stir up a similar heat in a stove <note>original: "hypocausto"</note> or another suitable and fit place. And at that time, the son, having received the heat of the sun, will be gradually refreshed and brought back to life by the spirit of life; but the dragon, being more urgently pressed by that same heat, will be utterly consumed and reduced to nothing. 

The King, however, seeing that the heat of the sun is too weak to entirely free his son from the dragon's poison, orders a bath to be prepared for himself and his son. And with the dragon extinguished, he himself enters the heated bath with his son, whom he fosters with continuous embraces out of paternal love. Meanwhile, by providing "virgin’s milk" <term>virgin's milk: in alchemy, a term for a mercurial or acidic liquid used to nourish, wash, or dissolve materials</term> to him daily in great abundance for the restoration of his limbs, he continues this bath of nourishment until the son—all the impurities of the poison being consumed—recovers his former bodily strength and beauty. 

He emerges in dignity, virtue, and splendor entirely like his father, so that you can scarcely recognize a difference between them. The father does not desert the son for eternity, nor in turn the son the father. For just as a shadow follows the body, so the son continually follows the father; for they remain joined to one another with such perfect and constant love that no external force of the elements—whether fiery, airy, watery, or earthy—can any longer dissolve such a firm pact of friendship.

Especially the son—to say nothing now of the father, who is like the son in all things—is a leader in this new generation so powerful and strong that he passes through the midst of fires of villages or houses without any harm. And just as fire has no right over gold, so also it has no power over this golden hero, who therefore deserves by the highest right to be called the **Magnificent and Illustrious Knight of the Golden Spur**, or the **Golden Knight**. <note>The "Golden Knight" is a personification of the perfected Alchemical Stone, which, like gold, is purified and unchanged by fire.</note> Furthermore, he is endowed with such great wisdom that many philosophers flock to him daily from distant regions, just as the Queen of Sheba came to Solomon. They seek to acquire from him a solid understanding and knowledge of philosophy (for from whom should an understanding of things be more sought than from him who draws it abundantly from the light and river of Nature itself, as if from the very fountainhead?). Having attained or mastered this knowledge—from which philosophers are called **Adepts** <term>Adept: from the Latin 'adeptus' (one who has attained), specifically referring to an alchemist who has successfully discovered the secret of the Stone</term> by Paracelsus, and from which **Adept Philosophy** takes its name—they modestly return thanks for such great benefits, as is fitting, and return in peace to their own region.

### 9. HERMES.

> *Come, sons of the wise, and now let us rejoice, and let us be glad together, because death is consumed, and our son reigns; and now he is clothed in a red robe and kermes.* <note>original: "Chermes," a red dye derived from insects, representing the final "rubedo" or reddening stage of the alchemical process.</note>

### SCHOLIUM.

Just as a great-hearted victor returning from war celebrates a public and solemn triumph, and everywhere in the public streets the shouting of the people is heard as a sign of joy and congratulation; so too Hermes believes that—with the sons of the wise shouting and congratulating together after the victory won in this **Chemical War** <note>original: "Chymico bello," the strenuous laboratory process of purifying matter</note>—there should now be a triumph, and we should clap with hands and feet as a sign of joy. For he has conquered so many horrendous monsters, put to flight so many terrible dragons, so many poisonous serpents and malignant spirits, and has finally overcome death itself, which has been brought to an end. But to whom is the first palm of glory more due for such a great victory obtained than to the **King's Son**? For like another Hercules, he sustained immense and insurmountable labor in defeating such atrocious enemies. Therefore, he has also obtained the highest degree of dignity as the legitimate heir of the philosophical kingdom, clothed in a red and purple robe; and like the most invincible monarch of the world, he protects and defends his kingdom from every assault and attack of enemies. ## 1. HERMES.

<margin>1. g.</margin>
> Understand, sons of the wise, that this stone cries out: protect me, and I will protect you; give me what is mine, so that I may help you.

->S C H O L I V M <note>A 'Scholium' is an explanatory note or commentary on a primary text.</note><-

I have spread out my hands, says the Lord of Hosts in Isaiah 65, all the day to an unbelieving people, who walk in a way that is not good, following after their own thoughts. Who, I ask, is more like this people than the erroneous and ignorant Chemist <note>The author uses 'chemist' here in a derogatory sense to describe "puffers" or amateur experimenters who lack the spiritual and philosophical grounding of true alchemy.</note> who hears neither the stone crying out nor the one philosophizing correctly: but is continually occupied in the ways of deception? But how should he hear the stone, which he does not recognize? Or how should he lend a kind ear to the philosopher, whom he neither understands nor desires to understand? For a vain persuasion of knowledge—when he nevertheless knows nothing—so blinds him that he often does not grasp a great mystery even when it is spoken of openly. Only his own ideas please him. He may have much experience in chemical operations, yet he does not wish to be taught, but rather to teach others. Hence he also bears the title of doctor or some other dignity (and not without reason), which the infamy of disgrace would perhaps stain if he acknowledged anyone more learned than himself.

This vain persuasion, I say, has harmed many until now, and still harms them daily, preventing them from reaching the goal of the art. For flying by a certain rashness higher than is right, and like Icarus approaching too close to the sun, they are plunged with him into the deep sea of error, from which they can later hardly escape without the greatest labor. The student of truth hears the stone and the philosopher speaking as if with one mouth. The stone indeed exhibits the matter itself nakedly without words; but the philosopher expresses the essential truth of the matter in words and demonstrates it by the work itself, if the matter requires: so that, even if one

->SCHOLIVM <note>A 'Scholium' is an explanatory note or commentary on a primary text.</note><-

When the philosophers speak of the rays of the Sun, of the light of the Moon, and of the lights of the other stars, this should not be understood as a bare external splendor, such as that of a lamp or a lit candle, which makes only the neighboring air clear and bright by illuminating it, without any other vital and animated force or impression. For philosophers care nothing for a shadow or a dead surface of that kind—or a "chaff-like" one <note>original: "relollaceam." Likely a reference to *lolliaceam*, meaning something resembling darnel or husks; a term Paracelsus used to describe the useless outer shell of matter.</note>, as Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist who emphasized the "internal" properties of substances.</note> speaks of it; but they seek only the true marrow of things hidden within, and they hunt for this alone with singular artifice through their essential rays and internal philosophical light. To make the twofold difference between these rays more known, for the sake of clearer teaching, we will bring forth an example of a lightning ray: whose science or natural property is such that it is not carried indiscriminately with light into any part of the air, nor [does it fill] the air with light...

not only illuminates externally, but by a certain magnetic and innate power is driven and snatched into a certain place, more agreeable and familiar to its nature, which alone it touches and strikes among all others, remaining unharmed, and clearly demonstrates its active power by a visible mark impressed upon it.

Hence we often see a sword or iron dissolved within its scabbard by lightning, while the leather of the scabbard remains whole and unharmed; likewise, sometimes a man's skin is scorched by lightning while his outer garments remain untouched, or vice versa. One may see many such examples in natural histories. From these things it is clearly evident that the philosophers are least concerned with rays that—lacking the energy of vital virtues—provide only an idle and sterile light; rather, they care only for those which, along with light, administer a simultaneously effective and living economy of forms or essential powers. The author explains their extraordinary effect in the following words: where he asserts that from such rays of light, many good things come to the skillful seeker, such as joy, gladness, glory, riches, and delights. He so magnificently extols this science that he prefers to call it divine—due to such a noble and excellent subject—rather than human.

### SCHOLIUM <note>A scholium is a marginal note or explanatory commentary on a difficult text.</note>:

It is not certainly established concerning that word of seven letters in which the author says the whole science is hidden. For it is impossible to extract all the riddles of the philosophers exactly; in searching them out, one may more quickly find the sense than the words. For what sort of word that might be, to confess the truth candidly, I am entirely ignorant; and although someone might seem to come closer to the author's mind by guessing, it would always remain in doubt, since no one, in the author's absence, can completely remove this splinter of hesitation. Therefore, leaving the dispute over the words aside, we will only strive to elicit the true sense and the very essence of the matter. My opinion is this (while leaving others free to think what they wish) that he would not seem to wander far from the truth who says that this seven-letter word is the seven bodies of the metals,

...[things], which are not absurdly understood under a single word, namely **PLANET**.

Add to this that if it is written in Greek <note>The Greek word for planet is πλανήτης (planētēs).</note>, after the first two letters an *alpha* follows, and a little after that, *yda* <note>original: "yda." Likely a phonetic transcription of the Greek letter Eta (η), which in some medieval pronunciations sounded like "ita" or "yda."</note>. And because of this, our preparation arises through locks and keys that open the latches, which is to say, the obscured riddles." Thus far his words. However it may be, you will hardly wring another meaning from the author’s words; which is clearly proven by the words that follow, where he says: The Sun is to be joined with the "water of the son" or Jupiter, and this is a hidden secret. For by the "son of water" he implies <term>mercury</term>, and by the sun he implies fixed and incombustible sulfur: in the union of these two, the whole secret lies hidden. But because the philosopher says above that the wise prepare their Stone from these metals and through "this," he understands nothing else by "this" than gold, or the Sun. For just as the Sun alone possesses such brilliance in the heavens that, once it has risen, it appears alone while all others are obscured; so the Sun of the Philosophers—whether born of the metal or born in the <term>philosophical vessel</term>—contains the other bodies of the metals within itself in a hidden way, and while the others are hidden, it alone appears. For it is called *Sol* [Sun], as if it were *solus* [alone], because it is one and not many; and it is of such great magnitude that, like a leader, prince, and moderator of the lights, it illuminates and fills all things with its light.

### SCHOLIUM:
<note>original: "SCHOLIVM." A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary written in the margin or as a supplement to a text.</note>

He who believes easily is easily deceived. Therefore, just as he did above, the author here warns again that his words should be weighed on the scale of right reason: and they should not be taken in a crude manner, according to how the naked letter sounds. And just as he does not handle the matters he proposes with a "light arm" <note>original: "levi brachio." A Latin idiom meaning to do something superficially or without effort.</note> (as they say), nor does he immediately insert into his book whatever comes into his mouth: but in their description and demonstration he employs the most subtle investigation and profound contemplation: so it also befits the reader to be diligent and painstaking in reading and meditating upon these same writings. For he who presumes anything in this work drowsily and without understanding is like a lame man who, with one leg broken or injured, rashly enters a running race. Concerning sincere investigation—by which he understands nothing other than right reason, which is true and consistent with the laws of Nature—this has been discussed above.

Next, he teaches that a species must be propagated through a species like itself. For he labors in vain who tries to gather grapes from thorns, as we said above <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 7:16.</note>. For from a human nothing is born but a human, nor from beasts except their own kind. For the order of propagating species, which God established at creation, remains inviolable. God, therefore, added to all things subject to this order His own blessing of growing and multiplying. However, every generation established outside of this order is undoubtedly subject to divine curse. We have a most clear example of this in mules, who, born from the mixture of horses and she-asses, or asses and mares, did not obtain a second seed for the multiplication and propagation of their species <note>The author is highlighting the sterility of hybrids as proof that "mixing kinds" is against natural law.</note>. Since such a confusion of species is not included under this divine order of creation, that power of growing and multiplying was rightly not bestowed upon them by divine blessing.

I speak here, however, of complete and perfect species—whether you wish to call them <term>Platonic Ideas</term> <note>The philosophical concept that every physical thing has a perfect, non-physical "form" or "idea" behind it.</note>, or certain and specific <term>ratios of seeds</term>, or special fiery sparks, or specific forms, or by many other names: all of which, spread throughout the entire world and distinguished from one another in a most beautiful order, God produced in creation through the single word **LET IT BE** <note>original: "FIAT." The Latin command used by God in Genesis to bring the world into existence.</note>. Against this sacred and undefiled order, however, the counterfeiters and false alchemists strike most forcefully; through a certain rash daring and a more-than-Babylonian confusion, they attempt the mixing of species with one another. For they join those things which God disjoin-

# CHAPTER IV.

He comes forth into the light without delay, and, increased by far greater strength, he distributes various gifts to his brothers. Mindful of the benefits by which he was helped in many ways by them, he seriously mandates, wills, desires, and commands that they be equally adorned with royal honors. When all these things were completed, the invisible was made visible, and the hidden was made manifest.

-> ## COMMENTARY <-
<note>original: "Scholium"</note>

Here the author faithfully desires his disciples to be forewarned, and he repeats this twice as an absolutely necessary and most momentous admonition: he wishes that nothing else be sought than the principle of Nature, from which man is generated. For the same principle which is the cause of procreating a human being also promotes the generation of the Stone <note>The "Philosophers' Stone," the goal of the alchemical work</note>. This principle is Nature, which the Philosophers everywhere urge their disciples to investigate and to know rightly. For the knowledge of Nature is so necessary that without it, any craftsman loses his "oil and labor," as the saying goes <note>original: "oleum & operam perdat"; a Latin idiom meaning to waste one's time and effort</note>. For Nature alone rejoices in nature: and nature overcomes and surpasses nature: and nature contains nature: and yet they are not diverse natures, nor many; but one only. Of this nature, the Rosary <note>original: "Rosarius"; referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational 16th-century alchemical text</note> speaks in these words: *O blessed Nature, and blessed is your operation, by which you make the perfect from the imperfect through true putrefaction <note>The alchemical stage of "Nigredo" or blackness, where the substance must "die" to be reborn</note> which is black and dark. Afterward, you make new and diverse things germinate, and with your greenness you make various colors appear.*

# 764
# ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICAL STONE

Many indeed recognize Nature, but they are ignorant of its power; if they truly knew it, they would certainly not hold it in such contempt. Our Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, known for walking about while lecturing.</note> seem to themselves to know this best of all, and when asked what Nature is, they recite Aristotle’s definition quite promptly and from memory, even without a book: **Nature is the principle of motion and rest** <note>original: "Natura est principium motus & quietis"</note>. But if you were to ask whether Nature exists through itself from eternity, or whether it proceeded from some prior principle—good God!—you would see how much drowsiness they show in responding, and how much fear and inconsistency. For whichever way they turn, they find no way or opportunity at all to escape. If they were to say that nothing existed before Nature itself, they would be marked with the greatest brand of impiety.

For, conquered by their own conscience, they know the matter is otherwise. But if they were to confess that God is the author of Nature, as he is of all other things, the entire building of their philosophy would suddenly collapse. For upon this foundation of Nature and the eternity of the world, that structure was built, which, if destroyed, must cause everything to fall at once.

For if Nature is from eternity, and is the principle of motion and rest, it will differ in no way from **GOD** himself. For God alone is from eternity, and the principle of all things. But so that they might cast a shroud over this tumor <note>A metaphor for covering up a glaring flaw in their logic; "struma" refers to a swelling or scrofulous tumor.</note> with their worldly foolishness (I meant to say wisdom), they have devised this distinction: bringing forward a twofold consideration of "principle," they assert that one belongs to *creation* and the other to *generation*. Thus, against all rational sense and Theological truth, they wrongly establish double principles of things, not without the stain of impiety. For never, even with the most subtle and sharpest moments of reasoning, will they be able to demonstrate any difference between these principles. Whether one looks at the origin of both, or the nature, or the essence, or every other individual property, they do not differ by even a hair's breadth. For the same Word that was the principle of creation was also the principle of generation. For from the one God proceeded both the word **Increase and multiply** <note>original: "Crescite & multiplicamini"; from Genesis 1:28</note>, which is the true principle of generation, as well as the word **Let there be** <note>original: "Fiat"; from the creation account in Genesis</note>, which is the principle of creation.

I greatly marvel at your imprudence, or rather your extreme madness, O Academics <note>Refers to university scholars or followers of the Academy.</note>, that while you are otherwise conspicuous for your erudition and knowledge of letters, and hold the keys to the Philosophical kingdom, you do not finally recognize this childish error of yours. By subscribing to the truth, you might come out from this laby-

## SCHOLIUM.
->Commentary<-

There are two "stones": the white and the citrine (or red). This latter one he calls "the clusters," which he commands to be extracted from the red node—that is, from the **Sulfur of Nature** <term>Sulfur of Nature: In alchemy, this is the active, internal heat or "soul" of matter that drives its transformation.</term>. But a little later he says that if it should become citrine, you need not worry, even if you do not extract further from the red. The reason is that both the white and the red are born from one and the same root, according to those well-known Philosophical axioms: *What whitens me, that same thing reddens me; and what kills me, that same thing gives me life; He who dies with me, rises with me.*

Therefore, all those are seen to err who say they possess the knowledge of the physical tincture <note>The "tincture" is the liquid form of the Philosopher's Stone, capable of "dyeing" or transforming metals.</note> or the Philosophical Stone up to the stage of whiteness <note>original: "albedo"</note>, but claim they are ignorant of the way to progress further to the redness <note>original: "rubedo"</note>. Believe me, if they had once known the right way of arriving at the whiteness, they would not speak so foolishly <note>original: "ἀσόφως" (asophos) - unwisely or without skill.</note> and ineptly. 

For if a peasant said he knew the way of producing grapes on the vines while they were still immature and white, but was ignorant of how red ones come about, would he not expose himself to be laughed at and hissed at by everyone? For the same vine, through the same external heat of the Sun and the kind mercy of the air and the weather, produces grapes both in the beginning and in the end—that is, both in the time of immaturity and maturity. Others again say that they have the best knowledge of the preparation of the white tincture (which they call the **body**) and the red (which they name the **soul**), but that the way of joining them is hidden from them: where...

### COMMENTARY
->Scholium<-

By the "body of the copper," by the "fleeing," and by "cambar" which is destroyed, nothing else is understood than **volatile Mercury**, which must be "fixed" (made stable) in the fire by means of **fixed and incombustible sulfur**. This is done so that it may rest in the fire, even if the fire is most vehement and of the "fourth degree"—that is, a melting or "reverberating" fire <note>A furnace designed to reflect or "reverberate" heat onto the material.</note>. Yet, it should feel no destruction or detriment from the fire at all, but rather remain constant and fixed within it. Since, however, there is nothing in the world that is not subject to corruption—except for the heavens or all the celestial bodies—the Philosopher leads his Mercury to such a state of perfection that it corresponds to the perfection of the celestial bodies, or, as Aristotle says, to the **element of the stars**. From this, it can easily be gathered that the nature of this fixed and incorruptible Mercury is entirely celestial and astral. If, indeed, anyone desires to search deeply into the cause of such great perfection within the celestial bodies themselves, he will find it without great labor through the technique of the mentioned **Philosophical Mercury**, by which that supreme and perfect constancy in fire is won for it. For just as the fire separates all impure and different elements in the Mercury, and finally turns it into a nature so fixed and permanent that it yields to no more fire, but rather rejoices freely in it: so too, by the same fire at the beginning of the world, the corruptible elements were separated from...

### CHAPTER IV.

...incorruptible things. But the corruptible things, like thick and heavy dregs sinking downward, have formed the triple globe of the elements: the earthy, the watery, and the airy. The incorruptible things produced an equal number in the heavens, so that all celestial bodies are either earthy, watery, or airy. But just as those lower elementary things are thick, foul, and impure, so on the contrary, these celestial things are separated from all thickness and foulness; they are pure, translucent, bright, and perfect. Fire, however, occupying its place in the midst of these six globes, partakes partly with the celestial and partly with the elementary. If you ask, therefore, why the lower elementary bodies are not also perfected by the same fire, since they are joined to it with no less proximity than the celestial bodies themselves? The answer is: this cause depends entirely on the power and action of fire, which by its nature always acts upward and never downward. Hence it happens that nothing enters heaven unless it has first been purified by fire; and thus in heaven all things remain pure and perfect through this same fire.

<margin>~</margin> For if fire acted with as much force on these lower things as on the higher ones, all impurity and imperfection would immediately be removed from the lower things, and they would become entirely like the celestial ones. But **GOD** has reserved this great and universal separation for Himself alone until the final day of judgment. In the meantime, however, He has also bestowed upon His faithful and elect members in Christ certain specific <term>masteries of fire</term> <note>original: "magisteria" - refers to specialized alchemical processes or the "master-works" used to transform matter.</note>, through which they separate the impurity of these lower bodies and perfect them to such a degree that they attain the same nature and perfection as the celestial bodies. From this we understand that it was rightly declared by Paracelsus: the entire secret of transmutation consists in fire. Therefore, in this art of fire, or <term>pyrotechny</term> <note>original: "protechnia," likely a variant of "pyrotechnia," the art of using fire for chemical transformation.</note>, unless one has been properly trained, he will hardly ever achieve anything worthy of mention or praise in Chemistry.

# 768

->**ON THE SECRET OF THE PHYSICIAN’S STONE**<-

As the Wise Man <note>original: *Sapiens*, referring to Solomon</note> testifies in Ecclesiastes 2: **And all things are subject to vanity**, that is, every body of the metals—with the sole exception of gold, or the Sun—is still imperfect and full of impurity, so that they remain liable to corruption. Therefore, so that all corruption may be removed from them, they must be reduced into the fixed and perennial nature of gold. This is achieved through gold alone, and not through any corruptible or foreign thing, as the erroneous alchemists are accustomed to do in their applications. These men, through things that are imperfect and still subject to vanity—namely, their gradual waters, cements, layerings <term>stratificationibus: the process of layering materials in a crucible for heating</term>, whitenings, reddenings, and similar follies—wish to draw forth perfect bodies. But it is vain to seek a perfect thing among the imperfect, or the living among the half-dead. For just as man is twofold, the old and the new, so also the bodies of metals must be considered in two ways: some are old, while others are new. The old are corporeal and dead; the new are spiritual and living. Those which are dead, buried in the tomb of impurities, must be raised by the power of the living. For Christ our Savior, who according to the testimony of Paul <note>Galatians 3:13</note> was made **a curse** for us by **GOD**, raised His own body from the tomb, not by the power of the old Adamic man, but of the new man, who was **GOD** and man in one person.

Therefore, those curious "little women" <note>original: *mulierculae*, a dismissive term likely used here to describe superficial or uninitiated practitioners</note> fatigue themselves in vain with anxious cares, who come to the tomb very early on the first day of the week, after the Sun has already risen, in order to anoint Jesus. For Christ had already been anointed with another far more excellent Ointment—namely the Holy Spirit—invisibly by the Father from eternity, and again visibly at his baptism. By the force of this anointing, as if by His own power, He was able to raise Himself and all the dead with Him, and to preserve them from all corruption of eternal death. Thus, He had no need of such ointments prepared from corruptible things like the spices of myrrh and aloe. Furthermore, the concern of those same women—though undertaken out of pious zeal—regarding the rolling away of the stone from the mouth of the tomb was superfluous. For this stone is nothing other than the heart of man, hardened like a stone by the weight of sins. Therefore, so that this stony mass of sins may be taken away from our hearts, and the charming, mild softness of the new man may be brought in, it is necessary that an angel from heaven—that is, the spirit of regeneration—descend into our hearts and roll away the Adamic stone of sins from the tombs of our hearts. Then Christ will rise in us, and by Him as the sole victor, we shall overcome the world with its dead and fleeting lusts, and in the kingdom of His celestial and unfading glory,

# CHAPTER IV.

...we shall live and triumph with him forever. In exactly the same way, the regeneration of metals must also be understood; it does not happen through corruptible tinctures <note>original: *tincturas*; in alchemy, a substance capable of changing the color and quality of a metal</note>, but through those that are fixed and perennial. Nor does it occur through foreign or alien substances, but through the inherent virtue <note>original: *virtutem*; meaning the internal power or essence</note> of those very same metals—not of the dead and imperfect ones, but of the spiritual and perfect ones. For from spiritual things alone is the true **Oil of the Philosophers** produced, for the anointing and tinting of the imperfect bodies of metals into perfect ones. This is no different than how Christ himself is the true oil of salvation and of the recovery of life. ## ON THE SECRET OF THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE

...[Morie]nus <note>likely Morienus, a legendary figure in alchemy often cited as an authority</note> says with these words: Our Art begins with Mercury, and ends with that same Mercury. For the nature of Mercury is marvelous, inasmuch as:

->*To him it is given to transform himself into various forms.*<-

And he is like a second Proteus <note>A sea god in Greek mythology known for his ability to change shape at will; here, he represents the volatile and transformative nature of Mercury</note>, who, crawling upon the earth, suddenly assumes the form of a serpent; soon, immersed in the waters, he represents a fish; but soon, like a bird, feathered and winged, he flies through the highest orb of the air. And yet, in the meantime, there are not many Mercuries, but only one and the same Mercury always and everywhere. For having first arisen from that golden and simple unity—which the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe</note> named Apollo <note>original: *Apollinem*; here symbolizing the Sun or the Monad/Unity</note>—he utterly turns away from every multitude of things. For this reason, he either remains entirely in the fire, or he flies away from it entirely. 

It will therefore be necessary that whatever matter our Mercury must be composed of, it must above all else strip off "multitude" and collect itself back into the first number of unity. Since this unity is the beginning and the end of all things, it also contains all things within itself. Let the craftsman stick close to this unique Mercury, and with it undertake whatever labors are necessary in this work. For it is fit and suitable for all things: for putrefying, distilling, coagulating, mortifying <note>the "killing" or chemical breakdown of a substance</note>, reviving, sublimating, and tinting <note>original: *tingendū* (tingendum); the final stage of alchemical transformation</note>. Without this, the Sophists <note>Deceptive or false alchemists who work with "sophisticated" or impure materials</note> labor in vain in all their operations. For they do not see this simple Mercury of unity; instead, being blind, they are occupied with the unhappy number of the "dyad" or duality <note>original: *diadis sive dualitatis*; the number two, representing division, conflict, and the separation from the divine source</note>, which is said to be the author of strife and confusion.

Furthermore, just as all who wish to be partakers of eternal salvation in the life to come must withdraw their minds from various and diverse worldly cares, and rather—along with Mary, the sister of Lazarus—sit continually at the feet of our only Savior and Lord Jesus Christ (choosing the "better part," unlike her sister Martha, to whom the Lord said, "Martha, Martha, you are anxious about many things"), they seek from Him with constant sighs and prayers that "living water," which becomes in them a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. 

In the same way, the true Philosophers seek nothing except this unique and true Mercury of unity. Once recognized, it becomes for them a living fountain, from which they draw that perennial Philosophical water to wash their bodies and cleanse them from all filth—so that in such a simple perfection of unity:

->they may remain pure and immaculate<-
->forever.<-

# CHAPTER FIVE.

## HERMES.

<margin>1. 2.</margin>
**M**y son, that which is born from the crow is the beginning of this art. Behold, by speaking in riddles <note>original: *circumscribendo*; literally "by drawing a circle around it," referring to the alchemical practice of using metaphors to hide secrets</note> I have obscured the matter for you, and deprived it of light; and
<margin>6.</margin>
this I have called "dissolved," that "joined," and this "nearest" the "farthest away."

## SCHOLIUM.
<note>A scholarly commentary or explanatory note added to a text to clarify a difficult passage.</note>

**W**e read in the first chapter of Genesis that in the beginning, when God created the heaven and the earth, the earth was void and empty, and that darkness was upon the face of the deep: and that God said, **Let there be Light**. From which it is to be gathered that darkness existed before light. Today, all generations of all things seem to emulate and sacredly observe the very same order that God held in creation. For nothing is generated, or brought forth into the light, which does not take its beginning from darkness, or from the "Night of Orpheus" <note>A reference to the ancient Greek Orphic creation myths where Night is the primordial source of all things</note>, that is, from invisible principles. And although according to the common opinion until now, those visible seeds have been held to be the true seeds or principles of things: yet they are not the true principles or seeds, but only certain rough drafts <term>rudimenta: the raw, introductory materials</term> and bodily dwellings for the true seeds. Although not even the spirit itself hiding within the bodily seeds can be called the "true seed" in its own right: because, held back by its body (which is dead), it conspires together in the economy of death <note>The natural cycle of decay and physical existence</note>, nor can it act or produce anything by itself without a third spiritual, living, and true seed, which is entirely invisible and free from every bond of the body. From this it becomes clear that the consideration of the seed is threefold: for the seed is either the body; or the mixed and bodily spirit; or the unmixed and incorporeal spirit. From this third unmixed, or incorporeal and invisible kind—as if from a crow hiding in the blackness and obscurity of the night—is taken the beginning of this art, which Hermes says is properly called the "seed." Moreover, there are especially three birds of this kind, of which Hermes and the rest of the Philosophers make mention here and there in their writings. They are called "Hermetic birds" after the name of Hermes; they fly at night without wings. The first is the crow, which from its blackness is called the beginning of the art; and it reflects the nature of the element of earth. For near the earth, in fields, meadows, lands, and low places, or upon trees...

In the preceding parts, the author has dealt for the most part with those things which concern theory: now, however, he passes to the practical work <term>opus practicum: the laboratory stage of alchemy</term>, and commands the matter, which he demonstrated above in various ways, to be roasted and cooked in that which proceeds from the belly of horses—that is, in horse manure <note>original: *fimo equino*; horse dung was used in alchemy as a source of gentle, steady heat for digestion, acting as a natural incubator</note>, or a similar heat, which clearly corresponds to the heat of a horse’s belly: and this for 7, 14, or 21 days. There is no doubt that this multiplication of the sevenfold number includes some hidden secret: but because that doubtful or elective particle "OR" is repeated so many times, I do not sufficiently see what is to be predicted from it regarding the certainty of the time. In the meantime, however, a little later the measure of time is revealed more manifest and clear: where the author says, that the "times of the earth are in the water," and it is done until you place the earth upon it. Which can be understood in this sense: the knowledge of the matter simultaneously embraces all things necessary for the work. If you know this, you will also be certain about the method of acting: so that the true matter and time are joined—

[conjun]ction <note>Continuing from the previous page: "know that the times of conjunction..."</note> are reciprocal and convertible with one another. For unless you have investigated the perfect and complete time of the conjunction, you cannot assert anything certain regarding the perfected matter; and conversely, you will hardly have knowledge of the perfected matter unless you know rightly how to join the whole with the whole. All these being ground into a very fine powder, let them be incorporated with the juice of plantain and the white of eggs to the proper consistency of a lute. If the orifice of the vessel is smeared with this lute and properly closed, no further evaporation of the spirits need be feared.

...it is burned into ashes. For these ashes are that Phoenix hidden by the Philosophers, which, worn out by old age, burns and consumes itself in fire; from its ashes rises a small worm, which in the course of time is reformed by itself into a bird. Thus the Phoenix, through the medium of **Pyrotechny** <term>Pyrotechnia: Literally "fire-art"; the alchemical practice of using controlled heat to transform matter</term>, exchanges its old age for youth and, as it were, becomes young again.

After a person’s death, a similar small worm remains, which is not corrupted along with the rest of the body’s substance, nor reduced to nothing: but it is reserved in the spiritual world of the dead until the general resurrection. At that time, all people, clothed in new and incorruptible bodies, shall grow young again. This, however, is that "worm of conscience"—whether good or evil—which does not die, of which we read in the Prophet <note>Referring to Isaiah 66:24, often cited in period texts to link physical decay with spiritual immortality</note>. No more certain argument from nature is given for establishing the resurrection of the dead than this very thing. If the dwellers of our world—whose whole heart clings only to the fleeting, vain, and corruptible treasures of the world—would examine this more deeply and diligently, they might perhaps take greater care to secure the eternal, stable, and forever-lasting goods than, alas, they usually do. 

But the author proceeds and calls these ashes "the brain," because of the most subtle spirit hidden within them. Just as the brain is the seat and home of the animal spirit—the purest and most subtle in the whole human body, or microcosm—so these ashes are also the dwelling place of the most noble and precious spirit of the entire greater world, or macrocosm. Therefore, with the sharpest vinegar or the "urine of boys"—that is, the **Metallic planets** <term>Planetarum metallicorum: Alchemical code for the seven metals associated with the planets (e.g., Lead/Saturn, Tin/Jupiter, etc.)</term>—these ashes are ground, that is, dissolved until they rot and the first color of the work appears, which is blackness. Concerning the three primary colors of the work, much has been said until now. But it must now be known that each of these appears twice in the Stone. For the Stone becomes black twice, white twice, and red twice. This, then, is one reason why the author repeats the "putrefaction" <note>original: *putrefactio*; the stage of the alchemical process where the matter decays and turns black</note> here, which he had also treated a little earlier. But he himself clearly declares the reason for this where he says:

> When reiterated, it dies again; that is, once it has been corrupted and rotted, it will rot a second time.

By "the brain," however, as I have said, is understood the spirit or the most subtle mineral substance to be dissolved in the "rooted vinegar" <note>original: *aceto radicato*; a potent alchemical solvent, likely a concentrated or distilled acid</note> of the Philosophers.

If the rectification or preparation of this rooted vinegar were known to students of Philosophy, no other solvent of the Philosophers would need to be investigated—neither any other metallic and mercurial water of life, nor any other water of the Stone—because this preparation of rooted vinegar contains all these things within itself.

### SCHOLIUM.
<note>original: "SCHOLIVM" — an explanatory commentary or note on a scholarly text.</note>

Whenever the Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists, the "Philosophers of Fire."</note> spoke of "spirits," or said that their Stone was fashioned by the work of spirits, many people interpreted the word "spirit" in a sinister way. They imagined for themselves some strange notion about conjuring up evil spirits or demons <note>original: "cacodæmoniis"</note> and summoning or calling them into the service of their work. But history bears witness all too well to the kind of end such people met—those who rashly abandoned this **natural magic**, the most noble and divine of all sciences, for that dark and diabolical necromancy. Indeed, there is no pious man who is not shaken with the greatest horror upon hearing of them.

From this, many are also found who, being ignorant of true magic or Philosophy, slander that great and distinguished Philosopher, Theophrastus Paracelsus. <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous physician and alchemist known for revolutonizing medicine.</note> Although he was most justly named "Theophrastus"—that is, "speaking from GOD" <note>original: "ex DEO"</note> and not from his own brain or a demon—they shamelessly lie, claiming he also used the works of demons, despite his great merit. He was a **Magus**, I admit—that is, a Philosopher. <term>Magus: Historically, this referred to a wise man or a student of nature’s hidden powers, not necessarily a "sorcerer" in the modern sense.</term> Therefore, he followed the "magical" way or method of speaking. Spurning the lifeless corpses of dead matter, he was concerned only with the investigation of natural spirits, as befits a true Magus.

Of these spirits, some are good and kind, being those which have been exalted by art and reduced into a "secret remedy" <note>original: "arcanum"</note>. Others, however, are wicked and malignant; their substance still flows with corporeal dregs and a malignant, poisonous quality. How differently these two are endowed with powers is made manifest in those who enjoy either good or poor health. Those who live in health owe this benefit and greatest gift to good spirits alone, as the true authors of health. This benefit is certainly not small, but is to be valued so highly that all other kinds of happiness easily yield to this one. Hence we rightly say in the French proverb: *Health surpasses everything* <note>original: "La sante surpasse tout"</note>; that is, nothing is more desirable or more excellent than good health. For men living in perpetual health in this worldly Paradise become, in this regard, like the angels in the heavenly Paradise, who alone [possess...]

...they live immune and secure from the contagion of diseases. On the contrary, however, those who are distressed by the frequent, or even continuous, tyranny of illnesses can attribute the cause of this to nothing except malignant spirits <note>In this context, the author refers to "spirits" as biological or environmental forces—what we might today call pathogens or toxins—rather than literal ghosts.</note>: by which they are so often afflicted with such great and intolerable tortures that a greater kind of punishment can scarcely be imagined. Thus, all who spend their lives in such misery and calamity experience a fate in this world almost similar to that of the damned and cursed **evil demons** <note>original: "cacodæmonibus"</note>. Truly, these spirits, both good and bad—that is, healthy and unhealthy—are found mixed in all natural bodies: but especially in our **Physical Chaos** <note>original: "chao nostro Physico" — the raw, unrefined prime matter used in the alchemical process</note>, from which we draw out our catholic <note>meaning "universal" or "all-encompassing"</note> or universal medicine.

Hence **Hermes** affirms that life and death are also brought about by these same spirits: specifically, death when the good spirits are taken away, and life when they are restored. In this, he seems to agree entirely with **Paracelsus** himself, so much so that anyone who does not notice it must be of a completely dull brain. Paracelsus speaks only of *natural* spirits, which they sometimes call "malignant" or "demonic" by way of a metaphor <note>original: "per similitudinem"</note>, because of such horrendous effects of diseases and symptoms. But those who falsely attach another meaning to Paracelsus either do not understand him or distort him out of singular malice. But let us return to the author’s text, in which it is clearly shown: the cause of life and death is to be sought in the spirits—namely, in natural spirits, which are divided into three kinds: **animal, vegetable, and mineral.** He who knows how to revive the mineral spirits as if they were dead, and to purify them through preparation so that they may exert their vigorous and animated powers upon the human body, has reached the greatest **arcanum** <note>a deep secret or mystery of nature</note>.

And this is what everyone seeks: if they should obtain it, being filled with the greatest joy, they will deservedly give infinite thanks to the most great and good GOD. For they will possess not only the highest medicine for the human body, but they will also be able to **fix** <note>to make a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</note> any perfect and impure bodies, and **tinge** <note>to transform or "color" the internal nature of a metal</note> them into the highest perfection of silver and gold.

## SCHOLIUM <note>A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary intended to clarify a difficult text.</note>.

The author indicates that the ancient Philosophers shadowed forth the knowledge of the art through figurative expressions and analogies. But because they are no longer among the living, the author has now demonstrated in their place the goal of the art, at which all wise men ought to aim; yet he has done so in such a way that none but the skilled—that is, the genuine and legitimate disciples of the art—shall taste the flavor of truth from it.

For he has hidden away the occult <note>In this context, "occult" simply means hidden or "secret," referring to the internal properties of matter.</note> matters, according to the saying: what you wish to remain hidden, tell to no one. He has completed the **separation of things**. He has joined diverse things together—that is, the higher and the lower—and he has made peace between the **death-dealing** and the **life-giving spirits**, so that now both conspire in a perpetual fellowship of harmony.

Therefore, those who are unable to grasp the secret of the art from what has been said thus far should incessantly petition the divine majesty with prayers, so that He might bestow upon them the spirit of understanding and truth.

->*The end of the fifth chapter.*<-

By that **fixed sulphur** <note>original: "sulphur fixum"; in alchemy, 'fixed' refers to a substance that is stable under heat and does not evaporate.</note>, which is so often mentioned among the philosophers, nothing else is understood than the true **balsam of Nature**, by which the dead bodies of metals, once anointed, are preserved from perpetual corruption. Therefore, from such things abounding in this balsam, our **universal medicine** <term>Universal Medicine<note>Also known as the Panacea or Elixir of Life, a substance believed to cure all diseases and indefinitely prolong life.</note></term> is to be drawn forth, so that it may be more effective for preserving human bodies in a state of health, and for driving away and radically extirpating diseases—whether they arise from a poor diet, hereditary propagation, or any other occasion.

Do not think, therefore, that such sulphur is to be found in nails, hair, verdigris, tragacanth, bones, and similar momentary and quickly perishing things: but these are only external names, which the author uses out of "philosophical liberty" <note>This refers to the practice of alchemists using 'Decknamen' or cover-names to hide their true ingredients from the uninitiated.</note> to hide the internal essence of things from the unworthy and the impious.

### HERMES.
<margin>3</margin>

<margin>S</margin>
*Furthermore, we must set forth the disposition of the ointment which contains tinctures, coagulates fleeting things, and adorns sulphurs; it is of a different form from all other ointments, for it is a hidden and buried ointment, of which no disposition is seen, and it dwells in its own body just as fire dwells in trees and stones; which we must extract with the most subtle art and ingenuity without burning.*
<margin>0</margin>

### EXPOSITION.

The author now explains the condition of the ointment, or the true philosophical sulphur, in more words: and first, he says that it contains **tinctures**. For the range of tinctures is vast. Whatever impresses a color or a property upon natural bodies by staining/dyeing it deserves the name of "tincture": thus, every medicine that preserves bodies in a good and natural constitution and removes diseases is rightly called a **tincture of health**; and conversely, things that destroy and bring sickness and corruption to bodies are called **tinctures of disease and death**. Therefore, as many things as are found in the world that cause health or disease, so many tinctures must be established: all of which, in general, this single ointment of the philosophers encompasses within itself. Furthermore, this same ointment has the power of **coagulating fleeting things** and **adorning sulphurs**—that is, of fixing volatile substances and illuminating what is dark.

Furthermore, such volatiles <note>original: *volatilia*; in alchemy, these are substances that easily vaporize or "fly away" when heated, usually representing "imperfect" metals like lead or tin.</note> are nothing other than all the lower and imperfect metals, which through this ointment are transmuted into the finest gold and silver. Finally, he says this hidden ointment lies concealed within bodies, not unlike how fire or natural heat—we are not speaking here of common fire, otherwise called "mechanical" fire, which burns and destroys all things—generates sap or "greenness" in trees during the springtime. As time progresses, it produces buds, leaves, and flowers, and finally completes the full ripening of fruits and seeds. Or, just as this same heat in the mountains and the innermost bowels of the earth (for the green line <note>The "green line" likely refers to the *anima mundi* or the vital path of nature that connects all things.</note> circles the universe) first mixes the simplest bodies of things or elements, and from there builds stones distinguished by various differences in their properties: so the **sulphur of nature**, or the true tinctures <term>Tinctures<note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a potent substance capable of infused its quality (like the color and purity of gold) into a base metal.</term></note> of the philosophers which it contains within itself, unfolds through the various revolutions of time. It brings the immature to perfection; it fixes the inconstant; it washes away the impure; and it ennobles the ignoble and the base. Because of such various and excellent gifts with which it is endowed, this sulphur is preferred far and wide above all others, so much so that it is not undeservedly called "divine" by the author. The **vessel** in this context is the matter itself, which contains the precious, celestial, and astral essence, impregnated with an abundance of vital spirits. These spirits, which like volatile Mercury have a fugitive nature, are extracted by an ingenious and wondrous art, and through sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify the "spirit" of the material.</note> are exalted more and more, and are finally fixed. But one must take precautions with the greatest industry lest an error be made in the degrees of fire. For too much heat will burn our matter—which, as we have said, is the vessel or dwelling-place of that celestial and astral essence—and thus, the prison being broken, the captive will fly away.

## COMMENTARY.

Here we treat the three parts of the stone. 1. The water. 2. The heaven, or "middle gold." 3. The gold, or terrestrial dross. Do not wonder, however, that gold here takes the place of dross, and is valued less than water and heaven. For the author speaks here not of common gold, but of **philosophical gold**, which contains <note>original: *continet*; the translator notes the catchword "tinet" at the bottom of the page.</note>...

### SCHOLIUM. <note>A scholium is a marginal note or explanatory commentary on a primary text.</note>

Within these three—that is, in a single subject composed of three parts, which is known in the chapters—lie hidden these three: smoke, blackness, and death. These are in fact only one thing: namely, the **dead head** <note>original: *caput mortuum*; the useless residue or "ash" remaining after distillation or sublimation.</note>. This is purified and brought back to life through dissolution alone. For unless the body is saved, no coagulation of the spirits occurs. Through the dissolution of the impure and smoky body, the purer and nobler spirits, like reinforcements <note>original: *succenturiati*; refers to soldiers kept in reserve to fill gaps in the line</note>, daily introduce new and more excellent strengths and properties. Once the blackness is removed, they bring forth the **white and red flowers of the philosophers** <note>These colors signify the "albedo" and "rubedo" stages—the final steps toward the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. But what "perfected philosophy" is has been explained at length in the previous sections. However, although Hermes here seems only to speak of the philosophy of transmutation <note>the alchemical change of base metals into gold</note>, elsewhere he explicitly confesses that all forms of wisdom are subject to his wisdom. Since Christ our Savior is the one and only true wisdom from eternity, I do not believe anyone can become a partaker of true wisdom unless they simultaneously possess the spirit of Christ. For through this spirit alone do we have free access to reach the hidden mysteries of both divine and natural things. For it is he who...

It is the [Spirit] who, as Paul testifies, searches all things, even the deep things of God <note>original: *scrutatur omnia, etiam profunda Dei*; a reference to 1 Corinthians 2:10</note>. For no one knows the things of God except the same Spirit of God whom we have received. By the power of this Spirit alone, we are made like Enoch and Elijah in this life. For just as these men, as scripture testifies, were taken up alive into heaven, so too are we—while still walking upon this earth—lifted up into heaven as living beings through the Spirit of Christ. 

Since "heaven" is understood to be nothing other than eternal life, and Christ himself is that very life (for speaking of himself, he said: *I am the way, the truth, and the life*), it necessarily follows that those who remain in Christ, and Christ in them, no longer dwell in the world, but in the heavens where Christ is. This means they are no longer earthly and worldly idolaters devoted to fleeting things, but are spiritual and immortal, clinging to Christ alone. 

Therefore, we should not wait for another Enoch or another Elijah to come into the world before the arrival of Christ. For just as the Antichrist does not dwell in only one individual, but reigns spread throughout the entire "Antichristian body" (which consists of many members), so too the spirit of Enoch and Elijah was not received by only one singular person. Rather, it is received by all true Christians and especially by pious philosophers. These, walking in the same spirit, hold an immortal and incorruptible treasure within their "vessels of clay" <note>original: *vasis suis fictilibus*; a reference to 2 Corinthians 4:7</note>—namely, Jesus Christ. 

From him, Elijah once received that same spirit, drinking from him as if from a spiritual rock; thus the spirit of Elijah was not belonging to someone else, but was the spirit of Christ himself. He alone is the true <term>Elijah the Artist</term> <note>original: *Elias artista*; a legendary figure in alchemy predicted by Paracelsus who would arrive to reveal the ultimate secrets of nature and transmute base metals into gold</note>, leading us into the truth of all arts. Indeed, he alone is the completed philosophy and the secret of all secrets.

# CHAPTER VII.
<meta>catchword: minimally</meta>

...[Philo]sophers preferred and magnified it, saying, *gold is held to reside in bodies just as the Sun in the stars is more splendid in its light: for by the will of God, every vegetable and every fruit of the earth is brought to perfection by it. Thus, gold contains and vivifies every body, for it is the ferment of the Elixir* <term>Elixir: originally "al-iksīr" in Arabic, referring to the "dry powder" or "stone" that acts as a ferment to transform metals</term>, *without which nothing is ever perfected.* <margin>9.</margin>

### SCHOLIUM <note>original: *SCHOLIVM*; a marginal commentary or explanatory note common in academic texts</note>.

The seven bodies are the seven metals: gold, silver, tin, bronze (or copper), iron, lead, and quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver," known today as mercury</note>. Among these, the most excellent is gold. For this reason, it is also called the "king" and "head" of the others by the author. But you err if you think this is said of "vulgar gold"—the kind used in the workshops of minters and goldsmiths. For our gold, *as the philosophers say*, is not the gold of the common people. Rather, it is "bronze" <note>original: *æs*; referring here to the "Philosophical Copper" or "Prima Materia"</note> or mineral electrum, whose composition encompasses all metals within itself. This is according to the saying: *All gold is bronze, but not all bronze is gold.* 

This bronze or gold is rightly compared to the Sun, who—*as Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the father of alchemy</note> *testifies*—governs the world after God and illuminates all worldly things, whether animate or inanimate. He is the governor of living things, the one who sustains and dispenses all vitality. Of him, Palingenius <note>Marcellus Palingenius Stellatus, a 16th-century poet known for his work *The Zodiac of Life*</note> sings:

> *O Sun, who changes the seasons,*
> *And with the seasons, whatever is generated in the world.*

This same generative and "seed-like" power, by whose force all things grow and multiply, is also present in the **greenness** <note>original: *viriditate*; alchemists believed this "greenness" was the physical sign of the life-force or "soul" within matter</note> of our bronze. Concerning this, the *Philosopher* says: *All that is perfect in bronze is that greenness alone which is within it; for that greenness alone is quickly turned into our truest gold through our mastery.* 

*O blessed greenness, which generates all things!* This is evident from the fact that no plant or fruit appears to bud unless the color green is present. From this, it is clearly gathered that this gold of the philosophers (or bronze) has properties and powers far different from the vulgar metal. For vulgar gold, *as Pico della Mirandola* <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who integrated Hermeticism and Kabbalah into Christian thought</note> *testifies*, flees from the fire when a small amount of powder is sprinkled upon it; it can be reduced to lime <note>original: *calcem*; a chemical powder resulting from heating a substance</note> and clear water; indeed, mercury destroys it completely. 

Thus, vulgar gold differs greatly from the true gold of the philosophers. Beyond the powers already mentioned, the true gold is also most perfect and incorruptible; it possesses the nature of an Elixir or a ferment. An Elixir is—*as the Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), an influential 16th-century alchemical text</note> *states*—a complete medicine, more purified and digested than gold or silver, because the Elixir itself has the power of converting all imperfect bodies into gold and silver, which they by themselves [cannot]...

# CHAPTER VII.

...leaven, says St. Paul, so that you may be a new batch <note>original: *nova conspersio*; see 1 Corinthians 5:7. Paul uses the metaphor of dough to describe the purity required of believers</note>. For the regeneration of the new man, a new leaven <note>original: *fermentum*; used here both for the sourdough-like starter in bread and the transformative agent in alchemy</note> is required, which is far more effective, purer, nobler, more heavenly, and more spiritual than that old one. Moreover, such a ferment of novelty, purity, sincerity, and truth is Christ himself, by whom in baptism through his death all true believers are leavened. Hence in Matthew 13, the kingdom of heaven is said to be like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened.

Therefore, as this new ferment is, so also must the dough leavened by it become. For unless the dough receives the same power and property as the leaven, it cannot be said to be truly and properly leavened. From this shines forth the evident distinction between true and false Christians. The true, by the power of the new leaven, work truth and life according to the new man; but the false work lies and death according to the old man. These latter works of darkness must be entirely avoided and fled by the regenerated man. For a little leaven <note>original: *Modicū fermentum*</note>—namely, of the old man—as Paul teaches in Galatians 5, corrupts the whole mass. Whoever, therefore, wishes to rightly leaven his mass, as much theologically as Chemically <note>original: *Chymicè*; in this era, "Chemistry" and "Alchemy" were the same discipline</note>: let him leave behind the old bodies of impurity and corruption, for he will never find anything stable or praiseworthy in them.

Moreover, fermentation is necessary in both sciences. For he who is ignorant of Christ in Theology will also be ignored by him. However, to know Christ in reality is to believe in his word and to keep his commandments. For in this way we will be one mass with him, and fermented by his own word into an essential and perpetual friendship with him. And now he will no longer call us servants, but friends. For you are my friends, he said to his disciples, if you do what I command you. In Chemistry also it becomes plain that fermentation is necessary from the fact that if you do not mix the leaven with the Elixir, the body will not be colored as it should be, because without the ferment neither the Sun nor the Moon <note>original: *Sol* and *Luna*; the alchemical code names for gold and silver</note> will go forth. For the ferment is the soul, which, by the mediation of water, grants life to the imperfect body—a life it did not have before—and brings it back into a better form.

### SCHOLIUM.

A great doubt seems to arise here regarding the ferment <note>original: *fermentum*; a substance added to a mixture to induce a transformation, similar to yeast in bread</note>, which we previously said was gold. Now, however, the author confirms that the ferment also whitens the preparation. But this is easily resolved by the philosopher <note>alchemical authors often referred to legendary predecessors simply as "the philosopher"</note>, who says: "it is not gold unless it was first silver." Likewise, "our gold" is the tincture, or the soul, or the kindling of the work, without which it is by no means completed. But when gold has been whitened—that is, the white body—it does not become silver unless it was first Mercury. Thus the Sun <note>original: *Sol*; the alchemical symbol for gold and the masculine principle</note> is imagined by philosophers to have three faces in the heavens: black, white, and red. So it is easily believed that this ferment not only whitens the preparation but also, as the author teaches a little later, protects the tincture from burning and fleeing <note>original: *combustione & fugâ*; referring to the risk of volatile substances evaporating or being destroyed by excessive heat</note>, and grants it "entry" <note>term: *ingressionem*; the ability of the alchemical medicine to penetrate and transform a base metal</note> during the projection <note>term: *projectione*; the final stage where the Stone is cast upon base metal to transmute it</note>. 

But because the ferment cannot enter a dead body except by the mediation of water—which creates the marriage and bond between the ferment and the white earth—the weight of each must be noted in every fermentation. If, therefore, you wish to ferment the "white foliated earth" <note>original: *terram foliatam*; a purified, flaky state of matter</note> into a white Elixir, so that it stands at the completion of the tincture over bodies diminished from perfection <note>referring to "imperfect" base metals like lead or tin</note>, then take three parts of the whitened or foliated earth of the "dead body," and two parts of the reserved "water of life" <note>original: *aquâ vitae*; here used as a technical term for a refined mercurial solvent</note>, and a half part of the ferment. Let the ferment be prepared so that it becomes a fixed and subtle white lime <note>term: *calx*; a fine powder produced by heating a substance until it is reduced to its essential, dry state</note>, if your intention proceeds toward the "white." If, however, it is toward the "red," then let it be a very yellow lime of gold, prepared, and there shall be no other ferment. 

Such is the excellence of fermentation that the author does not hesitate to call it the "key of the philosophers"—that is, the beginning and the end of the works, namely the white and the red. By its benefit, bodies are improved—that is, they are raised into a higher state of perfection—and thus at last the red and final work is perfected and led to its end by the inspiration of divine grace.

### CHAPTER VII.

<sig>D d d 2</sig>

...he considers that it is being corrupted rather than corrected and improved. The author proposes three examples, which he instructs should be observed in silence. For just as leaven <note>original: *fermentum*; a substance like yeast that causes dough to rise or change</note> does not ruin the mass of dough, nor rennet the milk, nor musk the spices, but rather they act so that bread is made from the mass, cheese from the milk, and the spices are preserved from corruption and decay by the pleasing scent of the musk; so also the ferment of the philosophers first corrupts our material, and converts it into blackness <note>term: *nigredo*; the first stage of the alchemical process, symbolizing death, putrefaction, and the stripping away of old forms</note>. However, this is not done so that the work, once reduced to that state, remains in the death of blackness, but rather that the entire mass of the composition may be fermented and colored through all the changes of colors. For heat acting on moisture first produces blackness; and heat in dryness causes whiteness <note>term: *albedo*; the second major stage, representing purification and the "washing" of the material</note>; and likewise in the white it causes yellowness and an exceeding redness <note>term: *rubedo*; the final stage of the work, representing the perfection and full power of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. This variety of colors is to be ascribed to the ferment alone; and thus the corruption of one thing is the generation of another. And the ferment is the "ferment of the ferment," as the philosopher says:

> He who has not tasted the savor of salts shall never arrive at the desired Ferment of ferment;

for it ferments the finished product through its excellence. Therefore, take for yourself the ferment, which is the soul before fermentation, so that it may be a powder calcined <note>term: *calcinatus*; reduced to a fine powder through high heat</note>, dissolved, and hardened; for if you do not prepare the ferment well, your mastery <note>original: *magisterium*; the "Great Work" or the technical skill required to produce the Stone</note> is worth nothing. And you should know that there is no ferment except the Sun and the Moon <note>original: *Sol & Luna*; the alchemical names for Gold and Silver</note>, which are assigned to these planets. For this reason—because just as the Sun and Moon dominate the other planets and convert them to their own nature—they are called "Ferment" by many. It is necessary, therefore, for the ferment to be introduced into the bodies, because it is their soul. And this soul brings life to dead and imperfect bodies, so that they may be quickened and perfected together with the living and perfect ones. For in this way the word of Christ is the true ferment, or the life-giving soul, in the dead Lazarus who had already been buried for four days and was stinking. For as soon as Christ says:

> **COME FORTH** <note>original: *EXI FORAS*</note> Lazarus:

behold, immediately the dead man rises and comes out of the tomb. For the word of Christ is so effective that whatever is pronounced through it is immediately brought into effect. This is proven throughout the sacred writings by almost infinite examples, performed both by Christ himself and by his disciples, and other holy men and prophets. And this is the complete and true word of God, proceeding from perfect and true faith. Therefore, all saints also essentially accomplish whatever they wish immediately through it. Indeed, many today boast in this word, but while they think they possess the complete and true version, they have achieved scarcely—if even scarcely—half of it. For from their effects or fruits, we clearly recognize that they possess nothing but the naked letter, and mor- <meta>catchword: mor- (likely *mortuam*, "dead")</meta>
