...your shadow of the word, and by no means the true word itself, which is essential and effective: so much so that they seem to be threshing mere empty husks, lacking any grain. For if they possessed the truth, they would demonstrate effects through it similar to the effects of the word brought forth by Christ himself, by the apostles, and by other holy men. For light that does not shine, nor illuminate the surrounding air, is not light, but only the empty and sterile name of light. However, light that brings both brightness and splendor to things truly deserves the essential name of light. For this reason, just as today there is an infinite number of those who use this empty and sterile word only to earn bread to feed their bodies—while there are very few, indeed scarcely one or two, who use this word effectively and essentially for the salvation of their own and others' souls—so also there is a huge multitude of deplorable alchemists who, in practicing the Chemical art, cling only to dead things or ferments <note>original: *fermentis*; agents of transformation</note> and certain specific deceptions. Truly, few are found who investigate and scrutinize the living and effective essence of Nature, and the universal medicine of all bodies, in the legitimate way.

### HERMES.

<margin>4.</margin> A certain golden color [tending] toward redness, <insert>5</insert> and its nature is not sweetness; therefore from it we have established the silk, which is *Ixfir* <note>term: *Ixfir*; a Latinized version of the Arabic *al-iksir* (Elixir), the substance used to "tinge" or transform base metals into gold</note>: and from it we have established the encaustic <note>term: *encaustum*; literally "burnt-in" paint or purple ink used by Roman emperors, here referring to the symbolic "coloring" of the work</note> which we have written: and with the seal of the king we stain the clay, and in it we have placed the color of heaven, which increases the sight of those who see it. <margin>1.</margin>

# CHAPTER VII.

<center>D d d 3</center>

...other things of this kind are smeared or stopped up; but there is a certain fixed arrangement of nature, by whose infallible law the things enclosed in the **philosophical vessel** <note>original: *vase philosophico*; the sealed container used for alchemical transformation</note> are marked with their own properties and colors, until the appearance of all of them has occurred. And finally, that most desired color, **Deep Blue** <note>original: *Cyaneus*; often associated with the "celestial" or "ethereal" stage of the process</note> or heavenly blue, comes forth. This color, by the healthy efficacy of its splendor, does not darken or dull the sight of the observer—as we see happen with the external splendor of the Sun—but rather sharpens and strengthens it. Nor does it kill a man with its gaze, like a **Basilisk** <note>a mythical serpent whose gaze was fatal; here used to contrast "dead" or toxic chemical light with the healing light of the Stone</note>; but rather, like the **Pelican**, it calls back those already near death by pouring out its own blood, restoring them to their former health. For the Pelican is said to strike its own breast with its beak bent in a circle, and by the blood flowing from there, to water its dead chicks and thus restore them to life. Hence **Chemists** <note>original: *Chymici*; practitioners of the chemical and alchemical arts</note> have a certain distilling instrument which reflects the shape of this Pelican's curve or circle.

But the true seekers of the art must be warned here regarding this **Pelican**: a great and difficult secret has been hidden in it by the philosophers. For just as the Pelican is a living bird, not a dead one, so also the philosophers require for their mastery bodies that are not dead, but living—that is, spiritual and endowed with the highest fertility of vital powers. Just as the blood flowing from the breast returns life to the dead chicks, so the **greenness** <note>original: *viriditas*; the animating "life-force" or potency</note> of our **Red Lion** <note>original: *Leonis rubei*; a powerful alchemical symbol, often representing the final fermented Stone or a potent mineral acid</note> resuscitates the life lying dormant in the dead and dark bodies of metals, restoring them to their former splendor and clarity.

And just as that blood is not drawn out unless a turn or circle is first made by the Pelican itself—for while it applies its beak to the breast, the whole neck and beak are bent into a circular form—so the craftsman will not be able to evoke the true and tinging blood of the Lion unless a **circulation of spirits** or a **circular distillation** occurs first. That is, the outer is driven in, and the inner is driven out; likewise, the lower is driven upward, and the upper is driven downward. In this way, the outer and inner, the lower and upper, meet together in one circle, so that you can no longer recognize what was outer or inner, lower or upper; instead, all things are one in a single circle or vessel. For this vessel is the true philosophical Pelican, and no other is to be sought in the whole world; without this, every **false alchemist** <note>original: *falsarius alchymista*; one who uses deceptive or purely material methods without philosophical understanding</note> labors in vain. But so that these things just said may be better understood, it has pleased us to include the following figure below.

Now the author openly confesses that the gold of the philosophers is the most precious stone, and he attributes many more gifts and duties to it than common gold possesses. And to say nothing of the rest, a clear distinction appears here between the gold of the philosophers and common gold: for common gold can by no right be called by the name of the "most precious stone," since, being adorned only with a simple perfection, it has not yet been freed from that bodily coagulation. And although it is pure, tempered, and safe and immune from the injuries of fire, air, water, or earth, it cannot, however, like a universal ferment, reduce all things to a tempered nature—as that yellow and true citron color can; that is, the star-like and heavenly **quintessence** <note>original: *essentia quinta*; the "fifth element," the purest and most potent extract of a substance</note> of gold, separated from its thick, impure, and earthly body:

### CHAPTER VII.

...not in body, but in spirit. For the spirit alone penetrates all things, however solid the bodies may be. Thus the <term>universality</term> <note>original: *Catholicismus*; the author uses this in the literal sense of the Greek *katholikos*, meaning "universal," to describe a spiritual unity rather than the Roman Catholic institution</note> of religion, or of the true Church, does not consist in a certain visible and corporeal assembly of men: but in the invisible and spiritual consensus and harmony of the pious and those who truly believe in the one Jesus Christ. For whoever—outside of this King of all kings, who is truly universal, in whom and through whom all things exist, and who alone is the one and only spiritual pastor, leader, and highest bishop of the true Church—subscribes to a particular specific Church, he is already a sectarian, a schismatic, and a heretic. *For the kingdom of God does not come with observation, but is within us*, says our Savior himself in Luke 17. Likewise, in the same place, he also exhorts his disciples to beware of the deceptions of such sectarians, where he says: *The days will come when you will desire to see one day of the Son of Man, and you will not see it: and they will say to you: "Look here! Look there!" Do not go, NOR FOLLOW THEM.*

From these words it is openly proven that one must not bind oneself to a specific external sect, as we see happening today; where many people, led astray by excessive simplicity, give their name to this or that sect, falsely persuading themselves that by being included among the number of certain sectarians—these or those—they can no longer err. They believe they will most certainly obtain the blessedness of the soul and eternal life from that association, since they wrongly believe that the Church, which each person thinks is alone the true one, cannot err. From this, so many dissensions and controversies in religion spring forth again, in which each party defends its own opinion tooth and nail <note>original: *mordicùs*; literally "with a bite," meaning to hold on tenaciously</note>. Most of them, however, seem to be more occupied with their own specific delusions regarding words and phrases than in seriously and piously examining the universal Holy Scripture and the word of God. For if they knew the power of this word, they would cease those infinite foolish, useless, and vain questions, which generate nothing but contentions and disputes; and they would avoid a heretical man after a first and second warning, knowing that such a person is subverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment. Titus 3.

But you will ask, where then are those true Christians who are free from all the contagion of the sectarians? To answer this question for you, I would have you know *that they are not to be sought on the mountain of Samaria, nor in Jerusalem, nor in Rome in Italy, nor in Geneva in France <note>original: *Gallia*; the author identifies the French-speaking city with the broader region</note>, nor in Leipzig in Germany, nor in Krakow in Poland, nor in Prague in Bohemia, nor in Olomouc in Moravia: but everywhere dispersed through the whole world, in Turkey, in Persia, Italy, France, Germany, Poland, Bohemia, Moravia, England, in America, and even to the furthest Indians.*

Gold and fiery water, however exquisitely they may be cooked and digested by art, are nevertheless found nowhere more perfect, better, or more excellent than in their own mines and roots, where they have not yet experienced any fire. This can be seen in gold just extracted from its earth, which still exists in a plainly raw state and has not yet been severed or separated from its superfluity. For this reason, such gold is more fit and suitable for the work of regeneration. Indeed, its spirits are still very free and are not held back by any strong coagulation of bodies.

Hence, they act more promptly and accelerate the preparation of the tincture <term>tincture</term> <note>in alchemy, a potent liquid or powder capable of transmuting metals or healing the body</note> more swiftly than if the body of gold, as it is commonly held, were taken. # CHAPTER VII.

...had extended their lives. For the bodies of men in those times were not yet so foully corrupted by that most hideous beast of lust—a corruption which has increased so gradually through the generations that in this, nearly the final age of the world, nothing appears healthy in its wake. This corruption was soon followed by the brevity of life. Whence it is now said:
->*In being born we die, and the end hangs from the beginning.*<-
<note>original: "Nascendo morimur pendetque ab origine finis." This is a famous line from the Roman poet Manilius, reflecting the idea that mortality begins at the moment of birth.</note>

The bodies of metals are also subject to this same yoke of calamity; as soon as they are torn from their mines, they are immediately shut up in the rigid, corporeal prison of death. From this, no liberation can be hoped for, unless that "golden key of life" were left to us, by which alone we may open all the closed gates in that prison of death, and lead the captive spirits out into the former theater of life. By this "key of life," however, I mean the vital roots of minerals; if the bodies are reduced back into these roots, they become fit for a new regeneration, so that you may then obtain the true tincture <note>a potent alchemical substance capable of transforming or "dyeing" base metals into gold</note> from them. Furthermore, there is the "fiery water," which is nothing other than the Philosophers’ Mercury <note>not common quicksilver, but a specialized substance believed to be the "living" spirit of metals</note> drawn from those same mineral roots. This water is the mother who dissolves the gold conceived in her womb, and during the process of digestion, provides it with the necessary nourishment until forty weeks have passed. Once the period of gestation for this Philosophical offspring is complete, the hour of birth finally arrives. Therefore, at the end of the digestion, when that hour of birth is imminent, the soul finally arises—but not before, nor any sooner. In this exact point, therefore, lies the whole danger. Once this point has passed, there is no longer any danger. Thus our "golden offspring" is brought forth into the light; and although it may seem inferior to "Aged Saturn" (or Lead) because of the weakness of its youth, it far surpasses him in weight, color, strength, constancy, and the other gifts of virtue. For Saturn <note>the planetary name for Lead</note>, too corrupted by cold qualities because of his lack of balance, can resist neither fire, nor air, nor the injuries of the other elements. But our "infant" is of the strongest and most temperate composition; it not only repels all external force from itself, but because of the fertile abundance of virtues in which it excels, it heals the infirmities of its own parents and tints any Mercury of the bodies into the highest perfection of gold.

### SCHOLIUM.
<note>original: "Scholivm" — a marginal note or explanatory commentary.</note>

Here the author distinguishes the **Great Work** <note>the *Opus Magnum*, the process of creating the Philosophers' Stone</note>, whether general or universal, into two specific types: namely, into the **vegetable** and into the **animal**, the latter of which he says is perfected in a **hen's egg** <note>a common alchemical metaphor for the vessel or the balanced proportions of the elements</note>. But although many and infinite works of this kind are imagined by the Philosophers, there is nevertheless only one true work. This work is firm and fixed, consisting solely of the equal and tempered mixture of the elements; for this reason, it is the greatest aid for health, and no less for the relief of poverty.

It is founded, moreover, in the **earth of gold**, which is deservedly called *Isir* <note>original: "Iſir" — likely a variant of *Elixir* or a reference to the Egyptian goddess Isis, used here to mean the essential transformed matter</note>, or the **Elixir**, or the **Leaven of the Philosophers**. We have already mentioned a little above that this leaven is twofold: namely, that of the **Sun** and that of the **Moon**. By the **leaven of the Sun** is understood the "seed of the male," and by the **leaven of the Moon**, the "seed of the female." From these, first comes the conjunction, and afterward a true and chaste generation.

The leaven of gold is gold, just as the leaven for bread is bread. And just as in the making of bread a small amount of leaven raises and ferments a great quantity of dough, so also that small amount of "earth" contained in this stone is sufficient for the nourishment of the whole stone. Whence **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational to later European alchemy</note> says: 
*Leaven reduces that which is added to it into its own nature, color, and flavor in every way—that is, from potentiality into actuality.* 
For it whitens the composition (or multiplies it), strengthens its spiritual nature, annihilates "combustion" <note>impurities that would normally burn away or "rust"</note>, and contains the **tincture** <note>the transforming essence</note> so that it does not flee. It lightens bodies and makes them enter and join one another, which is the end of the work—without which the Elixir is not completed, just as dough without leaven does not ferment. It is called the "leaven of leaven" and the "coagulum of coagulum" <note>the "rennet of rennet," or the ultimate thickening agent</note. 

For it does not only ferment lower and imperfect bodies <note>base metals like lead or tin</note>, but it also renders gold itself "more than perfect" from a "perfect body." It is the most fertile mother, who, the more often she is impregnated, the more often she conceives and gives birth; and she propagates offspring of her own species unto infinity. She alone is the **little key** <term>clavicula: literally "little key," a term used for secret manuals believed to unlock the mysteries of the universe</term>, which shuts and opens, and shuts again, and no one opens. Without this little key, no one in this age 

->can arrive at the perfection of this<-
->science.<-

## CONCLUSION OF THE ENTIRE TREATISE.

These are the things, most Noble and magnificent man, revered supporter and **Patron** <note>original: "Meccenas" — a reference to Gaius Maecenas, the Roman patron of the arts; here used to address the author's own sponsor</note>, which I have seen fit to comment upon regarding the seven chapters of this treatise for your sake. Would that there were something in me by which I might offer even the smallest sign of a grateful soul toward you: you would certainly find me most ready for all things. For as often as I heard that you had arrived in **France** <note>original: "Galliam"</note>, I congratulated myself, flooded with the greatest joy and gladness. To say nothing now of your other merits, by which you have bound me to you in many ways: from your conversation alone and our daily dialogue—from which you did not push me away, though I was eager to learn, but rather invited me as a friend and asked most kindly besides—I have drawn such great benefit in my **Philosophical course** <note>referring to his studies in Natural Philosophy and Alchemy</note>, that I may now truly say with **Alexander the Great**: that I received the principle of living from my father, but the principle of living well from you. <note>Alexander the Great famously attributed his life to his father Philip, but his "good life" or education to his tutor Aristotle.</note> Thus, though I was indeed fathered by my parents, I now seem plainly reborn through you by some **Aelian** <note>original: "Eliano" — possibly a reference to a specific teacher, or a play on "Helios" (the Sun), suggesting a solar or spiritual enlightenment</note>, or rather a divine spirit.

However, although I attribute this praise to you first and foremost, I do not wish to deny that I have also been present for the conversations of many other most learned men, both in **France** and in **Germany**—which, in its abundance and fertility of the greatest and most excellent wits, leaves other regions far behind, appearing somewhat faint (not to say lazy or entirely sluggish) in the investigation of **abstruse arts** <note>such as alchemy, hermeticism, or the "hidden" secrets of nature</note> of this kind. It would certainly be desirable that others, moved by a certain honorable emulation, should imitate the industry and great skill of the Germans in this regard. For this would be not only for honor and praise, but also of the greatest benefit to our common homeland.

Since, therefore, as I have said, I acknowledge the entire fruit of my studies as coming primarily from you, I have deemed it fair to offer you the first-fruits of the same, consecrated and dedicated as a due expression of gratitude. Whatever this may finally be, I ask that you do not allow it to fall into the hands of others until you have properly examined it according to the sharpness of your mind and your solid experience in these matters, and until, with your most polished and exquisite **refinements** <note>original: "limis" — literally "files," a common metaphor for the labor of editing and polishing a text</note>, you have rendered it more splendid and adorned. But if it should happen to reach the hands of others, and some should think they are not entirely satisfied regarding certain **obscure or barbaric terms** <note>a reference to the specialized, often non-classical vocabulary used in alchemical texts</note>...

*As I was frequently reflecting and revolving more attentively in my mind and memory, most distinguished Sir, in what sense **Fernel** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), an influential French physician who attempted to bridge the gap between traditional medicine and the hidden "occult" forces of nature.</note> asserts in the second book of* On the Hidden Causes of Things, *chapter 18, that the **seed of gold** <note>original: "Auri semen." Therefore, with what diligence and persistence I could, I sought out and scraped together from every quarter as many as had written on this matter—both published works and manuscripts, even those still being eaten away by moths and bookworms—the ancient, I say, as well as the modern authors...*

# DEDICATORY EPISTLE.

having read through [these works] with nightly and daily hand for twenty-two years, I have turned them over, noted them, annotated them, transcribed my notes, and organized these transcriptions into an order observed by no one until now. I did this with the intention that this **Compendium** <note>A concise summary of a larger field of knowledge; the author’s attempt to condense the sprawling and often contradictory literature of alchemy into a single system.</note> might serve as a **North Star** <note>original: "Cynosura." The constellation containing the pole star, used by sailors for navigation in the "sea" of opinions.</note> for me in that vast sea of so many conflicting opinions, so that after enduring long and infinite labors, I might be able to reach the desired harbor of true **knowledge** <note>original: "scientia."</note> safely, swiftly, and pleasantly. 

Indeed, it was not my intention to publish this **Harmony** <note>original: "Harmonia." Here meaning a systematic reconciliation of different alchemical views.</note>—which I had adapted and prepared for myself and my **Muses** <note>A poetic way of referring to his private scholarly pursuits and inspirations.</note> alone—for the general public. Nevertheless, the frequent encouragements—or should I say the anxious demands—of my friends have won out and extorted it from me, even against my will. It would be dishonorable to fail those who encourage me, and impious not to comply with those who ask. 

What finally drove me, while I was still wavering and hesitant, was pity for those who, not knowing how to manage these studies nor having learned to investigate the true sense of the **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to the ancient and medieval masters of the "Great Work" (alchemy), such as Hermes Trismegistus or Geber.</note> properly and methodically, are driven about by various errors. # DEDICATORY EPISTLE.

First, because your house is not only the oracle of our entire city—where you send away those who are uncertain of their affairs made certain and masters of their own counsel—but it also truly stands as an **all-receiving inn of wisdom and a sanctuary of every virtue** <note>original: "πανδοχὴς σοφίας πανδοχεῖον, καὶ πάσης ἀρετῆς σεμνεῖον." Lagneus uses Greek here to elevate the praise of Héroard’s home as a center of intellectual and moral life.</note>. You alone have been deemed worthy to whose care, vigilance, industry, and singular integrity our **Achilles** <note>A reference to the young King Louis XIII, whom Héroard served as physician and tutor. Achilles was the greatest hero of the Trojan War.</note> has been committed and entrusted, as if to another **Chiron** <note>In Greek mythology, the wise centaur Chiron was the tutor of Achilles, teaching him medicine, music, and hunting.</note>.

Second, I wish to testify in this way to the everlasting memory of the infinite benefits you have bestowed upon me. Finally, I desire that I might remain **safe and sound** <note>original: "sartus tectusque." A Roman legal phrase literally meaning "patched and roofed," used to describe a building in good repair or a person who is well-protected.</note> under your wings, as if in a sanctuary, from those who would strive to gnaw at these works with the **tooth of Theon** <note>original: "dente Theonino." A classical idiom referring to Theon, a notoriously slanderous poet; it signifies spiteful or malicious criticism.</note>.

This is surely a small and slight gift; yet, if you consider the spirit of the giver and the subject itself, it is not altogether to be despised. **Cyrus**, that great King of the Persians, declared that he had never drunk anything sweeter than the muddy and turbid water offered to him by a common soldier. **Augustus** did not refuse the reeds offered to him by a countryman, and **Louis XI** accepted even a withered radish from a peasant, which he ordered to be wrapped in precious fine linen and preserved among his own things **as something precious** <note>original: "ὡς τίμιόν τι."</note>.

Therefore, please receive our **Harmony**, offered as a favorable omen for this new year, with a fair and grateful mind, and continue to look kindly upon me, your most devoted servant.

From our **study** <note>original: "musæo." Literally a temple of the Muses; used by scholars to refer to their private library or place of work.</note> in **Paris** <note>original: "Lutetiæ." Lutetia was the Roman name for Paris.</note>, on the Kalends [1st] of January, in the year of restored salvation 1611.

### TO THE CANDID READER, GREETINGS.

From the more hidden secrets of Nature and the inner sanctuaries of the philosophers, this **Harmony** steps forth into the light, kind Reader; both to draw out more clearly (as they imagine themselves to see) those who are in this art from the thick darkness of ignorance, and to protect from a stumbling fall those who are on rugged, or even on flat, ground. To the former, it supplies **Ariadne’s thread** <term>Ariadnes filum: a classical reference to the guide used by Theseus to navigate the Minotaur’s labyrinth; here, it refers to a guiding principle through the complexities of alchemy.</term>, and to the latter, it provides an old man’s staff.

In this way, you will preserve for yourselves what is truly yours; you will send back **cucurbits** <term>cucurbitas: gourd-shaped glass vessels used as the lower part of a still.</term>, **aludels** <term>aludelia: pear-shaped pots used as receivers in the process of sublimation.</term>, **matrasses** <term>matratia: long-necked glass flasks, also known as "bolt-heads."</term>, and other instruments of that kind to the glassmakers, and **furnaces** <term>furnellos: small ovens or heating apparatuses used by chemists and potters.</term> to the potters. This, I say, is the **Harmony** which will convict of ignorance all those who mutter that those ancient philosophers of the early age never held any consensus among themselves. This is the same **Harmony** which, after twenty-two years of continuous labor and diligent vigilance, finally emerges victorious, soon to show to your eyes and touch what you seek so anxiously and with such great difficulty.

Finally, this is the accord and consensus of all the philosophers—attempted by many, but perfected and completed by none. Because without any squandering of money, without instructions or formulas for common recipes, and with little labor and few expenses, it offers you freely what neither the immense riches of **Croesus** <note>The last king of Lydia, legendary for his vast wealth.</note>, nor all the common recipes of **mountebanks** <term>Agyrtarum: from the Greek 'agyrtēs,' referring to wandering quacks, jugglers, or street-performers who sold fraudulent medicines.</term>, nor labors more than **Herculean** could ever—or could scarcely ever—attain. Therein, difficulties are uncovered and marked, and the unknown is made known. Furthermore, the sincerity of my talent and the candor of my soul are offered to you freely and with a generous hand—that which [was gained] not without great labor, much...

->To the most Noble and Distinguished man, Lord Doctor<-

# JEAN HÉROARD, LORD OF
# VAULGRINEUSE, COUNCILOR TO THE KING, and most worthy Chief Physician.

->*JEAN HÉROARD.*<-
->ANAGRAMS.<-

Go, flourishing, you honor. <note>original: "Vade virens honoras"</note>
An age of enduring honor. <note>original: "Ævies honor durans"</note>
You are a lasting vein of honor. <note>original: "Vena es honoris dura"</note>
From a vein of honor, you endure. <note>original: "E vena honoris duras"</note>
Ah, by this gift, I give spring-like strength. <note>original: "Ah dono vires vernas"</note>
Honor flourishing toward the truth. <note>original: "Honos virens ad vera"</note>
You look upon strangers with honor. <note>original: "Advernas vis honore"</note>
Live, O hero, who adorns. <note>original: "Vive heros adornans"</note>
<column-break/>
Honor is a difficult thing; come! <note>original: "Ardua res honos, veni"</note>
Persuading true things for honor. <note>original: "Honori vera suadens"</note>
Enduring in honor from Jesus. <note>original: "A Iesu durans honore"</note>
Healthy in a hero, O lasting things. <note>original: "Sanus in heroë ô dura"</note>
Richly honoring the truth. <note>original: "Dives honorans vera"</note>
A path rushing toward honors. <note>original: "Via ruens ad honores"</note>
Helping heroes with nard. <note>original: "Heroës nardo juvans" — nard is a costly aromatic ointment used in ancient medicine.</note>
Renewing the stars, I am carried. <note>original: "Sidera novans vehor"</note>

->A divine woman preserving with honor.<- <note>original: "Diva servans honore"</note>

---

Surveying all the peaks of Apollo <note>original: "Phœbeïa culmina"</note> with your eyes,
*Surveying the choirs of Apollo with your mind and spirit:*
*I see that nothing is more sublime than you in the Machaonian art,* <term>Machaonian art: Medicine, named after Machaon, the son of Asclepius and legendary healer of the Greeks at Troy.</term>
*And that you preside over the Paeonian choirs.* <term>Paeonian: Derived from Paeon, the physician to the gods; a poetic reference to the community of physicians.</term>
*What wonder is it if the other mountains look up to your summits,*
*And if they bring to you what they hold dear?*
*If they surrender themselves and their possessions to you, they who believe*
*That they stand, remain healthy, and flourish by your protection?*
*Shall I be the last to run to you? The gods forbid! I shall fly,*
*And though I am the lowest of hills, I shall follow the mountains.*
*Behold, L’Agneau himself* <note>David L'Agneau, the author of this work.</note> *dedicates to you his Harmony,*
*Which has unlocked for many those things that were once closed.*
*Your names, with their letters transposed,*
*Add a spur to the runner and wings to the one who flies.*
*These divine oracles give to me, in words of truth,*
*What the Delphic temples and the Sibyl* <note>A prophetess of the ancient world.</note> *are to me.*
*They sing golden sayings: what the path to the summit of true honor is,*
*And from where a living honor is prepared.*

<meta>This page continues the celebratory dedication to Jean Héroard, the chief physician to King Louis XIII. 805.

How excellent you are, you who preserve the French stars,
And those whom God wills to be the gods of earth and heaven.
Not with so many roses does Hybla <note>A mountain in Sicily famous in antiquity for its honey and flowers.</note> glow, nor Enna <note>A city in Sicily associated with the blooming of flowers and the myth of Proserpina.</note> with so many blossoms,
Nor do so many bright stars shine in the clear sky:
As many as the ornaments of high praise that your names bring back;
I bring to you these few things from the countless ones, and I bring you yourself.
Go, flourishing, for rich in honor you honor others;
Endure a difficult thing; honor, I conquer difficult things; come!
An age of enduring honor, and one persuading true things for honor;
The spring-like honor of Persuasion, perpetually flourishing.
You are a friendly vein of honor, lasting through the golden ages,
Always enduring by the honor of your Jesus.
From a vein you endure—but one of honor—flourishing with perennial praise,
Which the palm of virtue gave to you.
Healthy in a hero, O enduring one, you who govern the French scepters,
Wish many ages to your King.
Ah, by this gift I give spring-like strength to you, richly honoring
True things, an honor flourishing toward the truth by the gift of the King.
Rushing toward wonderfully bright honors by the gift of the gods,
Along a direct and legitimate path.
You look upon excellence; you flourish on the path with the honor of flowers,
Helping heroes with a more noble nard <note>An expensive aromatic ointment used in ancient medicine; here, a metaphor for Héroard’s medical treatments.</note>.
Live, O renowned hero, constantly adorning the Muses;
Say, "I am carried eternally, renewing the stars through my art."
The stars which shine most brightly in our sky,
The stars which wear the crown of the Franks.
A divine woman <note>original: "Diva"; likely referring to Divine Providence or the Queen Mother, Marie de' Medici.</note> preserving for a long time those things through which we are preserved in honor,
By which no greater Paeon <note>original: "Pæon"; the physician of the Greek gods, used here to describe Héroard as the ultimate doctor.</note> flourishes in the world.

->To you, most ready for all things,<-
->URBAN.<-

806.

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND LEARNED MAN, MASTER LAGNEUS, on his Harmony <note>Referring to Lagneus's famous work, *Harmonia seu Consensus Philosophorum Chemicorum* (The Harmony or Consensus of the Chemical Philosophers).</note>.

## DAVID LAGNEUS.

### ANAGRAMS.

->Go, praise of a worthy man. Vessel worthy of praise.<-
->Hail, forever worthy. Power <note>The Latin word *vis* means both "power/force" and "you wish." The poet plays on this double meaning throughout the following verses.</note> worthy of praise.<-
->A power very worthy.<-

*You wish <note>original: "VIS"</note> to bring forth many things hidden in the night,*
*You wish to set forth openly the secrets of the world,*
*To reveal to very many people things closed off to most,*
*You wish for the marvelous wonders of the rich world,*
*And at the same time to prove the wonderful power*
*Of the highest Avenger <note>A reference to God as the ultimate judge and sustainer of natural law.</note>, who, as the supreme Creator,*
*Bestowed such great power upon the lowest created things,*
*That He might crush the arrogant madness of the little man,*
*Who denies that the Olympian King <note>A classical metaphor for God.</note> could*
*Have done whatever pleases His divine will.*
*You wish that in our world there may be a Golden Fleece <note>A mythological reference to the prize sought by Jason and the Argonauts, frequently used by alchemists to symbolize the Great Work or the Philosopher's Stone.</note>,*
*And that the glittering brightness of the golden apple may be present.*
*You, fierce one, wish to have chased the Griffins <note>In mythology, griffins were the guardians of gold mines; here, they represent the obstacles or "monsters" that prevent the uninitiated from reaching secret knowledge.</note> from the Celtic mountains,*
*Unfolding the "griffins" of enigmas,*
*And untying knots tighter than the Gordian <note>Refers to the Gordian Knot, an architectural or literal knot that was impossible to untie, symbolizing a complex problem solved by bold action.</note> ones.*
*You wish to show how great is the power of your genius,*
*And how much sharpness; you wish, with a sincere heart,*
*To be of benefit to all, and to harm no one.*

It is necessary to bring forward many arguments against strongly held opinions, if one wishes to lead the listener away from a prior view and convert them to have faith in one’s own words. Indeed, I would not have even produced these things for the confirmation of my discourse, had there not been so many men who were opposed to my opinion. Hippocrates, *On Diseases*, Book 4, Section 15 <note>The author uses this classical authority to justify why he provides so many citations: he is trying to overcome deep-seated skepticism about alchemy.</note>.

Every thing which is bought at a great price is a lie. Morienes in the *Consolation of the Dawn* <note>original: *Aurora Consurgens*; one of the most famous alchemical treatises, often attributed to Thomas Aquinas. The expenses of our Art do not exceed the price of two gold coins <note>original: "duorum aureorum"</note> in its first purchase. An anonymous author in Theobaldus <note>Likely referring to the collection of alchemical writings edited by Theobald de Hoghelande.</note>.

Hold this firmly: that for all the chapters of this most precious art, the price of the medicines themselves does not exceed the expense of fifty silver pieces <note>original: "quinquaginta argenteos"</note>, calculating from the first operation. Arnaldus [of Villanova], *The Rosary*, Book 2, Chapter 7 <note>Arnaldus of Villanova was a prominent 13th-century physician. This quote reinforces the alchemical claim that the "First Matter" is common and inexpensive, unlike the costly minerals used by fraudulent alchemists.</note>.

#### *On the names of the physical Matter.*

<margin>Isaac Holland.</margin>
The Sages have bestowed many names upon the Stone. After they had opened the matter of the Stone and made it spiritual, they said the matter was a "vile thing" <note>Alchemy often emphasizes that the "Prime Matter" is something cheap or ignored by common people, despite its hidden potential.</note>. And when they had sublimated it <note>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then becomes solid again, used here to represent purification.</note>, they called it a "serpent," and a "venomous beast." When they dissolved it, they called it "water," and said it could be found in all places. When they had brought the matter to the state of an oil, they called it a "viscous thing" and "sold everywhere." But when they had congealed it, they named it "earth," and said that both the poor and the rich possessed it. When they had brought forth its whiteness <note>original: "albedinem exuissent"; the stage of *albedo* or whitening in the alchemical process.</note>, they called it "virgin’s milk" and "a certain white thing." And when they had sublimated its redness upward, they called it "fire" and "a certain red thing." And in this way, just as the matter of the Stone was converted into a specific nature, they bestowed a name upon it until it was brought to its final completion. John Isaac Hollandus, *Book of Mineral Works* 1, chapter 126.

<margin>Greverus.</margin>
After the materials have been amalgamated, this amalgam—in order to hide it from the unworthy—is accustomed to be called by the Philosophers "our copper," "our gold," "Magnesia earth," or "the whole composite." Jodocus Greverius, page 21.

Know, my son, that our seed is the true Salamander, which is conceived in fire, nourished by fire, and also perfected by fire <note>The Salamander was a mythical creature believed to live in or endure fire; in alchemy, it represents a substance that remains stable and is purified by high heat.</note>. Same author, page 36.

<margin>Alanus.</margin>
That blackness <note>The *nigredo* stage, or the "black of blacks," representing the symbolic death and decomposition of the matter.</note> is assigned a thousand names; for it is called "fire," "soul," "cloud," and the "crow’s head" <note>original: *caput corvi*; a standard alchemical term for the black stage of the work.</note>: and this blackness joins the soul to the body. Alanus, page 56.

<margin>Pontanus.</margin>
The Stone of the Philosophers is one, but it is named in many ways. For it is watery, airy, fiery, earthy, phlegmatic, choleric, me—

That composition made of three is called the <term>Blessed Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapis benedictus"</note>, *mineral, animal, vegetable*, because it has no proper name. *Mineral*, because it is composed of minerals. *Vegetable*, because it lives and grows. *Animal*, because it has a soul, spirit, and body just like animals. Our Stone has almost infinite names; for it is named after every thing that is black. Since it is luminous, it then has names of joy, according to white things, and similarly red things; and yet in the end, it is one single thing. The same author, page 74.

...[gold], glue of gold, red sulfur, and orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>: but while it remains raw, it is called lead of copper, the rod of metal, and the plate. They call the coin "copper": but the philosophers have called the blackness "lead." The same, page 142.

<margin>Vogelius.</margin>
The Sun <note>The Sun is the standard alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> or gold is called "the metallic body" by way of a certain excellence: because all other metals have not yet attained that perfection, which they can nonetheless reach through nature. Ewaldus Vogelius, chapter 1, page 7.

Oil is nothing else than the sliminess of all metals floating upon the <term>menstruum</term> <note>original: "menstruum"; a solvent or liquid medium used to dissolve solids</note> through their dissolution; it gathers upon its own water, so that if you mix it with our water, it will float on top and congeal in the manner of a very thin skin of diverse colors. It is also called water or ferment. The same, pages 8, 9, 10, 11.

*Oil, tincture, gold, soul, the philosophers' ointment, by which the whole mastery is completed, sulfur, light, alum, gum, blood, ferment, our earth, washed air.* Tincture: because it colors and dyes the earth that has been cleansed and purified of all filth. *Oil*, because after the dyeing, it remains upon the body like oil upon cloth. *Soul*, because just as all animals and plants live, grow, are nourished, and multiply through the soul: so the <term>physical stone</term> <note>The "lapis physicus" or Philosopher's Stone</note>, when the soul is poured into it after its birth, is illuminated with a metallic brilliance, adorned, nourished, and grows. *Ferment*, because just as leaven converts the whole dough into its own nature: so this oil turns the whole stone into its own nature. *Gold*, not of the common kind: because clearly it is no longer a solid body as before, but has been made thinned and spiritual; this is also to be understood regarding silver. *Ointment*, because just as all fats and ointments soften and make slippery those things to which they are applied: similarly this oil softens the hard parts of the stone, smooths the rough ones, and makes it flow. *Sulfur*, because it acts upon the matter like sulfur by coagulating and fixing it. *Light*, with respect to the soul, which illuminates the dead body. *Alum*, by an analogy taken from dyers, who often add alum in the dyeing of their cloths. The same, in the same chapter, page 33.

Simple matter is a dissolved body, as distinguished from a solid and hard body. The elements of the Chemists are called "composite," because they do not seek simple things, from which no generation would occur, but composite elements, of which each individual one has the other three annexed and joined to it, though one predominates over the other three. Thus they call it "water" when the qualities of water—namely cold and moisture—prevail in the water. The same, chapter 2, page 71.

The philosophers call <term>foliated earth</term> <note>original: "terram foliatam"; the purified, white, or layered state of the alchemical matter</note> a sulfur that has been perfectly cleansed...

# DAVID LAGNEUS

...given and purified and whitened. The same, Vogelius <note>Ewald Vogel, a 16th-century alchemical author</note>, chapter 4, page 151. Also Manuscript page 80, 46.

<margin>Arnold</margin> Our water is called *water of life, serene water, perpetual water*, and many other names. It is called *water of life* <note>original: "aqua vitae"</note> because it gives life to dead bodies and illuminates filthy matter. It is called *perpetual water* because it preserves the bodies it touches and leads them to the perfection of the <term>Adrop</term> <note>original: "Adrop"; a term often used for the lead or raw "body" of the philosophers' stone</note>. Arnold of Villanova, in the *Mirror of Alchemy*, pages 11 and 27.

<margin>Desiderabile</margin> While the work is raw, our quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> is called *permanent water, lead, spittle of the Moon, and tin*. When it is cooked, it is called *silver, magnesia, white sulfur*. When it has become red, it is called *orpiment, coral, gold, ferment, the stone, the lucid water of celestial color*. It is found *everywhere* because it shares in all the elements; it is named by every possible name to hide its true nature. It is most vile through its putrefaction, yet most precious through its inherent power. Philosophers do not care for names; they only use names to lead the mind to the reality of the thing. *Desiderabile* <note>A specific alchemical treatise title</note>, page 22.

When the stone is absolutely whitened, it is called *non-burning sulfur*, from which silver is made. And because redness is hidden within the whiteness, cook the whiteness until the redness emerges. The same, pages 26, 40.

<margin>14</margin> Our stone is called "natural" because it is found in nature and possesses the four qualities of the elements. It is *cold and moist* because of the Moon and Mercury, and it is *hot and dry* because of the Sun. It is called "animal" because it is red like blood, not because it is actually made from blood. It is called "herbal" because it has a vital or multiplying soul, and it is also called the *red servant*. The same, page 36.

Mercury is called by different names according to its various degrees of preparation. For while it is cold and moist, it is called the *soul*; while it is dry, it is called the *spirit*; and when it is more fully cooked and fixed, it is called the *body*. It is fixed—and cannot be fixed except—through great <term>decoction</term> <note>A process of prolonged heating or boiling to concentrate or mature a substance</note>. Philosophers call the Sun the brother of Mercury, and the Moon its sister. The same, page 50.

"My mother," says the physical Stone, "is *quicksilver*." This is according to the saying: *The wind carried it in its belly* <note>A famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, referring to the "volatile" or airy nature of the starting material</note>; that is, the airy quicksilver, which is also called *strongest vinegar, aqua fortis, dyeing poison, virgin's milk, the fountain of life, and burning fire*. The same, page 66.

Quicksilver is called the *father in the generation of metals, the true vine, the Lion, the Phoenix, the Pelican, Tantalus, Daedalus, the serpent, the fountain, the well, the door, the quicksilver of the Philosophers, the curd, milk, ferment, the fugitive servant*, and many other names. The same, page 71.

The stone is called Saturn; because just as Saturn is the highest of the planets, so our stone is more precious and higher than other stones. The same <note>referring to Arnold of Villanova from the previous page</note>, page 89.

There are four principal colors in the water: black, like charcoal; *citrine* <note>a yellowish-green or lemon-gold color</note>, like the foot of the bird called the Merlin <note>original: "Emerillon"; a small species of falcon</note>; *red*, like a ruby; and *white*, like a lily flower. *Citrine* is called *water*, *blackness* is called *air*, *whiteness* is called *earth*, and *redness* is called *fire*. The same, page 100.

In the stone, *quicksilver* <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> is the matter, and *sulfur* is the form. The same, page 103.

The philosophers called the compound *white earth* when it is white, and *red earth* when it is red. The same, page 114.

<margin>Bernard to Thomas of Bologna</margin>
The philosophers called the "earth" the body and its bones, because it is the part that binds the compound together and prevents the fluid elements from their raw tendency to flow, possessing fire symbolically within its dryness. They called the "water" and "air" the *Spirit*, because these are the moistening elements that dissolve the earth. They called the "air" and "fire" the *Soul*, because these are the forces that ripen, digest, and perfect the entire compound. Note that whoever speaks of the "soul" does so only metaphorically; it is not a spirit in the sense of biological growth, nor a body as a physical shape, such as is found in humans and other sentient beings. Bernard of Trevisan to Thomas of Bologna <note>a famous 14th-century alchemical correspondence</note>, pages 166, 167.

<margin>From a Manuscript</margin>
Take shining copper <note>original: "aeris nitidi"; likely referring to the "brass of the philosophers" or the purified metallic base</note>, colored fire, and radiant water, and mix them. Our dung <note>a common term for the putrefying matter at the base of the vessel</note> is quicksilver. It is called this because its natural moisture, by reason of its "fattiness," is preserved longer during putrefaction by its own internal heat. But the Philosophers gave many names to the Matter because of the different degrees of its "cooking." For while Mercury is cold and moist, it is called *soul*; when its moisture is <term>consumed</term> <note>original: "consumpta"; evaporated or dried out</note> through cooking and the Mercury becomes dry, it is called *spirit*; and further, when it is fixed and made solid by greater boiling, it is called *body*. Thus one single thing is called by three different names. An old manuscript codex.

<margin>The Correction of Fools</margin>
The solution of bodies is twofold: into Mercury, by means of Mercury; and into mercurial water. The first is for "particulars" <note>transmutation of specific metals</note>; the second is for "universals" <note>the creation of the Great Elixir</note>. The first is nothing other than resolution <note>breaking down into parts</note>; the second occurs through the putrefaction of the body and spirit in moisture. Putrefaction, however, is the solution of all natures that were bound to one another, and their separation. *The Correction of Fools* <note>original: "Correctio fatuorum"; an influential alchemical treatise often attributed to Richardus Anglicus</note>, page 15.

<margin>The Clangor</margin>
*Laton* <note>original: "Laton"; usually an impure alloy of copper, representing the matter before it is whitened</note> is a body composed of the Sun <note>Gold</note> and Moon <note>Silver</note>, or copper with Mercury. *The Clangor of the Trumpet* <note>original: "Clangor"; referring to the "Clangor Buccinae," a 14th-century text</note>, page 47.

Sulfur is an imperfect body with which ferment is joined, so that it may generate something like itself and become the Elixir. Ferment is—

### THE FIFTY-FIRST BY DAVID LAGNEUS.

...is called the body. The same <note>Arnold of Villanova</note>, page 51.

Common mercury is called *spirit*; the mercury of the body is called *soul*. And the spirit is not joined to the body except by the mediation of the soul; and conversely, the soul is not joined to the body except by the mediation of the spirit. The same, page 52.

In the first stage of the process, when the Stone is black, it is called *earth* and *Saturn*, and by the names of all black and earthy bodies. Then, when it is whitened, it is called *living water*, and by the names of all waters and salts, alums, and things possessing whiteness. After it becomes yellow <term>incitrinatur: the stage of citrinitas, or yellowing</term>, and is refined and made subtle, it is then called *air*, *citrine oil*, and by the names of all things spiritual and volatile. Finally, when it turns red, it is called *heaven*, *red sulfur*, *gold*, *carbuncle* <note>a deep red gemstone</note>, and by the names of all red, precious, and beautiful things, whether in stones, animals, or plants. The same, page 108.

<margin>The Child's Play.</margin>
Magnesia is that entire mixture from which our moisture is extracted, which is called quicksilver <note>original: "arg. vivum" or argentum vivum</note>. *The Child's Play* <note>Latin: "Ludus Puerorum," an influential alchemical text</note>, pages 136–137.

<margin>Aquinas.</margin>
Do not care much for the words of modern and ancient philosophers speaking in this science; for the whole alchemical art has established its seat in the capacity of the intellect and in experimental demonstration. The philosophers, however, wishing to hide the truth of the science, spoke of almost everything figuratively. Thomas Aquinas to Brother Reginald, chapter 1.

<margin>Flamel.</margin>
The dragon is the sulfur that is extracted from the bodies by the mastery [of the work]. Nicolas Flamel in his *Annotations*, page 133.

Whitened Magnesia does not allow the bodies to be broken, nor the shadow of Venus <note>referring to the impurities of copper or base metals</note> to be introduced. What is Magnesia, if not the whole compound? The same, page 180.

The illuminated body—that is, the body deprived of its blackness—is called the soul. The same, page 189.

<margin>The Rosary.</margin>
However much its names are varied, it is nevertheless always one single thing, and derived from the same matter. For nothing is introduced into Nature that is not already in her by its own nature. Therefore, it is necessary that the active and the passive agents be one and the same thing in their genus; but in species, they are different and diverse, just as Mercury distinguishes the woman from the man. For although they agree in one genus, they yet have a distinct difference between them, just as matter and form differ. *The Rosary of the Philosophers* <note>Latin: "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical compendium</note>, page 170.

Juice of the Lunaria <note>the "moon-plant," a metaphorical botanical name for an alchemical substance</note>, water of life <note>original: "aqua vitae"</note>, quintessence, burning wine, *vegetable Mercury*—all these are the same. The juice of the Lunaria is made from our wine, which is known to few of our sons <note>the "Sons of Art," or initiated alchemists</note>, and with it our solution is made, and our drinkable gold <term>aurum potabile: gold rendered into a liquid medicinal form</term> is made by its mediation, and without it, it cannot be made at all. The same, page 173.

The primary matter of bodies is not *common mercury* <note>original: "Mercurius vulgi"</note>, but is an unctuous and moist vapor. For from the moist part the mineral stone is made, and from the unctuous part the metallic body is made. For it is necessary that bodies be converted into such an unctuous vapor: and in this conversion, the bodies are destroyed, and the grain of the body is cast down into death and is totally mortified. And this happens by means of our white and red water. And such a vapor is called the *Stone* in the known chapters of books, and the principle of the matter of our *operation*, and *unctuous sulfur*, from which in the completion the *quintessence* <note>the "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated form of a substance</note> is extracted—the Mercury that stains every body into Sun [Gold] or Moon [Silver], according to how the stone was finally prepared. The same <note>likely Arnold of Villanova</note>, page 180.

*Our Stone* is composed of *body, spirit, and soul*. For the *imperfect body* is called the *body, the ferment of the soul*, and water is called the *spirit*. The *imperfect body* by itself is a body that is heavy, weak, and dead. *Water* is the *spirit*, which is the agent that cleanses, refines, and whitens the body. *Ferment* is the soul which grants life to the imperfect body, which it did not have before, and leads it into a better form. *Body* is Venus and female; *Spirit* is Mercury and male; *Soul* is Sun and Moon. The same, page 187.

The *Dragon* <note>a common alchemical symbol for the volatile spirit or crude mercury</note> is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> extracted from bodies, having within itself body, soul, and spirit. Concerning this, the Philosopher says: *The Dragon does not die except with his brother and his sister, that is, the Sun and the Moon: that is, with the extracted sulfur having in itself the nature of moisture and coldness by reason of the Moon*. With those the Dragon dies: that is, the quicksilver extracted from those same bodies from the beginning, which is the permanent water of the philosophers, which is produced after putrefaction and after the separation of the elements. And that water is called by another name, *fetid water*. The same, page 188.

The *Sun* [Gold] is *animal* <note>attributed to the animal kingdom</note>, because it receives three things: constriction, whiteness, and redness, and it is called the *great animal*: and *sal ammoniac* <term>sal armoniacus: a volatile salt used in sublimation</term> is made from it. And the *Moon* [Silver] is called a *plant*, and *alkali salt* <term>sal alkali: a basic salt, often derived from plant ashes</term> is made from it. But *Mercury* is called the *mineral Stone*, and common salt is made from it. The matter of this art, when dissolved, is called *sal ammoniac*: when *putrefied*, it is called a *vile thing, found on dungheaps*: when *converted into water*, it is called *that which the poor and the rich possess*, and it is found in every place, at any time, and in every thing. When *whitened*, it is called *arsenic* <note>here meaning a white sulfur or spirit, not necessarily the modern element</note>, and by the name of every white thing, and *virgin's milk*. When *red*, it is called *sulfur, hyacinth, blood*, and by the name of every red thing. The same, pages 189, 194, 204.

*Permanent or perennial water, or burning wine* <note>original: "vinum ardens," often referring to distilled alcohol</note>, is called the *water of the body*: that is, when the body is reduced into Mercury. It is also called the *water of life* <term>aqua vitæ: a powerful solvent or distilled spirit</term>. The *water of the philosophers* is called the *vessel*...

Of Hermes: about which the philosophers have written thus: *In our water all modes are performed, namely sublimation, distillation, solution, calcination, and fixation: in the said water they are performed as if in an artificial vessel: which is the greatest secret.* The same <note>referring to Arnold of Villanova, cited on the previous page</note>, page 193.

Grind pebbles <note>original: "calculos"</note>, or a marine animal, or copper <note>original: "æs"</note>, or the brain with the sharpest vinegar or the urine of boys, until it becomes dark. The same, pages 195, 197, 200.

Blackness is the name given to the earth which is produced by a gentle cooking <note>original: "decoctione"</note>, repeated so many times until the blackness floats on top. The same, page 204.

The ash which comes from those three is called by the philosophers the "unclean body": because it must be cooked and calcined until it reaches whiteness. The same, page 204.

The philosophers have named the Stone by diverse names, so that it might be manifest to the Wise, and hidden from the foolish. But by whatever name it is called, it is always one and the same and from the same source. The same, page 256.

<margin>Dastin <note>John Dastin (c. 1293–1386), a famous English alchemist known for his correspondence with Pope John XXII.</note></margin>
Do not worry about the diversity of names, nor the diversity of procedures, because if we wish to make the Sun [Gold] <note>original: "Solem"</note>, we apply the Sun; if the Moon [Silver] <note>original: "Lunam"</note>, we apply the Moon for the ferment. *Fire is the black earth.* Dastin, page 30.

That which ascends to the top is called air and oil: that which is below, pure fire. Because our earth is called fire, and our water is called oil, because it is not consumed by the dryness of the fire. The same, page 31.

<margin>The Flower of Flowers <note>original: "Flos florum," a title of a popular alchemical treatise.</note></margin>
The Stone is called air which is mixed with its own earth. Our Stone is called a Salamander, because it is nourished by fire alone. *The Flower of Flowers*, pages 35, 37.

<margin>Book of Two Words</margin>
When our black matter is whitened, it is called *foliated earth, ash of ashes, ferment of ferment, and white sulfur enduring fire:* yet without ferment neither the Sun [Gold] nor the Moon [Silver] will emerge, but something else that is of no value. *Book of Two Words*, page 47.

The vinegar of the philosophers is our blackening, which is the wood of true dissolution. *Book of Three Words*, page 48.

As many as there are colors, so many are the names. The same, page 49.

<margin>The Lord be with you <note>original: "Dominus vobiscum," here the title of an alchemical work.</note></margin>
*Magnesia* <note>a term for the "crude" primary matter of the stone, not necessarily the modern element magnesium</note> is the general matter containing the four elements. *Cooked Mercury*, treated so that the fiery virtue is not separated from it, is a perfect body without any volatility: and by reason of different degrees, it is called Mercury by various names. For while it is cold and moist, it is called *soul*; while it is dry, *spirit*; while it is more cooked and fixed, *body*: and it is not fixed except through great cooking. And it is manifest that Mercury comes to perfection more quickly with the addition of bodies than by itself. And this the philosophers confirm by saying,

<margin>Calid <note>Khalid ibn Yazid (died c. 704), an Umayyad prince traditionally considered one of the earliest practitioners of Arabic alchemy.</note></margin>

Therefore they said that the female has wings, but the male does not. The Stone is *old* because of its whiteness, *young* because of its redness, *Egyptian* because of its humidity, *Persian* because of its dryness. Wherefore the Egyptians...

red, saffron-colored <note>original: "crocus"; often referring to Crocus Martis or iron oxide</note>, cinnabar, minium <note>red lead</note>, hematite, burned human blood, egg yolk, calcined alum, coral, etc.; to put it in a single word, it is called by the names of all things that exist in the world. <margin>Assembly of the Philosophers <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages.</note></margin>
*Corsusle* <note>A technical term in the *Turba* for the matter in a specific stage of preparation.</note> is the head of this work, not the beginning; but after the union <note>original: "complexum"</note> it is rightly called by this name. Therefore, *Corsusle* is the whole compound, which must be roasted seven times, and then it tints every body; it is called a *coin, the flower of brass or of gold, or the flower of iron, even lead, tin,* and a thousand other names. *Assembly of the Philosophers*, Discourse 33.

Rust <note>original: "Rubigo"</note> is a fictional name, not a true one. I tell you, however, that *rust* becomes the second work according to what is made from gold alone; and for this reason they have called it a leech, because it is hidden in sulfurous gold just as a leech is in water. Rust is therefore the "reddening" in the second work. For in the first work, to make rust is the work of whitening: in which the philosophers commanded that the flower of gold and gold be placed in equal parts. The same *Assembly*, Discourse 50.

*Cambar, ethel a, auripigmentum, Zendrio, Ebsemech, magnesia, Chuhul,* are names for quicksilver <note>Mercury</note> sublimated from *Cambar*. When it has been made white, it is called *Lead from Ebmich, Magnesia, Martech, and white brass.* Discourse 54.

Cook the brass until the blackness <note>the *nigredo* stage</note> goes out, which they call the *coin*; mix the things of our art well, and you will immediately find the blackness, which is the *Lead of the Wise*, concerning which the Wise have treated much in their books. Discourse 70.

<margin>Exercise on the Assembly <note>The *Exercitatio in Turbam*, a commentary on the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note></margin>
It is called *water* at the start of the work; then, when the blackness appears, *earth*; then, once sublimated <note>vaporized and resolidified</note>, *air*; then, when reddened (for the air must be cooked by itself until it grows red), it is called *fire*. Next, when sublimated with some "luminary body" <note>gold or silver</note>, it is called *leaven* <note>fermentum</note>; finally, when added alone to the whole and composed matter, it is called *spirit*. And so, earth with water, air, and fire, is the body; the leaven is the soul, the final watering; the spirit belongs to Mercury alone. *Exercise 9 on the Assembly*.

<margin>The Rising Dawn <note>The *Aurora Consurgens*, a famous 15th-century alchemical manuscript often attributed to Thomas Aquinas.</note></margin>
He who desires to know many names and the reasons for them, let him see and read the book titled *The Rising Dawn*.

<margin>Rosinus <note>Zosimos of Panopolis, an early Greco-Egyptian alchemist, often called "Rosinus" in Latin translations.</note></margin>
*Foliated earth* or *earth of leaves*, that is, of garments. For leaves are the covering of trees, and our water is the garment of the earth of our water. Rosinus, page 297.

Just as man is composed of four elements, so also is the Stone: and so it is "of man," and you are its mine—namely, through the operation; it is extracted from you—namely, through division; and it remains inseparably in you—namely, through wisdom. The same, page 312.

<margin>Tauladan <note>An alchemical authority, possibly a corruption of a name like Zadith ben Hamuel.</note></margin>
*Soul, leaven, and form*, which are the same thing, are made when the Sun <note>Gold</note> and Moon <note>Silver</note> are dissolved. And this solution is named just like the other metals.

Whether **Gold** and **silver** are merely metaphorical expressions of the philosophers, see the same author, page 301, where you will see they are by no means metaphorical <note>i.e., they refer to actual substances or specific states of matter.</note>.

<margin>George the Venetian <note>Francesco Giorgio (1460–1541), a Franciscan friar and author of *De Harmonia Mundi*.</note></margin>
Gold is called *Or* in Hebrew, which is to say, **Light**, and *Paz*; and by the Latins it is called *Obrizum*, meaning **strong and most pure**, because it is never consumed by fire, but is purified more and more. George the Venetian in *The Harmony of the World*, book 8, chapter 1, page 735.

<margin>Libavius <note>Andreas Libavius (1550–1616), a German physician and chemist known for writing the first systematic chemistry textbook.</note></margin>
<term>Mercury</term>, which Nature has generated of itself in the mine, is called **the ostrich’s belly buried in the earth**. From this, it is also contrasted with "coagulated Mercury," which is nothing other than gold. Libavius, page 56.

All metals, when they have been prepared by Art, are then called **Sol** <note>Sun/Gold</note>, **Luna** <note>Moon/Silver</note>, **Mercury**, etc. For before that, they were simply **Gold**, **silver**, and **quicksilver** <note>original: "hydrargyrus"</note>. The same author, page 57.

<margin>John of Rupescissa <note>A 14th-century Franciscan chemist known for his work on the "quintessence."</note></margin>
The matter of the stone is one and the same thing of low price, which is found everywhere; it is a viscous water which is called **Mercury**. And because they say that it is found in vile places, many ignorant men, who do not understand according to the intention of the philosophers, have sought this stone in dung. John of Rupescissa, chapter 2.

The philosophers named the stone by many names so that the science might be more obscure: for when our stone is placed in the physical vessel, the more its colors change, the more names they bestowed upon it. Our stone after putrefaction <note>the "black" stage of alchemy</note> is called <term>Magnesia</term> <note>a term for the "crude" matter of the stone</note>, and during the process of putrefaction it is called **Saturn**. *The Mirror of Arnald*, page 18.

<margin>Vogelius <note>Ewald Vogel, a 16th-century writer on alchemical transmutations.</note></margin>
*Usis ur* <note>An Arabic-derived term often used for mercury or cinnabar.</note> of the Arabs is the **cinnabar** of the philosophers. Vogelius, page 88.

The **incombustible grain** of metals is their "radical moisture," and as it were a certain seed of the Sun and Moon, which Nature has placed in them, so that when the opportunity is given they might be cooked into gold and silver by Nature over a long time, or by Art in a short time. The same author, page 22.

<margin>Greverius <note>Jodocus Greverus, a 16th-century priest and alchemist.</note></margin>
<term>Amalgam</term>, that is, **softening**: because the hard seed of gold or silver is softened in the earth. Greverius, page 20.

### *Whether there are multiple ways of making the Philosopher's Stone.*

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>The Lilly.</margin>
The whole mastery <term>magisterium</term> <note>the complete alchemical process</note> is completed by one way, one thing, one disposition, and one act. *The Lilly* <note>Lilium Intelligentiae, a medieval alchemical treatise</note>.

<margin>Alphidius.</margin>
You need nothing but one thing, namely *water*, one boiling <note>decoction</note>, namely to cook it: and there is only one vessel to make the white and the red <note>the two major stages of the Work: the Albedo and Rubedo</note> together. Alphidius.

One vessel for the white and the red, one fire, one time—it is finished in the white and the red. Mahomet <note>Referring to pseudo-Mahomet, a persona used in medieval alchemical literature</note>.

<margin>Morienus.</margin>
Although the Sages changed their names and sayings, they always wanted it understood as *one thing, one disposition, one way*. The Sages knew this thing and have often proven that this thing is one. Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note>.

Our Art is not perfected in a multiplicity of things. For there is *one Stone, one medicine*, in which the whole mastery consists: to which we add no foreign thing, nor do we take anything away, except that in the preparation we remove the superfluous. Same author.

<margin>Rhasis.</margin>
The white and the red likewise spring from one root, with nothing of another kind intervening. For it dissolves and joins itself, it turns white and adorns itself with redness, it makes itself yellow and black, it weds and conceives itself, until it hastens the end of the work. Rhasis <note>Al-Razi, the 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note>.

No one has more than one path in sulfur. David.

<margin>David. Haly.</margin>
Know, brother, that this task is one stone, upon which no *garip* <note>original Arabic term meaning "stranger" or "foreign thing"</note> enters—that is, anything else: and the Sages work with it, and from it comes what they seek: and nothing is mixed with it, neither in part nor in whole, and it is called the *origin of the world*, and it rises like germinating things. Haly <note>Often identified with Khalid ibn Yazid</note>.

<margin>Turba.</margin>
Know that if you take anything other than our copper <note>original: "aes"; likely referring to the primary alchemical substance rather than common metal</note>, and water...

## On the number of things composing the physical Stone.

<margin>Aquinas.</margin>
Mercury alone is that which perfects our work, and in it we find all things which we need, to which nothing foreign ought to be added. **The Sun and Moon** <note>Gold and Silver</note> are not foreign to it, since they are reduced at the beginning of the work into their first nature (that is, Mercury), from which they took their origin. *Pseudo-Aquinas*, chapter 3.

Certain people misunderstand the Philosophers because they believe they can perfect the work from Mercury alone without its sister or partner. But I tell you with certainty: add nothing foreign to the Mercury; and know that gold and silver are not foreign to Mercury; rather, they participate more closely in its nature than any other bodies. Therefore, reduce them into their first nature—they are called the sisters and partners of Mercury—and from their fixation and composition the **virgin's milk** <note>original: "lac virginis," a term for the white mercurial water or the purified stage of the matter</note> will emanate. <header>DAVID LAGNEUS</header>

Learn how to correct the imperfect by means of the perfect. The **Sun** <note>Gold</note> is the father of all metals, and the **Moon** <note>Silver</note> is the mother, even though the **Moon** receives its brightness from the **Sun**: upon these two the entire mastery <note>the *magisterium*, or the completion of the Great Work</note> depends. Therefore, let them be reduced into **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note> that is not of the common kind—that is, not volatile, but fixed. Common quicksilver is indeed volatile and full of phlegmatic coldness; for that reason, it needs to be reduced by means of a **fixed quicksilver**, which is hotter and drier, possessing qualities contrary to those of common quicksilver. Therefore I advise you, O my friends, that you work only with the **Sun** and **Moon**, reducing them into the first matter: our **sulfur** and our **quicksilver**. Therefore, sons, you should make use of this venerable matter. And I swear and promise you that unless you take the **quicksilver** of these two, you proceed toward the practice like blind men without eyes or sense. The same author, in the preface to the *Clavicula* <note>The "Little Key," a title often given to foundational alchemical treatises</note>.

<margin>Greverus</margin>
Just as from man comes man, from a donkey a donkey, from a hen’s egg a hen, and from grain, grain is generated and brought forth: so from every like thing its like is made—from gold indeed comes gold, and from silver comes silver. From this, therefore, you understand what matter you ought to take and handle in this work. Greverus, page 8.

Before the Philosophers begin their work, they must judge the **gold** and **silver of the common people** they have taken in their hands, to see whether it be healthy or sick. And if they find it to be sick, let them bring it back to its proper health with a suitable medicine, which is the preparation itself. This **gold**, thus medicated, healthy, and purified, is the **Sun of the Philosophers**; and the same must also be understood regarding the **Moon**. Now it appears clearly enough that although the Philosopher takes the gold, silver, and **common Mercury**, nevertheless he does not put them into this work until he raises them from the common earth to the philosophical grade. The same author, page 10.

For the work, choose new gold that has not been through many labors of the goldsmiths, but has recently come from the mine and has not experienced much fire; of the best color, at twenty-four carats or near to it. And in this kind, the best is that which is found by its own nature raw in small pieces in the earth itself. If you can obtain such as this, you need no other preparation for this work than to spread it out into very thin plates by hammering. And you should consider the same thing said of silver. If you cannot obtain such, purge the gold by means of antimony <note>a metallic element used to separate gold from other metals</note>, or by the royal cement <term>royal cement: a purification process using salts and heat to draw out impurities from gold</term>, by melting one ounce of the **Sun** with 5 ounces of antimony. If you find fixed gold leaf in sufficient quantity in the apothecary shops or with the painters, you can use that for pure gold...
