<header>OF DAVID LAGNEUS</header>
<meta>catchword: Rebis</meta>

...animals, vegetables, minerals, and whatever is made from them; let the operator take the metals, and in them seek the principles of metals, namely, **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> and **sulfur**, since these are in them by nature, and metals are generated from them. Yet let them remember that the form of gold and silver can give nothing that they did not first possess: accordingly, neither imperfect metals, nor quicksilver, nor sulfur can attain the form and fixation necessary for the **Elixir**, unless they are first informed and fixed by the form of gold and silver. *The same author, page 121.*

<margin>Arnaldus</margin>
Our **quicksilver** is *most clear water*, and *our arsenic is pure silver*, and *our sulfur is pure gold*, and in these three consists all perfection. So that it may be more easily understood, we say that the whole philosophical science consists of the **Sun**, the **Moon**, and **Mercury**. By the **Sun**, we understand gold: by the **Moon**, silver. He who therefore knows how to tinge <note>to color or transform through alchemical tincture</note> **Mercury** with the **Sun** and **Moon**, comes to the secret which is called *white sulfur*: and when it is made red, it will be *sulfur for gold* <note>the Red Sulfur, or the final stage of the Philosopher's Stone used to transmute base metals into gold</note>. *Arnaldus in the Mirror, pages 41, 44, 47.*

With those bodies, namely the **Sun** and the **Moon**, **Mercury** is mixed and fixed by them through the greatest skill, which is hardly attained by a stiff-necked <note>original: "duræ cervicis," meaning a stubborn or unteachable</note> craftsman. *The same author in the Rosary, book 1, chapter 5.*

*He who knows how to tinge quicksilver with the **Sun** and **Moon**, comes to the secret which is called white sulfur, the best for silver. Which, when it is made red, will be the best sulfur for gold. From those bodies our white and red sulfur is extracted.* *Ibid, chapter 7.*

You who wish to work, you need first to labor in the solution and sublimation of the **two luminaries** <note>the Sun and Moon, signifying Gold and Silver</note>, because the first step of the operation is that **Mercury** may be made from them. *Ibid, chapter 9.*

**Sun, Moon, and Azoth** <note>a name for the universal agent or the "Mercury of the Philosophers" that contains the beginning and end of the work</note> are our dead stones upon the earth; they do nothing except through human industry. **Azoth** is indivisible, because it withdraws invisibly, and therefore it is called the *fugitive servant*, and it is incombustible. *The same author, On the Secrets of Nature, page 36.*

<margin>The Desirable One</margin>
The whole benefit of the craftsman consists in **Mercury**, the **Sun**, and the **Moon**. What you have sown, these you shall reap. *The Desirable One <note>original: "Desiderabile," likely referring to the alchemical text "The Desired Book"</note>, page 21.*

There is a difference between the *solar* and *lunar medicine*: because the solar contains solar sulfur, and the lunar contains lunar sulfur. For the lunar needs the purest white sulfur, and the solar needs the purest red sulfur. *The same author, page 25.*

From the dissolved *common Sun* <note>standard gold</note> and *common Moon* <note>standard silver</note>, the preparation of *common Mercury* is made. However, from these three, without any foreign species, the **Physical Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> is generated, and from no others can it be generated through physical skill. *The same author, page 114.*

# CHEMICAL HARMONY

The **Rebis** <note>original: "Rebis," a "double-thing" representing the union of opposites, often depicted as a hermaphrodite</note> is the first part of the work; the **Elixir** is the second; the **Tincture** <note>the substance capable of transmuting metals</note> is the third; and the **Medicine** is the fourth. It is clear, therefore, that the **Elixir** is required for the **Azoth** <note>original: "Azoth," the essential "spirit" or universal solvent of the alchemists</note>: because the Elixir precedes the Azoth in this work. For the Azoth is drawn out and extracted from the Elixir. Indeed, the Azoth is that which is extracted from dissolved bodies by **Mercury** itself: which is surely proven to be more mature. *The same author [Arnaldus], pages 169, 170, 193.*

The **Elixir** is nothing other than a body dissolved into mercurial water; after its dissolution, the **Azoth** is extracted from it, that is, the animated spirit. *The same author, page 194.*

One single metal, namely **gold**, is entirely necessary for the composition of the **Philosophers' Stone**. For the red and white bodies <note>Gold and Silver</note> are one, although the Philosophers have named them as two bodies or two works. *The same author, page 202.*

He who believes he can produce the **tincture** without these two bodies, namely the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>, proceeds blindly to the practice. *The same author, page 274.*

They who, with the **Sun** and **its shadow**, tinge the **poison**—that is, **Mercury**—perfect our Stone, which is called the **perfect and great gum**. *The same author, page 275.*

<margin>The Correction of Fools <note>original: "Correctio fatuorum," a well-known alchemical treatise</note></margin>
*Sow gold and silver, and they shall bring you a thousand-fold fruit with your labor*, through the mediation of Nature, because she alone possesses what you seek, and no other thing in the world: since all other things are as filth, and yield to nature through the persistence and testing of the fire. *Correction of Fools, page 9, and Richard, chapters 10 and 13.*

<margin>The Ladder <note>original: "Scala [Philosophorum]"</note></margin>
The Stone is one: yet this *one* is not one in number, but in kind: just as male and female are sufficient for procreating offspring without any other addition. And thus the **Philosophers' Stone**, composed of *two*, suffices for the intended medicine, namely the **spirit** and the **soul**, which are the **Sun** and the **Moon**. And some say that to these two a third is added, namely the **metallic body**. However, the number of the two is not multiplied, nor are the names, because the metallic body is composed of these two. *The Ladder of the Philosophers, page 106.*

<margin>Child's Play <note>original: "Ludus puer[orum]"</note></margin>
In our Stone or composite are the **Sun** and the **Moon** in virtue and power, and **Mercury** in its nature. For if this were not in our Stone and composite, they would create neither Sun nor Moon. *Child's Play, page 137.*

<margin>Aristotle <note>Alchemical works attributed to Aristotle were common, though likely written by later authors</note></margin>
*Take your most beloved son, and join him equally to his white sister: offer him the cup of love until they are intoxicated, and are divided into the smallest parts. Yet remember to keep this: that all pure things harmonize with pure things; otherwise they generate for themselves unlike sons.* *Aristotle, page 163.*

-># DAVID LAGNEUS<-

...unless he recognizes the principle of true nature and its governance; which once known requires no more than one thing, nor does it demand great expense: since there is one stone, one medicine, one vessel, one regimen, and one disposition. <note>The "one-ness" of the work is a common alchemical trope, emphasizing that despite complex metaphors, the process relies on a single underlying natural law.</note> *The Rosary, page 170.*

The **Dragon** <note>In alchemy, the dragon often represents crude matter or the volatile state of mercury that must be "tamed" or "killed" to be fixed.</note> does not die, except with its brother and its sister. *The same author, page 179.*

Three species suffice for the entire mastery, namely **white smoke**, **celestial water**, and the **green lion**—that is, the **brass of Hermes**, and the **foul water** <note>original: "aqua fœtida," likely referring to lead acetate or a sulfurous solution</note>, which is the mother of all metals, with which the **Elixir** is prepared from beginning to end. *The same author, page 184.*

Philosophy has three parts, namely, the **Sun**, the **Moon**, and **Mercury**. From these joined together, father **Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> knew how to fashion the tincture. *The same author, same page.*

There a conjunction of two bodies takes place, and it is necessary in our mastery. And if only one of those two bodies were in our Stone, it would never in any way give the tincture. *The same author, page 186.*

Join **Gabricus** with **Beya** <note>Gabricus (the brother/sulfur) and Beya (the sister/mercury) are famous alchemical figures whose "incestuous" marriage represents the union of the fixed and volatile principles.</note>, and do not take Nature itself unless it be pure, clean, raw, pleasant, earthy, and straight. Indeed, if you do otherwise, it will be of no use. See that nothing contrary enters with our Stone: put in only the Stone itself. *The same author, page 191.*

The **secret of the art of gold** is made from male and female: because the female, receiving the power of the male, rejoices, for the female is strengthened by the male. Take a dog of the same age, and a bitch of Armenia: join them together, and these two will bear for you a son, a dog of a heavenly color <note>The "heavenly color" refers to the blue or violet hue that appearing during certain stages of the chemical reaction.</note>, and he will guard you in your house from the beginning, in this world and in the other. *The same author, page 192.*

The **matter of the Philosophers** is water. And it is understood as the water of those three: nor should there be more, nor fewer. The **Sun** is the male, the **Moon** the female, and **Mercury** is the sperm. But for generation and conception to happen, it is necessary that the male be joined to the female, and beyond this the seed is required; and thus before fermentation, conception and impregnation must occur: and when the matter is multiplied, it is said that the infant grows in the mother's womb: and when it is fermented, it is said that the soul is infused into the body, and the **Crowned King** <note>The "Crowned King" is the perfected Philosophers' Stone, symbolized by gold.</note> is born. **Dissolve the bodies and soak up the spirit.** <note>original: "Solvite corpora & imbibite ſpiritum." This is a variation of the famous alchemical motto "Solve et Coagula" (Dissolve and Coagulate).</note> They say "bodies" in the plural; because it is necessary that there be at least two. And they say "spirit" in the singular: and thus it is necessary that it be one. And there is no sperm without the matter of the bodies, except **Mercury**. And when it is said, "Soak up the spirit"; that operation is understood which fixes the Mercury, and the Stone is multiplied. Multiplied, that is, reiterated. *The same author, page 204.*

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, David Lagneus persists in his collection of alchemical authorities, here focusing on the specific "Harmonia" or agreement between various masters regarding the necessity of combining the Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver) through the medium of Mercury to achieve the Stone.</meta>

### CHEMICAL HARMONY. ###

But do we not need gold alone and no other body? Listen to Hermes: *His father—that is, the father of the first composition—is the Sun; his mother is the Moon. The father is hot and dry, generating the Tincture; his mother is cold and moist, nourishing that which is brought forth.* <note>Hermes Trismegistus here uses the "Emerald Tablet" imagery to explain that the Stone requires both active/masculine and passive/feminine principles.</note> Therefore, if in our Stone there were only one of these, the medicine would never flow easily, nor would it give a tincture; and if it did give one, it would not tint except for what remained of the other, and the Mercury would vanish into smoke: because there would be no receptacle for the tincture within it. But our final secret is to have a Medicine that flows before the Mercury can flee. Therefore, the union of these two is necessary in our work. *The same author, page 227.*

<margin>Peter of Valencia</margin>
*With patience, by a most slow fire, up to the white stage inclusive in one vessel, with continuous color, due weight, and mixture. It consists of one thing in species, and two individuals, and it is perfected first to the white, and finally to the red, by strengthening the fire.* <note>The "white" (albedo) and "red" (rubedo) are the two final major stages of the alchemical Great Work.</note> *Peter of Valencia, page 4.*

<margin>Dastin</margin>
*Minerals ought to be chosen which are made from living Mercury and sulfur: from these work gently and not hastily.* <note>John Dastin was a famous 14th-century English alchemist.</note> *Dastin, page 30.*

<margin>Benedictus</margin>
*The Stone consists in one book, which is made of silver on the outside, having leaves of gold within.* <note>A poetic metaphor for the philosophical stone containing both silver and gold principles.</note> *Benedictus, page 55.*

<margin>Zininus</margin>
In the first regimen, let the raw and pure elements be placed upon a light fire, and let them be mixed, and joined, and governed until they are dried out and become black: in which blackness is hidden the whiteness that is extracted from there, and afterwards the redness through this kind of decoction <note>cooking or boiling</note>. And when it is in the state of whiteness, it is in an impalpable powder. *Zininus, page 68.*

<margin>John Duns</margin>
*From the dissolved Sun and Moon of the common sort, the preparation of the common Mercury is made.* <note>original: "Ex Sole & Luna vulgi," referring to ordinary gold and silver rather than the secret "philosophical" versions.</note> *From these three, however, without any foreign species, the physical Stone is generated, and from no others can it be generated by physical ingenuity.* *John Duns, page 114.*

<margin>Saturninus</margin>
The generation of metals and of the Philosophers' Stone is to join the proper principles: namely the male with the female, the active with the passive, and sulfur with quicksilver, so that from these may come generation and corruption. And quicksilver is the Stone receiving the form, and Gold is the philosophers' stone. *Saturninus, page 71.*

<margin>Tersin</margin>
*The whole work consists in the Sun, the Moon, and Mercury.* *Tersin, page 103.*

<margin>Ripley</margin>
No impure body, except one, which is commonly called by philosophers the **Green Lion**—which is the medium for joining the tinctures between the Sun and the Moon—enters our mastery with perfection. Both the material and formal principles ought to be dissolved; otherwise they would be of little moment. <note>Sir George Ripley was a highly influential 15th-century English alchemist; his "Green Lion" often refers to antimony or a strong mineral acid used as a solvent.</note> *Ripley, page 70.*

# DAVID LAGNEUS #

<margin>Libavius.</margin> *Gold, silver, and Mercury are the material of the physical Stone, after they have been prepared as they ought to be.* <note>original: "Aurum, argentum, & Mercurius sunt materia Lapidis physici." Andreas Libavius (c. 1550–1616) was a German physician whose work "Alchemia" is considered the first systematic chemistry textbook.</note> Libavius, Book 1, Paraphrase of Arnald, chapter 6, page 463.

In Philosophical Mercury, the *Soul, Body, and Spirit* all meet. It is the animal, vegetable, and mineral Stone: all perfect in their own way. The vegetable Stone is the Moon; the animal is the Sun; and the mineral is water—or spirit—and quicksilver. <note>In alchemical symbolism, "Moon" refers to Silver and "Sun" refers to Gold.</note> The same author, regarding Philosophical Mercury, pages 56, 63.

<margin>The New Pearl.</margin> We are nourished and perfected by the same things from which we are born, and not from outside things. Therefore, gold must be generated, nourished, and perfected from these same things, and not from outside things. Since gold is generated, nourished, and perfected by Nature from *quicksilver* alone, digested by an internal sulfur and finally purified of it; therefore, the Philosophers' Stone must also be generated, nourished, and perfected from these same things—namely, those which make up gold—and not from outside things. For just as the knowledge of a thing is taken from its essence, nature, and principles, so too is the work itself. <note>The "Margarita Pretiosa Novella" (The New Pearl of Great Price) is an influential 14th-century text by Petrus Bonus of Ferrara.</note> *The New Pearl, page 128.*

<margin>The Assembly.</margin> From man comes man, and from beasts comes their like. Therefore, join the red male servant <note>Gold</note> to his fragrant wife <note>Silver</note>, and together they will give birth to the Art. Do not introduce anything foreign to them, neither powder nor any other thing. Let the conception be enough for you, and a true son shall be born. <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, framed as a debate between ancient Greek sages.</note> *Assembly of the Philosophers, Proposition 31.*

We must join two things together (a mixture which the Philosophers have compared to a married couple), from whose embrace results the *golden water*. But this concerns the second stage of the work. I will say a little about the first stage. Stir up a war between *bronze* and *quicksilver* until they come to destruction and are corrupted; then the bronze, conceiving the quicksilver, coagulates it. The quicksilver, conceiving the bronze, is frozen into earth. Therefore, stir up the fight and destroy the body of the bronze until it becomes powder. *The same source, Proposition 46.*

The first composition, namely the body of Magnesia, is made from many things! Even though they become one thing, and are called "One" by the ancients—namely, the *whiteness of copper*. When it is governed, it is called by ten names taken from the colors of Nature, which appear during the governance of the body of Magnesia. It is necessary, therefore, for the lead to be turned into blackness, and then the ten aforementioned names will appear in the ferment of gold with Sericon, which is the composition called by ten names. <note>"Sericon" is a term often used for red lead or a mineral extract used in the "Red" stage of the work.</note> *The same source, Proposition 77.*

<margin>The Exercise.</margin> Just as Mercury is the beginning of all metals, so the *Sun* is the end and ultimate state of metals. All metals, both clean and unclean, are found in the Sun, Moon, and Mercury; but there is only one true... <note>The "Exercitatio in Turbam" is a later commentary on the Assembly of the Philosophers.</note>

It uses metaphors of marriage and warfare to describe the chemical reactions and color changes necessary to achieve the final "tincture."</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the materials of the Stone, this page focuses on the biological analogy of metallic generation, emphasizing that "like creates like" through the union of masculine and feminine principles, as supported by the Aurora Consurgens, Rosinus, and Tauladanus.</meta>

### CHEMICAL HARMONY ###

[...] the Sun <note>original: "Sol"; the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> which is drawn away from them. Just as a husband procreates offspring from his wife, who is nourished by menstrual blood: so similarly it happens in the artificial generation of metals, that from masculine Mercury and feminine Mercury mixed together—cast into the "field of Nature" <note>original: "agrum Naturæ"; a metaphor for the alchemical vessel or the base matter in which the "seed" is planted.</note> and brought to life through "menstrual Mercury" <note>original: "Mercurium menstrualem"; this refers to the solvent or "life-blood" that nourishes the growing metallic seed.</note>—an offspring is generated similar to the parents. It is not that the whole metallic body is converted by some artifice into masculine and feminine Mercury, and afterwards joined, fermented, and procreated into a solar or lunar body. Rather, it is otherwise. For from the masculine metallic body, masculine Mercury is drawn out, and from the feminine metallic body, feminine Mercury is drawn out. From these two Mercuries—joined together according to the due proportion and also coupled with the menstrual Mercury according to the due proportion, and placed in the field of Nature—then by the power of those two seeds, with the vegetation of the menstrual Mercury, guided by a due and tempered heat, an infant is generated according to the nature of the parents, either masculine or feminine. *Exercise 3 on the Turba [Philosophorum].*

<margin>The Aurora</margin>
Nothing is suited to a thing except that which is closer to it in its own nature, and in that thing a similar offspring is generated. That is, if you seek a medicine that cures metals, its origin will be from metals, since a species is tinted by its own kind. <note>The "Aurora Consurgens" is a famous 15th-century alchemical manuscript often attributed to Thomas Aquinas.</note> *Aurora, chapter 3.*

<margin>Rosinus</margin>
Things do not generate anything except what is like themselves, nor do things bear fruit except their own fruits. The Water of the Philosophers is the "ferment" <note>In alchemy, a ferment acts like yeast, transforming a large mass of material into the nature of the ferment itself.</note> of bodies, and the bodies are their earth, even after these have been blackened through the preparation of fire. They call this by the name "black fire," just as in the second stage of blackening, they call it *mountain coal and pitch, antimony, alkali, and salt of alkali, and marcasite, magnesia, quicksilver extracted from Cambar, and its ash, and lime, and glass*, and clean water, which has been cleansed from darkness and from the matter of blackness. *Rosinus at the end of the first book to Euthicia.* <note>Rosinus is the Latinized name of Zosimos of Panopolis, an early Egyptian-Greek alchemist.</note>

When we wish to create gold and silver, it is necessary to take the same. From man, man is generated; from a tree, a tree. *The same author, pages 580, 606, 607, etc.*

<margin>Tauladanus</margin>
Unless Art borrows the form-giving power of gold from gold, and that of silver from silver, and applies it to the remaining metals; it will never be able to ennoble base metals, no matter how much it washes and boils them. <note>Robertus Tauladanus was a 16th-century commentator on the works of John of Rupescissa and other alchemists.</note> *Tauladanus, page 246.*

Gold and the Moon <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical symbol for Silver.</note> are those metals from which the golden and silver Elixir is to be fashioned. *The same author, page 284.*

Gold alone is the ferment of the red Elixir, but silver is the ferment of the white. For to these two alone has Nature granted rays of splendor.

# THE WORKS OF DAVID LAGNEAU #

...with which they could illustrate the remaining metals with golden and silver beauty. All other metals are to be considered as the dough, or the material of the stone; they can never take on the nature of a form or a ferment <note>In alchemy, a "ferment" acts like yeast in bread, a small amount of a "perfect" substance that transforms a larger mass of "imperfect" matter into its own nature.</note> unless they are first ennobled, so long as *gold-making* <note>original: "chrysopœia"</note> or *silver-making* <note>original: "argyropœia"</note> remains the goal of Chemistry. But if *iron-making* <note>original: "sideropœia"</note> were the goal proposed for Chemistry, then the form or ferment of that *Elixir* would necessarily be *Mars* <note>The alchemical name for Iron.</note>. For just as the ferment of gold is gold, and of silver is silver: so the ferment of iron is iron, of tin is tin, of copper is copper, and of lead is lead. For every agent acts according to its own form. Same author, pages 296, 297.

Gold and silver are not spoken of metaphorically here <note>Lagneau is emphasizing that the "Gold" and "Silver" used in the work are the actual physical metals, not just symbolic terms for other substances.</note>. Same author, pages 301, 302, 303, 304, 305, and following.

By the testimony of all Philosophers, there are three parts of the *Elixir*: namely, *soul, body, and spirit*. The *soul* <note>original: "anima"</note> is nothing other than the ferment or the form of the *Elixir*. The *body* <note>original: "corpus"</note> is the dough or the matter. These two parts must be drawn from the metals alone: specifically, the form from the *Sun* <note>Gold</note> and the *Moon* <note>Silver</note>, and the matter from *Saturn* <note>Lead</note>, *Jupiter* <note>Tin</note>, *Venus* <note>Copper</note>, and *Mars* <note>Iron</note>. The third part of the Stone is the *spirit* <note>original: "spiritus"</note>: which, since it is the seat and vehicle of the soul, pours the soul into the body, and joins and couples these two extremes with an indissoluble bond of alliance. If this mediator were removed, the soul could never enter into a pact with the body. This *spirit* is nothing other than that liquor which thins the form and matter of the Stone, calling them back into a spiritual nature. This *spirit* is sometimes called by the Philosophers *heaven, solvent Mercury, menstruum, azoth, quintessence*, and by innumerable other names. Same author, pages 338, 339.

Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum"; Mercury.</note> is the other extreme of the Stone, and that from which motion arises. Same author, page 349.

Where Nature ends, Art begins. Nature ends in the perfect metals, and especially in the *Sun* <note>Gold</note>, because it is more perfect and cannot receive a higher degree from Nature. Therefore, Art should begin from the *Sun* and the *Moon* as its midpoint, by way of "corruption" <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to breaking a substance down into its base components so it can be reborn in a higher form.</note>. But why should so many reasons be brought forward here, since these things are so clear and manifest? Anyone who would dare to deny them should deservedly be considered blind, or one who gropes about at midday; such a person lacks sense no less than that philosopher who denied that snow was white. Same author, pages 309, 354, and 355.

The power of ignoble metals to be promoted to perfection must be elicited from only two sources—namely, the *Sun* and the *Moon*—and not from the imperfect metals themselves, since that power has been denied to them by Nature. Same author, page 226.

<margin>Geber</margin> The thing, however, which brings perfection in metals, is the substance of silver...

Lagneau argues that because Nature has already reached its peak in Gold, the alchemist must begin by breaking down these perfect metals to create the transformative Stone.</summary>

### CHEMICAL HARMONY ###

...of mercury <note>original: "vivi," referring to *argentum vivum* or quicksilver</note> and sulfur mixed proportionally, thickened and fixed through long and temperate boiling in the bowels of the clean earth; produced with the preservation of its radical moisture—not corrupting, but rather brought to a solid substance that melts when properly heated and can be stretched under the hammer. Geber, *On the Investigation of Perfection*, chapter 2.

<margin>Richard</margin>
Tinge with gold and silver: because gold provides a golden color and nature, and silver provides a silver one. For this reason, you should despise all other things: since there is no fruit in them, but only the loss of resources, as well as time and labor. Richard <note>Likely Richardus Anglicus, a 13th-century alchemist</note>, page 13.

<margin>Unknown Author</margin>
The Elixir must be made from things that are of a homogeneous and uniform substance. Unknown Author.

<margin>A New Chemical Light</margin>
Take a living male and a living female: join these together so that they may conceive between them a seed to procreate fruit of their own nature. For let no mortal believe that he is able to create the first matter <note>The "First Matter" or *Materia Prima* was the primordial, undifferentiated substance alchemists sought as the starting point for the Great Work.</note>. *A New Chemical Light* <note>A famous 17th-century alchemical text attributed to Michael Sendivogius</note>, page 31.

*Our water is a celestial water, which does not wet the hands of the common people, but is much like rain. The body is gold, which gives the seed: our Moon <note>In alchemy, the Moon is the standard symbol for Silver.</note> is that which receives the seed of gold (not common silver). It is afterwards governed by our continuous fire for seven months, and sometimes ten, until our water consumes three parts and leaves one, and this in double measure. Afterward, it is nourished by the milk of the earth, or the fatness of the earth, or the fatness of that which is born in the breasts of the earth; it is ruled or preserved from putrefaction by the Salt of Nature: and thus that infant of the second generation <note>The "Infant" is a common metaphor for the Philosopher's Stone in its developing stages.</note> is born.* Same author, page 53.

Give gold and silver to our Old Man to swallow, so that he himself may consume them, and finally, he too, being about to die, may be burned. Let his ashes be scattered in water. Cook them until it is enough, and you have the Medicine for curing leprosy <note>In alchemical texts, "leprosy" is a metaphor for the "sickness" or corruption found in base metals (like lead or iron) that must be "cured" to turn them into gold.</note>. Same author, page 64.

<margin>Bernard of Grana</margin>
*Those who recognize the mercury and sulfur of the Philosophers: they know that these are made from the purest gold, from the finest Moon (silver), and from the mercury which are seen every day, from which our mercury is drawn.* Bernard of Grana, page 1 of a very old manuscript.

<margin>The Secret of Secrets</margin>
First, we say that our Medicine is made from *bodies* and *spirit*. The *bodies* are gold and silver: because if they were not there, neither gold nor silver would be produced. And the *spirit* is *Mercury* or quicksilver, which is figuratively called by many names. An old manuscript called *The Secret of Secrets* <note>A widely circulated medieval text often attributed to Aristotle or various Arabic authors</note>, page 88.

## *What should be taken for the physical Stone, etc., and in what manner.*

# CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Isaac <note>Referring to Isaac Hollandus, a legendary Dutch alchemist whose works emphasize the use of "spirits" and the "Great Work."</note></margin>
A middle spirit must be taken, or a material which is always found in the middle: and it is this spirit which we seek, which lies between the fixed and the non-fixed. Isaac, Book 1, Chapter 5.
If you listen to me, you will avoid the separation of the elements, whether in the Mercury of the mineral or vegetable work, or in the Stone, which God gives to us freely. Wherever there is talk of this matter, and it is said that the elements must be separated, avoid all such works because of their uncertainty. Above all, labor in the Great Work <note>The *Opus Magnum*, the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. For in it there is no concern, neither distillation nor congealing, nor purification, nor foreign bodies, nor foreign things, nor unclean things containing dregs. You do not calcine <note>To reduce a substance to powder by heat</note>, for there is no need: you do not separate the elements, for they are indeed clean: it needs nothing. *There is one kind, one thing, one vessel, one furnace, and one work for the white and the red* <note>The "white" and "red" refer to the stages of the work: the *Albedo* (white stone for silver) and *Rubedo* (red stone for gold).</note>, and no danger can occur in the work. For the Great Work dissolves itself, sublimates itself, fixes itself, melts and perfects itself. The same, Book 2, Chapter 3.

<margin>Alan <note>Alanus de Insulis, or Alan of Lille, a 12th-century theologian and scholar to whom alchemical works were often attributed.</note></margin>
*He who does not know how to extract the soul from the body of the Sun and Moon, and to restore the same to the body in projection, should know that he wanders entirely from the path.* <note>In alchemical symbolism, the "Sun" is gold and the "Moon" is silver. "Projection" is the final stage where the Stone transforms base metals into gold.</note> *Indeed, it is extracted by the middle spirit of Mercury. For our physical water dissolves the bodies of the Sun and Moon.* Alan, page 31.

The extraction of the soul through the spirit of Mercury does not happen all at once and at the same time, but in many stages over time and days, as well as every single hour and moment, a little at a time, until the work has been brought to perfection. The soul does not leave the body all at once, but is drawn out in many stages; nor is it dissolved in one go in the vessel containing the solution (or in which the body is dissolved): but every day a little bit in there, and then again another small amount, according to the guidance of the operator and of Nature.

Therefore, do not think that the solution of the body happens all at once, but *in the course of time and gradually*, just as the sayings of the Philosophers above clearly attest.

Do not believe that the Tincture <note>The transforming essence or "dye" of the Stone.</note> is drawn out or extracted in only one single turn, but constantly a little bit, and then again a small amount; for a blackness occurs daily until the work is completed in the course of time. The same, pages 54, 55, 56.

<summary>This page cites Isaac Hollandus and Alan of Lille to argue that the Great Work requires a single "middle spirit" and a patient, gradual process of extracting the "soul" from gold and silver, rather than complex chemical separations.</summary>
<keywords>Great Work, Isaac Hollandus, Alan of Lille, middle spirit, extraction of the soul, Sun and Moon, alchemy, gradual process, Tincture</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the collection of alchemical authorities within David Lagneau’s "Harmonia Chymica." While the previous page focused on the choice of materials and the necessity of a "middle spirit" according to Isaac Hollandus, this page presents specific methods for extracting the "oil" or "spirit" of metals using authorities such as Garlandius, Ventura, Aegidius, and Vogelius. It transitions from theoretical advice to practical laboratory instructions.</meta>

->### CHEMICAL HARMONY.<-

->Ggg 4<-

<margin>Garlandius <note>John Garland (c. 1195 – c. 1272), an English grammarian and scholar to whom several alchemical treatises were attributed.</note></margin>
If you wish to make the Philosopher’s Stone from this (Gold, Silver, Mercury), do so: Separate the spirits as diligently as you can; for you cannot do this so subtly that it does not retain within itself some substance of the "wind-phlegm" <note>original: *ventiphlegmatis*. In alchemy, this refers to a watery, airy, or crude byproduct of distillation that must be removed.</note>. That spirit is called "burning water" <note>original: *aqua ardens*. This usually refers to a highly rectified spirit or alcohol used as a solvent.</note>, and it is like pitch. Garlandius.

<margin>Ventura <note>Laurentius Ventura, a 16th-century Italian alchemist and physician known for his work "De Ratione Conficiendi Lapidis Philosophici."</note></margin>
This is the oil of the Philosophers, made from the joining of the soul and the body, from which body the soul was extracted by that subtle thing itself, which is water and airy vapor: which spirit is not joined to the body again, except by means of the soul. And therefore it is necessary first for the extracted soul to be united with the spirit, so that afterwards both may be joined together with the body, and they may vivify the body itself, and manifest its hidden nature. Ventura, chapter 21, page 118.

<margin>Aegidius <note>Likely Aegidius de Vadis, a 16th-century alchemist who wrote on the "Art of Distillation."</note></margin>
That which is to be taken is not those things from which metals are made, but that which comes *from* the metals themselves. Sulphur and quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*, meaning Mercury.</note>, from which metals are generated, are not those things from which the Stone is made, because they are combustible; but rather that which comes from the metals themselves, which is non-burning <note>original: *non urens*.</note>. Aegidius, page 16.

This Stone is the potential vapor of the metal. You must be cautious in how you acquire it. The same [Aegidius], page 71.

<margin>Vogelius <note>Ewaldus Vogelius, a pseudonym for an alchemical author, possibly Benedictus Figulus or similar 16th-century figures.</note></margin>
Take the calx <note>The powdery metallic oxide or residue left after a substance has been roasted or "calcined."</note> or earth of any prepared and washed imperfect body <note>A "body" in alchemy refers to a metal; "imperfect" bodies typically refer to lead, tin, copper, or iron.</note>, and pour over it enough similarly purged Mercury so that it floats two or three fingers deep in a vessel with a long and narrow neck. Then apply a very slow fire, lest the Mercury should rise, until you see an oil like a film of various colors rise above the Mercury; separate this and set it aside. From here, with the vessel closed, light the fire again for several days until you have extracted all the oil and see nothing more rising. Then separate your Mercury from the calx, and pour it onto another quantity of the purged calx of any body, and do as before, continuing the slow fire until you have drawn from it all the vivifying humor. You can repeat this operation as often as you wish, according to the quantity of oil you desire, adding more Mercury if it has diminished. Finally, place all the collected oil in a cucurbit <note>A gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the bottom part of a distillation apparatus.</note>, and add six parts of that Mercury (with which you extracted the oil) for every one part of oil. And if the quantity is large, you can divide it among several cucurbits. Digest them together for a month; finally, separate the Mercury with a slow fire, lest the oil should rise with it. When nothing more evaporates at that degree of heat (which you detect by placing a copper or iron plate over the mouth of the vessel), know that the precious oil of sulphur resides at the bottom, which must be made subtle by twelve or fifteen distillations...

<margin>Arnald <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note></margin>
You require labor in the solution of the Stone, so that you may separate its purer parts from the impure and heavier ones: and you will complete the work with the lighter parts, having cast away the heavier parts. From this, once the first form of the bodies is dissolved into ***our Mercury***, a new form is immediately introduced, their [former] form having been destroyed. This new form is first black in color, foul in smell, and subtle and fragmented to the touch. Arnald in the *Mirror* <note>original: *Speculum Alchimiae*.</note>, page 55.

Nevertheless, collect the black material floating on top, for that is the oil and the true sign of dissolution: because that which is dissolved reaches the limit of sublimity. For this reason, it is separated from the lower things, ascending upward and seeking higher places, like a golden body. But guard it carefully, lest it fly away in smoke. The same author, in the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarium Philosophorum*.</note>, book 2, chapter 3.

<margin>The Monk <note>original: *Monachus*. Likely referring to a monastic author such as Efferarius Monachus or a similar cited authority.</note></margin>
It is necessary that the Stone, before it becomes the elixir, be extracted from the nature of two bodies. The Monk, page 15.

There must be a light fire, until the spirit is separated from the body, ascending in black clouds over the body. The same author, page 35.

By means of the crude spirit, the digested spirit is extracted from the dissolved body. The same author, page 167.

<margin>Richard <note>Richardus Anglicus (Richard the Englishman), a 13th-century alchemist.</note></margin>
If you do not resolve the body into ***Mercury*** by means of ***Mercury***, you cannot obtain the hidden virtue from it—namely, the sulfur digested and ripened by the work of Nature in the mine. Richard, chapter 11.

<margin>The Stairway <note>original: *Scala*. Referring to the *Scala Philosophorum* (The Stairway of the Philosophers), an anonymous 14th-century treatise.</note></margin>
He who seeks our radiating sulfur, let him make peace between the Sun <note>gold</note> and his wife <note>silver or mercury</note>, so that they are not separated from each other, but mixed inseparably. And this will happen when you have extracted the husband partly from his nature, and similarly his wife partly from her nature. Once this is done, let them be killed, and when they have been killed, let them be raised by a new, incorruptible resurrection, so that afterwards they are immortal. *The Stairway*, page 100.

<margin>Libavius <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a German physician and chemist known for his systematic work *Alchymia*.</note></margin>
Our newborn infant—whether you call it absolute putrefaction <note>decay or breaking down</note>, or the "crow’s head" <note>original: *caput corvi*. A term for the *nigredo* or blackening stage, the first main phase of the Great Work.</note>—must be as black as soot: for which reason it is called "the blacker than black." If you touch it with your fingers, it clings so finely that it cannot be removed except by washing. If you sprinkle it into water, it sinks, where previously, when mixed exactly with the water, it turned it black. This blackness is also called the beginning of the true tincture, the true seed, the ash not to be despised, the black earth which in the beginning stands upon the water, "virgin’s milk" <note>original: *lac virginis*</note>, "doubled Mercury" (consisting of the Mercury of the bodies and the crude Mercury), sulfur, and the "soul of gold" <note>original: *anima auri*</note>. Libavius, book four, page one hundred twelve.

<margin>The Correction of Fools <note>original: *Correctio fatuorum*. An alchemical treatise often attributed to Richard of England.</note></margin>
The Sulfur of the philosophers is a simple living fire, giving life to other dead bodies and maturing them: so that it supplies the defect of Nature, since it is of a superfluous maturity, according to which it is perfect in its own nature, and is more and more purified through artifice. Whence a certain author says: *Such sulfur is not found upon the earth except insofar as it exists in those bodies, the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note>, and another thing, which is that which is told to no one, unless it be revealed to him by God. In the Sun, however, it is more perfect: because it is more digested and decocted <note>original: *decoctum*, meaning thoroughly cooked or processed by heat</note>.* *The Correction of Fools*, chapter 6, page 7.

The Medicine is produced from Mercurial water, in which the Sun and Moon were previously dissolved. If you do not resolve the body into Mercury with Mercury, you cannot have the hidden virtue from it, namely the sulfur digested and decocted through the work of Nature in the mine. The same author, chapter 8, page 10.

<margin>Aristotle <note>Referring to Pseudo-Aristotle, the name given to various anonymous medieval authors who wrote alchemical texts under the name of the Greek philosopher.</note></margin>
In clean Mercury put clean bodies: and when you see blackness appearing on the surface of the water, collect it cautiously and set it aside, knowing for certain that your stone is now partly dissolved. *This blackness is the origin of the Art, the crow’s head <note>original: *caput corvi*, the symbol for the 'nigredo' or initial stage of putrefaction</note>, and the body is dissolved and reduced into its first matter.* Aristotle, page 163.

<margin>The Rosary <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a seminal 16th-century alchemical text.</note></margin>
*Our sulfur and that of the Wise is not found upon the earth, except that which is extracted from those bodies.* Therefore, let those bodies be subtly prepared, so that we may have sulfur upon the earth. For the perfect body, through our mastery, helps and perfects the imperfect one, without the mixture of any foreign thing. *The Rosary*, page 181.

*The tincture <note>The transformative substance sought by alchemists.</note> exists only from two perfect bodies, from which those sulfurs can be elicited.* The same, page 184.

*It is necessary that our stone be extracted from the nature of two bodies, before the complete Elixir is made from it. Since it is necessary that the elixir be more purified than gold and silver. Our Mercury is not obtained except from bodies liquefied by a non-vulgar <note>Distinct from ordinary metallurgical melting; refers to a chemical or philosophical dissolution.</note> liquefaction, but only that which lasts until the spouses are joined and united in a true marriage. And this is until the whiteness <note>original: *albedinem*, the 'albedo' stage of the work following the blackness</note>.* The same, pages 186–187.

*That which becomes spiritual <note>Volatile or refined into a gaseous/vaporous state.</note> ascends upward in the vessel: but that which is thick and coarse remains below in the vessel. And unless you have so blackened and destroyed the body, until the water does not wish to be mixed with it, or be received by the earth; you will achieve nothing. For when it becomes spiritual powder, it remains below in the vessel. Therefore, unless you turn everything into spiritual powder, you have not yet crushed it. This ash lacks fusion.* The same, pages 188–189.

*Our stone is named Mercury among the philosophers; which*

...is not born, as many think, but extracted from the body. The same author, page 194.

Burn <note>original: *combure*, meaning to calcine or subject to heat</note> our copper with a light fire, just like a nurse incubating eggs, until the body is established and the Tincture <term>Tincture: the soul or transformative essence of the metal</term> is extracted. However, you should not extract it all at once, but little by little; let it emerge every day, until it is completed over a long period of time. The same author, page 197.

From the male and the female make a *round circle*, and from that extract a quadrangle, and from the quadrangle a triangle: *make a round circle, and you shall have the physical Stone*. The same author, page 198.

<margin>Khalid <note>original: *Calid*, referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince and legendary figure in alchemy.</note></margin>
The Stone is cheap, black, foul-smelling, not bought for a price; it is never found without its companion, and it is light in weight. And they call it the origin of the world, because it arises like germinating things. And this is its revelation and appearance to the seeker. Khalid, chapter 9.

<margin>Benedictus</margin>
The soul is extracted from its body by means of the spirit: and this is called the key of the Art, and it becomes a black matter, which is called the **crow’s head** <term>crow’s head: *caput corvi*, the symbolic name for the black stage or *nigredo*.</term> Benedictus, page 56.

Blacken the earth by *separating its soul*: afterward pour water over the earth, whitening the whole, and you will have the mastery so that it may be turned into redness. The same author, page 59.

<margin>Gerard of Viviers <note>original: *Gerardus de Viariis*.</note></margin>
The second regimen <note>regimen: a specific stage or method of heating and treating the material</note> is that the processed material be taken and placed in a glass vessel <note>original: *urinali*, a vessel shaped like those used for medical exams</note> over sifted ashes, continuing for four days. For a certain *blackness* will come upon it: collect this, keeping it carefully to one side. Thus continue the work with a uniform fire until you have extracted all the black, with the clear substance remaining in the middle. And this is the second work, or the philosophers' stone. Then the third work is that you take that same blackness and put it in a glass vessel, over a slow fire on the ashes, placing on top some of the clear, pure middle part, just enough to float four fingers deep: continuing thus, and do not hasten the boiling <note>original: *decoctiones*</note>, until it becomes a **great white**. Gerard of Viviers.

<margin>James of Saint-Saturnin</margin>
Our Mercury is extracted from the lime <note>original: *calce*, the powder resulting from calcining or burning a metal</note> of metals through putrefaction, until the composite material casts off its old nature and puts on another. And thus, through operations of this kind, the Mercury of the philosophers is produced. James of Saint-Saturnin, page 72.

<margin>The Path of the Path <note>original: *Semita Semitæ*, a medieval alchemical text.</note></margin>
Place the water in a glass vessel and boil it over a slow fire, until you see blackness appear on its surface: remove this by collecting it skillfully every day, as often as you best can: and by boiling again and removing the blackness, until no more blackness appears. Then take all that earth—that is, the blackness you collected—and put it in a glass vessel, and pour water over it, and cook it with a light fire for ten days. Again add water and boil: repeat this until the earth becomes white and clear. *The Path of the Path*, page 72.

<margin>The Assembly of the Philosophers, Statement 37 <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous early alchemical text depicting a gathering of ancient sages.</note></margin>
> Unless you grind the body, break it down, saturate it, and govern it diligently until you extract its fatness <note>original: *pinguedinem*, referring to the "oil" or essential sulfur of the metal</note> and make it a fine, impalpable spirit, you labor in vain. And for this reason the Sages said: *Unless you turn bodies into non-bodies, and make non-bodies into bodies, you have not yet found the beginning of this work.* However, bodies become incorporeal when *Ethelia* <term>Ethelia: an alchemical term for a volatile spirit, vapor, or "soot" that rises during heating</term> is ground until it becomes dust; and this dust is not produced except by the strongest cooking <note>original: *decoctione*</note> and continuous grinding; it is performed by fire, not by hands, through the process of soaking, putrefaction, and *Ethelia*. And when the Sages said regarding this Art that *Nature is cheap and sold for a small price*, they caused the common people to go astray. The Philosophers said, *the moist spirit is black, lacking defilement:* and just as in man there is moisture and dryness, so in our work there is nothing other than vapor and water.

<margin>The same, Statement 38.</margin>
> The philosophers said: Know that unless you turn all things into dust, you have not yet ground them enough. Cook, therefore, until it is broken down and becomes dust.

<margin>The same, Statement 39.</margin>
> When the water becomes dust, the copper <note>original: *æs*, referring to the "philosopher's copper" or base matter</note> has been diligently ground.

<margin>The same, Statement 47.</margin>
> That hidden soul cannot be drawn out except through *Ethelia*, which turns bodies into non-bodies by the continuity of cooking and the sublimation of *Ethelia*.

<margin>Anonymous:</margin>
> Take the stone suspended over the sea, its name is victor: with it kill the living and bring life to the killed, for within it are death and life. Anonymous author, in the work beginning *An Example of Science*, page 389.

<margin>Uncertain:</margin>
> The divine Art teaches how to extract the seed from the more perfect body. This seed, when cast into the philosophical earth prepared by art and continuously cooked with temperate heat into a white or red dust, is said to have converted the lower bodies into the nature of the higher ones. Uncertain author, in the work beginning *Of all things rightly*.

<margin>Lullius <note>referring to Ramon Llull, a major figure in medieval alchemy</note></margin>
> Bodies made as black as coal are the secret of our true dissolution <term>dissolution: the process of breaking a solid down into its constituent spiritual parts</term>. Lullius in the *Clavicula* <note>The Little Key</note>, chapter 1.

<margin>The New Chemical Light <note>original: *Novum lumen Chymicum*, a famous 17th-century text attributed to Michael Sendivogius</note></margin>
> Take that which descends to the bottom of the vessel, and that which is from the dregs: wash it with hot fire until its blackness is removed and its thickness recedes. Whiten it with a good whitening, and cause the additions of moisture to fly away from it; then it will be converted and become a white lime <note>original: *calx alba*, a powdered residue after calcination</note>, in which there will be no dark obscurity, nor impurity, nor opposition. Khalid <note>original: *Galid*</note>, chapter 9.

> The craftsman here does nothing except know how to separate the subtle from the thick, and how to place them in the proper vessel. *The New Chemical Light, page 38.*

DAVID LAGNEAU
On the removal of the superfluous in the physical stone.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>Aegidius.</margin> By the power of fire your Sun <note>The "Sun" refers to the philosophical Gold or the soul of the matter.</note> is purified: which purification is understood by the Philosophers as an exaltation. And because in Aries <note>The zodiac sign of the Ram, marking the start of spring and the Sun's exaltation.</note> the Sun begins to ascend to its zenith, that is to its highest point, beyond which it cannot ascend further: in the same way your Sun is always exalted until the end of the work. (Aegidius de Vadis, chapter 8, pages 22, 23).

<margin>Arnald.</margin> Take that earth and blackness which you have gathered, and place it in a glass vessel, and pour over it the aforementioned water until it floats upon it, and cook it over a slow fire for four days: then set the water aside and cook, and so on thereafter, until the earth becomes white and clear. And this is what the philosophers have said: *This water putrefies and is purified with the earth; for when it has been purified, by God’s help the entire mastery will be directed.* Once it is cleansed and clarified or whitened by means of the water, etc. (Found in Arnald of Villanova's *The Flower of Flowers*).

<margin>Greverius.</margin> Geber and the practitioners of this divine work call the choosing and cultivation of seeds and earth "preparation," without which neither the Sun, nor the Moon, nor the earth of the philosophers can be obtained, nor is any entrance open to the inner chambers of such a great Art. For the gold of the common people is impure, contaminated, sick, diseased, and for that reason even sterile; silver is similar, and common earth is uncultivated and unplowed. But the earth of the philosophers is cultivated by bulls breathing fire <note>An allusion to the myth of Jason and the Golden Fleece, symbolizing the intense heat required to "plow" or prepare the matter.</note>. Although the philosopher may take the gold, silver, and Mercury of the common people, he does not put them into this work until he raises them from the common soil to the physical grade <note>The "physical grade" is the state where a metal is purged of its mundane impurities and becomes alchemically active.</note>. Therefore, nothing unclean, sick, or uncultivated enters our work, even though we may take things that are unclean, sick, and uncultivated before the work begins. (Greverius, page 9).

<margin>The Rosary.</margin> Our matter has within itself all that we seek, to which we add or diminish nothing, but in the preparation alone we remove the superfluous. We remove, I say, the physical humidity which is suitable for the work, which will be as clear as tears, in which the metallic quintessence <term>Quintessence: The "fifth essence" or purest part of a substance, beyond the four elements.</term> dwells: and that is the "placable" <note>original: *placabile*, meaning receptive or harmonious.</note> metal: and in it is the medium for joining the tinctures, because it has the nature of sulfur and quicksilver. (*The Rosary of the Philosophers*, page 208).

<margin>Geber.</margin> In the preparation of the bodies, nothing superfluous is to be removed from their depth, but rather from what is manifest <note>Visible or external qualities.</note>. (Geber, *On the Perfection of Mastery*, book 2, chapter 68).
What is lacking in them is a scarcity of Mercury, and the improper thickening of the same. Therefore, the completion in them will consist of a large amount of quicksilver [multi-]

These processes transform common, "sick" metals into the exalted, "healthy" materials required for the Great Work.</summary>

### On the operations of the Art of the philosophers.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Libavius</margin>
<note>Andreas Libavius (c. 1555–1616) was a German physician and chemist known for his textbook *Alchymia*.</note>
All purifications of Mercury through sublimation by means of salty substances are vain and irrelevant—indeed, they are harmful to the perfection of our work. Therefore, those who believe that Mercury must be sublimated seven times from salt and vitriol <term>vitriol: a sulfate mineral, often used as a corrosive or solvent</term>, and afterwards reduced with hot water or through the "fat of tartar," understand poorly; they do so because they read that "Latona" <note>original: "Latonem"; in alchemy, Latona represents the impure copper or base metal that must be "washed" or whitened to become silver.</note> must be washed. But they are deceived. (Libavius, pages 91, 92, 93).

<margin>Aquinas</margin>
<note>Attributed here to Thomas Aquinas, though likely a "Pseudo-Aquinas" alchemical text common in the Middle Ages.</note>
When our Stone has been dissolved into its first nature—namely into the "first water," or "virgin’s milk," or the "tail of the dragon"—then the stone itself calcines, sublimes, matures, distills, reduces, washes, and congeals itself. By the power of a proportional fire, it perfects itself in a single vessel without any other manual operation by the craftsman. (Thomas Aquinas to Brother Reynaldus, chapter 3).

<margin>Greverius</margin>
<note>Jodocus Greverus, a 16th-century author of the *Secretum nobilissimum*.</note>
The amalgam, which is the first work, is made with one ounce of the Sun <note>The "Sun" is the philosophical term for Gold.</note> and four ounces of Mercury, just as goldsmiths do. The philosophers have called this "beginning of their work" by many names, such as "our brass," "our gold," "the earth of magnesia," or "the whole composite," because they wished to hide it from the unworthy. (Greverius, pages 20, 21).

In the first cooking <term>decoction: a process of boiling or heating to extract essences</term>—that is, while you are in the "black" stage—a certain humidity like quicksilver will rise from your earth like a cloud and will cling to the sides of the upper part of your empty egg <note>The "egg" or *ovum philosophicum* is the oval glass vessel used in alchemical heating.</note>; you must leave this untouched. (The same author, page 25).

Turn these clouds into rain when you notice that no more vapors exhale from your earth, and those which have already ascended no longer multiply; these will irrigate your field so that it may bear its fruit in its own time. (The same author, page 31).

This reduction of clouds into rain is called by some "the tail of the dragon," augmentation, or multiplication; others say that "new Mercury" must be added. (The same author, page 32).

The cooking softens the seed through putrefaction <note>The stage of breaking down the matter, often associated with the color black.</note>, pushes forth the sprout, raises up the shoots and stalks, expands the flowers, forms the seeds, and finally directs those formed seeds to their expected maturity—all in one and the same vessel, and by a single operation of the craftsman, which consists in the administration of the coals. (The same author, page 35).

<margin>Alanus</margin>
<note>Alanus de Insulis, or Alain de Lille, a 12th-century theologian to whom alchemical works were often attributed.</note>
There is no reason to persuade yourself that when we mention sublimation, we are actually sublimating—that is, separating the part which is above from the part which is below. For in our "sublimation," the fixed parts are not raised, but only the non-fixed <note>The "volatile" or gaseous parts.</note> parts. (Alanus, page 49).

<summary>This page outlines the core operations of the alchemical "Great Work," emphasizing that once the matter is correctly prepared in a sealed vessel, the various stages—from the "black" stage of putrefaction to the "rain" of condensation—occur naturally through the steady application of heat. It warns against common chemical shortcuts like salt-based sublimation, advocating instead for a "philosophical" process that mirrors natural growth.</summary>

# DAVID LAGNEUS
<note>David de Planis-Campy, also known as Lagneus (1589–c. 1644), was a French physician and alchemist who sought to harmonize the various and often contradictory instructions of the ancient masters.</note>

Decoction, mixing, sublimation, grinding, drying, watering, ignition, whitening, and reddening—and by whatever other names it may be called—it is nonetheless only one regimen, which grinding and decoction can rightly achieve. (The same author, page 55).

Our beginning, when the body and spirit are already joined while being joined in the work, is called calcination. (The same author, page 56).

Every thing is destroyed by the same cause through which it grows; nor is anything more consistent with Nature than that each thing be dissolved and liberated from the bonds by which it is bound, through the medium of that thing from which it took its origin. (The same author, page 59).

Whoever knows how to destroy gold or silver, so that they cannot afterwards be reduced back to gold or silver, has reached the mastery. For it is more difficult to destroy bodies than to build them. (The same author, page 61).

<margin>Arnaldus</margin>
<note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous physician and alchemist. Here, he refers to the "White and Red" stages—the secondary and final goals of the work.</note>
White and red earth, cleansed and refined, are found for sale. (Arnaldus in *The Little Garden*, page 31).

There are seven dispositions of this mastery. First is called sublimation, second Calcination, third Solution, fourth Washing, fifth Waxing <term>ceratio: the process of softening a substance until it has the consistency of wax</term>, sixth Coagulation, and seventh Fixing. (The same author, in *The Mirror*, page 26).

Know that all operations—namely, putrefaction, solution, coagulation, washing, and fixing—are contained within sublimation alone, and they are performed in one vessel and not in many vessels; the work is finished in one furnace and not in many furnaces. Since there are seven operations within sublimation alone, we place seven dispositions in our book, through which the wise and understanding person may reach true perfection. (The same author, pages 39, 42).

To dissolve, to calcine, to sublime, to dye, to wash, to cook, to cool, to water, to extract, to coagulate, to moisten, to soak, to fix, to grind, to dry, and to distill are all one thing; namely, they denote the extraction of the soul or spirit from the body, and they signify the application of truths—that is, that the fire be made gentle. (The same author, page 65).

<margin>Lullius</margin>
<note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a Majorcan philosopher; many alchemical works were later attributed to him.</note>
Distillation happens through the "veins" of the glass <note>original: "venas vitri"; likely referring to the neck or tubes of a distillation apparatus</note> without the separation of materials; rather, it occurs with their conjunction in our secret furnace, and this is our sublimation. (Lullius in *The Codicil*, page 69).

<margin>Aegidius</margin>
<note>Aegidius de Vadis was a 16th-century alchemist known for his "Dialogue on the Art of Alchemy."</note>
Words cannot be published and printed; for the industry of manual operation lies in the experience of each individual, and it cannot be printed by type—indeed, it can scarcely be handed down by mouth, except through the hands <note>A classic alchemical sentiment: the "Art" is a practical craft that must be learned by doing, not just reading.</note>. (Aegidius in the *Preface*).

The acts of active things are within the disposed patient: that is, the form acts according to the disposition of the matter. (The same author, page 2).

Consider the nature of the mineral body, from whence it took its origin, and reduce it to its own matter. (The same author, page 5).

### CHEMICAL HARMONY

When men and women come together, they are then reduced to the first matter <note>original: *primam materiam*—the primordial substance from which all things originate</note>: because from their bodies crude seeds <note>original: *spermata*</note> are generated, from which they themselves first came forth; yet their bodies are not destroyed, as would happen if they were reduced to the remote first matter. Wherefore it is necessary that you do likewise *in your work, that is, under the preservation of the species*—which indeed you ought to note very well. Note, however, that it is not to be taken from that which metals are made, but from that which is out of the metals themselves. (The same author [Lagneus], pages 6–7).

In one glass vessel all things must be done, similar in shape to an egg, and well closed. (The same author, page 75).

Know that the philosophers have made many chapters concerning the Stone, and sublimation, distillation, separation, putrefaction, waxing, and calcination: all of which are one and the same operation, in one vessel. (The same author, page 106).

<margin>Vogelius</margin>
<note>Ewald Vogel, a 16th-century alchemist often associated with the author Hoghelande, known for reconciling different alchemical schools of thought.</note>
Bodies must first be refined <note>original: *subtilianda*</note> through dissolution, which is the first step of the work. This dissolution, however, is nothing else than for bodies to return into Mercury and sulfur, from whence they had their origin. Moreover, no other body can be resolved into Mercury than a metallic one consisting of Mercury and sulfur. (Vogelius, page 45).

Unless all things have been turned into powder, you have not yet ground them. Therefore cook and grind until they are converted, and by nature become dust. (The same author, page 62).

Our "sublimating" is not to ascend or elevate upward; rather, physical sublimation is to make a precious thing out of a vile thing, and from a thing most low and small, to make it high, great, and pure. When, therefore, we speak of sublimated bodies, understand them as refined, and converted into a high, pure, clean, and most noble nature. (The same author, page 83).

The mode of acting, digesting, and shaping belonging to the Art is different from the natural way, and likewise the instrument or the place and time, although they are equivalent toward the same ultimate end. (The same author, page 103).

<margin>The Monk</margin>
<note>Likely referring to a specific manuscript tradition attributed to an anonymous monk (Monachus), a common authority in 16th-century chemical compendiums.</note>
When the matter ascends through the wind, that is, through smoke, the philosophers have called this sublimation; and when the matter was turned to the bottom of the vessel, and converted into water, they named it solution or distillation; when the earth was thickened, they named it corruption; when the matter begins to change to a black color, they named it washing <note>original: *ablutionem*</note>. And the mastery consists in this: when the water is extracted from the earth, and the letting down of water over the earth occurs, until the earth putrefies and is cleansed. And when the philosophers saw the water decrease and the earth increase, they said it was waxing <term>ceratio: the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</term>; and when the whole becomes earth, they say it is congelation; when the matter becomes white, it is called calcination <term>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</term>. (The Monk, from a Manuscript, page 21).

<margin>The Desirable <note>Original: *Desiderabile*—likely referring to the alchemical treatise *Liber Desideratus* or a similar "desired" work.</note></margin>
Crush with fire, not with hands. For first, water strives to dissolve the earth, so that it may have a subtle nature after its own fashion. Secondly, the earth coagulates the water, so that it may endure the fire along with itself. And this is the dissolution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit. *The Desirable*, page 23.

The dissolution of bodies is the foundation of the Art, and it is a reduction into water: and from the reduction of water, there is then a reduction into earth, by adding nothing external, but only by removing what is superfluous. *The same author*, page 87.

Through a crude spirit, a digested spirit is extracted from bodies. *The same author*, page 264.

<image-desc>A manicule (pointing hand icon) in the left margin pointing towards the following paragraph.</image-desc>
Dissolution gives birth to blackness <note>The *nigredo* stage</note>, reduction to whiteness <note>The *albedo* stage</note>, fixation to yellowness <note>The *citrinitas* stage</note>, and waxing <term>inceratio</term><note>The process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note> to redness <note>The *rubedo*, or final stage</note>. Blackness is earth, whiteness is water, yellowness is air, and redness is fire. *The same author*, page 269.

<margin>Richard <note>Likely Richardus Anglicus, a 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note></margin>
Art imitates Nature, not in that it builds something new, but because it refines the power of that Nature. To these things Art begins to profit where Nature fails: to uncover the subtle nature enclosed within a thing, and to manifest it. *Richard, chapter 1.*

Crude Mercury dissolves bodies and reduces them into the first matter: but the Mercury of bodies <note>Mercury extracted from metals rather than common quicksilver</note> cannot do this. *The same author, chapter 1, pages 242–243.*

<margin>Dastin <note>Johannes Dastin (Daustricus), an influential 14th-century English alchemist.</note></margin>
Those things which are made of dissimilar parts possess their seed within themselves, from which they are multiplied and grow, as is seen in all living creatures and shrubs. But those things which are made of similar parts are not multiplied unless they are reduced to their first matter. *Dastin, page 2.*

Many Philosophers have put forward techniques for the veneration, concealment, and modification of their art—lest anything filthy or impure be introduced—such as mixing, cooking, sublimating, roasting, grinding, coagulating, rotting <term>putrefacere</term>, whitening, reddening, etc. Yet their regimen is only one: namely, to cook <term>decoquere</term>. *The same author, page 12.*

<margin>The Lord be with you <note>Original: *Dominus vobiscum*—a common title for anonymous alchemical tracts.</note></margin>
To dissolve is nothing other than a certain composition, complexion, or conjunction—that is, a binding of the primary virtues into one harmony, namely of the agents and the patients. *The Lord be with you.*

<margin>Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath; many alchemical works were attributed to him in the Middle Ages.</note></margin>
Note that entry, submersion, conjunction, complexion, composition, and mixing signify the same thing in this Art. *Avicenna, chapter 3, page 81.*

The spirit of metals is the other part of our stone, which it is necessary to evacuate from the bodies of metals: namely, from the two perfect ones through putrefaction, the division of elements, and their<gloss>m</gloss> fixation. *Lully in the Compendium of the Transmuting Soul, page 95.*

### CHEMICAL HARMONY.
<note>original: *Harmonia Chemica*</note>
4. Vol. H h h

To dissolve, to wash, to join, and to fix. To **dissolve** is to divide bodies and to create the "matter." To **wash** is to bury <note>The process of "inhumation" involves placing the vessel in a warm, dark place, often horse dung, to maintain a steady temperature.</note>, to distill, to ascend, and to descend. To **join** is to impregnate, to whiten, and to turn red. To **fix** is to ferment and to marry <note>original: *desponsare* — the "chemical wedding" or union of the volatile and fixed parts</note>. Dissolution converts the Stone into its first nature, which is its Water. Washing converts it into Air. Joining converts it into Fire. Fixing converts it into a spiritual and "tinging" <term>tingentem</term><note>A substance that has the power to permanently change the color and nature of another substance, usually into gold or silver.</note> Earth. *The Ladder of the Philosophers*, page 103.

<margin>Child’s Play <note>original: *Ludus puerorum* — a common title for alchemical treatises suggesting that, once understood, the Great Work is as easy as children's play.</note></margin>
Know for a truth that the Philosophers never intended for our Stone to be divided into four separate elements, as the foolish alchemists do. *Child’s Play*, page 142.

*To mix, to cook, to sublimate, to roast, to calcine, to whiten, to grind, to water, to tinge, etc.—these are many names, yet there is only one single regimen, which is performed in a single vessel by the power of fire. For Alphidius says: When we dissolve, we simultaneously calcine, sublimate, separate, and compose, and between the dissolution and the composition of the body and spirit, no interval of time passes. Chapter 19.*

<margin>The Rosary <note>original: *Rosarium* — likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational 13th-century alchemical text.</note></margin>
Conception and betrothal occur in the "putrefaction" at the bottom of the vessel. Putrefaction <note>The stage where the matter rots and turns black (nigredo), a necessary precursor to rebirth.</note> is achieved by the very gentle heat of warm, moist dung, and by no other means, so that nothing rises up. For if anything were to ascend, a separation of the parts would occur, which must not happen until the male and female are perfectly joined and one receives the other. The sign of this is a perfect dissolution or blackening on the surface, which is the "tincture," and therefore it must be preserved. *The Rosary*, page 198.

Burn in water, wash in fire: the whole work stands in dissolution. When the dissolution of the Stone is accomplished, it is then called the *first element*, namely Water. When the body is impure, it is called the *second element*, namely Earth. When the earth is calcined <term>calcinata</term><note>Reduced to a fine powder by high heat.</note>, it is called Fire; and when the fire is dissolved, it is called Air. *The same author*, page 203.

*To tinge* <note>To color or transform</note> is nothing other than transforming the substance being tinged into its own nature, and for it to remain with it without any further transformation; it is Nature teaching nature to fight against the fire. For the nature of the tinging agent and the nature of the thing tinged are in harmony. *The same author*, page 226.

It is asked: are the "red work" and the "white work" one and the same? It is answered that the Lunar <note>Silver</note> and Solar <note>Gold</note> stones are the same in essence, because both are perfected from their own Mercury. There is also one way in the method of acting, because the work is carried out through the same operations and in the same way and order. Therefore, it is one medicine according to all the philosophers, yet they differ in their fermentation. *The same author*, page 250.

These are the modes of operation for our Stone: 1. *sublimation*, 2. *descension* <note>Collecting a liquid as it flows downwards during heating</note>, 3. *distillation*, 4. *calcination*, 5. *dissolution*, 6. *congelation* <note>Turning a liquid into a solid</note>, 7. *fixation* <note>Making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, 8. *iteration* (which is sublimation), 9. *ceration* <note>Softening a hard substance until it has the consistency of wax</note>. *The same author*, page 256.

<margin>Dastin <note>John Dastin (c. 1293–1386), a famous English alchemist known for his correspondence with Pope John XXII.</note></margin>
To convert the elements is to make the moist dry, and to make the fleeing <note>volatile</note> substance fixed, strong, and capable of fighting against the fire. For when heat with cold—
