Thus a tempered mixture is formed, and the moist with the dry is blended. It is mixed for forty days, and conception <note>In alchemy, "conception" refers to the initial union of the "male" and "female" principles within the vessel.</note> occurs in the bottom of the vessel. This is done by a small fire, for a slow fire preserves moisture and perfects the melting; whereas an external fire consumes moisture and disturbs the melting. Nothing is dissolved unless the spirit is frozen, nor is the spirit frozen unless the body is dissolved. For when they are joined together, each acts upon the other: the earth is not made subtle except by the water, nor is the water thickened except by the earth. The soul flees the fire, but the earth endures it. Dastin <note>John Dastin (c. 1293–1386), a famous English alchemist.</note>, pages 31–32.

<margin>The Assembly of Philosophers <note>original: *Turba* — referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note></margin>**Calcination** is the removal of moistures; **dissolution** is the beginning of the Art; **preparation** is the taking away of the superfluous and the retention of the necessary; and **sublimation** is the sticking of a dry thing to the vessel. It is an elevation upward by means of fire, and from these things the body shall become spirit, and vice versa; the fixed shall become volatile, and the hard shall become soft, and vice versa. Thus the corporeal becomes incorporeal, and vice versa. For earth is turned into water, water into earth, and air into fire; and these things do not happen without heat and moisture. *The Assembly*, page 44.

<margin>Book of Three Words</margin>the Stone is divided into seven parts, which are *Conjunction, dissolution, Putrefaction, distillation, congelation, fixation, and projection*. *The Book of Three Words*, page 48.

<margin>Benedictus</margin>The Work is divided into seven parts: *solution, distillation, coagulation, sublimation, calcination, whitening, and reddening*. The first part to occur is *solution*, which takes place in heat and moisture because of weakness, so that from this a resolution occurs, which is called *dissolution, putrefaction, and digestion*. In this, you must temper the fire greatly, so that the soul may be drawn from its body by the spirit through this digestion—this is called the "Key of the Art." Then the matter becomes black, which is called the <term>Raven’s Head</term><note>Latin: *caput corvi* — a symbol for the *Nigredo* stage, where the substance "dies" and decays before its eventual purification.</note>. It is a mixing of earth with water, and vice versa, in the smallest parts, until they become one by means of this tempered fire. Therefore, in solution the fire should be gentle; in sublimation, moderate; in coagulation, tempered; in whitening, continuous; and in reddening, strong. Take note: although the philosophers have set down many ways of working, they did so to blind the minds of the ignorant. For there is but one medicine, one vessel, one regimen, and one disposition for making the White and the Red in succession. The **White** is completed by three things in which there is no fire <note>Likely referring to the stages of "cooling" or stabilizing the white tincture.</note>, but the **Red** is made from four, by which the true "tinging" <note>The power to transform the color and nature of metals.</note> is achieved. Benedictus, pages 56, 57, 58, 59.

<margin>Scotus <note>Michael Scot (c. 1175–1232), a medieval scholar and polymath often associated with alchemy.</note></margin>There are four regimens of the Stone: *to dissolve, to coagulate, to consolidate, and to fix*. Scotus, pages 61–62.

<margin>Ripley <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist and author of *The Compound of Alchymy*.</note></margin>Our **sublimation** is not understood as the common people understand it; rather, it is to make a high thing out of a low and corrupt thing. The same, page 63.

<meta>This page continues the technical definitions of alchemical processes found in the previous page's excerpt from the "Assembly of Philosophers." ### CHEMICAL HARMONY.

**Calcination** <note>The process of reducing a substance to a powder through heat.</note> is the cleansing of our stone, which restores it by its own natural heat and brings about the **solution** <note>original: *solutionem* — the liquefying of the solid stone into a "mercurial water."</note> that is primarily necessary for our stone. *Ripley, page 72.*

<margin>Saturninus.</margin>
**The fire of solution and putrefaction** <note>The "rotting" or breakdown of the matter, the first stage of the Work.</note> must be so weak that nothing of the nature to be sublimated rises up. Thus, a light fire is useful, for it gives Mercury entrance into the clean body; but by a strong fire, everything is lost. **The second fire** tempers and nourishes the stone gently. **The third fire** causes the alteration of the stone, making colors appear and emerge; this is called the **fire of drying and calcination**. **The fourth fire** brings the work to its end by fixing the spirit with the body, so that the whole becomes red. The first color is black, and it is generated by the first fire. After the blackness, various colors appear, and it is often dried and often liquefied before its perfection—which perfection proceeds from fire and Mercury with much patience. *Saturninus, page 71.*

<margin>Evalerandus.</margin>
**Inhumation** <note>original: *inhumatio* — burying the vessel in warm earth or dung.</note>, **putrefaction**, **distillation**, **decoction** <note>boiling or concentrated heating</note>, **digestion**, **descension**, **sublimation**, **separation of the elements**, **dissolution**, **congealing**, **waxing** <note>original: *ceratio* — softening the material to a wax-like state.</note>, **fixation**, **whitening**, **reddening**, **calcination**, and **mortification** <note>the symbolic death of the metals.</note>; to perform all these operations is actually just one single work—namely, the "cooking" of the Stone. All these operations occur within the same vessel, and in the same fire and furnace. *Evalerandus, page 113.*

<margin>Aureola</margin>
One must not labor to achieve transparency in the **Mercury**—that is, reducing it to a clear, see-through water as many "cooks" <note>A derogatory term for amateur alchemists who followed literal "recipes" without understanding theory.</note> do. For if Mercury were reduced into such a water, it would be uncontrollable in our work; it would neither be fixed nor congealed. *The Seventh Aureola, page 196.*

<margin>The New Pearl</margin>
Whatever the philosophers have said in their books—*Cook, roast, melt, descend, reiterate*, and so on—there is but one single operation in the fire. *Pythagoras in the New Pearl of Great Price, page 38.*

<margin>Richardus</margin>
Art begins where Nature leaves off, by uncovering the subtle nature hidden within a thing and making it manifest. Hence the philosophers say: "Nature generates metals, but it cannot generate **tinctures** <note>Elixirs capable of transforming base metals into gold or silver.</note>. Even though Nature contains the full tincture hidden within itself, and holds everything it needs, it is not perfected unless it is moved by Art and practical operation." *Richardus, chapter 1.*

<margin>Bella Ripa</margin>
To **sublimate bodies** is not the common sublimation intended by the ignorant, who believe that to sublimate is for a body to rise upward. Rather, the **sublimation of the philosophers** is to make something high and great out of a thing that is low and corrupt. That is, to transmute the black earth into white. Then the bodies are "sublimated"—meaning they are refined and converted into another nature, moving from blackness to whiteness. *Bella Ripa.*

<meta>This page continues David Lagneus’s compilation of alchemical authorities, transitioning from the technical definitions of fires and preliminary operations to the core processes of sublimation, solution, and the "nutrition" or growth of the Stone. # DAVID LAGNEUS

Through the **sublimation** <note>original: *sublimatione* — the process of vaporizing a substance and then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</note> of the stone itself, superfluities are removed, while the parts that are not **fixed** <note>Stable or resistant to heat.</note> are raised by smoke and wind away from the fixed parts. But we desire that these two be fixed together and offer an easy melting. Therefore, he who perfectly sublimates, also refines, and completes the entire work. *The same author.*

<margin>Roger Bacon</margin>
If the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>original: *Sol & Luna* — alchemical terms for Gold and Silver.</note> were more than perfect—whether by double, quadruple, a hundredfold, or beyond—they would perfect that which is imperfect. *Roger Bacon, page 53.*

<margin>Calid</margin>
**Solution and coagulation** <note>The liquefying of a solid and the solidifying of a liquid.</note> are in one operation, and they deserve to be called a single act; this occurs before the composition. But after their composition, the work will be different. These two which I have named—solution and congelation—are the **solution of the body** and the **congelation of the spirit**; they are two things, yet they share a single operation. For the spirit is not congealed except through the solution of the body; and likewise, the body is not dissolved except through the congelation of the spirit. When the body and soul are joined together, each of them acts upon its companion, making the other like itself. *Calid, chapter 1.*

Unless you convert the bodies into such **subtlety** <note>Finest powder or essence.</note> that they are refined and impalpable to the touch, you will not be guided to what you seek. *And if they have not been ground down, return to the operation until they are ground and become subtle. If you do this, you will be guided toward what you desire.* *The same author.*

**Composition** is the name given by many to the state after solution and congelation. *The same author.*

## C H A P T E R  V I I.

<margin>Isaac</margin>
Moisten the lower world with **May dew** <note>original: *rore Maiali* — a prized alchemical solvent, often collected from morning dew in spring, believed to contain universal life force.</note> until it bears white, yellow, and red flowers. Or, nourish the King with his own milk until he has grown up. Thus, every **solution** <note>The process of liquefying a solid.</note> is a **mortification** <note>Death or destruction of the previous state.</note>, just as every **congelation** <note>Solidification.</note> is a **vivification** <note>A bringing to life.</note> and the most immediate cause of life. *Lullius in the Codicillus, page 69.*

When the black matter is imbibed with water after separation through a filter, the black material on the **porphyry** <note>A hard igneous rock used as a grinding surface.</note> turns white; but as soon as the material is ground, the whiteness is hidden within the matter. This continues until the power of the water overcomes the power of the earth. However, before it reaches its true goal in the color of the earth, many and almost infinite colors will appear, of which no one could certainly give a full understanding. For in its **decoction** <note>Prolonged heating.</note>, the earth creates many gland-like or hump-like shapes, like bubbles, in which all the colors of the world appear, so radiant that one would rarely believe it unless they had seen it or experienced it themselves. *The same author, in the Summary Conclusion of the Testament, pages 66–67.*

Our **quicksilver** <note>original: *Argentum vivum* — Mercury.</note> enters and mixes equally with the other common kind, drying out its phlegmatic moisture and removing the coldness from the body, blackening it like coal, which it afterwards converts into powder. *The same author in the Clavicula, chapter 1.*

# DAVID LAGNEUS

The mastery is nothing other than to **perfectly dissolve** the stone and to **coagulate** it; and flee haste in these things, so that this happens by the gradual habituation of its own fire. <note>original: *assuefactione sui ignis* — refers to slowly acclimating the substance to the heat of the furnace.</note> *The same author, page 68.*

Water and fire suffice in the **whitening**. <note>original: *dealbatione* — the process of turning the "black" matter into "white" matter, a key stage in the Great Work.</note> *The same, page 69.*

Our water washes the filth from our earth. *The same, page 93.*

In this work, in its first composition, nothing foreign to its nature enters: thus, nothing multiplies it that is not of its first disposition. This Stone is nourished by much feminine seed—namely **Mercury**—applied to it unitively and sensibly in a composite way, though by means of **digestion**. <note>A process of gentle, continuous heat, similar to how a stomach digests food.</note> For like assumes like by composition and not by vegetable multiplication. For nothing nourishes and multiplies the aforementioned Stone under the generation of its own form except the seed that nourishes it through commingling. *The same, pages 192, 193, and the Fifth Aureola, page 193.*

### DAVID LAGNEUS

When water is mixed with the bronze <note>original: *æri* — referring to *aes*, meaning bronze, brass, or the impure metallic body being worked upon</note>, it whitens it from within. This whitening is called by some **impregnation**, because the earth is whitened. For while the water dominates, the earth grows and multiplies, and the increase of new offspring is generated from it. Take that which descends to the bottom of the vessel, and wash it with hot fire until the blackness is taken away from them and its thickness recedes, and make the additions of moisture fly away from it until it becomes an exceedingly white lime <term>calx: the powdery residue left after a substance has been roasted or "calcined"</term> in which there will be no stain. For then the earth is fit and ready to receive the soul. Join the dry with the moist—that is, the black earth with its own water—and cook it until it is whitened. That whiteness is called **air**. *The same author, pages 206, 207.*

*Dry earth does not produce much fruit unless it is moistened frequently from above by rain-water, and without water, it produces hardly anything or never.*
*The same, page 209.*

Pour in the water first by turns while grinding <note>original: *conterendo* — refers to the physical act of trituration or pulverizing the matter</note>, and afterward by lightly calcining, until the earth itself has drunk a fiftieth part of its own weight in water: knowing that it is necessary for the **Earth to be nourished first with a little water**, and afterward with more, just as one sees in the raising of an infant. Therefore, grind the earth much, gradually soaking it with water every eight days: because it makes the earth white. Beware, however, that you do not soak the earth except little by little, with long grinding—<insert>additionally</insert> after the drying of the earth. Then the weight <note>original: *pondus* — also implies "balance" or "proportion"</note> must be noted everywhere in this matter, lest excessive dryness or superfluous moisture corrupt it during the administration: namely, that you cook away by roasting as much as the dissolution added: and by soaking, you dissolve as much as the roasting removed. Therefore, every time after the calcination of the earth, pour water over it moderately, neither too much nor too little. Because if it is too much, it will become a sea of confusion; but if it is too little, **it is burnt into ashes**. For this reason, you shall irrigate the earth gently and without haste every eight days; you shall cook it in dung <term>fimo: horse dung was used in alchemical laboratories as a source of steady, gentle heat for incubation</term>, and you shall calcine it until it has drunk the fiftieth part of itself. And note that after the soaking, it must be **buried for seven days** <note>original: *inhumari* — "inhumation" or burial, referring to placing the vessel in a warm, dark place like a heap of dung or a sand bath</note>. Repeat the work many times, even though it may be long. For you will not see the tincture, nor the perfect profit, until it is completed. Therefore, if the earth is not white, grind it with water, and afterward calcine it again: because **Azoth and Fire wash the Laton, and take away the darkness from it**. <note>original: *Azoth & Ignis Latonem abluunt* — "Azoth" is the universal solvent or mercurial spirit; "Laton" refers to the impure, "black" state of the metal</note>. For the preparation is always made with water. Therefore, as is the clear water, so is the clear earth: and the more it has been washed, the whiter it becomes. *The same, pages 238, 239.*

*Fire and water wash the Laton, and wipe away its blackness.* *The same, page 248.*

# CHEMICAL HARMONY

The earth is mixed with its water, and the water is gradually diminished because of the temperate cooking <note>original: *decoctionem*</note>, and the earth grows: then it is said that the **ceration** <term>ceratio: the process of softening a hard or dry substance to a wax-like consistency</term> is perfected. This is because the earth is softened with the water, it is soaked, and by the temperate cooking of the "sun"—that is, the heat—it is dried out, and the whole nature is turned into earth. *The same author, page 257.*

<margin>Khalid</margin>
Unless you have refined the body until it becomes entirely water, it will not rust <note>original: *rubiginabitur* — in this context, it refers to the chemical change or "reddening" that precedes the final work</note>, nor will it rot; and it will not be able to congeal the "fleeting souls" <note>likely referring to volatile spirits like mercury or sulfur</note> when the fire touches them. For it is the fire that congeals them with its own help toward them. Likewise, the Philosophers have commanded us to dissolve the bodies, and we have dissolved them so that their heat might cling to their depths. Afterward, we return to dissolving those same bodies and to congealing them after their dissolution with the thing that has approached them, until we join all the mixed things in a good and suitable mixture, which is a temperate quantity. *Khalid, chapter 5.*

Take a male dog of Khorasan <note>original: *Corascenen* — referring to a region in Persia famous in alchemical lore</note> and a bitch of Armenia, and join them together, and they will give birth to a dog the color of the sky. Then, let him drink in a single thirst from the water of the sea, for he will guard your friend. Know that this work is a single stone, upon which no **stranger** <gloss>original: *Garib* — an Arabic term for a stranger or foreign substance</gloss> enters; that is, nothing else. *The same author, chapters 8, 9.*

Take the honored Stone and place it in a cucurbit <term>cucurbit: the lower, gourd-shaped vessel of a still</term>, and cover it with an alembic <term>alembic: the cap or "still-head" used for distillation</term>, and seal it well with the **lute of wisdom** <term>luto sapientiæ: a specialized sealing clay or paste used to make vessels airtight</term>, and let it dry. You shall do this as often as you seal it with the lute of wisdom. Afterward, place it in the hottest dung <note>rotting dung was used as a natural, steady heat source for "temperate" digestion</note> until the moisture is dried up and dryness prevails over it. *The same author, chapter 15.*

Make a light fire until a "patience" is established between the water and the fire, and until the spirit and the body become one. *The Monk, page 14.*

The dragon born in blackness feeds on its own Mercury, and is submerged in it, and by it, he is whitened a little bit. *The same, page 15.*

<margin>The Desirable</margin>

<margin>Arnaldus</margin>
Take the Stone and grind it with white milk, and it will be white: or grind the cheap with the dear, and it will be whitened. *Arnaldus de Villanova, On the Secrets of Nature, page 36.*

<margin>Dastin</margin>
The fire is the black earth at the bottom of the cucurbit; this fire, when it has drunk its own burning water, remains blackened for forty nights. *Dastin, page 30.*

# DAVID LAGNEUS

<margin>Benedictus</margin>
The mixing of water with earth occurs, and vice-versa, through the smallest parts <note>original: *per minima* — a term used to describe mixing at the most fundamental, almost atomic level</note>, until they become one, using a temperate fire. *Benedictus, page 56.*

<margin>Saturninus</margin>
Pay attention that in coagulation, the heat cannot be too light; and I advise you to always maintain a gentle fire, even if it delays perfection, provided that it is continuous. *Saturninus, page 73.*

<margin>Trevisanus</margin>
Just as nothing foreign to its nature enters into this work in its first composition, so it does not multiply anything that is not of its first disposition. This work does not "eat," because it does not grow biologically <note>original: *vegetat* — refers to vegetative or plant-like growth</note>. And although there is a body and a soul or spirit in the aforementioned **Philosophers' Stone**, it is not biologically animated like trees and plants, nor is it biologically nourished. Instead, there occurs in it a *multiplication by the addition of a nature similar to itself, and not by biological growth.* For like takes to itself like by addition; and the more it takes to itself and is multiplied, the heavier it becomes in quantity, and the more active and perfect it arises and emerges in quality. Thus, the flame of the fire does not multiply this stone of ours as if it were its required food—since fire is not of its primary composition, but is an external accident that warms it. He, therefore, who nourishes and multiplies the **Stone** in this way will not go astray, because that which multiplies it is converted into its very same species. *Trevisanus to Thomas, pages 157, 158, 159.*

<margin>Aegidius</margin>
When you are hungry and see food, you do not know how much of it is sufficient for you; but by eating, you immediately feel by the power of your stomach how much is suitable for you. Therefore, do the same in your mastery <term>magisterio: the technical process or "grand work" of the alchemist</term>. *Aegidius, page 27.*

Believe me, all your labor is lost unless your earth is revived by water; you will never see a true congealing <note>original: *congelationem*</note>. *The same author, page 81.*

<margin>Libavius</margin>
You who are a student of the Art, take this as a conclusion: you must first join quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note> to Mercury. When these reach the stage of cooking <note>original: *coctionis*</note>, they become the matter that dissolves gold—which does not simply form an amalgam with them as is known to goldsmiths, for such an amalgamation is of little use to the Art. Secondly, you shall join gold or the Moon <note>original: *Lunam* — the alchemical name for silver</note>, and cook it with a similar skill. *Libavius, in Defense of Alchemy, page 508.*

<margin>Ventura</margin>
Water assists in the whitening <term>dealbationem: the "albedo" stage of the work where the matter is purified until it turns white</term>; it is continually soaked into the earth and exhaled by heat—or rather, it is incorporated with the earth and dried out. Therefore, grind it often with its own water, and calcine it again, until the darkness completely recedes through the washing of water and fire. *Ventura, page 153.*

<margin>Isaac</margin>

You shall always sublime and fix the matter with a tiny fire, even though that time may be long. For when one works with a tiny fire, the matter better retains its own moisture. *Ibid. chapter 43.*

You must sublime with a very tiny fire indeed, so that the subtle, volatile spirit can first fly out from the **dregs** <note>original: *fecibus* — the "feces" or solid residue at the bottom</note> into the upper part of the vessel, before the middle spirit begins to exit from the dregs. *Ibid. chapter 113.*

## CHEMICAL HARMONY

[mate]rial <note>original: *[mate]riam* — completing the word from the previous page</note> blacken like pitch, even more so than before. Then increase your fire by a small degree; increase it significantly, so that it is perceived to be a little hotter than before. And keep the fire at that heat until you see another color, which is a reddish-ash, as if it were ashes. Then increase your fire still a little more, but not too much, so that it is like the Sun shines in April; and keep the fire at that heat until you see a greenish color, like the color of a **parrot's feather** <note>original: *plumæ psittaci* — a vivid green stage in the alchemical process</note>. Then increase the fire still a little more until you see a color like the **peacock’s tail** <note>original: *cauda pavonis* — the iridescent display of many colors appearing just before the transition to the white stage</note>, which has a hundred colors. Then increase your fire to that heat which is like the Sun in June, and no greater. And you shall not increase that fire until you see a perfect whiteness, and the **White Stone** <note>original: *Lapidem album* — the penultimate stage of the Great Work, capable of transmuting metals into silver</note> is perfect. Then add fire until you see the material take on an ash-like color. Then increase the fire a little, just one small degree, until you see a honey-yellow color, just like the curd with which tanners prepare their hides. Then increase your fire still one more small degree, and keep that governance of fire until you see a color just like crushed brick, between red and reddish-brown. Then increase your fire still a small degree, until you see an ash color again, as if it were bluish-gray ashes. And then increase the fire still a small degree. Truly, the ash color is the last of all the remaining colors to show itself. And now you shall increase your fire no more until the Stone is perfect. The first color you will see after this ash color will be a ruddy color, as if it were a rose, and gradually the color will sometimes become deeper, and little by little it will redden more and more, so that the material will turn out so red and of such a deep color that such a redness has never been seen by any human eyes. Then exult with the Philosophers: the Stone is perfect. *In the same place [Isaac], p. 131.*

<margin>Libavius</margin>
In an **aludel** <note>original: *aludele* — a pear-shaped ceramic pot or series of pots used for sublimation</note> vessel, let all that material be spread at its bottom: then let the fire be increased until its part, surpassing the whitest snow in its whiteness, clings like a dead thing to the joints of the vessel. *Libavius on Azoth, p. 92.*

<margin>Thomas</margin>
Believe me, that our whole mastery lies solely in the **governance of fire** <note>original: *regimine ignis* — the precise control of heat levels</note> through the capacity of industriousness. For we perform no work, but the power of well-directed fire works our Stone with modest labor and little expense: namely, that our Stone, when it has been once dissolved into its first nature—that is, into the first water or **virgin’s milk** <note>original: *lac virginis*</note> or the **dragon's tail** <note>original: *caudam draconis*</note>—then the Stone itself **calcines**, **sublimes**, **distills**, **reduces**, **washes**, **coagulates**, and by the power of proportioned fire, perfects itself in a single vessel, without any other manual operation. *Thomas Aquinas to Brother Reginald, chapter 3.*

<margin>Ventura.</margin> Let the fire be mild and equal, so that it neither increases in strength nor becomes weak. **Ventura**, chapter 20.

Fire is threefold among the Platonists: shining and burning, shining but not burning, and burning but not shining. A. Laurentius, *History of Anatomy*, book 11, question 3.

<margin>Libavius.</margin>
The whitening heat <note>heat used for the albedo or whitening stage</note> must not be excessive, otherwise it [the spirit] escapes. Note that in this passage he speaks of the first white color, which comes from nutrition. Libavius, p. 117.

<margin>The Assembly of Philosophers.</margin>
Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note> is fiery, burning every body more than fire, and mortifying bodies: and whatever body is mixed with it is ground down and given over to death. *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]" — one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts</note>, Statement 47.

<margin>Bacon.</margin>
Although we always speak of a slow fire, in truth we feel that in the governance of the work, the fire must be increased and made greater little by little and in turns until the end. Bacon, chapter 4.

## *On the Philosophical Vessel for making the physical Stone.*
### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Greverius</margin>
Carefully place your amalgam into a glass flask <note>original: "bociam"</note>, which is of such capacity that your sown and harrowed field <note>A metaphor for the alchemical ingredients prepared in the vessel</note> fills only a third part of it, leaving two parts empty. Afterward, seal the opening of your flask with the lute of wisdom <note>original: "luto sapientiæ" — a specialized airtight sealant used by alchemists to ensure the vessel was hermetically closed</note>; then you will have the Egg of the Philosophers, which is to say it is nothing but one vessel, one Stone, one cooking. Greverius, pages 21, 22.

It is very rare for a vessel to last from the beginning to the very end of the work. Yet you should not think the Philosophers lied when they say the Mastery <term>magisterium|The successful completion of the Great Work or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> is perfected in a single vessel. For when you hear this said, think immediately of the species <note>the specific type or design</note> and not the individual vessel, and thus you will grasp the truth. The same author, p. 39.

<margin>Alanus.</margin>
The vessel should be buried in ashes for half its part, and you shall take care that the other half stands out, so that you can inspect it daily. Alanus, p. 56.

<margin>Vogelius.</margin>
The vessels should be made of glass, wide at the bottom and ending in a point, like the figure called a Cone, or even convex and vaulted without a beak <note>i.e., without the delivery tube of a standard still</note>, like a "blind" alembic <note>original: "alembici cæci" — a vessel where vapors condense and fall back down into the base rather than being collected elsewhere</note>, to whose chambers and sides the sublimated spirits may adhere. The lower bowl should be made of earthenware, which may fitly receive the upper vessel within its walls. Vogelius, p. 89.

<margin>Libavius.</margin>
There ought to be several glasses of differing capacity. For in the beginning the quantity is small, but afterwards it grows. And yet nonetheless, if you look at the nature of the matter, it can be completed in one form of glass. Others have crescent-shaped and egg-shaped instruments; others prefer the form of an aludel <note>original: "aludelis" — a series of pear-shaped pots or tubes used in the process of sublimation</note>, so arranged that a narrower and cut-away neck can be

It emphasizes that while the process is said to take place in one vessel, this refers to a consistent design rather than a single physical object that must survive the entire operation.</summary>

*...[the neck of the] lower [vessel] into another glass, serving as a lid, just as if you were enclosing two segments of a sphere within one another. And this glass seems to me to be more suitable for frequent openings. For it is closed in the middle of the neck with paste smeared around the outside. But whichever vessel you use, let it be carefully obstructed <note>sealed or plugged</note>. Libavius on the Philosopher’s Stone, p. 110.*

<margin>The Desirable Thing <note>original: "Desiderabile"</note></margin>
*The Vessel of the Stone is one, in which the whole mastery <note>original: "magisterium"—the complete alchemical process</note> is completed; it should be thick, half a cubit long, round and flat at both bottom and top, and sufficiently wide. Its base should have a slight curvature, and the head should be wide so that the matter may ascend more freely. Let it be made of glass, so that the fumes do not escape, and therefore very tightly closed, lest our Mercury <note>The volatile "spirit" of the matter</note> be able to exit through the vessel itself. Desiderabile, p. 22.*

<margin>Book of Three Words</margin>
*The glass vessel must be round, with a long neck, whose mouth must be sealed with some lid, and it must be enclosed in another vessel, so that the heat does not immediately enter the matter; and thus it is cooked in a triple vessel. Book of Three Words, p. 49.*

<margin>The Game</margin>
*Hermes says: The Vessel of the Philosophers is their water. Children’s Game <note>original: "Ludus puerorum"</note>, p. 139.*

<margin>Flamel</margin>
*We need nothing but one vessel, one furnace, and one arrangement—which you should hear of after the preparation of the first stone. Flamel in Annotations, p. 150.*

<margin>Ventura</margin>
*Let the vessel be made of glass, firmly closed, round in the belly, and long and narrow in the neck to the measure of half a foot or thereabouts; and one vessel suffices. This vessel is called the egg, the sublimatory, the sieve, the sphere, the tomb, the prison, the ancient lion, the green lion, the urinal, the gourd <term>cucurbita</term>, the flask <term>bocia</term>, and by various other names. Laurentius Ventura, chapter 15.*

<margin>The Rosary</margin>
*In the work of our Mastery <note>the Great Work</note> we need nothing but a single vessel, one furnace, and one arrangement—which you must understand to apply after the preparation of the first Stone. The Rosary <note>original: "Rosarium Philosophorum"</note>, p. 211.*

*It should be noted that after the Stone has been purified and perfectly cleansed of every corrupting thing, and after it has been fermented, it does not need to change the vessel further, nor to be opened, but only that God might guard it lest it be broken. And for this reason the Philosophers said: In one vessel the whole mastery is completed. The same, p. 252.*

<margin>The Lord Be With You</margin>
*The vessel shall be of round glass, and it shall have a narrow and long neck, and the matter should not be placed within it without leaving two parts empty. The Lord Be With You <note>original: "Dominus vobiscum"</note>, p. 51.*

<margin>Scotus</margin>
*Place your matter in a strong round glass vessel, having a narrow and sealed orifice. Scotus, p. 60.*

<margin>The Women of Greece</margin>
*Take the Stone known to you and ground up: place it in an alembic <note>A distillation lid or apparatus</note> having but one hole at the top, which you must seal carefully, and place it in a very slow bath <note>Likely a "balneum Mariae" or water bath</note>. The Women of Greece, p. 92.*

The vessels necessary for this mastery <note>original: "magisterium," the complete alchemical process</note>, namely the aludels <note>pear-shaped glass or ceramic vessels used for sublimation</note>, are called by the Sages "cemeteries" or "sieves," because in them the parts are divided and cleansed; in them, the matter of the mastery is perfected, completed, and purified. *Khalid, chapter 2, pages 280, 281.*

->On the time for completing the physical work.<-

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>Thomas <note>Pseudo-Thomas Aquinas, to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note></margin>
Our matter perfects itself into the complete Elixir by turning itself into a very fine powder, which is called the "dead earth," or the "dead man in the tomb," or "thirsty magnesia" <note>a term for the crude matter at a specific stage of dryness</note>: because the spirit hidden within it is as if in a tomb, and the soul has, as it were, withdrawn. Therefore, allow it to stand from the beginning for up to twenty-six weeks; then the coarse has been made fine, the light heavy, the rough soft, and the sweet bitter, by the conversion of natures, secretly completed by the power of fire. *Thomas, chapter 5.*

<margin>Greverus</margin>
The Art cannot be perfected in a short space of time. Therefore, let the craftsman be patient. *Greverus, page 34.*

<margin>Ventura</margin>
The fewer days of preparation consist of the circuit and revolution of the greater luminary <note>the Sun; usually implying a year</note>. The Stone must be kept in the fire until it can no longer be changed from one nature into another, or from one color into another, but becomes like the reddest blood, flowing in the fire like wax, yet so fixed that it is never diminished. *Ventura, chapter 22, pages 121, 122.*

Let the craftsman be diligent and long-suffering in his work; let him not hurry, but without any madness of heart, anger, or fear, let him wait quietly and peacefully for the appropriate fruits after the due time, just as farmers do. *The same, chapter 28.*

<margin>Ripley <note>George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist</note></margin>
We take a year for our expectation. For in a shorter space of time, our lime <note>original: "calx," the powdery residue of a substance after heating</note> cannot be prepared. *Ripley, page 73.*

Those seeing the black color and the darkness and the evil depart after a long time, and a certain whiteness like the color of ash emerge, have called this "incineration" or "whitening." *The same, chapter 112.*

<margin>Libavius</margin>
The time in which the whole is finished is not defined with certainty among all authors. Some have referred it to ten months, or nine, in which a conception is perfected in the womb: although even this becomes une- <note>original: "fit inæ-", likely "fit inæquale" or "inæqualis," meaning "becomes unequal" or "varies"</note>

# CHEMICAL HARMONY #
Iii 3

...becomes unequal. Some have determined a three-year period, others even less. But many causes of inequality occur. Therefore, without an exact description of the time, they command the craftsman to act until perfection, and they determine individual actions by their own signs, so that they may know what should be instituted and when. *Libavius, page 108.* <note>Andreas Libavius was a 16th-century German chemist who attempted to organize alchemical knowledge into a systematic textbook.</note>

<margin>The Monk</margin>
The variation of times happens because of the quantity of the Medicine <note>original: "Medicinæ," referring here to the alchemical substance being transformed</note> and according to the industry of the craftsman. *The Monk, page 17.*

In purification there cannot be a limited time, but in ninety days the red work <note>original: "opus rubrum," the final stage of the alchemical process where the Stone reaches full power</note> is completed. *Ibid, page 20.*

In the first fifty days, the raven’s head <note>original: "caput corvi," a term for the "Nigredo" or black stage of decay</note> is made, and from there in one hundred and fifty the dove <note>original: "columba," the white stage or Albedo</note> will be made, and in another 150 it will become red: use a slow fire until whiteness. *Ibid, page 72; and also Saturninus.*

<margin>Unknown Author</margin>
The Medicine is not made in a few days, nor months, nor in a short time, since it is necessary for it to be tamed and nourished by the fire for a long time, indeed for quite a long time. *Unknown author.*

<margin>The Ladder</margin>
In the decoction <note>original: "decoctione," the long process of heating or "cooking" the matter</note> of this Art, the Philosophers have set many time limits. Some within a year, others within a month, others in *one day*, others in *three*. But just as we call that space from sunrise to sunset a "day": so they called that space between the beginning of the cooking and the end "one day." Those who say by the *month* speak in respect to the Sun, which runs through one sign of the heavens in a month. Those who say *three days* do so because of the beginning, middle, and end. Those who say a year, because of the four colors. *Ibid.* <note>Referring to the *Scala Philosophorum*, or "Ladder of the Philosophers," a popular alchemical treatise.</note>

<margin>The Ladder</margin>
When it has stood in Eclipse <note>original: "Ecclipsi," a period of darkness in the vessel representing the death of the matter</note> for five months, with the darkness receding and the light arriving, let the heat be increased. *The Ladder of Philosophers, pages 117, 118.*

<margin>Lully</margin>
The entire course of Nature is a space of two years. Hence the Stone is *one year and three months* old, because according to how it is destroyed, so it is generated. *Lully in Vademecum, page 160.* <note>Ramon Lully was a 13th-century polymath to whom many later alchemical works were attributed.</note>

<margin>The Rosary</margin>
The time for the perfection of the Elixir is at least *one year*. *The Rosary, page 179.* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* is one of the most famous illustrated alchemical texts.</note>

Know that this is the *longest way*. Therefore patience and delay are necessary in our mastery. *Ibid, pages 183, 210.*

I tell you that you should endure patiently, because perhaps it is delayed, and indeed haste is from the devil. Therefore, he who does not have patience should withdraw his hand from the work: because belief hinders him as he hastens. *Ibid, page 247.*

In forty days and nights the work for the white <note>original: "opus ad album," the stage of purification and silver-making</note> is completed after the true purification of the Stone. Because in purification there can be no determined time, except according to how well the craftsman works, and in ninety days and nights the work for the red is completed. And these are the true terms for the whole perfection. Understand this regarding the coagulation which happens after...

### C H A P T E R  X I.

<margin>Isaac</margin>
In a short space of time you will see all the matter turn black; then you may know that the true conjunction <note>The joining of the chemical "male" and "female" principles.</note> has occurred, and that whiteness lies hidden beneath the blackness. And know that unless the blackness <note>original: "nigredo," the first major stage of alchemy, signifying death, decay, and the stripping away of old forms.</note> shows itself in the work, there will be no mixture nor conjunction: nor could one ever be fixed with the other. And where no blackness shows itself, there no fixation between soul, spirit, and body happens. *Isaac <note>Likely referring to Isaac Hollandus, a famous alchemical author.</note>, book 1, chapter 64.*

When the blackness is seen, be certain that the true conjunction has been made. *The same [Isaac], ibid. c. 67.*

Before the clear, shining color arrives, all colors—as many as exist in the world—will appear and pass away; then you will see a great and remarkable whiteness, so that it will seem to you: "this is the true whiteness." But it will not be the true whiteness. Before the true whiteness comes, you will see around the edges of the glass, in the matter of the Stone, as if there were Oriental gems marked on the glass, like the eyes of fish. And when you see this, be certain that in a few days the perfect whiteness <note>original: "albedo," the second major stage of the work, representing purification and the "White Stone."</note> will manifest itself. And when you see the matter as white as snow, and having a brilliance like Oriental gems, which are highly notable for their clarity, as the matter...

...which is in the glass; rejoice. For the **White Stone** <note>The "White Stone" refers to the stage of the alchemical process where the matter has been purified enough to transmute metals into silver.</note> is perfect. Let it cool of its own accord. *The same [The Monk], chapter 131.*

Join the water well with water and the moist with the dry, so that afterward you may see the **blackness of the sea**, that is, the dark color, which you will see in its **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrefactione," the stage where the matter "dies" and rots, a necessary step before rebirth into a higher form</note>, which takes place in the space of twenty-nine days at a small fire: which is the perfect sign of a proven **conjunction** <note>The union of the opposing alchemical principles, often symbolized as a marriage.</note>. *The same, book 2, chapters 6 & 33.*

The secret of our true dissolution is the **Blackness** made like a coal from the **Sun and Moon** <note>The "Sun" and "Moon" are the alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver, or the masculine and feminine principles.</note>: and from this at last they are truly joined together, so that they are never separated from each other, and they become a very white powder, which are the male and female generated by the true bond of love. *Lullius, chapter 1.*

<margin>Greverius</margin>
When the predetermined days have passed, consider whether the first color has already changed from whiteness into a dark gray, or a black diluted with a certain whiteness. If you see this, rejoice: because you have supplied the legitimate heat, and now your **female** <note>The "female" usually refers to the passive or volatile principle in the crucible, often associated with Mercury.</note> is seen to germinate by this very sign. *Greverius, pages 24, 25.*

The first sign of the matter will appear as a color of dark redness almost turning black, showing a brick-color, which you recognize as neither black, nor red, nor brown, but a certain mixture of all these. Another sign is the **dryness of the earth**: which you will understand from this, if there is no more increase of exhalations than before. Signs of perfect maturity are a red color with intense yellowness <note>original: "citrinitate," the yellowing stage of the work</note>, shining somewhat, and a lack of exhalations. *The same, page 36.*

Mostly in the space of forty days a certain blackness appears like pitch: which is nothing other than the indication of the dissolved body. For whatever has been made **spiritual** <note>In alchemy, a substance becomes "spiritual" when it is vaporized or refined into its essence.</note> seeks the upper parts or the height, and everything earthy remains at the bottom, and everything light tends upward, while everything heavy tends downward. But when the **raven** <note>original: "corvus." The raven is the primary symbol for the "nigredo" or black stage of the work.</note> has been dissolved from its water and reduced into blackness and an incomprehensible essence, then the tincture of the solution is ready in the blackness. Thus, finally, the four elements come together into one. Whatever has been dissolved with **Mercury** will raise itself again, although the larger portion continually remains below. *The same, page 56.*

<margin>Alanus.</margin>
When the matter has stayed in moderate heat for the space of 40 days, a certain blackness like pitch begins to appear above, which is the **Raven's Head** <note>original: "caput corvi," a famous alchemical term for the peak of the blackening stage.</note> of the Philosophers, and the Mercury of the Wise. *Alanus, page 63.*

<margin>Garland.</margin>
This Stone is three-fold and one, having four natures, and three colors, namely: black, white, and red. *Garland, chapter 13.*

<margin>Ripleus.</margin>
All colors will appear before the perfect white, and after that the yellow and false yellow: then the unchangeable blood-red.

<page-num>872</page-num>
<header>OF DAVID LAGNEUS</header>

Then you have a medicine of the third order <note>Alchemists categorized the potency of their "medicines" or transmuting agents into three orders; the third is the most powerful and capable of being increased in volume and strength.</note>, multipliable in its own kind. *Ripley, p. 90.*

<margin>Arnold</margin>
Once the form of the bodies is first dissolved into our Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium nostrum," referring not to common quicksilver, but the "philosophical" mercury used as a universal solvent.</note>, a new form is immediately introduced, their original form having been destroyed: which form is first black in color, foul in smell, and subtle and fragmented to the touch. *Arnold [of Villanova] in The Mirror, p. 55.*

Heat acting upon moisture generates blackness first, and within blackness, whiteness; in the white, yellowness; and in the yellow, redness. *The same author, ibid., p. 22.*

In the hour of conjunction, the greatest wonders appear. For all the colors in the world that can be imagined appear during the operation, and the imperfect body is colored with a firm coloration by means of the ferment <note>The "ferment" is the substance added to the base matter to initiate the transformation into gold or silver, much like yeast in bread.</note>. *The same author, in The Flower of Flowers.*

Matter can in no way be so destroyed that it does not always remain under some form. Whence, the first form of the body having been dissolved into Mercury, a new form is immediately introduced, the form of those [the perfect bodies] having been corrupted. This form is indeed black in color, foul in odor, and subtle and fragmented to the touch. And this is the sign of the perfect dissolution of the bodies, because heat acting upon moisture first generates **blackness**: which blackness is the **raven's head** <note>original: "caput corvi." A classic alchemical symbol for the stage of deep putrefaction and the beginning of the Great Work.</note> and the beginning of our work. *The same, book 2 of the Rosary, chapter 4.*

<margin>The Monk</margin>
When you are in the work, see to it that you first have the black color, which is the key of the Art: and then you will be certain that you are proceeding correctly. *The Monk, p. 16.*

<margin>Dastin</margin>
When it first turns black, we say it is the key of the work, since it does not happen without blackness. For it is the very tincture <note>A "tincture" is the concentrated essence or soul of the metal that allows it to change the color and nature of other substances.</note> that we seek. *Dastin, p. 16.*

The whitening <note>original: "Dealbatio." The Albedo stage.</note> does not occur except by cooking and the congealing of the water: and the more it is washed, the more intensely it is whitened. *The same, p. 47.*

As long as the blackness appears, the dark female <note>In alchemical allegory, the "female" often represents the lunar, moist, or passive principle (Mercury) which must be purified.</note> dominates. And she is indeed the first power of our Stone; since unless it is first black, it will not become white nor red, because red is composed of black and white. *The same, p. 28, and The Children's Game, p. 144.*

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
When the earth is not **white**, grind it with its own water, and calcine <note>To "calcine" is to heat a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder or ash.</note> it again, because Azoth <note>A term for the universal spirit or solvent.</note> and fire wash the brass <note>original: "latonem," referring to the base or unrefined metal often called 'laton'.</note>, and snatch away its darkness from it. For preparation is always with water, and as the suitability of the water is, so will be the clarity of the earth: and the more washing there is, the more the earth will be white. *Avicenna, chapter 5, p. 83.*

<margin>The Ladder of Philosophers</margin>
When it has drunk its burning water, it turns black, and remains in the shadow of purgatory <note>A metaphorical term for the transitional state of purification between the death of the old form and the birth of the new.</note> for one hundred and fifty-six nights. *The Ladder, p. 129.*

### CHEMICAL HARMONY.
Lii 5
<meta>catchword: with you</meta>

<margin>The Children's Play</margin>
Regarding our copper <note>original: "Æs nostrum." In alchemy, "copper" or "bronze" usually refers not to the common metal, but to the base material of the Great Work at a specific stage of its preparation.</note>, the more it is cooked, the more it is dissolved and blackened, and it becomes a more subtle and spiritual water. Secondly, the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened and dried, and it becomes of a greater whiteness. Thirdly, the more it is cooked, the more it is colored and reddened, and it becomes a tincture of a deeper *redness*. *The Children's Play <note>A common alchemical title, "Ludus Puerorum," suggesting that once the secret is known, the work is as easy as a child's game.</note>, pages 143, 144.*

<margin>Flamel</margin>
The colors of the elements in the work are: from the feet to the knees, the earthy element, which is *black*; from the knees to the navel, the watery element, which is a *shining white*; from the navel to the heart, the airy element, which is a *citrine yellow*; and from the heart to the neck, the fiery element, which is *glowing and red*. Democritus, cited in Flamel's Annotations, page 176.

<margin>The Rose Garden</margin>
That black earth in the beginning stays above the water, and gradually it is submerged into the bottom of the vessel. *The Rose Garden of the Philosophers <note>original: "Rosarium," a famous 16th-century alchemical text.</note>, page 182.*

Its disposition is first to *blacken and rot*. The same author, page 195.

When you see your matter *blacken*, rejoice: for it is the beginning of the work. Therefore, burn our copper with a light fire, just like a nurse tending eggs, until the body is established and the tincture is extracted. The same author, pages 197, 200, 201.

Some have said that *all colors* that can be imagined in the whole world appear in the work of the stone. This is a sophistry of the philosophers, since only *four* principal colors appear. And because all others draw their origin from these, they therefore said "all colors." And if they do not appear to you, do not worry, as long as you can separate the elements. For *Citrine* <note>A pale yellow-green color.</note> signifies burnt choler and fire; *Redness* signifies blood and air; *Whiteness* signifies phlegm and water; *Blackness* signifies melancholy and earth. Having four colors, there are four elements. <note>The author is linking the stages of alchemy to the Four Humors of ancient medicine: yellow bile (choler), blood, phlegm, and black bile (melancholy).</note> The same author, pages 201, 203.

<margin>Dastin</margin>
The fire is the black earth at the bottom of the cucurbit <note>original: "cucurbitæ," a gourd-shaped chemical glass vessel used in distillation.</note>; which fire, when it has drunk its own burning water, remains blackened in the shadow for forty nights. And thus it conceives in the baths and gives birth in the air. *Dastin, page 30.*

The emergence of the black tincture is a sign of solution and full putrefaction. For blackness is the beginning of the medicine. The same author, pages 31, 32.

<margin>Book of Three Words</margin>
Blackening is the sign of solution, and it is called the "vinegar of the philosophers," and from there it comes to whiteness; but many intermediate colors appear, and after the whiteness follows *redness*. *The Book of Three Words, page 48.*

<margin>Example of Science</margin>
Our body is liquefied when it has been **made black** and thickened. *The Example of Science, page 93.*

<margin>The Master</margin>
The colors are only three: *black, white, and red*. Those which come between are called *intermediate* and they change; and when they no longer...

<margin>Ventura</margin>
To the whitening <note>original: "dealbationem." This refers to the transition from the black stage (nigredo) to the white stage (albedo).</note>, the water cooperates, which is continually imbibed with the earth itself and exhales by heat; or rather, it is incorporated with the earth and dried. Therefore, grind it often with its own water, and calcine <note>To "calcine" is to heat a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances and reduce it to a powder.</note> it repeatedly, until the darkness completely recedes through the washing of water and fire. Ventura, p. 153.

<margin>Libavius</margin>
*The whiteness that comes through nourishment is compared to the brightness of white lead <note>In alchemical symbolism, "white lead" often refers to tin, the metal of Jupiter.</note>. Therefore, it is not to be believed that this is the one desired in the perfect Stone. Thus, this dominion is assigned to Jupiter, whose whiteness is not fixed and still retains a certain lividness. Therefore, the whitening heat must not be excessive; otherwise, it flees.* Libavius <note>Andreas Libavius (c. 1555–1616) was a German physician and alchemist known for his attempt to organize alchemy into a coherent science.</note>, p. 117.

*It is asked whether the raven’s head <note>The "Raven's Head" (caput corvi) is a traditional name for the black stage of the alchemical work, symbolizing decay, death, and the separation of elements.</note> came from the dissolved body or from burnt Mercury? For those who consider it a mere impurity judge most poorly.* The same author, in *The Key of Lull*, p. 281.

*Do not believe that the water itself—which remains white—is blackened, but it appears black because of a floating spirit or black sulfur; once this is separated, its native brightness returns, which later, with the help of fire, is the cause for that earth also to be whitened.* The same author, *On Azoth* <note>Azoth is the "universal solvent" or essential spirit sought by alchemists.</note>, p. 89.

<margin>Turba</margin>
*When the water is whitened (which is called Ethelia <note>Ethelia is a term used in the Turba Philosophorum to refer to a sublimated spirit or vapor.</note>), it makes white and colors.* Assembly of Philosophers <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" is a famous early Latin alchemical text that takes the form of a debate among ancient philosophers.</note>, Maxim 56.

<margin>Another Turba</margin>
*What is it that produces blackness? Certainly the watery and combustible humidity; it is a watery smoke, of which it is said that watery and combustible humidity corrupts the work and stains it into blackness. This is called Saturn <note>Saturn is the planetary symbol for lead, the "heaviest" and "darkest" metal, associated with the beginning of the work.</note>, or lead, or bronze by the Sages of this art, because of its blackness and impurity; from which blackness and impurity a cleansing must be performed.* Another Assembly of Philosophers, from a very ancient manuscript, p. 65, 66.

*When coldness and humidity begin to be altered, the body is made black like a coal.* The same source, p. 70.

<margin>Rosinus</margin>
*Blacken the earth, and separate from it its soul and water; afterwards whiten it, and you will find what you seek.* Rosinus to Eutichia.

*The second work is done thus (the first work, which is the amalgam, having been listed): Place this water in an earthen vessel over a slow fire until you see blackness appear on top; remove it carefully whenever it appears. Then you will have water and earth. Over this earth, or blackness enclosed in a glass vessel, pour the blessed water <note>original: "aqua benedicta." In alchemy, "blessed water" is a metaphorical name for a specific purified solvent, not necessarily holy water in a religious sense.</note> until the water becomes white and clear.* The same author, to Sarratanta, p. 282.

<margin>The New Pearl</margin>
The first of the colors is black, which, as it appears first, so it appears more difficultly than the others; it shows that heaven has lain with form and has conceived: and without doubt there shall arise the desired perfection and the perfecting "poison" <note>original: "venenum informans." <margin>The Phoenix</margin>
When blackness appears in the work, know that you have already found the right way of operating. Therefore you ought then to rejoice, since the greatest gift has been granted to you by God. *The Phoenix*, p. 75.

### The method of fermenting the physical Stone.

## CHAPTER XII.

<margin>Isaac Hollandus</margin>
Take four parts of the ferment, two parts of your prepared spirit, and grind them together finely, so that they might be painted with a brush. Dry it; and once dried and fixed, take for every four parts of the matter one part of spirit, which together make five parts. Mix and dry as before; once dried, take again a fifth part of spirits, as before, for four parts of matter. Then put it into its own glass as before, and do this for so long until the matter melts like wax. Isaac Hollandus <note>Isaac Hollandus was a legendary Dutch alchemist, likely a pseudonym for a group of writers, whose works focused on practical laboratory procedures.</note>, book 1, chapter 9.

The ferment must perish <note>That is, be completely dissolved or transformed.</note> with the spirit and body, or earth, otherwise you lose your labor: and in ascending it becomes subtle and of great virtue, and is united to its own body. Wherefore the Sages have called the ferment the Soul, when they say: *The spirit attracts the soul into the higher regions, and it descends again into the lower regions.* Same source, chapter 35.

Then indeed take eight parts of ferment—that is, if you have eight ounces of ferment, weigh out one ounce of your sublimated spirit—and also put it in a small glass, and pour distilled water over it, and also pour distilled water over the ferment. Same source, chapter 64.

I teach you to take eight parts of ferment and one of spirit: because you will often fix the work, and often calcine <note>To heat a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder or change its chemical state.</note> and congeal it, and the work will turn out as subtle as possible in the bottom, so that afterwards it may arrive at a higher projection <note>"Projection" is the final step where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver.</note>. Same source, chapter 69.

<margin>Lullius</margin>
*The ferment is made after the birth of the child <note>The "child" or "infant" is a common alchemical metaphor for the Stone in its early, developing state.</note>. Moreover, the ferment is nothing other than nutritious food, convertible into the essence of the child, so that the entire work may be made of a single nature. This nutritional fermentation ought to be of its own proper nature and be assimilated to itself; for unless it were assimilated to it, it would never be incorporated into their nature, nor converted into the nature of sulfur.* Lullius in the *Codicillus*, p. 70. <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315) was a Majorcan philosopher; many alchemical works were later attributed to him.</note>

<margin>Ripley</margin>
*Fermentation is the incorporation of the soul with the body, restoring to it its natural odor, taste, and color, through the natural thickening of separated things.* Ripley, p. 85. <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490) was a famous English alchemist and canon of Bridlington.</note>

<margin>Vogel</margin>
*The ferment shall not be of this or that thing, but only of the Sun and Moon <note>In alchemical code, the Sun (Sol) refers to gold, and the Moon (Luna) refers to silver.</note>. For we seek nothing except that the stone be converted into its like: because the whole temperament is from them: nor is there a ferment before the said bodies are converted into their first matter.* Vogel, chapter 1, p. 10. <note>Ewald Vogel was a 16th-century physician and alchemical writer.</note>

<margin>The Desirable Thing</margin>
*In fermentation, see to it that the quantity of the volatile does not exceed the quantity of the fixed; otherwise the marriage bond of the body will be turned to flight. But if a little sulfur is projected upon much of the body, so that it has power over it, it quickly converts it into a powder, the color of which is like that of the body. One ounce of powder to four ounces of the body.* *The Desirable Thing*, p. 26. <note>Original title: "Desiderabile," likely referring to the "Desiderabile Desideratum."</note>

<margin>Arnald</margin>
*Know that there is no ferment except the Sun and Moon, that is, gold and silver.* Arnald in the *Flower of Flowers*. <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311) was a celebrated physician and alchemist.</note>

<margin>The Blare</margin>
*Fermentation is the animation of the stone itself.* *The Blare*, p. 46. <note>Original title: "Clangor Buccinae" (The Blare of the Trumpet), an influential 15th-century alchemical text.</note>

*The white ferment is made thus: Feed one part of the purest Moon <note>Silver</note>, filed into tiny bits or finely beaten into leaves, with double its weight of Mercury, which must be very clean and white. Grind them together strongly in a stone mortar until the Mercury drinks up the filings and becomes like butter, so that nothing of the filings can be found. Then wash it with <term>oxalme</term> <note>original: "oxalme," a cleaning mixture of vinegar (oxos) and salt (als).</note>, then with water, and afterwards dry it with fire. Add one part of white sulfur, grinding the whole until it returns to being as one body. Then soften it <note>original: "incera," literally "to wax," meaning to bring to a soft, waxy consistency.</note> with one part water, and send it to be sublimated. In the same way, the red ferment is made with the purest Sun <note>Gold</note>.* Same author, p. 50.

*If you do not mix the ferment with the elixir, the body is not colored as it ought to be: because without the ferment, neither the Sun nor Moon will emerge, but something else which does not remain in the tincture of a metallic nature, unless you have prepared it—namely, the imperfect body.* Same author, p. 51, 58.

<margin>The Rosary</margin>
*The imperfect body is colored with a firm coloration by means of the ferment; this ferment is the soul of the imperfect body, and the spirit is joined and bound to the body by means of the soul,*

Son, extract from the ray its shadow <note>original: "extrahe à radio suam umbram"; a famous alchemical aphorism meaning to extract the essential light or spirit from the material body</note>. Take, therefore, a fourth part of it—that is, one part of the ferment and three parts of the imperfect body <note>the base metal intended for transmutation</note>: dissolve the ferment in an equal amount of Mercury-water <term>Mercury-water: a specialized solvent or "philosophical mercury" used to break down metals</term>. <margin>Dastinus</margin>
If we wish to make gold <note>original: "Solem" (the Sun)</note>, we apply Gold; and if silver <note>original: "Lunam" (the Moon)</note>, we apply Silver for the ferment. If you do not provide a ferment, it will not be colored; and if you do not prepare the body, it will not withstand the fire; and if you apply too little ferment, you will have too little of the tincture <note>the concentrated power of the Stone to change other metals</note>. *Dastinus, page 30.* <note>John Dastin (c. 1293–1386) was a prominent English alchemist and member of the papal court at Avignon.</note>

<margin>The Lord Be With You</margin>
Take four parts of the ferment (*now, the ferment is something other than cooked Mercury; for it is cooked by "drinking" and "feeding"—because the dry substance drinks the moist*) and one part of the total Mercury, and amalgamate them thus: Heat the ferment by itself, and heat the Mercury in another vessel; and when the Mercury begins to boil and the ferment to glow with heat, cast the Mercury upon the ferment. Afterward, stir it with a rod so that no more of the Mercury appears. This being done, heat as much Mercury as you did before; but do not heat the ferment further so that it glows (lest the Mercury should escape), but it is enough that it be hot. When the Mercury begins to boil, cast it upon the ferment, stirring as before, and it will be swallowed up immediately, and the matter will be dry. Again, heat more Mercury and do as before, until there is as much Mercury as there is ferment. Then place the whole in a vessel, just as at the beginning, over a slow fire, for two days; and for another two days, increasing the fire slightly. Do this every two days until twelve days have passed. In this way, the whole matter will be ferment. If you wish to increase it further, do as before, infinitely. *The Lord Be With You, p. 55.* <note>*Dominus Vobiscum* is the title of a medieval alchemical treatise frequently quoted in compendiums.</note>

<margin>The New Pearl</margin>
"Ferment" is understood in two ways: either for the black powder, while it reduces the Mercury to itself; or for Gold or Silver. And it is called ferment, as if from "fervor" <note>original: "fervore," meaning boiling or heat</note>, because it causes the paste <note>the alchemical mixture</note> to boil, bubble, and grow. It possesses a single substance that is uniform throughout, and it holds a victorious and dominating hidden power that converts the paste into its own likeness. For by rectifying the matter, it leads it back to a worthier and better state. *The New Pearl, pages 110, 111.* <note>The *Margarita Preciosa Novella* (The New Precious Pearl) was written by Petrus Bonus of Ferrara in the 1330s; it is famous for comparing alchemical transformation to the way leaven works in dough.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of fermentation in the alchemical process, specifically focusing on the philosophical union of the three parts of the Stone: soul, spirit, and body. It transitions from the general theory of Lagneus to practical recipes found in the "Semita" (The Path) and the writings of Rosinus.</meta>

<header>DAVID LAGNEUS</header>

...the soul can be detained without its body. Such a union, however, takes place by means of the *spirit*: because the soul cannot have life in its body, nor any permanence, except through the spirit: and such a union and conjunction is the end of the work. It is necessary that the soul be joined with its own first body from which it came, and not with another. Unless you do this, you will fail in your purpose, as many of the ignorant do, because they are unaware of this secret. Just as matter has no being without form, but its entire being and dependency is upon form: so the soul, by means of the spirit, cannot exist in the stone itself except through the body: because their being and perfection depend upon the body. Similarly, therefore, it is clear that the body is the form: because that which disposes a thing in its final disposition, and completes it, is its specific form. But the body is of this kind. Therefore [the body is the form]. Similarly, since every composite is made of matter and form, and the spirit itself is the matter: Therefore the body will be the form <note>Lagneus uses Aristotelian logic here, arguing that the "body" of the metal gives the final "form" or identity to the alchemical Stone</note>. *Ferment* whitens the confection, inhibits combustion, and contains the tincture <note>the transforming power</note> lest the bodies flee <note>evaporate or escape the vessel</note>; it softens them, and causes them to enter and be joined to one another, which is the end of the work. *Ferment of gold is gold*: just as the leaven of dough is dough. *The same, and page 112.*

When the stone has been liquefied through decoction <term>decoction: a process of boiling or heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence</term>, it must then be coagulated. This coagulation, however, is done with the ferment, or with its own body, which is the same thing. And this is properly Alchemy, in an instrumental sense. *The same, page 116.*

In this conjunction of resurrection, the whole body becomes spiritual just like the soul itself, and they thus become one like water mixed with water, and they are not separated from one another for all eternity: since there is no diversity in them, but rather unity and identity of all three, namely spirit, soul, and body, without separation forever. *The same, page 120.*

<margin>The Path</margin>
Take of any ferment whatever its fourth part: for example, if there were one pound of the imperfect body—that is, of value—take from the ferment, which is the *Sun* <note>Gold</note> or the *Moon* <note>Silver</note>, three pounds: and let that ferment be dissolved and made into earth, just like the imperfect body, and prepared in the same way and order. Join them together and imbue them with the aforementioned blessed water <note>original: "aqua benedicta"; usually refers to a potent alchemical solvent like philosophical mercury</note>, and cook for three days or more. Then imbue it again with its water, and cook as before: and reiterate this as many times as necessary until these two bodies remain as one, that is, they are reduced into one. You will weigh this when the color in them does not vary. Then pour water over it little by little, and let it drink as much as it can drink, always giving it new water. *Semita, p. 72.* <note>The "Semita Semitae" (The Path of Paths) is a practical alchemical manual often attributed to Albertus Magnus</note>

<margin>Rosinus</margin>
If there be one pound of the imperfect body, let the ferment be a fourth of a pound. <note>Rosinus, or Zosimos, was a famous Greco-Egyptian alchemist; here he offers a different ratio of ingredients than the previous text</note>

...pounds. For the Ferment is the Sun and the Moon <note>original: *Sol & Luna*; in alchemy, these represent gold and silver</note>, and there are no other ferments. And when the ferment is thus dissolved and turned into earth like an imperfect body, prepared in the same way and order, join and soak <note>original: *imbibe*; the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it is saturated</note> them together, etc. Rosinus, page 283.

<margin>Rackaib</margin>
The powder released by the first release is called the first elementated ferment. Therefore, give to it the second fermented ferment, composed equally of every elementated element, which is gold: give it a fourth part. However, this should first be calcined <note>reduced to a powder through heat</note> and dissolved into water, for this is the "elementated water" balanced by all the elements. Give it the second ferment. When I say the second, I bring the "second retainer," and in it is the sulfurous <term>tincture</term> <note>the substance that possesses the power to transform other metals</note>, and it is called the "oil of retainers." Give it saffron-colored water: give it dry and hot water, with a subtle soaking, namely drop by drop. For if you were to give it less of these drinks, Rachaidib would be ruined. Page 399.

<margin>Khalid</margin>
Spirits are fleeting <note>volatile; they evaporate easily when heated</note> until bodies are mixed with them and strive to fight against the fire and its flame. Yet these parts agree very little except through good operation and continuous, long labor. This is because the nature of the <term>soul</term> <note>the volatile part of the metal</note> tends upward, which is where the soul's center lies. And who among the practitioners is capable of joining two diverse things whose centers are different, except after the conversion of their nature and the change of the substance and the thing from its own nature? This is a difficult thing to seek. Therefore, he who is able to convert the soul into the body and the body into the soul, and mix subtle spirits with it, will transform every body. Khalid, chapter 6.

### *The method of multiplying the physical stone.*

## CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>Isaac</margin>

This powder should be placed in a vessel <note>original: *metretio*; a Greek-derived term for a liquid measure or jar</note> sealed hermetically and kept over a moderate fire for four days; increase this up to eight days. Then place the matter within two crucibles luted <note>sealed together with "lute," a specialized airtight clay</note> together, and apply a strong fire for the space of twenty-four hours. Then cover it with coals, and once cooled, repeat if you wish, and you will have a marvel. For the Moon <note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical code for silver</note>, take equal parts of Mercury and white medicine, and proceed as above. Anonymous.

### C H A P T E R  X V.

<margin>Isaac.</margin>
If you wish to perform a Projection upon Jupiter <note>alchemical name for tin</note>, you shall melt it in a crucible, and place one ounce of pure Luna <note>silver</note> upon a pound of Jupiter, and melt them together; then cast your white stone upon it, and then the Jupiter will be transmuted into true Luna, more or less, depending on how refined <note>original: *subtilis*</note> your stone is. And if you wish to work with your red stone, you shall cast it upon Luna, melting it, and cast your red stone upon it, and it will become true Sol <note>gold</note>. *Isaac, book 1, chapter 80.*

<margin>Ripley.</margin>
No projection can be made with the red stone, except upon silver. *The same author, ibid. chapter 81.*

<margin>Ripley.</margin>
See that you cast your medicine upon your ferment <note>a substance added to the Stone to "prime" it for a specific metal</note>; then it will be as brittle as glass. Cast that brittle substance upon cleansed bodies <note>purified base metals</note>; then you will have metal proven by every judgment. *Ripley, page 89.*

<margin>Ewald.</margin>
You must not be ignorant of this secret: that our red male, nor his spouse, do not dye <note>meaning to "tint" or transform the metal's nature</note> until they are dyed themselves. *The same author, page 90.*

If powders are found to convert greater or lesser weights of metal, this happens not from a difference in the medicine’s nature, but from its own greater or lesser refinement; or because their power has been diminished or exhausted by several projections. *Ewald in the Preface, page 10.*

Does anyone wish to change lead into gold or silver with the physical stone? It is necessary that he first mix the substance of lead with the stone, so that together they become one single thing. The same must be done for tin, copper, and silver. *The same author, page 123.*

<margin>Manuscript.</margin>
Take your stone and divide it into three parts: wrap each in white wax, and so three pills will be made. And afterwards take one part of pure Sol <note>gold</note>, and let it be melted in a clean crucible. Once melted, put in one pill and let it be mixed with a rod, and after an interval, let another pill be added. Do as before, and then the third, doing as before. Then let it be drawn out, and place one part of this mixture upon ten parts of imperfect metal, and one of those [newly transformed parts] upon another ten, until the color pleases you. *Manuscript, page 70.*
