->*On the quicksilver and sulfur of the philosophers.*<-

### CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>Tauladan:</margin>
The ancient philosophers called quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*, literally "living silver" or mercury</note> *dry water* <note>original: *aquam siccam*</note>. Tauladan, p. 171.

It is clear enough what that quicksilver is which Geber <note>a Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> indicated in his *Summa* was to be chosen: namely, the pure substance of fixed Mercury enclosed within Sol <note>gold</note> and Luna <note>silver</note>. The same author, page 193.

<margin>Richard:</margin>
*Sulfur* arises from the fatness of the earth in the mine, thickened by a temperate decoction <note>slow heating</note> until it hardens and becomes dry; and when it has been hardened, it is called sulfur. But *Quicksilver* in its first root is composed of a white, subtle earth, excessively sulfurous, with clear water strongly admitted and united by such a union of the smallest parts, until the moist is tempered by the dry and the dry by the moist equally, until it becomes one substance, not resting on a flat surface, nor adhering to what touches it because of the dryness which has altered the wateriness within it. It is, however, homogeneous <note>consistent throughout</note> in nature: for either the whole remains in the fire and is fixed, or the whole flies off in smoke, since it is incombustible and airy. And this is the sign of perfection. Richard, ch. 7, p. 541.

<margin>Libavius:</margin>
*Crude Mercury* dissolves bodies and reduces them into the first matter. But the *Mercury of the bodies* <note>mercury extracted from processed metals</note> cannot do this. The same author, ch. 15.

The Mercury of the philosophers is composed of crude Mercury and the Mercury of the bodies, in an intimate and inseparable union, just as simple water mixed with simple water cannot be separated. Libavius, p. 62.

### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>The New Pearl:</margin>
This work is not caused by the motion of the upper bodies <note>the planets and stars</note>: because it can be performed at any time. *The New Pearl* <note>original: *Margarita novella*, a 14th-century text by Petrus Bonus</note>, p. 18.

<margin>Book of Three Words:</margin>
Begin the work at any time. *Book of the Three Words* <note>original: *Liber trium verborum*</note>, p. 48.

<margin>Libavius:</margin>
The contemplation of the heavens is not necessary. Libavius, on the Mercury of the Philosophers, p. 65.

The stars change by the hour, and they have not been so well investigated by any man that their full power is clear. Indeed, if they cannot prevent you from breaking a glass, how will they ward off other harms? It is not necessary to observe the position of the stars, nor to wait for them to compose our work. Geber, Book 1, ch. 11. <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational 8th-century figure of Islamic alchemy.</note>

<margin>Ventura.</margin>
It is not necessary to observe the rising and courses of the celestial signs, or the aspects of the Planets, or the times of the year, or the days, or the hours: because the generation of this stone of ours is entirely natural, just like other things that Nature produces, and its effects are similar. Ventura, ch. 13. <note>Laurentius Ventura was a 16th-century Venetian alchemist who argued that alchemy was a purely natural, physical process rather than a magical one.</note>

### *Whether all the riddles of the philosophers can be understood.*

## CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>Various.</margin>
He who wishes to examine every riddle will lose the Art rather than acquire it. For it is impossible to explain the allegories of everyone with certainty, since the authors have looked now here, now there, and the application itself is ambiguous. Libavius, page 65.

It is foolish to offer lettuce to a donkey when thistles suffice for it. He who reveals mysteries diminishes their majesty. Whatever can cause harm if made common should rightly be hidden in mystical speech. Various authors, here and there.

<margin>Aegidius.</margin>
Our science is a part of the Cabala <note>original: *Cabalae*; here referring to the general concept of "received tradition" or oral transmission, though often associated with Jewish mysticism</note>, which is interpreted as reception through conversation. For the philosophers, in treating it, involve it in such great riddles, metaphors, puzzles, enigmas, and problems, that Pythagoras teaches as much by his silence as they do by their writings. Aegidius, ch. 10, p. 28. <note>Aegidius de Vadis was a 16th-century writer who emphasized the spiritual and intellectual preparation needed for alchemy.</note>

Prophetic, natural, Spagyric <note>a term for alchemy involving the separation and recombination of substances, popularized by Paracelsus</note>, and poetic secrets are almost all hidden. Same, p. 102.

<margin>Vogelius.</margin>
One must attentively consider in what point the authors most agree. For there lies the truth, which is only one and simple. Vogelius in the Preface, p. 10. <note>Ewald Vogelius, author of several alchemical compendia.</note>

<margin>The New Pearl.</margin>
There are books written on this science in symbols <note>original: *sub figura*</note>, the greater part of which are very obscure and connected in their meanings, such that they cannot be understood except by their own composers. *Margarita Novella* <note>original: *Margarita novella*, "The New Pearl of Great Price," a highly influential 14th-century alchemical text by Petrus Bonus</note>, page 45.

## Powers or faculties commonly ascribed to the physical stone.
### CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>Hermes</margin>
Truly, without lie, certain and most true: That which is below is like that which is above. And that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of one thing, etc. <note>original: "Verum sine mendacio, certum & certissimum. Quod est inferius, est sicut quod est superius..." This is the opening of the famous *Emerald Tablet* of Hermes Trismegistus, the foundational text of Hermetic philosophy.</note> *Its power is complete if it has been turned into earth. Thus you will have the glory of the whole world's brilliance. Therefore all obscurity (that is, poverty and sickness) will flee from you.* This is the strongest strength of all strength, because it will conquer every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing. Hermes Trismegistus, in the *Emerald Tablet*.

<margin>Geber</margin>
We have found one medicine through long inquiry, the greatest labor, and certain experience, by which the *hard becomes soft, the soft is hardened, the fleeting is fixed, and the foul is enlightened* <note>In alchemical terms, "fixing the fleeting" refers to making a volatile substance stable under heat, a key step in creating the Stone.</note> with a wondrous splendor. Geber, cited in Libavius’s *On the Philosopher’s Stone*, p. 130. <note>Andreas Libavius was a 16th-century chemist; "Geber" refers to the legendary 8th-century Islamic alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan.</note>

Gold is a medicine that brings joy, *and preserves the body in youth.* The same, book 1, ch. 33.

<margin>Calid</margin>
Moreover, it has many properties and virtues. For it cleanses bodies from the additions of accidental sicknesses, and keeps substances safe, so that disturbances of opposites do not appear or be seen in it, nor the flight of its bond. For this is the soap of bodies, and their spirit and their soul: when it is mixed with them, it dissolves them without harm. This is the life of the dead and their resurrection, a medicine preserving the body, *and purging away excess.* And let him who knows it, know it; and let him who does not know it, not know it. For the function of this thing does not arise from a price, nor is it associated with selling or buying. Understand its virtue, value, and honor, and work. Calid, chapter 14. <note>Calid refers to Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince traditionally considered one of the first Arab alchemists.</note>

<margin>Unknown author</margin>
Since man is the most worthy of creatures, for whose sake and love all things were created by God and subjected to him, and whose body receives every excellence by any divine or human law; therefore, that *which preserves him in health and youth, by repelling all weariness from him and turning away from excesses,* is rightly to be sought with the greatest diligence. For this works upon nature beyond every medicine of Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, and other philosophers, or any potion or confection, so that even leprosy is driven away from him: since it is the antidote and medicine for curing and purging all bodies. Unknown author, *On the Composition of the Great Stone*, inserted at the beginning of volume 3 of the *Chemical Theater*, chapter 51. <note>The *Theatrum Chemicum* (Chemical Theater) was the largest compendium of alchemical writings in the 17th century. Hippocrates, Galen, and Avicenna were the traditional authorities of ancient and medieval medicine.</note>

<margin>Clangor</margin>
It is to be known that the ancient Sages *joined four principal effects or virtues in this glorious chest of treasure—* <note>The text cuts off here, referring to the *Clangor Buccinae* (The Sound of the Trumpet), a classic alchemical treatise.</note>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the miraculous powers of the "Philosophical Medicine" (the Philosopher's Stone) as described by David Lagneus. It transitions from the general praise of the previous page to a specific list of its medical and transformative applications.</meta>

<header>DAVID LAGNEUS</header>

...they discovered it through art and the assistance of science. First, it is said to heal the human body from many infirmities. Second, it restores imperfect metallic bodies. Third, it transmutes base stones into certain precious gems. Fourth, it makes all glass ductile or <term>malleable</term> <note>The legend of "flexible glass" (*vitrum flexile*) was a common theme in alchemical lore, signifying a substance that combined the clarity of glass with the durability of metal.</note>. Regarding the first power, all philosophers have agreed. For it cures every infirmity when taken internally, and heals when applied as an ointment externally. 

Indeed, the philosophers say that if a portion of it is given in water or in warm wine to those suffering from paralysis, frenzy, dropsy, or leprosy, it cures them. Other wise men say that it drives away <term>rosacea</term> <note>original: "guttam rosaceam," a chronic skin condition causing redness and pustules on the face.</note> through frequent anointing. From this medicine, heart palpitations, wasting fevers, intestinal obstructions, colic, jaundice, and <term>St. Giles' disease</term> <note>Historically associated with various ailments including leprosy, lameness, or "the falling sickness" (epilepsy).</note>, as well as epilepsy and all types of fevers, are cured, mostly by taking it internally. Arthritis is cured by anointing with it, and it repels all melancholy or sadness of the mind when taken on an empty stomach, and it dries up all rheumatic discharge. 

It is also the best healer for weak eyes. For it binds the flow of tears, thins the discharge of bleary eyes, drives away redness, and softens the skin or membrane by wearing it away. <term>Films</term>, <term>white spots</term>, <term>horn-like growths</term>, <term>nail-like growths</term>, <term>cataracts</term>, <note>original: "Tela, albugo, cornu, ungula, cataracta." These represent a variety of corneal opacities and growths described in medieval ophthalmology.</note> inversion of the eyelids, inflammation, and even darkness and swelling of the eyes—all these, I say, are most easily cured by this philosophical medicine. It strengthens the heart and the <term>vital organs</term> <note>original: "spiritualia," referring to the organs of breath and spirit, namely the heart and lungs.</note> when drunk, and mitigates headaches when rubbed on the temples. 

It even grants hearing to the deaf and assists with all ear pain; it rectifies contracted nerves through anointing, restores corroded teeth by washing, and sweetens the foulness of the breath. All kinds of <term>abscesses</term> <note>original: "apostematum."</note> are also healed by it, whether by anointing, applying as a plaster, or by applying its dry powder. Ulcers, wounds, cancer, fistulas, <term>corrosive ulcers</term> <note>original: "noli me tangere," literally "touch me not," a term used for particularly malignant or sensitive skin cancers and ulcers.</note>, anthrax, rashes, ringworm, chilblains, scabies, itching, and scales are healed through it. Scars are smoothed by it so that new flesh is regenerated. 

Corrupted and sour wine is restored if it is mixed in. A <term>stone</term> <note>original: "calculus," referring to kidney or bladder stones.</note> is dissolved if it is drunk. It deletes wrinkles in the face or all blemishes through anointing and makes the face youthful. It assists women struggling in labor; if applied as a plaster, it brings out a dead fetus and it provokes urination. It excites and increases sexual union, prevents drunkenness, induces memory, increases the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>A foundational concept in medieval medicine; the "radical moisture" was the innate fluid that fueled the body's life-force and determined lifespan.</note>, strengthens nature, and indeed shows and provides many other benefits to the human body. 

For this medicine is more excellent in odor, flavor, power, and effect than all the medicines of Hippocrates, Galen, Alexander, Constantine, Avicenna, and all other doctors of the medical art. And it should be noted that this medicine is always to be mixed with the medicines of the apothecary to drive away disease.

And then one possesses the *truest Potable Gold*.

<margin>The Rosary.</margin>
In this is completed the precious gift of God, which is above every secret of the world's sciences, and an incomparable treasure of treasures. For he who possesses this gift of God holds dominion over the world: since he has reached the end of riches and has broken the bond of Nature. Yet this is not merely because he has the power *of converting all imperfect bodies into pure <term>Sun</term> and <term>Moon</term>* <note>original: "Solem & Lunam"; in alchemy, these terms refer to Gold and Silver.</note>: but rather because it preserves man and every animal in the maintenance of health. Indeed, the crystalline plate, which is the *White Elixir*, if given in the amount of a mustard seed to one suffering from a fever, cures him. Even a leper, if purged with the *red* powder—from which <term>Gold</term> is made—twice a year throughout the four seasons, is cured. And both the white and red powders heal those with <term>sciatica</term> <note>original: "ischiadicos"; refers to chronic hip or leg pain.</note> who are in danger of death; it also heals paralysis. Likewise, if the powder is held to the nostrils of women laboring in childbirth, they are delivered. So says **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts are attributed.</note>. **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–c. 815), a Persian polymath and father of early chemistry.</note> also says that the *Red Elixir* cures all chronic infirmities of which doctors have despaired, and makes a man grow young again like an eagle, and live for five hundred years and more—as some **Philosophers** have done, who used it three times a week in the amount of a mustard seed. Wherefore note, that all infirmities generated from the crown of the head to the sole of the foot are cured in a single day if they have lasted a month; in twelve days if they have lasted a year; and in a month if they have lasted a long time. For just as it cures all metals infected by any disease, so it also cures human bodies. Whence **Hermes** says: *If you take the weight of a carob seed of our Elixir every day for seven days, your gray hairs will fall from your head and grow back black, and thus from an old man you will become young and strong.* Therefore **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says: This stone of ours has the effective power to heal every infirmity above all other medicines of the Physicians. For it gladdens the soul, increases strength, preserves youth, and removes old age. For it does not permit the blood to putrefy, nor <term>phlegm</term> to dominate, nor <term>choler</term> to be burned, nor <term>melancholy</term> to be exalted <note>These refer to the "Four Humors" of ancient medicine; the stone was believed to keep these four bodily fluids in perfect balance.</note>: rather, it multiplies the blood beyond measure, purges the contents of the <term>vital organs</term> <note>original: "spiritualibus"; in this medical context, it refers to the heart and lungs, the seats of the "vital spirits."</note>, effectively restores all bodily members, and guards them from injury. Generally, it most strictly heals all illnesses—whether hot or cold, dry or moist—above all other medicines of the Physicians. In short, it expels all bad humors and introduces good ones; it brings love and honor to those who carry it, as well as security, boldness, and victory in battle. *The Rosary of the Philosophers, near the end of the book.*

# CHEMICAL HARMONY.

He who completes this Art once, even if he were to live a million years and were to feed four thousand men every single day, would not lack for anything. For he is so rich, possessing the Stone from which the **Elixir** <note>A substance believed to be capable of changing base metals into gold or of prolonging life.</note> is made, just like one who has fire: he can give it to whomever he wants, and when and as much as he wants, without danger or loss to himself. *The same author, page 229 of the Basel edition.*

<margin>Lullius</margin>
It is effective against all diseases, except for the fixed limit of decreed death. With this tinting Spirit, we make glass that can be worked with a hammer and is unbreakable. From crystal we make the **Carbuncle** <note>original: "Carbunculum"; a term for a deep red gemstone, here referring to a perfected alchemical stone.</note>, just as the planets are mixed with them. *Lullius, cited in Libavius, Book on the Philosopher’s Stone, page 144.*

It remains, therefore, to seek the thing that, within the limits of our life, can preserve our body from decay, cure the sick, and restore what is lost, until the final death comes at the time appointed by God the highest Creator, etc. But no medicine in this world can do this except our **celestial vegetable animal menstruum** <note>original: "menstruum vegetabile coeleste animal"; in this context, "menstruum" refers to a universal solvent or the life-force extracted from substances.</note>, which is called the **fifth essence** <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the purest substance in the universe, beyond the four elements of earth, air, fire, and water.</note>. For it preserves flesh from corruption, strengthens the elemental forces, restores original youth through itself, digests the raw, hardens the thin, thins the hardened, makes the lean fat, weakens the fat, cools the inflamed, inflames the cooled, dries the wet, and moistens the dry: in whatever way one and the same thing can have contrary operations. Only the action of a single thing is diversified according to the nature of the receiver: just like the heat of the Sun, which has contrary operations, because it dries clay and melts wax. *The same author, Book on the Fifth Essence, distinction 1, page 21 of the Nuremberg edition.*

<margin>Valescus</margin>
Without doubt the Stone, or the medicine of the Philosophers, among the best properties and operations it performs in the human body, has the property of breaking the stone in the kidneys and bladder, and cleansing both, as Berjensis says. *Valescus de Taranta* <note>A famous 14th-century physician.</note>, *book 5, chapter on Strangury.*

<margin>Ripley</margin>
When Raymond <note>Referring to Ramon Lull.</note> was near death because of old age, he made **potable gold** <note>original: "aurum potabile"; gold in a drinkable liquid form, thought to be the ultimate medicine.</note> from the oil of the Philosophers, which revived him. *Ripley in the preface to the Twelve Gates.*

<margin>Bacon</margin>
The final step in which the Art reaches its completion, with all the power of Nature, is the prolongation of life for a great length of time. That this is possible, many experiments have taught. For **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist.</note> recounts that a soldier, strong in body and mind, lasted beyond the usual age of man by using mead internally and oil externally. Likewise, a peasant digging in the fields found a golden vessel with his plow together with a noble liquor; thinking it was dew from heaven, when he had drunk it and washed his face with it, he was renewed in spirit, body, and the excellence of wisdom: and from a cowherd he was made the bearer for the King of the **Osci** <note>An ancient people of southern Italy.</note>. And it has been proven...

### OF DAVID LAGNEUS

...by the testimony of Papal letters, that a German <note>original: "Almanicus"</note> who had been taken captive among the Saracens received a medicine that prolonged his life to five hundred years. For the King who held him captive received messengers from a Wise King <note>original: "Regis Magi"</note> with this medicine. But because he was suspicious of it, he wished to test what had been brought to him upon the captive. Similarly, the Lady of Tormery in Great Britain, while searching for a white doe, discovered an ointment with which the guardian of the forest had anointed his entire body, except for the soles of his feet; he lived for three hundred years without decay, except for pains and sufferings in his feet. We have also experienced many times in our own days that rural men have lived for one hundred and sixty years, or thereabouts, without the advice of Doctors. These things are also confirmed by the behavior of animals—such as the stag, the eagle, the serpent, and many others—which renew their youth through the power of herbs and stones. And therefore the Sages dedicated themselves to this kind of secret, moved by the examples of brute animals, believing that what is granted to brute creatures is possible for man. For this reason, Artephius <note>A legendary alchemical figure often cited as having lived over a thousand years through the use of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, in his *Wisdom of Secrets*, searching the powers of animals, stones, and other things to understand the secrets of Nature—and especially for the sake of longevity—boasts that he lived for one thousand and twenty-five years, etc. Roger Bacon, *On the Marvelous Power of Art and Nature*, page 150, Basel edition.

<margin>Richard</margin>
This is the most secret secret of all Philosophy: a most excellent body, which adorns a man with morals, enriches him with benefits, *helps the poor, and preserves the human body unharmed, providing it with health.* Richard the Englishman <note>original: "Richardus Angl"; a 13th-century alchemist.</note> in *The Correction*, chapter 2.

Furthermore, since among the common people and the aforementioned Philosophers, **Gold** <note>original: "Aurum"</note> holds the reputation that, remaining in its primary state, it cures leprosy <note>In alchemical texts, "leprosy" often refers both to the human disease and to "diseased" or base metals that need purification.</note> and possesses many other virtues, this is solely due to its complete **digestion** <note>original: "digestionem"; in alchemy, the process of maturing a substance through gentle, continuous heat.</note>. Because the excellence of fire acting within it consumes all the bad humors existing in sick bodies, whether arising from hot or cold causes. (But **Silver** <note>original: "Argentum"</note> cannot do this, because it does not have such a great surplus of fire, and it is not so well digested and cooked by natural maturity. Nevertheless, this notwithstanding, it possesses a "fiery nature" within itself secretly and potentially, but not so fully, because as of yet the fire does not overcome the other elementary qualities as it does in gold. And therefore **Silver**, remaining in its primary state, does not cure leprosy so powerfully unless it is further digested by Art until it possesses the highest degrees of Gold and all maturity.)

# CHEMICAL HARMONY

<meta>catchword: bea- (from "beatus" or "beata")</meta>

...wherefore other diseased metallic bodies are less able to cure infirmities, insofar as they differ more in perfection and maturity from [Gold]: some differ less, others more, and accordingly they heal less, which results from a defect of the infected, foul, and burning sulfur from which they were made in their generation and coagulation from the beginning. Therefore, they do not heal, since the fire within them is so infected with elemental dregs and is burning, with an admixture of other elemental qualities. 

When, I say, Gold is of such vigor, and remains in its first disposition; what wonder is it if it be reduced into a medicine (as has been experienced) through the ministry of Art following Nature, and its virtue be refined through the digestion of decoction and the purging of qualities, so that it might then have the power to cure many, infinite, or even all sicknesses? 

This is evident through Arnald of Villanova <note>Arnaldus de Villa nova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician, alchemist, and diplomat.</note>, a most skilled Physician, who liberated the Lord Pope Innocent from an infirmity incurable by other medicines (others say from the plague) with this medicine. *It makes an old man young and brings him back to life; it preserves health, strengthens youth, and expels every sickness of the body; it drives poison from the heart, moistens the arteries, dissolves the livid impurity from the lung, heals the wounded, purifies the blood, breaks the stone <note>Refers to kidney or bladder stones, a common ailment in the early modern period.</note>, cleanses the contents of the vital organs <note>original: "spiritualibus" — in medieval medicine, this refers to the organs of breath and spirit, namely the heart and lungs.</note>, just as it is for rheum <note>a watery discharge from the eyes or nose</note>, it purges the flow, and strengthens the stomach in its natural heat.* 

And if the sickness has lasted one month, it heals it in one day or hour; but if the sickness has lasted one year, it heals it in eight days. If, however, the disease has been ancient for a long time, incurable by other medicines, it heals it in half a month. O happy science with the one who knows it! Therefore, not without merit, this medicine is to be sought above all other medicines of the Physicians: because he who has it possesses an incomparable treasure, was born under a healthy constellation, and in this age is enriched with infinite riches above the kings and princes of this world. Who would not love such things which, *preserving the healthy and long-lived above all the medicines of Physicians, keep them, while enriching the person and not impoverishing others.* These are good and just things before God and men, not acquired through usury, etc., because this Art is a special gift of God. The same [author], chapter 14.

<margin>Greverus</margin> <note>Jodocus Greverus, a 16th-century German alchemist known for his work "Secretum nobilissimum."</note>
This is the powder that cleanses every stain and brings back to life all who are dead. O most noble science, which is the theater of all Nature and its anatomy, terrestrial Astrology, an argument for the omnipotence of God, a testimony of the resurrection of the dead, an example of the remission of sins, an infallible experiment of the future judgment, and a mirror of eternity.

*With this medicine, you will be able to heal every infirmity, even those despaired of, and also to produce gold, silver, and precious stones. <margin>M. Scotus</margin>
*If you mix a grain’s quantity of that Elixir with some clear wine, it heals leprosy, removes scabies, skin eruptions, every fever and heat instantly; it plucks every corrupt humor from the human body, raises every contracted limb, and preserves youth. No one who uses this food or drink knows infirmity for any length of time; they will always be joyful and ruddy. — Michael Scotus <note>Michael Scotus (c. 1175–1232), a mathematician and scholar at the court of Frederick II, often associated with legendary magical and alchemical powers.</note> on the Nature of the Sun and Moon, page 201.*

<margin>Ventura</margin>
This Stone has the most excellent virtues above all other stones. *There is, specifically, a triple immense virtue to it. For, Morienus <note>Morienus: A legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says, this is the secret of this mastery: that one part of this substance converts a thousand parts into the purest Echeb <note>original: "Echeb" — an Arabic-derived alchemical term for refined, pure gold.</note>. And it performs all these things more than all the medicines of Physicians, or any potions or concoctions whatsoever. This medicine, when applied in finished form, also preserves and protects so that no disease can come to the person in the future. And thus it becomes an antidote and medicine for all bodies to be cured and purged, both metallic and human, etc. The third is because many wonders are performed with it in other things. For it makes malleable glass <note>A legendary lost invention where glass could be dented or bent rather than shattered.</note>, and from fused crystal with it we draw out a Carbuncle <note>original: "Carbunculum" — a mythical, glowing red gemstone believed to have its own internal light.</note>, and from a thousand pearls we compose one very large and most natural-looking one. ### CHEMICAL HARMONY

...[the stone’s] worldly riches and inferior treasures, and more than drinkable gold <note>original: "aurum potabile"</note> (which ignorant and reckless practitioners so name, making and understanding it from common gold), by which Kings, Princes, and Magnates, when placed in their medicinal confections, seek to preserve their health. For this [stone] of ours is truly divine, more spiritual and subtle than any physical dissolution, and far more effective than all other things in value, virtue, and any immortal praise whatsoever. — Laurentius Ventura, *On the Philosophers' Stone, chapter 31*.

<margin>Dorn</margin>
Regarding the fabrication of precious stones through metaphysical Art, and regarding the reduction of many *unions* <note>original: "unionum" — specifically refers to large, singular pearls of great value</note> or precious stones into a single one, see Gerard Dorn in *The Supernatural Artifice, chapters 16 and 17*.

<margin>The Game of Children</margin>
If you wish to use our medicine by ingesting it, then take of our *Elixir* the weight of two gold ducats to one pound of some medicinal confection, and eat the weight of one drachma <term>drachma: a small unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</term> of that confection in winter. If you do this, it dispels all bodily infirmities, from whatever cause they arose, whether they be hot or cold: it will preserve health and youth in man, and from an old man it makes a youth, and causes grey hair to fall out. Likewise, our philosophical venom <note>original: "venenum" — used here as a technical term for a potent, transformative substance rather than a toxin</note> cures leprosy instantly; it sharpens the sight, all the senses, and the intellect in a wondrous way, above all the medicines of the Philosophers. Therefore, our medicine cannot be sufficiently valued; for all things were created for the sake of man. — *The Game of Children* <note>original: "Ludus puerorum," a famous alchemical treatise</note>, found at the end of the book.

<margin>Vallentis</margin>
That Chemical powder—whether you call it the Philosophers’ Stone, or molten salt, or sulphur, or the Elixir, or the medicine, or drinkable gold—certainly has a wondrous power over three classes of things: *Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral.* In the *Animal* kingdom: for it restores every animal, whether man or beast, sick internally or externally, to health in the shortest time. For it leads back to their own nature the primary qualities, or the elements themselves, which deviate from natural symmetry, as well as weakened actions and offending humors—the causes of imbalance and corruption, whether internal and arising from within, or incident from without. For it is almost incorruptible, being tempered by the purified elements themselves and separated from the dregs of the four elements, which are the primary cause of corruption. Therefore, it produces a tempered and healthy body, like the *spirit of life*, by whose power and help Nature digests the indigestible and leads out everything undigested; *it cuts away all superfluous and offending qualities, vivifies the spirit, hardens the soft, softens the hard, thins the thick, thickens the thin, makes the lean fat, thins the fat, cools the hot, warms the cold, dries the moist, moistens the dry, and [restores] natural heat, or...*

# OF DAVID LAGNEUS

It strengthens and confirms the substantial moisture <note>original: "humidum substantificum" — also known as "radical moisture," the vital fluid thought to sustain life in medieval medicine</note>. It is, as it were, a universal medicinal body into which all the specific properties and powers of other medicines are reduced and infused. This is because it is that "fifth nature" introduced by the ancient philosophers—whether called an essence or a most subtle soul—which is most pure, resisting putrefaction or corruption for the longest time. It is corrupted only with the greatest difficulty and labor, consisting of equality and homogeneity, freed from all mortal concretion. It is a celestial and simple substance of the elements, as if tempered from the elements themselves, purified and secreted from coarser matter and the heterogeneous superfluity of the four elements by that chemical sublimation.

Disease, the Physicians say, is an immoderation or imbalance of the four elements, or of the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance determined health</note> from which the human body is composed, falls ill, and thrives. Yet that chemical medicine, or potable gold <note>original: "aurum potabile" — a legendary liquid alchemical preparation of gold believed to cure all diseases</note>, *is a homogeneous and uniform substance consisting in equality, a most subtle soul separated from the dregs, and like a simple substance of the elements; it is therefore temperate and least liable to corruption or decay. For this reason, it tempers the elements or humors of the human body, and strengthens the innate heat and substantial moisture, restoring the sick person to health, moderation, and balance.* In this way, the person will be preserved safe and whole from disease until the limit predefined by God, provided that by using that medicine prudently, they do not otherwise injure the powers of their nature and the complexion of their body beyond measure.

For since this supreme medicine is nothing other than *natural heat multiplied in the substance of fixed Mercury, and the power of heat is to gather homogeneous things and separate heterogeneous ones; this medicine, by its life-giving heat, will necessarily separate heterogeneous things in the bodies of animals, while preserving the spirits and humors,* and more quickly in man than in the nature of metals. This is because man, by his own proper natural heat, separates out heterogeneous wastes, which metals are least able to separate by their own connatural heat.

Regarding the method of administering and dispensing this medicine to the sick, in potions and pills, consult the book of Arnaldus on the *Water of Life* <note>Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note>, likewise Lullius on the *Water of Life or the Fifth Essence*, John of Rupescissa on the *Consideration of the Fifth Essence*, book 2, and William of Paris in the chapter on the effects of this Art.

In the Vegetable realm <note>original: "Vegetate"</note>, it performs these actions: *For in the springtime, it vivifies all plants, trees, shrubs, bushes, and herbs with its great and wondrous heat, and it strengthens and excites their generative power;* since it is nothing other than natural heat, as it were, fixed in its radical moisture. Indeed, if a certain quantity of that medicine is dissolved in water and placed into the heart or center of the trunk...

### ->CHEMICAL HARMONY<-

If you inject it into the trunk of a vine, flowers and leaves will be born, and it will produce fruit in the month of May. So it is with other plants. In the Mineral genus: For it transforms every imperfect metallic body—namely lead, tin, copper, and iron—as well as common quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, into either silver or gold. It achieves this with every distinction of perfection: purity, weight, fixation <note>the ability to remain stable under heat</note>, color, ductility, and the test or trial by ash <term>cupellation: a process of refining gold or silver by heating it in a cupel made of bone ash</term>, cementation <note>a method of refining gold by heating it with salts</note>, ignition, fusion, exposure over sharp vapors <note>acidic or corrosive fumes</note>, the mixing of adhering sulfur, quenching, calcination, and the repetition of reduction; as well as the easy or difficult reception of quicksilver. Furthermore, it cures and perfects the "sicknesses" or imperfections and deficiencies of precious stones—whether in their transparency, color, hardness, or weight—and restores them to their natural virtue, or rather to perfection, and transmutes one into another. Their sicknesses are cured, their hidden qualities are made manifest, or their manifest flaws are covered. For by that art, these stones are most perfectly composed: the Emerald, the Carbuncle (also known as the Anthrax or commonly the Ruby), the Diamond, the Beryl, the Balas Ruby <note>original: "Balagius" or "Palatius"—a variety of spinel</note>, the Chrysoprase, the Chrysolite, and others. These things and many more are found in *Robertus Vallensis on the Truth and Antiquity of the Chemical Art, chapter 3.*

Regarding the opinions of *Arnaldus* <note>Arnald of Villanova, a celebrated medieval physician</note> cited above—*It wards off poison from the heart*, <margin>Odomarus</margin> *It makes a young man out of an old one*, and *It expels every sickness*—see the fuller explanation by *Master Odomarus* in the *Question: Whether the physical Stone is effective against the plague*, in *Volume 3 of the Chemical Theater, page 181*, where among other things he says: *The Philosopher’s Stone is nothing other than Gold multiplied in its degrees, the proportion that was in the first gold remaining, so that what was one whole degree of "gold-ness" is now a hundred or a thousand. If, therefore, gold of one whole degree, dissolved philosophically, expels every superfluity harmful to itself (as experience teaches), then surely Gold of a hundred or a thousand whole degrees—which is the Philosopher’s Stone—will expel all poison from the human body. In this Stone, all natures are open and abundant, ready to communicate their "gold-ness" to other metals and to transmute them suddenly into the truest gold. "From an old man it makes a young one," that is, by casting away all dross <note>original: "scorioso"</note> and impurity, it recalls the power of the pure parts into action and mends the lapse of the human constitution, bringing it back toward the temperament of its own nature; thus a seventy-year-old thrives <note>original: "luxuriat"—becomes vigorous or full of life</note> and does those things he did at age 50 or 40. "It expels every sickness," except perhaps in chronic hereditary diseases, such as the joint-disease <note>gout or arthritis</note> left over from the father’s seed, Leprosy, and similar passions which remained in the seeds of the parents at the time of conception. For the root of such infirmities is uprooted with difficulty, or perhaps in no way at all.* *The same author, in the same place.*

### CHAPTER XX.

<margin>The Assembly</margin> <note>original: "Turba" — referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>
ALL you seekers of this Art, know that you cannot arrive at the knowledge and benefit of this Art unless you are of a patient and enduring mind. He, therefore, who is long-suffering and gladly enjoys patience, shall walk in the right path of this Art. But he who thinks he can harvest the fruit from our books more quickly is mistaken; it would have been better for him not even to look at them than to have ever touched them. For our books seem to do a great injustice to those who read our writings only once, twice, or thrice; frustrated in their understanding and all their study, they also—which is worst of all—lose the wealth, labor, and time they have spent on this Art. Nevertheless, he who bends his back over our books and studiously devotes himself to them, who applies and perks up his memory and mind, and is not entangled in various distracting thoughts, and prays to God (as **Solomon** did) for the granting of wisdom rather than for riches—he shall reign in our kingdom without end until he dies. Therefore, fear God, O seekers. For that which you seek is by no means of small value. You seek the greatest treasure and the most excellent gift of God. — *Bacafer in the Assembly of the Philosophers, page 34, Basel edition.*

<margin>Arnaldus</margin> <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>
Let no one neglect to dig out from hidden places the final and chief mother of all **Philosophy**, which adorns a man with morals, enriches him with benefits, exalts the poor, keeps the body unhurt, and restores the sick to health. For he who is lazy in reading books will not be able to be prompt in preparing things. For "book opens book," and speech explains speech: because what is diminished in one is completed in another. For a person cannot become well-accustomed to **Practice** whose mind is not grounded in **Theory**.

...refuses to exert himself: because he proceeds to Practice <note>The physical laboratory work, as opposed to "Theoria" or study.</note> as a donkey approaches a banquet, not knowing how or why he offers his snout and mouth. — Arnaldus <note>Arnaldus de Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> in the prologue of the 1st book of the *Rosary*.

*Therefore, most beloved, exert yourselves in this with persistent labor, especially in the long duration of immense meditation: for with that you shall find the completed <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "Physical Stone" in its liquid or medicinal form, capable of transmuting metals or healing the body.</note>, and without it, never.* — The same author, Book 2 of the *Rosary*, chapter 32.

<margin>Richard.</margin>
*Study, according to the Doctors, removes ignorance and restores the human intellect to the true knowledge and understanding of every thing.* Therefore, it is first necessary to acquire knowledge through the study of this sweet work, and to sharpen one's wit through philosophical sayings, since the known path of truth is within them. If, therefore, those who labor do not despise the work, they shall sweetly taste the fruit arising from it. But those who abhor study, yet still wish to labor, should weigh carefully whether their Art is an imitation of Nature itself—especially of that thing whose nature their Art is meant to improve. For without the imitation of Nature, it is impossible for them to bring the secrets of the Philosophers to a perfect end. These people, as the Philosopher says, proceed to Practice like a donkey to hay, not knowing toward what it stretches its snout, except insofar as the exterior senses, without intellect, lead it to the fodder through sight and taste. Thus these "donkeys," without good and true principles and fruitful studies, and without knowledge of natures, seek to perfect the works of Nature. Therefore, all those who love the benefit of this Art are bound to persist in their studies, and to draw the truth from books, and not from fictional fables and faulty works: since this Art is in no way truly found (although many deceptions appear to men) except after the period of study, and knowledge of the sayings of the philosophers, or through the faithful instruction of a knowledgeable person when it is taught. For he who has been idle in reading books, etc. — Richardus Anglicus <note>Richard the Englishman, a 13th-century author to whom several alchemical works, such as the *Correctio Fatuorum* (Correction of Fools), are attributed.</note>, *Correction*, chapter 2.

<margin>Geber.</margin>
Know, most beloved, that he who is ignorant of natural principles within himself is already far removed from our Art: since he has no true root upon which to build his intention. And he who knows his natural principles and all the causes of minerals, yet has not yet achieved the true end and profit of this most hidden Art; he has, however, a more easy access to the principles of this Art, the causes of minerals, and the manner of generation which consists of the intention of Nature—yet little is taken from him concerning the completion of the work, etc. *Labor, therefore, to study in our volumes, and strive to revolve them very often in your mind, so that you may [grasp] the true intention from the manner of our speech...* <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan; the text here likely refers to the *Summa Perfectionis*, a foundation of Latin alchemy.</note>

### Lll 3

...philosophers, it is nothing but a perfect divine inspiration, and a secret of the glorious God, who bestows it upon and withholds it from whom He wills; it is fitting, above all, for him who desires to be initiated into this to ask the triune and one God <note>The "Triune and One" refers to the Christian Trinity, a common invocation in later Latin alchemy to align the work with religious orthodoxy.</note> with a supplicant mind, that He might deign to illuminate his understanding and confer wisdom upon him. For there is no wisdom except from God, who does not deny it to those seeking and asking with a sincere heart and good intention. Wherefore Alphidius <note>An alchemical authority, possibly of Arabic origin, frequently cited in the Middle Ages.</note> says most rightly: *Son, I preach to you the fear of the Lord, and likewise love with unfeigned obedience.* And Senior <note>original: "Senior" refers to Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century Arab alchemist.</note>: *You who shall be studious in the fear of God shall see the secret and apparent power of this Stone, and shall find it, being instructed by the spirit of the Most High, etc.* Theobald de Hoghelande <note>A 16th-century alchemist known for his defense of alchemy against skeptics.</note> at the beginning of his book.

The prudent Artist <note term="Artifex">The "Artist" or "Artifex" is the standard term for the practicing alchemist who performs the "Art."</note> should be wise, and naturally possess a subtle and deep wit, and excel in outstanding judgment. Furthermore, let him be learned, so that whatever he does not achieve through wit, this defect may be aided by learning. For "whoever wishes to reach this science," says Arnaldus <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note>, "and is not a philosopher, is a fool: because this science is only concerned with the secrets of the Philosophers." Let him be industrious and hardworking, and of a constant will. For in this business, if the difficulty of the task and tedious fatigue make the worker negligent, it deprives him of the expected joy, stifles hope, and destroys effectiveness. Let him not be headlong into anger, but patient and long-suffering. For "haste," says Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the "father of chemistry," though this quote likely comes from the "Latin Geber."</note>, "is from the father devil." Let him be of his own judgment and free, not distracted by other cares or business. Likewise, let him be particularly tenacious of the secret, lest he bring danger upon himself and offer a handle for wrongdoing to others. Let him be neither a spendthrift nor a miser, but sufficiently wealthy, and let him have a great supply of books. (The same author, pages 138, 139, 140, Volume 1 of the *Chemical Theater*).

<margin>Unknown Author</margin>
However, an artist filled with a coarse wit and a hard mind should not approach the investigation of this science, nor one who is greedy, nor one sparing of expenses, nor a double-minded man, entirely changeable in his purpose, nor one too hasty, nor one who is infirm or weak in hands or eyes, or too old: nor so poor that he cannot afford the means to investigate this costly science. But rather let him be a "son of doctrine," a man graced with a most subtle wit, sufficiently wealthy, generous, healthy, firm in purpose, patient and mild, temperate, and well-disposed and ordered in his organs and limbs. And let it not weary the artist to study this book quite often, and to extract the true understanding from it, and to carry that extracted knowledge secretly in his heart, and commit it to perpetual memory, and only afterwards to work. For it is not fitting to investigate it through books alone, because he who follows it only through books will find it most slowly: for the books of this science are not written for its instruction, just as... <note>The text ends here as a catchword for the next page.</note>

<summary>This page outlines the necessary virtues of an alchemist, emphasizing that the "Great Work" requires divine favor, intellectual depth, and specific character traits like patience and secrecy. It warns that those who are poor, infirm, or impatient will fail, as the science requires both deep study of books and practical labor.</summary>

->Unknown author, *Theatrum Chemicum* <note>The "Chemical Theater," a massive and influential compendium of alchemical writings first published in the early 17th century.</note>, Volume 3, page 1.<-

<margin>Greverius</margin>
For I know well enough that no one can take these things for themselves unless he is one to whom God himself has granted it, who alone illuminates the darkness of these mysteries or clouds their clarity: so that one understands not even the clearest things unless he has been illuminated by Him; nor follows any of the most obscure things if they have not been illustrated by Him. Moreover, I adjure you, whoever has this writing of mine, not to hand it over to the unworthy or the greedy, nor to those who would apply it to the disadvantage or even the oppression of their neighbors: such as are tyrannical, unjust, adulterous, soft men <note term="molles">In this period, "soft" (Latin: *molles*) referred to those lacking moral discipline or being overly devoted to luxury.</note>, and those whose "God is their belly" <note>A reference to Philippians 3:19, describing those driven by physical appetites rather than spiritual truth.</note>. # CHEMICAL HARMONY

*Observing the innermost footprints of Nature everywhere,*
*Then a delay, having slowed down anxious haste, will follow:*
*Soon Labor, setting in motion the noble steps of Industry,*
*Will not be absent; indeed, it will bring one single glass vessel,* <note>The "one vessel" refers to the alchemical flask or "Philosopher's Egg," signifying that the entire process should take place in a single, sealed environment.</note>
*One work, and finally it will bring with it one single matter.* <note>A central tenet of alchemy is the "unity of the matter," the belief that the Great Work starts from one primary substance.</note>
*He, therefore, surrounded by such a great company, will enter*
*Upon a long journey, and traversing all things with a slow step,*
*Will continually feed his eyes and mind with marvelous discoveries,*
*And the sights beheld will beguile his constant toil:*
*Until he reveals the treasures hidden in the secret earth,*
*An unknown weight of silver and of gold.*
*And even proceeding further, he will find the secrets*
*Of the outermost things, in which completion Nature*
*Delights herself; and he will fashion gems by a similar art.*

Augurello, Book 2 of *Chrysopoeia* <note term="Chrysopoeia">The art of making gold; the title of a famous alchemical poem by Giovanni Aurelio Augurello (c. 1441–1524).</note>, page 222, Volume 3 of the *Chemical Theater* <note>The *Theatrum Chemicum*, a massive compendium of alchemical literature.</note>.

# 904.

->GREETINGS TO THE READER.<-

*Since that passage by Fernelius <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558) was a prominent French physician and natural philosopher. This reference is to his work "On the Hidden Causes of Things" (*De Abditis rerum causis*).</note>, in Book 2, Chapter 18, regarding the extraction of the seed of gold, provided the primary occasion for compiling this Harmony, it seemed to me that it would not be out of place if I were to transcribe it here in its entirety. Furthermore, so that some few pages would not otherwise remain empty, I have appended one or two enigmas. I hope you will look upon this with a kind and favorable eye. Farewell.*

<margin>Fernelius</margin>
The Philosopher’s Stone <note>original: "Lapis Philosophicus"</note>, known as the Elixir to the Arabs, the true seed for the generating and propagating of gold, is to be sought and tracked down not from sulfur, nor from quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, nor from any of the other substances which many people offer through deceit, but from gold alone, and that of the purest kind.

> *He who has a heart for barley, at last sows barley; so you*
> *should not now prepare the origins of gold from elsewhere; in gold*
> *are the seeds of gold, although they may recede, hidden*
> *at a distance, and must be sought by us with much labor.*

There is nothing in any part of nature that does not contain within itself the seed of its own kind, but it is such that it can scarcely be drawn out by art. However, it can be drawn from gold alone. The greatest power of the seed resides in a certain oil; in other things, that oil is usually ignited and consumed by fire, but in gold, it cannot be. For this reason, it cannot be scorched or consumed by the heat of any fire, and it withstands every force of the art.

> *...Since nothing of gold is lost*
> *to fire; just as no old age consumes it alone,*
> *and neither rust nor tarnish destroys it at all,*
> *so firmly do all things there cling together in their structures.*

Furthermore, extract that fertile seed in this way: take two ounces of the purest gold and mix them with ten times as much quicksilver prepared with great artistic skill. Dissolve them with a gentle fire until the quicksilver expires <note>i.e., evaporates</note> entirely, and the original weight of the gold settles, reduced to a black powder, which nevertheless, if melted, could return to the proper nature of gold. From this powder, next, by means of a very sharp fire to produce vapor, you will continually draw out water until the entire powder turns into the whitest ash and a calx <note term="Calx">The powdery substance remaining after a metal has been roasted or "calcined" in fire; a foundational step in alchemical purification.</note>. Sprinkle the calx seven times with the water which has been drawn out from it by that same evaporation. Labor with every skill so that, by this repeated impulse and incursion, they may thin themselves out and be rendered most pure from every filth and dreg, having attained the highest powers. These two are the primary principles of the entire art and of the work to be completed, in which the four elements of the world are bound together.

<meta>catchword: For</meta>

<summary>This page features an excerpt from Jean Fernel explaining that the "seed" of gold can only be found within pure gold itself, rejecting other common alchemical ingredients. It details a process of mixing gold with mercury and repeated heating to produce a purified "calx" or ash, which serves as the foundation of the alchemical Great Work.</summary>
<keywords>Jean Fernel, seed of gold, Philosopher's Stone, Elixir, quicksilver, mercury, calcination, alchemy, purification, chemical elements</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the excerpt from Jean Fernel’s "On the Hidden Causes of Things," as introduced on the previous page. Fernel is explaining the theoretical and practical composition of the Philosopher’s Stone.</meta>

For air is also present in water, and in the lime <term>calx: the roasted or burnt residue of a substance, seen here as the "earthy" component</term> both earth and fire reside: thus what we read in the *Emerald Tablet of Hermes* <note>The *Tabula Smaragdina*, a foundational Hermetic text attributed to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus. It provides the philosophical basis for alchemy.</note> comes to pass as if it were a mystery carved in stone: *It ascends from the earth to the heaven, and again descends to the earth, and thus receives the power of things superior and inferior.* <note>original: "Ascendit à terra in cœlum, iterumque descendit in terram, sicq; vim recipit superiorum & inferiorum."</note> Those who have woven these secrets into riddles call this water "quicksilver" <note>original: "argentum vivum," referring to mercury</note> and the lime "true sulfur," from the mixture of which the Stone is formed, just as bread is made from water and flour. Others have called the water the "living spirit" and the earth the "ferment"; still others have called the former "male" and the latter "female," from whose embrace and union the infant <note>The "infant" or "offspring" is a common alchemical metaphor for the resulting Philosopher's Stone.</note> is procreated.

To complete the final stage of the work, store the pure lime in a sealed vessel buried in warm horse dung <note>In the days before regulated laboratory heaters, buried vessels in fermenting horse dung provided a constant, gentle "moist" heat for the process of digestion.</note> for forty days, until it melts into a white and thick liquid. Into this, pour water gradually at proper intervals of days, following the exact method and reasoning that masters of the art have explained to a T, so that the lime, gradually drinking in all its water as if nourished by it, may solidify into a true stone. The various changes of color that the Stone must undergo during this period, and the signs of its completion and perfection, have also been clearly expressed and revealed by those masters.

This is the immense treasure, this the true elixir, this the fruitful seed of gold, a <term>drachma: a dram; a small unit of weight used by apothecaries and alchemists</term> of which, if it be poured into two hundred and fifty drams of
->melted lead or tin,<-
->will convert the whole into<-
->the purest gold.<-

<summary>Jean Fernel describes the alchemical synthesis of the Philosopher's Stone using the principles of the Emerald Tablet, comparing the process to biological procreation and culinary fermentation. He concludes by asserting the Stone's power to transmute base metals into gold at a ratio of 1 to 250.</summary>

# THE SECRET OF THE PHILO-
# SOPHERS, ONCE WRITTEN BY A
## most learned man in hexameter
## verse.

->In the name of the living and life-giving God.<-

---

->I.<-

*Earth provided my body, and fire granted me strength,*
*I seek a home on high, yet my seat is always in the depths:*
*And the moisture that quickly leaves me drenches me.*
<note>In alchemy, the "body" is the solid state (Earth), while fire provides the energy for transformation. The "moisture" often refers to the process of distillation where vapors (the spirit) leave and then return to the substance.</note>

->II.<-

*I have tears, though there is no cause for sorrow,*
*My path is to the heavens, but heavy air hinders me:*
*And he who fathered me is not born without me.*
<note>"Tears" are a common alchemical metaphor for the droplets formed during condensation. The "path to the heavens" refers to sublimation or evaporation, while the "heavy air" represents the cooling or pressure that prevents the spirit from escaping the vessel.</note>

->III.<-

*Thin water of dust, gliding with a modest weight,*
*Soaked by the sun, flowing in summer, dry in the cold,*
*About to create rivers, I first occupy all the lands.*

->IV.<-

*I shall relate to you the wondrous beginnings of our life:*
*I was not yet born, nor was I then in my mother’s womb,*
*Once the birth was delivered, no one saw me born.*
<note>This describes the hidden or "occult" nature of the Philosopher’s Stone, which exists in a potential state before it is "born" through the alchemical process.</note>

->V.<-

*I cannot be born if I do not kill my mother:*
*I killed my mother, but the same end awaits me.*
*My death suffers that which my origin has already done.*
<note>A classic alchemical paradox: the "mother" (the initial raw material) must be destroyed or dissolved to produce the "son" (the Stone). This cycle of destruction and rebirth is central to the Great Work.</note>

->VI.<-

*Life to me is death; I die if I begin to be born:*
*But the fate of death comes before the origin of light:*
*Thus I consider the spirits of the dead to be my only parents.*
<note>original: "manes" — refers to the souls of the deceased or ancestral spirits. In this context, it suggests that the Stone arises from the "dead" or blackened matter (the nigredo stage) of the previous substance.</note>

<summary>A collection of six alchemical riddles written in verse, personifying the Philosopher's Stone as a paradoxical entity that must die to be born and exists across all elements. These verses use the language of classical poetry to encode the stages of chemical transformation, such as distillation and dissolution.</summary>

<keywords>Secret of the Philosophers, alchemical riddles, hexameter verse, Materia Prima, elements, distillation, killing the mother, life and death cycle</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the sequence of alchemical riddles from page 907. ## VII.

*I am not great indeed, but the greatest power resides within me,*
*The spirit is great, although in a small body,*
*Neither does my seed hold harm, nor does my fault bring a blush.*
<note>In alchemical literature, the "spirit" (volatile essence) is often described as a vast power trapped within a small "body" or vessel of matter. The lack of "blush" or "shame" suggests the purity of the refined substance.</note>

## VIII.

*We are both stones, we are one, we both lie together:*
*As sluggish as one is, so much the other does not go slowly;*
*This one remains unmoved, while that one does not cease to be moved.*
<note>This describes the union of the "Fixed" (the stone that stays unmoved) and the "Volatile" (the stone that moves or evaporates). In alchemy, these are often represented by the King and Queen or Sulfur and Mercury.</note>

## IX.

*No one can split me, yet many can cut me off.*
*But I am many-colored, destined eventually to be white.*
*I prefer to remain black; I shall fear the final fates less.*
<note>The "many-colored" state refers to the *cauda pavonis* (peacock’s tail), a stage of shifting colors before the substance reaches the *Albedo* (the white stage). The preference for remaining black refers to the *Nigredo* (the stage of putrefaction and death), which the alchemist must navigate before "resurrection."</note>

## X.

*No shape is certain for me, and none is foreign.*
*A brilliance resides within, shimmering with radiant light,*
*Which shows nothing, unless it has seen something before.*
<note>This riddle suggests the "Mirror of the Philosophers," a state of the matter (often associated with refined Mercury) that is reflective and takes the shape of its container while containing an internal "light."</note>

## XI.

*I do not immediately die when the spirit departs.*
*For it returns constantly, although it also often withdraws:*
*And now I have a great capacity of soul, and now none at all.*
<note>This describes the process of "circulation" or "distillation," where the vapor (spirit) leaves the solid matter (body) and then condenses and falls back down, repeatedly animating and leaving the substance.</note>

## XII.

*I have endured more than one body ought to have.*
*I had three souls, all of which I held within.*
*Two departed, but the third almost followed.*
<note>The "three souls" likely refer to the *Tria Prima*—the three primary principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury. Alchemical transformation involves separating and recombining these aspects.</note>

It cannot be denied more clearly than by saying, No.
And it cannot be affirmed more clearly than by saying, So be it.
To whom it has not been given, he does not understand. For every gift comes
->from above.<-
<note>original: "ab alto"</note>

# ON THE CHEMICAL HAR-
# MONY OF THE MOST RENOWNED AND 
### most learned man Master Lagneus, from his
### closest of friends.
<note>David Lagneau (D. Lagneus) was a 17th-century French physician and alchemist. His "Harmonia Chemica" (1611) attempted to reconcile the diverse and often contradictory writings of various alchemical authorities.</note>

*Do you see the glowing fleece of Phryxus the Aeolian*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*While Jason, son of Aeson, seeks it, what dangers he undergoes?*
<note>original: "Aeolii rutilantia vellera Phryxi." Phryxus was a mythological figure who escaped on a golden ram; its fleece became the goal of Jason's quest. In alchemy, the "Golden Fleece" is a common metaphor for the Philosopher's Stone.</note>
*Both gods and men roar, the sea resounds, and the heavens*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Thunder, and a crash is returned with the dark blue rain.*
*The Cyanean crags rise up: and you would think the rocks*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Against other rocks wish to destroy the fearful ship.*
<note>The Cyanean crags are the Symplegades, the "clashing rocks" that Jason had to navigate. They represent the volatile and dangerous early stages of the alchemical "Great Work."</note>
*And now, having traversed the immense journey and reaching the Phasis,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*The harsher Aeetes delivers these wild commands.*
*He said: "Stranger, if you wish to carry back the shining back*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Of the golden-haired beast to your Greek homes;*
*Then, being strenuous, yoke the bronze-footed bulls to the plows,*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Blowing out flames in a pitch-black whirlwind of Mars.*
*And sow my fields with the teeth of a serpent.*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*Thus shall you possess the gold of my beast."*
*He was stunned by these words, and at the shores of the Phasis*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*He groaned at the effort tried in vain (though too late):*
*When wise Medea, pitying the youth's labors,*

# ALBERTUS MAGNUS
## ON THE HARMONY OF THE PHILOSO-
### phers regarding the Stone.

Although in this matter the Philosophers seem to disagree literally, yet by bringing them into harmony, they all say the same thing in essence. For though they speak of one thing, they have named the stone itself by different names—according to different reasoning, different methods, their various symbols, and the operations of the stone. They call it at one time male, at another female, at another the thing joined together as a *rebis* <note>original: "rebis." A Latin-derived term (*res bina*) meaning "double thing," symbolizing the union of opposites like male and female or spirit and matter.</note>, and then as one single thing, then as various things. According to this logic, all the arguments and various authorities of the masters speaking on this matter can be resolved toward a single goal <term>terminum: end-point or goal</term> of the paths of this stone, which will be described hereafter. For there is but one way, namely mercury <note>In alchemy, "mercury" often refers to a philosophical principle of fluidity and transformation, not just the liquid metal.</note>, whether natural or artificial, or extracted from bodies—and especially from the most perfect ones [such as gold]—because in these, the substance of Mercury is at its most subtle and pure. It is prepared for the "fixation" <term>fixionem: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</term> of the Philosophers more than any other mercury in the whole world, as will appear more broadly through the authorities at the end. And yet, at every goal of the paths mentioned later, the authorities of the philosophers can be excellently explained to mean the same thing and in the same way. For there are, and can be, many paths to one single intent.

Nevertheless, from the different ways of applying fire as the "efficient cause" <note>A term from Aristotelian philosophy meaning the primary agent that produces an effect.</note>, the operation receives its direction, and consequently, the Philosophers' Stone receives different names according to its appearance; yet all things tend toward the same end. Namely, toward SUBTILIZATION <term>subtiliationem: the process of making a substance finer or more "spiritual"</term>, which is called sublimation <note>The process where a solid turns into vapor and then back to solid, used to purify the "spirit" of the matter.</note>. And toward the COMPLETION, which is called waxing <term>inceratio: "inceration," the addition of liquid to a dry substance until it has the consistency of wax</term> or calcination <note>Reducing a substance to a powder through high heat.</note>, and is known by many other different names. Therefore, from the repetition of that operation—namely, sublimation and its thickening—there naturally follows "waxing" or the "fixation" of the philosophers. This is achieved through the skill of the fire, using only one thing or with other scouring agents <note>original: "rimantibus," likely referring to auxiliary substances that help "open up" or cleanse the matter.</note> which, however, should not remain in the final result, as they all tend toward the same goal. And because of the speed of the progression and the quickening of the work, the excellence of the work results; and also, once the same "ferment" <note>A substance, often gold or silver, added to the alchemical matter to "ripen" it and give it the quality of the desired metal.</note> has been added, if one wishes to proceed further, an "augmentation" <term>augmentatio: increasing the quantity or potency of the Stone</term> can be made, as is clear to anyone looking at the sayings of the philosophers.

<summary>In this opening section, Albertus Magnus argues that the apparent contradictions among alchemical writers are merely differences in terminology, as all paths lead to the same process involving mercury and fire. He defines key stages of the Great Work, such as sublimation, fixation, and the use of a ferment to reach the final Stone.</summary>

<keywords>Albertus Magnus, Philosophers' Stone, Mercury, alchemy terminology, sublimation, calcination, fixation, rebis, ferment, augmentation</keywords>

# CHAPTER ONE CONCERNING THE
## *matter of the stone.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' featuring scrolling foliage and a human figure within the letter's frame.</image-desc>

Therefore, something must be said specifically about this matter, because some philosophers—indeed, nearly all of them—maintain that the Philosophers’ Stone is, in its beginning, a substance of mercury most refined of all earthiness, which would otherwise hinder its fixation <term>fixionem: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</term> and fusion. The philosophers would have it emerge from a totally purified matter, which is said to be produced through sublimation <term>sublimatio: the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</term>, as is evident through Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century chemist whose writings were the foundation of medieval alchemy.</note> in his *Summa*, in the chapter on the Solar medicine of the third order <note>original: "medicina Solari tertii ordinis." In alchemical hierarchy, a "third order" medicine is the most potent, capable of permanent transformation into gold.</note>, where he says that mercury is the stone known in the chapters.

And in the chapter on Mercury, he says that the tincture <term>tinctura: the transformative essence or "dye" that changes the properties of a metal</term> is produced and elicited from it. He also says that, by means of separation, you should divide the purest part and set it aside. But concerning this Mercury, the philosophers have differed, as is clear in their books. For some have asserted that this Mercury is the mercury of the common people <note>original: "Mercurium vulgi." Ordinary quicksilver as sold by merchants, as opposed to the "philosophical mercury" prepared by the chemist.</note>, yet not simply so, but purified through sublimation or through certain methods and "revivification." This must be done so many times that it becomes pure without any earthiness—whether this is done in the manner of the common people, or in the manner of the philosophers, namely, that the Mercury is held in a fire of endurance and balance. From that point on, by the continuity of the fire, the nature within it will be transformed, and the more refined part is separated into an upper vessel, about which we shall speak later regarding this path. Thus, the whole Mercury in its purest substance is born in such a way that its earthiness remains behind as dregs in the bottom to be discarded, as a certain philosopher says in the *Turba* <note>original: "turba." Refers to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>. You must hold to such a method of working for our stone; we add nothing and take nothing away, except that we remove the superfluous. Many sayings of the ancient philosophers and authorities placed in the books of philosophers have moved them to hold to this path, which are clear to anyone looking closely at the books of the philosophers. And here I will first attempt to bring in some authors who lean toward this path. For Senior <note>Senior Zadith, the Latin name for the 10th-century alchemist Muhammad ibn Umail al-Tamimi.</note> says, concerning the power of the Philosophers’ Stone and its one method of working: "Consider, my son, whatever is said in our books about waters, sulfur, vinegar, and salts—understand nothing else but our one divine thing, which, according to the difference of signs and preparations, is called at one time the soul <note>original: "anima." The vitalizing, volatile spirit of the chemical matter.</note>, and at another time sulfur." And he adds: "Do not pay attention to many things, although the philosophers say it is made of many things and a thing composed of three certain parts; this is said through a likeness [metaphor], as will be discussed below." Likewise, he says: "Our Philosophers’ Stone is one thing; if other things participated in it that were not of its own nature, we would not have called it 'our stone,' because all
<meta>catchword: men (continuation of "homines" from "omnes homines" / "all men")</meta>

It cites major alchemical authorities like Geber and Senior Zadith to argue that despite the many names used in alchemical texts—like sulfur, salt, or soul—the true work involves only one "divine" substance purified of all "earthiness."</summary>
