...humans share with other things. And he says further, "Some indeed have added sulfur." Likewise, according to Aristotle <note>In the Middle Ages, many alchemical texts were falsely attributed to the Greek philosopher Aristotle to give them authority; these are now called "Pseudo-Aristotle."</note>, nothing is completed except with a refined ferment like spirit. And consider this diligently. And when we said that its preparation is nothing other than sublimation <term>sublimatio: the process of purifying a substance by heating it into vapor and then solidifying it again</term>, this also includes the refinement, distillation, fixation <term>fixio: the process of making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand heat</term> of the philosophers, and inceration <term>inceratio: "waxing," or softening a substance until it has the consistency of wax</term>, because all these follow one another in nature, solely through the governance of fire according to the demands of the labor and the degree or endurance of the fire, which I shall declare more specifically below. Likewise, another philosopher says in the *Turba* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum" or "The Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a meeting of ancient sages.</note>:

"All things that are bought at a high price are found to be useless in this art." Nor should it be an obstacle that it is said in the *Book of Seventy Precepts* <note>An influential alchemical work attributed to Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan).</note> that this "thing" is made in "every thing," since the Senior <note>Referring to "Senior Zadith," the Latinized name of the 10th-century chemist Ibn Umail.</note> explains it thus: that in this one thing are all powers, namely whiteness <term>albedo: the second stage of the alchemical work, representing purification</term> and redness <term>rubedo: the final stage of the work, representing the perfection of the Stone</term>. Geber confirms this in his *Summa*, saying that it is found only in those things from which it is elicited; and for this reason they called this stone "one thing," as a certain philosopher says, because in that one thing alone is what it requires, such as sulfur, salt, and elixir <term>elixir: the refined substance capable of transforming base metals into gold or curing disease</term>. Likewise, the philosophers say that this "thing" does not consist in a multiplicity of things. And they also say to those intending to labor in this art: if they walk the right path, they should work around one thing through our stone; if you say you do not know this thing, you are wandering in error. Likewise, some say that from one thing, by one way, and by one disposition, the entire mastery is perfected. Likewise, someone said: "Do not forget that you need only one thing in the work." Likewise: "Do not support a plurality of compositions." Many envious authors lead people astray by speaking in figures <note>Alchemists often wrote "enigmatically" to hide secrets from the uninitiated; "envious" was a standard term for authors who deliberately obscured the truth.</note>, for our truth is one, in which there is a mighty spirit we seek that overcomes all natures; and therefore many philosophers have called this one thing "all things." Likewise, in the same place: "You do not need many things, for it is completed by one thing alone." And these are great words from the one who says: "Nature rejoices in nature, and nature contains nature" <note>original: "Natura natura laetatur & natura naturam continet." A famous ancient alchemical maxim attributed to Bolos of Mendes/Pseudo-Democritus.</note>, which the wise man governs by himself and extracts from the thing that overcomes every nature. Many other authors agreeing to the same are omitted here.

## CHAPTER TWO.

There are other philosophers who place the Philosophers’ Stone in Mercury—not the common kind <note>original: "non vulgi." Alchemists distinguished between "vulgar" mercury found in shops and "philosophical" mercury created through their art.</note>, but that extracted by ingenuity from perfect metallic bodies, namely the Sun and Moon <note>In alchemical code, the Sun (Sol) refers to Gold and the Moon (Luna) refers to Silver.</note>. And they say this method of extraction is done so that the extracted perfect bodies are so refined and transformed into true mercury...

It emphasizes the "governance of fire" as the primary tool and introduces the concept of "philosophical mercury" extracted from gold and silver.</summary>

...similar to the natural in a true manner, just as perfected bodies are sublimated <term>sublimatio: the process of purifying a substance by heating it into vapor and then solidifying it again</term> through skill and ingenuity—namely with "sharp waters" <note>original: "aquis acutis"; likely referring to corrosive acids used to dissolve metals</note> and the water of Sal ammoniac <note>original: "Salis armoniaci"; ammonium chloride, highly valued in alchemy for its ability to help cleanse and refine metals</note>, which greatly refines these bodies. And by continuing this refinement until the body becomes spiritual, mercurial, and volatile. This body, thus dissolved or prepared, they called Mercury, the Stone of the Philosophers. And then they persisted with the methods of working, as will be said hereafter, until a tincture <term>tinctura: a potent substance capable of transforming or "dyeing" base metals into gold or silver</term> was made from it, which can be increased and multiplied infinitely. 

And they are moved toward this path for such a reasonable cause, saying there is no doubt that in a perfected body—specifically in the Sun <note>The "Sun" (Sol) is the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note>, in which there is said to be the tincture of redness and whiteness, or even from the Moon <note>The "Moon" (Luna) is the alchemical symbol for Silver.</note> in which there is a white tincture, and by the continuation of fire it will become red. Others, however, call the Mercury of bodies "male and female." Still others take three parts of the male and five parts of the female, or even both mixed together as male and female—that is, body and spirit—as some say, because of the speed of the bodies' simultaneous corruption <note>In alchemy, "corruption" is a necessary stage of decay or breakdown that must occur before a substance can be reborn in a higher form.</note> compared to the living [mercury] alone. 

And then the bodies thus dissolved into "living mercury" <note>original: "Mercurium vivum"; quicksilver or a purified metallic essence</note> have within themselves a Mercury prior to all natural ones and even more disposed toward physical fixation <term>fixio: making a substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated</term>, and because of this, it accomplishes everything more quickly than any natural mercury, provided it is worked according to the previously written sayings of the philosophers. Furthermore, it is not inconsistent to assert, as those do who place the stone of the philosophers in the refinement through "strong waters" <note>original: "aquis fortibus"; usually referring to nitric acid</note> of perfected bodies, that it may fly or rise upward even in common sublimation. And to refine the body in such a way that it truly flies—that is, that it is sublimated and refined to such an extent that it becomes spiritual and easily melted, penetrating and dyeing. 

For in this way, through such sublimation, perfected bodies are changed from nature to nature and become incorporeal, until through "roasting" <note>original: "assationem"; a slow, dry heating process</note> they produce from themselves kinds similar to themselves, such as Gold the Sun, Silver the Moon, and so on infinitely. And they say this belongs to the perfection of any nature: that it should be able to generate its like; but gold and other things cannot do this naturally. And therefore they say the craftsman ought to **begin where nature has left off.** And thus make the philosophical tincture, perfectly discovered through this most noble science and art.

to the most noble substance of Mercury, or of a body refined to such a degree that it is judged to be the same; and this is confirmed by these authorities. For Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary figure in Islamic alchemy whose works were foundational to European alchemy.</note> says in his *Summa of the Perfection of the Magistery* <note>original: "summa sua perfecti magisterii"</note>, in the chapter on the sun and the moon: "By God, the sun is the tincture of redness and the moon of whiteness." And elsewhere in the same book he says: "For it is necessary that the tincture be more subtle than the bodies from which it is drawn." Geber also says in the same place that the tincture is found both in bodies and in Mercury. In bodies, however, it is more difficult; it is difficult to resolve perfected bodies of the strongest composition so that they are destroyed and compared to Mercury in subtlety and penetration, as will be clear where Geber says in his *Summa of the Magistery* that the bodies from which the tincture is drawn must be refined, and this cannot be achieved by a "hard-necked" <note>original: "duræ cervicis"; a metaphor for a stubborn or unskillful practitioner who lacks the patience for delicate work</note> craftsman. 

But why it is not "more perfect" in Mercury, but rather "easier," can be shown thus: First, because a longer labor is required in Mercury. For before natural <term>☿: the symbol for Mercury</term> is prepared to such an extent that it matches the purity and goodness of a metal body reduced into Mercury, a long time passes, and it requires a long digestion <term>digestio: the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat to mature it</term> with methods of refinement, as is said later. And because it requires much digestion and very hidden processes for its perfection, it consequently becomes more accustomed to the fire; thus the tincture is most perfectly worked and generated. Therefore, he says that in Mercury the tincture would be easier, but not more perfect. 

Likewise, toward this same path—namely, that the Stone of the Philosophers exists in the bodies of metals—Geber seems to lean strongly in the book *On the Investigation of the Perfection of the Magistery*, speaking practically of tinctures of the "third order" for the white and the red. For he says: "For the white, take the moon <note>Silver</note>, and for the red, take the sun <note>Gold</note>, and dissolve them in their own strong water <note>original: "aqua forti"; a corrosive acid, likely nitric acid, used to dissolve precious metals</note> and make small stones." Then he immediately adds: "And this is our fixed body dissolved into our fixed Mercury," and so on. And in the same place, he teaches how to govern it further by sublimating and fixing it, as we have handed down in our *Summa*. 

Note here, however, that although Geber says to take the moon for the white and the sun for the red, he does not mean to deny that both tinctures are in each body by itself (as they are in the mixtures), or even that the white is in the red body and the red tincture is in the white, as is clear from a certain philosopher who says: "Although our stone is outwardly red or white, inwardly it is white if it is outwardly red." And if it were outwardly white, through the decoction <term>decoctio: the process of boiling or heating a substance in a liquid</term> of the fire, it will become red. And Plato adds in the fourth book: "Convert the natures, and you shall find what you seek." Likewise, another says: "Make the hidden manifest and the manifest hidden, and you shall find the magistery <term>magisterium: the finished work or the "Masterpiece" of the alchemist</term>." To this same path belongs what a certain philosopher says in the *Assembly* <note>original: "turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "Unless the bodies in..."

# ALBERTUS MAGNUS

...you have made corporeal things, and yet you have not found the rule of operating to make incorporeal things corporeal. Likewise, the philosopher Archelaus <note>Archelaus was a 5th-century BCE Greek philosopher, though in alchemy, his name is often associated with later apocryphal texts.</note> says: I advise that you begin with perfected things, for you will sooner run out of life than you will bring imperfect things to their final perfection. Likewise, Hermes says in that treatise of his titled *On the Secrets of Hermes*: "If you should consume a third part of your camels..." <note>original: "Si camelorum tuorum tertiam partem consumas"; a metaphorical instruction regarding the proportions of the "beasts of burden" or raw materials in the chemical process.</note> And Plato agrees with him in the *Book of the Fourth* <note>original: "libro de quarto"; likely referring to the *Liber Quartorum*, a Latin translation of an Arabic work attributed to Plato</note> where he says: It is necessary for gold to be turned into vapor, and this cannot be done except in a triangular figure. And a certain Master, who wrote a discourse on the truth of this art, also holds to this path. And the philosophers commonly say: **Our Mercury is not the common Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius noster non est Mercurius vulgi"; a standard alchemical warning that the "Mercury of the Wise" is a specially prepared substance, not the quicksilver found in shops</note>, but you should understand it to be Mercury when it has become the elixir. Likewise, Senior and Calib <note>"Senior" refers to the 10th-century Arabian alchemist Zadith ben Hamuel; "Calib" refers to Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince credited with being the first Muslim alchemist.</note> say the same: This gold of ours comes forth from gold. And it is air; and furthermore, Senior says: O, if you only knew this stone of ours, the air or the aerial thing in which the metals are understood to be contained! Likewise, Senior says in the same place: It is the "thing" of all philosophers, which has within itself everything that it needs, and it is the mother of gold. And it is also said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic.</note> that it is more excellent by nature, yet viler than all other things. For gold is not vile by nature. 

Behold how the same Senior seems to disagree in his own words, and how the other philosophers seem to disagree among themselves, as can be seen from the authorities already written here and previously. Nevertheless, all philosophers cry out one thing: **One matter, one vessel, one preparation** <note>original: "Res una, vas unum, præparatio una"</note>, which is <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collecting the purified solid as it cools</term> or thinning, which we call the sole operation; but according to the requirements of the degrees of the fire, different operations follow—namely, <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</term>—and the thing itself receives different names, as was said before. 

It remains, therefore, to approach the reconciliation of the philosophers, and not without merit. In concluding, therefore, as it seems to me, it must be said that all philosophers and their authorities agree on Mercury. This is because the Stone of the Philosophers is always Mercury. And this appears clearly from their writings. However, they seem to be in discord regarding "natural Mercury" and "extracted Mercury," as was said before. Here it must be said that the authorities leaning toward the path of natural Mercury are to be understood as not speaking by way of denial—that is, it is not that another "abstracted" Mercury is not, or cannot be, the Stone of the Philosophers. But because such philosophers, knowing the method of investigation and the thorough cooking <note>original: "deconcoctionem"; the slow heating or "digesting" of materials</note> by which natural Mercury is found, discovered the art in that alone. And they did this so that men would not spend their money on more precious things, since the art can be found even in a viler thing; thus they set down their authorities—namely, that the "thing" is bought for a cheap price, as was said before. Truly, those who placed the Stone of the Philosophers in the "bodies" <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to the seven metals, particularly gold and silver.</note> did so, and they did not place it there by the denial of the other understanding, since no one doubts...

### ON THE CONCORDANCE OF PHILOSOPHERS CONCERNING THE STONE

It must be acknowledged that they all aim toward the same path and intention. From this arise many modes, methods, and paths—one easier, another more difficult; one longer, another shorter—yet they always intend the same result. Therefore, those speaking in such a way intend this path: namely, that once the **Mercury of the perfected body** <note>original: "Mercurio corporis perfecti"; this refers to mercury extracted from gold or silver rather than common quicksilver</note> is obtained, or once the perfected body is dissolved and refined, it is certain through the refinement of the operation that this thing is purer, more perfect, and more suitable for further perfection. Such a substance can generate its own likeness from itself without its own <term>tincture</term> <note>A "tincture" is the concentrated essence or "soul" of a metal that has the power to transform other substances.</note>. Furthermore, this process is completed in a shorter time, is less difficult in the manner of working, and is less prone to error. 

In contrast, many have erred greatly by working with **common mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio vulgi"; ordinary quicksilver purchased from a merchant</note>, laboring over its preparation—namely the <term>philosophical fixation</term> <note>Fixation is the process of turning a volatile liquid substance into a solid that can withstand fire.</note>—for long periods of time until they are driven to the very edge of despair. This would likely not have happened to them if they had worked with the material of the perfected Mercury. Indeed, that which is already perfect is more quickly and more thoroughly perfected, and it is destroyed with greater difficulty. Consequently, fewer errors are made with it, since "nature rejoices in nature, and nature delights in and befriends nature," as a certain philosopher says. "In things that possess a shared quality, the transition is easy." <note>original: "in habentibus symbolum est facilis transitus"; a principle derived from Aristotle's physics, meaning that substances sharing a common element or quality transform into one another more readily.</note> 

This authority is natural in this art regarding the unity of our **blessed stone**. Through it, many paths are revealed, yet many have labored in them and been led to extremes, and therefore they ultimately denied that the art was true. These are the ones who have labored and continue to labor in the joining of bodies and spirits through <term>amalgams</term> <note>A mixture of mercury with another metal.</note> and in "waters," or by working with bodies alongside other bodies. In this way, they wished to convert a body into a spirit, and afterward to fix together one body with a spirit, or one spirit (or many) with one body (or both perfected bodies). They claim that the <term>tincture</term> cannot be made except with the joining of a marriage: namely, the **Sun** as the husband and the **Moon** as the wife, with **Mercury** acting as the medium for joining their tinctures. <note>In alchemical allegory, the Sun (Sol) represents Gold, the Moon (Luna) represents Silver, and their marriage is the chemical union required to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

These things are said through many authorities which are written perhaps literally, or perhaps out of jealousy or allegorically, as when they speak of **distillations**. In truth, there is but one stone, as everyone proclaims, which contains within itself everything it needs. According to the different signs appearing during its preparation, it is called by various names, as I have written to you more diligently earlier in this treatise. 

It is no wonder that those who labor so long in the "fixations" of bodies and spirits have found nothing. For the less simple and more composite a thing is, the less of a "shared quality" <note>original: "symboli"</note> there is within it. Therefore, the transition is more difficult because when the required refinement of fire is needed, it can only with great difficulty be applied to things of diverse natures that are tending toward a single end. For perhaps while one part is being "fixed" (made solid), another might become volatile; or while one is being sublimated and refined, another might perhaps become thickened or coarse.

And yet it is quite true that the spirit is joined to bodies through solution in **sharp waters** <note>original: "aquis acutis"; typically refers to corrosive acids like nitric acid or strong vinegar</note> or in those waters themselves, whether by the body or in amalgamations or other ways. For whether that Mercury is natural (yet purified, and thus not common but of the philosophers) or whether it is abstracted from a perfected body or bodies by whatever method or device—either by itself or by addition for the sake of shortening the labor—as long as the Mercury extracted from the body is subtle and not deprived of its humidity <note>original: "humiditate"; in alchemy, the "radical moisture" that allows a metal to be flexible and alive</note>, but pure like a pure body refined into the likeness of Mercury (provided that the added things do not remain), then that Mercury of the philosophers—through devices and fire as the efficient cause according to the modes and devices of Geber (who in this says the whole truth in a few words) and the greater philosophers agreeing with him—if it is continued with the persistence of the work, the **true tincture of the philosophers** can be made from it; and thus it is evident.

...already known, and let it be prepared in a single glass vessel like an *orobus* <note>original: "orobo"; likely referring to a small, pulse-shaped or bean-shaped vessel, or perhaps the plant-based shape of the glass</note>, or in a vessel that sits atop another in the manner of a **cucurbit** <note>a gourd-shaped boiling flask</note> and an **alembic** <note>a distilling cap with a beak or "nose"</note> or nozzle, and let them be skillfully joined if you work with one vessel atop another as certain philosophers say, just as I will write later, in such a way that it cannot "breathe" <note>the vessel must be hermetically sealed so no vapors escape</note>. Let the work of the **sublimation of the philosophers** be applied steadily upon it—which is to say, <term>refinement</term> <note>original: "subtiliatio"; the process of making a substance finer, purer, or more "spiritual" through repeated heating</note>—so that the stone may be perfectly refined, reaching the ultimate fineness and purity through the persistence of the work and the tempering of the fire, or rather through a greater, continuous, and successive endurance of the flame, continuing all things toward the same task of refinement.

The reason for this is that the entire <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; the completion of the Great Work or the production of the Philosopher's Stone</note>, as all philosophers agree, consists of nothing but sublimation through the continuation and endurance of fire. All other operations follow naturally; namely, once refinement is achieved, there follows thickening <note>original: "inspissatio"</note>, then the reduction to ash <note>original: "incineratio"</note> of some part, and from this follows **fixation** <note>making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>. No one should doubt that through refinement alone, and through the use of a greater fire, that same specific part is fixed and reduced to ash by itself—as will be said later—a part which then fixes many other non-fixed parts.

Secondly: let it be refined again, and thus fixed again. Thirdly: let it be refined yet again. **Geber** <note>the famous 8th-century alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan</note> sets forth his precise intention on this: using only the Stone itself, only fire, and only a single vessel if you wish, the entire Stone will thus be perfected into a **tincture** <note>the final medicine capable of transforming metals</note>.

And you should not find fault because some have said that "aids" <note>additives or secondary reagents</note> are necessary so that Mercury itself may be so refined, since it is of a homogeneous—that is, a very strong—composition, and is spiritually **Sun and Moon** <note>original: "Sol & Luna"; symbolic terms for Gold and Silver</note>. If Mercury must be extracted from it and thus refined into Mercury, it is extremely difficult. Consequently, this might lead the practitioner into error.

I say to the first point that although natural **Mercury**—or the Mercury of the philosophers, or the Mercury of perfected bodies—is of a very strong composition, nevertheless, through the continuation of fire, some part is always separated from the other by refinement in the manner of a vapor. And because it cannot "breathe" out of the vessel, it thickens and descends again. And again, by means of the governance of the fire—namely a slow heat, as the purpose of the work requires—it refines another even finer part along with itself, and so on until the whole work is thus completed. This is the primary intention of the philosophers who write the truth in this art; however, other methods (some of which I will set down below) are not denied by this, provided they tend toward the same goal of the philosophers in their way of working, even if they use different methods and clever ways of laboring.

## CHAPTER FIVE CONCERNING
### *perfected bodies.*

But regarding the second part—that is, the <term>perfected bodies</term> <note>original: "corporibus perfectis"; in alchemy, these are the noble metals, gold and silver, which are "perfect" because they do not rust or decay in fire</note>—as was just touched upon above. I confess that it is exceedingly difficult to digest these bodies by themselves in such a way that they are changed into the nature of Mercury, or become "Mercurial." Indeed, a human life might not last long enough to witness such a perfect <term>refinement</term> <note>original: "subtiliationem"; the process of making a solid substance more fluid or spiritual</note> through natural means alone. However, this is not impossible, because through the application of fire—that is, the fire of heat and moisture, as in <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the process of breaking down a substance through gentle, moist heat, often compared to the biological decay that leads to new life</note>—even substances of the strongest composition can be altered and consequently well-refined into Mercury.

Therefore, because of the great length of time required, it is not unreasonable to assert that one may rightly allow preparation with external substances—namely, with salts, <term>sharp waters</term> <note>original: "aquas acutis"; mineral acids like nitric or sulfuric acid used to dissolve metals</note>, putrefactions, solutions, <term>roastings</term> <note>original: "assationibus"; heating a substance in a dry state</note>, calcinations, and any other methods—so that these perfected bodies of the philosophers may be refined or prepared into the nature of Mercury, and then those external agents may be removed. 

Afterward, when the bodies have been prepared to such a Mercurial fineness, the result is called the **Philosopher's Stone**. With this, one must then proceed—principally as if with one Mercury and then another, according to the sayings of the philosophers—entirely and not in one single way. This is the consensus of all the philosophers, as has already been demonstrated many times through their own words. This specific part concerns the method of refining perfected bodies into the *nature* of Mercury, and not into <term>living Mercury</term> <note>original: "vivum Mercurium"; liquid quicksilver</note>. While there is a way of working that resolves bodies into living Mercury—similar to the way one works with common Mercury—the "preparation of the philosophers," as previously stated, is different. 

Some have adopted a way of working similar to that of common Mercury, and they claim this method belongs to **Plato** in his *Book of Quarters* <note>original: "Platonis in quartas"; likely referring to the *Liber Quartorum*, a famous alchemical text attributed to Plato</note>; they also agree with the intention of **Geber** <note>an influential 8th-century alchemist (Jabir ibn Hayyan) known for his rigorous laboratory methods</note>, as has been said, and other philosophers. For sometimes the work must be done by taking a perfected body such as <term>the Sun</term> <note>original: "solem"; alchemical code for gold</note> and refining it with sharp waters, converting it into "little stones." These they dissolve in a <term>solution of dung</term> <note>original: "solutione fimi"; using the steady, gentle heat of a fermenting manure pile to keep a vessel warm for long periods</note>, and then they congeal the matter by roasting; this they call the "work of refinement." 

As many times as they repeat these solutions and congealings, the whole mass is refined into the nature of Mercury, so that it flows with easy fusion and "entry," and this matter may <term>tinge</term> <note>original: "tingat"; the ability of the Stone to "dye" or transform base metals into gold</note>. Then afterward, holding that refined part as the "fixed part" and the "ferment," they cook it again with four parts of the body (which has been reduced into their fusible Mercury and into little stones). They dissolve it by roasting, as before, continuing the labor until the matter tinges again, and

Some indeed intend to perform this refinement of the body or bodies using <term>spirits</term> <note>volatile or gaseous substances</note>, namely with <term>sublimated Mercury</term>—whether "living" [liquid] or in other forms—or other spirits of salts, joining these spirits with the bodies through <term>sharp waters</term> <note>original: "aquas acutis"; mineral acids like nitric or sulfuric acid</note> by means of decoction. And then, by sublimating from these spirits or even simply, they say some part of the body is "lightened" or raised up with the spirits; and they continue this until they have a good portion of the body converted into spirit.

And then, through separation with a gentle fire, they take the more refined part of the sublimation from the top; but they say the other part remains at the bottom, which they later call the "fixed" part. They then cook this fixed part again with the non-fixed part in a good quantity by gently roasting it until the part is "fixed" once more and converted back into <term>fixed earth</term>. They continue this to fix a good portion. And they call this the prepared <term>earth of sulfur</term> <note>original: "terram sulphuris"; a vital alchemical stage representing the active, combustible, and masculine principle of the work</note>.

Then they raise this earth again with a good quantity of the non-fixed part, and they repeat this until the whole is raised. And thus they fix it once more. And this, repeated four times, they say will be the <term>tincture</term> according to the sayings of <term>Geber</term> <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry" whose Latinized works were foundational to European alchemy</note> and also <term>Hermes</term> in the <term>Emerald Tablet</term> <note>original: "Telešmo"; referring to the "Tabula Smaragdina," the foundational text of Hermeticism. The word used here, 'Telesmus,' suggests the 'completion' or 'perfection' described in that text</note> where he says: *You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently and with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth to heaven and descends again, until it retains the power of both the inferior and the superior.*

And although these sayings of Hermes agree so well that they could apply to the method of the Philosophers' Stone previously mentioned and its way of working, as was stated before, nevertheless—to satisfy their opinion, which does not seem irrational, and because they aim entirely for refinement and a <term>mercurial</term> state—I say such ways of working are well supported. Provided, however, that in the labor one takes care that the bodies or the matter in such refinement are not dried out too much or entirely stripped of their nature. For as was said before, in whatever way Mercury is refined, and through whatever path, as long as such preparations and decoctions are done according to the path and intention of the philosophers of which we spoke earlier.

...philosophers and the writings in this treatise of mine, many philosophers are inclined toward the way which is in <term>natural Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurio naturali"; mercury as a base elemental substance</note> prepared, or rather in the Mercury specifically <term>resolved</term> <note>dissolved or broken down into its essence</note> from bodies or from a <term>perfected body</term> <note>original: "corpore perfecto"; usually referring to gold</note>, more than toward those ways written just above. This is because the ancient philosophers paid much more attention to the unity and uniformity of the matter and the labor than to multiplicity, since in one thing there is greater unity and a stronger <term>link</term> <note>original: "symbolum"; a shared essence or correspondence between the material and the goal</note> than in many. Consequently, the labor is easier and less prone to error, provided that the method of fire and preparation—which all philosophers have hidden—is duly completed. 

Nevertheless, for the completion of this treatise concerning the intent of the <term>philosophers' stone</term> and the way by which the philosophers principally understand their own sayings, I propose to write a little about the <term>regimen</term> <note>original: "regimine"; the controlled administration of heat over time</note> according to the writings, considering that very stone of the philosophers which consists in one thing and in one labor. 

Furthermore, I subsequently propose to validate such things through the authorities of the philosophers, then finally concluding this treatise in this way. Just as, therefore, in the second principal part of this treatise something was said concerning the preparation of our stone, now therefore speaking conclusively, I say it must be totally asserted only in the modes or the mode of preparation of the stone which the philosophers principally intend—which you cannot know from my writings alone—the whole preparation of which stone consists in <term>sublimation</term> alone, that is, in <term>subtiliation</term> <note>the process of making a substance "subtle," volatile, or refined through heat</note>. 

And this operation, through the length of the labor and with the persistence of diligence upon the stone itself, and the <term>regimen of fire</term> toward the intention of the work and the endurance of our Mercury, our whole <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; the successful completion of the alchemical work</note> is fulfilled. And all the various operations written, on account of the different intentions of governing the stone itself, naturally follow one another: as after sublimation (which is subtiliation), there is <term>thickening</term> <note>original: "inspissatio"</note>, and then <term>incineration</term> <note>original: "incineratio"; reducing to ash or a dry powder</note>, whence comes <term>waxing</term> <note>original: "ceratio"; making a substance soft or meltable like wax</note> and our <term>philosophical fixation</term> <note>original: "fixio philosophica"; making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates in fire</note>, etc. 

And so that you may better understand this term "philosophical fixation": it should be known that one must take the greatest care lest the stone, through the endurance of its fire, be deprived of its <term>moisture</term> <note>original: "humiditate"; the "radical moisture" or vital fluid that alchemists believed held the matter together</note>, because then its moisture could never—or only with great difficulty—be restored to it, and thus the whole work would be destroyed. This has happened to many philosophers, even those whose stone was developing well, for which reason they even denied the art; and others among them who wished to deny the art can be mistaken, not noticing that all philosophers cry out that their work is "sublimation alone." But they themselves purified and subtilized the stone known to them in some way, and then they intended toward fixation once sublimation was dismissed and purification completed, and thus they [fixed] the stone to such an extent...

...concluded <note>original: "verunt," completing "concluserunt" from the previous page</note> that they deprived it of moisture, and through this they were led to destruction. They did not notice that all Philosophers cry out for one work and one labor, which are followed by various signs according to the utility of the stone and its different dispositions. These, however, consist in <term>sublimation</term> alone <note>original: "sublimatione"; the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then condenses back into solid form</note>, the regimen of which is the fire of sublimation. Through this, various operations are performed in the stone: now sublimation, now thickening, now <term>incineration</term> <note>original: "incinerationem"; reducing a substance to white ash or powder through heat</note>. Following this incineration, through the heat of its own endurance, comes the hidden <term>Philosophical fixation</term> <note>original: "fixio Philosophica"; making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</note>.

And therefore, Philosophical fixation must be considered most carefully—namely, that the stone be fixed, and that during the time it is being fixed, the power of refining the fixed part (for the purpose of fixing what is not yet fixed) is not taken away. Rather, these works should be carried out for a long time in one or two vessels, as was said before, with a single labor and a single method of administering the fire in the first work, which is the sublimation of the stone. Then, through a medium fire of the greatest endurance, the <term>thickening</term> <note>original: "inspissatio"; the process of a liquid becoming dense or solid</note> of the stone follows; and further still, the incineration of the part which, by nature and through the continuation of fire, is more suited to fixation. Subsequently, it will be fixed by that Philosophical fixation mentioned above. Thus, your work continues as a single labor until, through the signs to be described later, the matter itself reaches <term>perfect Mastery</term> <note>original: "perfecto Magisterio"; the completed alchemical work or Great Work</note>.

However, it must be noted here—lest we be criticized by the <term>envious</term> <note>original: "invidis"; a common alchemical term for critics or those unworthy of the secret knowledge</note>—why the Philosophers did not properly write down the regimen of fire by its specific degrees. I say that it cannot be very well determined in specific detail regarding such degrees of fire and their proportions, nor have any Philosophers fully set these down. Although one may have said more about such matters than another, they committed the rest to the industry and practice of the workers. From these workers, other notable points can be well drawn out below from the authorities of the Philosophers speaking on this matter.

## CHAPTER SIX, IN WHICH
#### *the whole Regimen consists.*

The whole regimen of the degrees of fire and the preparation of the stone consists, therefore, as I can determine from the sayings of the Philosophers, in this: that our stone, being one, is held in a single vessel (as has been written) over a slow fire. This is done so that its subtler part remains in the fire for a good length of time, ensuring that another labor—namely, thickening—is not applied to it too quickly. This continues until, through the long duration of the fire and the seasoning of the stone within it, you see that part naturally thickened by the steady heat of the fire. Then, by strengthening such fire a little, and thus

...continuing until you see some part desire to be <term>incinerated</term> <note>original: "incinerari"; reduced to a fine white ash or powder through heat</note>. Then, simply with a greater vigor of fire—yet without departing from the first or second works through the violence of the flame—once some part is already incinerated by itself and naturally (on account of the multitude of other subtle parts), such a part will begin to be refined again or <term>sublimated</term> <note>original: "sublimari"; in alchemy, this refers to the purification of a substance, often by vaporizing and condensing it, though the author later clarifies its specific meaning here</note>. 

And so, proceeding again continually as has been said, and doing this through the endurance of a greater fire until these powders become sublimated and incinerated. You will find that for this work, the first step is the <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixio"; making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</note> of the stone through long cooking by fire. Our stone itself will reach such an endurance for fire because such a great heat would be required even in the second work and labor regarding the persistence of the stone for sublimation—that is, its refinement—just as it was in the first for its thickening. 

And so consequently, concerning <term>inceration</term> <note>original: "inceratione"; the process of softening the stone to a waxy consistency so it can "melt" into other metals</note> and fixation, you must urge the process forward continually until, ultimately, the whole stone—sufficiently purified—readily offers its fusion through this method of ruling the fire upon the stone with its own ignition. In this state, it transforms metals or <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurium"; quicksilver, considered the "spirit" of all metals</note> into a true <term>Sun-maker</term> <note>original: "Solificum"; something that produces gold</note> and <term>Moon-maker</term> <note>original: "Lunificum"; something that produces silver</note> through its own perfections and tests. 

This happens either according to the whole mass or according to a part. I say "according to a part" notably here because there is no worry if the whole of your placed matter is not entirely prepared; it does not harm the work if some part of it remains in any particular stage—namely sublimation or inceration. The reason for this is that it serves as a sign that the stone has not been directed with too much speed, and this is more useful. Therefore, one must take the greatest care that the stone is not so accelerated in any part of even the prior work. For the <term>sublimation</term> of the Philosophers must be continued for so long upon the stone, and it is not an upward elevation, but a "remaining within" <note>original: "infra remansio"; a crucial distinction where the substance is refined in place rather than vaporized to the top of the vessel</note> until the whole mastery is completed in its perfection. 

Prove this perfection by <term>projection</term> <note>original: "projectione"; the act of casting a small amount of the Stone onto molten base metal to transform it</note> upon a spirit or a body. If you find the stone itself whitened and purified to such an extent that it yields a pure whiteness, and you then see the stone so sublimated that it penetrates to the interior of the thing to be tinted—and once that penetration is made, the stone remains so fixed that the tested matter withstands all judgments <note>i.e., survives the tests of the assayer, such as acid or intense heat</note>—then it is sufficient, and you have operated rightly. 

If it is not so, repeat the first work upon it, and so on as has been written, until it becomes so, and it shall be with God’s cooperation. Behold, however, you can consider that it is very erroneous to agitate the operation of the stone in such a way that, once one operation is done, one intends to move to another and the first is abandoned. For if the mastery is not in its completion—as happens to many who, because of this, are led to the ruin of this art—the first work cannot be repeated upon it, and thus...

## CHAPTER SEVEN, THE REGImen of the stone proven by authorities.

### *The control of the stone proven by authorities.*

Now I speak according to the promises; I shall not omit to insert some authorities of the ancients regarding the said regimen of the stone as it pertains to fire and its preparation, committing the rest to the diligence and understanding of anyone reading the books of the Philosophers. For **Senior** <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemist whose works were highly influential in the Middle Ages</note> says first: in the preparation of the stone and the regimen of fire, the preparation of our stone becomes difficult and especially hidden. Likewise, he says elsewhere: the common people having eyes are asleep, for when they have the thing, they do not know its preparation, etc. Likewise, the Philosophers, speaking of the fire, say: It is necessary for this fire to be the heat of the **Sun** when it is in its own state, and for this reason they called it <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefactionem"; the stage of "blackening" where the matter is broken down by gentle heat</note>. Likewise in the same place: let your fire be the **fire of baths** <note>original: "ignis balneorum"; a water bath or bain-marie, providing steady, gentle heat</note>. Likewise in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: Let your fire be gentle in <term>whitening</term> <note>original: "dealbando"; the *Albedo* stage where the matter becomes pure and white</note>, that is, with that moderation by which the <term>tincture</term> <note>the soul or coloring power of the stone</note> is made white; it requires a smaller tolerance of fire than when it begins to be rectified with the matter of the stone through the persistence of fire alone. Then, when the stone is worked toward the <term>red</term> <note>original: "rubeum"; the *Rubedo* or final stage of the work</note>, it requires as much a degree of fire for the first work toward red as is perhaps required for the second work in whitening. And in this, a man ought to be cautious, that he does not rule the stone before the time of perfect whitening—that is, until the tincture is perfect in the white regimen—through the degrees of fire which belong to the red. And concerning this the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> cries out, saying: **Do not mix the white work into the red.** These matters, however, are to be committed to the greatest exercise of the one laboring. Likewise, in the same place: concerning our stone in a vessel placed above, a gentle fire is to be made for 40 days, because through it the corrupting moistures are drawn out. For all the Philosophers commend the lengthiness of their work, and they condemn speed and <term>combustion</term> <note>original: "combustionem"; excessive burning that ruins the delicate balance of the matter</note>—namely, so much that the stone cannot return to its first work, and is thus destroyed in its entirety. Likewise, it is said in the same place that we must beware of our <term>vinegar</term> <note>original: "aceto nostro"; an alchemical solvent or acid, not common vinegar</note>, lest it...

Likewise, it is said in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: In our work, first all things are **blackened**, that is, when the "first matter" is, as it were, reduced to ash <note>original: "incineratur"</note>, it is not yet perfection. In the second stage, all things are **whitened**, that is, in the second work the matter is prepared for greater whiteness and transparency. And thirdly, it is necessary to incinerate the whole composition—specifically upon reaching perfect whitening. Thus, it is not totally incinerated until it is perfectly whitened, as was said before. 

Likewise, it is said in the same place: "Do not despise these ashes," for again its "sweat" or liquefaction—that is, its <term>sublimation</term> <note>the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again</note> or solution, which here are the same thing—will return to it through a somewhat greater application of fire. And so, fourthly, the **golden crown** is then perfected in the <term>tincture</term> <note>the final medicinal or transforming essence of the Stone</note>. 

It must be known, however, that some matter becomes yellow <note>original: "citrina"</note> after the blackness; sometimes red <note>original: "rubea"</note> before the whiteness. One should not worry about this, provided that such states are not maintained until perfection (as has been said), because the "red work" would then be mixed with the "white," which ought not to happen. Instead, the degrees of fire should be moderated when such an effect is seen, lest one deviate from the intention which I have already written to you most correctly. Thus, the work is directed from **blackness** <note>original: "nigredine"</note> to **whiteness** <note>original: "albedinem"</note>, so that the work may always be able to return to its principles. 

Whence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> says, and it is also said in the *Assembly*: "Let the crude and fresh elements be received at the beginning of the mixture, and let them be mixed until the elements are joined to one another; and let them be ground—not by the grinding of hands, as is said in the *Assembly*—but when they are washed with water, they then conceive; thereafter let them be extracted and nourished, so that the 'offspring' may be produced." 

And he adds: "And know, that this **marriage** <note>original: "desponsatio"; the chemical union of substances</note> occurs in **putrefaction** <note>the breaking down of matter</note> at the bottom of the vessel—not the 'rot of the common people' <note>original: "putredine vulgi"; a warning that alchemical putrefaction is a specialized chemical process, not biological decay</note>, but through incineration." For the ancient Philosophers nowhere suggest anything regarding common rot or the distillation of waters, but perhaps speak allegorically and figuratively of it being "in the air"—that is, in the upper part of the vessel, or in a superior vessel, if one works with one vessel placed upon another, as **Senior** <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemist</note> seems to think, as will be clear below.

Likewise, it is said in the same place: "Take things from their minerals, and exalt them to higher places, and reap them from the summit of mountains, and lead them back upon their roots." And these are manifest words, written without any envy <note>i.e., written transparently for the student</note>, and confirmed by authority. 

Certain people wished to pull this way of working toward [a different method], namely that they converted **Mercury** into water through "affusions" <note>pouring liquid over a substance</note>, either with other things or by itself, and they distilled it through an **alembic** <note>a type of still used for distillation</note>, and they moistened the "earth" at the bottom with the water, and thus they converted the water into earth; and they did this until...

...the perfect <term>tincture</term> <note>the final transforming essence of the Stone</note> must be continued. Whatever the case may be regarding this, whether in the universal or the particular work, this does not seem to me to be the intention of the ancient Philosophers—although I do not see it refuted anywhere. For even though it proceeds through the <term>refining</term> <note>original: "subtiliationem"; the process of making a substance more spiritual or ethereal</note> of prepared Mercury, and through its purification with natural moisture and <term>fixation</term> <note>making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, it does not seem to agree literally with the operations of those same Philosophers. For others say: "our work is to digest things, and to convert them into water and vapor, and to thicken them again." Likewise, they allege: "nothing is more useful to us than that water be <term>sublimated</term> from vapor," along with many other things.

Likewise, the Philosophers say in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> that the beginning of our work is that when the stone is worked with a gentle fire, it is made to look like something dead. And afterward, its **soul** is returned to it, and thus it continues so that the soul becomes permanent in the fire.

Likewise, according to **Geber** <note>an 8th-century Arabic alchemist known in Latin as the father of chemistry</note>, it is said that a **triple fire** is required in its preparation:
1.  **First**, a very slow fire, so that the substance of the stone does not rise, but only our vapor begins to thicken.
2.  **Second**, so that a part may be incinerated <note>reduced to ash</note> according to the methods written for you.
3.  [Implied third stage of completion].

Likewise, **Senior** <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemist</note> commands that when that "one thing" of theirs—to which we add nothing and from which we take nothing—is sufficiently purified, it is called the "natural Mercury" of the Philosophers, provided it is purified of earthiness. However, the other "Mercury of the Philosophers"—namely, that made through the dissolution of the **perfect body** <note>usually gold or silver</note>, as has been said—is said to need such purification less.

And **Senior** adds that then the stone must be "divided into parts." He says this according to the opinion of those who work with several vessels, or a double vessel, or a vessel upon a vessel, so that the matter can be digested better and more certainly. According to the intention of the craftsman and the prepared fire, the work is perfected more quickly. Yet, the same operation aims at the same goal: namely, to **fix** one part of the stone, and then to refine it with the part that is not fixed, as I wrote to you before. Although all things can be done in one vessel and with one thing, individual steps can also be done excellently with natural Mercury alone, just as with "artificial" Mercury previously purified of earthiness.

Master **Archa** was of this same opinion in his *Book of the Concordances of the Philosophers*, saying that "purified Mercury should be taken." I say the same, and even better (as was said before), that it should be the Mercury of the perfect body, or rather the most perfect: namely, of **Gold** <note>original: "Sole"</note>. And let it be placed in its vessel, and be cooked with itself alone in one vessel over a slow fire until it is divided and dissolved into the most refined parts, like vapor. And thus...

# ALBERTUS MAGNUS
## THE COMPOUND OF COMPOUNDS.

---

I will not hide the talent for trading <note>original: "talentum... negotiationis"; a reference to the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25, where a servant is expected to increase the value of what his master entrusted to him</note> entrusted to me by the Lord, lest I suffer the curse of the wicked servant. Hidden knowledge or a buried treasure—what is the use of it? And therefore, the knowledge which I have learned without deception, I share without envy; for where envy festers, knowledge fails, because such a person shall not be a participant in the friendship of God. All wisdom and knowledge is from the Lord God, but in whatever way it is expressed, it is always from the Holy Spirit. Since no one can say "Lord Jesus Christ" unless he be a son of God in the Holy Spirit, so too my teaching, which is true, cannot exist without Him who sent me. Yet I am not sent to everyone, but only to those who are called worthy by God, and who praise the Lord in His wonders. Therefore, he who has ears for hearing such God-given <note>original: "Deificæ"</note> grace, let him hear the secret which has been betrothed to me by the grace of God, and which is by no means revealed to the unworthy. Nature is the model and foundation of art, for which reason art imitates nature as much as it can. It is necessary, therefore, for the craftsman to look upon nature, and proceed from the same things from which nature proceeds.

### *Concerning the Procreation of metals in general from quicksilver and sulfur.*
### CHAPTER I.

Furthermore, as we have come to know, it has been found that the nature of metals for the procreation of any of them is naturally and generally composed of <term>sulfur</term> <note>often associated with the "soul" or "combustible" principle in alchemy</note> and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury, associated with the "spirit" or "fluid" principle</note>; the diversity of the boiling and digestion <note>original: "decoctionis & digestionis"; the application of heat to mature the substance</note> produces the diversity in the species of metals. I have learned by my own senses that from one and the same vessel—one vein—yet in different parts of it, it produces both minerals and silver naturally. For it has been most clearly proven in our books on minerals that the generation of metals is circular <note>the theory that metals exist in a cycle of transformation and can be brought back to a primary state</note>. Nevertheless, in all things that have circular generations from one another, the transition is easy; and for those things which have in themselves—

<column-break/>

<summary>This page serves as the prologue to Albertus Magnus's treatise, establishing his theological justification for sharing alchemical secrets and introducing the core theory that all metals are composed of sulfur and quicksilver.</summary>
<keywords>Albertus Magnus, alchemy, sulfur, quicksilver, mercury, imitation of nature, generation of metals, circular generation, Parable of the Talents</keywords>

--- Page 951 ---
<meta>This page continues Chapter I of Albertus Magnus's "The Compound of Compounds." The previous page introduced the idea that Art (Alchemy) must imitate Nature by using the same base components that Nature uses to create metals.</meta>

<page-num>930</page-num>
<header>ALBERTUS MAGNUS</header>

mutual affinity <note>original: "convenientiam"</note>, for this reason gold is more easily made from silver than from any other metal. For it is not necessary to change anything in it except the color and weight, which are both easily accomplished. For with a more compact substance, weight will certainly be present. And because the solution is aqueous with a suitable white-yellow sulfur, the color is changed accordingly. This method is also used in other cases. For sulfur is like the father, and quicksilver <term>argentum vivum (mercury)</term> is like the mother of metals. However, it is more fittingly stated if sulfur is said to be, in the mixing of metals, like the substance of the father’s seed, and quicksilver like the menstrual blood <note>In medieval physiology, it was believed that an embryo was formed by the action of male seed "curdling" or "coagulating" the female menstrual blood.</note> coagulated into the substance of the embryo. Sulfur does not generate within its own substance, just as a father does not. And just as the male generates from his substance within another, and within the other’s menstrual blood, so sulfur generates within quicksilver, and in itself it does not generate at all. Let us say, therefore, in other words, that in order for the Alchemist to remove from the metal the specific form <note>original: "speciem"; in a philosophical sense, this refers to the "species" or essential nature of the metal</note> which nature gives, he must proceed from those same things from which nature proceeds: that is, from sulfur and quicksilver prepared and purified according to the likeness of nature.

### *On sulfur, which follows.*

Sulfur, as we know, is found to have three humidities <note>or "moistures"</note>. The first is very airy and fiery, adhering to the external parts due to the evaporation of those elements, which likewise fly away and consume the surface of the things in whose mixture they meet. It has another humidity that is phlegmatic or watery, standing just beneath the former in the parts of the thing. It has a third humidity which is radical <term>radical moisture (humidum radicale), the life-sustaining fluid thought to exist in all things</term>, fixed and immersed in the parts that determine the composition; and this alone is generative, and therefore it is not easily separated from the thing without the destruction of the whole. The first humidity, therefore, does not withstand fire, but is combustible on the outside; it is ignited in fire and burns the substance of the metal with which it is cooked. Therefore, it is not only useless, but even harmful to our purpose. The second humidity moistens the parts of things but is not generative, nor does it increase; it evaporates in the fire and contributes nothing to the purpose. But the third is radical and essential, soaked into the parts of the thing, and from it the essential parts are also composed. It is necessary, therefore, that sulfur be cleansed of the first two superfluities, and the refinement of the third makes the best mixture. For the heat of sulfur is a vapor, and especially sulfur that is well-cleansed and sublimated <note>sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it becomes a gas and then solidifies again, used here as a purification method</note> whitens most excellently and thickens most strongly; because of this,

Skilled Alchemists, through sharp washes, are accustomed to remove from sulfur the two aforementioned impurities—using substances like yellow vinegar, sour or goat’s milk, the urine of boys, and strong lye. This is done through washing, boiling <term>decoctions (boiling a substance to extract its essence)</term>, and <term>sublimations (the process of heating a solid until it becomes vapor and then solidifies again upon cooling)</term>. Afterward, it is refined further through dissolution, so that only the pure substance remains. This pure core contains the active, perfecting, and immediate power of the metal. Thus, we have the "father" of this miraculous work.

### *On the nature of Quicksilver.*

Quicksilver <term>argentum vivum (mercury)</term> possesses two unnecessary substances: namely, one earthy and the other watery. The earthy substance contains a portion of sulfur and turns red when exposed to fire on its own. The watery substance contains excessive moisture. Quicksilver is best purified from these earthy and watery impurities through sublimations and very sharp washings. Indeed, Nature herself sublimes it into a dry state from sulfur, and it is cleansed of its earthiness by the heat of the Sun and the stars.

Therefore, when Nature has well-washed the pure mercury from its earthy substance and dried its excess moisture with pure sulfur—as mentioned before—it generates a pure and clean metallic body within the veins of the earth; likewise, it creates something impure from impure materials. Thus, the diversity of metals found in these veins depends on how well they were cleansed and "digested" <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to a process of slow, consistent heating, similar to how the body processes food, to mature a substance.</note>—specifically the sulfur and the quicksilver. This is the process of ripening <note>original: "decoctionis"</note>.

### *On Arsenic.*

Arsenic shares the same nature as sulfur. Both provide the "tincture" <note>A "tincture" in alchemy is a substance capable of infusing or changing the color and quality of a metal, specifically to white or red.</note> for redness and whiteness. However, there is more moisture in Arsenic, and it flees from fire more slowly than sulfur—unlike sulfur, which ignites quickly and burns all metals except gold. Arsenic moderates the dryness of sulfur when the two are combined. Once joined, they cannot be separated from each other; instead, the coloring power of both is improved.

For Arsenic contains many parts of quicksilver, as Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-9th century scholar whose works were foundational to medieval European alchemy.</note> says; therefore, it should be prepared in the same or a similar way. Conversely, one should know that the spirits hidden in sulfur and the oils extracted from animal parts are called the "White Elixir" by the Philosophers. However, it is not joined or mixed with that fiery power and substance through which the Elixir is perfected into the "Red Elixir," because it is subdued in the melting, as is certain among us—

through experiment, not only because it removes foreign qualities, but it also purifies when it is joined with those same melted substances and <term>arsenic (an alchemical mineral used for whitening metals)</term>, and because there is a common proportion at the end of the elements. Metals differ according to the purity and impurity of their matter—namely, of sulfur and quicksilver—and the heat from which the metals are generated. According to the philosopher <note>original: "philosophum," likely referring to Aristotle</note>, however, there is one medicine or <term>elixir (the agent of transformation)</term>; for in minerals, bodies are called "animals" <note>This refers to the alchemical idea that minerals possess a kind of "life" or spirit that can be manipulated.</note>. Let us say, therefore, that the hidden spirit is sulfur, arsenic, and the oil extracted from bodies. That is the spirit we seek, with which we may dye any body and lead it from a state of diminution to natural completion.

That spirit is called "water" and "quicksilver" by the Philosophers. Quicksilver, as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a famous 8th-century alchemist</note> says, is nothing but a medicine, a proportion of the moist and the dry, and the dry and the moist. I say, observe the proportion: make earth from fire, and air from earth, and from air also moisture, since it prevails over heat. These things are to be noted as the secrets of the whole world. Yet none of those things received in this work have power of themselves, because they are subjugated within the metals; they neither bring them to perfection nor do they remain.

Hence it requires a double substance: one which may be mixed with the melted things, and another "fixed" substance by which they may always be fixed so that they remain. Thus says Rhasis <note>Al-Razi, a Persian polymath and alchemist</note>: There are four substances which are changed by time, each of which is composed of the four elements, taking its name from the dominant element. Their wonderful essence, thus united there, is said to be "air from water," which provides nourishment to certain things and embraces a secret worthy of admiration. It is so gathered within them that it melts from heat; thus it is shown to our estimation that the stones which Alchemy receives, and the stones which work Alchemy, have an impression and an operation upon melted bodies if they are prepared.

Truly, the stones which primarily and principally work—to not hide the truth—are four: two of which make white <note>for the creation of silver</note>, and the other two effect red <note>for the creation of gold</note>. Thus the whole consists of whiteness and redness: sulfur, arsenic, and <term>Saturn (the alchemical name for Lead)</term> for one body. And regarding this, many raise doubts as to why "perfect bodies" <note>Gold and silver</note> are not taken or used first. To these it must be answered: because in imperfect bodies there is their <term>aqua acuta (sharp or acidic water)</term>, which is bitter and vinegary, and this water is entirely necessary in the art. For it dissolves and <term>mortifies (kills/breaks down)</term> the bodies it encounters, and again quickens and composes them. Hence Rhasis speaks in his third epistle: We seek our <term>Entelechy (the vital principle or realized perfection)</term> from where the bitterness of the waters and elements proceeds. Then the fiery power and oil remain—which are entirely necessary to us in the water itself—and they cannot be separated from the water in any way, yet they do not remain useless. Therefore, it is necessary that we have another preparation, by which we extract from them the "water of sulfur," the oil, and its thinnest spirit, which is truly the dyeing tincture we seek when it is prepared.

Similarly, the other aforementioned bodies are prepared either by being separated through "separation," or through distillation alone. These are taken from all those things that are united by nature; through the thinning of their parts, they remain partly in a state of simplicity and enter into other parts to bring them to that same simplicity.

However, some who are ignorant of the arrangement of this <term>mastery (the "Ars Magna" or Great Art of alchemy)</term> wish to complete our work using quicksilver alone, claiming that it possesses a soul, a body, and a spirit, and that it is the sole matter of gold and silver. For it is not possible to find within a thing that which is not already in it. But quicksilver does not possess the tincture of redness; therefore, the body of the <term>Sun (gold)</term> cannot be made from it alone. ->*On Putrefaction.*<-

### CHAPTER II.

Death and life are brought about by fire. For by a gentle fire, the moisture of a body is extracted; the accidental cause of this is the external fire approaching a substance, which stirs the element near and similar to itself already existing within that body. This internal element is the **natural heat**. This natural heat moves and incites the "first fire" of that element extracted within the body's composition. Once incited, a conjunction occurs which brings the **radical moisture** <note>original: "humiditatem radicalem"; the essential, life-sustaining fluid of a substance</note> of the body itself to the surface. As the external fire acts continuously, this radical moisture—which preserves the internal harmony of the parts—is drawn outside its proper place. From this, death, corruption, and dissolution happen to the body, because the **knot of nature** <note>The bond that holds the different elements together in a specific form.</note> within it is untied. 

And although this must be carried out by an external fire acting as an instrument, nevertheless, since fire by its own nature dries and constricts, it cannot achieve this dissolution without some particular thing aiding the process between the fire and the body—especially if it is a solid, compacted body like an element. Such a body requires an "attractive medium" which, after the separation, can itself be separated from the corrupted body. This process is achieved through the nature of the **Sun** <note>original: "Solis"; likely referring to gold or a specific "solar" quality of heat that is both generative and transformative.</note>. Therefore, that attractive medium is effective because it is of a hot and moist nature relative to the other elements.

## CHAPTER III.

There are four <term>Regimens <note>original: "Regimina"; these are the specific stages of management or operational procedures in the alchemical process.</note></term> of this Stone. The first is to divide. The second is to wash. The third is to reduce. The fourth is to fix. Through the first regimen, the division of the "natures" occurs, because unless they are divided and cleansed, they cannot be joined together. Through the second regimen, the washing and purification of those divided natures takes place, so that by this process they are brought back to a state of simplicity. Through the third, our <term>sulfur <note>The active, combustible principle of the work.</note></term> is "reduced" or brought back to its mineral source—namely, that of the Moon and the Sun <note>Silver and Gold</note>—and likewise for the other natures. Through the fourth regimen, the union, composition, and fixation of all things and bodies arising from our stone occurs, so that they may remain stable together.

There are, however, some who assign five stages to the management of this <term>mastery <note>original: "magisterii"; the Great Work of alchemy.</note></term>. The first of these is to dissolve the substances down to the <term>prime matter <note>original: "materiam primam"; the formless, fundamental substance from which all things are made.</note></term>. The second is to reduce it to a state close to nature—specifically that of sulfur and quicksilver—by means of our "earth" or <term>black magnesia <note>A term often used in alchemy for the dark, unrefined stage of the matter, not necessarily the modern chemical magnesium.</note></term>. The third is to properly reduce the sulfur to its most immediate nature: that is, to its mineral matter and the nature of the Sun and Moon. The fourth stage is to compose the <term>white elixir <note>A medicine capable of transmuting metals into silver.</note></term> from several parts. The fifth is to perfectly burn the white elixir and convert it into red <term>cinnabar <note>original: "cinoborum"; here referring to a deep red, stable state of the matter.</note></term>, and upon this foundation, by adding more, to compose the <term>red elixir <note>The final medicine for transmuting metals into gold.</note></term>. There are also others who set different stages in the process of this art: some say four, others three, and some only two, who divide the whole work into the "direction and washing" of the parts, and the "composition" of those same parts.

**Note.** The nature or matter of the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> is a thing of low price found everywhere, because it is a "viscous water," just as <term>quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note></term> is. Because of how it is extracted from the earth—and because it is viscous like quicksilver extracted in latrines—some have said it could be found in every place. Many "beastly" people, taking the intent of the Philosophers too literally, have actually sought it in dung <note>The text warns against taking alchemical metaphors for "base" or "foul" materials too literally.</note>. However, Nature works this by removing something—namely, its "earthiness"—just as it does by adding something—namely, the "Sulfur of the Philosophers." This is not the common sulfur of the markets, but an invisible sulfur of a red tint, which is certainly the spirit of <term>vitriol <note>A sulfate mineral, often copper or iron sulfate; here specifically "Roman vitriol."</note></term>. And these two preparations are made together as follows: ℞ <note>Take</note>. Saltpeter and Roman vitriol, two pounds each; grind them finely as will be shown in what follows. In this way, the saying of Aristotle in the fourth book of his *Meteorology* is explained—

...of those who say: "Let the practitioners of Alchemy know that the species of metals cannot be changed," which is true, as he adds, "unless they are first reduced to their <term>prime matter <note>original: "primam materiam"; the formless, fundamental substance that underlies all physical things.</note></term>." The reduction of these into prime matter is easy, as will be clearly explained in what follows. Therefore, as the <term>Philosopher <note>original: "Philosophus"; likely referring to Avicenna, whose work "De Congelatione" was often attributed to Aristotle and cited by alchemists.</note></term> says, there is no passage from one extreme to another except through a medium. For the nature of the medium is always to contain the extremes of the parts within itself. 

Now, the extremes of our <term>philosophical stone</term> are, on one side, the two <term>luminaries <note>The Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver).</note></term>, which are perfect bodies. Just as ice is resolved into water because it was water originally (by the mediation of heat), so in their own way the bodies of metals are resolved into their prime matter, our water of life.

How we ought to arrive at this water of life will be clearly revealed in the following sections, for it alone has the power to reduce all metallic bodies into their prime matter.

## *On the sublimation of Mercury.*
### CHAPTER IV.

Take, therefore, in the name of the Lord, a pound of pure <term>Mercury <note>Quicksilver.</note></term> from the mine, and of <term>Roman vitriol <note>Iron or copper sulfate.</note></term> and of roasted common salt; grind them finely together. Let it be stirred with a wooden spatula so that the very dregs of the Roman vitriol and common salt "swallow" the Mercury, so that nothing of it appears, but it is entirely turned into a paste by this method. 

When this is done, you should dry the material in the moderate heat of a furnace overnight. In the morning, take the material thus dried and grind it finely and very well upon a stone. Once it is crushed and powdered, place it in its vessel for sublimations which is called an <term>aludel <note>A pear-shaped ceramic pot, open at both ends, used in the process of sublimation.</note></term> for sublimating as you know. Then place its cover upon it, and seal well around the joints with the <term>clay of wisdom <note>original: "luto sapientiæ"; a specialized airtight sealant made of clay, hair, and other binders.</note></term> so that the <term>Mercury <note>original symbol: ☿</note></term> cannot escape. Then let the vessel be placed upon its furnace and fitted with clay into the furnace so that it cannot tilt in any way to the side, but stands directly upright. Then kindle a fire, first a slow one...
