### The second water by means of Sal ammoniac.

In the name of the Lord, take one pound of the first water and dissolve in it four <term>lots <note>original: "lot."; a historical unit of weight used in Germanic and Central European regions, roughly equivalent to 1/30th of a pound.</note></term> of pure and clear <term>sal ammoniac <note>original: "salis armoniaci"; ammonium chloride, used here to increase the solvent power of the water, likely creating a form of Aqua Regia.</note></term>. Once dissolved, the water is immediately qualified and colored differently. For the first water was green in color and a dissolver of silver, but not of gold; and immediately after the addition of the sal ammoniac, its color turns to lemon-yellow, and it dissolves gold, mercury, and sublimated sulfur, and it stains human skin a very bright yellow color. Keep that water aside, etc.

### The third water qualified by sublimated Mercury.

Take one pound of the second water and ten lots of very clear sublimated Mercury, which has been well prepared from <term>Roman vitriol <note>original: "vitriolo romano"; likely iron or copper sulfate used in the preparation of corrosive materials.</note></term> and common salt. Add this to the second water gradually and successively. Seal the opening of the glass vessel well so that the power of the added mercury does not suddenly exhale, and place the glass in warm, tempered ashes <note>A "cinder bath" or sand bath used for gentle, even heating.</note>. This water will immediately begin to work upon the Mercury, dissolving and incorporating it into itself. Thus, allow the glass to stand in the warm ashes and in the dissolution of the water until the water no longer appears as it was, but instead completely dissolves the sublimated Mercury itself. Indeed, the water always acts upon the Mercury by way of <term>imbibition <note>The process of a solid absorbing a liquid until it is saturated or dissolved.</note></term> until it is entirely dissolved. 

But note: if this water is not able to totally dissolve the added Mercury, then whatever has been dissolved of the Mercury <note>original uses the symbol: ☿</note> by this water should be poured off, and the undissolved portion at the bottom should be dried with a slow fire, ground up, and dissolved again with new water as before. Repeat this order until all the sublimated Mercury is dissolved into the water. Then join all the solutions of this third water together into a clean glass and seal its opening well with wax and keep it diligently. This is the third thick philosophical water, qualified in the third degree of perfection—

### *The fourth qualified water, through which all calcined bodies are reduced into the first matter.*

Take the third clarified water, the Mercurial water, which has been qualified to the third degree of perfection, and place it for putrefaction <note>The process of breaking down a substance through gentle heat and moisture.</note> in a <term>horse’s belly <note>original: "ventrem equi"; a common alchemical term for a heap of decomposing horse manure, used to provide a steady, gentle heat for weeks at a time.</note></term> that is well-digested. Place it in a clear glass vessel, well-sealed and with a long neck, for fourteen days. Let it putrefy so that the dregs reside at the bottom; then this water will be transmuted from a lemon-yellow <note>original: "citrino"</note> color into a golden-yellow. When this is done, take out the glass and place it among the ashes over a very slow fire. Attach the <term>alembic <note>The lid or "head" of a still used for distilling liquids.</note></term> with its receiver and begin to distill, drop by drop, the very clear, clean, and heavy "water of life," the "virgin's milk," and the "sharpest vinegar," continuing always with a slow fire until you have distilled all of the serene water of life. Then stop the fire and let the furnace cool, and carefully keep this aside. Behold, this is the water of life, the <term>philosopher’s vinegar <note>original: "acetum philosophorum"</note></term>, and the <term>virgin’s milk <note>original: "lac virginis"</note></term> through which bodies are resolved into the first matter. It is called by infinite names.

The signs of this water are these: if one drop is cast upon a red-hot copper plate, it will immediately penetrate it and leave a white mark; it smokes over fire, and it congeals in the air like ice. Furthermore, when this water is distilled, its drops do not run together continuously like other drops, but one drop follows one path and another follows a different path <note>This likely describes a high surface tension or a particular way the liquid beaded on the glass.</note>. This water does not act upon metallic bodies like other strong corrosive waters that dissolve bodies into water; rather, this water reduces and resolves all bodies placed in it into <term>Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"; in this context, it likely refers to returning the metal to its "living" metallic essence or a liquid state, rather than just common quicksilver.</note></term>, as you shall hear later. 

For after its putrefaction, distillation, and clarification, it is purified and brought into a better state, cleansed of all sulfurous and corrosive heat. Thus, it is no longer a corrosive water that dissolves bodies into liquid, but a reductive water that turns bodies into Mercury. It receives this power from the Mercury that was first dissolved and putrefied through the third degree of perfection, nor do any earthy turbidities or dregs remain within it. Because through the final distillation, all things were separated <note>original: "sincopata"</note>, as the black turbidities remained at the bottom of the vessel. The color of this water is sky-blue and clear yellow. Keep it carefully aside, because through it all <term>calcined <note>Reduced to a powder through heat.</note></term> and putrefied bodies are resolved into their radical first matter,

The "Water" must be extracted from a moist substance and from no other; the "Air" and "Fire," however, must be extracted from a dry substance and from no other.

### *The practice follows, using the Mercury of the Sages.*

This is not the mercury of the common people, but that which is called <term>primary matter</term> by the philosophers. It is a watery element, cold and moist, a permanent water, the spirit of the body, an oily vapor, blessed water, virtuous water, the water of the wise, the <term>vinegar of the philosophers <note>A common alchemical term for a sharp, acidic solvent used to dissolve metals.</note></term>, mineral water, the dew of heavenly grace, <term>virgin’s milk <note>A traditional name for a white, milky liquid produced during alchemical reactions, often associated with the early stages of the Work.</note></term>, corporeal Mercury, and is called by infinite other names in the books of the philosophers. Although these names are indeed varied, they always signify one and the same thing: namely, the <term>Mercury of the Sages <note>original: "☿ sapientum."</note></term> alone. From this alone is drawn every virtue of the art of Alchemy, and in its own way the white and red <term>tinctures <note>The "white tincture" was believed to turn metals into silver, while the "red tincture" (the Philosopher's Stone) turned them into gold.</note></term>, etc.

Take, therefore, in the name of Jesus Christ, the previously mentioned venerable Mercury, the water of the philosophers, the first <term>hyle <note>original: "hile." From the Greek word for "matter," referring to the fundamental substance of the universe.</note></term> of the wise, and the Stone known to you from these chapters—which is called the primary matter of the perfect body, as you well know. Place it into a clean, clear, bright, and round <term>vessel <note>original: "furnum alveolum." A small furnace or specialized glass flask used for heating.</note></term>, with its opening well-closed with the <term>seal of Hermes <note>An airtight seal, usually made by melting the glass neck of a flask shut.</note></term>, so that it cannot breathe out in any way. Place it to be smothered in its "bed"—well-layered, well-tempered, and warm—for a <term>philosophical month <note>Typically 40 days, the traditional time required for alchemical putrefaction.</note></term>. Keep it continuously warm, preserving it in the <term>sublimation <note>The process where a substance turns to vapor and then solidifies again.</note></term> of its own "sweat," until it no longer sweats through the process of ascending and descending. Continue until the matter begins to putrefy, smother, and coagulate from within by the power of the preserved fire, becoming fixed. Thus, it shall no longer ascend as a smoky, airy substance, but will remain at the bottom, dry, its moisture exhausted, putrefied and coagulated, converted into a black earth. This is called the <term>black raven’s head <note>original: "caput corvi nigrum." A famous alchemical stage (nigredo) symbolizing the death of the old form before rebirth.</note></term>, the dry, earthy element. When this is done, the true sublimation of the philosophers is complete, in which all the aforementioned methods have been performed: the sublimation of the quicksilver, distillation, coagulation, putrefaction, calcination, and fixation—all in one vessel and one furnace, as has been said. It is a change of temperaments, such as from a cold and moist temperament into a dry **choler** [<note>original: "coleram siccam." In medieval medicine, choler or yellow bile was the humor associated with heat and dryness.</note>], according to the physicians. Likewise, what was spiritual is made corporeal according to <term>Aristotle <note>The famous Greek philosopher, whose physical theories regarding the four elements and the "prime matter" formed the basis of alchemical science.</note></term>. Likewise, what was liquid is made thick according to <term>Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval Latin texts.</note></term>. Likewise, the hidden is made manifest according to <term>Rudianus <note>Likely a reference to a philosopher cited in the "Liber Trium Verborum" (The Book of Three Words), an influential alchemical text.</note></term> in the *Book of Three Words*. Thus the understanding of the philosophers is clear when they say the operation of our stone is nothing else but a transmutation of natures and a revolution of the elements. It is clear, indeed, that through such a deprivation of moisture, we make the stone dry, the volatile fixed, the spiritual corporeal, the liquid thick, the watery fiery, and the airy earthy. In this way, we truly change natures because we have revolved the four elements in a circle and changed their natures; blessed be God forever. Amen.

Now, therefore, we must pass by a simple declaration to the **second preparation** under God’s blessing, which is the whitening of the whole earth. Take, therefore, the aforementioned earth which is called the **crow’s head** [<note>original: "caput corvi." This represents the black stage or *nigredo*, the initial state of decomposition in the Great Work.</note>] and grind 2 parts of it finely and carefully upon a very clean <term>porphyry <note>A hard red stone used as a slab for grinding chemicals into fine powders.</note></term>. Add to it one part of the saved **philosophical water** [<note>original: "aquae philosophicę." Likely the mercurial solvent described on previous pages.</note>] which you know, using your skill to make them into one mass by soaking the dry earth with the water gradually, until it has "drunk" its designated draught. Mix these well together into a single **chaos** [<note>A term for the undifferentiated, raw state of the matter being worked upon.</note>] by grinding, so that a good and deep union of body, soul, and water is produced in the mixture, even to the very depths of the body.

When this is done, let it be placed back in its little <term>cucurbit <note>A gourd-shaped chemical flask used in distillation.</note></term>, firmly closed so that it cannot breathe [leak], and let it be placed in its well-layered, moderately and continuously warm **bed** [<note>original: "lectulum." Likely a sand-bath or a warm part of the furnace designed to maintain a steady, gentle heat.</note>] so that the draught it drank may be evaporated through sweating in its entrails for the space of eight days, so that the earth is partly whitened. After this, let the stone itself be taken out again and ground, and let it be soaked with **virgin milk** [<note>original: "lacte virgineo." A poetic term for a purifying white liquid or a specific grade of mercurial water.</note>] as before by way of union, so that it may drink its draught again. Then put it back into its tray in the warm, tempered bed, so it may dry by sweating once more as before.

This order of repetition—soaking the earth, uniting it with the saved water, drying, and <term>calcining <note>Heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder.</note></term>—must be repeated four times; thus you have sufficiently administered the earth to the most precious stone through boiling. Thus, by these stages of boiling, continuous grinding, soaking with water, drying, and calcining, you have sufficiently cleansed the **crow’s head** and the black and stinking earth, and brought it to whiteness by the power of fire, heat, and the whitening water. Then carefully keep this white earth and set it aside; for this is the sought-after good: **white foliated earth**, **white sulfur**, **white magnesia**, etc. And this is what the philosopher **Morienus** [<note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the art to the King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>] means when he says: *“Let this earth putrefy with its water, and thus it is cleansed, and with God’s help the whole mastery is finished.”* Also, as **Hermes** says: *“You wash the <term>Azoth</term>”* [<note>original: "Azot." The universal solvent or essential transformative agent in alchemy.</note>]...

As for the third stage, we must proceed to the fermentation of the whitened earth so that the dead body may be animated and revived, that its power may be multiplied infinitely, so that the desired white **elixir** may be perfected, which tints Mercury into the most perfect and true body of the **Moon** [<note>original: "lunam." The alchemical name for silver.</note>]. But note that the ferment cannot enter the dead body except by means of water, which makes the marriage and union between the ferment and the white earth; therefore, in every fermentation, the weight of each component must be noted. If, therefore, you wish to ferment the white foliated earth into the white elixir so that it stands in the fullness of the **tincture** [<note>The "tincture" is the soul or color-giving property of the elixir that allows it to transform other metals.</note>] over that which is diminished in perfection, then take three parts of the whitened earth or foliated dead body, and 2 parts of the reserved **water of life** [<note>original: "aqua vitæ." In this context, a powerful alchemical solvent or distilled spirit.</note>], and one and a half parts of the ferment. However, let the ferment be so prepared that it is a white, subtle, and fixed **calx** [<note>A fine powder produced by heating a substance to remove its moisture.</note>], if your intention proceeds toward the white work. If, however, you proceed to the red work, then let it be the most yellow calx of prepared gold, and there shall be no other ferment. The ferment of silver is silver, the ferment of gold is gold, and there shall be no other fermen-

...ferment. The reason for this is that these two glowing bodies contain brilliant "dyeing rays" that can tint other substances with true whiteness [silver] and redness [gold]. For they are, by their nature, found to be substances of the purest **sulfur** [<note>original: "sulphuris." In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of a substance.</note>], belonging to the category of stones. 

Therefore, combine each species with its own species, and each genus with its own genus. For the **White Work** [<note>original: "opus album." The stage of the Great Work that produces silver.</note>] is intended for whitening, while the **Red Work** [<note>original: "Opus vero rubeum." The final stage of the Great Work that produces gold.</note>] is intended for reddening. Do not mix the process of one stone with the process of another; if you do otherwise, you will fall into error. 

Thus, all the philosophers say that **our stone** is composed of three parts: namely, from body, spirit, and soul. For the **white foliated earth** [<note>original: "terra albafoliata." This refers to a purified, flaky, or layered state of the alchemical matter during the whitening process.</note>] is the **body**. The **ferment** is the **soul**, which grants life to the body by means of the **water**, which is called the **spirit**. 

Therefore, mix these three parts into one "matrimonially" [<note>original: "matrimonialiter." This implies a chemical marriage or permanent union of the ingredients.</note>] upon a clean grinding stone, grinding them well so they are united in the smallest particles into a single "confused chaos," until everything becomes one inseparable body. Afterwards, wisely place this in its fitted vial and return it to its "warm bed" [<note>original: "thorum suum calidum." Likely a reference to an incubator or a furnace at a steady, low heat.</note>] so that they may coagulate and be **fixed** [<note>original: "fixentur." To 'fix' a substance in alchemy means to make it stable and non-volatile under heat.</note>], and it will become a single white body. 

Once this is done, take up that blessed white stone again and grind it finely on a very clean stone; once more, **imbibe** [<note>original: "imbibas." To imbibe is to saturate the solid matter with a liquid, like a sponge soaking up water.</note>] it with a third part of its "water," repeating the process until it has swallowed the draught. Put it back once more into a clean, similar vessel in its tempered and warm bed so that it may begin to "sweat" again and drink the draught of water; allow it to dry within its own **bowels** [<note>original: "visceribus." A metaphorical term for the internal parts or center of the alchemical vessel.</note>]. 

Reiterate and multiply this process until you have prepared the most excellent **White Stone** through these steps of repetition. It will be fixed and permanent, penetrating the smallest parts of other bodies very rapidly, flowing like "fixed water" over a fierce fire, and **dyeing** [<note>original: "tingentem." To 'dye' or 'tinct' is the alchemical process of transforming the inner nature and color of a base metal into a noble one.</note>] Mercury and all **bodies diminished from perfection** [<note>original: "corpora à perfectione diminuta." This refers to base metals like lead or tin, which alchemists believed were simply 'unripe' or 'sick' versions of gold and silver.</note>] into true silver that surpasses all natural silver. 

Note that the more this sequence of completion is repeated—by dissolving, coagulating, grinding, and roasting—the more the potency of the medicine increases, and its "goodness" is multiplied further and further. For every time you work upon the stone to enhance its stored virtue, you will gain a corresponding increase in the power of its **projection** [<note>original: "projectione." Projection is the final stage where a small amount of the Stone is thrown onto molten base metal to transform it.</note>] upon imperfect metals. For instance, if one part of the medicine from the first repetition is used, it converts one hundred parts of any metal into **Moon** [<note>original: "Luna," the alchemical name for silver</note>]. 

After the second repetition, it converts a thousand parts. 
After the third, 10,000. 
After the fourth, 100,000. 
After the fifth, 1,000,000. 
After the sixth, infinite thousands, and so on unto infinity. This is the great saying of the philosophers which the wise everywhere praise.

**Take** the white stone itself and then divide it into two parts. One part you shall increase toward the white elixir, as was said before, with its reserved "white water," so that it never ceases to be itself. But the other part you should place in a "new philosophical bed" [<note>original: "thorum philosophorum." A metaphorical term for a clean, round glass vessel or flask.</note>] that is clean, clear, bright, and round. Place it thus in its furnace for its digestion [<note>original: "digestionis." Among the philosophers, this is called "blood-colored," "purple gold," "red coral," and "red sulfur." 

When you see the stated color shine red as predicted, like dry burnt saffron, then joyfully take out the King itself and save it carefully. If you then wish it to become a tincture of redness of the highest elixir—transforming and tinting Mercury, the Moon, and every body into the truest Sun—then ferment three parts of it with one and a half parts of the purest gold. This gold must be prepared so that it is a most subtle and lemon-yellow powder [<note>original: "calx." A metal that has been reduced to a fine powder through heating or chemical action.</note>]. With two parts of water that has been artificially "solarized" [<note>original: "aquæ solificatæ." Water that has been treated to contain the "spirit" of gold.</note>], you shall reduce these into one "chaos" by mixing them into the smallest particles until the body is hidden. Place it in its "womb" [<note>original: "alvo." Another term for the vessel.</note>] with a maturing fire so that it may be digested to its final completion, until the true blood-red stone shines forth. 

Once more, you shall increase it using its reserved "solarized" part, proceeding step by step by means of a stronger fire of digestion. In this way, you proceed in the increase of its perfection and the accumulation of its goodness by repeating the work with its reserved part, which is of a solarized nature suited to it. Finally, its goodness is multiplied even unto infinity. Even in the first degree of its perfection, one part of it [will transmute] a hundred parts of Mercury (which has been washed with vinegar and salt, as you know, and placed in a crucible over a small fire until it smokes) or the Moon. It immediately tints and transforms it into the truest Sun, better than any natural gold. Thus, it is clear that through the reiteration of the stone, one finds the means by which Mercury and the Moon are converted into infinite gold.

And thus, indeed, is completed the precious secret [<note>original: "archanum." A profound mystery or specialized chemical secret.</note>] and incomprehensible treasure. Wherefore the philosophers say: our stone is of three colors—namely, first black, then white...

...[white] in the middle, and red at the end. And another philosopher says: Heat acting upon the moist first generates blackness [<note>original: "nigredinem." Now, therefore, let the sublime God of all natures be praised, glorious and blessed, who created that substance and gave it such a unique property that it cannot be found in any other natural things. For within it is found a great struggle, and it is the only substance that powerfully resists the battle over the hearth and the fire. Indeed, all other things flee and are consumed by fire. [<note>This refers to "fixity." While most substances evaporate or burn away, the perfected Philosopher's Stone is said to be fire-constant.</note>]

Note these words, therefore; mark these mysteries, for here, within the brevity of this discourse, the most hidden understanding of the entire art of Alchemy [<term>Alchemy: The medieval precursor to chemistry, focused on the transformation of matter and the search for the Philosopher's Stone.</term>] has been collected and recorded. It has been compiled briefly in simple language and a plain series of words, without any concealment; God is my witness that in the individual books of the philosophers, nothing better is found than what is written above. 

Therefore, I ask that you reveal this to no one, nor place it in the hands of the impious, since it clearly encompasses the secrets of the ages of all philosophers. Truly, such a precious portion of pearls must not be cast before swine [<note>A reference to the biblical warning in Matthew 7:6 against sharing sacred knowledge with those who cannot appreciate or respect it.</note>] or the unworthy; for if it were done otherwise, I pray to Almighty God that this divine work never reaches its desired conclusion for them.

# THE BOOK OF ALBERT THE GREAT
## OF EIGHT CHAPTERS,
### *On the philosopher's stone.*

I shall divide this book into eight chapters.
In the first chapter, I shall speak of Mercury and its nature, as well as the sulfur which it contains within itself.
In the second chapter, I shall speak of the nature of the perfect bodies and their sulfur.
In the third chapter, I shall speak of the conjunction of body and spirit, and the dissolution of the stone into its first matter.
In the fourth chapter, I shall speak of the extraction of water from the earth.
In the fifth chapter, I shall speak of the reduction of the water back upon its earth.
In the sixth chapter, I shall speak of the method for the sublimation of the earth.
In the seventh chapter, I shall speak of the fixation and the multiplication of the stone.
In the eighth chapter, I shall speak of the method of projecting the medicine and of dyeing any metal whatsoever.

->C H A P T E R  I.<-

Quicksilver [<note>original: "Argentum vivum," literally "living silver." In alchemy, mercury represents the fundamental "spirit" of all metals.</note>] is cold and moist, and God created all minerals with it; and it is of the nature of air and flees from the fire. Depending on how long it has remained in the fire, it will perform miraculous and high works. It alone is the living spirit [<note>original: "spiritus vivus."</note>], and in all the world there is nothing equal to it, nor is there anything else that can perform the works which it performs. It is that which enters every body, penetrates, washes, and excels. It is the ferment for the bodies to which it is mixed, and then the whole will be an elixir for both the red and the white [<note>The "red" and "white" refer to the two goals of alchemy: the White Work to create silver and the Red Work to create gold.</note>]. It is the perennial water, the water of life [<note>original: "aqua vitae."</note>], the virgin's milk [<note>original: "lac virginis." A common alchemical term for a transformative solvent or purified mercury.</note>], the fountain, and the alum from which he who drinks shall not die. When it is "living," it has certain effects; when it has been "killed" [<note>In alchemy, "killing" mercury refers to the process of fixing it so it no longer evaporates when heated.</note>], it has other, even greater effects. It is the serpent luxuriating in itself, impregnating itself, giving birth in a single day, and killing all metals with its poison. It flees from the fire, but the wise, through their artistry, have made it so that it awaits the fire, feeding it with

# CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE

...its earth, until it awaits the fire, and then it performs works and transformations. For just as it is changed—that is, altered—so it changes others; and as it is dyed, it dyes; and as it is coagulated, it coagulates. Therefore, among all minerals, the generation of quicksilver [<note>original: "argenti vivi," literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note>] is to be preferred. For it is found in all minerals and shares a common bond [<note>original: "symbolum," indicating a shared essence or correspondence</note>] with them all. It is made of a moderate amount of earth and a moderately subtle watery or "living oil," and a very subtle spirit. From its earthy wateriness, it possesses weight and downward motion, brightness, fluidity, and a silvery color. For it issues out of the earth, bounces back into the earth, spreads itself drop by drop, and reunites itself with moisture. By heat and a dried spirit, it is fixed and mixed with all minerals, and it will adhere firmly to whatever it sits upon, wherefore it is called the father of minerals and metals.

Quicksilver clearly appears to have a dense substance, so that as a unique entity [<note>original: "monocalus," likely a reference to its singular or uniform nature</note>] through the heaviness of its immense weight it even outweighs gold while it remains in its own nature; and it is of a very strong composition and uniform nature, since it cannot be separated. It allows itself to be divided into parts in no way, because it either retreats from the fire with its entire substance, or remains standing with the fire. Therefore, the cause of perfection is necessarily noted in it. For it alone suffices for the perfection of fixation in every degree—namely, with ignition—because of the good adherence of its parts and the strength of its mixture; if its parts are thickened in any way by the fire, it does not allow itself to be corrupted any further.

Neither by a furious entrance into the furnace, nor further, does it suffer itself to be separated or raised up. Because it does not tolerate its own thinning [<note>rarefaction</note>] due to its density and its lack of burning [<note>adustion</note>], which is caused by sulfurousness (which it does not have), it is perfected. Quicksilver is clearly the most perfect in all its works. For it protects against burning and causes melting when it is fixed. For it is a tincture of the most abundant redness and refreshing brightness, and it does not withdraw from what it is mixed with so long as it exists. For it is friendly and pleasing to metals, and a medium for joining tinctures, since it is mixed with them in the smallest parts [<note>original: "per minima," meaning it blends at the most fundamental, quasi-atomic level</note>], and it naturally adheres to them in their depths because it is of their own nature. 

Nevertheless, it mixes more easily with the Sun [<note>gold</note>] and Moon [<note>silver</note>], because it happens to share their pure nature, and then nothing is joined to it except the Sun. From this you may especially draw out the secret: that Mercury receives into itself what is of its own nature, but rejects what is foreign, because it rejoices more in its own nature than in a strange one. From this, it clearly shines forth that those bodies are of greater perfection which contain more Mercury...

### CHAPTER II

Gold is the most noble of bodies, the lord of stones, the King and head of all others, which neither the earth corrupts nor burning things consume; nor is it diminished in fire, nor altered in any way, but rather is improved in it, because it is moistened by a certain humidity within it; nor is it changed at all, because its temperament is balanced [<note>original: "complexio ejus est temperata," referring to the balance of the four elemental qualities</note>], and its nature is direct in heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Neither is there anything in it that is superfluous, nor anything lacking. For it is created from the most subtle clarity of the substance of quicksilver, and from a small amount of the substance of clean and pure sulfur—fixed, clear redness, changed by its own nature—dyeing that Mercury of gold, as it were. It holds every body and is the ferment [<term>fermentum: an agent that leavens or transforms a mass, like yeast in bread</term>], the elixir of the white and the red; it is not improved except with it, nor completed with anything else, just as a mass of dough is not completed without another ferment. Gold is a body lasting and remaining for ages upon ages, and therefore the philosophers have preferred it, magnified it, and said: That gold stands among bodies just as the sun stands among the stars. For the sun, by its light and splendor, generates all growing things and perfects all fruits BY THE WILL OF GOD. For Hermes [<note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>] said that a true tincture [<note>the essence or medicine that transforms base metals</note>] is never made without the red stone.

Silver is a body less [noble] than gold, and its weight is less than the weight of gold; it belongs to the parts of the Moon in its moisture, and in a moist place it is corrupted, and its taste is acid. In fire it is diminished and it is burned by sulfurs. Nevertheless, gold excepted, no body is better than it or closer to gold. For the interior of gold is the exterior of silver [<note>an alchemical theory suggesting that silver is "immature" gold, or that their internal/external qualities are inverted</note>]. Its nature is cold and dry, and it receives the tincture. Furthermore, gold is a perfect and masculine body without superfluity or diminution. Which if in the earth, mixed with it by liquefaction alone...

DE LAPIDE PHILOS. <note>original: "On the Philosopher's Stone"</note>

Ooo 4

...[if it] would perfect [the imperfect], it would be the **red elixir** <term>elixir ad rubeum: a medicinal or chemical substance capable of transmuting metals into gold</term>. **Silver**, however, is a body that is almost perfect and feminine; if it were to perfect [other things] by fusion, it would likewise be the **white elixir** <term>elixir ad album: a substance capable of transmuting metals into silver</term>, which it is not, because they are only perfect within themselves.

But if that perfection were capable of being mixed with the imperfect, would not the imperfect then be perfected by the perfect? However, if they were "more-than-perfect"—whether by double, quadruple, a hundredfold, or a thousandfold—to that same extent would the imperfect be perfected. And because Nature always works simply, and perfection within her is simple, inseparable, and unmixable—unless perhaps they were reduced to their pristine state, that is, into flight with the volatile, because the total amount of **volatile sulfur** overcomes the total amount of the **fixed body**. And since we can obtain a perfect body from the purest **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"</note> and from such **red sulfur**, why would we not choose [them] as our material for the red elixir, and silver likewise for the white elixir? For these two bodies are simply so perfect, without any clever cleansing, and so strongly digested and cooked by natural heat, that we are scarcely able to work upon them with our artificial fire. And although Nature perfects something, yet she does not know how to inwardly cleanse or purge it. For she simply works upon that which she has.

For there is a leader in sulfurous bodies, because we say a certain substance is enclosed in silver at the beginning of its mixing, while another truly foreign substance arrives that is alien to its nature and corrupts it.

And it must be noted most diligently that the joining of these two bodies is necessary in this art for the Red and for the White. There are two reasons: one is that **gold** is the most noble among metals and more compact, perfect, and fixed; yet if it is dissolved into its smallest parts, it is separated and becomes "spiritual" and flies from the fire just like **Mercury**, which is its soul—which is a marvel. This is by reason of its good elemental makeup, and then it possesses a **tincture** <term>tincture: the color-giving and transformative power of the Stone</term> without number; and this tincture is called the **hot red masculine sperm** <note>original: "sperma masculinum rubeum calidum"</note>. If, however, silver is dissolved, it has no tincture, yet it is prone to receiving and fixing that tincture in a temperament of cold and heat; it is called the **cold and dry feminine sperm**, and their joining is a containing [of one another]. Also, there is another reason that the joining of these two bodies is necessary: because while gold by itself is of most difficult fusion and liquefaction, yet if they are joined together they flow easily, namely with Mercury; and those who work in gold <note>original: "auri fabrifacientes," i.e., goldsmiths</note> know of the solders for gold.

It emphasizes that while Nature creates perfection, the Alchemist must use art to "super-perfect" these substances so they can transmute the imperfect.</summary>

# ALBERTUS MAGNUS

<meta>catchword: De con-</meta>

Therefore, if in our stone there were only one of these two principles, the medicine would never flow easily through any mastery of the art, nor would it bestow a **tincture** <term>tincture: in alchemy, a substance capable of infusing its color and qualities into another material</term>. Even if it did bestow a tincture, it would only dye as much as the substance itself weighed, because there would be no "receptacle" for the color to spread. And our final secret is to possess a medicine that flows before the **flight of Mercury** <note>original: "ante Mercurii fugam" — referring to the tendency of quicksilver to evaporate or escape when heated before it is "fixed"</note>. Thus, the conjunction of these two is necessary. For there has never been a body more worthy or pure than the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> or its shadow, the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>, without which no coloring **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> is generated. Anyone who strives to produce a tincture without this body of quicksilver proceeds to the practice blindly, **like a Donkey to a feast** <note>original: "sicut Asinus ad cœnam" — a proverbial expression for someone attempting something for which they are entirely unsuited or unprepared</note>. For gold bestows a golden color, and silver bestows a silver color. Therefore, he who knows how to join quicksilver with the sun or the moon has arrived at the **Secret** <note>original: "Archanum"</note>, which is called the "sulfur of the art." From these bodies, then, is extracted **living sulfur**, either white or red, since within them resides the purest substance of sulfur, purified by the ingenuity of supreme Nature.

I advise you to work with nothing except **Mercury**, the **Sun**, and the **Moon**, because the entire benefit of this art consists in them. For **whatever a man sows, that he shall also reap** <note>a reference to Galatians 6:7</note>; for a seed corresponds to its own kind, and every shrub brings forth its own fruit according to its genus. Indeed, Nature is wise and always desires to be perfected, because she always contains her own seed within herself—that is, the seminal virtue within the seed. For this reason, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational to European alchemy</note> says: "Unless I saw gold and silver, I would say for certain that Alchemy was not an art found in nature. But when I see gold and silver, I see most certainly that Alchemy exists in nature." It is possible for other bodies to be worked upon, but they will never be as good as these. Indeed, it is impossible to give a medicine that they do not possess, just as it is impossible to fix that which is not fixed, or to cleanse that which is unclean. For nothing is found in a thing that was not in it before, nor can anything give what it does not have.

Indeed, because your Mercury is by its own nature transformative, it becomes one with each of the planets it embraces; for with the good it is good, and with the evil it is evil. For if it is joined with lead, it will be lead; if joined with iron, it will be iron; and when joined with other bodies, it will be similar to them. But if it is joined with these two **rays** <note>Sun and Moon</note>, it becomes a complete and perfect elixir,

ON THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE

->*On the conjunction of the body and the spirit, the dissolution of the stone into the first matter, and its putrefaction.*<-

### CHAPTER III.

It is indeed certain that every thing is made of, or from, that into which it is eventually resolved. For instance, ice is turned into water by the mediation of heat; it is clear, therefore, that it was water beforehand. Truly all metals are generated from **Mercury**; therefore, they are resolved back into it. The first **regimen** <term>regimen: a specific stage or systematic procedure in the alchemical process</term> of the stone, therefore, is to dissolve it—reducing the solid mass into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>—so that it may be returned to its **first matter** <term>first matter: (materia prima) the primal, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made</term>. All of this is accomplished through quicksilver, which has the power to bring the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and the **Moon** <note>Silver</note> back to its own nature and to the first matter.

But because quicksilver contains within itself dregs and a tendency to scorch <note>original: "adustionem" — a technical term for the impurities that cause a substance to burn or oxidize poorly</note>—even without actual flame—as well as a watery substance, it is necessary to remove its excesses and supply what is missing if you wish to make or create a complete **medicine** <term>medicine: in alchemy, the Elixir or Stone used to transform base metals into gold</term> from it. Its earthiness and dregs must be entirely removed and cleansed through **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the material</term>, so that it does not create a leaden or "livid" color during the **projection** <term>projection: the final step of casting the Stone onto base metal to transform it into gold or silver</term>. 

Likewise, its wateriness must be removed so that it does not cause the entire matter to become "fugitive" <note>original: "fugitivam" — meaning it evaporates or escapes when heated</note> during projection. For the essential property of the medicine is to preserve the substance so it is not scorched, to be defended from burning, not to be put to flight, and to make the substance **fixed** <term>fixed: a stable state where a substance no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire</term>. 

Therefore, it sometimes happens that one creates **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note>, **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, or sometimes **Mars** <note>Iron</note>, which must necessarily happen because of impurity. From this process, sometimes the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> is created, and sometimes the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>, which necessarily results from purity. 

Whence the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "quarto Metheororum" — a foundational text for medieval science</note> mocks the sophists <note>fraudulent or ignorant practitioners</note> of this art, saying: "Let the craftsmen know that the species of metals cannot be changed." This is indeed always true, as the Philosopher writes, *unless* those species are first reduced to their **first matter**. This matter is indeed quicksilver, since it is the element of all ductile <note>malleable</note> metals; then they are indeed changed into a form other than what they were before. 

For it is not the "species" <note>the abstract essence or "gold-ness"</note> but the "individuals of the species" <note>the specific physical pieces of metal</note> that are changed, because these individuals are subject to sensory actions, in that they are convertible among themselves. The species of silver, which is "silverness," is not changed into the species of gold, which is "goldness," nor vice versa, because the species of nature cannot be changed; but the *individuals* of the species can be, when they are reduced to their first matter. For when the form of this or that individual has been destroyed <note>original: "corrupta"</note> and resolved into the first matter, another form is easily and even necessarily introduced, because the destruction of one thing is the ge- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword for "generation"</note>

...generation of another. And because matter can in no way be destroyed without remaining under some form—whereby, once one form is destroyed, another is immediately introduced for this operation or another disposition. For it must be noted that the **first matter** <term>first matter: (materia prima) the primal, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made</term> is of two kinds: one is "near" and the other is "remote." 

The "near" matter is indeed **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum," i.e., Mercury</note>. The "remote" matter is truly water, because before it was quicksilver, it was water. Therefore, the true beginning of our work is the **dissolution of the stone** <term>dissolution: the process of breaking down a solid into its liquid or "spiritual" components</term>, because dissolved bodies are reduced to the nature of a spirit, except that they are more fixed. For it belongs only to the body to exist with the congealing of the spirit. 

Therefore, be patient, endure, and cook, grind, and soften with wax <term>incera: (inserration) a process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a wax-like consistency</term>, and do not let it weary you to repeat this very thing. For those things which are soaked in water are softened, and the more you grind, the more you soften, and the more you refine the coarse parts until they are broken down and divided from one another; since spirits are made into a paste with the body, and all things that are made into a paste are entirely dissolved. This "impastation" occurs through excessive grinding with water, **incineration** <note>original: "incineratione" — reduction to ash</note>, and **roasting** <note>original: "assatione"</note>. 

For through the grinding of waters, roasting, and fire, the parts bound by the viscosity found in bodies are separated. Truly, dissolved bodies are reduced to the nature of spirits, and they are never separated, just as water mixed with water cannot be. Indeed, because nature rejoices in nature, for the **bridegroom and the bride** <note>A common alchemical metaphor for the union of male/sulfur/spirit and female/mercury/body</note> are joined; however, those parts that are not dissolved are neither refined nor softened.

Therefore, dearest one, you must labor in the dissolution of the stone to separate its purer parts from the impure and heavier parts; once the dregs are cast aside, the work may be perfected with the lighter parts. This is because the intent of our work is nothing other than to select the purest substance of **Mercury** in the bodies themselves, since the **elixir** <term>elixir: the perfected substance capable of transmutation and healing</term> consists only of these. 

Now, it is necessary for the first movement to be **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the decomposition of a substance, often through gentle heat, to release its inner essence</term>; however, since there are many types of decay and corruption, we speak only of that which is used for our purpose. Therefore, the first natural principle is the material matter... just as I said above. The second is the heat that moves this matter toward putrefaction. The signs of perfect putrefaction are a black color, a foul odor, and the material becoming subtle and discontinuous to the touch, as if it were the first Mercury. Because heat acting upon moisture first generates blackness; this blackness is the **Raven’s Head** <note>original: "caput corvi" — the *nigredo* stage, symbolizing the death of the old form</note>, which is the beginning of the work.

Also note that entrance, submersion, connection, conjunction, complexion, composition, and commixtion all mean the same thing in this art. For nothing is added, joined, or converted...

...without being mixed. For a mixture is a union of things capable of being mixed through their smallest parts—that is, joined to one another through indivisible parts. Know also for certain that the entire strength of this **mastery** <term>magistery: (magisterium) the complete process or "work" required to create the Stone</term> lies only in **putrefaction** <note>In alchemy, putrefaction is the "death" of the substance, where it turns black and decomposes before it can be reborn in a purified state.</note>; if it has not been putrefied, it can neither be dissolved nor melted. And if it has not been dissolved, it will come to nothing.

Likewise, know that in every body there are three dimensions and depths, and this clearly appears from the body. And that which first lies open to our sight—for example, our Stone in its **first creation** <note>original: "prima creatione," referring to the initial state of the raw materials</note> is white, and so it appears on the surface. Wherefore we call it cold and moist, because it is such from its origin; hence we should study why our stone is watery, because it is cold and moist. For such a disposition is called the **manifest** or obvious state of the body.

**Width** <note>original: "latitudo," often used in alchemy to describe the intermediate range of qualities between two extremes</note>, however, is that middle disposition through which one goes to the depth; it is truly the middle between the depth and [the surface], as if between two extremes or contraries. And it is impossible to pass from one contrary to another, or from one extreme to another, except through a middle disposition, because our stone is of a cold and moist complexion. If, therefore, we wish to make it pass to the middle disposition, it is necessary that one quality be destroyed in it. It is destroyed in it by means of putrefaction. For the cold and the moist, by nature and by putrefaction, are thickened.

And its moisture is turned into a nature of dryness according to **Alfidius** <note>Alfidius is a legendary Arabic alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval Latin manuscripts.</note>, and the transition to the middle disposition is made, which is coldness and dryness. This is called the "width," namely of water, because it holds coldness from the cold and moist, and dryness from the hot and dry—namely, fire. Previously, indeed, through the heat existing within by means of the coldness which remained in the body, a transition is made to the opposites or extremes by destroying coldness and introducing heat. This disposition is called the **depth** or the **hidden part** of the body, which appears best in the book *The Mastery of Aristotle* <note>original: "Magisterii Aristotelis," a title for pseudo-Aristotelian alchemical works.</note>.

He, therefore, who wishes to profit in this art, must especially compose this mineral mixture or **secret** <term>arcanum: a profound mystery or "inner secret" of nature that the alchemist seeks to unlock</term>, so as to first find it moving from nature to nature, from color to color. # ALBERTUS MAGNUS
## On the extraction of water from the earth, and the return of water upon its own earth.

### CHAPTERS IV & V.

After the matter has been **putrefied** <note>In alchemy, putrefaction is the stage where the substance turns black, signifying the breakdown of its initial form.</note> to achieve the union of body and spirit—which is only possible in "air" (that is, in a state of heat and moisture)—this is done through **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and kemudian solidifies again, used here to mean "refining" the substance into a spiritual or oily state</term>, which is its resolution into an oil. You should know, therefore, that our stone is divided into two principal parts by the **mastery** <term>magistery: (magisterium) the entire technical process of the alchemical work</term>: namely, into an upper part, which ascends on high, and a lower part, which remains **fixed** <note>original: "fixa"; in alchemy, a "fixed" substance is stable under heat and does not evaporate.</note>. Yet these two parts agree in their power, and therefore the Philosopher says: **That which is above is like that which is below.** <note>original: "Superius est sicut quod est inferius." This is the most famous axiom of the "Emerald Tablet," a foundational alchemical text.</note>

And this division is necessary to perform the miracles of the "one thing"—that is, the Stone. The lower part is the earth, which is called the **nurse** and the **ferment** <note>The "ferment" acts like leaven in bread, transforming the rest of the material into its own nature.</note>, and the upper part is the **soul** <note>original: "anima"</note>, which gives life to the whole stone and makes it rise again. Thus, once the separation has been made and the **conjunction** <note>The "marriage" or re-joining of the separated parts.</note> of the stone has been celebrated, many miracles are performed.

It should be noted that although our stone is divided by some into four parts during the first operation—which are the four elements, as was said above—there are nevertheless two principal parts: namely, one which ascends on high, which is called **non-fixed** <term>volatile: (non fixa) a substance that easily evaporates or "flies" when heated</term>, and the other which remains below, which is called **fixed**, or earth, or ferment, which nourishes and ferments the whole stone, as has been said. 

Indeed, it is necessary to have a good quantity of this non-fixed part. It must be given to the Stone—which has been made most pure and free from filth—repeatedly through the mastery until, by the power of the non-fixed spirit, it carries the whole stone upward by sublimating it. And this is what the Philosopher says: **It ascends from the earth into heaven.** <note>Another quote from the Emerald Tablet, describing the refinement of the matter into a spiritual state.</note> Afterward, it is necessary to repeat the process with the stone thus exalted upon **marble** <note>original: "marmore"; likely referring to a porphyry grinding stone used to mix alchemical ingredients</note> with the "element" extracted from that same stone in the first operation. 

This element is called the **water of the stone**, and it must be subtly **roasted** <note>original: "assari"; referring to the application of dry heat</note> so many times until the entire stone descends once again into the earth. In this way, it will receive the "superior power" by ascending and the "inferior power" by descending. Thus, that which is corporeal becomes spiritual by ascending, and that which is spiritual becomes corporeal by descending. In this way, you shall have the **glory of the clarity of this world** <note>A state of perfect purity and enlightenment</note>, and all darkness, all want, and all sickness will flee from you.

For the stone composed in this way cures every sickness. This stone is "strong with the strength of all strength," because there is no comparison between this stone and the other strengths of this world. For it overcomes every subtle thing and will penetrate every solid thing; it passes through and conquers almost everything, and by conquering, it converts **Living Mercury** <term>quicksilver: (Mercurium vivam) liquid mercury, which the Stone is said to "fix" or turn into solid gold or silver</term>, which is subtle, into these bodies.

# ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE

It will penetrate hard and solid things, for *Morienes* <note>Morienes was a legendary 7th-century hermit-alchemist, traditionally said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says that the "whole black" is nothing other than the extraction of water from the earth, and the returning of this water back onto its own earth—that is, its own substance—until it rots. And this water rots and is purified together with the earth; once it has been purified, with the help of divinity, the whole mastery <term>magistery: (magisterium) the complete technical operation of the alchemical art</term> will be directed. This water indeed contains within itself the soul of its own body. This soul, I say, exists in the spirit in the manner of an oil; this soul is a dissolved tincture carried within the spirit, which some Philosophers call the "white smoke" <note>original: "fumum album"; a symbolic term for a purified, volatile substance that rises during heating.</note>. It is so regarding the white smoke, because the white smoke is the soul of dissolved and dead bodies, whose souls we have extracted from their bodies. For every body that lacks a soul is dark, and when the white smoke is returned to the dead body, it flows into the body and carries away its blackness and impurity, because it consolidates the bodies into one and multiplies them; then its beauty will appear, and the tincture <term>tincture: a concentrated spiritual essence or "dye" capable of transforming the properties and color of a substance</term> will work within it. And know for certain that if the white smoke did not exist, the art of *Alchemy* would not exist. For *Pythagoras* says, speaking of the water of *Mercury* extracted from the stone—that is, the earth of gold:

**THIS** water is indeed the sharpest vinegar <note>original: "acetum acerrimum"; in alchemy, this refers not to kitchen vinegar but to a powerful universal solvent or "mercurial water" used to break down metals.</note>, which makes pure gold become a spirit, without which neither whiteness, nor blackness, nor redness, nor rust can be produced. And when it is mixed with the body, it becomes one with it, and turns it into a spirit and colors it with varying colors. *Philosophers* say that water alone does everything by itself: it dissolves all things, congeals all things, and breaks down all things without anyone's assistance. In it colors are accustomed to appear ...... body in which is the tincture of any body. Furthermore, there is a difference between the tincture of the water—namely the *Lunar* <note>Lunar: referring to the moon or silver</note> water—and the tincture of the oil—namely the *solar* <note>Solar: referring to the sun or gold</note> water. For the tincture of the water washes and purifies, while the tincture of the oil tints and colors. An example of this is if a cloth is dipped in water: it is cleaned by it, because when it is dried, the water recedes, and the cloth remains in its original state and color, except that it is cleaner. On the contrary, it is like oil: when a cloth is dyed in it, it cannot be separated from it even by the heat of fire, unless the whole cloth is destroyed. Therefore, the oil is the likeness of the soul existing in the body, which cannot be extracted.

### ALBERTUS MAGNUS

Boil it down, and afterwards calcine <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a fine powder</term> it moderately in the fire, and do not let it weary you to repeat this very thing, for the earth does not bear fruit without frequent irrigation. For the body is a disconnected element because it has been entirely deprived of its own soul; therefore, since it is dry and empty, and thus very thirsty, it freely drinks up its own watery moisture. Grinding shall not cease until the water becomes one with the earth; otherwise, the body itself gains nothing. You must not, therefore, stay your hand from the grinding <term>trituration: the act of grinding or pounding a solid into a fine powder</term> and the roasting until it makes the earth white. 

Be careful not to soak the earth except little by little, with long grinding after the drying of the earth, for in this balance is found everywhere. It should be noted that an excessive administration of moisture should not ruin the dryness, nor should a superfluity of dryness ruin the moisture; specifically, you should boil it down by roasting just as much as it requires for dissolving by soaking. Note that every time after the calcination of the earth, you should pour the water over it temperately—neither too much, clearly, nor too little—because if it were too much, it would become a "sea of confusion" <note>original: "pelagus conturbationis"; a common alchemical phrase describing a state where the proportions of the elements are so unbalanced that the chemical reaction fails or becomes unmanageable.</note>. If, however, it were too little, it would be scorched into ashes. 

Therefore, gently and without haste, you shall irrigate the earth every eight days, boil it, and calcine it until it has drunk its own water. Thus, continue the work many times, for although it is a long process and you will not see the tincture <note>original: "tincturam"; the spiritual essence capable of transforming metals</note>, you will not reach perfection until the work itself is perfected. Studeas therefore, when you have worked, to record in your mind all the signs that appear in any boiling and to investigate their causes. 

There are indeed three principal colors: black, white, and yellow <note>original: "niger, albus & citrinus"; corresponding to the three major stages of the Great Work: Nigredo, Albedo, and Citrinitas.</note>. When the blackness emerges, it is perfect but not complete; every time, strengthen the fire in the calcination until the earth comes out white from the intensity of the fire. For just as heat acting upon moisture generates blackness, so heat acting upon dryness generates whiteness. Therefore, if the earth is not white, grind it in its own water and calcine it again. 

Azoth <term>Azoth: the "universal solvent" or the essential mercury of the philosophers</term> and fire wash the Laton <term>Laton: (latonem) a term for base metal or "impure brass" that must be purified into gold</term>, and being placed by it, they snatch away its impurities. For its preparation is always with it. And just as the clarity of the water shall be, so shall be the clarity of the earth; the more it has been washed, the more white it shall be. 

Wherefore another philosopher says: "When you have found it already black, know that this is the first key of the Stone; afterwards, however, it grows red after the putrefaction—not a true redness—and it even turns yellow." Regarding this, a certain man said: "It often turns red, and often turns yellow, and often liquefies, and often coagulates before the true whiteness." Whence another said: "It dissolves itself, and it coagulates itself, and it adorns itself with redness before the whiteness; it even becomes green." [All colors] that can be imagined in this world appear before the whiteness, and then the true whiteness follows. You must therefore temper this mastery. For the composition will not be without marriage and putrefaction. And the "marriage" <term>marriage: the chemical union of opposite substances, such as the 'subtle' spirit and the 'thick' body</term> consists in mixing the subtle with the thick; and the "putrefaction" of the earth is to roast and moisten it until they are mixed together and become one, and there is no distinction, like water mixed with water. Then the thick part will try to hold back the subtle, and the soul will try to purify with the fire and endure it, and the spirit will try to be submerged in the bodies and be poured into them. Know that when the body has mixed itself with moisture and the heat of the fire finds it, the moisture is turned upon the body and dissolves it; and then the spirit cannot escape from it, for it drinks itself in with the fire and its flame. Yet these parts do not unite except with good tempering, continuity, and long labor.

Truly, the ancient Philosophers bestowed many names upon our stone: they called it "animal," "gum," "vitriol," "blood," and "red urine" because of the red color, and they called it by infinitely many other names. They called it "iron" because of its inability to melt, and they said this: for when this body is deprived of its moisture through boiling—which previously made it flow easily—the body must necessarily be dry and not flow; hence they called it "iron," because among other bodies iron is said to be the driest, just as that body, through the deprivation of the moisture that first made it volatile, must now remain fixed. For all things that are not fixed are made fixed through such a deprivation of moisture, which was called "calcination" by many Philosophers. Wherefore Geber <note>Geber: The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an early authority in alchemy whose writings emphasized rigorous laboratory techniques.</note> says: "Calcination is the purification of a thing by fire, or its reduction to powder by removing the moisture of the consolidating part; and the reason for the invention of calcinations is so that the spirits themselves may be better fixed." So it is, through the deprivation of moisture...

According to **Geber**, this is changing from nature to nature, and from water into fire according to the naturalists, as stated in the *Turba* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" or Assembly of the Philosophers, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>. Because if you kindle the fire before the red growth, it becomes red [too soon], which is of no use to you, because you desire whiteness, as **Lucas** says. For all Philosophers assert that a mild fire ought to be used for the reasons aforesaid. For they require that we must govern it smoothly until the sulfur becomes incombustible <note>original: "incremabile"; sulfur that can no longer be consumed by fire, a sign of the Stone's stability</note>; hence, from the seed, the woman ought not to reap except after the harvest. Our Philosophers have called this our **Salamander**, because just as the Salamander lives on fire alone, so our stone is nourished by fire alone. Wherefore another also says: "Unless the soul becomes a body, it will not endure the fire." But he who has been able to convert the soul into a body, and the body into a soul, and to mix with it the subtle spirits, tinges every body to perfection.

Know that this stone, which the Philosophers recognize and which possesses powers above all the powers of stones, as we have taught, should be placed in the Philosophical vessel to be sublimated; and with it the stone is sublimated until it reaches the ultimate purity of sublimation. This is the first order, or what is called the first operation. And these are the words of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a famous 8th-century scholar often called the "Father of Chemistry"</note>, who placed the whole art in sublimation and repetition. And know that this sublimation is not that of the common folk, because in this sublimation all the previously mentioned sublimations are left behind, which I will define for you. 

The FIRST is purification, so that the most subtle and purest substance may be extracted. The SECOND is solution, so that the whole matter is dissolved into water. The THIRD is <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the stage where the matter "dies" and turns black before its rebirth</note>, as Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: "Never has anything been animated in any way or brought forth from birth, nor has it grown, except after putrefaction and a change of appearance." Whence the Wise One says: "That all strength," etc. For he says if it has not become putrid, it will not be dissolved; thus it is necessary that putrefaction occurs there. Hence the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says, "The corruption of one thing is the generation of another" <note>original: "Corruptio est generatio alterius"</note>. 

The FOURTH is washing, as it is necessary that this putrefied and filthy thing be washed through ablution, and cleansed from corruption and impurity. And they have rightly said: "Because as long as the water remains over the earth, the more the earth is cleansed and washed," so that washing and <term>ceration</term> <note>the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note> are the same thing. 

The FIFTH is coagulation, according to which, by drying gently in the Sun, the water is united with the earth, then dried and coagulated together until it is turned into a powder. And thus is coagulation completed. 

The SIXTH is <term>calcination</term> <note>reducing a substance to powder through high heat</note>, from which you should know that a calcined thing is more suitable than one not calcined. And it is, simply put, close to <term>fixation</term> <note>making a substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</note>, which is why many Philosophers spoke of calcination as fixation, and they spoke well. For all these modes are within sublimation; because I say that he who perfectly sublimates completes and performs the entire work. 

And know that all of this is accomplished in one furnace and one vessel. In sublimation alone are all these operations we have spoken of and the seven dispositions, which any intelligent person can complete from them. Therefore, do not be negligent in sublimation, for the work is perfected through sublimation; and as the cleansing shall be, so shall be the perfection. Now I wish to demonstrate to you what sublimation is.

# ALBERTUS MAGNUS

Sublimation is the elevation of the most subtle parts from the coarse parts, and likewise the separation of the <term>volatile</term> <note>original: "non fixarum," meaning parts that evaporate easily</note> parts from the <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "fixis," meaning parts that resist the fire and do not evaporate</note> parts. The volatile parts are raised up by smoke, that is, by "wind," because as we have said, one must take care that they do not escape; rather, they should be fixed together with the fixed parts so that they remain and provide a faster melting for the coarser parts. Understand that true sublimation occurs when we create a separation of the parts that are raised to the top from those that remain at the bottom. Indeed, we want them to come together simultaneously in their own proper way. Because in our <term>stone</term> <note>the Philosopher's Stone or the primary material of the work</note> after the first purification, which is completed through <term>solution</term> <note>the process of dissolving a solid into liquid</note>, we find nothing diminished and nothing superfluous. It is for this reason that Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century "father of chemistry"</note> said that the stone should be sublimated with it until it reaches the ultimate purity of sublimation; and for this reason Geber said that we must perform our sublimation with it alone, without any other addition or external thing. Because of this, all those workers are deceived who sublimated with <term>dregs</term> <note>original: "fæcibus," refers to the waste material or "lees" often added by amateur alchemists</note>; they do not know what they are doing, or they are ignorant of what the Philosopher’s Stone is, and even if they sublimated a hundred times, they would not succeed because they are ignorant of the Sublimation of the Philosophers. Whence Geber says:

> For there is one Stone, one medicine, in which the whole <term>mastery</term> <note>the "magisterium" or the completed alchemical process</note> consists. To which we add no external thing, nor do we take anything away, except for that which we remove as superfluous during the preparation or operation.

And the first purification which is completed through sublimation, I have already sufficiently demonstrated to you. Know that when you wish to perform sublimation, you should add or take away nothing from our stone; rather, place it with its whole substance in our vessel as we described in the first arrangement, closing the vessel tightly. Place it in the furnace and cover it with ashes below and underneath, in such a way that two parts of the vessel are uncovered until the matter is dissolved, and afterwards manage it with a slow fire until the greater part is turned into powder, which will happen within thirty days. And when these operations which we have mentioned are done, then <term>sublimation</term>, <term>solution</term>, <term>distillation</term>, <term>descension</term>, <term>putrefaction</term>, <term>ablution</term> <note>washing</note>, <term>ceration</term> <note>softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note>, and <term>calcination</term> <note>reducing to powder through heat</note> or <term>fixation</term> have all been accomplished. Know that the Philosophers said many such things—namely, about each operation mentioned above—so that the science would be more obscure to understand. When our stone is in our vessel and the matter feels "our Sun" <note>likely referring to the controlled heat of the furnace or the "sulfur" principle within the matter</note>, it is immediately dissolved into water, so that it ascends to the top, to the "head" of the vessel, and afterwards descends to the bottom of the vessel. And it was their opinion that what ascends should be named the **first sublimation**. Afterward, seeing this matter descend to the bottom and turn itself into water, they judged in their hearts that this was the **second sublimation**. Likewise, seeing such an ascent and descent convert into water, they said that there was **distillation**, which is the **third mode**. And seeing these things thicken and turn into black earth—and this thickening at first stood upon the water, and thus by letting it go and gradually thickening, they saw the earth submerge into the water and stand at the bottom under the water—which earth was black and dreggy, they judged within themselves that this operation should be called **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrefactio," the stage of decomposition where the matter turns black, often called the "raven's head"</note>, which is the **fifth mode**.

Seeing still more—that the whole remained under the water and grew while the water diminished due to moderate boiling—they all said that this was perfect **ceration** <note>original: "ceratio," the process of softening the matter until it has the consistency of wax</note>, and thus it was a new beginning. Wherefore the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle</note> said that the water is waxed and soaked with the earth, and through moderate boiling it is dried out, and the whole matter is turned into earth. Hence the Philosopher says: "This is its entire power, if it be turned into earth," <note>original: "vis eius integra, si versa fuerit in terram," a famous line from the Emerald Tablet</note> and this is the **seventh mode**. 

Likewise, seeing still that the whole matter became earth and reduced itself to a single substance that did not flow, but rather stood firm—seeing this, they said that this was the whole [work], because Plato said: "Dissolve our stone and coagulate it afterward"—that is, turn it into earth—and do this with great caution, and you have almost the entire mastery; and this is called the **eighth mode**. Wherefore Plato said: "Take our stone in thin plates, cook it and place it in our vessel firmly closed, and roast it with a light fire until it is broken apart." Afterward, cook it in the heat of the Sun until it is coagulated. *And know that the whole mastery is nothing other than making a perfect solution and coagulation.* Wherefore the Philosopher said: "**Dissolve and coagulate** <note>original: "Solvite & coagulate," the fundamental axiom of alchemy</note>, and you shall have the whole operation and art."

### *On the fixation and multiplication of the stone.*

## C H A P T E R   V I I.

Next follows the planting of the powders, so that they may bear fruit and their fruit may remain forever. And I will teach how to **fix** <note>original: "figere"; fixation is the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</note> the sublimated powders, so that they may be able to remain in the fire, and be united and mixed with bodies. Now, fixation is the suitable adaptation of a "fleeting thing" to the fire. Truly, the cause of its discovery is so that every **tincture** <note>the coloring principle or essence of the Stone</note> and every alteration may be prepared in another and not be changed. It remains, therefore, after the sublimation of the matter, to proceed to its fixation.

It is fixed thus: Take that which is sublimated, and divide it among <term>cucurbits</term> <note>gourd-shaped glass vessels used for boiling</note>, or among <term>urinals</term> <note>tall, narrow-necked glass flasks</note>, according as the quantity of the matter requires. And let the sign of its fixation be when the matter no longer ascends to the <term>alembic</term> <note>the "still-head" or cap of the distilling apparatus</note>, even when one is able to increase the fire greatly; then it appears immediately; or place some of the body upon an iron plate: if it remains fixed and does not fly away, do not repeat the process. And divide it equally among the aforementioned urinals, place them upon a <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>a furnace designed to reflect or "reverberate" the heat from the roof back down onto the vessels</note>; having done this, first apply a slow fire all around for several days until you see that by such a slow fire nothing more ascends; and thus strengthen the fire, and continue with such a stronger fire until you see nothing being raised; and thirdly you shall give the strongest fire, which you must continue until the aforementioned matter is fixed.

And it must be known that the spirit and soul are not united in a true way except in the white color, because then all the colors that can be imagined by an impure man appear there, and then they are strengthened and complete the work in one color, namely that of <margin>10</margin> whiteness, and there all colors meet. For the **whitening** <note>original: "dealbatio," referring to the <term>albedo</term> stage of the work</note> is the beginning and foundation of the whole work; nor is it finally changed into different colors, except into the red, in which...
