...is the final end. Truly, **incineration** <note>original: "cineratio"; the process of reducing a substance to ashes or a gray-blue state through heat</note> is that which occurs into blue and red, and it is not called a color <note>Likely meaning it is a transitional phase rather than one of the primary "Great Colors" of alchemy</note>. In the process of **decoction** <note>slow, steady heating</note>, one cannot go wrong after the **whiteness** <note>albedo; the stage signifying purity and the creation of the "White Stone" for silver</note> has been reached. For by gradually increasing the governance of the fire after true whiteness, one arrives at incineration before the **redness** <note>rubedo; the final stage representing the "Red Stone" for gold</note>, as I have said before. 

And know that **mercury** <note>original: "argentum vivum" or "living silver"</note> is the fire that burns, kills, and binds bodies under a single governance; and the more the bodies are ground and mixed, the more they are broken down and thinned out. And know that the body cannot tint unless it is tinted itself, and unless the spirit is extracted it will remain hidden in the belly—that is, buried—and it becomes a body and soul without spirit. This spirit is the spiritual nature from which the colors will appear. Wherefore the **Philosopher** <note>Usually a reference to Aristotle, though here referring to the collective wisdom of alchemists</note> says: *I command you to make bodies no longer bodies, even incorporeal bodies.* For through this governance the compound is purified, and the hidden part of its nature is extracted. For unless the thick bodies and the corporeal nature are broken down until they become incorporeal—namely, a most subtle spirit—you cannot extract that most subtle and tinting soul which is hidden in the natural belly.

It must also be noted that the body or "earth," which is the stable thing receiving the **tincture** <note>the essence that transforms base metal into gold</note>, is said to have greater power than its brothers, namely the soul and the spirit. For it overcomes all things that are mixed with it and transforms them into its own color; and the spirit is the carrier of the soul’s virtues through the body. Similarly, the more our **bronze** <note>original: "æs"; used here as a code name for the starting material of the Stone</note> is cooked, the more it is thickened, until it becomes what the envious <note>those who hide alchemical secrets</note> call the "Stone of all metals." Afterward, it is burned until it becomes like saffron or burnt blood; then, being incorporated, it is imprinted upon and tints into true gold. **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek mathematician was often cited in medieval alchemy as a primary authority on the harmony of elements</note> says: *Our Stone must be cooked in its own water until the whole becomes most pure, and made as if spiritual, and then the inseparable union of body and spirit occurs.* Let the color then be permanent, because the **fugitive** <note>the volatile spirit that usually evaporates</note> has become "without flight" <note>meaning it is now fixed and stable under heat</note>.

Pythagoras also said that in **Mercury** and in **Sulfur**, all elements must be so purged that they are rendered unburnable by fire, uninflammable by air, and of an unvaporizable wateriness from water.

Furthermore, "distance" and "proximity" exist in the matter; these aforementioned things can also be understood this way: namely, that those two spirits, mercury and sulfur, are very far apart, both because of the aforementioned impediments and because of their nature. This is because that moisture is subtly mixed with one oily, viscous earthiness, and also because of the long decoction which digests it; and this is...

...distance. But "proximity" is called the embrace <note>original: "complexio"</note>... by embracing, which immediately after digestion becomes an indissoluble union of both. Or this **decoction** <note>the process of slow, steady heating in a sealed vessel</note> acts here upon the entire substance of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii"; refers here to the "Philosophical Mercury," the living spirit of the metal</note>, but it acts especially upon the corporeal substance, because then it breaks down the body and it becomes powder. It is therefore necessary that the body of Mercury within, which that noble smoke contains, be continuously and most subtly broken down, corrupted, and entirely purified, so that it is turned into a refined corporeal nature. And then our two spirits and the body are made subtle and embrace each other inseparably, and one holds the other; they do not flee from the fire nor are they consumed by it. They penetrate metals and strengthen them perfectly, [using] a heat almost like the heat of a hen incubating her egg <note>A common alchemical metaphor for a gentle, constant warmth (the "fire of the first degree")</note>, especially at the beginning of the governance. 

Because through such heat, all the muddy force of **quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti vivi"</note>, the superfluous moisture of the powder, and the thick yellowness—the vaporous oiliness which it has from the nature of **sulfur** <note>In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, combustible principle, while Mercury is the passive, fluid principle</note>—is gradually purged and refined without the rising of said oiliness. Once these are thinned, the body of Mercury is produced, appearing like a hidden virtue, and then the fire is increased a little. And the said virtue will be collected and joined to its purified body, and then their indissoluble marriage <note>original: "desponsatio"; the chemical union of the fixed and volatile principles</note> occurs. In the first decoction it becomes **black** <note>the *nigredo* stage, representing putrefaction and the death of the old form</note>, and then it is known that it is rightly guided. In the second decoction it becomes **white** <note>the *albedo* stage, representing purification</note>, and in the third, **red** <note>the *rubedo* stage, representing the final perfection of the Stone</note>. 

Some make the whiteness appear faster through greater haste, which can be done by increasing the fire, but the body will not be purified, nor reduced into its proper nature. And therefore the hidden, fleeing spirit is never mixed with the thick body; instead, it flies away from the fire immediately if the burning of the fire does not cease—that is, the external or artificial fire. For if the artificial heat exceeds too much, it removes the intrinsic heat, because the intrinsic heat cannot draw to itself the moisture at the root by which it might defend itself from the fire. Nor will the burning of the spirits from the intrinsic heat cease—about which **Aristotle** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher; his work was the foundation of medieval science</note> spoke excellently in his book *On Meteorology* <note>original: "libro Meteororum"</note>. 

And so, by altering and breaking down through continuous and slow heat, the muddiness is consumed and the superabundant moisture evaporates. These two things—the muddiness and excess moisture—were impeding the subtle parts (namely the earthy and the radical watery parts) so that they were not able to embrace entirely. And yet, with these two removed, the place for true mixing is made, because it allows that earthy part to be joined to its radical water, and be decocted again until they liquefy and one is incorruptible with the other through all its parts, so that the smallest bit of earth is mixed with the smallest bit of water, so that no...

...in them there should be a place where there is no true mixing, and when it is soaked with **permanent water** <note>original: "aqua permanente"; a specialized alchemical solvent that does not wet the hands but dissolves metals</note>, because in this **decoction** <note>the process of slow, steady heating</note> it becomes red and is dyed with a true and perfect redness. For he says that intense, over-abundant heat causes the moisture to evaporate, but the "cold of the fire" <note>an insufficient or inconsistent heat</note> causes the work to perish. Note the **governance of the fire**: if it is to be governed according to nature, it should be governed by the example of the four seasons. In the first season, namely winter, the earth conceives. In the second, namely spring, it produces herbs and flowers. In summer, the fruits are ripened. In autumn, they are gathered. 

Hence, in our work, it is similar: In the first operation, **Mercury** <note>the spirituous principle</note> is killed and the whole body is turned to powder. In the third <note>The original text lists these stages out of order: 1st, 3rd, 2nd, 3rd, 4th</note> it conceives so that it may be turned into another nature; hence in that decoction it becomes black. In the second, it shows its nature by whitening itself. In the third, the fruits already appear, because then the redness appears, which is at the end of the work. In the fourth, the fruits are ripened and gathered from it. And let these things said concerning **fixation** <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable in fire</note> suffice.

But it must be known that one metal is further removed from perfection than another; and although any metal may be led to perfection by the elixir, nevertheless those that are naturally closer to it are reduced more easily and much more perfectly than those far away. And when we find a metal that is already near-perfect and very close to perfection, we are excused from working with those very far removed. Which metals are very close or far away can be found clearly enough in many books. ...already done. It is also difficult to <term>project</term> <note>the final act of adding the alchemical Stone or Elixir to a base metal to transform it</note> over a million parts and to present them immediately; therefore I will hand down to you a more hidden secret. One part must be mixed with a thousand parts of a **neighboring body** <note>original: "corporis vicinioris"; likely a metal considered "close" in nature to the target metal, such as lead for silver or copper for gold</note>. Put all of this into a firmly opened <note>the original Latin "firmiter aperto" is likely a transcription error for "firmiter operto," meaning "firmly closed"</note> vessel, and place it in the **philosophical fusion furnace** with a slow fire at first, always increasing it for three days, until they are inseparably joined. This is the **work of three days**. Then, once again and finally, any one part must be projected over another thousand of any neighboring body; and that is the work of one day, or an hour, or even a minute.

There is also another way of proceeding in this manner: Take a hundred parts of **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note> washed with salt and vinegar and put it in a **crucible** <note>a heat-resistant melting pot</note> over the fire. When it begins to flow, add one part of your **elixir** prepared in the said manner; project it over the 100 parts of washed Mercury as I have said, and the whole will become a **medicine** for washed Mercury. Then, place one part of this congealed medicine over 100 parts of washed Mercury in a crucible glowing in the fire, and the whole will still become medicine. Afterward, place one part of this final congealed medicine over 100 parts of washed Mercury, and it will be **gold or silver**, the best by every judgment, according to how the elixir was prepared.

There is also another method of projecting: place one part of the aforementioned medicine over 60 parts of Mercury and put it in some glass vessel, sealing the mouth of the vessel with **lime** <note>original: "calce"; used as a sealant to make the vessel airtight</note> so that it does not breathe. Then, place it over a fire of ashes for three days. If the <margin>*</margin> Mercury is retained, know that the medicine is then perfect. And take note, because then all those 60 parts of Mercury will be a medicine and elixir over others. Note that by this method, by always increasing the Mercury, you will be able to prove the excellence of the Medicine; for sometimes one part converts a hundred, sometimes 200, sometimes 40, sometimes a thousand into infinity, and the whole becomes medicine, whatever Mercury it retains with itself.

The method of operation, however, is this: project one part of the aforementioned medicine over a hundred parts of melted **Sun** <note>original: "solis"; gold</note> and it will make it brittle, and the whole will be medicine. One part projected over 100 parts of any melted metal converts it into the best "Sun" <note>gold</note>, than which no better can be found. And if you project it over the **Moon** <note>original: "lunam"; silver</note> in a similar way, it converts all bodies into "Moon." And by the same method, you could convert the Sun and Moon into **Venus** <note>original: "venerem"; copper</note>, **Saturn** ♄ <note>lead</note>, **Jupiter** ♃ <note>tin</note>, and **Mars** ♂ <note>iron</note>; regarding which, by my advice, do not do it and do not proceed. If, however, the aforementioned medicine or elixir has no **ingress** <note>the ability to penetrate and permeate the metal</note>, take equal parts from that stone extracted in the first operation, and mix and incorporate them together upon a marble slab. If it seems right to you, mix it by distilling via a **water bath** <note>original: "balneum"; a gentle heating method</note> so that they [combine] together...

# THE LETTER OF AVICENNA TO KING HASEN
## On the Proper Procedure.
### *On the Proper Procedure.*
#### CHAPTER I.

<margin>
1.
By observing 
the secrets 
of nature, 
the Method of 
the art is 
discovered.
2.
3.
4.
</margin>

Various matters have been discussed between me and Hasen <note>Likely referring to a patron or local ruler, possibly Al-Hasan ibn Ali</note> regarding what he himself knows; he asked me to write down a portion of these things in a treatise for delivery, so that they might be better understood, and so that I might make him understand the ways in which I applied myself to that subject. I have considered this according to what I have thought and known, examining natural things with a double subtlety. The opinion affirmed by those professing Alchemy <note>original: "Alchimiam"</note> was one of those things which those who work toward goodness and science mostly oppose, and they have annihilated the alchemists' opinion. For my part, however, there was no excuse in my own art <note>referring to his expertise in medicine and philosophy</note> for not knowing the intentions of both sects. I therefore considered the books of those affirming the art and found them empty of the reasons that exist in every true art, and I found most of what is contained in them to be more akin to madness <note>original: "alienationi," implying a lack of rational sense</note>. I also looked at the books of those who contradict the art and found their contradiction weak and their reasoning light, such as would not be enough to destroy the art.

Therefore, I returned to my own thoughts and began to meditate: if this thing is possible, how is it so, and how is it not? I knew, therefore, that it is possible for us to dye the moon <note>the alchemical symbol for Silver</note> into the color of the sun <note>the alchemical symbol for Gold</note> and Venus <note>the alchemical symbol for Copper</note> into the color of the moon. To do this, we require a red tincture <note>a concentrated medicinal or chemical coloring agent</note> that reddens, and a white one that whitens. I knew, furthermore, that the mixing of tinctures with [metallic] bodies to produce the Stone is not possible before they are made light and "run" <note>original: "currant," referring to the metal becoming fluid or mercury-like</note>. Furthermore, their softening and their flowing are not possible at the start of the work before they are liquefied. When, however, they have been liquefied, not every red or white tincture allows us to attain our goal. For when a substance is treated over the fire, it may be burned up, corrupted, and fail to complete the work. Or, if it is not burned, but is not "fixed" <note>stable</note> in the presence of fire, it instead flies off and escapes. It is of no value if it neither burns nor flies off yet fails to enter or mix with the metal. Or if it enters and mixes but does not remain in a fixed state—but rather is purified and flies off or is separated by any mode of separation—it does not complete the work. Or if it is not separated and does not fly off, but it fails to make those things which are burnable unburnable <note>i.e., it fails to protect the base metal from oxidation in the fire</note>.

<summary>Avicenna introduces his letter to King Hasen, critiquing both the irrationality of alchemical proponents and the weak arguments of its critics, while outlining the physical requirements for a successful transmutation of metals.</summary>

# ON THE PROPER PROCEDURE.

...as it stands in the moon <note>original: "luna"; referring to silver</note> and does not make the moon un-burnable <note>In alchemy, "adustion" refers to the oxidation or "burning away" of base metals in a furnace</note> by those substances which do not burn the sun <note>original: "solem"; referring to gold</note> but do burn the moon—such as salt and other things by which the sun is purified but by which the moon is consumed. Similarly, if it does not make Venus <note>copper</note> such that it is not burned by those things which do not burn the moon but do burn Venus; and likewise for lead and the rest. We require, therefore, a Medicine of a yellow <note>citrine</note> or white tincture which may be mixed with putrefied bodies and not be burned by those sharp substances that burn everything else, and which does not permit those burning agents to separate the parts of the body <note>the metal's substance</note>. I considered, therefore, whether among simple medicines there might be a medicine having these operations, and I found no medicine among those available that achieves this effect, except for that which was answered to you regarding the discovery of a plant whose nature and logic is this; and red sulfur <note>original: "sulphur rubeū"</note> found in fragments and white arsenic <note>original: "arsenicum album"</note> also have these operations. Nevertheless, what remains in my estimation is that this is vanity. For no such medicine as described in these accounts has ever come to any of those who were truly wise. It is therefore necessary for us to discover this operation for ourselves. Let us therefore seek a tincture which fire cannot destroy, a substance that may be mixed with liquefied metals, a consolidating substance, and a coagulating, uniting substance fixed over the fire, and the ingenuity to mix these things with one another so that, by uniting, they become 

<margin>Once the union of the root is made, let it become one thing.</margin>

one substance upon which fire leaves no mark; let it color with that tincture which is within it, be mixed by that mixable substance within it, be forever consolidated by its consolidating substance, and be forever fixed by that

### *On Tinctures.*
## CHAPTER II.

Regarding the white tincture, it must be known that we have found "living Zaimbar" <note>original: "Zaimbar vivum"; an archaic term derived from Arabic, here referring to Mercury or quicksilver</note> to whiten [metals], and we have found that with its whitening it adheres to bodies and penetrates them. ...it possesses the virtue that it is not burned by fire at all, but is only heated by it. And we know that when it is prepared so that it may be mixed with liquefied metals and remains white within them according to its own nature, we have seen that at the beginning of its processing, the drying and the destruction of its wateriness <term>aqueitas</term> <note>original: "aqueitatis"; the philosophical quality of being liquid or volatile</note> is necessary. This is done so that it may be heated until it can be powdered, broken, or ground, so that when it is prepared and we wish to grind and mix it with other substances, it is no longer "living" <note>original: "vivum"; referring to the liquid, mobile state of "quick" mercury</note> or hidden. It must be made receptive so that we may drench it with the "waters" <note>chemical solutions or distillates</note> if perhaps the necessity for them arises among those things we cannot do without if we desire a proper conjunction and mixture. Therefore, the method is to cook it over the fire in such a way that its flowing parts are separated from it and its dry part remains; furthermore, this is possible so that the flowing part evaporates and the dry part settles, since this is the nature of the whole, or at least its dominant part. This becomes especially apparent when our method involves mixing it with medicines from which we cannot later separate it. The procedure <term>regimen</term> is therefore to take its moist and dry components, distill the moist part, and conceal the dry part within its inner essence. Then, let us repeat this many times so that it is never hidden thereafter; and thus, when any part of it is burned, it is burned at the bottom of the instrument, and the foreign matter is purified with it. The dry substance is then sublimated from the essence of its wateriness, resulting in a white, crushable substance in which there is no combustion at all—a white coagulated mass entirely free from "burning."

Let us turn it and place it in a glazed earthen vessel, and let us coat the vessel with the **lute of wisdom** <term>lutum sapientiæ</term> <note>original: "luto sapientiæ"; a specialized sealing clay used to make vessels airtight</note> and dry it. Then, let us place it in an **Athanor**, that is, in a baker’s oven <note>original: "furno panis"; implying a furnace that provides steady, moderate heat</note>. And we shall indeed describe after this how **mercury** <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>original: "argentum vivū"; literally "living silver" or quicksilver</note> is "mortified" <note>killed or stabilized so it no longer evaporates</note> and how the lute of wisdom is made. Then, after the roasting, we grind it and leave it in the vessel of sublimation, and the vessel is called an **aludel** <term>alludel</term> <note>a series of pear-shaped pots used for collecting vapors</note>, and we sublimate it in there many times. And as often as we sublimate it, we renew the mixture for it and return it upon that same dregs <note>original: "fecē"; the solid residue left at the bottom</note>. We do this many times until it "dies" and is made white; sometimes this is completed in seven cycles, and sometimes we wait upon it for up to 12 times, which is the ultimate limit. And sometimes we place it in a chemical vessel <term>Kimiam</term> coated with the careful lute of wisdom and we bind its head after we have taken up its "wheel" <note>original: "rotē"; possibly a circular support or a specific part of the apparatus</note> as we shall say later. Then we sublimate the medicine so that it may ascend and be perfected; it will be produced in the neck of the vessel, transformed like crystal, sometimes like tin, and sometimes like rock salt. After we have sublimated it from there, and these things emerge through reasoning and experience, I shall then know that the intention in this is to dry the mercury and make it "pervium" <note>original: "pervium"; meaning permeable or capable of penetrating other metals</note>. After we have done this, we find a power that is **tinting** and lasting—indeed, of a better tincture and penetration—so that it does not differ from the color of pure silver in any way; rather, it is a more reflective tincture and of a more complete whiteness. And these things were known to us before the experiment through long and intense, subtle thought. Thus, the **white tincture** has come to us, stripped of the things we [otherwise] require.

### CONCERNING THE RED TINCTURE.

According to what we have found, we did not find anything in the beginning that produces **red**. Rather, we found that all things which penetrate into silver—and the rest of the things which tint it—lead it toward blackness. Furthermore, we see silver take on a **yellow color** <term>citrinitatē</term> from sulfur. Then, when it remains, it turns it black, and similarly as it remains, the blackness becomes stronger; and when it is thrown upon it in liquefaction, it burns it and pierces it. And we know that there is no way of reaching its whiteness [once] it is blackened by burning through the path of greenness—rather, it is through the path of yellowness and redness because of the principles which we already know. Therefore, since we know that when it is dissolved into water and is clean and also green, it does not make it "fall" green but turns it red, we know that it is possible for us to make [the tincture] flow from things that blacken **silver** <term>lunam</term> <note>original: "lunam"; literally "the Moon," the alchemical name for silver</note>.

<margin>Commendation and preparation of Sulfur.</margin>
Since sulfur is better than all other minerals, let us find the way to use it; let us boil it in water with a gentle fire so that the fiery power within it is processed and extracted, yet without burning away the actual substance of the sulfur or the fiery power itself, and so that nothing of the sulfur's essential virtue is lost. ### On the substance capable of mixing with what is melted.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>The subject of melting.</margin>
The **second element** <term>elementum secundum</term> is that which is necessary for a substance that can be mixed and melted, so that it may be melting within its own substance. When we later thought about and investigated how we might find something that, when thrown upon a melted metal, would adhere to it, mix with it, be submerged in it, and not ruin it, we found nothing among minerals except **sulfur** <term>sulphur</term> and, among the mixed substances, **arsenic** <term>arsenicum</term> <note>In this context, arsenic refers to arsenic-based minerals like orpiment or realgar, used to color or harden metals</note>. These, however, flee [evaporate] and do not stay, except for a very brief time when they are found beginning to proceed toward a connection with the metal. Therefore, we found no ingenious way except their **rectification** <term>rectificationem</term> <note>The process of purifying a substance or altering its properties, often to make it "fixed" so it does not evaporate under heat</note>, so that the power of adherence remains in them and the "burning" [combustibility] is destroyed. I have found, therefore, that because of the necessary burning, that which is evaporated by the fire—and by its own nature it is prone to evaporate quickly—is lost; and we found that the cause of adherence is the melting. Then, we considered the likeness it imitates and the proximity it has in nature with the metal; we looked into the natural principles. Thus, the **subject of melting** <term>subjectum liquefactionis</term> is a running moisture mixed with dry, earthy parts in which it moves when the fire dissolves them and does not...

<meta>This page continues the technical discourse on the properties of elemental qualities—specifically moisture and dryness—and how they react to fire. While the previous page focused on the practical "reddening" of quicksilver and sulfur, this page provides the underlying natural philosophy, explaining why some substances burn to ash while others turn into glass or vapor.</meta>

<page-num>978</page-num>

-> **A V I C E N N A** <-

It is possible for it to be moved by them because of the intensity of the mixture; and we have found the cause of **evaporation** <term>evaporatio</term> to be moisture that is not intensely mixed within it, but rather it is raised up from it and departs. And we have found the cause of **combustion** <term>adustio</term> <note>original: "adustio"; literally a burning or scorching, referring here to the chemical breakdown of a substance into ash</note> to be that the substance is already "cooked" <note>digested or processed by heat</note> and thoroughly mixed with dryness. This occurs so that it reaches the substance through the dryness mixed into it, because the moistures share in or exchange an excessive accidental heat when joined with fire, so that the substance is "fixed" for us until the destruction of the moisture is found. This happens when the fire is powerful enough to convert certain "waters" <note>liquid components</note> of the body, or the substance of the fire itself, either before or during evaporation. Then, the fire is separated or its dregs remain as ash—and this is what is called "burned." Indeed, when this evaporates, having already been converted, it turns into flame.

As for the power of this regarding **vitrification** <term>vitrificatio</term> <note>the process of turning a substance into glass through heat</note> and its indicative and essential causes, this is a matter that this book does not expand upon, but experiment bears witness to it. The rule is this: excessive moisture does not burn; rather, when heat first finds it, it is **sublimated** <term>sublimatio</term> <note>turned into vapor or raised to the top of a vessel</note> before any combustion can occur. But if the moisture is hidden within something and it is not its nature to evaporate—so that it remains drier and like ash—nothing of it is burned, as is seen in liquified bodies <note>metals in a molten state</note>.

Furthermore, when this is contained in the body of a plant or animal in which there is innate heat and a "mixable" power, then if it is cooked with the dry part so that it is not fully incorporated and becomes an ointment or oil, it is ignited or burned. Similarly, even when it is not an oil, it may become an intense mixture with the dry part, and despite all this, it is not emptied of its primary oiliness. For we see that if the combustible power is purged from it and its oil is destroyed so that only moisture remains in it, it liquefies or adheres to it, following what we shall say regarding the highest and most extreme estimation. 

I believe that the moisture in such bodies is not emptied out by the intense mixture with the dryness within them; thus, when fire moves the moisture toward evaporation, the dominant dryness and dregs are not separated. Instead, it flows and liquefies or becomes light, just as it is in **glass** <note>original: "vitro"</note>. If the moisture is dominant, it expands and evaporates so that the vapor is like smoke mixed with the dryness within it, and it is among those things that are not purged into pure water. Furthermore, after we have proven this by experiment, it was most frequent; indeed, they take the dryness whitened by "cooking" through sublimation. Therefore, the third point for us is that a substance is not destroyed by evaporation, nor is it diminished by evaporation, because its moisture and dryness are mixed with its [own] dryness. And when we persevere...

<page-num>979</page-num>
# ON THE CORRECT METHOD <note>original: "DE RE RECTA"</note>

<margin>Methods of purifying sulfur.</margin>
By working upon it, we shall destroy its "combustibility" <term>adustio</term> <note>the quality of being easily burned or charred, which alchemists sought to remove so the substance would remain stable in fire</note> and we have seen many ways to do this. One of these ways is roasting it with burning substances that cause a separation <note>original: "periurium"; likely a transcription error for "purgationem" (purification) or "permixtionem" (thorough mixing)</note>. Next is **sublimation** <term>sublimatio</term> <note>the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify substances</note>. For without doubt, during sublimation, that which is not burned is scorched and purified in a healthy way. If indeed any part of it is burned, we shall repeat the process until we find, at the end of the work, a **white sublimate** in which there is no mixture of combustion. When we project this upon silver, it will neither burn it nor corrupt it; this was certain to us through proofs, the explanation and recollection of which would be too long—namely, that this operation does not destroy its substance, its depth, or its adherence, and it does this with moisture more quickly than can be imagined. Just as the innate earthiness of bodies is removed through sublimation, so through the **dissolution** <term>solutio</term> of their substance is every impurity separated from them. Thus says Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the father of chemistry; his works were the "gold standard" for medieval alchemists</note>.

<margin>Combustion</margin>
**Combustion** <term>adustio</term>, however, occurs when the "substantial moisture" of a thing is mixed, burned, or corrupted. Since we have already destroyed that moisture, it is no longer burned; we have also dissolved a great deal of the superfluous moisture, for these things are congealed. Because of this, the superfluous and combustible moisture is destroyed, and there remains a moisture intensely mixed with dryness. For those moistures are congealed because they have been liquefied like oil over a fire.

<margin>Fixation</margin>
Therefore, after we gained knowledge and experience, we found that it adheres, and we found that it whitens that which is not white when that liquefaction is held so that it is not separated from it—either by "retainers" mixed with it or by the construction of the **head of the flasks** <term>capitis ampullarū</term> <note>the top part of a still or alembic, designed to trap vapors</note>, so that it finds no way to escape. Indeed, we knew this by reasoning before the experiment, and the experiment verified the reasoning: for a "white mixture" makes things white. After we found it adhering and appearing as it should, we attained what we desired.

<margin>Another method of sulfur preparation</margin>
And sometimes it is not sublimated; instead, we boil it in oil or water until the "fiery power" is separated from it and much of the moisture that overwhelms the dryness evaporates. What remains is the moisture contained within the dryness, which is not separated; rather, when it is purified and moved within it, it causes the substance to liquefy. Therefore, they do not delay when they are physically gathered in oil or water and presented over the fire.

## On the fixed substance.
### CHAPTER V.

We have sought the **fixed substance** <term>substantia fixa</term> <note>a material that remains stable and does not evaporate or "fly" when exposed to the heat of the furnace</note>, which is found among those things we have mentioned. We take this fixed substance and find it to be everything that does not flee from the fire. These include both bodies that can be melted and those that cannot. We found that all of these hindered us from our work; however, the melted ones are closer in similarity. Their condition improves while they remain bodies possessing a "conjoined liquefaction," for it is not possible to mix anything else into them. And when the parts that are able to flow are **sublimated** <note>turned into vapor and resolidified to purify them</note>, they become "fixed," making it possible for them to return to their state over the fire.

It is necessary, therefore, that we burn them and **calcine** them <term>calcinemus</term> <note>the process of heating a metal or mineral to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder or "calx"</note>. If it is possible to calcine them after combustion, let us do so until they become a powder that perhaps will not flow. In this way, the "specific form" <note>the essential nature or identity of a substance in Aristotelian philosophy</note> of these species will be destroyed, as **Aristotle** declared in his *Natural Hearing* <note>original: "auditu naturali"; this refers to Aristotle's *Physics*</note>. Since experiment destroys the specific form, when it reaches this state, it will be possible for us to achieve our intention through them.

We have seen, and we see clearly, that we should take **Moon** <note>the alchemical name for Silver</note> from Moon—which is better—or from lead. We take **Sun** <note>the alchemical name for Gold</note> from Sun—which is better—or from **Venus** <note>the alchemical name for Copper</note>. It is also possible for us to take a lime <term>calx</term> from the Moon, which is **white lead** <term>cerusa</term> <note>a white pigment made from lead</note>, and it will be one of the whitening agents. From the Sun, it will be a red powder like **cinnabar** <term>usifur</term> <note>specifically refers here to a red mercuric sulfide or a red lead pigment</note>, and it will be one of the reddening agents.

## On Composition.
### CHAPTER VI.

After the oil, the tincture, the lime, and all other whitening agents have reached the state of "white"; and the tincture, the oil, and all other reddening agents have reached the "red," it will be necessary for us to **compose** a mixture between them so that they become one single substance. This is not possible except through their "entry" and through their thorough mixing.

...and we now see in those things, by the methods of experience we have already used, that when they are mixed with water they do so vehemently, then they are dried, coagulated, and glued together. It follows that 
<margin>When the fixed flies with the volatile, or the reverse.</margin>
if the quantity of the volatile substance overcomes the quantity of the fixed, it will "fly" <note>evaporate or sublime</note> with it; and if it does not overcome it, it will be "fixed" <note>remain stable and solid</note> with it. And we have seen many things dissolved and coagulated, and their power remains in those things from which they are made, such as salt, saltiness, and **tragacanth** <term>dragantum</term> <note>a natural gum used as a binding agent</note>. And we know through many principles of natural science that it is possible for things of a slippery substance—whose roots are from earth and water—to be dissolved and made flowing. Then we know through other rules that when these aforementioned elixirs are dissolved, this dissolution does not prevent them from performing their fundamental operations; rather, there remains for us that power of theirs which we desire. For experiment bears witness to the belief of meditation. We have therefore seen that for this purpose, dissolution and flowing are most suitable, followed by a thickening so that, the union of the root having been made, it becomes one thing: stable, dyeing, penetrating, consolidating, and persevering. And we considered that when we use "contrition"—that is, the grinding/wearing down by means of 
<margin>Grinding that is done with water.</margin>
mixed hot waters, dissolved and blended through constant application—that this would take the place of dissolution. We therefore did the same things to experiment, and sometimes it was successful and sometimes it was not, either because of the weakness of the instruments, or a defect in the work, or because of particular 
<margin>He seems to reject the waters.</margin>
accidental things that are not understood. Therefore, our intention was directed toward these two chapters in the summary of the completion of the art of the elixir. Thus, with the praise of God, the sought-after intention arrived: the 
<margin>The roots of his art or materials.</margin>
**roots of the white** <note>the ingredients for the "White Elixir," used to transmute metals into silver</note> were: prepared **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>mercury</note>, whitened sulfur, the **calx** <term>calx corporis</term> <note>the powdery ash or oxide left after heating a metal</note> of the body, and their **ceruse** <term>cerusa</term> <note>white lead</note>; when these are joined and mixed, they become a complete elixir. And the **roots of the yellow** <note>the ingredients for the "Yellow" or "Citrine Elixir," used to transmute metals into gold</note> were: prepared sulfur, prepared quicksilver, whitened and fixed salt, and gold-calx. And it is better for that purpose if all these things are "rubified" <note>turned red through heat</note>. Then they are composed, and from them a complete elixir is made.

->*On Hair, Egg, and Blood.*<-

### C H A P T E R VII.

After we heard many times that it is possible for an elixir to be made from hair, egg, and blood, and many parts of animals, we began to experiment whether they might have any staying power or ability to leave an impression in liquefied metallic bodies. We found, therefore, that these things do not leave an impression themselves, but their smoke does; for the smoke itself is suspended in the bodies so that the silver begins to take on a yellow color, and if the ignited silver is marked when it is submerged in it, the impression is made.

We therefore knew that in these things there is a **tincture** <note>original: "tinctura"; the dyeing or transforming essence</note> and that in them there is a **suspension** <note>original: "suspensio"; likely referring to the state of being held in a fluid medium</note>. And we knew that the hair, blood, and eggs of false decoctions are coagulated from waters into salt. And we knew that when we wish to separate the tincture and the suspension from them, it is not possible unless it be done with fire and **sublimation** <note>the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note>, so that it does not dye <note>original: "tingat"</note>. And we knew that the first thing distilled from them is water, then oil, because the oil is more **fixed** <note>stable and resistant to heat</note> over the fire. We therefore distill these things with a subtle fire in a **cucurbit and alembic** <term>cucurbita & alembico</term> <note>the two parts of a traditional still: the lower boiling vessel and the upper cooling cap</note>. Thus, the water was distilled first, then the oil began to be distilled; we therefore distilled from that point on for as long as it took until they were finished and the dregs remained. These dregs we burned with fire for so long until there came forth a **fixed calx** <term>calx fixa</term> <note>a powdery residue that has been purified by fire and no longer reacts to heat</note> over the fire; thus, from it, a calx was produced for us. Then we knew that the tincture comes from the oil, so we rectified it. Then we boiled it in nothing else but its own water, since its water is hot and salty, and since it is congealed into **sal ammoniac** <term>sal armoniacum</term> <note>ammonium chloride, a pungent salt used as a flux in alchemy</note> by a gentle boiling, for as long as it took until we extracted its tincture. Then we took and boiled it in nothing else but its own water, etc. Then we took the oil and boiled it in waters tempered in sharpness until they purged it and whitened it, and removed the **combustion** <note>original: "adustionem"; the charred or burnt quality</note> from it; through this, liquefaction and suspension were achieved, and the burnt quality was destroyed from it. And we purged its calx for as long as it took until it became a white powder, and we found its water just as in minerals we find **quicksilver** <note>original: "arg. vi." or "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>, and its oil just like the **sulfur** in minerals, and its calx just as the calx in minerals. And the **elixir** <note>the transformative medicine or agent</note> joined together from these—just like the elixir which is from minerals—is truly more abundant, better, more widely acting, and more sublime.

<margin>Sublimation of Mercury ☿.</margin>
We mix it with salt and vitriol <note>original: "attramento"; likely green or blue vitriol used as a reagent</note>, afterward it is sublimated <note>the process of heating a solid until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note> from them many times. Indeed, every sublimation and binding occurs after distillation.

*Concerning Arsenic and Sulfur.* Regarding Arsenic and sulfur, it has seemed appropriate that they be ground strongly with iron filings and boiled in vinegar until they are dried out; then let them be roasted, and afterward sublimated. This should be repeated with salt, vitriol, talc, "new" lime, and "lesser" lime. And when they are bound by glass and burnt bronze <note>original: "ære usto"</note>, either individually or together, they are congealed like salt or crystal; and let the sublimation be repeated many times until they reach their end.

*Concerning the Oil of Hair.* Regarding the oil from hair, blood, and the rest: after its coagulation with a steady, non-boiling heat, let it be processed until it thickens. Then, to receive the tincture <note>the transforming color or essence</note> from it, let it be boiled in water in which talc or lime—a gentle nourishment—has already been boiled, for as long as it takes until its blackness departs from it and it is whitened.

## On Calcination.

### C H A P T E R  I X.

<margin>Calcination.</margin>
Indeed, bodies <note>refers to the seven metals</note> are processed when they are supported by sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum</term> <note>ammonium chloride, used as a powerful flux and cleansing agent</note> and vinegar, and when they are burned with caustic materials for so long until they allow for grinding with salt, sal ammoniac, and sulfur. Sometimes they are "fed" with quicksilver <note>mercury</note> until the quicksilver is sublimated away from them many times, until only a powder remains. <margin>Soaking.</margin> Then, that which is sought for the "white work" <note>the stage of creating silver</note> should be soaked with distilled salt-water and waxed, and left in the aludel <term>aludelle</term> <note>a series of pear-shaped pots used for subliming substances</note> continually until it becomes a substance that does not separate into parts. And that which is sought for the "yellow work" <note>the stage of creating gold</note> should be soaked with the water of vitriols—either one by one or joined together—with the redness of sulfur and other things, and with oil of eggs; let its roasting be maintained until it is reddened, so that it becomes a powder that does not separate.

### C H A P T E R  X.

The easier method which we have seen for resolving these things is the conversion of the nature of the species into substances that naturally accept resolution, such as salts and vitriols.

And we have seen that the strongest among them is sal ammoniac <term>Sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to help dissolve metals and volatile substances</term>. Indeed, we have resolved it and performed the constant soaking <term>imbibition: the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it is saturated</term> of the waxed material by grinding it and roasting it with heat, until the whole is congealed into sal ammoniac. And this is done so that a certain quantity of dissolved sal ammoniac may be poured over it; then let us leave the body itself until it is dried. What comes from this we place in a transfer-bag within the vessel-sanctuary <note>original: "sacrarium"; here referring to a specific type of alchemical heating chamber or specialized vessel</note>, which is a type of vessel for infiltration, and we approach it with a gentle fire. When it begins to smoke, let us remove it, then soak it, and afterward repeat this ten times. Then let us repeat the soaking again, doing this until it is "waxed" <term>ceration: a process where a substance is softened until it melts like wax on a hot plate without smoking</term>, which is when it liquefies upon a glowing iron. Then let it be dissolved into water until no trace of it remains, through twenty to thirty soakings. For if we proceed by these paths, it will be resolved within a period between forty days and three months. 

When the waters are resolved, we shall gather them and "bury" them until they are thoroughly mixed. ## CONCERNING THE ELIXIR.

This elixir <term>Elixir: the transformative substance of alchemy, believed to be capable of changing the properties of metals</term> colors by means of its own tincture <term>tincture: the concentrated essence or "soul" of a substance that imparts color and quality</term>, it is submerged or integrated by its own oil, and it is fixed <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated</term> by its own lime <term>calx: the powdery residue left after a metal or mineral has been burned; it represents the "body" or solid foundation of the matter</term>. Indeed, the oil is the agent that gathers the water and the very subtle tincture together. And quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury, viewed as the "messenger" or carrier that moves the transformative power through the metal</term> is that which carries the tincture; when the aforementioned oil is deeply infused along with the dyeing lime, it carries the tincture deep into the substance along with it. When the lime is fixed, the rest of the mixture is fixed with it because of the intensity of their blending. The archetype of lime is the element of earth. Furthermore, the white work <note>original: "album"; referring to the Albedo, a stage of purification and whitening in the alchemical process</note> is completed in three cycles <term>wheels: "rotis" in Latin, referring to the repetitive rotations of the alchemical process, such as distillation or circulation</term> in which there is no fire <note>this may refer to "cold" digestion or the use of gentle, indirect heat rather than a literal flame</note>. And the red work <note>original: "rubeum"; the Rubedo, the final stage of the alchemical process representing perfection</note> is completed in four cycles.

# DECLARATION OF THE STO-
## NE OF THE PHYSICIAN AVICENNA
### to his son Aboali.

My son Aboali <note>Aboali: Abu Ali ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna (c. 980–1037), the famous Persian physician whose name was frequently attached to later alchemical texts to lend them authority</note>, understand what I tell you regarding the knowledge 
of the stone. My son, where the Philosophers say in 
their books "Take sulphur and orpiment" <term>orpiment: "auripigmentum," a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral; alchemists used it as a code for various volatile substances</term>, 
it does not enter into our mastery <term>mastery: "magisterium," the secret process or "Great Work" of creating the Philosophers' Stone</term>. But they 
named sulphur and orpiment while explaining the 
Stone of the Philosophers, for within that stone the sulphur and 
arsenic <note>original: "arsenicum"</note> of the Philosophers lie hidden or are concealed. And indeed the Phi-
losophers say: it is a stone and not a stone, and it is worthless in the courtyards, and 
cast out in the streets it is trodden under the feet of men, and by any 
poor person it can be acquired; and it is sulphur that is not sulphur, and 
it is orpiment that is not orpiment, and it is a hen’s 
egg, a toad <note>original: "buffo"; a common alchemical metaphor for the "black stage" of matter or a poisonous, earthly substance</note>, human blood, hair—and they did not speak such 
names except to hide the mastery; and know for 
certain that the Philosophers cared for no names, except 
one name, and one action: namely, to cook the stone and 
to bring forth its soul. For their stone is always one, in which 
they expect every good thing, and there is no other in this world 
which is of such power and effect besides this stone. This, there-
fore, is the stone and not a stone, without which nature performs nothing, whose 
name is Living Mercury <term>Living Mercury: "Mercurius vivus" or quicksilver; in alchemy, this is often the "secret" mercury that has been purified and "animated" for the work</term>; yet the Philo-
sophers have named or called it by many names, 
whose names cannot be numbered because of the nature of its excellence. 
This is truly the Stone of the Philosophers, and there is no other besides it, 
which receives and drinks the work, from which every body appears. And 
this mastery does not belong except to Kings and those of higher rank and those filled 
with riches, because this mastery is eternal; and for one who does not have 
riches, how shall he work? For it is proper for the practitioner to have 60 
pounds <note>original: "℔," the symbol for the libra or pound</note> of pure Mercury—that is, quicksilver that is not adulterated—at the least, for the 
purpose of extracting its moisture to complete the whole work <note>original: "op^a," abbreviation for "opera"</note>, 
because the entire mastery is in the vapor. My son, now fools come 
daily and work just as they find in books regarding sul-
phur and arsenic, and regarding mercury <note>original: "☿," the symbol for the planet and metal Mercury</note> through sublimations, calcinations 
of bodies perfect and imperfect, and through the dissolv-
ing of various waters, salts, and vinegar, and through coagulations 
and fixations, and through amalgamations, and they cannot 
reach true perfection; and it is no wonder, for those idiots

<page-num>987</page-num>

# OF THE PHYSICIAN’S STONE.

...they do not understand the mention of the Philosophers, and they always say that the mastery <term>mastery: "magisterium," the secret alchemical process for creating the Stone</term> is not true, and that these Philosophers err as liars. Therefore, my son, I have composed this chapter and illuminated the blind and opened the treasures and chains; I will make the foolish understand what they did not understand, and I have loosened the bindings of words. I have told you, my son, with the truth of God, the secret of the Philosophers and their intention, and therefore I command you that you give this book to no one except your son, and your son to his son, and so from generation to generation, and this only to the wiser among them. And know, my son, that I have done wrong in that I revealed to you the purity of that gift. You shall not reveal this holy, laudable work. And I tell you, my son, in truth that the Philosophers did not work with other things, except with the "blood of hair" and "eggs" metaphorically <note>original: "exemplariter"</note>—that is, they worked with nothing except the four elements. And it is to be noted today concerning the preparation of the four elements, which stood in warm horse manure <term>horse manure: "fimo equino"; used as a source of gentle, steady heat for digestion and fermentation</term> as was necessary. And first distill, and that which first comes out, keep aside, because that is water. Repeat the water by distillation, and that which will be distilled, keep, and that is simple; place it under manure and keep it, and that which will remain in the bottom of the flask <term>flask: "cucurbitæ"; the lower vessel of a distilling apparatus</term>, keep aside because it is earth.

**Definition of the science of the secrets of natural philosophy.** It is the extraction of water from the earth, and the conversion or reduction of that same body upon its own prepared earth. Indeed, this earth putrefies <term>putrefies: "putrefcit"; the "blackening" stage where matter decomposes before it can be purified</term> and is washed with its own water; when it is or has been made clean by the help of God, the whole mastery will be directed. For first, one strives to dissolve the earth so that it may have a subtle nature in its own way, which happens when the qualities of the water have overcome it. Then, when the earth strives to condense the water so that it may be fixed with it and withstand every fire, this happens when the qualities of the earth have overcome it; since the foundation of this art and the beginning of the work is the resolution of the body into water, which the Philosophers call corruption or putrefaction, without which the circular transmutation of metals into one another does not occur. For the corruption of one is the generation of another. Because the principles of generation and corruption are the same.

The Philosophers’ Stone arises from a vile thing into a most precious treasure, namely, from the seed of Sol <note>Sol: the Sun, the alchemical symbol for gold</note> cast into the womb <note>original: "matrice"</note> of Mercury through union; that is, through the first mixing. And this is its proximate matter from which it is drawn out. Truly, the most immediate is the seminal fluid separated by the act of generation from the individual parts of each parent—namely the body and Venus <note>Venus: represented here by the symbol $\unicode{x2640}$, usually signifying copper or the feminine principle</note>. Because only the radical humors of the bodies are the essential parts of the stone itself. And also, from two beings in nature, one does not become one unless they are related to each other as the acting and the <margin>except <unclear>rarely</unclear></margin> passive, or unless one becomes the potentiality of the other.

# THE DECLARATION OF AVICENNA

Therefore, the elixir of the wise and the medicine for perfecting and transforming every imperfect thing must be drawn from the clearest species which take their origin from the first mineral fountains, and not from any others. For the Philosophers command us to take crude, clean, sincere, and upright elements and to cook them over a light fire, saying that if it is done otherwise, it will profit nothing. They also say: take things pure, fresh, close, and better from their minerals, and exalt them to the summits of mountains or to the stars of heaven <note>This refers to sublimation or distillation, where the substance is "raised" into the upper part of the vessel</note>, and also reduce them to their roots, and thus the whole mastery <term>mastery: "magisterium," the secret alchemical process for creating the Stone</term> of the clarifications and fixations of the thing is accomplished. And you who seek to usefully compose the tincture <term>tincture: a concentrated substance capable of dyeing or transforming metals</term> of the wise, know the mineral roots, preparing your work from them. Because once the qualities of the bodies and the nature of their principle and governance are known, the work is easily perfected.

<margin>*</margin>The medicine itself is elicited from physical things that are most suitable in nature. For it is highly necessary to take the tincture primarily from those things in which it most consists. It is, moreover, found in bodies as well as in the spirits <term>spirits: volatile substances, such as mercury or sulfur, that can evaporate or "fly"</term> themselves according to nature, since they are discovered to be of a single nature. But it is elicited from bodies with more difficulty, while from spirits or quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"</note> it is elicited more easily and closely—though not more perfectly—which is the tincture itself or medicine of bodies; for which reason, there is the white and the red. They proceed from one root, with no body of another kind of offspring intervening. For there is one stone and one operation for it, which is digested and perfected successively in one vessel, by one fire, and a single cooking <term>cooking: "coctione," the process of slow heating and ripening the alchemical matter</term> into white and red non-burning sulfur.

It is necessary, however, that they lead out the form of the Great Elixir from the power of its nearby matter in which it naturally consists. But it lies hidden and concealed in that same viscous thickness of the elements; therefore it is called the "vegetable stone," "stone and not a stone," and "original and primordial vapor," because it is in the making—that is, in the way of digestion—not yet fixed by nature, nor finished in the specific being of a perfected metal. And it relates to the cause of common mercury <note>original: "☿ vulgi" or "mercurius vulgi"</note> just as rennet relates to milk, and it is known through that which it coagulates. Since before the specific forms of the metals can exist, the temperaments of sulfur and quicksilver must pre-exist, along with their purification and alteration.

It is also expedient that the elements of the stone be of the same kind and not different, otherwise they would not have mutual action and passion toward each other. Since one would not tint the other if something foreign were introduced, because a thing is not suitable unless it is closer to it by its own nature. To which, if anything strange is added, it stains—

# OF THE PHYSICAL STONE

<note>original: "LAPIDIS PHYSICI"</note>

...the work is corrupted, nor will that which is sought by the craftsman be produced from it; instead, another effect will follow which does not exist within the care of nature and art. For no true generation occurs except from things that are compatible in their nature.

It is necessary, finally, that the corrupting, disfiguring, and combustible coarseness of the composition of the elements be deleted through ingenious preparation. The stony, earthy, and useless density must be divided from the metallic substance before a univocal and perfect complexion of the elements themselves can be made. This is achieved by roasting, grinding, and digesting <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the application of gentle, consistent heat over a long period, similar to how a stomach processes food</note> patiently and gently until the substance is reduced to its simplest form and into a true **fifth essence** <term>fifth essence: the "quintessence," or the purest, most concentrated part of a substance that remains after the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) have been purified</term>. This is, namely, a most simple and pure fiery entity that does not burn; it is indeed nothing other than pure natural heat infused into its **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: the fundamental life-giving fluid thought to exist within all matter, maintaining its vitality</term>. For fire, continually cooking by its very function, unites homogeneous parts, while it marks and consumes the heterogeneous parts as fuel, turning them into ash.

The Philosophers further desire that the "manifest be hidden and the hidden of the thing be made manifest." This means that the earthy, sulfurous, and flammable density appearing on the surface of the mixture must be removed by the skill of the artist. That intrinsic, pure, and splendid substance—planted in the root of the thing from nature's beginning—should be brought into the manifest through the "corruption" and stripping away of its outward accidents. This experience is easy and possible because the intrinsic part of a thing is the opposite of its extrinsic quality; the study of contraries is the same, as they seem to shine more brightly when placed near one another.

Furthermore, the **mortification** <term>mortification: the process of "killing" a substance to strip it of its volatile qualities, often resulting in a black color (nigredo)</term> of volatile things so that they are fixed and do not flee from the fire, and the **vivification** <term>vivification: the "bringing back to life" or sublimation of a substance into a higher, more potent state</term> of the dead or fixed things lying there, is undoubtedly necessary. For he who knows how to mortify, and how to resuscitate after death, is a master of this doctrine; he who is ignorant of this should withdraw his hand from the work and not weary his mind with things he cannot reach. You indeed revive those things whose species and spirit you restore through elevation. For when the dead rise, they are perpetual, and they die no more, but are glorified to an immortal life that will endure without end <note>The author uses the language of Christian resurrection to describe how chemicals, once "fixed" so they no longer evaporate, become "immortal" or stable under heat</note>.

The singular genius of the Art of Philosophy does not seek, as the unrefined common folk <note>original: "rude vulgus"</note> usually object, to make gold or silver from scratch. Nature is already accustomed to generating these in the bowels of the earth. Instead, the craftsman works only organically and instrumentally, eliciting the form of gold and silver from matter already disposed for this and giving motion to nature, so that through the temperate cooking of the art...

# THE DECLARATION OF AVICENNA
<note>original: "AVICENNÆ DECLARATIO"</note>

<margin>
+
r. 6.
</margin>
...[that which was] stirred up may be led from potency into act. For although the **Philosopher's Stone** naturally contains within it the tincture which was created perfectly in the belly of the earth, it does not transform <note>original: *tingit*, literally "dyes" or "tinges," referring to the alchemical transformation of color and substance</note> by itself in act, nor is the **Elixir** made from it, unless it is moved by the industry and operation of the craftsman. And nature works with the craftsman himself serving as its minister. From which it is not doubted that the entire effect of its power consists in the practice of the exercise. In the artificial decoction <note>the process of heating or "cooking" a substance to extract its essence</note> of imperfect or incomplete bodies, it is necessary that the external and moderating heat of the fire be so proportioned that the internal power—acting and perfecting—is not smothered or overcome in any way, etc. This is the force of the most subtle **sulfur**, pure and simple, fiery but not burning, which is called the **Light of Lights** <note>original: *lumen luminum*</note>, because it is the form and splendor of all metals; it illuminates all bodies, since it is the light and tincture illustrating and perfecting every body. And if the craftsman of this mastery does not know this light, he wanders through many devious paths like one walking in darkness, because of his distance from the truth and unity of this science. For what is good is done in one way, but what is evil in many ways, with almost infinite errors. For once one absurdity is granted, many more frequently follow.

If the active principles are well applied to the passive, and the passive to the active, so that they best embrace one another, and if the heat of the fire is proportioned in the required manner, as has been said: then, according to the Philosophers, there will be no difference between the digestion of nature and art, since digestion is a perfection brought about by natural and proper heat from the opposite passive things—that is, from contrary qualities or elements. For the **transforming Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius tingens*</note> is not found in act upon the earth unless it is taken from liquefied and clean bodies <gloss>us</gloss>—not by a common liquefaction indeed, but by that through which the **male and female** are united inseparably in a true marriage openly over the fire. Because only from the male and the female does true generation occur.

The perfectly completed **Elixir**, or the **Tincture of the Sages**, acts as the form and most powerful agent in respect to metals diminished in their operation, provided that it is mixed with them once they have been prepared as its proximate matter in a state of flux. For then it completes, fixes, and perfects them, and colors them with an invariable dye that always remains even in the harshness of the fire. And this is the true medicine of men and metals, gladdening and transforming; nor, after God, is there any other which puts poverty to flight and expels all listlessness <note>original: *languorem*; can also mean weakness or disease</note> from human bodies, preserving them in health, to whose...

# ON THE PHYSICAL STONE
<note>original: "LAPIDIS PHYSICI"</note>

...[to which] knowledge very few physicians of our time have arrived.

<margin>
<unclear>preparing</unclear>
<unclear>preparing</unclear>
</margin>
In matter that is poorly prepared, it is not fitting to work anything; for **proportion** is the Treasure of this matter and the omen of its completion. Indeed, the repetition of proportion is the **Secret** <note>original: *Arcanum*</note> of the art. Preparation is, in fact, the act that disposes the matter toward the boundary of motion or perfection, through which imperfect things are brought to the specific boundary of a metal’s essence; and this is achieved through **motion, light, and heat**. However, when heat is lacking, motion is lacking, because every action—whether natural or artificial—has its own motion and due time, in which it is perfected or finished over a span of greater or lesser time, because nothing acts beyond its own species. Therefore, when the specific form arrives, it completes the work and causes the motion to cease, and the agent is then forced to be separated from the matter.

Furthermore, for there to be a true, total, and perfect mixing of things—which is the union of altered substances capable of being mixed—an identity of natures is required in the proportion and equality of **subtlety and purity**; otherwise, they would not be mixed through their smallest parts <note>original: *per minima*, referring to a microscopic or atomic level of blending</note>, nor would they embrace each other mutually before they had been sufficiently prepared. For the **spirit and soul** of the stone are not united with the body except by the **white color** <note>original: *albo colore*, referring to the stage of Albedo or "Whiteness" in the Great Work</note>. In the joining of the spirit and the body, the craftsman’s entire intention must be focused, because until the whiteness is reached, the corruption of moisture and the **dominion of the woman** <note>The "woman" represents the feminine principle, often identified with Mercury or volatile moisture, which must be stabilized</note> thrives. But in the true whiteness, this corruption is ended and consumed, and then thereafter the **husband** <note>The "husband" represents the masculine principle, Sulfur, which provides stability and "fixity"</note> begins to dominate his wife, decorating her with his own stable color.

It is necessary only that bodies which are thick by nature be thinned and refined until they become spiritual, light, and clean. Conversely, spirits—which are rare <note>thin or volatile</note>—should be embodied and thickened, until they remain with the bodies even in the fire. For the ancient Sages asserted: **unless you make the bodies bodiless and the spirits bodily**, you have not yet found the way and the rule of operating. This means rarefying that which is thick and lightening that which is heavy, since everything subtle is more worthy than the thick, just as everything rare is worthier than the dense. For heavy things cannot be raised higher except by the company of light things, nor can light things be held down and **fixed** below except by the power of heavy things. The body does not act upon the spirit, but only the spirit acts upon the body by penetrating it; therefore, so that they may act and be acted upon in turn, let the bodies be **calcined** <note>reduced to powder through heat</note> and washed by frequent watering with their own "water." Let the spirits, however, be cleansed by **sublimation** <note>the process of vaporizing a solid and collecting its purified deposit</note> unto the ultimate degree of purity.

<vocab>matter, preparation, motion, heat, species, mixture, spirit, soul, stone, whiteness, bodies, let them be calcined, sublimation</vocab>

# AVICENNA’S DECLARATION
<note>original: "AVICENNÆ DECLARATIO"</note>

<margin>
<unclear>Matter...</unclear>
<unclear>water...</unclear>
</margin>
...[until they] come to their proper degree. Which, once dissolved or mixed with water, are inseparably united and remain so, such that the violence of fire cannot separate them hereafter. Because every kind of **calcined** <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or reduce it to powder</note> substance is more fixed and easier to dissolve than one without calcination; without this, the sulfurous <term>combustibility</term> <note>original: *ustibilitas*</note> cannot be removed, nor can we reach the inward purification of the bodies without it.

The spirit in this art is twofold: namely, the **preparing** and the **dyeing** <note>or tinting</note>. The <term>preparing spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus praeparans*</note> is that which putrefies, breaks down, dissolves, and reduces bodies back to their **prime matter** <note>the fundamental, formless substance from which all things are made</note>; it contains within itself a rectifying moisture by which the bodies are soaked, washed, cleansed, and set right. For it is the washing-bath of the purifications and the antidote without which the true **tincture** <note>the permanent, transformative color or essence of the alchemist’s goal</note> is not completed. But the <term>dyeing spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritus tingens*</note> is extracted from clean bodies through the benefit and power of the preparing spirit. For one must choose that which is uniform and common to both the "lights of the world" <note>referring to the Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver)</note>, which is sulfur from sulfur and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*, literally "living silver"</note> from quicksilver, and one quicksilver from two quicksilvers. This is called "the extracted" by men, because by human ingenuity it is drawn out from the "man" and "woman" <note>the masculine/sulfurous and feminine/mercurial principles</note> of the art, through the mediation of solution and putrefaction.

No water is suitable for the bodies in their dissolution except that which is coagulated with them while remaining through the cooking; and there is none other except a clean, viscous mineral water, clear like a tear from the eye or the dew of May. There is nothing else in the world that could stand in its place or take its role. It is called by the Philosophers the <term>water of life</term> <note>original: *aqua vitæ*</note>, the sharpest vinegar, the strongest water in the whole world, divine water, and <term>permanent water</term> <note>original: *aqua permanens*</note> after it is governed by maturing. Yet, it cannot remain permanent without its body with which it was joined by a gentle fire and made into one union. Just as accidents cannot exist without substances, so spirits do not remain in the burning of fire unless they are joined to fixed bodies. 

Therefore, when the Philosophers in their books make mention of <term>azoth</term> <note>a universal solvent or the essential spirit of mercury</note>, quicksilver, mercurial water, clean sulfur water, <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>literally "strong water," usually referring to nitric acid, though here a philosophical version</note>, living water, sharp water, and other liquids that dissolve bodies, they were not speaking of common things simply as they are given by nature. Instead, they intended to be understood as speaking of the moist vapors extracted from the **Philosophers' Stone** by ingenuity. They say that the entire preparation of the stone is done with its own water from the beginning of the work to the end, without the addition of any foreign thing. This is the medium for joining the tinctures, which purifies and illuminates their inward filth, protecting them from the burning of a violent fire.

<summary>In this declaration, Avicenna explains the dual nature of alchemical spirits (preparing and dyeing) and emphasizes that "philosophical water" is not a common substance but a refined vapor extracted from the matter itself.</summary>
<keywords>calcination, spiritus praeparans, spiritus tingens, quicksilver, aqua vitae, aqua permanens, azoth, aqua fortis, prime matter</keywords>
