<page-num>993</page-num>
<header>->OF THE PHYSICIAN’S STONE<-</header>

...by defending, but it is difficult to strike the middle path <note>original: *medium tangere*; a reference to the alchemical "Golden Mean" or perfect balance required in the work</note>. Therefore, by various processes entirely alien to the work of nature, it happens that for the most part, one wanders wrongly through extremes. That which does not enter and is not mixed does not alter nor effect transformation in the bodies of metals. It is necessary, therefore, that the **tincture** <note>the transformative essence or "medicine" of the stone</note> or the medicine itself, having been reduced and made capable of transforming bodies, enters and penetrates into the very depths of the thing to be changed. It must be like a **fixed oil** <note>an oil that does not evaporate when heated</note>, flowing easily over a glowing plate of some metal without producing smoke. It must melt or liquefy before the flight of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum* (mercury); "flight" refers to its tendency to evaporate quickly when heated</note>, dyeing the metal and making it permanent and fixed over the fire without any evaporation. Furthermore, no violence of fire should be able to squeeze out or separate the tincture from the bodies it has transmuted, until they have reached the perfected stability of <term>Lunar</term> <note>Silver-like</note> or <term>Solar</term> <note>Gold-like</note> bodies.

The wise are further advised here that no <term>projection</term> <note>the act of casting the alchemical medicine onto a base metal to transform it</note> of any tincture should be made upon unpurified bodies, unless their due purging precedes it. Otherwise, after the strict tests are applied, the bodies transmuted without preparation would be destroyed upon the trial of fire, and the tincture would likewise be separated from them. For the intention of this art is nothing other than to attribute the nobility of the superior metals to the inferior ones. And because every tincture proceeds from its own likeness among the metals to be dyed, it cannot come from any other things whatsoever that did not draw their origin from the pure substance of <term>quicksilver</term> and <term>sulfur</term>. It is also a common principle that the matter of all metals is very closely related; among things that share a common symbol in their matter and natural powers, transmutation into one another is easy. Their differences are judged only by which is more purified and better "digested" <note>in alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow maturation or cooking of a substance through gentle heat</note>. Therefore, let the dregs be cleansed, and let the undigested be better matured; in this way, through the steps of preparation, the corrupting accidents <note>external or non-essential qualities that mar the metal</note> will be removed from them. For only when their pure metallic substance remains, incorrupt, can they be converted into the species of a perfect metal. Indeed, the actions of active agents only take hold in a subject that is already predisposed for them.

There are only three species found in mines that are fruitful for the perfection of the <term>dyeing stone</term> <note>the Philosopher's Stone in its role as a color-changer</note>. When these are duly prepared, the entire benefit of this art is achieved: namely, the <term>Solar stone</term> <note>Gold or a gold-like mineral substance</note> in which there is pure **sulfur**, a pure red that does not burn; and the <term>Mercurial stone</term> <note>Mercury or a mercury-like mineral</note>, which is intermediate and encompasses both natures. These species, therefore, you shall firmly hide from the ignorant and the unworthy. Permit the fools to wander by laboring in every other kind of thing; they shall not arrive at the effect of this sublime mastery...

# AVICENNA’S DECLARATION OF THE PHYSICIAN’S STONE

...until the <term>Sun and Moon</term> <note>original: *Sol & Luna*; alchemical code for Gold and Silver, or the masculine and feminine principles of matter</note> are reduced into one body, which is impossible to achieve before the divine will. <page-num>995</page-num>

# AVICENNA ON THE CON-
## GELATION AND BINDING
### of stones.

Pure earth does not become stone, because it does not create continuity, but rather discontinuity; for the prevailing dryness within it does not permit it to be <term>bound together</term> <note>original: *conglutinari*; the process of sticking together like glue</note>. Stones are formed in two ways: by binding and by <term>freezing</term> <note>original: *congelando*; in this context, it refers to the solidification of liquids into solids, not necessarily through cold</note>. In some, indeed, earth is dominant; in others, however, water. Sometimes first the mud is dried, and something is formed which is intermediate between mud and stones, and then it becomes stone; mud, however, is more suited to this transformation if it is viscous, for that which is viscous is connective. Also, on the banks of the <term>Geon</term> <note>original: *Geon*; the Gihon River, one of the four rivers of Paradise. In medieval geography, it was often identified with the Nile or the Oxus</note>, earth has been seen that appears to be converted into stones in the space of 33 years. 

Stones are also made from water in two ways: one is when water falling drop by drop is frozen <note>a description of the formation of stalactites and stalagmites</note>; the other is when something descends from running water which settles on the surface of the bottom of that water and becomes stone. For there are certain places upon which poured waters are converted into stones, which are of various colors; and waters which are not frozen when taken up from above, are frozen if they are poured near their own bed, and they become stones. We know, therefore, that in the earth there is that <term>mineral power</term> <note>original: *vis illa mineralis*</note> which freezes waters. 

Therefore, the principles of stones are either made from a muddy or viscous substance, or from a substance in which water prevails, which is frozen by a certain mineral virtue; or earth prevails in it, causing it to coagulate. In the same way <term>sal armoniac</term> <note>original: *sal armoniacum*; ammonium chloride, a volatile salt used in alchemy to clean metals and encourage chemical reactions</note> is frozen, but the earthy power is not sufficient to change it into salt; rather, heat assists it. For the arriving heat coagulates it by a hidden virtue; and perhaps it is made from cold, dry earth and from water, and thus earth [is formed] when the qualities of earth prevail over it, and vice-versa. 

There is, however, a certain thing which someone of ingenuity uses when they wish to coagulate a dry thing, which is composed of two waters and is called <term>Virgin’s Milk</term> <note>original: *lac virginis*; in alchemical practice, this usually refers to a milky white liquid produced by mixing solutions of lead or mercury, used as a powerful reagent for "fixing" substances</note>, which is its most certain effect. Stones are therefore made from mud by the heat of the sun, or from water coagulated by a dry earthy virtue, or from dried hot water. Similarly, certain vegetables and certain animals are also converted into stones by a certain <term>stony mineral virtue</term> <note>original: *virtute quadam minerali lapidificativa*</note>, and this happens in a stony place, or by some sudden discordant power which comes out of the earth at the hour of an earthquake, which converts what it encounters in that hour into stones; this transformation occurs in the bodies of animals and vegetables, and is as near as the transformation of waters. It is, however, impossible that any <term>complexioned thing</term> <note>original: *complexionatum*; a biological body composed of a specific balance of the four elements</note> should be entirely converted into a single element, because elements and those things composed of elements [transf...]

...changed into one another, they pass into that which is dominant. Wherefore, that which falls into salt-flats becomes salt; and that which falls into fire becomes fire, though some do so more quickly and others more slowly, according to the power of the active forces and the resistance of the passive ones. There is a place in Arabia which colors all bodies within it with its own color. Bread placed near a <term>torrent</term> <note>original: *toratem*, likely a transcription error for *torrentem* (a rushing stream)</note> was converted into stone, yet it still retained its original color. Such things are wonders because they happen rarely, yet their causes are manifest. Often, however, stones are also made from fire when it is extinguished, because it frequently happens that earthy and stony bodies fall with <term>lightning flashes</term> <note>original: *coruscationibus*; Avicenna is describing the phenomenon of meteorites, which were historically associated with thunderbolts</note>, because the fire becomes cold and dry upon its extinction. And in Persia, aerial bodies also fall with lightning, similar to hooked arrows; they cannot be melted, but are forced by their internal moisture to evaporate into smoke through fire until only ash remains. There also fell at <term>Lurgeam</term> <note>original: *Lurgeam*; likely referring to Jurjan (Gorgan) in modern-day Iran, where a famous iron meteorite fell in 1021 AD</note> a piece of iron weighing one hundred <term>marks</term> <note>a medieval unit of weight</note>, which because of its hardness was almost unbreakable. A part of it was sent to the Ruler, who commanded that swords be made from it, but it was unbreakable and impossible to forge. The Arabs say, however, that <term>Germanic swords</term> <note>original: *enses Alemanici*; referring to high-quality swords from the Germanic regions, highly prized in the medieval world</note>, which are the best, are made from this iron. When that mass fell, it sometimes rebounded from the earth like a ball, because it was composed of tiny pieces clinging to one another, about the size of large millet grains. A similar process occurs among terrestrial things. In this way, therefore, stones are made; their generation will either be sudden, through a great heat reaching oily mud, or gradually over a long period of time.

### *On the cause of mountains.*

### CHAPTER II.

Mountains also are made sometimes from an essential cause, and sometimes from an accidental cause. From an essential cause, such as when the earth is elevated by a <term>violent movement of the earth</term> <note>an earthquake</note> and becomes a mountain. From an accidental cause, such as when a deep excavation happens because of winds or the flow of water, occurring gradually until a vast depth is created. Thus, a great prominence emerges next to it, and this is the chief cause of mountains. There are also certain lands that are soft, and some that are hard. The soft ones are carried away by water-flows and winds, while the hard ones remain, and thus a prominence is formed. Just as the generation of mountains occurs, so does the generation of stones, because the water-flow continually brought viscous mud to them, which over a great length of time is dried and becomes stone; and it is not unlikely that there is a <term>mineralizing power</term> <note>original: *vis mineralis*; a theoretical force in medieval science believed to transform matter into minerals</note> converting waters into stones. And for this reason, there are found in many stones certain <term>parts of aquatic animals</term> <note>a remarkably early and accurate recognition of fossils as the remains of living creatures</note> and others. <summary>Avicenna describes the formation of stones through elemental dominance and "mineralizing power," citing meteorites in Persia and Jurjan as evidence. He also provides an advanced geological explanation for mountains, attributing them to earthquakes and the erosion of soft soil around harder rock, while identifying fossils as remains of aquatic life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the text traditionally attributed to Aristotle but authored by Avicenna (*Ibn Sina*). It transitions from explaining how geological forces like tides and erosion form mountains and stones to a formal classification of mineral substances into four categories: stones, fusible substances, sulfurs, and salts.</meta>

<page-num>997</page-num>
->On the Solidification of Stones<-
Rrr 3

stones have been formed, as it were, over long periods of time, as we said before, provided they are not eroding. However, the muddy substances found on high ground do not consist of that original stony matter; rather, they are made of material worn away from mountains, or they are earthy, or some other substance brought by waters along with mud and plants. These become mixed with the mud of the mountain, or perhaps they are the ancient mud of the sea, which acts as a single substance because part of it becomes stone and part does not. Instead, it is softened and dissolved by some dominant quality. It is the <term>retreat and advance</term> <note>original: *recessus & accessus*; referring to the tidal movements and the long-term changes in sea levels that ancient geologists believed shaped the earth's surface</note> of the sea that hollows out certain places and raises others; at one time it covered the entire earth, and from that it wore away soft materials and left the hard ones behind, piling them up in certain places. The soft materials gathered by the sea were dried out when they were cut off from the water and were eventually turned into mountains.

---

### *Of the four species of mineral bodies.*

### CHAPTER III.

Mineral bodies are divided into four species: namely, into stones, <term>liquefiable substances</term> <note>original: *liquefactiva*; substances that can be melted or fused, typically metals</note>, sulfurous substances, and salts. Some of these have a <term>loose substance</term> <note>original: *raræ substantiæ*; literally "thin" or "porous," referring to a weak internal structure</note> and a weak composition, while others have a strong substance; some are <term>ductile</term> <note>original: *ductibilia*; meaning they can be hammered or drawn out into wires or sheets without breaking</note> and some are not. Among those with a weak substance, some are salts, which are those that quickly liquefy from moisture, such as <term>Alum</term> <note>original: *Alumen*</note>, <term>Vitriol</term> <note>original: *Calcamentum*; likely a transcription error for *Chalcantum*, a sulfate of copper or iron</note>, and <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> <note>original: *Sal Armoniacum*; ammonium chloride</note>. Others are oily and do not liquefy easily by moisture alone, such as sulfur and <term>Orpiment</term> <note>original: *Auripigmentum*; a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>. However, <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver"</note> belongs to the second group, even though it is the foundational element of ductile metals, or similar to certain ductile ones. All things that can be melted are ductile, and for the most part, things that are ductile can be melted, though they do not soften except with great force. The matter of ductile things is a watery substance mixed with an earthy substance in a strong mixture, and one cannot be separated from the other. Its watery substance is frozen with cold after the action of heat upon it, which is <term>epthesis</term> <note>original: *epthesis*; a Latinized Greek term used by Avicenna to describe a "cooking" or "boiling" process that thickens a substance through heat</note>. An example can be seen in wine, which does not freeze because of its oiliness, and therefore it is not ductile. Stones, however, among mineral substances, are materially watery, but they are not frozen by water alone, but also with a dryness that alters both the wateriness and the earthiness. There is no overly oily moisture in them, and therefore they cannot be hammered out; and because their solidification comes from dryness, they are not easily dissolved for the most part, except through natural dissolving techniques. Furthermore, Alum and Sal Ammoniac belong to the genus of salts because the portion of <term>fire</term> in Sal Ammoniac is greater than the earth; thus the whole of it <term>sublimates</term> <note>original: *sublimatur*; turns directly from a solid into a vapor when heated</note>, and it is itself water to which smoke is mixed.

->AVICENNA ON CONGELATION<-

...extremely subtle heat, and much fieriness coagulated by dryness. The wateriness of sulfurous substances is mixed with earth by a strong mixture through the boiling of heat, until they become oily, and afterwards they are coagulated by cold. 

**Atramenta** <note>original: *atramenta*; literally "blackings," but referring to the category of vitriols or metallic sulfates like copperas</note>, however, are composed of salt, sulfur, and stones; and there is in them a mineral power of certain liquefiable bodies which are formed from them. For instance, <term>calcamentum</term> <note>original: *calcamentum*, likely a corruption of *chalcanthum*; blue vitriol or copper sulfate</note> and <term>alathar</term> <note>original: *alathar*, a Latinization of the Arabic *al-zāj*; likely yellow vitriol or copiapite</note> are generated from larger grains of vitriol. Their saltiness is not dissolved except in combination with the sulfurous part contained within them; it then coagulates, having already received a mineral power from certain metallic bodies. Therefore, that which receives an iron-like power will be red or saffron-colored, like *alathar*. That which receives a copper-like power will be green. Hence, it is possible for these two to be produced artificially. 

Quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver," mercury</note> is like water that is mixed with an extremely subtle sulfurous earth in a strong mixture, to the point that it does not rest on a flat surface; this is due to the great dryness inherent in it, and for this reason, it does not stick to the hand when touched. Its whiteness comes from the clarity of that water and from the whiteness of the subtle earth within it. Its unique property is that it is coagulated by the vapor of sulfur; perhaps it is also "frozen" [solidified] by lead in this way, or easily by sulfurous vapor. 

It appears, moreover, that <term>argentum vivum</term> [mercury], and substances similar to it, is the primary element of all liquefiable <note>original: *liquebilium*; metals that can be melted</note> substances. This is either because all liquefiable things are converted back to mercury when they are melted—though they do not melt until they are heated, and when melted they appear red. Lead, without a doubt, is mercury when it is melted, but it does not melt unless it is heated; once liquefied, it turns into a color common to all melted metals, namely a fiery redness. Therefore, mercury mixes with these bodies because it is of the same substance. 

However, these metallic bodies differ in their composition from mercury in the same way that mercury differs from things similar to it, based on the mixtures combined with them until they solidify. If the mercury is pure, the power of white, non-burning sulfur will coagulate it; this is the best material that those who practice <term>Alchymia</term> [alchemy] can find to convert it into silver. If, however, the sulfur is of the highest purity and clear with a red color, containing the power of simple, non-burning fieriness, it will be the best thing alchemists can find to make gold, for these qualities transform the mercury into gold. 

And if the mercury is of good substance but the sulfur is impure—possessing a "burning" <note>original: *vis adurens*; a quality associated with acidity or the ability to corrode, which alchemists believed prevented the formation of "noble" metals</note> power—it will convert the mercury into copper. If the mercury is of poor quality, impure, and earthy, and the sulfur is likewise unclean, iron is produced from it. Tin [stannum], however, seems...

<page-num>999</page-num>
<header>AND THE CONGEALING OF STONES.</header>
<sig>Rrr 4</sig>

[it appears] to possess good Quicksilver <note>original: *Argentum vivum*; mercury</note> but bad Sulfur, and these are not well ground together, but are as if composed of small parts; therefore, such a substance does not form. Truly, the quicksilver of coarse lead <note>original: *Plumbi... grossi*</note> is bad, heavy, and yellowish, and its sulfur is also bad, possessing a foul, stinking, and weak vapor. For this reason, it does not congeal well. 

Craftsmen produce a coagulation nearly similar to this artificially, although artificial things are not made in the same way as natural ones, nor do they possess such certain similarities. Thus, it is believed that natural composition occurs in this way, or in a manner close to it. But art is weaker than nature and does not follow it, despite how much the craftsman may labor. 

Let the practitioners of Alchemy <note>original: *Alchymiæ*</note> know that the species of things cannot be transmuted. They can, however, make things similar to them, such as dyeing a red substance with a lemon-yellow color <note>original: *citrino*</note> so that it appears to be gold, or painting a white substance with whatever color they wish until it is very much like gold or bronze. Furthermore, they can wipe away the impurities of lead, yet it will always remain lead, even if it looks like silver. But then, other qualities will be so well represented in it that men are deceived, just as those who take salt and sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum</term> <note>original: *salem armoniacum*; ammonium chloride, used in alchemy to clean metals or as a flux</note>. 

Moreover, I do not believe it possible that the specific difference <note>the essential quality that defines what a thing is</note> can be removed by human ingenuity. It is not possible for one temperament <note>original: *complexio*; the specific balance of the four qualities</note> to be converted into another, because these sensible qualities are not the "differences" by which species are changed; rather, they are accidents <note>non-essential characteristics like color or smell</note> and properties. The true differences between species are not known, and since the difference is unknown, how can one know whether it has been removed or not, or how it might be removed? 

One can achieve the stripping away of accidents—such as vapor, color, and weight—or at least their reduction, but the proportion of these substances will not be the same in all things. Therefore, one [metal] cannot be changed into another, unless perhaps it is reduced to prime matter <term>primam materiam</term> <note>the underlying, formless substance that Aristotle argued was the basis of all elements</note>, and thus they are changed into something other than what they were before. This, however, does not happen through simple melting <note>original: *liquefactionem*</note>, but rather external things happen to it.

->**The end of Avicenna’s treatise on Minerals.**<-

# THE BOOK OF WILLIAM
## OF TECENO, Provin-
## cial of the Order of Friars Prea-
## dichants. <note>The Order of Preachers is better known today as the Dominicans.</note>

->*Which is called THE LILY AS IF PLUCKED FROM THORNS.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring an intricate floral and scrollwork design.</image-desc>
This art <note>Alchemy</note> is to be preferred far above others, since in it there is small expense, small labor, a short time, great gain, pleasant security, and a generosity accompanied by cheerfulness. All those who are practitioners of this art are physicians; for whatever they do, they do so that they may have things in abundance, which they cannot achieve or attain without this art. It is proper to know that the actions of this art are deeply entwined with logic; for if they taught it openly, everyone would know it, and it would be rendered worthless—or perhaps because the first person who read it would afterwards burn those books out of envy, lest it should reach posterity. Do not despair if you are deceived once.

<margin>The intention of nature.</margin>
You have learned that all metallic bodies, by the intention of working nature, ought to have been Gold <note>original: ☉, the symbol for Sol or Gold</note>, but because of a deficiency in material or form (or both), they are weak and incomplete, and they stand distant from the substance of Gold to a greater or lesser degree.

<margin>The intention of the art.</margin>
Hence, the intention of the present art is how they may be led back from infirmity to health, and from deficiency to completion, by adding or taking away from each that which was applied too much or too little by nature.

---

<margin>
The material of metals:
Mercury and Sulfur
</margin>
Regarding this, one should know that all things are born in the belly of the earth from Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> and the fieriness of Sulfur <note>original: *, a symbol for sulfur</note>, cooked according to various qualities; indeed, individual things dissolved by fire return into Mercury, except for the heat, which it is the part of a wise man to remove. For just as a sick body is led back to health through a medicine prepared by opposites—because often that which is faulted by nature is corrected by art—so it is also in these metallic bodies. For example:

<margin>The Elixir.</margin>
The Elixir is a medicine composed, or prepared, which heals the infirmities of metals just as Theriac <note>original: *tyriaca*; a famous ancient "universal" herbal jam used as an antidote to poison</note> heals all poisonous bodies. Therefore, the utility of this elixir is twofold: for it both enriches the soul with joy, and it frees the body from poverty and servitude.

It asserts that all metals are naturally composed of Mercury and Sulfur and can be perfected by the Elixir.</summary>

<header>PLUCKED.</header>

...intended. Therefore, greetings to those intending nature concerning Gold <note>original symbol: ☉, representing the Sun and the metal Gold</note> and Silver <note>original symbol: ☽, representing the Moon and the metal Silver</note> and the other planets <note>In alchemy, the seven classical planets corresponded to the seven metals: Sun/Gold, Moon/Silver, Mars/Iron, Venus/Copper, Jupiter/Tin, Saturn/Lead, and Mercury/Quicksilver.</note>, and regarding their medicine, and to their exaltation.

In this true and perfect doctrine, many fictions and many errors of writers are contained; let these be uncovered so that any fruitless and vain expenses in the labor of persons may be avoided, in which nothing is established without mastery. I have found nothing else in the books of the philosophers except what pleases individuals, and what is repeated many times in each, so that if by chance something is omitted or imperfectly expressed in the preceding parts, it may be found more fully joined in the following sections. The title of this little book, however, is designated as **THE LILY PLUCKED FROM THORNS** <note>original: *Lilium de Spinis Evulsum*</note>.

Lest it be left in doubt in anyone’s mind regarding the order of the subjects for one wishing to inquire: why the medicine of Gold <note>original symbol: ☉</note> is more worthy, yet the medicine does not precede Gold; rather, first comes Silver <note>original symbol: ☽</note>, second Gold <note>original symbol: ☉</note>, and the other planets with certain other extraordinary things, as will appear below, and thirdly the medicine is placed. Let his doubt be satisfied in this way: either because the end is better than the beginning, or because it is more worthy, or—more truly—in another way. Since the same things are whitened and made red, and the red cannot be made unless the white precedes it, Simon <note>likely Simon of Hungary or a figure from the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical assembly text</note> says: "Know that unless you whiten this stone, you cannot make it red," through which red the other planets are tinged, nor does the beginning of the medicine proceed except from that same red.

By necessity, therefore, the order had to be such: that first the white is placed, that is, Silver <note>original symbol: ☽</note>, through which one arrives at the red, that is, Gold <note>original symbol: ☉</note>. Concerning this, hear the philosopher saying: "All you researchers of this art, seeing that apparent whiteness above all others, be secure, for the redness is hidden within that whiteness; and then you must not extract it, but cook it until the whole becomes red. Then, secondarily, in a moment, Gold <note>original symbol: ☉</note> or the elixir <note>The "elixir" or "medicine" is the substance capable of transmuting base metals into noble ones.</note> of the medicine itself follows, from which perfection the perfection of the other planets and even of the medicine itself proceeds, and this not without Reason." Thirdly and finally, let it be understood concerning the medicine proceeding from the gradual perfection of both preceding stages. Just as the Son proceeds from the Father, and from both the Holy Spirit <note>original: *S. S.*, abbreviation for *Spiritus Sanctus*</note> (who may assist our weak beginning), so that through this medium there may be a praiseworthy and glorious ending of the same without end.

<margin>Permanent water.</margin>

<margin>Body, soul, spirit</margin>
For nature is one, which conquers and overcomes all things, and nature rejoices in nature, and nature contains nature; in this single word the whole work is encompassed. And Dardanis <note>Dardanus is a legendary figure in alchemy, often associated with Greek or Hermetic wisdom</note> says: Have you not heard what the masters have told in many ways about the permanent water <term>permanent water: a symbolic term for the universal solvent or "mercury of the philosophers" that does not wet the hands</term>, and that in the whole process <note>original: *regimine*</note> it is not suitable to use anything except that permanent water? And he who does not know this process labors in vain, and without it nothing is done, because it is spiritual blood; and therefore they named it the first and permanent water. The blood, cooked by the will of God—which the master before me narrated—is turned into a body, and the body into a spirit; mixed together and reduced into one, they are incorporated and embrace one another. Robert says: "Behold, in that water is what you seek," and indeed another says: "It is not found except in that thing which corrects itself." And Aros <note>Aros or Horos is a common authority cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> says: The process, O Theodore, and that which operates is one; therefore, cook it. And Simon says: I signify to posterity that the round copper <note>original: *rotūdu æs*</note>, which is turned into the four elements, is one. And Constans says: Nature is one, which overcomes all; therefore the masters said that what is perfected is to be called one. And Mundus says: For different things or natures do not correct that thing, but one nature, having in itself the things and the nature which suffice for it. And Gregus says: Truly there is one thing which makes itself germinate. For Lucas says: This white copper in summer, until it makes itself germinate. And Mergeris says: Thus this composite is made perfect in all four elements. He also says the same: This egg <term>egg: the alchemical vessel (the philosopher's egg) or the primordial matter contained within it</term> extracts from itself the life which it has from generation, the soul. For if this copper is roasted until it makes itself germinate—and no different things correct or contain that thing—it is perfected in all four elements, so that from itself it extracts the life which it has (the soul from generation); it well follows that it is only one thing and not different ones. However, this thing is said to be composed of three: namely body, soul, and spirit, as Lucas says. For this thing, like a man, has a body, soul, and spirit; for a man's inspiration is from the air, which is his life after God. Similarly, this copper is inspired by moisture, by which, receiving power, it is multiplied, and that copper is increased like all other things. And therefore the philosopher Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian physician whose name was often attached to Latin alchemical works</note> says: When copper is burned and the process repeated many times, it becomes better than it was, as Bonellus also says; and Hermogenes says that copper, like a man, has a soul and a body. Wherefore the philosophers said that body does not penetrate body, but rather the subtle thing in nature which is the soul, which is penetrating and dyeing <note>original: *tingens*</note> the body. Therefore, one nature is body and soul—namely, the hidden part—as Democritus says.

Now they are called "sulfurs" which were hidden in the four bodies. However, there are four bodies, whether males, or the male who is properly called "male"—the liquefaction or water from our copper. Arisleus says, saying: and of the *ehelia* <note>this likely refers to *chelia* or *ethelia*, obscure terms for the vaporous or spiritual state of matter in the *Turba*</note> with its own water...

### CHAPTER III.

When the poison penetrates the body, it colors the body itself with an unchanging color, and the body never allows the soul—which is similar to itself—to be separated from it. For with one pursuing, another fleeing, and another meeting, flight is taken away from them, and they contain one another, because nature has taken its companion as an enemy, and they embrace and contain each other; and when sulfur is mixed with sulfur, a precious color is produced, which does not change nor flee from the fire, because the soul enters the innermost parts of the body, and contains and colors the body. Similarly, Arsuberes says that this water is of a cold nature, as Pythagoras <note>the famous Greek philosopher, often cited in alchemical texts as a master of the elements</note> says: "Know that the moisture is cold at first." Therefore, beware of excessive fire, because fire is the enemy of cold moisture; as Pythagoras says, the moisture is cold at first.

...investigators of this Gum. For some of them have discovered certain applications which, however, are unable to endure the punishments of fire, for they are diminished within it. # EXTRACTED

...nothing is generated by heat alone. An intense bath or intense heat causes evaporation; if, indeed, it is cold, it causes the work to perish. But tempered heat makes the body suited to its nature and well-disposed.

<margin>Spirit.</margin>
Sometimes, however, all three are called SPIRIT, and not without reason. For even the third of them, or the density which is called earth, may be spiritual, airy, and subtle—all of which consist in the same thing, or in our brass <note>original: *æs*; in alchemy, this refers to the "Philosophical Brass," a base state of the material undergoing transformation</note>, which brass is a body, or composed of bodies.

<margin>Body.</margin>
As to what the BODY is, Aisleus <note>Aisleus is likely a variant spelling of an alchemical authority such as Archelaus or a figure from the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> says:
> Take the body which the Master ordered you to take, and showed to you, and fit it into thin plates.

And Bonellus says:
> Take the brass which is from a metal having a certain color of the sun <note>original: *color solis*; referring to a golden or solar yellow hue</note>.

Likewise, Simon says:
> Know that it is the body in which gold resides.

<margin>Water.</margin>
Likewise, Speras says:
> And know that it has been carefully ground with water.

<margin>Note.</margin>
If, however, you ask how water becomes powder, it should be noted that the philosophers' intention is this: the body, which was not water, falls into water; and that water is mixed with another water, and being made one together, they are water.

<margin>Note.</margin>
It must therefore be made known that unless you convert everything into water, you will not reach the completion of the work. It is necessary, therefore, for the body to be occupied by the flame of fire so that it may be broken down; and when it is duly combined with water, it is turned into water until the whole becomes water.

<margin>Permanent Water.</margin>
Fools, hearing of "water," think it is common water or water from a cloud. But if they had read the books of the philosophers, they would surely know it is "permanent water" <term>Permanent water: A stable, non-evaporating alchemical solvent, often identified with philosophical mercury</term>, which cannot remain permanent without its own body with which it is dissolved and made one over the fire. Concerning this, Eximideus says:
> Take the stone of gold and mix it with its own moisture, which is the permanent water, and place it in its vessel over a light fire or heat, so that it becomes earth. This earth, because it is stable, receives the tincture <note>original: *tincturam*; the "dye" or power of transformation that changes the color and nature of the metal</note> from the spirit latent within it.

Concerning which Hermogenes says:
> Look upon the latent spirit, and do not despise it, because when it remains, it is a great secret <note>original: *archanum*</note>.

It is also said to have greater power than its brothers—that is, the spirit and the soul—and this happens when it receives the tincture, after the companions are truly joined; that is, after the whitening <note>original: *dealbationem*; the *albedo* stage where the matter becomes white and pure</note>.

<margin>Conjunction. Male ♂ female ♀ *.</margin>
For in the true whitening, the spouses are united and associated in truth. That which first acted as the female then begins to be acted upon by the male, that is, by the quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo*; mercury</note>. And she who was first called the female, or the sulphur, used to attract, but then she is drawn by the male or by the quicksilver. And that which first dominated is then transferred into being dominated.

For the male, who first allowed himself to be drawn, was drawn by the permanent female, who was first the attractor or the ruler; now he dominates by drawing her back, and he receives the staining spirit, namely when the male himself draws the female to him, which is called the prior force of the stone...

<margin>The first power of the stone is the sharpest vinegar.</margin>
...of our honorable stone, and it is called the sharpest vinegar <note>original: *acetum acerrimum*; in alchemy, this usually refers to a potent acidic solvent or "philosophical" vinegar rather than household vinegar</note>. <margin>Women’s work and children’s play.</margin>
preparation is understood, it is nothing other than women's work and children's play <note>A common alchemical phrase implying that once the secret "key" is discovered, the physical labor is as easy as domestic chores or simple games</note>. For the secret of the work of gold is made from the male and the female. For the female rejoices when she has received the strength of the male, because she is aided by the male. <margin>Two natures.</margin>
stone, you cannot make the true red, because the two natures are nothing other than the white and the red. For when the water enters the body, it turns it into spirit, then into earth, and then into dust or ashes. If you wish to test this ash at its perfection, take it in your hand; and if you find it to be like impalpable water <note>meaning a powder so fine it feels liquid or weightless</note>, it is well. If not, manage it until it becomes so. And know that if you take anything other than our brass <note>original: *æs*; the base metallic material of the work</note> and manage it with our water, you will not find what you seek. But if you take our brass and manage it with our water, you will find what you seek. And although this stone of ours already naturally contains the true tincture within itself—for it was created in the body of magnesia <note>original: *magnesia*; not the modern chemical, but a "prime matter" or "perfect earth" often described as the mother of the stone</note>, that is, the perfect earth—nevertheless, it has no motion of its own unless it is perfected by art and operation. <margin>Infant.</margin>
Mosius, Theophilus, and Hermes say. Therefore, operation is necessary for us, just as it is to be seen in an infant, who is born perfect in terms of creation, but truly imperfect in terms of function, unless it is first nourished with a little milk, then with more milk, and then with more and stronger food. See, therefore, to this kind of operation of the stone according to the saying of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note>; for he says in the *Book of Roots*: "For this purpose the operation and preparation are done, so that its tincture may be improved more than it is in its own nature, and also that it may become an <term>elixir</term>—which, according to the allegory of the wise, is a compound made of clear species—a seasoning, an antidote, and a medicine for all bodies to be cured, purified, and transformed into true gold-making and silver-making <note>original: *solificum & lunificum*; substances that turn base metals into Gold (Sun) and Silver (Moon)</note>."

<margin>1. Alchemy.</margin>
For what else is Alchemy than an art demonstrating or ministering, containing the essence of the seven metals, and showing how their forms may be naturally led from a state of diminution to a natural completion?

<margin>2.</margin>
Or otherwise: Alchemy is a certain hidden kingdom, which becomes manifest by the light of the begotten sons, and that which grows young again upon the sons...

...does not know, as Secundus the philosopher says, or otherwise. Alchemy is a corporeal substance, composed of one thing and through one thing, joining more precious things to each other through effect and knowledge, and by that same natural conjunction, naturally converting them into a better kind. <margin>Our stone</margin> For our stone is that corporeal substance composed of one and through one, which contains two very thin moistures—namely soul and spirit—just as if they were clear vessels. It grows young and manifests itself through the light of the begotten sons <note>likely referring to the "children of the sun," or planetary influences</note>, and it contains the essence of metals in such a way that within that substance resides a strong dyeing spirit <note>original: *spiritus tingens*; the active agent that changes base metals into gold</note> which we seek, by which we may dye any body and naturally lead any of them from a state of diminished value to their natural perfection.

### CHAPTER IV

Mercury <note>original: *arg. vi.* or *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver," the common name for quicksilver</note> is called the spirit—that is, the carrier of the virtues of the soul (which is sulfur)—through the body (meaning the bronze of magnesia or the earth). When this earth is made spiritual, it is called gold, which was hidden within the body of magnesia, according to the understanding of the saying: "Son, extract from the ray its shadow," meaning from the sun its terrestrial nature or density. Truly, magnesia is so named because a great secret <note>original: *magnum archanum*</note> resides within it, as the philosopher says. 

However, before we arrive at the operation of our stone, let anyone seeking this science take heed at the beginning so that they do not fall into wandering and error. This is because philosophers <margin>Names of the stone.</margin> name our stone in many different ways; for sometimes they call it the stone of animals, sometimes of vegetable things, sometimes of salts, sometimes of alums, sometimes of spirits, sometimes a body, sometimes an egg, sometimes a cock, or they call it by the name of any thing whatever. This is because in its operation, all colors that can be imagined in the world today appear, and thus the philosophers vary its names according to the colors appearing during the work. 

There is also another reason: because this stone is perfected from all four elements, they call it by the name of any elemental thing. There is also a third reason: namely, so that the foolish might not recognize this stone. For if they knew it, they would not sell it for such a low price as they do. Although this stone of ours is cheap in its physical state, it nevertheless contains a near potential for what is precious—namely, the dyeing spirit, which is hidden invisibly in its secret body, like the soul in a human body. For nothing precious is made without the vile, nor the vile without the precious. This stone is ground with its own water until it drinks all that moisture and receives an eminent power against the battle of fire; and then <margin>Rust.</margin> it is called rust <note>original: *rubigo*; often refers to the deep red color of the final stage of the work, the "Red Lion"</note>, and it is carefully putrefied until it becomes a spiritual powder.

...this color of burnt blood, which fire introduced into the unwilling belly of nature as a separate humor, and colored with an unchangeable hue. ## CHAPTER V.

Therefore, let everyone who wishes to work know, before they proceed to the operation, what they are working upon, so that after much labor and expense they are not frustrated in their purpose. Having cast aside other things, consider the operation of our stone, which from the beginning requires a light fire, and for many days appears like a dead thing, like a man in his tomb. Afterward, God restores life to it—that is, its soul and spirit—and then, its infirmity having been taken away, it is purged. Truly, after corruption it is improved, until it becomes ash <note>original: *cinis*; the calcined or powdered remains after heating</note> by a fire more intense than the first. And know that when the work is ash, you have mixed it, because that ash has received the spirit; and again moisten it with that humor with a more intense fire, until it assumes the sign of dry saffron, or the color of burnt blood, or of pomegranate syrup. Do you not see that seed <note>original: *sperma*</note> is made from blood, and from seed a human being is formed, until it is seen to have a deep and uniform color, carefully processed in the liver <note>original: *epate*; in ancient physiology, the liver was the source of the body's blood and heat</note>? Yet nothing new is created in that seed. Similarly, our bronze <note>original: *æs*; likely referring to the "Philosophical Copper"</note> becomes a spiritual seed through putrefaction, as Pythagoras and Bonellus say. However, if there is anyone who says he knows this art or its operation, and wishes to bring in some infusion for working or for making expenditures on this work, let him at least feel that he has gained this utility from my book: that he cannot be deceived or misled by anyone, even though from what has been said, he may not be able to reach a true knowledge of our stone, perhaps because of the clouding of his own intellect. For if anyone seeks this knowledge and is ignorant of it, God has hidden the truth from him. For if God knew he had a faithful mind, He would certainly reveal the truth to him, as Diomedes says. Therefore, let no one blame the wise, but himself. Nor—

Understand, therefore, the sayings of the philosophers, lest you wander.

<margin>Vessels.</margin>
...if he attends diligently to the things received, and understands, considers, and observes them, he will not be able to be deceived nor misled by an erroneous craftsman. ## CAP. VI.

<margin>One vessel.</margin>
<margin>A stone vessel.</margin>
It must be known that the philosophers attributed only a single vessel to this operation of ours. For **Bonellus** <note>a recurring authority in the *Turba Philosophorum*, an early alchemical text</note> says: "Place it in its own vessel, and then extract the things existing in the vessel." Likewise, **Epistenus** says: "And place it in its own vessel." **Miredis** says: "Place it in a vessel with a narrow opening." **Mireris** says: "It must be sieved in its own sieve." And many others seeking that operation always speak of the vessel in the singular. Regarding which vessel and operation, hear **Theophilus** saying: "I notify you that the **Dragon** <note>the 'Dragon' usually symbolizes mercury or the raw, volatile matter that must be 'killed' or stabilized</note> never dies unless it is killed with its brother and its sister. However, the philosophers have given their wife and consort over to death; for that woman's belly is full of arms and poison. Therefore, let a grave be dug for that Dragon, and let the woman be buried there with him. He is strongly joined to that woman; the more he is bound and the more he rolls around her, the more his body is separated into many parts, and mixed with the woman's limbs, he is entirely given over to death and turned completely into blood." 

Now, this stone and circular vessel must not fear fire or fires, since it is subtly composed of its own water. However, few of these stone vessels, such as those used by glassmakers, last when they are corroded in the work or the vessels split; but glazed ones should be coated. Let the vessel be concave in the manner of a half-moon, having a capacity of 40 or 50 pounds, although the master would not have placed more than 25 of **our brass** <note>original: *nostri æris*; likely referring to a specialized alchemical copper or alloy</note> fitted into thin tables or drawn out into plates, as **Theophilus** and **Arisleus** say—pure, clean, raw, pleasant, sincere, and upright. In this vessel, sight rather than writing is to be sought, according to the description. And as **Pandolphus** and **Orsoltus** say, let it be made round in the manner of a celestial half-moon. The Master indeed placed 25 of the body, of which a third part is for a fine and fit decoction, as **Ascanius** says. This vessel must be placed within a furnace in which the flame may thus **reverberate** <note>original: *reverberet*; to reflect heat back onto the substance, common in 'reverberatory' furnaces</note> over the vessel and next to the vessel in the furnace. The place for the fire is in the furnace, and the vent <note>original: *spiramen*; an air hole for draft or exhaust</note> should be above the fire, but not above the vessel.

...that the airhole <note>original: "spiramen"; a vent or breathing-hole in the alchemical vessel</note> must be covered, so that the flower—or rather the smoke—does not escape through it, but keeps its neighbor <note>the volatile part keeping the fixed part</note> with itself and causes its **whiteness** to be kindled, as **Lucas** says. For as **Bonellus** says, nothing useful is made from the elements without governance and composition, because the seed is generated from blood and desire; for when the man is joined to the woman, the seed is nourished by the blood’s moisture and heat while the moisture of the womb is present. After forty days have passed, the fetus is formed, and if the moisture of the womb were not there, the seed would not be preserved nor would the fetus be completed. 

God, moreover, ordained that blood and humor to nourish the seed until you extract it at will. Once the fetus is extracted, however, it is nourished only by milk, and by a small fire, and gradually while it is an infant. As it grows larger and the bones are strengthened, it is led into youth, and upon reaching that stage, it is self-sufficient. So, therefore, you must act in this **Art**, knowing that nothing is ever generated without heat; yet intense heat causes destruction, and a cold composite bath causes it to flee. Through a temperate heat, however, the body becomes smooth and fitting, for by a light fire the corrupting moistures are drawn out. 

All the **Philosophers** testify that they have found no other fire that extracts corrupting moistures than a light one, commending slowness and blaming haste—and rightly so, for if the composite is forced more than it should be, it is extinguished. Thus it must be burned—that is, whitened—just as if by the nourishment of eggs, which is to say, by a light decoction <term>decoction: the process of boiling or heating a substance to extract its essence</term>, as **Mofius** says. For the water knows the battle of the fire through the long duration of corrupting, cooking, putrefying, and thickening, and its flight is prevented, as the same **Mofius** says. For by the heat of the sun—that is, by the light decoction of the fire—things are congealed; therefore, the composite ought to be introduced into a temperate bath or chamber <note>original: "caenaculum"; literally a dining room or upper room, here referring to the heating chamber</note>. Intense heat causes this bath to perish—that is, by too much fire, as **Bonellus** says. Because if you intensify the fire before the proper time, it becomes red, which is of no use to you, because in the beginning of the governance you desire **whiteness**, as **Lucas** says. 

Regarding the manner of the fire, seek the philosophers: **Bonellus**, **Ascanius**, **Arfuleres**, **Gregorius**, **Balgum**, and **Marcus**. For they say: we must govern gently until the **sulfur** becomes incombustible.

### ->CHAPTER VII.<-

Since I have said above that all these things are made from one thing, some of the **Philosophers** say that **fire** and **Azot** <note>Azot is a term for the universal solvent or the "Mercury of the Philosophers"</note> are sufficient for you. Others say that **water** alone through itself does all things, for it dissolves all things, binds or congeals all things, and destroys all things without the help of another. And in it are all things: the dyer and the dyed. It is made through it, and in it alone is that which makes the colors of the soul appear once the body is **punished** <note>original: *punito*; in alchemy, this refers to mortification, the breaking down or "killing" of the material to release its essence</note>, in which the tincture <note>The coloring principle or transformative essence</note> of any body resides, as **Mireris** and **Democritus** say. Others, however, assert that all things are made by the fire of **ethelia** <note>A term for the volatile spirit or "vaporous" essence of the matter</note> and by moisture, or liquefaction.

<margin>Azot, that is, <term>Fire</term> <term>Mercury</term>.</margin>
It must be understood that all things are made by fire, that is, they are nourished. But **Azot**—that is, the **water of mercury** or **ethelia**, which is to say, by moisture or liquefaction or **permanent water** <note>water that does not evaporate when heated</note>—cannot exist without its body, with which it is dissolved, and they have been made one permanent thing. This water is also called spirit of spirit, and sulfur of sulfur, and **quicksilver of quicksilver**; for everything is called **ethel**, that is, permanent. Likewise, it is also called **vapor**, regarding which hear **Victimorum** saying to his disciples: "Nothing else is suitable for you than to sublimate the water and the vapor."

For when you see the natures become waters, purified by fire, and the whole body of **magnesia** <note>A traditional name for the primal matter of the Stone</note> just like molten water, then all things have been made into vapor. By right, then, the vapor contains its mate; wherefore the **Envious** <note>original: *Invidi*; a term for alchemical authors who hid their secrets from the uninitiated</note> named both of the pair "vapor" because in the cooking of the one, the other is joined, and the one contained the other. Then, though born to flee, it found no path; for although flight is essential to it, the other nevertheless contained it and did not permit it to flee, and it found no place to escape, and they were made permanent. Therefore, when the hidden things fall into the body, it is congealed with it, and its color is changed, and its...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "one thing" from the previous page, expanding on the elemental nature of the Work and the philosophical principle that "Nature rejoices in Nature." It transitions from the general theory of water and vapor to the specific process of removing the "blackness" to reach the "whiteness."</meta>

# THE LILY AMONG THORNS

It <note>The Stone or the philosophical matter</note> ingeniously lays aside its nature, which God has suggested to His learned ones. And it has received the power not to flee <note>original: *ne fugiat*; refers to volatility, where the substance escapes as gas. Here, it is "fixed" or made stable</note>, and just as there is moisture and dryness in a liquid, so our work is nothing other than water and vapor. These are the two things which the envious <note>The "envious" (*invidi*) is a common alchemical term for previous masters who supposedly hid their secrets to prevent the unworthy from succeeding</note> have called "composites," because those two are actually four: namely, moisture, dryness, spirit, and vapor. 

And although I say these two become four, do not forget, however, that in our work you require only one thing. Concerning this, hear **Mundus** <note>Likely a reference to an alchemical authority or a speaker from the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> saying: Do not care for a plurality of compositions, nor those things which the deceivers have narrated in their books through figures. For the truth is one nature, which naturally changes nature, because that natural secret <note>original: *archanum*</note> is hidden in its belly; it is neither seen nor known except by the wise. Therefore, he who rules sparingly—that is, through itself—and knows its temperament <note>original: *complexionem*; the balance of its qualities</note>, extracts from it a nature surpassing all natures. 

And then the words of the Master shall be fulfilled, namely: **Nature rejoices in nature, nature contains nature, nature overcomes nature** <note>A fundamental alchemical axiom attributed to Pseudo-Democritus</note>, and yet they are not diverse natures, nor many, but only one, having its own things and natures within itself, by which it diminishes all other things. And this water, called by so many different names, is called by the philosophers **whitening water**, **cleansing water**, or **imbuing water**, or the **infusion** that removes blackness from bodies. And this is that water which the philosophers, in the washing of the body, have divided into two parts.

The first part of this water cleanses the composite from metallic corruption, having been gently managed with a light fire, as has been said. Otherwise, if the composite is ruled and nourished by too much fire rather than a light one, it is extinguished. This liquefaction in that light fire must be continuously repeated so many times until the blackness, appearing at the first face in the work, recedes. For **Florus** <note>An alchemical author</note> says: "And finding the blackness appearing above on the first face." And know that the redness is extracted from that blackness after the **whiteness** <note>The *albedo* stage</note>, because that black thing is refined; and by composing peace between the "fleeing" <note>volatile</note> and the "non-fleeing" <note>fixed</note>, it has reduced them into one. 

And why does this "flee" <note>volatilize</note>? Because the tormented thing, when it is joined within the body, turns it into an unalterable, immutable, and indelible nature by repetition. It is necessary, therefore, for you to know this **sulfur** <note>In alchemy, sulfur often represents the active, combustible, or "soul" principle of matter</note> by which the body is blackened, of which **Mireris** says: "I command those who follow to make bodies non-corporeal, and the incorporeal corporeal." EXTRACTED

...by the man, and through **echelia** <term>echelia: a specialized alchemical term, likely derived from the Greek *echeia*, referring to a transformative brine or "divine water" used as a solvent</term> a hidden nature is extracted, through which bodies are colored. By this governance, you must understand that bodies become non-bodily, and the incorporeal becomes corporeal. If you diligently perform these matters by fire and by **echelia**, they become "non-fleeing" <note>original: *non fugientes*; meaning the substance is "fixed" and will no longer evaporate or sublimate when heated</note>. And know that **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum: mercury</term> is a corporeal fire, burning, killing, and binding under a single governance. And the more the bodies are mixed and ground, the more they are broken down and thinned by the application of fire. When, however, you grind the bodies diligently and prepare them as is required, you will possess the nature of **echelia**—a heat that does not flee, and a tincture that endures the fire, which overcomes, binds, and contains. This is because copper <note>original: *æs*; this can mean copper, bronze, or the "base" metallic state of the matter</note> does not color anything unless it is first colored itself; once it is colored, it colors others. 

And know that a body cannot tint unless it is tinted, and unless its spirit, which is hidden in its belly, is extracted, and the body and soul are made without the spirit. This spirit is the spiritual nature from which colors will appear, because a thick, earthy nature cannot tint. Rather, it is the thin part of the nature—the incorporeal part—that pierces through and colors. When you govern the body, it will belong to the tinting agent, and from it you extract the thinnest part; then it will be turned into the tincture by which it is colored. Therefore the Wise Man said that copper does not tint unless it is tinted. 

And know that the body cannot be contained or tinted without this. But this "torturing" <note>original: *crucians*; in alchemy, "torture" refers to the intense chemical processing, such as purification by fire or acid</note> tints, and that blackening sulfur is the body which opens the door to the "non-fleeing" <note>the stable substance</note> and turns that which flees into that which stays. Do you not see that this "torture" does not cause harm or corruption, but rather union and utility? For if its suffering were harmful or improper, the matter would certainly not embrace it until it had extracted from it those unalterable and indelible colors, which we call **water of sulfur** <note>original: *sulphuris aquam*; a name for the "Divine Water" or the transformative solvent</note>, and which is suited for the tincture of redness—a cooking that produces blackness, and which cannot happen without that blackness.

### CHAPTER VIII.

Behold, I have notified and shared with you the key of the work: for as long as the blackness <term>nigredo: the initial stage of the alchemical process, symbolizing decay and the stripping away of old forms</term> lasts, the female dominates, right up until the whiteness <term>albedo: the second major stage, representing purification and spiritualization</term>. Regarding this vinegar in our work, one must be careful that it is not turned into hay <note>i.e., scorched or dried out</note> by too much fire. For through a light decoction, the male—that is, the **quicksilver**—receives the spirit from the female—that is, from the tinting **sulfur**. This spirit...

### LILY AMONG THORNS

### 1018

...[nourish]ing and vivifying spirit is introduced after the corrupting humidity has receded—and not before—which occurs once the state of whiteness <term>albedo: the second major stage of the alchemical work, representing purification</term> has been reached. And this is what Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian physician whose works on medicine and chemistry were foundational to medieval European science</note> says in his third book on humors: "For heat in a moist body produces blackness; it then strips away that blackness when its humidity is entirely finished. And when heat overflows in it, it turns it white," as can be seen in the colors used by common people, which is well worth committing to memory. 

<margin>The true process of the art is fourfold.</margin>

For first in our work, as I have said, all things are turned black; secondly, they are whitened; thirdly, by the intensification of a greater fire, the composite must be incinerated—that is, reduced entirely to ash. And this is the end of which Aziracum speaks: "Mixing therefore the ash with water," etc. Micedius also speaks of this, saying: "Do not despise the ash," and he explains the reason there. For again, its own "sweat" is returned to that same ash once it is liquefied—namely, through a greater intensification of fire—and thus, fourthly and lastly, the King is crowned. 

And this is the King of whom Diomedes says: "Venerate the King and his wife, and do not burn them, nor put them to flight by burning with too much fire, since you do not know when you will have need of those things which improve the King and his wife. Cook them, therefore, until they become black, then white, then red, then let it become a tinting poison <note>original: *venenum*; in alchemy, "poison" often refers to a potent, transformative substance or the "solvent" that kills the old form to create the new</note>." These things, moreover, must be done through the division of the water, as Ixistius says: "I command you, however, not to pour the water all at once, lest the elixir be submerged." 

But when you have divided the water, as Thelus says: "Cook the male with the vapor of the female until both are coagulated and become the stone which is called **Atos** <note>original: *Atos*; a specific name for the matter when it reaches the pure white stage</note>, or the white stone, for you have already divided the water." Now, the white state arises from combustion and moisture or liquefaction, through which "death" is said to follow; this is apparent in the blackness <term>nigredo: the "blackness" or first stage, symbolizing the death of the base matter</term> appearing first in the work. In this mortification <term>mortificatio: the alchemical "death" or breakdown of the substance</term>, the souls are punished—that is, they are dried out—because unless the bodies are dried, the colors of the soul (which are called the blackness and the cloud) will not appear. 

Of which Lucas says: "Take the cloud which your predecessors commanded you to seize, and cook it with its own body, because that smoke is white and whitens everything; by this smoke, whatever is commanded to be whitened is whitened." Therefore, mix that smoke with its own dregs <note>original: *faeci*; the sediment or dregs remaining after distillation</note> until it is coagulated and becomes a white body. Roast this copper <note>original: *æs*; while literally copper, it refers here to the base metallic matter of the work</note> also until it causes itself to sprout, since when it is whitened with **magnesia** <term>magnesia: in alchemy, this refers not to the modern element, but to a "primitive matter" or mineral used to "fix" the volatile spirits</term>, it does not allow the spirit to flee, nor does it allow the cloud or shadow of the copper to appear. This is because nature contains nature due to the proximity of their being to one another; for natures meeting their own nature rejoice, and one thing performs what many operate...

# UPROOTED

### 1019

...[mat]ters, you have no need of anything except one thing. Indeed, that one thing is present in every stage of your operations, though it is turned into another nature. Truly, when the **blackness** <term>nigredo: the initial stage of putrefaction and darkness</term> fades, the spirit is restored to both parts—that spirit which, as far as the eye could see, appeared almost separated from them, yet was not so in its substance. For the spirit, as it is said, never dies, because there is nothing that can separate or corrupt it; rather, it vivifies <note>brings to life</note> both the body and the soul. 

And in a similar way, one must understand that saying of the Philosopher: "Nature rejoices in nature," that is, in the meeting of its own kind. "Nature contains nature," that is, by the proximity of its own kind. "Nature overcomes nature," namely, by killing and bringing life to the body, since it is made from itself, and is converted into itself, and is increased, and is multiplied; for God extracts many from one, because He creates nothing that lacks governance, and indeed it is purified by ingenious means. 

Similarly, our **copper** <note>original: "aes nostrum"; in alchemy, this refers not to common copper but to the base material of the Work</note> when it is cooked, becomes water; then, the more it is cooked, the more it thickens, until it becomes a stone. This is what the envious <note>The "envious" (invidiosi) was a common alchemical term for authors who hid their secrets from the uninitiated</note> call the stone that looms over every metal. First, it is broken and soaked, and then roasted with a fire more intense than the first, until it becomes like dry saffron or burnt blood; then it is projected upon bodies and tints them into gold, as **Bonellus** <note>Bonellus is an alchemical authority often cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*, likely a corruption of a Greek name like Apollonius</note> says. 

And although I have said in the preceding sections that this stone of ours contains two very thin liquids—namely, **soul** and **spirit**—it is not necessary for anything foreign to be introduced to it, nor for anything to be removed from it. For like a plant from its root, everything green and every **tincture** <term>tinctura: the power of the elixir to change the color and nature of a metal</term> is taken from it according to the root it contains, as has been said, and all things are founded upon that same root. Because this foundation of the work has but a little of the root, the power of this root does not abound equally, just as the splendor of the Sun does not shine equally upon the planets. 

Patience and delay are therefore necessary. And for this reason **Simon** says: "If anyone introduced to this art knew its natures, he would endure the lengthiness of the cooking until, by the will of God, he extracted his purpose." He would not seek it from another thing or things, for from its belly the hidden flowers are drawn out, and it makes itself germinate. For this, which possesses the life of all things, draws its soul and generation from itself and not from others; and what is inside it sends outside, so that the internal corrects the external, and the external corrects the internal, until the **redness**, which is naturally hidden in the body, is turned into **whiteness**—that is, in the first part of the work—and the white is turned into a red that is no longer hidden as before, but is now apparent in the final part of the work. And thus they mutually correct one another according to the saying of **Rosinus to Euthesia** <note>Rosinus is the Latinized name for the 3rd-century alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis; Euthesia is a corruption of Theosebeia, his female student</note>: "Therefore, turn the red into white, and the white into red," etc., and thus they mutually correct each...

## CHAPTER IX.

<margin>The red elixir.</margin>
Since the Philosophers have set down various accounts of these burnings or roastings, nonetheless, because of the diversity of environments—namely, the wet and the dry—the matter coagulates faster in the wet and more slowly in the dry. You should keep this work in your mind, along with Hermes, as Ascanius says: let the work be operated and repeated continuously by cooking in dung <note>fimo: a common alchemical method for providing gentle, steady heat using fermenting horse manure</note> until it becomes visible to the sight. Thus, let the very transformation of the work teach you; follow the saying of anyone else. Theophilus says that in 100 days the entire work is turned into earth. Bonellus and Ascanius seem to mean the same. Aristeus says the completion occurs in 80 days; Socrates in 150 days; Balgus and Azirarus likewise in 130; Rosius in 80 days; and the Master of Perfection says it is completed in 80 days. 

And it should be known, as I said before, that the spirit and soul are not united with our true body except in the white color, because then, in that whitening <term>albedo: the second major stage of the Great Work</term>, all the colors that can be imagined in the world today appear, and then they are fixed and complete their work in one color, namely whiteness, in which all colors meet. For whitening must be awaited. It is the beginning and the foundation of the whole work, and then it is called the **Greater Elixir of Whiteness**. Nor does it thereafter vary into different true colors, except into red, which is the final end: the **red elixir** <term>rubedo: the final stage of the alchemical process</term>. Indeed, the "ashing" <note>cineratio</note> that occurs between the white and the red is not called a color; in the cooking after the whiteness, you cannot go wrong, for once the governance of the fire is increased after the white...

...[red]ness, one arrives at ashing <term>cineratio: a stage where the matter is reduced to a gray, ash-like substance</term> before the final redness, as I have said. It should also be noted that Maria <note>Maria the Jewess, a legendary foundational figure in alchemy credited with inventing various laboratory apparatus</note> called this water—which produces blackness, whiteness, ashing, and redness—a "fiery poison" <note>original: "venenum igneum"</note>, and not without cause, for it conquers the battle of the fire. For it is through this water that the body is turned into spirit. Unless these dense things are separated by a nature that lacks a body until they become incorporeal—that is, a most subtle spirit—you cannot extract that most subtle and tinting soul which is hidden in the natural womb. And know that unless the body is broken down until it dies, and you extract from it its soul, which is the tinting spirit, you can in no way tint anything with that spirit; nor does the body tint unless it itself is tinted. Neither does body penetrate body, but rather it is the subtle nature, which is the soul, that penetrates and tints the body. For when the Gold <note>original: "☉", the astrological and alchemical symbol for the Sun or Gold</note> made into water has been generated as a liquid, it returns to its progenitor, the magnesia <note>In alchemy, "magnesia" refers not to the modern element, but to a primal, "transformed" state of matter</note>; it becomes airy and subtle because of its offspring—namely, from the spirit or water or liquefaction—which occurs through the stage of whiteness alone. For then both the fleeting things—that is, the soul and spirit—are turned into the non-fleeting earth and make it spiritual, cleansed of its earthiness; that is, they make it airy and subtle. Thus the son is said to improve the father, first by killing him <note>mortificando: the process of breaking down the "body" of the metal</note> and afterwards by bringing him to life, so that finally, the spirit having been altered by the body, the soul rejoices in it, having been made incorruptible. In this way, one transmutes the other, and each receives the power of the other as nature disposes. Every body is dissolved with the spirit, as Orfoltus <note>An alchemical authority, likely a corruption of a name like Ortholanus or Avicenna</note> says, and then it is not impossible that, although the order of the elements is varied, one is transmuted into another. But lest you marvel while working (so that we do not seem to have omitted these things), it must be known that in this operation, the composition first becomes black, as was said. Then it becomes yellow, then red—though not a true red, because it turns yellow and red many times, and is dried and liquefied many times—and all these things happen before the "whitening" <note>original: "dealbationem"</note> or the white stage. Keep this in mind, however: one should not care about those colors that appear before the whiteness, for they are not true colors. Whatever happens with the colors, one must wait for the whitening, which is the beginning and the firm foundation of the whole work, as has been said. For the final red cannot be achieved unless the white precedes it.

...clean, and subtle, and made into an airy spirit from sulphur—which is called the **Sulphur of Sulphur** <note>original: 🜍 de 🜍</note>—and from mercury, which is the **Mercury of Mercury** <note>original: ☿ de ☿</note>. Since, therefore, as has been stated many times, the entire mastery is completed with one thing (that is, our one stone), by one way (namely the way of Hermes), by one arrangement (namely first blackening, second whitening, third ashing, and fourth and finally reddening), and by one act, which is cooking.

Therefore, let the false Alchemists and those who believe them cease from all their dissolutions, sublimations, conjunctions, separations, congealings, preparations, grindings, distillations, whitenings, and reddenings and their other deceptions. Nor is there any elixir other than ours, nor any whitening or reddening other than those we have mentioned, nor any other animal other than ours which is called **Kenkel** <note>a symbolic name for a creature in alchemical allegory, possibly representing the mercury of the philosophers</note>, or any other egg other than ours which is called an "egg" by way of a metaphor, or any other stone other than ours (which is called **Artos** <note>Greek for "bread"</note> or "the white one"), or human blood, or gum, or any other elixir extracted from vegetable things or from man or from a brute animal, that would be suitable or useful for our operation. 

For in this matter men are deceived: because our stone has as many names as there are things, or names of things (as was said above). Let them also hear the many Philosophers who say—for Diomedes says: "Know, all you seekers of this doctrine, that nothing comes out of man but man, nor from brute animals or vegetables except what is like themselves." Therefore, this is treated briefly; pay attention, for by omitting long-windedness, I have raised you up to the true stone. Since nature is not mended except in its own nature, just as you are not mended except...

->E V A R S U M<-

...in your son, namely man. Beware, therefore, lest you disregard my precepts, and use the venerable nature; for from her the work is made, and not from another. And know that unless you receive and govern her, you will have nothing. Join, therefore, the male son of the **red servant** <term>servi rubei: a common alchemical code for a specific mineral or state of matter, often associated with sulfur or the "solar" principle</term> to his fragrant wife; once this is done, they will come together and perform their union.
