O, how most precious is the nature of that servant, without whom the governance cannot stand! Otherwise, followers seek after certain errors and false applications; because of such predicted things, they are themselves deservedly called counterfeiters, and for this reason they abandon their purpose. 

They even teach those who believe them that our work is made from a tortoise, or some other similar brute animal, or from the powder of the **Basilisk** <note>original: Basilisci</note>, based on the aforementioned reasons. Yet nothing is born from man except man, and nature is not improved except in its own proper nature. In this they are perhaps deceived, because the Philosophers say the smell of our stone is like the "smell of tombs" <note>original: sepulchrorum odorem</note>. Because of this, they perhaps believe it to be the Basilisk, as it is a foul-smelling animal, or they believe it to be a Dragon, or a tortoise, or a foul serpent whose smell is similar. However, do not let this deceive them, for in the operation of our stone, the smell is indeed like the smell of tombs, and almost intolerable.

## C H A P T E R  X I.

Hear then, most dear sons, humble and devoted, who seek after this most noble science, and fix this most secret and truest word in the depths of your heart: That our virtuous **elixir** <term>elixir: the perfected substance capable of transformation, often called the "medicine" of metals</term> is not made except from minerals, and incombustible things, and the purest substances, by the natural way or governance. Know, however, that if you find this thing, it ought to be nourished like an infant in the womb, as certain Philosophers say. Draw it toward similar things, not according to the quantity of the time itself, but to the gentleness of the cooking and the fire. For as it is said: the thing is congealed by the heat of the Sun; and when it is said this thing is nourished by the **fire of wings** <note>original: igne alarum</note>, this means just like the nourishment of eggs <note>This refers to the "incubation" stage of alchemy, where a very gentle, consistent heat—like a bird sitting on an egg—is used to mature the substance.</note>. 

Likewise, hear what **Rosinus** <note>Rosinus is the Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, an early alchemist from the 3rd or 4th century</note> says to Euthesia when she asks about this operation: "Consider that there are four seasons of the year, namely winter, spring, summer, and autumn. Understand that just as in these four seasons or parts of the year we begin from winter, which is humid, so in this operation we begin..."

Afterwards, in the spring, by using a greater heat of the fire after the **whitening** <term>dealbatio: the stage where the substance turns white, also called the albedo</term>, reaching the stage of incineration—just as heat increases in the summer—and finally arriving at the **redness** <term>rubedo: the final stage of the alchemical process, representing solar perfection</term> through a greater heat, by which fruits are ripened and gathered from the trees. This is true unless, speaking generally, I were to say that one person is more fit than another for performing or doing something; but descending to the specifics of this work, far be it from our age to believe such things to be true. For all things written in this art were written to hide it, not as in other writings meant for our instruction. Wherefore the **Philosopher** <note>original: Philosophus; likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle, the traditional authorities in alchemy</note> says: Do not love or care for a plurality of compositions, nor those things which deceivers have told in their books using figurative language. For our truth is one, and it is one thing in which is the spirit we seek, with which we may tinge any body whatsoever; and this likewise I leave to the judgment of those skilled in this part.

### Chapter XII.

From the aforementioned things, briefly and summarily, clearly and appropriately, collect the signs which ought to appear in the operations at the beginning, the middle, and the end. These will always be an indication to you so that, as they always appear in their due order and course during the operation, you may know you are working correctly; otherwise, **blackness** <term>nigredo: the "blacker than black" stage of putrefaction and beginning of the work</term> will not be the first thing seen in the work. Likewise, the work often turns yellow <note>original: citrinatur</note>, and often turns red. Likewise, the work often dries out and melts, and all these things happen around the beginning of the work and in the process before reaching the degree of the greater stage, namely the **whiteness** <term>albedo</term>, which is the same thing. Likewise, even before the whitening in the operation itself—that is, in the **conjunction of the soul, body, and spirit**—all the colors that can be imagined appear, and then you know that you are near the whiteness.

...it is whiteness <note>original: "albedinem"</note>, for by the approach of this whiteness all the aforementioned colors are formed, and they come together into the single color of the expected whiteness, as Mireris, Mundus, Morienes, and Pythagoras say. And from that point—that is, after the **whitening** <term>dealbatio: the stage of purification where the matter turns white</term>—that which first pulled is now pulled, and that which was first being pulled now pulls that which first pulled it. This is always to be understood by means of the **black** and **white** colors <note>original: "nigro & albo colore"</note>, by which all things are first washed clean. If, however, in that operation, the black and white colors appear and that "pulling" or treatment were false, it would be of no value.

And this is what Lucas says, and why it was stated above: whatever may happen regarding the colors between the blackness and the whiteness, one must not care; the whitening must always be waited for, which is said to be the beginning and the firmament of the work. Likewise, note that he says "firmament" so that you cannot easily go astray afterward. From then on, we must increase the fire, and the operation turns into **ash** <note>original: "cinerem"</note>; once turned to ash, the sweat and liquefaction are returned to the ash itself through a greater intensity of heat. Thus, through this portion of the water, the **King is crowned** for the fourth and last time, and finally, one arrives at a **redness** <term>rubedo: the final, most perfect stage of the Great Work</term> such as is found in saffron or dried blood. Regarding this red, we say with Simon: *This is the spirit which we seek, so that with it we may tinge any body, and naturally lead whatever is diminished from perfection to its natural completion.*

Hitherto I have set down what is approved by the sayings of the Philosophers; from now on, however, I shall subjoin things only from the notes of the Master whom you know well, and which I heard him confirm with his own living voice, and in the manner I describe. For he asserted that with this **red elixir**, or with this tinging spirit, **malleable glass**—that is, glass that is not fragile—could be made so that it might be hammered. Furthermore, from common crystal, a **carbuncle** <note>a deep red gemstone, like a ruby or garnet</note> could be made using a small quantity of this elixir of ours; for instance, if the crystal is mixed in an operation of the planets, specifically one weight in 1,000 pounds of **mercury** <term>☿: the alchemical symbol for mercury, representing the fluid, transformative spirit</term>, and each part of this (namely the 1,000) into another 1,000, until the said number is completed (namely 1,000,000), which is to proceed almost into infinity according to Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note>. And these are those two extraordinary things, namely concerning glass and crystal, which I said at the beginning I would explain.

...therefore, it is not so easily to be proven or believed unless experience precedes it. For what reason could be assigned in this matter that might lead one to believe such a marvel? For the Master spoke thus:

> Since man is the most worthy of creatures, for whose sake all things were devised and to whom all are subject, and whose body is beyond any price, as every thing divine or human testifies. This medicine, when taken in youth, removes old age, and in old age conserves a healthy and long life, by expelling all languors from the body and preserving it from impending infirmities.

He asserted and attested that our **elixir** <term>elixir: the supreme alchemical preparation, also called the Philosopher's Stone, capable of both transmuting metals and healing the body</term> works beyond the medicines, potions, or any concoctions of Galen, Hippocrates, Avicenna, and all other philosophers. Thus, in the bodies of the sick—which have natural heat and motion within themselves, ready and appointed to expel all superfluities—this medicine will expel any nurtured or fostered languor. 

This medicine, when applied gradually in preparations, protects so that no disease may come to the person in the future. Thus, everyone should be mindful of what is common knowledge among the nations: for the great nobles seek to preserve their health and youth for themselves by adding filed gold to their own specific antidotes and concoctions. There are four species which pertain to the work of the Elixir: namely, Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum," or mercury</note>, yellow fleeing living sulfur <note>original: "Sulphur vivum citrinum fugiens"; "living" means native or unrefined sulfur, and "fleeing" refers to its volatility when heated</note>, green sulfur—that is, Vitriol <note>Iron or copper sulfate, often used as a source of sulfuric acid</note>—and white fixed sulfur, which is Saltpeter <note>original: "sal petræ," or potassium nitrate</note>; and it is necessary that these species be fresh and select, not consumed by age or poor storage. Nevertheless, all these things, according to the said Philosopher, are "one thing" after they are joined to one another. Wherefore it is concluded that the operation or creation of this Elixir contains within itself all things previously mentioned; the composition of this elixir is as follows. And just as the aforementioned Author testifies that he completed the work in the space of seven days, from the first to the last, so by the grace of God I have decided to set down the said work here in order.

Take 12 ounces of choice vitriol <note>Iron or copper sulfate, used here to produce sulfuric acid vapors</note>, and three drachms each of saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note> and cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide</note>; let them all be ground together with strong rubbing, as finely as possible, so that it becomes a single fine powder. Let the said powder be placed in a urinal <note>a glass vessel shaped like a bladder, commonly used in distillation</note>, or in a glass gourd <note>term: <term>cucurbita</term>—the bottom part of a still</note> well-sealed with lute <note>original: "perlutata"; a paste of clay, dung, or flour used to airtight-seal laboratory glass</note>. Place the alembic <note>the "head" or cap of the still</note> on top, and let them be well-sealed together either with paste or with linen cloth, so that the material has no breathing-hole. Position the said gourd among ashes to the thickness of one finger all around, and let a slow fire be made beneath for six or eight hours so that the phlegmatic water <note>original: "aqua phlegmatica"; the watery, inactive first distillate</note> may come out. Let the first sixteen drops fall before it is collected.

A certain sign that the phlegmatic water has finished coming out is this: a man should place a slightly heated knife under the nose of the alembic and wait until one drop falls upon the knife; if it boils and turns black, then the phlegmatic water has departed and ended, and the water following it is to be collected. If this does not happen, one must wait until it does, and afterward all the water is to be collected entirely in a clean receiver <note>original: "receptaculum"</note>. See well that the receiver is well-fitted and joined to the nose of the alembic. Strengthen the fire moderately and gently until the alembic is well-reddened and the drops are slowed in their exit; then let the fire be given with a flame for six hours or thereabouts, until nothing more distills and the redness of the alembic fades; then it is done.

And note that four vessels ought to be placed at the fire at one and the same time with the aforesaid species from which the water is to be composed, and in each vessel there shall be similar weights—except in one vessel, from which the water is extracted in which gold must be dissolved. The first weights vary somewhat from the weights previously mentioned at the beginning of this chapter. These are the weights of the species which enter into the making of the water in which gold is to be dissolved: Take 12 drachms of the purest fresh vitriol, no more and no less, because its weight is always equal in the making of all these waters. Then take nine ounces of white sulfur—that is, saltpeter—and nine ounces of red earth—that is, cinnabar. Let them all be ground finely and mixed with one another, and placed in one well-sealed urinal. Let the urinal be of such capacity that half of it is—

Place the alembic <note>the "head" or cap of the still</note> on top, so that the openings of the alembics enter the mouths of the urinals <note>glass flasks</note>, and let them be joined well with a linen cloth and paste or the sealant of the mastery <note>original: "luto magisterii"; a specialized alchemical paste used for airtight seals</note>. Then this water must be carefully poured off and saved, and other water of the same power and strength poured over the said red powder; and thus always use three times as much water by weight as there is of gold filings. Let it stand again among hot ashes for two hours, and it will be dissolved in part or in whole. If this does not happen, pour this [water] off and put in new [water] again, and the whole will be dissolved by the grace of God, if the order is followed as previously described.

And note, that gold is dissolved much more easily by means of a small quantity of sal ammoniac <note>original: "salis armoniaci"; ammonium chloride, often used to create *aqua regia*</note>, but the author of this book completely forbids sal ammoniac to be added in this work, because he says that sal ammoniac infects and consumes all bodies <note>refers to the "bodies" of metals</note>; for it destroys and corrupts their radical moisture <note>term: <term>humorem radicalem</term>—the essential, life-sustaining fluid thought to exist within metals</note>, therefore he forbids its entry into this work.

Furthermore, a great secret is to be noted here, of which the author speaks regarding the composition of all these aforementioned waters. When you wish to make any of those previously named waters, see well at the beginning that the fire is so slow that the species do not melt in any way until all the phlegmatic water has been distilled. For before the species are melted by the power of the fire, they emit watery "sweats" and vapors with a gentle heat, which ascend to the alembic and form drops like a clear tear; and this watery moisture is called phlegm.

### ALCHEMICAL PRACTICE

And note, that if it happens that the substances <term>species; the chemical ingredients</term> melt before the separation of this phlegm <note>the watery, low-potency byproduct of distillation</note>, know that this phlegm can never be separated from the "good water" <note>the potent acid</note>. In this case, the water would lose its power and perish, and the craftsman would fall into error, never obtaining the desired end because of the water's weakness. Regarding this, the Author of the present work testifies that after he reached the state of this secret, he completed in seven days what he previously could scarcely finish in eighty days. He also says that he later labored with arsenic, sulfur, and other things for seven years and found nothing. Nevertheless, he advises that no one should undertake to complete this work in such a short space of time unless they have first become experienced in all the matters mentioned above. Now I have recited the secrets of this work in part, and how gold is prepared and dissolved through the power of the aforementioned water.

Now I shall speak of the other three waters of the first composition. Let each water be taken by itself in its own receiver, because one part contains as much power as the other. In the first part of the water, let two drachms <note>a small unit of weight</note> of pure calcined <term>calcined; reduced to a powder by heat</term> silver <term>argentum; the alchemical Moon</term> be dissolved. In the second part of the water, let two drachms of raw mercury <term>mercurius; quicksilver</term>, well washed, be dissolved. And in the third quantity of said waters, let two drachms of well-powdered cinnabar <term>cinobrium; a bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide</term> be dissolved. See that all the aforementioned are dissolved well and purely without dregs. And however much silver is dissolved here in one quantity of those waters, the same amount of gold must be dissolved in its own water (which was spoken of above), neither more nor less. 

And note that the Author says that in the composition of either elixir—both the white and the red—it is absolutely necessary to apply both the ferment of the Sun <term>Sol; gold</term> and the ferment of the Moon <term>Luna; silver</term>. Otherwise, a true generation will never occur, because by the ferment of the Moon, the "female seed" is understood, and by the ferment of the Sun, the "male seed" is understood. From these, the union <note>original: "coitus"</note> first occurs, and then true generation follows, for our Blessed Stone <term>Lapis benedictus; the Philosopher's Stone</term> is impregnated by these seeds. Concerning this, Hermes says:

> Its father is the Sun, and its mother is the Moon.
<note>original: "Eius pater est Sol, Mater vero Luna"; a famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, emphasizing the dual nature of the chemical work.</note>

Once this is done, let all the aforementioned waters be joined together immediately: both the waters in which the gold was dissolved and the remaining waters in which the other substances were dissolved. See that each vessel is half-full. This can be checked through the hole in the lid of the vessel with the iron wire. The present author says that the first beginning of this work is winter, whenever it is started, and he assigns the reason for the comparison. This work—namely the crushing or grinding <term>trituratio; the mechanical breakdown of materials</term> of the species—is called **Winter** by the philosophers through a similarity: just as it is seen that winter is destitute of all fruit and active natural virtue, so this work of grinding still seems to be, and is, destitute of any active operation of the elixir, because as of yet nothing of the aforementioned substances has been mixed. Thus it is clear that it always begins in winter, and every time is the "winter of the elixir." When the time of winter is complete and finished in the grinding of the said species, the work of composition and the mixing of the said species by the hands of the Artist immediately begins. This is called the work of **Spring** because just as natural things are naturally united in spring to bear fruit, so every single thing from which the elixir is generated or composed is united in this work to bear fruit or generate the philosopher's stone. ...and the Artisan will not err, unless he chooses to wander from the path and the order of the things described above.

I have spoken above, in the best and shortest way I could, how this renowned and most excellent work must be begun, carried out, and completed, so that through its power—and with the assistance of divine grace—the sick and infirm metallic bodies <note>In alchemy, base metals like lead or tin were considered "sick" or "imperfect" versions of gold.</note> may be cured, so that they arrive at the full maturation and perfection of true **gold-making** <note>original: "solifici"; literally "sun-making," referring to the production of gold</note> or **silver-making** <note>original: "lunifici"; literally "moon-making," referring to the production of silver</note>, and be purged of their **leprosy** <note>original: "leprositate"; a common alchemical term for the impurities or corrosion found in base metals</note>, and remain meanwhile fully perfected, better than all other minerals. Now it remains to see how, with this medicine, sick and infirm human bodies may be cured, so that all **superfluities** <note>Excess or unbalanced humors that were believed to cause disease.</note> may be purged and deleted from them, such that the old and the decrepit—namely those destitute of natural heat—may be relieved and recreated, to such an extent that they may arrive at a youthful appearance and strength. Likewise, every kind of leprosy may be evacuated, regardless of its type or how it drew its origin from the **complexion** <term>complexionis; the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within an individual</term>; and it not only evacuates and roots out one kind, or two, or three kinds of infirmities, but it roots out and expels all kinds of infirmity from the human body. Furthermore, it restores, strengthens, and confirms the lost nature and natural color, the practice of which perfection follows here.

Take of the best wine, white or red as you prefer, which is clear and limpid without dregs, and put it in a clean glass or copper **gourd** <term>cucurbita; the lower, bulbous vessel of a distillation apparatus</term>, and place your gourd with the **alembic** <term>alembicum; the "cap" or still-head that fits onto the gourd to collect and condense vapors</term> set on top, among hot ashes. Know well how much wine you put in, because it is necessary that the whole be separated into five parts, as will be distinguished below. For the fourth part of the water which is distilled from this wine is worth nothing at all, because it is entirely **phlegm** <note>In this context, "phlegm" refers to the watery, non-alcoholic portion of the distillate which lacks medicinal power.</note>, lacking the spirit of the **fifth essence** <term>quintæ essentiæ; the "quintessence" or pure spirit (alcohol) extracted from organic matter</term>, and therefore it is to be thrown away. Know truly that the fifth part of the whole remains in the dregs; therefore, three parts of the whole are to be kept or taken, and no more. The reason why the fourth part is not kept is because—just as was aforesaid in the previous work—the phlegmatic water is the first which comes out in order, so it must be understood here that the corrupting and infecting phlegmatic water is the *last* which comes out in order <note>The author is noting a difference in distillation order compared to earlier processes: here, the valuable spirit comes over first, and the useless water comes last.</note>. Thus it is clear that the extraction of this water takes the opposite order of the extraction of the first water treated above. Therefore, it must be considered here how much wine is put in, for the whole must be divided into five parts: the first part of the three parts of water is the strongest, worthiest, and most noble, since it contains more of the spirit of the fifth essence; the second is less strong; and the third is even less strong than the second; but the fourth is worth nothing at all. Therefore...

# MASTER ORTHOLANUS
<note>original: "Magistri Ortholani"; likely referring to Ortholanus, a 14th-century alchemist known for his commentaries on the Emerald Tablet.</note>

It must be considered that the parts should be divided equally, so that one part does not have more in quantity than another, and that each part is kept cleanly in its own vessel; the method of separation is as follows.

Take as much of the stated wine as you wish, as I have described above; let it be fitted into a suitable vessel and placed among hot ashes for distillation. Let the water that comes out be received in a clean **receiver** <note>original: "receptaculo"; the vessel used to collect the distillate</note>. When a fifth part has been distilled, then remove that receiver with its water, and place another in its spot at the **beak of the alembic** <term>nasum alembici; the downward-pointing spout of the still's head through which the vapor condenses and drips</term>. When an equal amount is distilled again—that is, when it can be estimated that another fifth part of the whole has been distilled—then set aside that receiver with its water and apply another, namely a third vessel, to the beak of the alembic. Let a third part of the whole be received in that receiver, and let a fourth also be received; then let [the fourth] be cast away immediately, for it is worth nothing. 

However, these three preceding waters are called **burning waters** <note>original: "aquæ ardentes"; early terms for distilled alcohol or brandy</note>. The first is stronger than the second, and the second stronger than the third, according to how much more of the **spirit of the fifth essence** <term>spiritu quintæ essentiæ; the most purified and potent form of a substance, believed to be a celestial element</term> each one possesses compared to the others. These aforementioned waters are called "burning" because if a linen cloth is soaked in them and brought near a fire, it immediately catches flame, yet the cloth is not consumed. This is because of the **phlegm** <term>flegma; in distillation, this refers to the watery, non-alcoholic residue or impurities</term> that is within them; for each of them still contains a portion of phlegm, and this phlegm must be separated in this way:

Let each part be placed by itself for one distillation, and let them be distilled with a moderate fire, not too strong. When it is observed that a third part of each of them has been distilled, then separate the receiver from the alembic, and let a fourth part distill and be cast away. Afterward, let these three waters be joined together, since they are partially improved, and let them be distilled again in a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbita; a gourd-shaped chemical vessel used as the base of a still</term>. Here also, let a fourth part of the whole be separated and cast away, just as was noted before in all other operations for the composition of this water. 

Now you have the **rectified water of life** <note>original: "aquam vitæ rectificatam"; "rectified" means purified through repeated distillation</note>, which is the water that dissolves **mercury** <note>original: "mercurium"; likely referring to its use as a powerful alchemical solvent</note>. And if a linen cloth is soaked in it and brought near a fire, it catches flame and *is* consumed. This is the certain sign of perfection. But if it is not yet of such great power that it can do this, let it be distilled again, always setting aside the fourth part, until that sign occurs; then it is the perfected **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitæ"</note>. 

And it is said that the **second stone**—namely the **vegetable stone** <note>original: "lapis vegetabilis"; a branch of alchemy focusing on substances derived from plants rather than minerals</note>—is contained in this water and in its dregs from which it was drawn, after it is prepared in the proper manner. However, because it would be a long task to tell this entire story, and its usefulness is not of great value, I cease to put its composition here. Nor should this water be prepared so universally if the dregs themselves did not also need to be purified and prepared.

### ALCHEMICAL PRACTICE.

And because in a certain book, which by the grace of God I am about to write for you, I propose to describe all things universally, I therefore omit for the present, on account of the length of the discourse, the composition of the said **stone** <note>original: "lapis"; the "Philosopher's Stone" or a similar alchemical catalyst</note>, and I return to our purpose—what should be done with the said water—according to the intention of the often-named author.

The most precious **secret of secrets** <note>original: "Arcanum arcanorum"</note>, exceeding all other secrets, and showing itself most excellent and most illustrious above them, and truly and deservedly the beginning of the secrets of making and composing the **water of life** <term>aqua vitae; literally "water of life," referring to highly concentrated distilled alcohol used as a solvent for medicines</term>, I weigh out to you, reverend father, in these words. Take the aforesaid **rectified** <term>rectificatam; purified by repeated distillation</term> water of life, as was said, in whatever quantity pleases you, and place into it bit by bit, part after part, some of the aforesaid perfected stone, as much as it can dissolve. And in that solution, burning or flaming golden sparks will emerge, and as many colors will appear as can be imagined. And when the colors have ceased to appear and the water has become clear, then it will be golden, or a clear, limpid, and serene reddish-gold. This is the perfected water of life and a true bodily medicine, prevailing over the medicines of **Galen**, **Avicenna**, **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Galeni, Avicennæ, Hypocratis"; the three most authoritative figures in medieval medicine</note>, and all other physicians, powerfully extirpating, eradicating, evacuating, and expelling all infirmities from the human body. 

And if an infirmity has lasted for a hundred years, it shall be perfectly cured in one month; and if it has lasted fifty years, it shall be perfectly cured within fifteen days. And if any infirmity has lasted for 20 years, it shall be perfectly cured in the space of eight days. And if any infirmity has lasted in the human body for seven years, it shall be cured within three days. And if any infirmity has lasted for one year, it shall be cured in one day. And this truly seems to be the secret of secrets, the virtue of which cannot be bought, and it is deservedly called the **blessed stone** <note>original: "lapis benedictus"</note>, because there has been nothing more precious in this world given by God Most High to men. 

And the medicine should be taken thus: let one draught of good wine be taken according to the strength and appetite of the patient, and let one drop of the aforementioned water of life be placed in that draught; if the patient is gravely ill, let two drops be added, and no more at one time. Let it be warmed a little by the fire, and the medicine will immediately begin to mix with the wine; and when they have been perfectly mixed, then let the draught be offered to the patient. And he shall recover in the name of the Lord and be saved by the grace of God; and this shall be done every third or fourth day until the patient is made safe and sound. This same medicine can also be taken in whatever **confection** <term>confectio; a medicinal preparation made by mixing drugs with sugar, syrup, or honey</term> pleases the patient, in the event that the patient is weak or feverish and cannot drink wine; then the medicine is to be given with some confection suitable to the patient, yet following the stated proportion and observing the dose in all things.

# THE TEACHINGS OF MASTER ORTHOLANUS

...so that with the true and universal practice, the artisan may more easily be able to gather the specific practice.

In the name of God the most high, pious, and merciful, let **strong water** <term>aqua fortis; typically nitric acid or a powerful solvent used to dissolve metals</term> be made from the aforementioned species, namely from green sulfur, white sulfur, and red earth—made from **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; mercury</term> and sulfur—observing the proper weights in the composition of all the waters, both for the "red" and for the "white," just as was clearly enough stated above in the first specific practice. 

In the water made for the **white** <note>The "White Work" or *albedo* aims to create silver or the white elixir</note>, two ounces of white earth—that is, **nelu** <note>original: "nelu"; an alchemical cover-name for a specific white substance, likely a purified salt or silver compound</note>—shall be dissolved. In the other water made for the **red** <note>The "Red Work" or *rubedo* aims to create gold or the red elixir</note>, two ounces of red earth—that is, **filos** <note>original: "filos"; a cover-name for a red substance, likely a gold compound or antimony</note>—shall be dissolved. Once these are dissolved and turned into a clear water, take half of each water and keep the other part in its vessels until the proper time. Mix them together **in the smallest parts** <note>original: "per minima"; an alchemical term meaning to mix substances at the most fundamental, atomic level</note>.
<margin>1</margin>
This entire mixture is called the **Elixir**, and it truly contains within itself the four elements. Regarding this, we read in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "it is necessary that the thing be **elixated** <term>elixare; to boil or thoroughly refine</term> before it enters our mastery." To "elixate" means to make a dry thing moist, or to dissolve a dry thing into moisture; and thus this Elixir is understood. 

However, this is not yet the **True Elixir**, because the True Elixir "elixates" in an hour; it softens the metal bodies, and whatever in them is coarse or impure, it makes subtle and pure, and converts it to its own nature, as will be shown below. It is still asked why two bodies are dissolved here for one Elixir, since philosophers commonly say there are two Elixirs: namely one for the white and another for the red. And the Elixir for the white is made from a white body, and the Elixir for the red is made from a red body. 

To this I respond by saying that the True Elixir is composed of many things, yet after the union or unification of those things, they all become one single thing. Hence the excellent philosopher Ortholanus says that there are two parts of our Elixir: the first part is white, which is made from the white earth, and the second part is red, which is made from the red earth. Thus there appear to be two Elixirs, one for the white and another for the red, when in truth it is not so. In reality, these two parts make nothing but a single elixir, which serves both: namely, first for the white, and later the same—and no other—is brought to the red in the same vessel. This is because the true **Impregnation of the Stone** <note>The "marriage" of chemical principles to produce the Philosopher's Stone</note> does not occur except from the seed of the father and the mother. The mother’s seed is made from the white earth, while the father’s seed is made from the red earth. On this point, Hermes, the father of philosophers, concludes, saying:

> *Our stone is a strong staining spirit, whose father is the sun and whose mother is the moon.* <note>original: "Lapis noster est spiritus fortis tingens, cujus pater est sol, mater vero luna"; a reference to the famous Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus</note>

And why does Hermes say that our stone is a strong staining spirit, if not because our "bodies" are here made spiritual through universal solution, and are **altered**...

Then he took out the said gourd with its medicine, and found his medicine partially dissolved or liquefied. He immediately removed the cover of the gourd and left the gourd open to the air in a clean and suitable place where no uncleanness could fall in, nor rain—which must be completely avoided. He says that in a short time the whole was dissolved and converted into a **thick oil** without dregs <note>original: "fecibus"; the waste or sediment remaining after a process</note>, and this is the true and perfect dissolution. He used this method and no other, and in it he found the power. Once the solution was made, he placed the vessel with the oil over ashes and administered a gentle fire, like the heat of the sun in summer, and placed a fine linen cloth over the mouth of the vessel so that no ashes or uncleanness might fall in. Then he let it stand until it was entirely thickened and coagulated. Afterward, he repeated this dissolution three more times...

Once the arrangement of the blackness is completed and the regime of the earth is finished, as has been said, one must come to the arrangement of the whiteness of the earth of the blessed stone. For it must be noted that in this blackness of the earth, whiteness is hidden; therefore, it is black to the sight, but white to the intellect. Because of this, that which lies hidden within it must be made to appear on the outside, and that which is on the outside shall be made to be within.

Thus, the blackness of this earth, which is now on the exterior, shall become the interior, and the whiteness, which is interior, shall become the exterior; in this way, the hidden is made manifest, and the manifest is hidden. This arrangement is performed in the same vessel and without removing the aforementioned earth from it, in the following manner. Our aforementioned doctor knew the weight through his skill, and he placed it in his vessel in the open air until it was resolved into a thick oil, just as it was before its coagulation. Then he poured over it half of its water—that which he had extracted from it without any impregnation—and he placed a blind alembic <note>An "alembic" is the cooling lid of a still; a "blind" one has no spout, forcing the steam to condense and fall back down, a process called reflux</note> over it as was previously described. He sealed it well so that it could not breathe <note>meaning it was hermetically sealed to prevent evaporation</note>, and placed it under warm dung, inspecting his vessel every eighth day until the whole became one single substance. And note what he himself says: that this order of dissolutions can be done just as well among warm ashes as in horse dung, and that he himself sometimes performed this dissolution over ashes for the reason that he considered this "dissolution of Mercury" to be done more rapidly and more quickly than the other in dung. However, I do not doubt that the dissolution made under dung is better and more useful than that among ashes. Then, once the dissolution was finished, he removed the cover of the vessel—namely, the blind alembic—and placed another alembic...

### MASTER ORTHOLANUS

...the blessed and perfect red [stone], the father of every <note>original: 'telesmi'; a term from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus meaning 'perfection,' 'completion,' or 'miracle'</note> miracle, and of every secret or treasure of this world, which God grants to whom He wills and withdraws from others. Many are called to the perfection of its discovery, but few are found chosen for the effect of its perfection. And if a few do find this sublime art, it is because our art is reserved within the power of God; it comes from the gift of God and His grace, after many errors, and with immense labor and expense.

Therefore, let the most high Creator of all be praised, who created the same thing for the white stage and the same thing for the red stage—namely, those whitened and reddened things which are made one through "marriage" and composition, as has been stated. And this was revealed by God’s grace to a certain man searching for this renowned science, while he was wandering in the error of his own investigation.

Now that all these things regarding the creation of our <term>blessed stone</term> <note>The 'Lapis Benedictus' or Philosopher's Stone</note> have been determined: it remains to briefly recap all the regimes <note>The 'regimes' are the specific stages or 'reigns' of different chemical/symbolic states</note> in a single series of words, so that these dispersed ideas may more easily be gathered and retained in the heart. The form of this recapitulation is added here: Take two ounces each of the two "earths," namely the white and the red, and dissolve the white earth in its own water, and the red earth also in its own water. Then take half of each part, set each aside by itself, and join these two parts together, shaking the vessel well by hand until they are thoroughly mixed. This mixture is called the <term>Elixir</term>. You should place this matter in a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped glass vessel used for boiling or distilling</note>, with an <term>alembic</term> <note>A still-head or cap that fits onto the cucurbit to catch vapors</note> well-fitted on top as taught above. It is situated in warm <term>horse manure</term> <note>original: 'fimo equino'; a standard source of gentle, consistent laboratory heat</note>, and let the phlegmatic <note>watery or dull</note> water be evacuated. Then, let a clean receiver be joined to the "nose" of the alembic and allowed to stand until the water has distilled, the stone has thickened, and it has turned to a black color, appearing somewhat transparent in the break. Then, determine the weight through your own skill, and pour over it half of its weight of that same water extracted from it. Close the cucurbit tightly with a <note>original: 'alembico caeco'; a 'blind' alembic is a still-head without an exit spout, used for refluxing or circulating vapors back into the liquid</note> blind alembic, and again place it under horse manure for a month at least, or for forty days at most.

And note that this timeframe of days is not set here because other dissolutions would also take so much time, but only for this specific dissolution alone. For it is to be feared in this first stage that if the water is to be drawn away from the matter through the alembic, the entire matter might rise together through the alembic, because the <note>original: 'luminaria'; the Sun and Moon, representing Gold and Silver</note> luminaries are "philosophically dissolved" and therefore volatile. It must be reasoned, therefore, that the first solution is the most difficult; the second and third are...

# THE NEW LIGHT OF THE EXPERIENCED 
# YOUTH BEGINS, etc.

->*Reverend Father and Lord, although I remain ignorant of the liberal sciences, etc.*<-

## HERE BEGINS THE TREATISE IN WHICH 
## he names the Philosophers' Stone.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a figure or landscape scene.</image-desc>

UNDERSTAND, therefore, the saying of the Philosopher: that the actions of active things take place in a pre-disposed subject <note>original: 'patiente prædisposito'</note>. By this, it is understood that the Elixir <term>Elixir</term><note>The transformative substance sought by alchemists to change metals or prolong life</note> cannot be made except from matter having a perfect disposition for it. I testify to you that such a capability exists in the matter from which, by my own hands and witnessed by my own eyes—though by another's teaching, as I said before—the elixir was made, converting Saturn <note>The alchemical name for lead</note> into gold, that is, into the Sun <note>The alchemical symbol for gold</note>. This matter I have already named for you: it is the magnesia of the Philosophers <note>original: 'Philosophorum magnesies'; not modern magnesium, but a secret 'first matter'</note>, from which the Philosophers extracted gold hidden in its body, and in which they found quicksilver <note>Mercury</note> from quicksilver and sulfur from sulfur. It is a stone in appearance and in action, but in its nature, it does not imitate the natures of a common stone. For this reason, it is called the "stone that is not a stone" <note>original: 'lapis, non lapis'; a famous alchemical paradox</note>, and it is our "quicksilver" mentioned in the mixture, not quicksilver in its ordinary nature. We are still within nature, to which it is led through the ore. But our quicksilver exists in the nature to which our craftsmanship leads it. This is our "bronze" <note>original: 'æs'</note> from which the true tincture <term>tincture</term><note>A potent liquid or powder used to 'stain' or transform the properties of a metal</note> is made, from which the marriage of Gabricus and Beia <note>original: 'Chabrichim & Veijæ'; symbolic figures representing the union of the solar/male and lunar/female principles</note> is formed. In this marriage is the King with his wife, and these things that commend them are within the bronze itself, as the instruction will make clearer through the operation. This is the spirit by which we dye, and it is the body spoken of in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: 'Turba Philosophorum'; one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>. This is the path called "quicksilver." Therefore, it is obtained from liquefied bodies—not by common melting, but by that which lasts as long as the spouses are united in true marriage, namely, until the whitening <note>albedo</note>. This is the stone found on the mountain tops, and it is rightly called mineral. It is also said to be animal when it possesses a soul. For this reason, it is said in the *Assembly* that bronze, like a human, has a body and a soul. Likewise, everything that has a spirit also has blood—

...perfection of the natural philosopher, scripture now commands, saying: "It rises gently with great ingenuity from the earth to the sky." <note>original: 'suaviter cum magno ingenio ascendit à terra in coelum'; a famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus</note> Likewise, know that when it is mixed with the body, it becomes one with it, and turns the body itself into spirit. And Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century chemist; here referring to the *Summa Perfectionis*</note> commands the same in the chapter on the medicine of the third order, and all the Philosophers cry out the same; and this work is called by the Philosophers "washing" <term>ablutio</term><note>A process of purification or cleansing the matter</note>, through which *achilefne* <note>original: 'achilefne'; a technical term likely derived from Arabic, referring to the joining or purification of substances in the vessel</note> occurs, since in the rising, both ascend into smoke or the spirit of smoke. And because this matter also liquefies while it ascends, it is clear that it is of the nature of warm water. For that which liquefies and is coagulated by cold, and when it is stripped of superfluities, is washed, imbibed, and [joined] by its own water—namely, the aforementioned spirit proceeding from that same germ—this, therefore, is the physical dissolution which is accomplished by fire.

->*whiteness.*<-

Therefore, a furnace <term>furnus</term> of such a disposition must be made, that in it a slow fire may be administered, which cannot be increased. And the vessel <term>vas</term> containing the matter must be made of glass, covered by an iron vessel of the same shape, split through the middle; and it ought to be a vessel one cubit long, narrow at the top, so that the structure allows nothing of the spirit to exhale, and its length may precipitate the smokes, if any happen to be raised, and consume the corrupting humidities within itself. The vision of this furnace and vessel should be sought from the "Lily" <note>original: 'lilii visio'; likely referring to an illustration in a text titled 'The Lily of the Philosophers' rather than written instructions</note> rather than from writing; and the heat must circulate around the vessel from every side, so that there is equality of heat everywhere; otherwise, it would be called a "bath" in vain. And at the top of the furnace there must be a hole, through which should emerge a round and long piece of glass, closing the orifice of the said vessel; by the touch of this piece, it is known if the matter is being cooked by a suitable heat. And if by chance any smoke should be seen to rise within the already mentioned vessel, the arranged dose <term>dosin</term><note>The specific measurement or proportion of matter being treated</note> does not allow it to exhale, however much the vessel might even be held open. Wherefore it is said by Geber that one is never truly separated from the other, although to the sight it may seem to be segregated or separated superficially, nor can one exist without the other; for their spirits are tempered through the way of nature so perfectly that they are not separated from one another.

<header>LIGHT OF THE YOUTH</header>

<margin>Matter below.</margin>
In this degree of heat, nature is made black, because the acting heat produces blackness in the moist substance. Therefore, it is said in the *Turba* <note>original: 'Turba'; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or 'Assembly of the Philosophers,' a foundational 12th-century Latin alchemical text</note>: "When you see blackness hanging over that water, know that the body has now been liquefied." Likewise, in the first stage of the work, all things are blackened. This result, however, occurs so that too much fire may be avoided; for forced heat causes the composition to perish and be pulled apart. Therefore, it must be pursued with a tempered fire, and cooked down just as a child is nourished with milk <note>A common alchemical metaphor for applying gentle, consistent heat</note>. In this, all the philosophers agree, and this is also shown in the practical work concerning the different colors contained within the black color.

### *On the Degree of Fire upon the Arrival of Blackness.*

When indeed everything is black, the fire of the same degree is maintained until the whiteness, hidden in its belly, appears. For in this way, the fixed substance approaches. It should be noted, however, that many colors appear in the blackness itself, which the Philosophers do not mention. For sometimes the whole becomes green, sometimes livid, sometimes of a violet color; sometimes it is even green on one side of the vessel and black or livid on the other, or green on the outside and livid on the inside. Nevertheless, all these colors are understood to be part of the black stage; and since no essential perfection exists in them, the Philosophers principally name only three among the other colors—namely, those which are called the "virtues of the soul": black, white, and red.

Therefore, in the *Turba*, we "venerate the king and his wife" <note>Symbolic language for the solar/masculine and lunar/feminine principles or chemicals like sulfur and mercury</note>; do not burn them, lest you drive them away with too much fire, since you do not know when you will need those who improve the king and his wife. Cook them so that they become black, then white, then red; then let the staining agent become a "poison" <term>venenum</term> <note>In this context, 'poison' refers to a potent, transformative elixir that 'penetrates' and changes the metal</note>. Likewise, let the white stone be made by combustion and moisture or liquefaction. Through the water, "mortification" <term>mortificatio</term> <note>The symbolic death or breakdown of the material to prepare it for rebirth</note> is said to follow, which appears in the first arrival of blackness. In this mortification, the spirits are united—that is, they are dried out—because unless the bodies are dried out, the colors of the soul (which are called the "blackness" and the "cloud") do not appear.

Likewise, Magnesia <note>original: 'Magnesies'; a cryptic name for the base matter of the stone</note>, when it is whitened, does not allow the spirit to escape, because nature contains nature. Therefore, the moisture which took care of the blackness during the cooking shows itself to be dried out when the white color begins to appear. For in the transformation of the blackness, before it was perfectly whitened, I saw a dusky whiteness which is commonly called the "brown color" <term>brunicies</term> <note>A transitional stage between black and white</note>. This brownness is afterwards made into true whiteness. At that time, while the brownness lasted, my master broke the vessel and the stone and inspected it inside and out; he found it brown on the outside, but inside there was still blackness, the cause of which he assigned to me—namely, that...

# EXPERIENCED ANEW.

The parts of the matter clinging to the sides of the vessel felt the heat near them more than the matter in the center. Therefore, they began to change color more quickly, and he told me that this brownness was rising because the <term>albedo</term> <note>whiteness; the second major stage of the alchemical work</note> was being drawn out from the belly of its <term>nigredo</term> <note>blackness; the initial stage of decay or 'putrefaction'</note>, as is said in the *Turba* <note>original: 'Turba'; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or 'Assembly of the Philosophers,' a famous alchemical dialogue</note>. For when you see it born, know that its whiteness is hidden in the belly of the blackness that first appears. And then you must extract that whiteness from its most subtle blackness. Do not wonder, however, that he still calls this matter a "stone." 
<margin>Why it is called a stone. As long as it is hard.</margin>
For you should know that as long as the whiteness lasts, and even after it has taken on the <term>rubedo</term> <note>redness; the final stage of the process representing perfection</note>, it remains hard for a long time and the spirit resides in a strong mass, until by the continuation of the <term>decoction</term> <note>the process of steady heating or "cooking"</note> it begins to break down by itself and rise up a little.

->*The cooking of the second degree follows, up to the redness, etc.*<-

When this stone has thus let go of its blackness, the degree of fire is changed, and it is placed in another furnace of subtle design, in which a stronger cooking is applied to heat the vessel and the matter all around. It must be cooked there, for then it receives the true whiteness, with which it is cooked in that same place until, the whiteness having been transformed, it is seen to take on a redness. Care must be taken, however, that this fire is not more intense than its degree requires, for in that white color, the body and spirit are joined by nature. And if the cooking were given in excess beyond what is due to its degree, the united parts would be separated. For this reason, it is said in the *Turba*: "Cook carefully, lest they turn into smoke and perish." It becomes yellowed <note>original: 'citrinatur'</note>, however, when it is transformed from a white color into a red one. The yellow color <note>often called <term>citrinatio</term></note> is the middle between white and red; it must appear before the true redness. The Philosophers have spoken of this practice, saying: "The spirit and the soul are not united except in the white color," because then all the colors that can be imagined in the world appear and are fixed, and then they meet in a single color, namely whiteness. For the <term>dealbatio</term> <note>whitening or bleaching</note> is the foundation of the entire work, nor does it vary from there into different colors (that is, "true" or stable colors) except into the red, which is the ultimate end. For the yellowing that occurs between white and red should not be called a color in its perfection. All the things I have said before are proven through these means, which the experience of the work also demonstrated to me to be true.

# LIGHT OF YOUTH

### The third degree of cooking follows, up to calcination.

And while it begins to turn red, it is placed to be cooked in another furnace by applying a stronger degree of fire, until it enjoys a true redness both inside and out. The sign of this is a breaking apart <note>original: "diruptio"; refers to the matter crumbling or fracturing as it dries out</note> and the aforementioned rising up, about which it is said in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "after the whiteness, you cannot go wrong." For when the fire is increased after the whiteness but before the redness, one arrives at incineration <note>original: "cinerationem"</note>. Likewise, seeing that eminent whiteness, one might think that the redness is hidden within that whiteness. It is then necessary to extract it—or rather, to cook it—until the whole becomes red. 

And if you are left with any doubt as to why the whiteness is extracted from the "belly of the blackness," while the redness is not extracted from the whiteness (even though it becomes red through cooking), I declare it to you in this way: while the blackness lasts, the matter remains, and it is moist in nature. This moisture shows itself to be dried out when the whiteness appears; indeed, the whiteness never appears until the corrupting moistures are entirely consumed. For these two reasons, it can be said that while it turns red, nothing is wasted, but it is merely cooked; and through strong <term>decoction</term> <note>the process of boiling or heating a substance to extract its essence or ripen it</note> the unchangeable red color appears, in which is perfection. Therefore, in the *Assembly*, when the compound is turned into a "red spirit," it becomes the principle of the world. Likewise, the dyeing and life-giving spirit is let in after the corrupting moisture has departed—which is to say, only after the whitening or <term>albedo</term> <note>the second major stage of the Great Work, associated with purification</note> has been reached. Therefore, when this red color appears, nature reveals its hidden perfection.

### *The calcination follows, in which the final degree of fixing is completed, and then the spirit is truly made into a body, truly permanent, and fixing that which is volatile.*

After this matter, possessing a red color, begins to break apart and rise, it shall be placed for <term>calcination</term> <note>the reduction of a solid to a fine powder through high heat</note> by means of a strong, reverberating flame within an earthen vessel. In this vessel, the fixed degree of fire is completed and the matter is made permanent through a true and perfect <term>fixation</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable so it does not evaporate when heated</note>. Therefore, Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> says in the chapter on calcination that "spirits are calcined so that fixations may occur and they may be better dissolved." And also in the chapter on the <term>medicine of the third order</term> <note>the highest level of alchemical preparation, the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone, capable of transformation</note>, it begins to calcine, and it must remain in the rigor of the calcining fire until the powder becomes impalpable to the touch, possessing a most brilliant redness. Therefore, it is said in the *Assembly*: "Know that when it is ash, it is best mixed, because that ash receives the spirit..."

...and that moisture is enclosed by the internal fire, until it takes on the color of dry saffron, or burnt blood, or its own natural color. Likewise, when the water entered with the "body," it turned it into earth, then into powder or ash; if you wish to test for perfection, take it in your hand. This very red, impalpable substance rises up within itself and even grows like leaven <note>original: "fermenti"; refers to the way the material expands or "yeasts" during the chemical reaction</note>. In the aforementioned <term>calcination|the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</term>, a very subtle and transparent black earth is separated from it, which is found at the bottom of the vessel beneath the said red powder. 

Hence my master used to tell me that the perfection of <term>fixation|fixio: the process of making a volatile substance stable so it does not evaporate or change when heated</term> appears to exist in this for two reasons: one, because through fixation and through calcination, the fire is introduced through the vessel, and a quantity of this elixir—when cast upon many quantities of "non-permanent" <note>unstable or base metals</note> bodies—confirms the fixation of gold within them. This it would not do unless the fixation within the elixir itself was superabundant. The other reason is that the aforementioned black earth is separated from the mixture during calcination—a substance which otherwise had been inseparable throughout the entire work because of its extremely strong union. Therefore, it was necessary for it to be separated by a most powerful artifice. If it remained mixed in, its impurity would block the entry of the pure nature.

->The ash made fusible through calcination follows, and it is<-
->once again a stone, which is the complete elixir.<-

Indeed, this ash lacks the ability to melt; how then shall it enter the metals to "tinge" <note>to transform or "dye" the base metal into gold</note> them? Certainly, liquefaction is restored to it—or a "sweat"—according to the method handed down by the Philosophers. What then is that method? Is it to be dissolved in water? Certainly not, because the Philosophers do not care for waters that stick to the hand and moisten it. For it is said in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, an influential early alchemical text</note>: "The fools, hearing of 'water,' thought it was common water; but if they had read our books, they would surely know that our water is permanent." What then is this water which truly does not stick to the hand, but runs over the surface without wetting anything, just like quicksilver <note>original: "arg. vivum"; literally "living silver" or mercury</note>? Who then shall make such a water? I say it is certainly he who knows how to make glass; for this matter wants nothing else but itself to be joined to it, for it possesses everything it needs within itself. And if those things I have said before are well considered, you will know how to obtain from this ash a red stone of intense color, slightly transparent, brittle with a modest blow, yet fusible and penetrating...

# AN EXCELLENT WORK FOR 

## BOTH [PURPOSES] BY THE MOST EXPERIENCED MASTER VALENTINE. Which he gave as a testament to his adopted son, who also wrote this little tractate with his own hand, John the Apothecary <note>original: "Joanni Apot."; likely an abbreviation for Joanni Apothecario</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a building and landscape.</image-desc>

**S**ince, indeed, in the flourishing of Philosophical study, a certain secret part—namely, a famous, renowned, and glorious science—is hidden from the foolish but manifest to the wise; a science through which, when it is possessed and discovered, every ecclesiastical rank serves the Most High God without poverty, etc. Kings and princes rule and subjugate the necks of their adversaries to themselves. The poor and needy are helped in their necessities. Out of love for you, my dearest son, I propose to declare this to you in this present little book by handing it over in brief speech—neither entirely hidden nor entirely manifest—lest the wicked, masquerading as the righteous, unworthily usurp such an eminent science and foster it in their sins and negligence.

Learn this before all things: that you know how to recognize the natures of **Metals** and their generation. Take care that you are not too hasty, or headstrong and greedy, or fickle of mind. But rather be a patient man, a "son of doctrine," and a man graced with a subtle wit, investigating all things; be also generous. And there are also sufficient [instructions] for you below. 

Nor is it fitting that you should wish to investigate solely through books. This is because the books of this science are not written for the instruction of the seeker, as in other sciences, but are only certain figures of the science itself. For they are written under hidden and diverse metaphorical riddles <note>original: "ænigmatibus Metaphoricis"</note>, that is, figures; and for this purpose only: that through these figures, the matter of the science may be known, so that it may be truly believed that this science is true and entirely correct. For this reason, no Philosopher ever wrote of this as it truly is in itself, but only enticed craftsmen to investigate it. 

The principal material of all metals in their mines, from which they are generated—that is, caused—is **Dry Water** <note>original: "Aqua sicca"</note>, which we call **living water** or **mercury** <note>original: "arg. viv." or "argentum vivum"</note>, and a **stinking spirit**, which we otherwise name **sulfur**. However, the radical principles of this science upon which it is founded are these: namely, a certain matter or substance close to mercury and sulfur, smoky and sub-

<header>A NOBLE WORK</header>

...the most useful [substance] generated from the nature of the two aforementioned things through our artifice, most limpid and clear, like a <note>original: "latrina"; while literally "latrine," in alchemy this often refers to a pit, a sink, or the bottom-most part of a vessel where the "dregs" reside but the spirit is found.</note> receptacle in which the **spirit of the quintessence** <term>quintessence: the "fifth essence," the purest and most medicinal part of a substance, extracted through alchemical processes.</term> hides and dwells, as we shall say below. This substance itself is not sulfur, nor is it quicksilver, as they are found in their own nature in the mines. But it is a certain part of these two, which is neither quicksilver nor sulfur. 

Note that by doing this, the craftsman generates the aforementioned famous substance from the substances of the two, namely **Mercury** and **Sulfur**, and their adjuncts; which said substance, once united, is a certain body from which a smoky substance exits, which the craftsman causes to ascend from the earth into the sky—that is, a certain material or bodily substance into a spiritual substance. And finally, afterwards, that spiritual material or substance is congealed and fixed, and is converted into a stone, many superfluous things having been set aside. 

Note that there are four species, neither more nor less, which are suitable for composing this elixir; namely, they require: **Mercury**, **Sulfur**, **Volatile Citrine**, and **Fixed Green Sulfur**—which has a black "belly," that is, an internal nature <note>original: "intellectum"; here meaning the hidden property or essence within the material.</note>, although it appears clear to the sight—and **Fixed White Sulfur**. And these three sulfurs are melting and flowing like wax. These species are better when they are new or fresh than when they are old. Good **green sulfur** is that which is in thicker chunks. And when it is broken, it has a clear, green, and shining fracture like glass; for which reason it is called **vitriol** or glass. 

**Fixed white sulfur** is better when it is thoroughly white, having a white, shining, and clear [color], and it comes in oblong grains, not very large but somewhat thick; it is more effective with thick grains. **Volatile citrine sulfur** is "living sulfur" <note>original: "sulphur vivum"; native sulfur found naturally in the earth.</note>, and is better in large chunks, clear and not porous. Furthermore, **quicksilver** <note>original: "arg. viv." or argentum vivum</note> is composed with **living citrine sulfur** so that they are changed together in a certain way from their first nature and become one and the same in a red and heavy mass, which we call **heavy red earth**. From this point, there are not, nor are there needed, more than three species in this art; the other two species are not composed [separately] as the work of this art teaches. 

℞ <note>original: "Recipe"; the standard command to "Take" ingredients for a formula.</note>. Therefore, take 1 pound <note>original: "℔"; the Roman libra, here specified as 12 ounces.</note> of **fixed green sulfur**, grind it well upon marble as best you can, and set it aside. 

Secondly, take 3 ounces (that is, a quarter part of one 12-ounce pound) of **fixed white sulfur**, and grind it in the same way as the first and save it. 

Thirdly, take 3 ounces of **heavy red earth**, and grind it most excellently and save it.

->This work of grinding is called by the Philosophers<-

Then, immediately and without delay, join all these powders together and mix them well into one. And then divide all that material into two glasses or put it into one, and place an **alembic** <term>alembic: the top part of a still, used to catch and condense vapors during distillation.</term> on top, so that the mouth of the urinal <note>a glass flask or vessel with a rounded bottom, often used in alchemy and medicine.</note> does not enter the mouth of the alembic as is done in common distillations, but conversely...

# MASTER VALENTINE

### XXX 4

...the mouth of the alembic <term>alembic: the top part of a still, used for distilling liquids</term> should enter the mouth of the urinal <note>original: "urinalis"; in early chemistry, this refers to a glass vessel shaped like a bladder or gourd, often used for boiling or distilling.</note>, and be surrounded by it and well luted <term>luted: sealed with "lute," a paste of clay and other materials that hardens to create an airtight seal.</term>, and carefully dried and hardened. This is done so that the alembic cannot be separated from it. Then, lute it again and dry it as before, so that the spirits <note>original: "spiritus"; the volatile vapors or gases released during heating.</note> can in no way escape. 

After all the drying of this luting is complete, wax it, and soak the dried luting with melted wax carefully and wisely, as the process requires, and thus you will be secure. This procedure is called by the Philosophers the **Work of Spring** <note>original: "Opus Veris"</note>, etc. Then, place the sealed vessel into an **Aludel** <term>aludel: a pear-shaped pot used as a condenser in sublimation or distillation.</term> upon sifted ashes, so that the thickness of the ashes is equal to the thickness of a little finger beneath the bottom of the aforementioned urinal vessel. 

Then place fire beneath; if there are two glass vessels, then place it in the middle of the aludels; but if there is only one, then proceed simply. Let that fire be so tempered that you can hold your hand at the base of the aludel inside the furnace over the fire without injury; otherwise, the whole work would be destroyed. 

With everything thus arranged, the vapor of this material then ascends upward in the alembic in the manner of a most subtle smoke, and that smoke is converted there into clear and limpid water—like a reservoir <note>original: "latrina"; here meaning a clear vessel or pit for collecting fluids.</note> having in itself the nature of all the aforementioned species from which it was generated—and it descends through the **stag's horn** <note>original: "cornu cervi"; the downward-pointing spout or "nose" of the alembic.</note>, that is, through the nose of the alembic itself. 

At first, the first 16 drops or more are of no value and should not be collected. Around the 16th drop, take one upon a heated knife or a cleaned iron blade; if it boils and turns black, then it is the time for receiving the water, and not before. Then you must have two glass vessels—if you have put in two vessels with material—which should be shaped like a vial, thick and long. Apply these receptacles to the alembics, putting the "horns of the stag" into them carefully and stopping them well with a dry linen cloth; do not use luting here, nor stop them too tightly, as they might be broken by the power of the water. 

This fire is to be continued at this low strength for a day or thereabouts. Afterward, not suddenly but little by little, the fire is to be strengthened, up to double or more if necessary; in this increasing of the fire, it is to be held until the alembic turns red. The fire must be kept at that redness until all the water has come out. 

And then the fire is to be strengthened further and made into a flame, so that the thicker and stronger parts of the water may come out. Such a flaming fire is to be held for six hours or thereabouts, until all the water comes out and the earth remains dry; thus the water will be perfected. 

This water is named after its mother, namely the **Stone**—but here it is pure, whereas there [in the raw material] it was impure. Likewise, it is called **Mercury water** and **Sulfur water**, which is generated from them. Likewise, it is called smoke, wind, oil, water, air, fire, life, soul, and spirit, which is a burning fire that dissolves all bodies by one regimen—that is, by one operation—and in several...

It concludes by listing the many symbolic names given to this potent distilled spirit, which is capable of dissolving all bodies.</summary>

-># EXCELLENT WORK<-

...by other names, the Philosophers themselves call it, and the **blessed stone** <note>original: "lapidem benedictum"</note>, which is not a stone, nor has the nature of a stone. And immediately after that water is made, the composition must be made within two hours, because the power of that spirit quickly vanishes, unless [it is fixed] through its composition with the body, so that it may be retained by the body itself. Therefore, it is necessary that it be done quickly. And that work is called **Autumn** <note>original: "Autumnus"; the alchemists often named their processes after seasons to indicate the stage of growth or maturation.</note>. It is also called **impregnation**.

Therefore, take 2 ounces <note>original: "2. ℥ . i. e. duas uncias"</note> of the purest white earth in very thin plates, and cast it into that water, and seal the glass very well with a linen cloth, and place it over warm ashes, situated in their **aludels** <term>aludel: a pear-shaped ceramic or glass pot used as a condenser in the sublimation process.</term> upon the furnaces. And as soon as this body has been cast into that warm water, the water then immediately begins to boil if it is good. If, however, it does not boil, an error has been made in its operation, and it is worth nothing. And therefore, it is necessary to repeat it and make another. 

The vessels must be kept continuously over hot ashes until that water ceases from boiling; and when it has ceased, it will be clear, and limpid, and green. And our earth will be dissolved and gathered to the spirit. Note: if, however, anything remains of the body which was not dissolved or liquefied, it is of no consequence, but take another vessel similar to the first, and pour into it that water, as much as you can, through a **glass clepsydra** <term>clepsydra vitrea: literally a "water clock," but here referring to a glass funnel or siphoning device used for careful decanting without disturbing the sediment.</term>, carefully, so that that which remained at the bottom undissolved does not pass through with the clear water. 

And with each of the vessels well-plugged with a linen cloth, keep the **blessed water** <note>original: "aquam benedictam"</note> for the hour of necessity. And then make new water again, and put in those things which were not dissolved in the first water, adding new earth—that is, 2 ounces as before—and proceed in all things as above, and pour the latter water with its dissolved earth into the first. And if the earth is still not entirely dissolved, then if you wish, do as before, until you have enough of that water at your pleasure. 

And this is the true beginning and middle. And this water in which the body is dissolved is called the **Tempering of the Wise** and **Water of Life** <note>original: "aqua vitæ"</note>, and the dissolved body is called the **gum of the Philosophers** <note>original: "guma Philosophorum"</note>, though it is not yet perfected.

It should be noted that this first part of the elixir is white, because it is from white earth, as has been said. And the second part of the elixir is red, which you shall make from red earth as we will describe. And thus there seem to be two **Elixirs of Birds** <note>original: "elixiria Avium"; this may refer to the "Bird of Hermes," a symbol for the volatile spirit that must be "tamed" or fixed.</note> in this art, although it is not so, because in truth, these two parts do not make anything but one true elixir, which is for both—namely, first for the white. Afterwards, the same thing and no other, and in the same vessel, for the red. For we have already spoken of the white part. Now we shall speak of making the red part. And then again, pay attention, my son, so that you do not wander into error, for the aforementioned species are to be taken for the red, just as before for the white. But when...
