### MASTER VALENTINE.

...by other weights alone. **Take 1 pound and 12 ounces of fixed green sulfur**, and in this the weights agree. Item: one part of a pound (12 ounces) of **medicine of fixed white sulfur**. Item: 6 ounces of **heavy red earth**. And in these two ingredients, the weights for the red work differ from the weights used for the "white water" <note>The "white water" refers to the stage of the work aimed at the transmutation of silver, whereas the "red" refers to gold.</note>. From these species, you should perform everything just as you have above: namely, the **Work of Winter, Spring, Summer, and Autumn**, using similar separation, grinding, and fiery decoction in similar vessels, **aludels** <term>aludels: pear-shaped ceramic or glass pots used as condensers in the sublimation process.</term>, furnaces, joints, and **lutes** <term>lute: a clay or paste used to seal laboratory apparatus airtight.</term>; with a similar separation of the **phlegm** <term>phlegm: in alchemy, the watery, tasteless, and inactive distillate that is often discarded.</term> from the water, similar reception, and similar projection—or the "conjunction" or "marriage"—of the red earth with the spirit of the stone in the aforesaid water.

Moreover, the red earth must be clean. But note: when it has been combined with the water, it will not be dissolved in it at first. For the water is not yet of such great power; rather, the earth will only be **calcined** <note>original: "calcinabitur"; reduced to a powder through heat.</note>, and reduced in a certain way to a red powder without being touched. 

This being done, remove the water carefully and pour it into another similar vessel, so that the red powder remains in its own vessel. And into that removed water, place some "white body," such as the white earth, and it will be dissolved in it; thus you have a useful result. 

As for the calcined red earth, dry it according to its proper method, just as you, **my son**, have seen me do; for I cannot repeat everything to you now. Keep that powder in a clean vessel until you have made another water in which those powders can be dissolved. 

Make this other water from the aforesaid species: namely, 1 pound and 12 ounces of **green sulfur**, 9 ounces of **white sulfur**, and 9 ounces of **heavy red earth**; and proceed through all the operations as before. Except for this: in the separation of the phlegm from it, you will separate twice as much (or more) as you separated in the previous instances. And afterward, collect the water as was said before, and place that red powder into it. If it dissolves and becomes a very red water, then the water is perfect. 

But if it does not, then again remove the water from it, just as you did before, dry the red earth, and keep it. The water must be made anew, always increasing the weight by three ounces in the white sulfur and in the red earth only—but not in the green sulfur, the weight of which is always the same in these waters. And you will always separate twice as much of the phlegm in that operation than in the previous one, until you find the water which dissolves the red earth into a **very clear, red water**. 

Some practitioners, however, remove everything that comes out of the **alembic** <term>alembic: a distillation apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</term> before it turns red, keeping that "white water" aside. They say that the white water dissolves the white body, and the second (red) water dissolves the red body. They speak well, provided the craftsman is observant; but you, my son, hold to what seems best to you. 

And when you have found the water which dissolves the red body, then keep it...

<header>### A Noble Work</header>

…and make for yourself as much of it as you wish. Understand that you should dissolve [the material] from the **body** <note>The "body" refers to the solid metallic or mineral base being worked upon.</note> by always making new water, and dissolving the body in it; you should always pour the solutions into a single glass vessel until you have enough. You should also do this for the "white" as described above, even if the whole is not dissolved. However, you should not use as much of the **red earth** as you did the white, but only **two drachms**—that is, a quarter part of one ounce. If you are able to dissolve more, add more, provided that it is well **calcined** <term>calcined: reduced to a fine powder through prolonged heating without melting.</term>.

And just as the first **white water** in this art is called the **virgin** or the **pregnant girl** carrying one breast—which is the white and cold **feminine seed** <note>In alchemical theory, substances were assigned genders; the "white" or silver-producing stage was considered feminine and cold.</note>—it is also called the **urine of girls** before the white body is dissolved in it.

In the same way, that aforementioned **red water** is called the **handsome youth**, just as you, my son, are a man, having a black head and a purple garment; because the **masculine seed** is hot, it is therefore red. Both, however, are called the **urine of infants** and by infinite other names.

And note that the bellies of the vessels should not be filled completely with the aforementioned matter, but only half-full. The **elixir** <term>elixir: the perfected chemical compound capable of transmuting metals.</term> for both [the white and red works] is completed in this way: Take as much as you made at one time of the **white water**, and I leave the knowledge of its weight to your own expertise. I could not write everything to you, my son, for a reason I shall declare to you below. And take <note>original: "℞." (recipe), the traditional symbol for "take."</note> as much of the **red water**, the weight of which I also leave to you. Pour both waters into a strong, thick **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation.</term>. Then, immediately, the entire water will become lemon-colored, clear, and bright; this will be the **true coupling** and the **true elixir**. In that place, there will be a true impregnation, from which a true birth follows.

This substance, made into one from two waters, is called **our gold** and **our silver**. Indeed, it is called **celestial water**, **our bronze**, **our vinegar**, **our magnesia**, and the **leaven of the stone** <note>original: "fermentum lapidis"</note> for both works. As soon as you have poured these two waters in, you must block the vessel well until they are thoroughly mixed and become one thing: namely, a clear, red water.

Know, my son, that the weight of each should be equal. Any remaining water, whether white or red, must be kept in its own vessel, most tightly closed. Pay attention, for you should only take half of each for the **conjunction** <note>The "conjunction" or "marriage" is the central chemical reaction where the two principles are joined.</note>; keep the other half, as I said, which is called the **dragon’s tail**, because it is kept so that the **dry dragon** may devour it, as will be shown below.

I also want you to know this, my son: that you cannot perfect one without the other. Just as you cannot generate offspring by yourself, neither can a virgin without a male. I do not wish this to be a secret from you because of the service you have shown me: **The Sun and the Moon, this is more than the Sun** <note>original: "σολ λωνα ηστα ιστ μᾶλλον σολαῶ" (Sol luna ista est mallon solao), a mixture of Latin and Greek meaning the union of Gold and Silver is greater than Gold alone.</note>. Unless you join these together, you will accomplish nothing. Now pay attention, my son, for it is now time to arrange the work of the aforementioned stone. Take, therefore, the elixir or the aforementioned compound exactly as it is in the vessel where you first placed it...

...you have been, namely in a **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</term>, and place a glass **alembic** <term>alembic: the "cap" of a still that redirects vapor into a collector</term> over it. Seal it well with lute <note>lute: a clay or paste used to make vessels airtight</note>, let it dry, and wax it in the same manner as you did for the extraction of waters in the first operation. 

When this is thus prepared, take that vessel and bury it in warm **horse manure** <note>Horse manure was used as a natural, steady heat source for slow "digestion" or fermentation.</note> and cause the **soul**—that is, the **water**—to fly away from the same; this means catching that very water from the **elixir** in a glass vessel and casting away the **phlegm** <term>phlegm: the tasteless, watery byproduct of distillation</term>, as you did before in the first trials, until a drop boils when placed upon a hot iron plate. 

Then proceed with the fire as described above until all the water gradually exits, and the matter appears without water. Likewise, continue the fire until the water becomes black and dry. That which was previously called the **seeds** <note>original: "spermata"</note>, or the **father** and **mother**, in the first operation, is now in this operation called the **earth**, or the **nurse**. 

Therefore, the Philosopher says: *Extract the shadow from the sun's ray.* The philosophers call this earth the **shadow of the sun**, the **dead body** <note>original: "corpus mortuum"</note>, the **winning crown**, the **shells of the sea**, **black magnesia**, or the **dragon** because it eats its own tail. It is known by infinite other names. 

The water, however, which exits from it, is called the **dragon's tail**, which is eaten by the aforementioned dragon, just as with the remainder of the two seeds named in the first operation. And therefore, you must put this totally extracted water into the **white body** to dissolve it, as you did in the first operation, so as to keep it aside with the other seeds for the hour of necessity. 

When these three are dried out, as has been said, extract them carefully from the cucurbit. Take note likewise of its weight. Afterward, place it in another vessel made of strong, thick glass, wide and large according to the quantity of the medicine you wish to make, so that it matches the weight of the aforementioned earth. Let the belly of the vessel be round and the neck long. 

And when the aforementioned **dragon** or **earth** has been placed in the vessel, the vessel must be placed—well-stopped—in an **aludel** <term>aludel: a pear-shaped pot used as a condenser in the sublimation process</term> over ashes. A fire must be made with three large coals and continued until the earth dissolves into itself and becomes a **thick, red water**. 

But according to others—and this is better—let it be buried in the warm "belly of a horse" <note>A metaphorical term for a manure digestion-pit.</note> until it dissolves. For in this way, it is dissolved in 40 days. Others place it in the open air with the vessel open, but they should take great care that no dust enters the glass. However, this work is completed more quickly in a moist environment and more slowly in a dry one, as has been said. 

This dissolution of the black and dead body we call **dissolution** when it dissolves by itself alone; but when it is dissolved by its own water, we call this dissolution **resurrection**, or **vivification**, or the **animation of the dead body**. I shall show this to you below, my dearest son. 

But since the dissolutions of this earth are diverse in themselves, I am compelled to explain them to you, my son, lest you should ever be discouraged. Listen to what I hand down to you: that dissolution which is done with the "phlegm of fire" or with horse manure are not properly dissolutions, but rather **liquefactions** or **fusions**, much like the melting of wax or metal as you have often seen.

<meta>This page continues the instructions for the "Work," specifically focusing on the treatment of the "earth" (the solid residue) remaining after the soul (water) has been extracted. It elaborates on the cycle of dissolving and congealing the matter to achieve the "black mass."</meta>

# THE NOBLE WORK
### (OPUS PRÆCLARUM)

-> PREPARATION OF THE EARTH <-

But this must first be done, through which it is clear that **melting** <note>original: "fusio"</note> is taken here for **solution** <note>original: "solutio"</note>, or conversely, solution for melting; and since it is its own property, as I have said. Then again, solution properly by itself is as if in the air. And therefore solution happens in two ways in this place. It is necessary that you consider that first you dissolve it by itself—that is, you liquefy it. And second, you dissolve it simply by itself in the air, then in the aforementioned vessel. 

That vessel with the dissolved earth must be taken and placed upon ashes, in an **aludel** <term>aludel: a pear-shaped sublimation jar used in alchemical condensed heating</term> upon a furnace; and in the furnace, let a slow fire be made, continuing this there until it congeals into one **black mass** <note>original: "massam nigram"</note>. It should become hard and black, like a mass of salt, the fracture of which will be shining like the fracture of glass. 

Again, grind it and place it with its vessel in its place so that for the second time, as said, it may be dissolved in the air as before. And for a second time upon the ashes, as before, congeal it in the same vessel. Others, however, after it has been dissolved once and congealed as permitted, determine its weight. 

Afterwards, they add to it a small amount—that is, a sixth part of its weight—of its own **tail** <note>In alchemy, the "tail" refers to the liquid or "water" that was previously distilled off from the same substance, following the symbol of the Ouroboros (the snake eating its tail).</note>; that is, of the water that came out of it, and not from any other. This water, if done thus in this place, must be entirely simple without any impregnation of body or spirit. 

And afterwards there are some who place it in the air to dissolve, as is permitted. And some of them make it dissolve in a **horse's belly** <note>original: "ventre equino"; a common alchemical term for warm, fermenting horse manure used as a steady heat source.</note>. And afterwards all these men dry it—that is, roast it, that is, congeal it—upon ashes with a slow fire, as was said. Take care, my son, what you do in this step. 

And thus, in whatever way you dissolve and congeal it, repeat this solution and congelation four times. On the fourth time, with **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify the matter</term> and congelation, it is completed. 

Then **our earth** <note>original: "terra nostra"</note> will remain fixed at the bottom of the vessel, shining and black in its fracture; and when cast upon [metallic] bodies, it will alter them into its own color. And with all these things thus completed, you have sufficiently performed the true regime of the earth of the **blessed stone** <note>original: "benedicti lapidis"; referring to the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. 

And note that however many more times this earth is dissolved and congealed as described, the subtler and more penetrating it will be. 

And note that some do not melt or liquefy it as said above, but only dissolve it by itself properly and congeal it. And if the aforementioned melting is omitted—since we call it "solution" above—there is no error. Nevertheless, if it has been blackened by cooking, consider the form of the vessel we described above in which this earth, after it has been blackened, must be placed for dissolving and congealing. 

Concerning this, note that we do not remove the said earth from its **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: the lower, gourd-shaped part of a distilling apparatus</term>. Instead, once the **alembic** <term>alembic: the "cap" or lid of the still</term> is un-sealed and removed from it, we place a thick and strong glass lid over it, seal it with lute, and wax it to the cucurbit; this lid is commonly called...

# MASTER VALENTINE

-> THE ANTONEARIUM AND THE WHITENING <-

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely continuing instructions for a specific vessel setup.</note> ...we call the **Antonearium** <term>Antonearium: a specialized alchemical receiving vessel, likely named after an inventor or a specific shape, used here for circulation</term>, because it has a slender and thick neck. And let that neck hang inside the **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped chemical vessel used in distillation</term>, and not outside, because the neck must be **luted** <note>original: "lutari" – sealed with a paste of clay or wax</note> and waxed so that the "flower" <note>the volatile vapor or essence</note> does not escape. And when there is a need, remove the cover and again attach the **alembic** <term>alembic: the "cap" or still-head used to cool and collect vapors</term>, and seal it; and again, having set aside the alembic, attach the Antonearium. Do this alternately as needed, and thus in one vessel you can complete everything. 

Look, my son, at what you have done; in this vessel we do not confine you, nor do we confine you to the openings of the vessel. For if you should know a more subtle and more profitable way, adopt it. Indeed, many things concerning this operation of the art would need to be written, which I leave to your own industry; and thus you will have the **blackening** <note>original: "denigratio"</note> completed as I said above. 

Now, however, let us come to the arrangement for **whitening** <note>original: "dealbandi" – the albedo stage, where the matter is purified to a white state</note>. Therefore, know the weight of that earth, as has been said. And afterwards, dissolve that earth by itself, just as you did in its blackening. Once it is dissolved, take half of its weight of the **unfixed spirit** <note>original: "spiritu non fixo"</note>—that is, of the water which came out from it, which is called the **Balsam Dog** <note>original: "Canis Balsami"</note>, or **virgin’s milk** <note>original: "lac virginis"</note>, or our **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, or the **soul**, or the **wind**, or the **dragon’s tail** <note>original: "cauda draconis"</note>, etc., as I said above. 

Place this upon the dissolved earth—or the dissolved dragon—through the neck of the cover of the cucurbit, the cover itself having been well-luted to the cucurbit beforehand, as was said. Block the neck of the cover well, and seal it well according to its manner. And if it should be another vessel, block it well with a dry linen cloth, tied firmly. Afterwards, place it in warm and moist **horse dung** <note>original: "fimo equino" – alchemists used the steady, gentle heat of fermenting manure for long-term digestion</note> or upon ashes—that is, dry it with a slow fire as was said. 

Continue this until the earth and water become one, or a single thing, yet much clearer and of a different color in some small measure than it was before. This having been done and completed, the whole is to be congealed and thickened into a mass and returned to the same place, and in the same continuous regime. And if it should be necessary, the cover of the cucurbit is to be removed and the alembic installed, as was said, and luted from above so that no moisture escapes, and the matter may thicken more quickly. 

The sign that the matter—that is, the **gum**—has been cooked in the decoction is this: if the vessel is set to cool and that **dragon** is hard, after the manner of hard or cold pitch, then it is sufficiently cooked and purged of its **phlegm** <note>original: "flegmate" – watery, inactive residue</note>. 

**Note:** The water which comes out from this gum or dragon during this decoction can be collected if any comes out. And if it should be necessary to work with it, as with the "tail," once this dragon is congealed, let it be placed in such a place where it may dissolve by itself into a thick water by its own existing heat. Once dissolved, place it upon the ashes just as you did in the blackening, and leave it there until it is congealed as was said in the blackening. And this decoction is complete, and it will be one body, still opaque, but in its fracture...

# PRE-EMINENT WORK
<note>original: "Opus Praeclarum"</note>

...eminent. See here, my son, for the philosopher says that one must take care lest the **elixir** <term>elixir: the medicinal or transmutative substance in its developing state</term> be submerged. As **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary 8th-century father of alchemy</note> says, the submersion of the elixir occurs when the volatile smoke <note>vapor or gas</note> overcomes the smoke of the fixed substance. And thus that decoction will be perfect; then finally, you shall determine the weight of all that congealed matter, just as you first learned to do through your own industry. Because I cannot write everything down for you, I leave many things to your own discretion, lest I perhaps be found a perjurer <note>one who breaks the sacred oath of secrecy common among alchemists</note>.

Afterward, place a fourth part of that congealed matter upon the "congealed earth," or the congealed matter itself from the aforementioned water, or with the non-fixed spirit, without the **dragon's tail** <term>dragon's tail: likely referring to the dregs or the "volatile" part of the matter</term> or the **white sperm** <note>original: "spermate albo" – an alchemical term for the pure, white seed of metals</note>—all of these are the same thing. Keep it in the same vessel, without extracting the "dragon" <note>the matter in the flask</note> from said vessel, and cook it as before with the vessel well sealed, as was said, until it is congealed and thickened, becoming a hard substance like pitch, and afterward let it be dissolved entirely by itself. 

And once it is thus dissolved by itself, let it be immediately congealed upon the ashes <note>an ash-bath for gentle, even heating</note> with a slow fire, as was said; it will then be a mass of a different color than the first, and somewhat more clear. And in a similar way, with a similar regime and weight—namely, a fourth part of the whole congealed mass, and **quicksilver** <note>original: "ar. vi." for "argentum vivum" (mercury)</note>, and the aforementioned white water—let the whole congealed mass be placed over it. By a similar dissolution and coagulation, let that dragon be dissolved and congealed both by its own tail and by its own self.

Moreover, let this arrangement be contained, governed, and repeated through the **alembics** <term>alembic: the cap of a still used for distilling</term> by means of this white water or "tail," by weights, and through these waterings, washings, soakings, thickenings, inspirations, vivifications, animations, dissolutions, and coagulations—so perfect either by the water or by itself—and in the same vessel, and without extracting the dragon. Do this until that dragon, or that whole dead mass, like a man in his tomb, is revived little by little by its spirit, or life, or the soul of which it was deprived during the **blackening** <note>original: "denigrando"</note>, as was said. 

In the meantime, let it be thickened, vivified, animated, resuscitated, and refined more than before, so that it becomes a single **white crystalline stone**, sharing a certain greenness, persevering in the fire, melting, flowing, and congealing **Mercury** and perfectly retaining it, and transmuting any imperfect body <note>changing base metals into silver or gold</note>.

It should be noted that many and diverse colors will appear in that stone before it becomes white. The first was black, and afterward white, which are two opposites. Because the philosopher says one cannot pass from one opposite to another without a middle state, it is necessary that in the stone's progress from black to white, many intermediate colors appear. Because of this, it says in the book that it often turns yellow, and often turns black; indeed, as many colors as can exist in the world will appear. Yet these are not true colors; in the end, the **whitening** <note>original: "dealbatio" – the albedo stage</note> is to be expected, which is the true color. And according to the variation of those colors, philosophers have called this stone by diverse names: some call it iron, others lead, others tin, others copper, others bronze, others gold, others silver—all of which names, though diverse in words, refer to one thing...

# MASTER VALENTINE. 1071

...they attain the intention. And this **white stone** has the weight of its father, that is, the **sun** <note>original: "solis"; in alchemy, the sun typically represents gold or the masculine principle, but here refers to the weight/density of the solar metal</note>. For one grain of this stone generates a hundred grains in **multiplication** <term>multiplication: the process of increasing the quantity and quality of the alchemical medicine</term>, through the **imbibition** <term>imbibition: the repeated process of "feeding" the stone with liquid (spirit) until it is saturated</term> of the gum by the spirit, which is non-fixed and white; and this ought to be done in the same way, and with a similar regime, in all things as you did before in the whitening. And thus it is not necessary to start again from the beginning, but only to multiply it as has been said. Do not be content with having only a little of it, since you can multiply it unto infinity through the method already described. 

And know that the more it is dissolved with its **soul** <note>the essential essence or tincture</note> or non-fixed spirit and is congealed, the more it is multiplied—not only in quantity, but also in the power of the **tincture** <term>tincture: the transformative substance that "colors" or transmutes base metals</term>, in its subtlety, and in **projection** <term>projection: the final step of casting the stone onto base metals to transform them into silver or gold</term> it will convert and transmute a greater weight. Regarding the projection and the manner of it, and the form of the furnaces and the names of the vessels, I shall tell you below.

Yet, if it should happen to dissolve, it would not be any worse for it because of this, but it must be congealed again by itself over ashes with a gentle fire, just as you did in the whitening. 

Also note that although we made our decoctions with the aforementioned white water with a weight of a fourth part of the entire congealed body, as was said: nevertheless, if you place a greater weight of it upon the body itself than a fourth part—so long as the **elixir** is not **submerged** <note>drowned in too much liquid, which prevents the proper "breathing" or circulation of the matter</note>—it will be better; that stone will be whitened and will be finer and more penetrable, and it will alter and convert with a greater weight, as was said.

Also note that the stone or medicine which converts **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note> is finer than that which converts bodies <note>solid metals like lead, tin, or copper</note>, and vice versa, unless it has been prepared to be finer. I indeed spent seven years occupied with various errors of that art, through various erroneous operations, before I grasped the true elixir; which, when I had finally understood it, I made and composed in seven days. It is clear, therefore, that the craftsman must learn through experience from many errors. Therefore be vigilant, my son; you have the foundation from me, which I hardly found through seven years of work. Thus it is clear what is said: our work is nothing but **women's work and children's play** <note>a famous alchemical maxim suggesting that once the secret is known, the work requires only gentle heat and patience, similar to laundry or simple games</note>.

Also note: to whiten and to redden are the same thing; that **calcining** <term>calcining: reducing a substance to a fine powder through heat</term>, dissolving, and congealing are the same as composing, making a composite, and joining. **Roasting** <note>original: "assare"</note> is the same as drying a thing or placing it in such a place that it can be properly reduced to a dry powder. Also, distilling, **sublimating** <term>sublimating: heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again in a purer form</term>, and dissolving are the same as making things "descend from heaven to earth." Also, dissolving in water is the same as sublimating. And to congeal the fixed and the volatile is the same as descending and making the volatile fixed. Also, to dissolve by itself is the same as making the fixed dissolved; and to congeal the dissolved is the same as calcining the dissolved by itself. And that calcining...

# A FAMOUS WORK
### [OPUS PRÆCLARUM]

...is the same thing as whitening and reddening, completed. And understand here, O son of doctrine <note>original: "fili doctrinæ"; a traditional address from a master to a student in hermetic texts</note>, that the diverse terms of this art agree in one intention; in which diversity of names many have erred, and still err and are deceived.

Likewise, Note that there is greater labor in whitening, on account of the weights and mixtures which are unknown before they are tested, than in reddening; because then, through the whitening, they are known, and similarly a more certain method of working is given, etc.

Likewise, Note that the fusion of the stone, which I mentioned above in the arrangement of blackening—this our true earth, designated and named concerning the solution—is by no means to be done, nor should you do it, because it is dangerous and harmful, because it is dry. But when I wrote that chapter, I did not then recall the harm of that fusion which I had incurred, and therefore it must be entirely dismissed, and another solution must be made, not a violent one, as was established and shown in that same place, and the arrangement of whitening will be perfectly completed.

And now we must come to the arrangement of yellowing <term>citrinatio: the stage between the white and red works where the substance turns a golden-yellow</term> so that from there we may arrive at the redness. Take 1 <term>ʒ</term> <note>a drachm, a unit of weight approximately 1/8th of an ounce</note> of the aforementioned white stone, and in the same vessel from which you extracted it, put it in again, or in one similar to it, and stop up the vessel in the same manner as you did before in the whitening, and make it dissolve there by itself, as has been said. 

Because once it is thus dissolved by itself, take of the red sulfur—that is, of red **mercury** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver"</note>, or the masculine seed, which you reserved to the side as was said—and let it be of that quantity of red water as much as you made from two ounces; and leave it there, mixing them together minutely until they are one and the same, and one clear yellow water tending toward redness. 

And close the vessel with an **alembic** <term>alembic: a distillation cap or apparatus used for refining substances</term>, just as you did in the blackening. And this water is called the **ferment of the sun** <note>original: "fermentum solis"; the solar principle used to produce the "Red Work" or gold</note>, just as the first compound is called the **ferment of the moon** <note>original: "fermentum lunae"; used for the "White Work" or silver</note>. 

Then take the aforementioned vessel, sealed with clay with the aforementioned water, and place it in a location where the water can exit from it little by little, just as you did in the blackening. And draw it out from the superfluity of the **phlegm** <note>original: "flegmatis"; in alchemy, this refers to the watery, inactive byproduct of distillation</note> and receive it, as before, and from it make the red, just as you did in the blackening for the white, and let the other water be thoroughly thickened. 

Know that what will appear in the bottom of the vessel will be bright and clear, red, and fusible like wax; and it is called a **ruby**, **hyacinth**, **coral**, or **jasper**, etc. These stones are so named because of their color. Or, dry and roast <note>original: "assa"</note> this whole thing as much as you can, as its nature requires, until it is dried and turned into the likeness of dry saffron or burnt blood; and this drying and roasting is called **incineration** <term>cineratio: the process of reducing a substance to a dry, ash-like powder through heat</term>, and the arrangement of incineration is complete. It should be noted that the whole white stone, without moving it from its vessel, can...

# MASTER VALENTINE
### [MAGISTRI VALENTINI]

...in the manner aforesaid, it is to be reduced to ash and converted into the ferment of the sun <note>original: "fermentum solis"; in alchemy, "ferment" acts like yeast, transforming the whole mass into the nature of the ferment—in this case, gold</note>, but it is more necessary to have red sulfur or sperm <note>original: "spermate"; refers to the "seed" or essential generative principle of the metal</note>; a glass vessel could hardly be found that would not break before the perfection of the stone. Now we must come to the arrangement of reddening <term>rubificatio: the final stage of the Great Work where the substance turns deep red, signifying the highest potency</term>, which is the final work of our stone.

Concerning this, I say that after the whitening <note>the albedo stage</note>, no error follows until the perfect redness is reached. This is because it is to be reddened in the same way it was whitened: in the same place, and in the same vessel. It requires the same weights of water and similar imbibitions <term>imbibitio: the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it is saturated</term> and irrigations. It follows all the same other regimens, but uses red sulfur, or red spiritual water, or red sperm (previously preserved), which are all the same thing. Reiterate the process as many times—cooking, imbibing, dissolving, and congealing—just as you did in the whitening, until the King is crowned with a red diadem <note>a poetic image for the appearance of the red color on the surface of the matter</note>, or until this whole composite is reddened as is fitting. Then it becomes one stone: red, clear, flowing, melting, persevering in the fire, and possessing the power of tinting, transmuting, and penetrating. It converts Mercury and every body, whether solid or soft, into true gold <note>original: "solificum verum"; literally "true sun-making"</note>, and it cleanses every body. It also cleanses the human body from every infirmity, preserving it from ill health; it makes glass malleable <note>original: "vitrum malleabile"; a legendary material that could be hammered like metal without breaking</note> so that it may be struck with a hammer without shattering, and it fixes all precious stones. And this is the blessed red stone, the father of all price and the treasure of the whole world, which God grants to whom He wills and withholds from others. Receive this from me constantly, most beloved son, for I have made it just as you yourself have seen. Take care, however, that you show these writings to no one, and be mindful of me, lest the same should happen to you. Now hear how you should project the medicine.

The projection <term>projectio: the final step where a small amount of the Philosopher's Stone is cast onto a molten base metal to transmute it</term> is performed in this way upon metallic bodies: according to how refined the stone is, use more of the metal and less of the Medicine. This method is to be held in every projection, whether for the white or the red.

Take 1 drachm <note>original: "ʒ"; a unit of weight approximately 3.9 grams</note> of gibar—that is, the Medicine—and four hundred and forty drachms of lead or tin, and melt it over a fire. Cast this drachm of medicine upon that molten lead or tin, and the whole will be converted into medicine. And if the medicine is not of such virtue that it can convert such a weight into medicine as was said, then take less of the metallic body, as much as you know can be converted. If it can convert more, take more. Then, from that material converted into medicine, take 1 drachm and project it again in the same way upon another four hundred and forty drachms of molten lead or tin as before. And still, that whole mass will be converted into medicine, though not as strong as the first.

# WORK FOR THE WHITE
### [OPUS AD ALBUM]

Also, take 1 drachm of this last converted substance, and project it again for a third time over two hundred and fifty drachms of brass or copper, and it will be perfectly converted into a true silver-maker <note>original: "lunificum"; from "Luna," the alchemical name for silver</note> or gold-maker <note>original: "solificum"; from "Sol," the alchemical name for gold</note> according to the color of the medicine. This gold or silver, generated in this way by this medicine, exceeds all natural gold or silver in all properties, both medicinal and otherwise. And in the same way, the projection <term>projectio: the final stage of alchemy where a small amount of the Stone is thrown onto molten base metal to transmute it</term> is performed upon mercury. From these things, therefore, it is clear that our mercury truly kills itself, generating and reviving itself. This projection, moreover, is done in an earthen crucible before the mercury flees <note>refers to mercury's tendency to evaporate or "fly away" when heated</note>. You ought to test, when the medicine has been made, how many weights it can fall upon, according to the manner aforesaid. You can, if you wish, so refine the medicine itself through sublimation and congealing (as has been said) that it would fall upon a thousand thousand parts and truly convert them. However, I leave this certainty of weights in projection and the refinement of the medicine to you and to your own industry; and likewise when you wish to make malleable glass <note>a legendary substance in alchemy—glass that can be hammered like metal without breaking</note> and to fix <term>figere: to "fix" a substance means to make it stable under heat so it does not evaporate</term> precious stones through those things which we have said in this chapter. I do not intend to limit you, my son, in the mode, form, or weights of projections, since you might do them otherwise with other weights, just as the strength of the medicine requires.

Now, however, this medicine, when taken by human beings, preserves their bodies in health, purges them of exhaustion, and defends them from approaching infirmities. For it works above all the medicines, drinks, syrups, and any concoctions of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, a famous 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note>, Hippocrates <note>the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note>, and other philosophers. This medicine, applied gradually to those who are infected, protects them so that no disease may ever happen to them. I omit other investigations of this medicine in detail for the sake of brevity, and I leave them to your industry, my son. For you yourself have tasted it when it was administered to you by me. 

Now, most beloved son, I have hidden nothing from you regarding this science, except for the secret of the art, lest I should be cursed for the revelation of the secret; nonetheless, I have set you on the path of investigation to find the secret of this matter, for which you are bound to return innumerable thanks to God and to me, even if you now value these things lightly. But that secret of this art is such that you shall learn it not from me, but from another, as Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher was often cited as an alchemical authority in the Middle Ages</note> says. You ought to know that glorious celestial water <note>original: "aquam coelestem"; likely referring to the purified mercurial spirit</note> of which I spoke above, which turns our body into spirit; this repeats the whole work. Likewise Alphidus <note>an Arab alchemist often quoted in Latin texts</note>, the philosopher, in the book called *The Key* [Clavis]. "Take," he says, "the whiteness and the blackness, divide them; when it is boiled with water, it descends into the alembic <term>alembic: the top part of a distillation apparatus, used to collect vapors</term>, which is the cover of the vessel; throw away the dregs <note>original: "faeces"</note>, take the water from there, wash the earth with the water, and clean the vessel; close it firmly and beware of the smoke; bring the fire closer..."

# MASTER VALENTINE 1075

[...due] regarding your putrefaction <term>putrefactio: a stage of alchemy where the substance is broken down, often turning black, symbolizing death before rebirth</term>, preserve the coldness and the warmth of life. Let the delay of cooking and purifying not weary you; surround the vessel in moist dung <note>Dung was used in laboratories as a source of steady, gentle, "living" heat for incubation.</note>. This is the order of our separation which happens all at once in a single hour: when our body is placed in water to be dissolved, then it immediately turns black, and is immediately separated into its smallest parts. And it is immediately calcined, and then immediately dissolved and sublimated; by dissolving and sublimating, it is joined with the spirit. And if there was anything foreign mixed with the body, it is not dissolved but remains at the bottom of the vessel, and the body is cleansed of any foreign thing that was in it. 

However, one must not wait until it is fully dissolved. Otherwise, the solution is somehow corrupted, and it is not obtained as it should be. Unless you watch with the greatest caution, you will hardly be able to perceive it happening because the operation is so quick, subtle, and brief. Nevertheless, in this and in all other operations of that Stone <note>original: "lapidis"; referring to the Philosopher's Stone</note>, guard yourself from the fumes of the materials as much as you can. If they enter you, there would be danger to your life, either in the present or in the future, unless you help yourself with some good medicines. You should always have these ready with you so that you can immediately assist yourself and apply the appropriate remedy, so that you may bring that glorious work to an end in good health. May He grant this to you and to me, He who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit and reigns forever and ever. Amen. 

And when, most beloved son, you find all things to be so, praise God and be mindful of me. And guard yourself from those by whom you see me imprisoned. Of what use is this glorious art to me, since you know, my son, in what danger I am placed? Therefore, I warn you to take care that you do not boast of knowing this or that, especially before great lords <note>original: "magnatis"; powerful noblemen who often exploited or imprisoned alchemists for their secrets</note>, lest the same thing happen to you. Farewell, and look diligently upon the love which I have for you. May my God, who gave me this art as you yourself have seen, grant it also to you, so that you may grow here into the best of men. Keep God before your eyes in all things so that He may direct your paths, and pray for your Master when it shall be well with you.

# THE WORK FOR THE
## WHITE.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' containing an illustration of an alchemist or scholar seated at a desk or workspace within a vaulted room.</image-desc>Behold the shortest, best, and easiest work for making a medicine that is both penetrating and fixed. When applied to 80 parts of crude Mercury <term>mercurius: quicksilver</term> that has been well washed, it transforms it into the truest Moon <term>Luna: the alchemical name for silver</term>, surpassing every test and judgment, forever and ever. Therefore, take in the name of Jesus Christ 1 pound of Roman vitriol <term>vitriolum Romanum: likely copper sulfate, used to create acidic vapors</term>, 1 pound of verdigris <term>viride aeris: the green crust on copper</term>, 1 pound of Jamen alum <note>original: "aluminis jameni". A specific type of alum, possibly sourced from Yemen, highly valued for its purity.</note>, or plume alum, and 1 pound of saltpeter. Grind each one by itself. Or do it this way: ℞. Take 1 pound of common vitriol, 1 pound of saltpeter, and 1 quarter-ounce <note>original: "fertonem". A medieval unit of weight.</note> of cinnabar <term>cinobrii: mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral</term>. Grind these as described above, as finely as you possibly can. Then mix them together, grinding them very forcefully upon a stone. Then place the aforementioned things in a glass aludel <term>aludel: a pear-shaped vessel used in sublimation and distillation</term> with an alembic <term>alembicus: the "still-head" or cap of the distilling apparatus</term> placed on top. The joints must be closed and very well luted <term>lutatis: sealed with "lute," a specialized airtight clay or paste</term> so that it cannot breathe out in any way. Proceed with the same material: first with a slow fire, then a stronger one. Collect the first water that comes off, then the second, as these are of no value. Afterward, collect the third water with a strong fire. Then the third water will come forth—most precious, turning yellow, piercing the hand, and dissolving all metals and all precious stones; it is penetrating and cleanses all things. Its praises are innumerable and unknown to men, for within its secrets lie worldly treasures. You shall take this water when the alembic begins to turn yellow. Truly, he who knows its secret should know that he possesses the most perfect way of the entire Art. For this is the way of kings and the beginning, both because of its ease and its stable perfection under the judgment of examination; this is made manifest by the help of God through writings and labors.

The receptacle, concerning the calcination <term>calcinatione: the reduction of a metal to a powder or liquid through heat or acid</term> of *fidda* <note>original: "fiddæ". An Arabic-derived term (fadda) for silver commonly used by medieval alchemists.</note> with corrosive water. Take sheets of the purest silver, hammered very thin to the thickness of a quill or a penny, to the length of the belly of the vial and the width of its mouth, so that they may enter. Observe this: there should be 4 parts of water for every part of silver—that is, for 2 *lots* of silver, use 8 *lots* of *barnaas* <note>original: "barnaas". Likely a specific term for the distilled corrosive water or "strong water" (aqua fortis) described above.</note>. When you have placed the Moon [silver] into the water, close the mouth of the glass well and place it to be calcined in warm ashes for half a day, so that the silver is dissolved into a white water. Then take it out and let it stand for half a day. You should also have ready Mercury, which you shall likewise place into the water in another glass, so that it too may be dissolved into a white water, following the same method as above for closing the glass and the weight of the water.

# THE WORK FOR THE WHITE.

So that when there are 8 lots <note>original: "lot." — a Germanic unit of weight, roughly half an ounce.</note> of Mercury <term>Mercurius: quicksilver</term>, you then add 1 pound of the water <note>Referring to the corrosive "aquafortis" described on the previous page.</note>. Then the Mercury will be dissolved immediately and calcined <term>calcination: the reduction of a metal to a powder through heat or chemical erosion</term> by boiling; it will settle at the bottom of the vessel, whiter than snow. Allow it to stand likewise for half a day or thereabouts. Regarding the joining and thickening of the sidda <term>sidda: a specialized alchemical term for silver</term> and Mercury, follow this: put the water in which the sidda was calcined into an earthenware vessel shaped like a small bowl, and place it by the furnace on the ashes. Then apply a slow fire underneath, and the "lime" <note>original: "calx" — the powdery residue left after a metal is dissolved or burned.</note> of the sidda is dissolved into a clear water. Do the same with the calcined Mercury. Then join those waters together—namely, the Moon <term>Luna: the alchemical name for silver</term> and the Mercury—in the aforementioned bowl. Next, draw off the water from the aforementioned Moon and Mercury with fresh water and allow it to dry in the sun. Then that dissolved mixture will congeal and remain at the bottom of the vessel as a white crystal stone. Then take it and grind it very finely upon a stone; once ground, place it into a large glass vessel with a long neck to dissolve in horse dung <term>fimum equinum: horse manure, which alchemists used as a source of gentle, consistent heat</term> for 7 weeks, such that half of the neck is outside the dung. It will dissolve into a clear water, which you should then congeal in the heat of the sun.

* Regarding the joining, it is also held thus: keep the solution of sidda in glass over a small furnace until the Mercury is also dissolved. Once they are thus dissolved and calcined, pour the Mercury solution with its water into the Moon [silver solution]. They will then join together into a white or green water, and the perfect marriage of Mercury with his sister <note>In alchemical allegory, Silver (Luna) is the feminine "sister" to the masculine Mercury or Gold.</note> is achieved. Then allow that glass to stand in warm ashes, roasting it moderately until a third part of the water is consumed. Then allow it to cool and place it in a location where neither the sun nor the air can touch it. Then, white stones descend to the bottom, and so forth.

Afterward, proceed as stated above. * Then you will have the most perfect elixir and the most excellent stone, which all the philosophers have hidden. It melts like oil, faster than wax, upon a glowing metal plate; it will penetrate deep into crude Mercury and fix it <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</term>, so that it remains with it eternally.

### On the method of casting the medicine.

Take a crucible <term>crucibulum: a ceramic or graphite melting pot</term> and place in it 70 ounces of Mercury that has been well cleaned with vinegar and salt. Then place the crucible among live coals, heating the Mercury gently and moderately. When it has been heated, cast upon it 1 ounce of the stone. It runs, melting through all the "veins" of the Mercury, penetrating it, and leading it to the state of most perfect and malleable sidda [silver], which can withstand every judgment of testing forever—namely, the ash-test <term>cinericium: cupellation, a refining process where metal is heated on a bed of bone ash</term> and every other trial.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the alchemical poem attributed to St. Thomas Aquinas. # THE BOOK OF THE LILY
## OF BENEDICT 26.
<note>Likely referring to a specific collection or chapter number within the larger alchemical compendium.</note>

->*Mercury the fugitive, while he drinks the Moon sixteen times doubled.*<-

In this verse, the Philosopher <note>A title usually reserved for an ultimate authority like Aristotle, or in this context, the author of the poem.</note> sets forth his intention. And the meaning of this verse is that when the Moon <note>Silver</note> shall have drunk of fugitive Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note> sixteen times doubled <note>meaning thirty-two times</note> in weight. This explanation is quite obscure. And therefore I speak according to the manner of our nature: that Mercury has four dimensions, namely two that are manifest <note>visible</note>, and two that are occult <note>hidden</note>. The two manifest qualities are Whiteness <note>original: *Albedo*</note> and fluidity; the hidden qualities are fixation <term>fixation: the process by which a volatile substance is rendered stable under heat</term> and Redness <note>original: *rubedo*</note>. Indeed, Mercury relates to metal as flour relates to bread. For flour is not bread, nor is bread flour; yet flour becomes bread if leaven and water are added and it is baked appropriately. By a similar comparison: Mercury is not Metal, nor is Metal Mercury. But Mercury can certainly be made into Metal—in accordance with its own impurity—through the addition of leaven and mixing water.

Let us see, then, what this leaven <note>original: *fermentum*</note> is. And first, let us consider the leaven of the common people <note>original: *fermentum vulgi*—standard yeast or sourdough</note>, so that we may better understand the philosophical leaven. Common leaven is dough taken from a previous batch of dough, with the addition of salt and vinegar, and it is kept until needed. Now, philosophical leaven is of two kinds: namely, perfect and imperfect. The imperfect is that which is made from imperfect metals <note>base metals like lead or tin</note>, and we shall not concern ourselves with that. 

But as to how the perfect leaven is made, the Philosopher speaks when he hints: *Mercury the fugitive drinks*, (as if he were to say) that the Mercury must be saturated with the Moon <note>Silver</note> until it reaches a sufficient hardness. And I understand it thus: that you must take as much of the refined Mercury as you take of pure Silver, beaten into thin sheets. And you must place them layer upon layer <note>original: *stratum super stratum*—a standard laboratory technique for alternating materials</note> in a glass vessel, and set it in the ashes <note>an ash-bath used to provide gentle, even heat</note> for four hours, and let the fire be such as is used for sublimation. When that time has passed, you must take it out and pulverize it once it is cold. To the pulverized material, add an equal weight [of Mercury] again. And put it back into the fire. And thus you shall continue pulverizing, adding, cooking, and cooling, until the Moon has drunk the required weight of Mercury. Just as

# THE BOOK OF THE LILY

The Philosopher <note>A title usually referring to the author of the poem or an ancient authority like Hermes Trismegistus</note> instructs you. And you must pay the greatest attention to the change in **color** whenever you remove it from the furnace: whether it has a **waxy color**, and whether it melts more easily. If it should not please you, place it in different glasses in various quantities. For if there were too much material in the glass, perhaps the upper parts would not be properly cooked; once all these things are prepared, pulverize it as finely as possible. And note that three Metals—namely Moon <note>Silver</note>, Mars <note>Iron</note>, and Venus <note>Copper</note>—can be dissolved with Mercury and imbibed. Gold, however, cannot, because it is perfect in itself with every natural perfection. Saturn <note>Lead</note> and Jupiter <note>Tin</note> cannot, because they do not lack moisture, as they are themselves like the roots of moisture. And the Philosopher touches upon this when he says: "Dissolve the bodies and imbibe the spirits." Note that Moon and Mercury, thus joined, are dissolved into pure water if they are placed in a warm and humid place. And I believe that when the "third water" is added—which the Philosophers call the **vivifying and animating water** <note>original: *aquam vivificantem & animantem*</note>—it brings life to dead and even fugitive spirits, etc.

->*And the fire holds and nourishes by the sharing of heat.*<-

In the second verse, the Philosopher differs in no way from the work of nature, except in the time required until the non-fixed spirit is well-mixed with the body through artificial decoction <term>decoction: the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or change its state</term>. Otherwise, just as bread is rendered unformed unless the flour has been well-kneaded, I believe he understands it in this way. And so I have done: after the composition and the incorporation of the body with the spirit in the manner described above, I took my powder and placed it in a glass vessel in warm ashes over a moderate fire. And I let it stand for three days upon the fire. If any Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note> ascended to the top of the glass, I subtly scraped it away with a feather. For an error often occurs in the "stomach" <note>the bottom of the alchemical vessel</note> when the undigested is placed upon the digested. In those three days, the Moon <note>Silver</note> and Mercury are made into one to such an extent, and are so notably befriended, that no Philosopher in the world could separate them; and there one of them appears—either the dryness of the body imbibes the humidity of the spirit into itself, or the humidity of the spirit absorbs the dryness of the body. But I tell you what it is, however, as one who has proven it: that if anyone should subtly grasp the perfection of this discourse, he could give so much Mercury for one good piece of Silver <note>original: *Argento*</note> to drink as there is in the world. And there is no doubt that this Mercury, thus drunk, could be reduced into the true species of the Moon <note>Silver</note>. And note a sufficiently marvelous business: just as Mercury is imbibed with Moon, so you may imbibe cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide</note> with copper, and you will find such a tincture <term>tincture: a potent alchemical substance capable of changing the color and quality of a metal</term> that, with a little Sophistite <term>Sophistite: likely a reference to a chemical additive used in "sophistication" or the imitation of precious metals</term>, it turns the whole into the species of the Sun <note>Gold</note>. And then it would not be, because neither color...

...nor are the bodies fixed. Above all, one must be extremely careful and diligent in the management of the fire, which ought to be perfectly tempered; otherwise, Mercury will not be mixed with the body, nor vice versa, and so on.

->*Add a lip of salt, as much as a sixth part of the two;*<-

In this third chapter, the Philosopher <note>likely referring to the author of the underlying poem</note> sets forth the doctrine of the **third element**. Let us see, then, what this "third" is. For many Philosophers, by varying their terms—that is, speaking in different ways—have spoken of a third, calling it the **medium** <note>the intermediary or "middle" substance</note>, and regarding this third they have not erred. For it is the medium for joining the "tinctures" <note>the color-changing alchemical essences</note>. It is a medium between two extremes; it is the medium between the hard and the soft. And therefore we see among these three things which of them is the medium in the sequence—namely Moon <note>Silver</note>, the spirit, then salt, which is deservedly called the medium between body and spirit. 

This is because salt attracts the humidity of the spirit with its own dryness, and by its "sweetness" it offers the hardness of the body to the Sun <note>Gold</note>; this salt, by its penetrative nature, grants entrance to the materials. In this depends the great power of our art. There should be a sixth part of salt relative to the joined material. It works like an arbitrating medium, joining two diverse things into a fixed and firm friendship. It also works by participating in the nature of both. 

And just as menstrual blood nourishes the embryo in the mother’s womb and makes it grow until the end of its term of life—serving as the medium between the seed of the male and the female—so our salt makes the spirit and body grow in the matrix (that is, in the "womb" of the vessel) until the matter lives; that is, until it receives life in the bowels of the earth. 

It is necessary, therefore, that we extract this salt from three things, which is done as follows. Note: Take <term>Salt of Tartar</term> <note>original: Sal Tartari; potassium carbonate derived from wine lees</note>, <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> <note>original: Sal Armoniacum; ammonium chloride</note>, <term>Common Salt</term> <note>original: Sal Commune; sodium chloride</note>, and <term>Alkali Salt</term> <note>original: Sal Alcoli; likely a carbonate or hydroxide salt</note>. And by portions of the weight from the first to the last, by division of the fifth, and doing this step by step, you should see that you separate each of these from the "brightness of the earth" <note>impurities or dross</note> within the matter that retains the earth. 

From all these you should make a pure and clear water, which you will congeal in a clean vessel. You will then have your salt in the **color of wax**: penetrative, sweetening, dissolving, and fixing. Honor it and hold it dear, for in this consist the secrets. For it fixes the volatile, gives life to the dead spirit, softens the brittle, and certainly also cleanses <term>Venus</term> <note>Copper</note> of its leprosy <note>corrosion or green oxidation</note>.

# BOOK 52.

...to place it gradually, until the six weights of the previously prepared medicine have drunk up one weight of the said salt. At this point, you must be extremely careful, because it often happens that the material rises so much upon the arrival of the salt that it seems to exceed its limits <note>Alchemical reactions often involved bubbling or expansion; the author warns of the vessel "boiling over."</note>. It must be noted that each component should be tested before they are mixed. The test for the **spirit** was given to you in the preceding chapter: namely, an easy melting, a waxy color, and a change of color without smoke. Now hear the test for the **salt**: a waxy color, an oily sharpness, no crackling sound while it is being melted, and no smoke if you have observed it well, etc.

Those Philosophers who have labored—and who labor still for the sake of knowing rather than possessing—held that every perfect <term>decoction</term> <note>the process of "cooking" or maturing the alchemical substance through steady heat</note> is completed in one month (thirty days). ### BENEDICT. 26.

...second. Because the first was like **blackness** <note>original: *nigredo*; the first stage of the Great Work involving decomposition</note> while the materials were being incorporated. The second is **whiteness** <note>original: *albedo*; the stage of purification</note> while they are united. The third sign is the easy dissolution of the congealed matter over fire. Note well, that everything which is congealed by cold is dissolved by heat. And vice versa. For it is necessary that medicines of this kind follow the nature of metals. If you have ears, let you hear what you well know: that all melted metals behave like Mercury. And if they could remain melted while cold, they would be purer. You may see, therefore, that "moist" metals, such as Jupiter <note>Tin</note> and Saturn <note>Lead</note>, are easily reduced into their Mercury. And I will teach you in its proper place that Mercury devours every metallic body and reduces it into itself. 

Now let us say why Mercury is called "fearful water," and in what way it is to be feared. I say it is to be feared—that is, to be honored—because through it and in it the desired work is perfected; that is, the work is brought back to its intended state. It is also to be feared because it dulls the senses, paralyzes the nerves, and kills or infects those who do not guard themselves against it. It corrodes whatever it touches. 

As to how and what the weights should be, heed the Philosopher saying: "Neither drowning nor intoxicating the future of the world, nor allowing it to dry out." He intended nothing else but to avoid excess and deficiency; therefore, you should add only as much as allows your material to be dissolved. This should be a weight similar to half of the whole compound. And because workers often proceed so prematurely that their "water" is neither strong nor capable of dissolving, I give you a remedy. 

After you have made your water, dissolve in it four ounces of **sublimated mercury** <note>mercury chloride</note> and two ounces of **crude arsenic**, and distill it again. And you will suddenly have a water capable of dissolving every body for the **White Work** <note>original: *ad album*; the process for creating silver</note>. If, however, you seek the **Red Work** <note>original: *ad rubeum*; the process for creating gold</note>, in place of Mercury you should put **cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide</note>, and in place of arsenic you should put **Roman vitriol** <note>copper sulfate</note>. 

But if anyone doubts how a staining and fixed medicine can come from something "corrupt," since everything there (except the "body") is volatile—namely the salts and spirits—I shall answer: let those understand who can understand. For the sperm of the man and the woman remain distinct in the woman's womb in the form of "milk" for three days. In the form of "blood," they remain for nine. In the form of "incomplete flesh," for twenty, and the limbs are formed by thirty. And in the end, God creates and infuses the soul, creating it from that same sperm of the "agent" (that is, the body) and from the sperm of the "patient" (that is, Mercury), with the nourishment of the *menstruum* <note>a term for a solvent, here linked to the biological cycle</note>, namely the **salt of alembroth** <note>a double salt of mercuric chloride and ammonium chloride</note>. Our work grows first for three days in "milk" while it is being incorporated; then in "blood" while the salt is added. Afterward, it grows in the manner of "incomplete flesh" when it is congealed and dissolved into water.

### THE BOOK OF THE LILY

Afterwards, the limbs are formed in the dung-bed <note>original: *simo*; a pit of fermenting manure used by alchemists to provide a gentle, constant heat</note>, and in the end, pious God grants the grace of a living day—that is, to one possessing power. This occurs according to the increase by which that same **Medicine** <note>The "Medicine" or "Elixir" is the final alchemical goal, capable of perfecting both metals and the human body</note> is nourished. And note, that the better it is digested during the process of refining, the more it is improved. *Verse:*

->*Afterward, you shall divide the world if the origin is repeated.*<-

The Author’s opinion is that just as the whole world was in a state of confusion during the composition and mixing of the elements—so much so that the four elements had lost their power, light did not shine, the earth did not sprout, the Air did not nourish, and the water did not flow—in the same way, our named **medicine** is affected by the mixing of these elements. It lacks any disposition suitable for anything useful. And certainly, it is called "the world" by its proper name. For if you look closely, the four elements are there. For **water** is the first; indeed, the first matter of these things seems to be there. **Fire** is there by reason of the **physical sulfur** <note>term: physical sulfur; in alchemy, this refers to the active, combustible, and "masculine" principle of matter, not common brimstone</note> lying hidden in our matter, and it reveals itself. For before the elements are perceived, there is a **tingeing spirit** <note>a spirit that "tinctures" or changes the color of the material</note>, burning with the color of fire. **Air** is also there, for the smoke and the odor are seen by the eye and felt. **Earth** is also there, which by its own weight is cold and dry—but these things are in a state of confusion. And therefore it is well said:

> The earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, while the spirit of the Lord moved over the waters. <note>original: *Terra autem erat inanis & vacua...*; a quotation from Genesis 1:2 linking the alchemical process to divine creation</note>

Now, how these four elements are to be separated is easy to say, but difficult to perform. Because whenever one element is placed into another, the work is disturbed. Certainly, if you put water into fire, you extinguish the fire, and conversely, if you put air into earth, you generate earthquakes and whirlwinds; if you put earth into air, you generate thunder and lightning, just as storms are generated in great waters, unless the air enters through the caverns of the earth and, seeking an exit, generates those powerful tempests. Therefore, it must be observed that in the separation of the elements, one should not be mixed with another. Secondly, it must be observed that you know the causes well in their proportion: that in the consideration of the elements, **Earth** is the smallest element, **Water** is the second, **Air** is in the third degree, and **Fire** is uniformly equal on every side, a small part of which illuminates the whole world. Let us come to the point and speak thus: after all the matter has been dissolved as has been said, the vessel must be placed upon its furnace by means of light ash. And the **alembic** <note>term: alembic; a chemical apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling volatile substances</note> must be placed on top, so that the water may be distilled, which is somewhat sweet, and this continues until the cap begins somewhat...

Now you possess the four elements, each one by itself. But here a great doubt arises: whether any part of one element is mixed with another element; namely, whether some of the **air** passed over with the **water**, or whether some of the **fire** passed over with the **air**. And I will tell you the way of recognizing and separating them. 

The method of separation is this: you shall examine your **water** to see if there is anything floating on the surface like oil. If so, know that this is the **air**; then you shall distill that by itself, and you will see the water come out first, and the air will remain at the bottom. You shall also examine the air and fire in the same way, and work in the same manner. 

But someone might doubt here: why does the water—which nevertheless weighs more than air and fire—ascend more quickly than these two lightest elements? And I will tell you the Reason: Because every contrary acts upon its contrary as much as it can, and retains its own like with all its power. Now, because material fire is totally opposed to water by reason of its nature (for fire is hot and dry), it therefore first forces the water to ascend. And because **air** shares one degree with fire—namely, heat—it is somewhat "loved" by it, yet in another degree it is contrary to fire—namely, moisture. Therefore, fire acts upon it as upon a contrary. 

And because air is homogeneous in those two degrees—namely, heat and moisture—and because fire's nature is to expel moisture, it is necessary that it also expel the heat; it extracts it and forces it to exit through the alembic. But I shall tell you how fire might expel fire, even though they share the same nature. 

**Our fire** <note>term: our fire; also called "philosophical fire," this refers to the internal active principle or "sulfur" within the matter, rather than the literal fire under the furnace</note> differs from material fire just as the soul differs from the body. An entire animated body is a human being; the whole of fire is fire. Just as the soul is subtle and, by its power, nourishes the body with a constant heat, so "our fire" relates to material fire as the soul relates to the body. And I tell you, this fire is understood as the **tincture** <note>term: tincture; the concentrated essence capable of "dyeing" or transforming base metals into gold</note>, because it is of a fiery color. And whatever it tinges, it tinges by the heat of fire. 

However, concerning the proportion of these elements, it is most difficult. And here truly **hang the Law and the Prophets** <note>original: *pendent leges & Prophetae*; a biblical allusion indicating that this specific point is the foundation of the entire system</note>. And here is the "weight of the art"; in this mixing of the elements, countless people are deceived, because they do not weigh the "heavy weight of knowledge," or because they rush, not waiting for the naturally assigned ends. But before I proceed further, let us move on to the fourth element, namely...

# BOOK OF THE LILY

The Earth that remains at the bottom of the vessel is like a certain white, fixed mass, which is not consumed by the fire, nor is it forced to rise; it is, in itself, coarse and heavy. It is necessary, however, to refine and lighten it. The method is as follows: Take <note>original: ℞, the symbol for 'Recipe' or 'Take'</note> all your earth out of the cooled vessel, and on a clean stone, you shall pulverize it well. And I would give you counsel that the glass should be closed with the Seal of Hermes <note>term: Seal of Hermes; a hermetic seal, created by melting the glass neck of a vessel shut to make it perfectly airtight</note> around the middle of the neck. Conduct yourself diligently and carefully, because if you fail here, you would lose your work. ### How the Earth of the Vulgar is to be Separated from the Earth of the Philosophers.

The Earth of the vulgar <note>original: "Terra vulgi"; common, unrefined matter, often associated with impure salts</note> is salt. And I say it is to be taken thus: the calcined <note>term: calcination; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile impurities and reduce it to a powder</note> earth, as before, is to be placed little by little into a glass or glazed vessel in which there is very hot, clean, and pure water. You must stir it with a glass rod until that which can be dissolved is dissolved. And know that the "good earth" will be dissolved, and the water will be made white like milk; once dissolved, set this aside. And again, grind the earth that remained undissolved, and add very hot water again, until you do this so many times that you clearly see that nothing more can be dissolved. The signs [of success] are that the earth which remains at the bottom, if placed upon the tongue, "bites" <note>This suggests the presence of caustic or alkaline properties remaining in the waste</note>; the second sign is if it is placed over the fire, it neither melts nor burns. And after you see this, then take all your earth thus prepared in the aforementioned water, and place it in a glass vessel and congeal it by strong drying. And after it has been congealed, then know that you have **Philosophical Earth**, clean and prepared, which you shall weigh and keep in a moderately warm place. And this is what the text means up to the point: "The base part descends."

### BENEDICTI 26.

[The author] places the conjunction of [the elements] in this part. And here we must note a very practical matter: namely, why the Earth, although it is a heavy element compared to the others, acts as a medium to support the entire machine of the firmament. Here, the coarse understanding of the laity is bold <note>The author suggests that common people are overconfident in their simple view of the world, whereas the alchemist sees a deeper, hidden structure.</note>, for they can neither truly know nor even conceive of this. It is a most high undertaking; it requires present contemplation, and it is necessary for the one working such a secret to understand other matters well: the science of the spheres and the scientific cause of why certain waters adhere to the whole earth. 

[He must know] how the waters may come upon the heavens, and how it is that a multitude of waters is bound by certain characters <note>original: *characteribus*; this likely refers to celestial influences or mathematical laws that govern the tides and rains.</note> so that they do not exceed their boundaries. The worker must also know how water is joined to the earth. I say that Earth shares one degree with Water and differs from it by one degree; it shares in coldness, yet there is a natural moisture by which Earth also differs from Water, so that between these two elements, they are made heterogeneous <note>original: *etrogema*, a corruption of the Greek-derived *heterogenea*, meaning "of different kinds."</note> in respect to one another. One thing is necessary: that a division be made in the <term>symbol</term> <note>In Aristotelian physics, a "symbol" is a shared quality (like coldness) that allows one element to transform into or join with another.</note> between the dryness of the Earth and the moisture of the Water, for they differ only in this. Observe nature well with all your heart: for if the dryness overcomes the moisture, you accomplish nothing, and vice-versa. 

Now let us speak the truth regarding the method of joining these. I tell you: <note>original: *Re.*, the standard abbreviation for *Recipe*, meaning "Take."</note> Take your earth and weigh it. To the weighed [earth], add a fourth part of water using a slow fire, and it becomes very well prepared. I tell you that the fire must not be stronger than a "feverish sun" <note>A technical term for a very gentle heat, roughly equivalent to the body temperature of someone with a mild fever.</note>. I alone have performed this using wood shavings [as fuel], and if it were summer, there would be nothing better for drying this <term>medicine</term> <note>In alchemy, the "medicine" refers to the substance being refined toward the Philosopher's Stone.</note> than the sun itself. 

After that fourth part has been dried, move the matter with a glass tool and add another fourth part of water. If you have a "glass stone" and even glass matter, I would advise you that you should work it in the sun, covered with a clean cloth. This being done—that is, the <term>imbibition</term> <note>The process of "feeding" a dry powder with liquid until it is saturated.</note>—add another fourth part of water. You must work this successively until there is as much moisture as there is dryness. Know for certain that if you have done well, your Earth—which is now deprived of all the "superfluous moisture of the common sort"—will drink up this elemental water with such a glorious appetite that the two can hardly be separated except by a very subtle wit. 

Now let us come to the question asked: namely, why Earth is the support for composing our whole firmament. I will tell you the cause which all the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>A term for the ancient authorities of alchemy and natural science.</note> prove, and in this our faith does not disagree. It is certain that there are three primary things that concur for the being or non-being of any element: namely, Matter, Form, and Privation. Matter is that confused <term>hyle</term> <note>From the Greek *hyle*, meaning the fundamental, formless "prime matter" of the universe.</note> in which the elements are mixed together. It cannot be said to have quality or quantity.
