# THE BOOK OF THE LILY
<meta>Catchword: earth,</meta>

from this material is drawn the element of earth, and the other elements as was said in the preceding sections. And now follows the second principle, namely, **Form**; and thus you ought to believe that something comes out of nothingness immediately, and form enters it immediately, so that the form shapes the very thing which must exist upon the earth. And just as the form recedes, corruption or "privation" <note>In medieval philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a form that should naturally be present.</note> enters immediately and introduces another new form. And this was the intention of the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle.</note> when he said: *The corruption of one (namely, a form) is the generation of another (namely, a form).* For it must not be understood that the corruption of a man like Saihardus <note>original: "Saihardi." This is a proper name used as a placeholder in logical examples, similar to how modern texts use "John Doe" or "Socrates."</note> is the generation of another Saihardus. And note this well: you must think of this in our work—specifically, that the corruption of the dryness of the earth is the generation of another kind of dryness. Instead, it is an equalization of two opposites and the reduction of them into a single identity.

And because it is necessary that the element which is water—which is heavy, transparent, and fluid—has a place in which it may rest, and none of the elements have this property except for the earth; therefore, it was necessary that the earth provide the support for the structure of the <term>firmament</term> <note>The "firmament" here refers to the stable, solid framework of the alchemical stone being created.</note>. And this is what was first sought.

The second doubt is whether water, which is not "fixed" (as is apparent, because it ascends through the <term>alembic</term> <note>A cap or apparatus used in distillation to catch vapors.</note> when joined to fixed earth), becomes fixed by reason of the fixation of the earth; or whether the earth is made "volatile" <note>To be "volatile" means to be easily evaporated or turned into vapor; "fixed" means to resist the fire and remain solid.</note> by reason of that non-fixed water. And I say that the water is first retained by the earth by reason of the dryness of that same earth, because the dry attracts the moist; and the moisture itself, which is in the earth, is cold. And you must weigh this carefully: that degrees of coldness hold themselves together in earth and water, while degrees of dryness attract moisture. Therefore, it is necessary that the water be fixed with the earth, and that they become one identity of substance, just as matter and form are made one by the introduction of the thing formed, etc.

Weigh your dried earth, and if you find that its weight has been doubled, then know that you have done well. If truly it has not, then know that some of the element has escaped through the violence of the fire. See, therefore, how much weight is missing, add that amount of water, and dry it as before, so that the weight becomes equal, etc. The verse follows:

->*And let it be nourished abundantly by Air,*<-
->*This [substance] of Mersugi will tinge the horns of the white Phoebe.*<-
<note>original: "Merſugi tinget in alba cornua Phœbe." "Mersugi" is a cryptic alchemical name or substance; "Phoebe" represents the Moon, symbolizing the "White Work" or the creation of silver.</note>

Here now the Philosopher proceeds to the conjunction of the third element, namely **Air**. And he says that the earth, already soaked with its water and dried out, ought to be nourished by its air abundantly. For your understanding, you must note here that air is one of the principal causes by which all things live upon

### OF THE BLESSED [WORK]. 26.
<header>OF THE BLESSED [WORK]. 26.</header>

...earth, and it is quickened and they grow even in the waters and in other places in which wine is quickened and grows. And vice versa. And from this we see that the principal cause of this mortality <note>In this context, "mortality" refers to the corruption or breakdown of substances during the alchemical process.</note> is the infection of the air, by which all things are nourished. And certainly I tell you that the air infects the lands and the waters, and the fire [infects] the air. Now let us see to it that our earth and water may have the air purely and well—pure and good. And note that there ought to be more of the air than of the water.

And the reason is this: because the degrees of coldness were two—namely, of water and of earth—let us set aside the other two degrees for their own time—namely, the moist and the dry—and let us harmonize those two degrees of coldness with the degree of heat which is in the air. For the air is **hot and moist**; hot by reason of the fire which stays above it, and moist by reason of the earth and the water which lie beneath it. Let us say, therefore, that there were two ounces of water and two of earth, which makes four degrees of coldness. It is necessary, therefore, that the elements be shared together in such a way that the air is four times in proportion to those four degrees of coldness in weight relative to them.

And you must in that manner imbue <term>imbibere</term> <note>To "imbibe" in alchemy means to slowly add a liquid to a solid until it is fully saturated or "drinks" the liquid.</note> the earth and the water with this air, just as you imbued your earth with its water. And you should know and observe diligently that when the air is added and dried, the material—feeling the fire by its own power—immediately melts and enters the bodies into which it must be mixed with a strong penetration, and it retains the **fugitive spirits** <note>Volatile substances, like Mercury, that easily evaporate when heated.</note>.

And if you were to dissolve this material in dung <note>original: "in fimo." Fermenting dung was used as a source of gentle, consistent heat in alchemical laboratories.</note>, and place the dissolved material into the "first phlegm" of **strong water** <note>original: "aqua fortis," typically referring to nitric acid.</note>, know for certain that there would be generated a stone like a crystal, which by its own power congeals Mercury into the true **body of the Moon** <note>original: "corpus Lunae." The alchemical term for silver.</note>. 

But how one is to proceed, the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle, or the specific author of an alchemical authority.</note> does not state, nor how the medicine is to be projected <note>"Projection" is the final stage of alchemy where the "stone" or "medicine" is thrown onto a base metal to transform it.</note>; he only taught that this fugitive Mercury colors [or tinges]. For the Philosopher did not wish to speak except to those who know, and those who have labored for long times. And for the sake of clearer evidence, I will say four things here:

1. First, how this medicine has its entry.
2. Second, upon how much [it acts].
3. Third, I will remove a doubt.
4. Fourth, I will provide a remedy if, by an unfortunate accident, the medicine does not melt or does not pursue its intent.

Regarding the first, I say that a vessel must be taken in which the **Mercury** is to be congealed, and it must be well-anointed on the inside with some fat [or oil]. This is so that the violence of the fire and the dryness of the vessel do not absorb the medicine. Once anointed, the Mercury is to be placed inside and a sufficiently slow fire is to be made. And know this: you must have the medicine wrapped in **wax**. And when your Mercury begins to "rage" <note>To boil or vaporize violently.</note>, you must apply your medicine. For this, you must also lift the vessel a little bit away from the violence of the fire, because while Mercury is being forced by the fire, it leaps...

<header>THE BOOK OF THE LILY</header>

...and by leaping out, it carries the medicine away with it, from which errors often arise, especially for those who do not consider the causes of things. Therefore, let the fire be tempered after the application of your medicine, and let it be **above**, not below. <note>In alchemy, "fire above" often refers to heat applied to the top of a vessel or a "reverberatory" heat, intended to keep volatile substances from escaping or "leaping" before they are fixed.</note> And understand this applies to the perfect medicine; for in medicines that are not yet perfect, the whole mixture must be maintained. And after the fire has remained above for some time—that is, for a quarter of an hour—then place it into the fire of fusion. And know that you then have Moon <note>original: *Lunam*; the alchemical name for Silver</note> which does not require cupellation <term>cineritio</term> <note>A refining process where metal is heated on a bed of bone-ash to remove impurities like lead</note>, because it is perfected with total perfection.

The second doubt is: how much medicine ought to be applied? And I say to you that you can think this through for yourself from what has come before: because just as much leaven as you put into dough, you must put that same proportion of medicine upon the Mercury. And commonly, just as a pound of leaven ferments one hundred pounds of dough, so one weight of our medicine congeals one hundred weights in the perfect work. And I tell you that if you had the time for multiple rounds of dissolving and congealing—as I believe can be done—it would "tinge" <note>original: *tingeret*; to transmute or "color" a base metal into a noble one</note> unto infinity with the addition of "nutriment."

And this is attested by Hermes, Geber, Avicenna, Albertus Magnus, Hermogenes, and Arnold of Villanova, who say that he who has once worked well and perfectly does not need to start over, but only to continue. The method of continuing, moreover, is to add the nutriment of the spirit and the body of the prepared elements.

I come now to the third doubt to be removed: whether any other "body" <note>A "body" in alchemy refers to a solid metal, like Gold or Silver</note> should be mixed with pure and clean Mercury. And I answer: if the medicine is perfect, it does not require the addition of a metal body. For if you were to put well-baked bread into the dough you are mixing, you know that you would destroy the dough and ruin the bread. Thus, if you put a metal body in with the Mercury, the medicine would draw that body to itself and would not allow the medicine to be mixed with the Mercury.

And therefore, take this from me: that Mercury will never be perfectly "moon-ified" <note>original: *lūnificabitur*; turned into Silver</note> with raw Moon <note>Silver</note>, nor will it become Sun <note>Gold</note>, because the raw and the cooked can never share in the same nature nor agree. Those people are therefore in error who believe they can achieve increase by dissolving Mercury together with Silver or Gold. For there is no doubt that salt has only as much red sulfur as is necessary for itself, and no more. How then shall it give some to the Mercury? It is certainly impossible; for if one pound of silver were placed into two pounds of gold, anyone would easily recognize that it is not pure gold. And it is seen on the parchment and in the "cement of judgment" <note>A reference to "cementation," a dry refining process used to test the purity of gold</note> that its weight would be diminished.

And someone might say perhaps that Mercury "carries" sulfur because it ascends with it into the aludel <term>aludel</term> <note>A series of pear-shaped sublimation pots used in alchemical distilling</note>, I believe. But I say that neither the Mercury nor the sulfur are fixed. As to how they ought to be fixed—not by gold, nor by themselves—let the worker look to this and say he is firm against the matter...

...to labor diligently, yet I do not deny that increases occur in the "bodies" <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to the solid metals</note>, of which one is more perfect than the other when combined with things that amplify the degrees of color. For example, the Moon <note>original: *Luna*; the alchemical name for Silver</note> joined with the Sun <note>original: *Sole*; the alchemical name for Gold</note> is easily amplified through the medium into the highest degree of the Sun’s color. Likewise, Venus <note>Copper</note> and the Moon are "silvered" to the highest degree of the Moon with things that amplify lunar or solar color.

I come to the fourth doubt, regarding remedies. Sometimes—alas!—it happens to those laboring that at the end of all their hard work, the medicine either does not enter the metal, or it enters but does not flow, or it does not dissolve. It also sometimes happens that they believe they are making something perfect, yet it is much more imperfect than what is found in nature. From this, it follows that they fall into despair and come to the fullness of poverty; for the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, though often used as a general term for alchemical authorities</note> says that small expenses made frequently have consumed the greatest riches. Therefore, we shall provide help as far as we are able. I tell you this: if the medicine does not have "entry" <note>The ability of the elixir to penetrate and transform the base metal</note>, I would give it a 1/16th part of dissolved salt alembroth <term>salis allembrat</term> <note>A double salt of mercury and ammonium chloride, used to help the medicine penetrate the metal</note>; if it does not flow, I would give it a fourth or sixth part of borax <term>lapidis Bore</term> <note>Used as a flux to lower the melting point of metals</note>; and if it does not dissolve, I would give it an eighth part of "fat of the eagle" <term>pinguedinis aquilæ</term> <note>A symbolic term, usually referring to sal ammoniac or a specific mercurial distillate</note>. And if I wished to use it perfectly according to any of the aforementioned weaknesses, I would cause the medicine to be dissolved in dung <note>A "manure bath" or *balneum ventris equini* provided a gentle, steady heat for digestion</note> with the remedy mentioned above that is appropriate for this weakness. A Verse:

->*If you give this, it will grant Gold and the tawny Lion.*<-
<note>original: *Quam si dederis Aurum dabit fulvumq; Leonem.* The "Tawny Lion" is a common alchemical symbol for the Red Tincture or the final stage of Gold.</note>

This is the final chapter given by the Philosopher to those who understand. In this chapter he wishes to set forth the conjunctions of fire with the other three elements, and he says: "If you give the fourth element, namely fire—that is, if you mix it with the aforementioned prepared elemental matter—you will have a golden, red, tawny color." This explanation leads those who do not understand into confusion, as has been sufficiently stated in the preceding pages. So that the ignorant may understand, I say this: the Philosopher understood by the "conjunction of fire" the tincture of redness <note>The *rubedo*, the final stage of the Great Work</note> applied upon Mercury, and even upon the Moon [Silver]. And know this: because the sphere of fire in the firmament is so expansive—stretching below, above, and to the sides—it is joined to the air in the sharing of heat. According to this, one can imagine that the air receives its heat from the fire itself. The Philosophers also consider that the Sun circles the entire Zodiac through the course of a single year. And according as its sphere is more closely approached to us, we judge it to be summer. And as it is further removed, we judge...

...we experience winter. And there is no doubt that the Moon <note>original: *Luna*; alchemical Silver</note> is seven times larger than the whole Earth, yet it completes its course in a single month; and the Sun <note>original: *Sol*; alchemical Gold</note> is many times larger than the Earth itself. It is therefore necessary to consider in this art that a very small part of fire is able to tinge <note>To "tinge" is to fundamentally change the color and nature of a metal, essentially "dyeing" it into gold or silver</note> a great amount of earth. I say that it is to be joined just as the air was joined in the preceding chapter. But because the prior three elements were dissolved by a tempered fire and mixed, this mixture is easy. And thus the four elements, composed within themselves, are joined and united through the conjunction of extremes. Now see how much is to be joined.

I say that a 1/16th part of fire should be placed in respect to the whole compound. For example: If there were 15 ounces of the three aforementioned prepared elements, then one ounce of fire should be added, and this suffices for tinging; this can be proven. Take <term>Recipe</term>: 10 ounces of good, fixed, and very pure Silver <note>original: *Luna*</note> and place it in a crucible; while it is molten, place within it one drachma <term>drachmam</term> of the perfect medicine, if the perfect solar tincture tinges it. Then you will know that you have labored well. If indeed the color is not sufficient when you test it on parchment, then add a little more fire. And if the color should be too excessive: add a little of the other preserved elements, according to the order of their weights, until the color is tempered. And rightly that verse follows:

It is nourished, cooked, dissolved, and coagulated, and also united with itself through conjunction, imbibition <note>The process of soaking a solid in a liquid until it is saturated</note>, and even calcination; and just as it was separated from the philosophical earth, it is separated from the common earth <note>original: *terra vulgi*; the unrefined material used by the uninitiated, as opposed to the "philosophical" matter of the masters</note>. Likewise, it is necessary that in the Sun and Mercury, the operation for the Red <note>original: *ad rubeum*; the "Rubedo" or final stage of the Great Work, resulting in Gold</note> be performed in this way, but through different actions. For gold cannot be destroyed as quickly as other metals, as was said before. And the Philosophers maintain that it is easier to construct gold than to destroy it. I say again, that if you revive Mercury seven times after it has been sublimated <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor and then collecting the solid deposit formed as it cools</note>, it will reduce every "body" <note>metal</note> into its first matter. You have understood this, for I have told you enough. But because Mercury is naturally white, I tell you openly of the additives that most greatly redden it; and if you were to sublimate it with these additives seven times, know without a doubt that the subtle spirits of redness would ascend with it. This occurs so that the degrees of the color of redness in the Mercury would extensively exceed the degrees of the Sun <note>original: *solis*; alchemical Gold</note>. And when it happens that Gold is joined with Mercury, animated, and nourished—just as it was with the Moon <note>original: *Luna*; alchemical Silver</note> and Mercury—you will find your tincture redder than the morning sun. 

And these are the additives. Take calamine stone <note>original: *lapidem calaminarem*; zinc ore</note>, Alexandrian tutty <note>original: *thutiæ Alexandrinæ*; zinc oxide</note>, hematite stone <note>iron ore</note>, and magnetite <note>loadstone</note>: of each an equal weight to the "living" Mercury; and of borax <note>original: *tintar borax*</note>, two weights; of Roman vitriol <note>original: *vitrioli romani*; copper or iron sulfates</note>, three weights; and of cinnabar <note>original: *cinobrii*; mercury sulfide</note>, four weights. Let all be powdered together very finely and incorporated with "fat of the eagle" <note>original: *pinguedine aquilæ*; an alchemical code name, usually referring to sal ammoniac or ammonium chloride</note> until it is well massed and kneaded. Then let it be placed in glass or in a clay aludel <note>original: *alludel fictili*; a pear-shaped pot used for sublimation</note> and left open until the moisture leaves; afterwards let it be closed and sublimated by the common method of sublimation. Let the vessel be broken and the sublimate joined with the dregs by grinding and kneading with vinegar. And let it be sublimated again, and let this be done seven times. When you bring it down <note>recover the material</note> as you know how, you then have the "destruction of gold"—that is, its solution—from which solution you must proceed as has been told to you. Concerning the projection <note>The final act of casting the elixir onto base metal to transform it</note> and the entry, it has been described to you in the preceding parts; observe and keep that method in all these things. 

A recapitulation follows:

*It conceives for three days: it is boiled for thirty days*
*In the belly of the earth it receives life for ten days*
*Then the chaos separates, the elements recede in turn*

a good and perfect <term>decoction</term> <note>The process of heating or "cooking" a substance in liquid to extract its essence or change its state.</note> should follow the course of the moon. I should therefore abhor and flee from the face of the one who labors [incorrectly]. Namely, those who labor with plants, with eggs, and with hair, and who meditate on forging <term>Sodomitical</term> <note>original: *Sodomiticas*; in alchemy, this refers to "unnatural" or "bastard" processes that attempt to create results through materials like hair or eggs rather than through the "natural" union of metallic principles.</note> natures. Above all, one must be most careful and diligent in the <term>regimen of fire</term> <note>The management of the furnace temperature.</note>, which must be extremely tempered. For if the fire is excessive, it will not permit the <term>Mercury</term> <note>Quicksilver.</note> to be mixed with the body, but will make it more and more "fugitive" <note>Volatile; evaporating or escaping as vapor.</note>. If indeed the fire is too slow, then the body will not be melted nor dissolved. And consequently, it will neither "drink" nor will the fugitive spirits be retained. Therefore, let your fire be a fire of coals somewhat surrounded by ashes; note one thing: sometimes a fire of juniper coals, surrounded by their own ashes, lasts for a very long time. Therefore, let your wise intellect provide carefully and keep watch over the timing.

Let us see; for the great Aristotle maintains that there is no passage from one extreme to another except through a middle state. For there is no doubt that Mercury is one extreme, and <term>C.</term> <note>Likely shorthand for *Corpus* (the Body/Metal) or *Calx*.</note> is the other extreme, and that both differ wonderfully, as if between act and potency. For Mercury exists in potentiality, while the Moon exists in the state of its own perfection—at least as far as the Moon is concerned. They also differ by a certain difference: Mercury is entirely volatile in itself, while the Moon is fixed according to the degree of the Moon. They differ by the difference between the past and the present, and the present and the future. In the past they differ because, undoubtedly, the Body was once Mercury. They differ in the present relative to the future because Mercury is potentially made into the Moon in the future; whence in the *Book of the Perfect Mastery*, Mercury is imagined to speak to all the perfect metals thus: "I am your father, and our earth; you were made from me. # MERCURY FLEES WHILE IT DRINKS.
<note>original: *MER FUGI DUM BIBIT*; this refers to the volatility of Mercury (quicksilver) which "escapes" or evaporates during the heating process unless it is properly "fixed."</note>

...[soaks] in your blood, it will generate for you by way of a third kind brothers and sisters who will surpass all things. Let us see, therefore, what this "third" might be.

### The Sun
<note>In alchemy, the "Sun" refers to Gold, the most perfect metal.</note>
Consider that in this there are three principal qualities: one is **penetrative**, another is **attractive**, and the third is **softening**. By its attractive nature, it wipes away superfluous moisture, concerning which the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or Geber.</note> says: "He who does not know how to wipe away stains and also to lift the dross <note>original: *furfures*, literally "bran" or "scales"; referring to surface impurities.</note>, his labor descends to corruption." By its softening nature, however, it eases the harshness of **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver.</note>. For Mercury is, by its own nature, incisive and corrosive through its hidden power; by its penetrative nature, it grants entry. 

In this depends the great force of the Art. For many labor and yet have no "entry" <note>the ability of the chemical agent to penetrate the base metal</note>; whence, when they think they have done everything, in the end they are deluded. Being ignorant and not possessing the understanding of the philosophers, they rail against books and the authors of books, saying they were liars. Note, therefore, that the medium for joining the **tinctures** <note>the transforming essences of the metals</note> is **our salt**, which certain philosophers have called by its right name in Chaldean: *alembrat*, which means the **key of the art**.

### Of the Earth
Some philosophers call this same thing the "key of the art," others the "elephant" <note>likely referring to its strength or stability</note>. Our philosopher, however, calls it the *labrum* <note>a basin or vat</note>, and sometimes the *labium* <note>a lip</note>; they are the same. It is called *labrum* or *labium* from *delibo*, which means "I purify." For it is not proper for the harshness of the salt to be smeared into our work. For that is the "earth of the common people." 

It is necessary that our substance be subtle and entirely **airy**. For this reason, **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century philosopher and theologian known for his writings on alchemy and nature.</note> says to the philosophers: "If our stone were not airy, it would not be joined to Mercury, and its part would not remain with the same." However, the philosopher does not set down exactly how the salt acts as a medium or how it joins two diverse things into a fixed and firm friendship, nor how it is made. Nevertheless, it is necessary because of the first three qualities that it be composed of three or four things from which these qualities draw their work. Because "no one gives what he does not have," it is made thus.

### Homogeneous Substances
Here the philosopher discusses their "befriending" so that they may become **homogeneous**. For just as the intellective, vegetative, and sensitive souls are first diverse among themselves, but afterwards through the unity of the structure are made one—having a total homogeneity within themselves so that one cannot be separated from the other—so it is necessary that these three diverse things become one. 

For they have within themselves the aforementioned powers, if you consider it well. Not yet actually, but **potentially**. Now, indeed, the philosopher reduces this diversity to unity; and it is nothing else but to reduce these three things to their first matter of salts and metals, which is to say, into **water**. If any coarse man [does not understand]...

"If a grain falling into the earth does not die, it remains alone. But if it dies, it brings forth much [fruit]." <note>original: *Si granum in terram...*; quoting John 12:24, a common alchemical metaphor for the stage of "putrefaction" or chemical breakdown.</note> How wonderfully God works, however, cannot be scrutinized by man. Because "Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and of His wisdom there is no end." <note>Quoting Psalm 147:5.</note> I shall come to the matter, and I will remove the doubt of some laymen who labor in this art: who do not understand what it is, why it is, or how it is. For we see the grain of which we spoke cast into the earth, bathed by the air, and having been bathed, it rots; having rotted, it germinates; having germinated, it is born. And once born, it grows; and having grown, it matures; and once matured, it returns another [crop], some a hundredfold, another a thousandfold, another less, another more, according to the disposition of the good earth.

Why this is referred to our art in a similar way can certainly be seen by anyone concerning natural sowing, if one imagines <term>Mercury</term> <note>quicksilver, the spirit of the metal</note> to be the grain, the **Moon** <note>silver or the feminine principle</note> to be the earth and the water—that is, the dew of heaven by which it is bathed in the earth. How much <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the breakdown or "blackening" of the substance</note> accomplishes is sufficiently touched upon by **Aristotle** when he says, "the corruption of one is the generation of another." But if some ignorant and mad person doubts how a <term>tinging and fixed medicine</term> <note>an elixir capable of changing the color/nature of metals and resisting fire</note> can emerge from corruption when all things that are there (except the body) are volatile—namely, the salts and spirits—I respond (though I know the wretched will not understand) just as with the seed of a man, etc.

...it is first reduced to its own first matter. And this is what the philosophers—Hermogenes <note>A common medieval variation of the name Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>, Avicenna, and the rest—intended. But as for what the first matter of metals was, we all know, for it was Mercury alone. How all metals are reduced into it, however, I consider to be the greatest secret of all the philosophers, which they have hidden above all else. Certain of my dearest friends have labored continuously for thirty years and found nothing. 

But I take <note>original: *Rx*, the recipe symbol for "recipe" or "take."</note> Mercury sublimated seven times, as much as I wished, and an equal amount of pure wheat flour; these must be kneaded together like a paste with simple water, until they are like dough or a thick porridge. This must be placed in a glass vessel having a long neck. Let the vessel be placed in ashes, so that the water may evaporate entirely and the material adheres well to the vessel. Then, once the vessel has cooled, place it in a completely round furnace, and let the beak <note>The "rostrum" or spout of the still.</note> descend through an opening below, and thus let it flow down into a cold vessel. 

This is the secret of secrets. For this Mercury, while hot, drinks and eats any thin body, and reduces it into its own matter, namely Mercury. And note well that in this is encompassed the entire meaning of the philosopher—that is, the intellect. For while you vivify the dead and mortify the living for the seventh or septenary time, you will have what is sought. Therefore, when questioned, Hermes, the father and prince of our art, said: "Ascend seven times with the dead, and descend as many times with the living, and you will have the end." <note>original: *ascende septies cū mortuis...* This refers to the process of sublimation (ascending as vapor) and condensation (descending as liquid) repeated seven times.</note> 

For what else is it, but to sublimate dead spirits, to make the sublimated spirits living? And know that by this same means I mentioned above, Mercury will drink and eat a perfect or imperfect body. From the perfect, it makes perfect; from the imperfect, it makes imperfect. And I said before and say again that solution is twofold: one is natural, and that occurs in the bowels of the earth; the other is an artificial and violent solution, because it acts excessively. For it is impossible, if fire is continued under one vessel for a single day, that in the final hour of the day the vessel is not hotter than in the first or second hour; thus that fire acts not uniformly, but in varying ways.

For otherwise we would not be able to work in a short time that which nature works in the belly of the earth through the cycles of many years. But what material fire works unevenly, our manure-heat <term>fimus; referring to *fimus equinus* or horse dung, used by alchemists as a source of gentle, constant, and uniform heat</term> repairs, disposes, and directs uniformly. For it softens the undigested and the hard, cooks the raw, and produces identity in the matter of its subjects. But now let us see in what vessel our medicine should be placed. I say that it should be in a simple vessel so that the heat may more easily penetrate the glass; and certainly it would be better if the dung did not touch the glass, but let it stand like a naked man in a bath, so that the heat might come from every side.

The longer it stands, however, the better it is. Because the better food is digested in the stomach, the more nourishment it provides to the eater, from which nature afterward separates the elements <note>The four basic building blocks of matter: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> one by one.

**Regarding the Opinion**, the origin of formed things is repeated a second time: there is no doubt that all things were in a state of confusion <note>original: *in confuso*, referring to the primordial chaos before creation.</note> before the elements were separated in turn. Therefore, it was the opinion of certain philosophers that the composition and state of the world occurred when the elements were properly separated and placed in their own proper locations. Once joined at their boundaries, they share in one another. If we examine the sayings of the philosophers and poets, we find that all have reached this approved truth: that the world consists of the four elements. And if it should happen that any element were not properly purged, the philosophers undoubtedly estimated that such an element would destroy the others. Because of this, they propose that a general flood is a natural event. Similarly, they believe that the darkness which has often come over the earth is caused by the air, and that the sphere of fire is sometimes fertilized with such excessive heat that a universal combustion of all worldly things would follow. And certainly, those higher elements are pure and hold themselves very much according to their nature, whereas the earth is in the middle like a weight <note>original: *pendiculum*, a plumb line or weight.</note>. It is carried around in a circle, surrounded on all sides by air and with water around it, while the fire remains above. However, how this happens and by what motion they are moved is not our present concern, except only to explain that verse: *afterward you shall divide the world.*

**Regarding the Method**, all those who preceded us laboring in **this art** <term>The Art: A common way for medieval authors to refer to Alchemy without naming it.</term> studied most greatly to work toward the desired end. Many have consumed infinite riches so that they might reach the perfect end of the art; kings, princes, and great high priests have breathed their last <note>original: *anhelaverunt*, meaning to pant after or long for, but also implying great exertion.</note> hoping they might know it. For knowledge is an inestimable treasure, and because science is nothing other than the habit of reaching a conclusion, as Aristotle says. For to know is to understand a thing through its cause. Therefore, if the laypeople <note>original: *laici*, meaning those without formal education or those outside the "priesthood" of alchemical knowledge.</note> understood these words, they would never set their hand to the plow of this art, but would instead arrange the rural works which they have learned. For this art requires men who are scientific, intelligent, diligent, and sober. And because they are of great heart, they are stable. For what can a greedy man do? He hurries. The drunkard runs about aimlessly and sleeps. The layman does not know what he does, but walks like a blind man. And yet everyone runs toward one goal, and everyone seeks the prize, <note>original: *hrainu*, likely a printer's error for *bravium*, the prize or reward mentioned in 1 Corinthians 9:24.</note> but only the wise man receives it. I have said these things because many labor...

A universal way in both. Take Mercury extracted from Cinnabar <note>Cinnabar is a bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide, the primary ore of mercury.</note>; of this, you should have a notable amount. Prepare for yourself the Gold of the Sun and the Silver of the Moon <note>original: *aurum solis & lunae*; alchemists referred to gold as the Sun and silver as the Moon.</note>, which must be prepared. These will be useful to you for the work. For the gold, beat it into thin plates and "cement" it <note>Cementation was a process of purifying gold by heating it with various salts and minerals.</note> with the following cement: Take Roman vitriol <note>Roman vitriol usually refers to copper or iron sulfate.</note>, calcined; Saffron of Venus <term>Saffron of Venus (crocus veneris): a powder of copper oxide created by heating copper plates.</term>; calcined copper vitriol; and calamine stone <note>lapis calaminaris: an ore of zinc.</note>. Grind these well with vinegar and dry them a little. Mix this with the oil of egg yolks and layer the gold plates with the aforementioned powder. Add also a little sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride, used as a flux in metallurgy.</note>, place it in an earthenware vessel, and begin with a small fire; afterward, strengthen the fire for 24 hours. The copper vitriol and Roman vitriol are calcined only with vinegar and dried. Also grind the Saffron of Venus with vinegar in the manner of these cement plates. Take 3 *loth* <note>A historical unit of weight used in Germanic countries, roughly equivalent to half an ounce.</note>, cutting the gold into small pieces, and with pieces of cinnabar. This much is also done with the gold, and these are cooked in glass for 6 days over a slow fire, then over a stronger fire for 12 days. Once cooled, let the glass be broken and the material ground and washed with water. But when the gold is placed with the cinnabar, verdigris <note>original: *viride eris*</note> is added. Then do precisely the same for silver as for gold, except for the verdigris. Thus you are certain that you have Mercury extracted from cinnabar; then it is not necessary to sublime the quicksilver <note>original: *ar. vi.* (argentum vivum)</note>, but only to wash it with salt and vinegar. These two are thus prepared. Take both together, place them in glass, and cook them with clean, raw, washed quicksilver so that it becomes like a paste. Place this in a vial and let it be cooked. In a short time, the color will change; first, a black color is produced by the flames, which is the first good sign <note>The *nigredo*, or blackening, was the essential first stage of the alchemical process.</note>. Let it be cooked in that heat for one month. Then the color will change into a dark matter; continue its fire for a month, and the color will become clearer. Then test if it does not smoke; if so, the labor is finished. If, however, it gives off smoke...

If, however, you wish to prepare this material further toward perfection so that you might receive 1 mark <note>A "mark" (marca) was a weight of roughly 8 ounces or 230 grams</note> every week, then proceed as follows: when you have added 2 lots of quicksilver <note>original: *ar. vi.*, an abbreviation for *argentum vivum*</note> four times and fixed it, do not take anything out for expenses. If you still take nothing out at this stage, and again add 2 lots of Mercury and cook for 14 days, and do this again four times, you will then be able to take out 6 lots every week for expenses. Continue this sequence, always adding and cooking 2 lots of Mercury according to the method already described, until you are able to take out 16 lots every week for expenses. By continuing to multiply in this way according to your desire, provided you observe this order—in the beginning, the middle, and the end—neither adding nor subtracting more or less, you may eventually proceed so that you take out 1 pound, or 2, or 3, or 4, etc., every week.

Likewise, concerning the Gold thus prepared as a ferment through cementation <note>A purification process where metal is heated with salts</note>: Take 1 lot of it and add 3 lots of sublimed Mercury, ground together. Take the Mercury that has ascended and grind it with what remains at the bottom, place it in such a glass again, and set it to sublime. Again, grind what has ascended with what remained; do this three times, or until the Mercury remains fixed with the Sun <note>The Sun (*Sol*) is the alchemical symbol for Gold</note>. Keep this gold, thus prepared, for your work.

**The Preparation of the Sun with the Moon** <note>Gold with Silver</note>

Take 1 lot of silver filings and 4 lots of small portions of cinnabar <note>Cinnabar is a red mineral, the primary ore of mercury</note> about the size of peas. Afterwards, take it out and wash it with vinegar and salt, and then with clean warm water until the material becomes very clear. Cook this purified material, adding 3 lots of clean Mercury, for 14 days. Afterward, wash it and keep these two together—that is, the Mercury and the Moon <note>Silver</note>. Add 3 lots of clean Mercury and cook in the sublimation furnace, repeating this four times as described above.

### The Sublimation of Mercury

Take saltpeter, vitriol, alum, sal ammoniac <term>ammonium chloride, often used as a flux in alchemy</term>, and common salt, one pound of each. Knead these into crude mercury, as much as the mixture can take, and place it over the furnace in a large glass vessel sealed with luting <note>original: *lutatum*; a clay or paste used to seal alchemical vessels against leaks</note> and provided with a vent. Manage the fire successively or by degrees. Once the water has evaporated, open the vessel, and you will find the Mercury above the furnace like snow. Repeat this labor by placing the Mercury back down into the dregs <note>original: *fæces*; the solid remains at the bottom of the vessel</note> and do this three times. The Mercury will become a very vibrant green and excellently purified. Join this to the "body" <note>likely the base metal being transformed</note>, and you will find what you desired, God willing.

### The Increase for Both Processes

<note>original: *Augmentum ad utrumque*; likely referring to the "White Work" for silver and the "Red Work" for gold.</note>

"The light of your countenance is signed upon us, O Lord; you have given gladness in my heart" <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 4:6–7</note>. Save us, our Lord. Note: Gold <note>original: *Sol*; the sun, the alchemical symbol for gold</note> is man. If you wish to have a single perpetual increase, both in the white and the red:

Take, therefore, 1 lot <note>roughly 15 grams</note> of gold leaf and 12 lots of Mercury, and combine them together in a goldsmith’s crucible. Make an amalgam <note>a blend of mercury and another metal</note>, just as goldsmiths do, and wash it well with vinegar for as long as it takes until no blackness appears. Then place it over a slow fire within ashes in a long-necked glass vessel. Let the fire be like the flame of a candle among the ashes, and continue this with a slow fire for 8 weeks. Afterward, bury it deeper in the ashes for 14 days and increase the fire.

Then, "trees" will grow there—most wondrous and golden—both inside and outside the material. Take these and grind them in a mortar and on a stone. Now, when you wish to multiply this same material: take as much Mercury as there is of the entire material and grind them well together. Again, place it in a suitable glass and set it in slow ashes as before for 8 days; then bury it deeper in the ashes and give it a greater fire, as before, for 8 days. Then take it out and grind it again on a stone or in a mortar, and once more add as much Mercury as there is of the whole material. Again, place it in the glass in the ashes and give it a slow fire as before for 8 days; afterward, bury it deeper in the ashes and give it a greater fire again for 8 days. Then take it out again and grind it as before, and so on. Manage the process in all things as before; you can multiply this infinitely.

However, when you wish to reduce it into a "true body" <note>return the alchemical substance to solid, usable metal</note>: Take 1 part of Gold and dissolve it in *aqua fortis* <term>nitric acid</term>, and do the same with the medicine <note>the alchemical substance produced above</note>. Then join both solutions together and draw off the *aqua fortis* <note>through distillation</note>. Finally, give it a good fire for a day and a night.

Put 8 lots <note>One lot is roughly 15 grams or 1/32 of a pound.</note> of pure **silver** <note>original: *lunæ*; the Moon</note> and set it to be dissolved; once dissolved, keep it well in a closed glass vessel. Likewise, for the second part of the water, put 6 lots of pure **sal ammoniac** <term>ammonium chloride, used as a flux and solvent</term>, so that it may be dissolved; afterward, set that water to be distilled over a slow fire. A very clear water will be distilled, into which you should put 4 lots of **cinnabar** <term>mercury sulfide</term> which is composed with an eighth part of **sulfur**, and let it be dissolved. But it dissolves with difficulty, perhaps over two natural days. 

Now, take the water in which the silver was dissolved, and pour it little by little into the water in which the cinnabar was dissolved; it will soon be colored like milk. Afterward, set it to be distilled, first with a slow fire, until half the part appears to have been distilled. Soon after, let the fire be increased successively until it no longer desires to distill. Immediately give it a very strong fire with very dry wood, and a certain **white powder** will ascend into the neck of the **alembic** <term>the upper part of a still</term> and the **cucurbit** <term>the lower vessel of a still</term>. Continue this fire until it no longer desires to ascend, or is unable to. After the glass has cooled, collect this powder carefully and diligently keep it for your work. 

As for the fused mass remaining in the bottom, take it out and carefully scrape off with a knife what has adhered to the glass, and reduce it in the **ash-cup** <term>a *cinericium* or cupellation furnace used to refine precious metals</term> with **lead** <note>original: *saturno*; Saturn</note>. And then, at the end, you will find the mass of your silver. Dissolve this mass in a crucible and pour it through a brush <note>original: *scopam*; likely a bundle of twigs used to scatter the molten metal into droplets</note> into cold water, as you know how to do, so that it may be granulated. Once granulated, dry it by the fire. Afterward, put these granules into **aqua fortis** <term>nitric acid</term> made from **saltpeter** and **vitriol** <term>sulfate minerals</term>, and the pure silver will be separated—namely, it will stay at the bottom of the glass in a black state, but the silver passes into the form of transparent water. 

Pour this water into another glass, but the **black gold** <note>original: *solem*; the Sun</note> found at the bottom, reduce it with prepared common salt, and you will have **natural gold**, which lay hidden in the silver. As for the silver water, set it to be distilled, first with a slow fire. And when the distillation has ceased, improve the fire with dry wood, almost to the point of melting the glass; and when the redness of the alembic changes to whiteness, then it is enough. Afterward, when the vessel has cooled, break it, and you will find the matter coagulated in the glass, which you should reduce with **litharge** <term>lead oxide</term> in the ash-cup, and you will have your silver back.

Now, take that very white powder which had previously ascended to the neck of the glass, and soak it with **water of Mercury** <note>a mercurial solution or "philosophical" mercury</note> so that it floats to the thickness of a finger. Then add to it the **ferment** <term>a substance used to "ripen" or transform the alchemical mixture</term>—namely, for one flagon-weight of powder, a weight of ferment the size of an **obol** <term>a small coin or weight</term>—so that it is well mixed. Then let this mixed material be placed upon very warm ashes and be covered with another glass or basin, and thus let it coagulate; and do not despair because it coagulates with difficulty. The sign of perfect coagulation, however, is when the whole material, above and below, appears white...

This sign occurred for me in 17 days. Once this is done, place the material, thus coagulated, in your cabinet so that it is not touched by the air or the sun, until it is dissolved into an oil as before; it will hardly dissolve in five or six days, or perhaps there is the same difficulty in dissolving it as there was in coagulating it. Then take some of the same material and let it be tested thus: put some of the powder in some humid or airy place; if any moisture still hides within it, it will immediately dissolve a little, but not entirely. Seeing this, it is not yet a sign of **fixation** <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>. Then place it again in the reverberatory furnace, as before. And test it again in the humid place, as before. And repeat this by reverberating and testing until it no longer dissolves in the humid place; and this is the sign of the fixed medicine and the perfect **tincture**, for tinging raw Mercury that has been washed and purified. Tinge it, therefore, as you know how, etc.

### *Preparation of the Ferment.*

Take one part of the purest **gold** <note>original: *solis*; "the Sun," the alchemical name for gold</note>, and three parts of **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurii*; quicksilver</note> well purified, and make an **Amalgam** <term>a blend of mercury with another metal</term>. Place it in a glass vessel and add to it some **aqua fortis** <term>nitric acid, literally "strong water"</term> made from one part **saltpeter** <note>potassium nitrate</note>, another part **vitriol** <note>iron or copper sulfates</note>, and an eighth part **cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide</note>. Place it over a small furnace, first with a slow fire, until the **alembic** <term>the top cap of a still</term> turns red; then strengthen the fire with small sticks, and a white substance will ascend. And when you see that the redness of the alembic has ceased, then strengthen the fire more; then the white matter will ascend to the neck of the alembic, and a little bit will even be distilled into the receiver. Save what ascends for your work; do this five or seven times. And always strengthen the same water with four or five drops of new *aqua fortis*. And thus you will have the ferment,

### Mercury Water.

Take **sublimated mercury** <term>mercury(II) chloride, a volatile and toxic salt</term>, **sal ammoniac** <term>ammonium chloride, used as a flux and for cleaning metals</term>, and the **lime of eggshells** <note>original: *calcem corticum ovorum*; eggshells burned until they turn into a white powder or lime</note>, equal parts of each, and grind them together and incorporate them. Place them in a glass vessel with an **alembic** <term>a specialized lid used for distillation that collects and directs vapors</term> placed on top, and **sublimate** <term>to heat a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again</term> with a slow fire. Whatever rises to the top, return it to its **dregs** <note>original: *fecibus*; the solid residue left at the bottom of the vessel</note>, and sublimate again. Do this repeatedly until the whole amount melts at the bottom of the vessel, which happens quickly. Afterward, take it out and grind it on marble, then place it in a damp place and it will be dissolved into a water. Keep this water in a well-closed glass vessel for its intended work. For this water whitens, **fixes** <term>original: *figit*; to make a volatile substance resistant to heat</term>, **incerates** <term>original: *incerat*; to bring a substance to a soft, waxy consistency</term>, and dissolves everything soaked in it, and it works wonderfully.

# A BRIEF WORK TOWARD THE
# RED WITH GOLD THROUGH
## strong waters.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter R featuring a floral and scrollwork design.</image-desc>
Take one pound of **calcined vitriol** <term>vitriol, or iron/copper sulfate, that has been heated until it crumbles into a dry powder</term>. Take one pound of **saltpeter** <note>original: *salis nitri*; potassium nitrate</note>. Make **aqua fortis** <term>literally "strong water"; nitric acid, used by alchemists to dissolve metals</term>. In this, dissolve or calcine crude mercury. And when it has been calcined or dissolved, congeal it and grind it into a powder. Afterward, take one pound of calcined vitriol, and one pound of saltpeter, and half a pound of **Roman vitriol** <note>original: *vitrioli romani*; often refers to high-quality blue copper sulfate</note>, 8 **lots** <note>a historical unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce</note> of **verdigris** <note>original: *viride æris*; the green pigment or crust found on weathered copper</note>, and 8 lots of **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *salis ar*; ammonium chloride</note>. And from all of these, make a "strong water," discarding the **phlegmatic** <term>the initial watery, weak distillate produced during the heating process</term> part. And of that water, take 8 lots and dissolve in it 1 lot of fine **laminated gold** <note>original: *auri fini laminati*; gold beaten into thin sheets or leaves</note>. And after it has been dissolved, take 9 lots of that powdered mercury [prepared earlier] and put it in a **vial with a long neck**. And afterward, pour over it little by little that water in which all the gold was dissolved. And see to it that only a third part of the vial is filled. And cover the vial and place it for one day and night upon **ashes** <term>an ash-bath used to provide gentle, indirect, and even heat</term> that are not very hot, and many colors will appear. Afterward, seal the glass with the **Seal of Hermes** <term>original: *l. Hermetis*; an airtight, hermetic seal made by fusing the glass or using a specialized clay</term> and place it in a **bain-marie** <note>original: *balneum mariæ*; a warm water bath</note> until it is all dissolved. And when it is all dissolved, remove it from the bath and place it in the air in a safe place so it is not disturbed. Then that water will gradually congeal. And when you see a **red circle** in the bottom of the water, then open the glass and place it on very gentle ashes so that the matter is well dried. Then break the glass and grind the matter well upon a stone into powder. Therefore, of this **stone** <note>original: *lapidis*; the "Philosopher's Stone" or the finished medicinal powder</note> take 1 part, and of mercury take 10 parts, or one hundred—test this for yourself to see if one part can **tinge** <term>original: *tingere*; to alchemically transform or dye a base metal into a precious one</term> a hundred—and do it thus: Take a **crucible** <note>original: *tigillum*; a ceramic or graphite melting pot</note> and put in the mercury, and on top of it put the medicine, and over the medicine put prepared common salt. And close the crucible with the **clay of wisdom** <term>original: *luto sapientiæ*; a specialized sealant or lute made of clay, hair, and dung to withstand high heat</term> and give it first a slow fire. Then give it a melting fire, and afterward
-> pour it out and you will find <-
-> pure gold. <-

# THE WORK OF PETER OF
## SILENTO.

<note>original: "Petrus de Silento"; likely a pseudonym, meaning "Peter of Silence," a common trope in alchemical literature emphasizing the need for secrecy.</note>

Give heed, sons of doctrine, to my words; perceive with your ears the speech of my mouth. A wise man says: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom <note>A reference to Proverbs 9:10</note>, and blessed is the man who hopes in Him. For all wisdom is from Him: therefore, whoever has bent their back in reading the books of the Philosophers, let them lift up their heart, praying to the Most High, that the spirit of understanding may be granted to them. This hidden Philosophy is a glorious science; after the science of faith, it excels all other sciences in the sweetness of its pleasantness and utility. It has been greatly hidden by the Philosophers, and reserved for the power of God alone, which must be reached by a seeker with the fear of God, a pious mind, a devoted soul, and lengthy study. 

However, let him who enjoys books in patience enter into this disposition. But he who desires to reach the goal more quickly should not look at the books of the Philosophers, because this science is an enemy to him; for one must not quickly believe the **literal** <note>original: "manifestis"; refers to the surface-level or "plain" meaning of the texts, which alchemists claimed were intentionally misleading</note> books of the Philosophers. Because he who then thinks he knows everything and possesses the whole world, finds nothing in his hands, and a rushed belief destroys him. For haste, as **Morienes** <note>Morienes Rufus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist famously associated with the introduction of alchemy to the Islamic world</note> says, is from the devil; appropriately to whom it is said: Alas for him who desires to have this offering of God after reading the book only once or after the **first regimen** <term>regimen; a specific stage or process in the alchemical Great Work</term>. 

I say therefore, that for this work these things are required: a perfect Nature, the purest substances, true weights with the proper conjunction, a vessel, fire, and the method of operating. And patience is necessary throughout all things, for indeed too much talk without understanding increases error. In this method, for your benefit, I will pass on those things which they have written extensively concerning this secret Philosophical science. If anyone reads this having some understanding of his work, he will rejoice. But he who does not reach the result through this book should not seek another, but should rest, for the truth has been hidden from him, perhaps because he has an unfaithful mind. I further advise you to keep it, and read it often, and guard it from the impious. 

**Aristotle**, in a vision of the soul, says: Take notice, seekers of this science, that the **envious** <note>original: "invidi"; alchemists often referred to themselves as "envious," meaning they were "jealous" of their secrets and intentionally obscured their writings to prevent the unworthy from succeeding</note> have divided this secret into various parts, namely, *Philosophy*, *Astrology*, and the *Magical art*. And they have treated of many...

...with various waters, and broths, and bodies, stones, and spirits, so that they might devastate this precious art by the multiplication of names. They also described various regimens and vessels in order to deceive all those seeking this amicable art, although in this art nothing is necessary except one thing, a unity, specified and named with one name, and it can be perfected by one action—namely, cooking—at whatever time or times it can be done. Therefore, dismiss those things which the deceivers have explained, and hold to the following. Behold, a certain fatty **Ore** <note>original: "minera"; refers to the raw mineral source or "mine" from which the work begins</note> is found in sufficient and abundant supply. This is called pitch, or incombustible sulfur, **Kibric** <note>original: "Kibric" or "alkibric"; from the Arabic "al-kibrit," meaning sulfur</note>, the head and father of alums, of salts, of all liquefiable metals, and oil. It is also called by the Philosophers **Azoth** <note>A universal solvent or the essential agent of transformation, often symbolized by the mercury of the philosophers</note>, the highest humidity, the permanent water, which, when it is joined with the fixed sulfur of the body, cannot remain in the fire without it. 

It must be known for greater clarity of the doctrine that this mixture—namely of the water—produces all metals in the ore according to the diversity of matter and form: that is, the mixture of Mercury and sulfur. This water itself, if it were not dug out from the depths of the earth, would be on the path of perfection of any mineral for a long time. 

Note: Peter said above, "In the ore there is a certain fatness," denoting by this the marrow of the fixed sulfur of the body, which is called pitch or sulfur; and that fatness, as **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar and saint whose writings on minerals were foundational to alchemy</note> says, is in all metals, and all metals arise from it. Most notable of all, however, is that from this water proceed **Soloma** and **Brumasar**. Here Peter speaks of the soul extracted from the Sun and Moon, and how it has different names. Thus the synonyms for the Sun and Moon are **Soloma and Brumasar** <note>Arabic-derived names for the solar and lunar principles</note>, which are the most noble among metals because they have fixed sulfur within themselves, which is extracted from them by the previously mentioned water. **Kibrit** <note>original: "Kibrit"; Arabic for sulfur</note>, the natural sulfur, is called by so many names because of the excellence of its dignity. Know therefore, my son, that in its **white sister** alone does the degree of our wisdom grow, and not in the other flowing minerals of the earth. And because of this, [through] the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and **Moon** <note>Silver</note>, we create the proximate philosophy. The Author says: The white sister is **quicksilver** <note>original: "ar[gentum] viv[um]"</note> extracted from the Moon by Mercury, and it is called the **Stone of the Philosophers**, and its brother is the Sun, from which Mercury is extracted through Mercury; and these two are called the "honored stones," of which one is the man—namely, **red sulfur**—and the other the woman, which is Mercury (that is, of the Sun and Moon). Although they are two in number, they are nevertheless one in kind <note>original: "in specie"</note>. This secret must be approached naturally, just like a man and a woman. Although these are two in number, they are yet one in kind for procreating a son—namely the "above" and the "below." Through the Sun and the Moon is signified the Mercury extracted from these two bodies. Whence **Theophilus** <note>A pseudonym used by various medieval technical and alchemical writers</note> says: "When these bodies are joined—namely Sun and Moon—they will be as planets when the sun rises; and yet their light (that is, the planets’) is turned into the light of the sun itself." Here the error of the art is shown. If anyone leaps away from this path, he undoubtedly moves toward the ruin of his work. What I have said—one in kind and two in number—actually consists of three: namely soul, spirit, and body. Because quicksilver <note>original: "arg[entum] vi[vum]"</note> is the spirit and the soul, and the other is the body. There are also the four **Elements**, as happens to be found in any composite thing, without which nothing useful is ever generated. Therefore the **envious ones** <note>original: "invidi"; a term for alchemical authors who hid their secrets in riddles to prevent the unworthy from understanding</note> called these the four bodies—namely dryness, moisture, spirit, and vapor—all of which make seven: namely soul, spirit, body, and the four elements. And there are ten, which are these seven plus the "two in number" and "one in kind" mentioned before; and one is rightly called the **soul**, because it is the perfection of all ten. There follows, God willing, that which is sought. The envious ones also called this **the egg** because of its similarity, since the four distinct elements appear within it. They also said it is an **animal**, and a **man**, because it contains within itself soul, spirit, and body. Yet they meant nothing else but this stone, which is "a stone and not a stone," cheap and dear, and dearer than gold, embodied in golden flesh. Here it is shown what the Stone of the Philosophers is like, which is embodied in gold; it is that very thing which is passed over in the streets and trodden upon in the dung-heaps.

Therefore, this is one thing, both cheap and exceedingly precious beyond all knowledge, not of one name but of many, without which stone nothing useful is generated. This **gum** <note>original: "guma"; likely referring to the thickened or "coagulated" state of the mercury</note> is also more precious than gold among the Philosophers. **Gum** refers to quicksilver, extracted from the Sun and the Moon. The spirit and the body of equal temperament and property are gladdened, etc. Also, spirits flee the fire unless they are associated with fixed bodies—namely the Sun and Moon. And the bodies lie as if dead unless they are vivified by the spirits. 

The Author says "vivified," <gloss>meaning they become spiritual when well-joined and mixed together.</gloss> When indeed they are thus appropriately "betrothed" in turn—that is, joined together—then the bodies are dissolved with the spirits, and they retain those spirits even during the trial of the fire. Of all these bodies, the most noble was described first, namely **Brumazar**. Even the lower body is not improved except from our gum. 

Therefore, the initiate must begin nothing in this art before he knows the power of this **permanent water** <note>original: "aquae permanentis"; a term for the universal solvent or a stabilized form of Mercury that does not evaporate</note>; for one must use nothing in the mixing, the grinding, and the whole process except that permanent water. He who is ignorant of this water and its proper management should not enter into this art, for its spiritual power is the blood [of the work]. Therefore I shall relate briefly, and I say that heavy things, namely bodies, cannot be lifted, joined, or thrust down except by the light things above, namely spirits; nor can light things [be handled] except by the heavy things below. Just as the moist cannot be tempered without the dry, nor the dry without the moist, nor the hard without the soft, nor the soft without the hard in any way; therefore take sulfur and quicksilver, and grind the Sun—that is, roast the Sun with it—until it becomes a tinting silver. Whence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: "The spirit does not tint unless it is tinted." This method is praised in all books. And it is the Stone of the Indians and Babylonians. Place it in dung <note>Dung was used by alchemists as a source of gentle, steady heat through natural fermentation</note> for weeks, open it, and grind it with sal ammoniac <note>original: "almisadis"</note>, which is the most intense of all salts. Therefore, let no one approach the proposal until he finds the method of the components and the complete weights. will reach the effect; but if he takes what he ought, and does what is fitting, that which he seeks will come to pass. The same have said: he who gives to the mastery what he ought will be safe from error and will err no longer. However, the Philosophers did not wish to make the tradition concerning the proportion of spirit and body <note>In alchemy, "spirit" usually refers to volatile substances like mercury or sulfur, while "body" refers to solid metals</note> so manifest, because then it would be women's work and children's play <note>original: "opus mulierum & ludus puerorum"; a common alchemical phrase suggesting that once the secret is known, the process is easy, yet it must be hidden from the "unworthy"</note>. He who observes these boundaries well commits little or the least error in the work. 

Such error is usually twofold: either because it is not well liquefied, or once liquefied, it is not well submerged. And then, when the mixture has been made, the error was in excessive heat, and this is one error. Another is that perhaps it is not quickly fixed, and although it appears fixed during the boiling <note>original: "decoctione"</note>, it nevertheless flies away during the examination <note>Testing the substance by fire to see if it remains stable</note>; then the error was in too much raw spirit. Or perhaps a universal mixture has not been made, which is the union of altered mixable things. To correct these errors, because many works are lost because of them, the Wise Men discovered fixing waters—namely for the bodies—and incinerations <note>original: "incineraturas"</note>—namely for the spirits—just as was described in the previous sections. 

The goodness of this tincture <note>The transformative essence</note> truly comes from the proper weights and from the repetition of solution and coagulation. And the reason is that none of those things which enter into this compound have the power of the compound by themselves in action. For this elixir is tinted by its own tincture, submerged by its own oil, fixed by its own heat, and dissolved by its own dregs or saltiness. Dissolve therefore by repeated turns under the proper weights, and this method corrects your errors and increases the tincture in color, weight, and power; for the more you lighten the body, the more it is worth. the fixed substance multiplies the elixir by its power, weight, and roasting <note>original: "assatione"; a process of dry heating or roasting in alchemy</note>. But the Ancients said regarding all these things: Reiterate the fire until it is completed. Nor should the long delay weary you, because fire thins the natures, and the liquid is separated from the turbid. The office of the fire is to bring about the red heat.

Therefore, in the "greater work," take one part of **white gum** <note>original: "guma alba"; likely a resinous or crystalline alchemical intermediate</note> of the most intense whiteness, and one part of **our yolk** <note>original: "vitello nostro"; a symbolic term for a yellow substance, often sulfur or a specific stage of mercury</note>—others say three parts of **rectified sulfur**, without which the work is not corrected—one part. And mix these together. However, he who undertakes the work of these things, if the parts are not equal in power, it is necessary that he take one part of our unprepared bronze and three parts of prepared **permanent water** <term>Permanent Water<gloss>original: "aqua permanente"; a term for a powerful alchemical solvent, often mercury or a mineral acid that does not evaporate easily</gloss></term>. The Envious <note>The "Envious" (Invidiosi) was a standard term for earlier alchemists who supposedly hid their secrets behind riddles to prevent the unworthy from succeeding</note> have said: Take one part of the dry body, and three parts of the bronze of our magnesia, and then join them; mix them with our vinegar and with the **male**. Likewise, join the **male** with the **wife**, and combine them with quicksilver <note>original: "arg. viv." or argentum vivum</note>.

Note: Generally, it must be maintained that fugitive humors <note>volatile substances that evaporate easily</note> are not multiplied, nor should the dry substance be placed in by itself; rather, mix it strongly with **dew** until it forms a mass, knowing that if you add too much water to the mass, it cannot be contained in the furnace. And if you dry the mass too much, it will not be joined or cooked in the furnace. Therefore, let there be one part of the **male**, three parts of the **female**, and as much rectified sulfur as you wish (because it has no fixed weight in the books), and one part of the **medium** <note>an intermediary substance that helps the "male" and "female" substances combine</note>; among these, do not introduce any foreign powder or any other thing, because there is sufficiency in this itself, by the help of God.

However, if the **ferment** and the **medium** are added in the beginning or the middle, the work is perfected more quickly and does not require repetition. And this rule must be observed in the greater work, which is perfected by fire alone, because it is aided by "inspirations," which are alums, salts, and **atramenta** <term>Atramenta<gloss>A class of black, vitriol-like minerals or salts used as reagents</gloss></term>, and by the "fountains" of animals and plants—all of which may be used at will with their respective grindings, provided that what I have said is observed. A gloss regarding the proportion of the spirit and the body, and the ferment and the medium, joining them both:

Behold, I have already named the thing from which it is made, and we speak with certain weights. And because it remains to see, under one name, its single path and action—namely, the cooking—therefore that which the Philosophers say must be done: The Work is completed in **four regimens**, which are: **Putrefaction**, **solution**, **calcination** or **sublimation**, **distillation** through an alembic, and **coagulation** by a light fire. Truly, some, on account of the difficulty, complexity, or length of the preparation, have omitted one of the aforesaid regimens, others two, and others three. And the work...

# THE WORK OF PETER

completed it under one regimen. And because of this, their opinions differed. For some said the mixture could not be made except with both fire and solution; others with solution alone; and still others with fire alone. It would be tedious to recount the processes of them all. However, more praiseworthy are the methods set down in the "Book of Perfect Administration" <note>original: "libro administrationis perfectæ"</note> to be transmitted through the **Kyma** <note>original: "Kymam"; likely referring to an alchemical vessel or a specific stage of fluid mass</note>, in which I have at times gladly practiced. Above all, when I performed the method—which involved both the way of solution, as **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in medieval alchemy</note> names it, and the "sublimation of spiritual gold through redness" according to **Bubacar** <note>The Latinized name of Al-Razi (Rhazes), a Persian polymath and alchemist</note>—I proceeded as follows:

I took four parts of **mercury** <note>original: "arg. vivo" (argentum vivum)</note>, one part of **gold**, three parts of **sulfur**, four parts of **Cyprian vitriol** <term>Cyprian Vitriol<gloss>A blue-green mineral salt, usually copper sulfate, used as a corrosive or coloring agent</gloss></term>, and four parts of crystalline **sal ammoniac**. I ground all these together for a long time with raw, red vinegar, and kept them for a long period in a dewy place <note>original: "loco rorido"; a cool, moist environment used for slow chemical reactions or "digestion"</note> until I made the substance volatile, exhaling it to perfection. Then, I waited and weighed the ground material in a glass vessel with a wide bottom, and I placed the roasted material there to the thickness of a fingernail. I sublimated it using the method of **sublimation** with a very strong fire. 

At the beginning, I did not collect its "dew" <note>the condensed vapor</note> until the entire sublimated mass had ascended to the top. I "drank" <note>saturated or dissolved</note> it with the aforementioned **water of atraments** <note>original: "atramentorum aqua"; a solution made from mineral salts or vitriol</note>, roasted the fixed material, and ground it repeatedly until it became a red, fused **cinnabar**. One part of this colored three parts of **Silver** <note>original: "Lunæ" (of the Moon)</note> into **Gold** <note>original: "Solē" (into the Sun)</note>. However, using the previously mentioned water, I dissolved the aforementioned waxy tincture in a bath <note>original: "balneo"; likely a water-bath or Mary's bath (balneum Mariae)</note> and purified it until the water was of a single color. I then coagulated it until it was dried out, and I fixed it with fire by degrees until it could withstand a strong heat. Finally, I lowered the fire until it was gently melted. By dissolving and coagulating this, and by adding tinctures at my pleasure, I multiplied it. 

This method is subtle and true, though it requires a long preparation. Afterward, I took a method using solution alone. I took three **lothones** <note>A "loth" was a Germanic unit of weight, roughly 15 grams</note> of the "matter of hair" <note>original: "de capillis"; likely a symbolic term for a substance rich in ammonia or sulfur, or literal hair used for its chemical properties</note>, and of the **sincere body** <note>the pure metal</note>, and of the salts in their proper portions. By putrefying them, I dissolved them until they were turned into water—of white and black colors, and all the colors in between <note>This refers to the "nigredo" (blackness) and "albedo" (whiteness) stages of the alchemical work</note>. At last, it was purified and thinned until it was beautifully, slightly reddish; this tinged plates quenched in it according to every judgment. However, it did not long withstand the **cement** <note>original: "cimentum"; a rigorous heat-test used to verify the purity of gold</note>. I believe this was because it was not "fermented" with Gold <note>original: "Sol"</note>. Because that preparation was so long and tedious, I tried the method which is done by fire alone, as follows:

I took the **spirit** and the **bodies** in their due weight, sometimes prepared and sometimes raw. However, they were pure, and through them the "body" was made more beautifully and more quickly. All these I mixed together strongly into one with a pure liquor, grinding them well, subli...
